Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a game that has a wonderful mix of jump scares, mystery, horror and story. The introduction to the game pulls you right in by sparking off a multitude of questions that can only be answered by descending deeper into the story. The story is flawlessly mysterious and satisfying as you go along and uncover the answers to countless questions on the way in which you ended up in the early 1800's Prussian castle. The lore and story that you follow throughout the game contribute to the bone-chilling fear of what lies deeper in a seemingly endless castle. Furthermore, the story conveys themes that subtly question the notions of good and evil. The main protagonist, Daniel, and the Baron of the Brennenburg castle, Alexander, have constantly evolving definitions on doing the right thing and sacraficing for the morally superior or perhaps inferior motive. The multiple endings are all quite satisfying based on your actions.
The gameplay is very smooth and simple, a perfect fit for a horror game. The developers of this game knew the importance of focusing energy on story and tone rather than overcomplicating the gameplay. The basic conflict where you are in danger of dying mainly lies within two main enemy types: the Kaernk and the Gatherers. The Kaernk is an invisible monster from another dimension that is only encountered in shallow water. You can detect the Kaernk by hearing its roar and the splash of its footsteps in the water. Avoiding the Kaernk is especially a spooky task because many times you will find yourself jumping from crate to crate in the water. Missing a step and falling into the water in presence of the Kaernk is a potentially fatal and very scary event. The Gatherers are soldiers from the 30 years' war who were turned into monsters by drinking Alexander's tainted wine after wandering too close to the Brennenburg castle in the Prussian forest. These soldiers turned monsters have two variations, the Servant grunt: a more common enemy who takes multiple hits to kill you, and the Servant brute: a rarer enemy who kills you in one hit. In any case, when encountering an enemy, the only way to deal with the enemy is to run and hide, further adding to the scary nature of the game.
The controls were solid. Everything was fluid and smooth. I especially enjoyed the immersive feature where object interaction was based on mouse movement rather than clicking. It makes you feel more into the game by having the tactile quality to object interaction.
Care must be taken when considering whether or not to seach a room or area. It takes away from sanity to be in a dark area, so one must risk using oil or tinderboxes to light a place of interest. Additionally, you run the risk of being killed by an enemy or not finding anything worthwhile while searching. In the vast majority of times I have searched an area, the risk was very well worth the reward, which is a good game mechanic.
The atmosphere and graphics contribute very nicely to the gloomy and scary mood of the game. The contrast between each area is stark, and the different areas end up giving different types of eerie chills as you progress throughout the game. When insane due to looking at too many grotesque objects or scenes, looking at gatherers, being in the dark or being in appropriate cursed ritual areas, Daniel views paintings as horrible hallucinations and hears whispering and distant screams that arent there. In some water areas even, Daniel hallucinates that the Kaernk is there when in reality it is not.
The various puzzles in the game are difficult enough to make you think about them, but are not frustrating in difficulty. The developers did a very good job of keeping Amnesia: The Dark Descent feeling like a horror game, rather than a scary puzzle game.
All things taken into consideration, this game is a solid horror game that is a must have if you are interested in the horror genre. The colorful story, carefully crafted gameplay and horror elements make it a classic for this genre.

If you don't mind solving puzzles in an action-adventure game, then please skip my review and buy this game. Darksiders runs smoothly, has great art style, fun and brutal combat and a cool sword.
BUT if you're not into puzzles, then this game might not be for you.
At first, the game feels very much like an epic metroidvania God of War, which is cool. There are puzzles here and there and that's fine.
But later in the game, the dev got too carried away with puzzles and the balance shifts heavily from action-and-puzzle to puzzle-and-puzzle-and-puzzle-and-puzzles. I don't mind repetitive combat and weapon/skill upgrades that don't evolve to anything much. However, running around trying to figure out seemingly endless stream of puzzles with not enough actions in between isn't something I expect from a guy named War.
Again, if you like a lot of puzzles in your action-adenture game, then you'll have a great time. But this isn't for me.

This game is absolutely amazing. I remember once trying it out when I was younger and I never really made it very far into the game. But then my friend gave me this as a gift because like me he likes Quake and I thought 'well why not lets give it a go' and that was one of the greatest decisions of my life. the singleplayer campaign gave me around 8 hours of gameplay and it was spectacular.
the game has fantastic atmosphere and goes from badass shooter to tactical shooter to♥♥♥♥♥♥scary 'oh sweet jesus may god have mercy on my soul' in a matter of minutes. the game is fairly difficult to be honest, enemies do quite a bit of damage even on Corporal, which I assume is the 'normal' difficulty but it's never too hard only requiring you take your time and don't rush in guns blazing hoping things die. The guns are absolutely lovely and each enemy seems to have a gun that works best to kill them, some flat out requiring you smash them with the local superweapon which may at first sound like a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but it really isn't, it's just the simplest way to take them down without using all of your ammo and I never found myself using the superweapon that often until the final level where I used the aforementioned 'rush in guns blazing and hope people die' strategy and it seemed to be the best way to go with little cover and all the strongest enemies trying to absolutely destroy you. One 'issue' I had though is that there never seemed to be more than a few enemies attacking you at any given time, wether this was an issue with ID tech 4 (the game engine) or wether this was just a design choice made by the developers to help with the fact that enemies do quite a lot of damage and you need to sit back and take your time and if you didn't constantly fire and risk getting shot right in the face then you would quickly be overrun.
all in all the dark setting, kickass weaponry and all round 'creepy' atmosphere (which makes sense, this is war time and your forces seem to be very heavily outnumbered by the Strogg) really work well to keep you very interested in the game and I never fealt myself getting bored and wanting to play something else. The story is pretty interesting (or I thought so atleast) and the characters aren't all that bad themselves though they do come off as ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s most of the time by making you walk off on your own to fend for yourself in this horrific setting with monsters potentially around every corner wanting to rip your face off but it made getting back to them so that you aren't dealing with the horrors alone all the more relieving and you never really go too long without someone there to watch your back which some may see as an annoyance that takes away from the dark and scary atmosphere but I don't really like that all too much and I'd much rather have that in bursts and still have someone there to keep me company so I don't go completely insane from time to time.
so all things considered this is a truely great game and I would more than recommend you buy this, I would recommend you get some friends to as well (I found a co op mod and haven't tested it myself but have high hopes). the game is fun, story is enjoyable and I found myself connecting with the character and found myself putting myself in their shoes which is a great thing for games to do and I don't get often. though I do wish that I could have more than two weapons with torches on them while it does add to the creepiness as they are the two weakest weapons in the game (well the lightning gun is pretty bad but atleast it looks cool).

Quake 4 was one of the first games I played on my Xbox 360 around mid 2006. I wasn't expecting much out of it, even though Quake 2 is one of my favorite games of all time (but for its multiplayer, not its singleplayer). Plus the reviews of the 360 version of Quake 4 were pretty bad.
Even though it was indeed a bad port, I really liked the game. It was a good shooter with a nice weapon upgrade mechanic   and a sweet story twist around the halfway point of the game. But now, in 2014, I'm afraid that it just hasn't aged well. I played Doom 3 before trying my hand again at Quake 4 PC, and Doom has aged much better. Quake 4's graphics look good from a technical standpoint, they don't have the crazy intense atmosphere of Doom 3 but they also don't have Doom's muddy textures. However from an artistic standpoint they're just...flat. Everything feels very generic, very "been there done that." The shooting feels like a relic from another era, your weapons feel powerful but you need a ton of bullets to take down your enemies and there's a lot of them, so in firefights all you do is shoot at everything that moves until they drop.  No real tactics here, just shooting. What made those 90's shooters so satisfying is the crazy amount of stopping power you had at your disposal. The double barreled shotgun in Doom 2 can take out a whole room of low level minions if aimed correctly. THAT'S satisfying. Needing 5 shotgun shells to down one guy while his two or three buddies use you for target practice? Meh.
So, yeah, leave this one in the past.

As a die-hard fan of the first KOTOR, having pumped countless hours into it across two platforms, it  saddens me that my hopes that the Restored Content Mod would've given me a better experience replaying the sequel after so many years, originally. To be frank, I pretty much got this game for that sole reason: I hoped that this patch would somewhat remedy the problems I had when playing this way back in '05 on the Xbox.
I didn't like it then because of its apparent rushed nature; it was glitchy, some storylines didn't follow through, lots of unanswered questions/quests, and plenty of other elements missing. While many kudos go to the guys who worked on the RCM, making it the tape to the pile of shredded documents that the original release was, despite their efforts that went into the mod, the major flaw is still apparent: it just isn't a worthy sequel and decent, bordering mediocre, as a stand alone.
It's hard not to hold this to the first game; you honestly can't do it. It has a lot of elements in the first game, both story and gameplay-wise, incorporated into it. The problem was that both elements just weren't up to par and as well polished as its predecessor. I completely understand it was trying to build on top of what the previous had done, but in doing so, the mechanics and, again, narrative buckle under its weight.
Example, you have two star villians: one feeds on death of stars and worlds, and another is held together by sheer will of the Force. In terms to the story, these two are immensily powerful; one can't die and the other can kill everything by himself. In terms of the game, your character can be overpowered to the point where you can kill either them with the greatest of ease. For me, I always play as a Force-user in these games over lightsaber combat (supposedly, making the game harder). By the end, I was the accumulative level of 29 when I killed Darth Sion with nothing but Force Wave and a handful of life support packs. With Darth Nihilus, I buffed myself so I was immune to his Force powers and my team and I just beat him death. To top that all off, all that meant nothing when you get to the end and you fight the final Sith Lord, easily the toughest boss fight in-game, but she was the one who was easily punched to near death in a cutscene in the beginning. Ludonarrative dissonance, if I ever heard it.
In the end, I can't recommend this game to anyone who was a fan of the first. It's just so flawed on so many dissapointing levels, that there is nothing but heart-ache to be had. If you were curious, like I was back in 2005 to see how this game was to the first and on it's own, then you'll probably check this out on that sentiment alone. Video Review:
Etherlords 2 is a collectible card game very similar to Magic: The Gathering.  The player collects cards to build a deck of spells and creatures.  When you approach enemies on the world map you have the opportunity to fight them.  This is where the actual card game starts.  The player takes turn with the enemy casting spells and attacking.  Victory is achieved by killing the opponent.  The card game is surprisingly complex and it feels rewarding when your deck works.  In addition your character levels up and can choose perks that will influence your strategy.  If you enjoy these types of table top games you will probably have fun with Etherlords 2.
The problem is...everything else outside the card game. The voice acting is sub par and the movement/animations on the world map are jerky and frustrating.  There is no camera angle that let's you properly see where you're going and there are no resolution options that I could fine.
I rushed thought the poor dialog and map navigation as fast as possible so I could get back to actually playing the card game.    If you like card games then I will grudgingly recommend Etherlords 2 because it can be quite fun, but everything else almost spoils the game.

Almost 6 hours into the game, and I have to say its AMAZING! If you enjoy some of the newer zelda art style games, you'll enjoy this one. Runs amazingly well. No problems what so ever running on max graphic settings, however I do have a high end gaming system.
I was very hesitant starting out, for the developers seem to just drop you into the game without any training. Didn't seem to get in the way, for the control options are extremely simple to master, and within 5 or 10 mins, I was running around as if I had a clue. Controls are very intuitive, and you can customize your buttons with no problem. Game has zero dialog, but that just doesn't matter. The creatures you encounter have an amazing ability to display all types of emotions, simply through the art and graphic motion. Wall paintings and clues are all over the place, all you have to do is immerse yourself into the game, and pay attention to your surroundings. The developers have done an amazing job with this puzzle game, and no puzzle I have encountered so far, is frustrating to the point you quit playing because of difficult jumps, timing, or almost impossible game physics. The day/night cycles add a lot of fun surrounding changes, and when you first encounter a “time machine” where you can advance or turn back time, I found myself just playing with the device to watch the sun and moon shoot through the sky, and watch shadow activity. Many of the puzzles depend on these game physics, and much of the game is very dependent on accurate shadow movement. Again, the developers did an amazing job dealing with those world physics. Pre-ordered this game with reservations about it, but all in all, I'm extremely pleased with RiME, and consider it well worth the time and money. Even after solving puzzles, I found myself looking forward to replaying the game to run the puzzles again.
Edit note: I've been scoffed at about running on max graphics settings without problems. Sorry folks, I've had zero shuttering or frame speed issues with all graphic settings on the highest. Not sure why others are having issues. I7 4930k casually overclocked. Dual GeForce video cards. I don't know what else to tell you, except I'm finding myself thankful that I'm not having issues.

I first started playing this game when it became available on steam, and now, 7 hours later, I have completed it. I cannot echo what others have said regarding optimization, as I experienced no issues. However, I can offer my perspective of the gaming having finished it in it's entirety.
First. The game is beautiful. The soundtrack is beautiful, the art is beautiful, the environments and storytelling elements are extremely well done, especially for a game without dialogue. I even found myself falling in love with the nameless NPC allies you meet about midway through the game.
The puzzles, while not mind-bending like some puzzles in Limbo or The Witness, among other games, were satisfying, and I found myself stumped in one or two spots. There are plenty of types of collectibles for completionists, and many of them provide insight into the overall lore of the game. Overall, the game was satisfying to complete.
Then came the last 10 minutes of the game.
Throughout the game there are several questions posed to you, the player. Mysteries that the game, and developers themselves ask you to solve. As I progressed through the game, I began to piece together these answers, but I fit the final pieces in too late to prepare myself for what was to come. The end of this game is an intense, emotional, viscerally heartbreaking experience for which nothing in my entire life could have prepared me. When the credits rolled, I had to get up and take a walk so that I could be composed enough to write this review.
This game is art. It is an experience. It is the embodiment of the love that the developers have for their families and friends. As difficult as the end might be, I think this is an experience that would benefit everyone.

For many Total War fans, and certainly for me, this is where it began. It still holds up today as a fantastically engaging and rich military strategy game, and has an easy and accessible feel to it that gets you hooked into campaigns that take many hours to complete. Still worth the purchase today, even though the graphics and some basic mechanics are starting to feel dated. With Mods, much of the games shortcomings can be patched and freshened up for new arrivals, but for the oldies even vanilla Rome Total War is a pleasure to dive into.
The aspect of Rome Total War that hooks fans, and that Creative Assembly really hasn't managed to re-create in many other releases in the series, is the role-playing element. You do get very attached to your characters in-game, and at times adapt your play style to the personality of the general you control: are you a brutal tyrant who destroys enemies mercilessly? Are you a strategic general who approaches conflicts with caution, or perhaps a political animal more suited to building a career as a governor close to the Eternal City? As your family grows you will understand that Valerius, son of Asinius, wants to avenge his father who was killed by the Carthaginians, or that the son of the good-for-nothing Gnaeus wants to prove his family can be great by conquering lands for the glory of Rome. This is part of the wonderful dynamic storytelling in the game, and something that is hard to find in other titles from the series.

If it's for cheap like a Daily Deal, then you save yourself the buyer's remorse I get for having bought this $60 at launch. But then I wouldn't recommend that unless you have a few bucks to spare and a sense of morbid curiousity for bile. That is to say, Duke Nukem Forever is not a broken game. It's not an incomplete game. Infact, nothing is overall glitchy or messy, and it's competent.
But does that make it good?
Forever tries to cash in on nostalgia to Duke Nukem 3D, but it reaches a point that Duke himself almost feels like a parody of his younger self, and that nostalgia is hollow at best with art design, ripped or altered quotes, and wholesale references. The Duke's lines seem like they were written by Comedy Central writers on a boring weekend, and a few very specific moments are just plain.. Unnecessary or even downright vexing as to how anyone thought it was a good idea.
When the game you're referencing is better than the your own game, however, that becomes a significant issue. And in all regards, Forever falls down the cesspit that is a modern shooter without much ingenuity. Regenerating health (coined as 'Ego', but extremely inconsistent on how much damage you can actually sustain), bland gunplay with no real kick or impact beyond the shotgun blast, dumb-as-bricks enemy AI that either stands perfectly still or rushes you, turret and vehicle sections thrown in for 'variety' that drags players down when they last way too long, rudimentary puzzles to pad out the game time, boss fights that arbitarily can only be hurt by explosions with magical infinite ammo reserves somehow implemented to keep you going...
For all of the callbacks, mythology gags, and attempts to appeal to the Duke 3D fans, the game plays nothing like it beyond being of the same genre. There's no depth, beyond finding boosts to your Ego meter by winning minigames or doing things like photocopying your rear end (and some objects you interact with give Ego, including easy-to-miss ones, but others that might reasonably do so.. don't). You can only carry four weapons at a time plus handheld explosives, and only two if you toggle that patched-in option off. Things like the Beer power-up are completely useless and outright detrimental. And it just keeps dragging
and
...
There is a multiplayer function to the title, make no mistake. It's fast-paced, much more so than the actual campaign mode of the game, and there's even a basic unlock and customization system. .. if unlocking aesthetics around a penthouse is your idea of a worthy set of unlocks, or being able to change Duke's shirt color, try on different glasses and put on hats is your idea of fun customization. At times the multiplayer's a bit
hectic, though, making it rather hard to keep up with and a likely cycle of 'die, respawn, die' with larger player counts. I don't have much to say, since this is basically Call of Duty meets Quake without any real polish.
If this were just another crummy modern first-person-shooter, no one would've given it the time of day. But because it's Duke Nukem and been in the making for twelve years, it's not even a case of expectations being too high; I went in with middling to low expectations even at launch, and this game was so medicore, so boring, so
that despite getting to the last portions of the game, I just don't feel like I'll ever properly finish this game. And considering I loved Duke Nukem 3D, as well as having had this game since day one, it breaks my heart to say that.

First and foremost if you plan on playing this game "Activate" and "Register" are two different things. You must activate the game by internet or phone with your cd-key, but make sure to uncheck the "register" box so you won't have to deal with the hassle of filling out a form with all your personal info.
I had an issue with this game regarding lag or slowdown where the game would go from running smooth 60fps then lagging heavily then back to smooth. I was able to resolve it by opening Nvidia Control panel and manually setting the profile of this game to run using "Adaptive V-Sync", "Triple Buffering ON" and "Single Display Performance". It still slightly lags in parts of the intro where you escape the prison but overall fixes the major slowdown issues across the game.
As for the game itself it has its charms and shortcomings. On the positive side the graphics hold up quite well in 2016 with max settings and environments have detailed design. You can have three active sets of gear so switching between fighting styles is easy. Voice over work is a massive improvement over the original game and feels more polished.
On the bad side of things the game relies heavily on combat and it is very clunky and frustating. For example if you melee and move while you press the attack button for combos, it will break the chain. You must stand still for your attacks to chain. Smaller faster enemies will do hit and run tactics where they will charge attack and immediately run away a few yards, making counters useless. Then there are enemies that will swarm you and attack you repeatedly and all you can really do is block and run away. The game also throws in random enemies that are much stronger then the rest. Problem is you can't really tell which ones they are until they hit you twice while you block and kill you. The animations aren't great either. Attacks look like that don't have any impact and your character looks like he is just flailing his arms around. Auto target is extremely unreliable with a high chance you will be dislodged and attack open space.
I haven't played too far into the game to get a strong grasp of the story but so far the prologue doesn't really offer anything special. The first bunch of characters that help you on your quest seem decent but the main character is annoying. I don't understand why he is so weak that he has to learn how to use a sword/staff/bow and he just talks way too much.
I haven't run into any major glitches (ie. crashing/corrupt saves) but a minor one is during dialog between the characters the lines would get cut off and the next character would begin talking.
Overall it's hard to give a definitive yes or no to recommending the game. I would recommend getting the game absolutely if it's on sale. I picked it up for a couple of bucks. It's a fun distraction if you are patient enough and give it a chance.
However, if you had just finished games like Skyrim or the Witcher 2/3, you might feel like this game is nothing but mediocre compared to those polished amazing experiences.

I'll be the first to admit, while the game might not be perfect (poor hit registration, flaky servers, bugs etc.), the developers are working hard to resolve all issues raised by the community and their own testing. Sure, you can blame them that things should've been working 100% from the get go, but that isn't going to help anyone. The game is in the shape that it is, the player base is growing because new content is being added (at no extra charge) and issues are being resolved. Thousands of gamers from Counter Strike, Call of Duty and Battlefield are migrating over to Siege for a reason.
There isn't much of a single player 'campaign', and given how much content has been released over the past almost two years the offline training missions don't really prepare you for the multiplayer modes. You will be beaten into a pulp and there is a tough learning curve given the number of maps and operators to learn, but persevere!
Practice makes perfect. This isn't your run of the mill action shooter, this game rewards skill - positioning, holding angles, call outs, team operator composition etc. There are operators to cater to almost any play style - fast/rushing, slow/anchoring objectives, support and trappers.
You earn your victories, and learn from defeats. You'll never feel an adrenaline filled clutch like you can in Rainbow Six Siege, I guarantee it.

Loads of fun. First playthrough i built out full ranged.
By the end I ran with a demon like pistol, that when fired, has a blast radius of 8 (i think it's feet). Great for clearing out destructible objects before a battle, sweeping a house and blasting apart everything and taking out rabbits.
Next was my sawed off shotgun with 3 barrels. At one point I put a mod on that fired all 3 at once, but it was overkill with a long cooldown (1.5 seconds). Slotted it with electricty mods. By the end, i would have used this more than any other weapon. The ability to dash at any time, no cost, no cooldown, means i can dash right into a back of baddies faces, then let loose and dash out again. Short range, wide spread, huge destruction and damage. WIth the electric mods anything that wasn't killed, was stun/dot'd to death a few seconds later. I used this for any swarms of small creatures and fighting medium ones that engaged at melee range.
Assault rifle for mid range combat. Finally got a decent one later on. This was my primary weapon for large enemies that were not elite/champion. It did plenty of damage to mow them down from a safe range. For elite/champion large baddies, I would use this as a secondary fallback.
Minigun! My favorite and comes in a number of flavors. Putting dozens of rounds down range every second. I slotted this with my best and strongest mods. I designed it to use with Fury and stacked amulet bonus and personal mods to increase fury damage. Nothing lasts for more than a few seconds with this combination except for the strongest of bosses.
Gauss rifles. Found quite a few near the end. I used arrows at one point. Arrow type you charge up for max damage but can fire again right away. Gauss rifle you fire instantly, but reload after each shot. I found the Gauss rifle to be ideal since it doesn't "Arc". They seem to all have a straight LoS fireline. Since i used this for opening sniper shots on large and/or hard targets, accuracy was key. With the distance, most things can't even find me and i can pick off an entire group without even drawing attention. Headshot + Element = massive damage. It's so strong that in the right situation, it was useful on bosses when my primary/secondary were out of ammo.
Rocket Launcher. Found one called, World Destroyer? Big toxic damage. Single shot. With mods on this thing, it has a single shot damage output of ~1200. Right after getting this and modding it, I came across a champion called "Destroyer of Worlds". (Hope i'm recalling these names correctly). Stayed a good 50m away from him, and decided to test the new rocket launcher. Killed him in a single shot. Later in the game it wasn't powerful enough to single shot champions. However with the right angle looking down on a group of enemies, this thing made their day very bad.
Very early on, melee weapons that consume ammo for force slash were strong. Once i had a decent arsenel with the ammo storage/find skills maxed out, it wasn't necessary to carry a melee weapon.
All in all, very satisfying. Played on normal. Switch to insane. Stopped after the first half dozen missions as insane difficulty was proving to be a bit easy. Probably pick it up again later.

FULL REVIEW HERE:
Wizards of The Coast are back for this year’s Magic: The Gathering digital trading card game, which is available on PC via Steam, Xbox 360, Amazon Kindle and Android on Google Play with an Xbox One version planned for release later this summer. Magic 2015 focusses on the Planeswalkers Garruk Wildspeaker, controller of forests and the powerful creatures that dwell there, and Liliana Vess, the black magic wielding necromancer who has cursed Garruk, now using him to take down other planeswalkers, and you. The campaign takes you on a journey to stop Garruk’s rampage, first witnessing the carnage he has created, then dueling on until you face the cursed warrior himself.
Whilst not much has changed visually compared to last year’s Magic offering, Wizards of The Coast has heard the community’s wishes for the practical aspects of Magic 2015 and now allows you to create your own trading card decks from scratch, rather than having to manipulate the pre-built decks and ultimately play how the game wants you to play. For the less experienced players who want to try their hand at deck building, the in game deck builder is surprisingly intelligent. By adding just a few cards that you want to build your deck around the game does the rest for you. This pushes the digital Magic games away from simply teaching you how to play to a more competitive direction, encouraging players to go out into the community and have fun playing against friends and strangers alike.
Microtransactions were made for impatient Farmville players, and their increased inclusion in serious games for content that should be and in previous versions has been free ruins the idea of skill rather than money leading players to victory. Their inclusion in Magic 2015 not only makes the game less fun, but the microtransactions are implemented in competitive online play, meaning that a pay-to-win trend is sure to emerge. Despite Wizards of The Coast limiting the number of these special paid for cards that can be had in a collection, the fact that these exclusive cards exist is a sad day for people who play Magic The Gathering to hone their skills, not empty their wallets.
Magic 2015As far as the cards available at the time of release, there is very little to be excited about. The previous block of cards Theros and this year’s core set are available, but the core set has more reprints than a poster factory, and for dedicated players of Magic: The Gathering, Theros feels ancient. Despite this, when you choose your preferred colour of deck to play you are given an inclusive choice of colour combinations, allowing for a variety of play styles and ways to approach the computer challengers.
Overall, Magic 2015 is another welcome instalment to the longstanding series. Its advances in deck building and story have made Magic 2015 the glue that holds the multiverse together, and for players interested in lore the digital games are a must play. The misty aesthetics and more dynamic challengers make Magic 2015 a progressive albeit expected improvement on last year’s offering, and provide an interesting and tactical challenge for new and seasoned Magic: The Gathering players alike.

I liked Magic the Gathering 2012. It was a great tool to teach me how to actually play Magic, which before was too daunting of a task. Now I buy the games every year, with each game adding more to the experience. As any iterative game, there are cool new features and drawbacks. However, Magic 2015 takes out all the features that I enjoyed for a system meant to manipulate you into microtransactions. I already paid money for the game, please give me the full game.
Negatives:
First Noticed that the game overall is slow. The menus are painful and AI is slower/dumber.  Another is no Custom Duels-- My favorite mode Two Headed Giant was taken out. Why? Each year they take great modes away, but this was a staple. I actually reinstalled the other magic games to replay those modes I loved so much. I also loved the decks provided in the previous games, which for this game doesn't have any themed planeswalker deck.
You can create your own deck?! Well yes, this year you can actually do that. However, to get the good cards you need to unlock them through the campaign (random chance boosters). To get all the cards... well you will have to pay to do that.
Positives:
The Art can be cool at times. Sometimes.
If you want to get into magic I suggest buying Magic 2013, or even Magic 2014. This game however is trying to ride the card game microtransaction systems of FREE to Play card games WHILE making you pay for the initial game. I regret two purchase in my life for games-- Dragon Age 2 and Magic 2015. I guess another postive at least I didn't spend 60 dollars and have to install Origin. But that is like saying, at least I didnt walk out my front door into traffic today.
So buyers beware.

I've been blown away by this game. Flying Wild Hog has always made interesting world design, decent combat mechanics, but everything else always kind of sucked. For example in Hard Reset the story was bad and the acting was distractingly awful. The first Shadow Warrior they made is fun for a little while, but it's old school by design and get's dull around the middle.
They have upped the ante this time. The things they added to the combat alone feels great. It especially feels good the way you can move around the field in combat with evasion into a double jump into sword slashes. I vaguely remember RPG like mechanics in the first game, but I found the first game forgettable so I can't recall completely. In this it's front and center and totally works.
You'll start with a few cards which you upgrade by leveling up (by finishing missions and killing stuff), but you can find more as drops or buy some at shops. There are tons of skills to level up, and there seems to be no end to skills you'd want. It adds to replayability as it would take a while to level all of them up.
The enemy system is similar to Diablo in that it's procedurally generated. You may find a sub boss (or three) in every level, and they have various vulnerabilities and resistances. The regular enemies can sometimes as well.
The maps themselves don't seem randomly generated, but where you can start in them is so it gives it a little flair (I could be wrong, but the maps themselves didn't seem random in my game). There are, however, a decent amount of maps in the game which is good as often you do missions in maps you've been to before.
There is a shocking amount of weapons in this game. You may say "So does Borderlands!" The difference is all the weapons you can find are completely different weapons. You can find an M60, or a Lazer Katana, or maybe a Pistol with 3 barrels. There's so many different kinds of weapons sometimes I'm not entirely sure which ones I want to use (you can assign 8 weapons at a time to quick slots and 4 to quick switch, by the way).
The final thing I should mention is the acting, and story. Flying Wild Hog isn't American, I know, and it still shows in the way they write dialogue. With Shadow Warrior (their first reboot) I mostly was fine with it because it came off endearing that they would say stuff in the wrong context or misuse euphemisms almost as if they didn't actually understand what they mean. They still do that, but it's significantly improved in this one. The writing is still not great, but their intent with the character (Lo Wang especially) is interesting in this game, and it's especially interesting how (like most reboots of old 90s first person shooters now a days) self aware they are about what the character is. This in turn means all the characters you interact with call your character out for being the donkey-hole he is. This also means sometimes he has to face it which is an interesting thing for a character like Lo Wang. It's a really good idea and I'm glad they went for it. They didn't nail all of the writing, but they made it interesting to read all the scrolls you can find or listen to the conversations (sometiems full of Lo Wang being really mean to someone and sometimes them calling him out on being the donkey that he is).
For me this game is fantastic. The combat is amazing, movement is fluid, the quick switching of guns is well implemented, and it just feels fun to kill demons in this game.
If I have one downside, though, it's very minor. The "crafting" system is completely meaningless, and only seems to be in the game in order to have another way to get rid of upgrades you don't want. I personally see no need for it and I just sell all of mine.
Overall, though, this may be the best game I've played this year, and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

Let me start off by saying that I wasn't a fan of the Shadow Warrior reboot. Like Flying Wild Hog's other game Hard Reset, it suffered from bullet sponge enemies and not-all-that-great gunplay. So when Shadow Warrior 2 was announced I wasn't really looking forward to it. However since I was pleasantly surprised by DOOM, and pretty much every review site/youtuber I followed gave Shadow Warrior 2 a very positive score, I figured I'd go into it with an open mind.
Unfortunately I found Shadow Warrior 2 to be a boring and frustrating mess of poorly executed ideas.
But let's start out with the positives. First off, the game looks and runs great on my PC and there's a nice amount of video options, as well as the option to configure parts of your HUD. The texture are really well done for the most part and there's a lot of color in the game, which is always welcome. I also found the music to be surprisingly enjoyable, the standouts being the main menu theme and "Warrior" written by Stan Bush specifically for the game.
Before I start tearing the game a new one, I'd like to say that I don't consider it a bad game. Objectively I'd say it's above average at the very least. Right then, let's talk about what's wrong with it.
1) The loot is pointless, boring and kills the pacing. The game showers you with loot, and at some point you WILL have to open the poorly designed menu that looks like an old website, and you WILL have to go through every single gem you find, since there is no way to quickly select a lot of gems. And about 80% of the gems you get are the boring "+X% stat" kind.  There are a few interesting gems which change the way your weapons work, but they’re so incredibly limited I didn’t really bother with most of them. Oh and the best quality gems have drawbacks to them, while the second most common quality gems don’t. Now I played through the game on Hard and got a fair bit into it on Insane and I didn’t notice the loot getting any better.
2) The maps are huge but empty and give you no incentive to explore. This being a game focused on loot, naturally you will have chests to open. But there’s almost never anything good. Unlike Borderlands, where you have might get a decent weapon every now and then, here you almost always get money, ammo and some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gem. Each map has one miniboss-type enemy who is GUARANTEED to drop either a skill or a weapon, so there’s no reason to explore every inch of the map, just kill the miniboss, then finish your objective and leave the map. Even though the maps are somewhat procedurally generated, there is very little variety to them and it feels like there are only 3  maps – a rural area, a town area, a sci-fi area. After about an hour of playing you will pretty much see all the level variety the game has to offer. That’s kinda sad. Even Doom had more variety than this. Hell even the Shadow Warrior reboot had more variety.
3) Having 70+ weapons sound like a good idea until you realize you can't properly balance all those weapons. And you wouldn't really need to, since a lot of the weapons feel pretty much the same (even down to the reload animations) or are just straight up upgrades. A better way to do it would be to have about 10 well balanced weapons, and like 2 or 3 skins for each weapon.
4) The enemies don’t get tougher, they just get more prefixes. The further you go into the game (especially on higher difficulties), the more special abilities the elite enemies will have. And by special abilities I mean resistances to damage. Near the end of the game you will be fighting groups of elites who are all resistant and vulnerable to a different element (and most of them will be immune to your powers) so fighting those elites becomes incredibly boring, since they don’t become smarter or change their tactics, they just get more health. One thing I wish Shadow Warrior 2 had copied from Borderlands 2 was the way certain enemies were always vulnerable to something i.e. robots are always weak to acid, shields are always weak to electricity and so on. But the enemies in Shadow Warrior 2 are randomized, so you can’t be prepared in advance.
Once again I'll say that I don't think Shadow Warrior 2 is a bad game. Flying Wild Hog have improved on a lot of things, and I give them credit for that. However for me there are just too many issues with Shadow Warrior 2, which stem from it's new direction towards the Diablo/Borderlands focus on loot. Since I can't give a "mixed" rating, I'm going to give this a negative review, because I hope someone at Flying Wild Hog takes note of these issues and fixes them for the next Shadow Warrior game. Just my two cents

As a die-hard fan of the first KOTOR, having pumped countless hours into it across two platforms, it  saddens me that my hopes that the Restored Content Mod would've given me a better experience replaying the sequel after so many years, originally. To be frank, I pretty much got this game for that sole reason: I hoped that this patch would somewhat remedy the problems I had when playing this way back in '05 on the Xbox.
I didn't like it then because of its apparent rushed nature; it was glitchy, some storylines didn't follow through, lots of unanswered questions/quests, and plenty of other elements missing. While many kudos go to the guys who worked on the RCM, making it the tape to the pile of shredded documents that the original release was, despite their efforts that went into the mod, the major flaw is still apparent: it just isn't a worthy sequel and decent, bordering mediocre, as a stand alone.
It's hard not to hold this to the first game; you honestly can't do it. It has a lot of elements in the first game, both story and gameplay-wise, incorporated into it. The problem was that both elements just weren't up to par and as well polished as its predecessor. I completely understand it was trying to build on top of what the previous had done, but in doing so, the mechanics and, again, narrative buckle under its weight.
Example, you have two star villians: one feeds on death of stars and worlds, and another is held together by sheer will of the Force. In terms to the story, these two are immensily powerful; one can't die and the other can kill everything by himself. In terms of the game, your character can be overpowered to the point where you can kill either them with the greatest of ease. For me, I always play as a Force-user in these games over lightsaber combat (supposedly, making the game harder). By the end, I was the accumulative level of 29 when I killed Darth Sion with nothing but Force Wave and a handful of life support packs. With Darth Nihilus, I buffed myself so I was immune to his Force powers and my team and I just beat him death. To top that all off, all that meant nothing when you get to the end and you fight the final Sith Lord, easily the toughest boss fight in-game, but she was the one who was easily punched to near death in a cutscene in the beginning. Ludonarrative dissonance, if I ever heard it.
In the end, I can't recommend this game to anyone who was a fan of the first. It's just so flawed on so many dissapointing levels, that there is nothing but heart-ache to be had. If you were curious, like I was back in 2005 to see how this game was to the first and on it's own, then you'll probably check this out on that sentiment alone. However, level-design, gameplay, narrative; all is flawed. Much respect to those who worked on the RCM, but you can only polish a turd so much when you realize, that in the end, it's still a turd.

Before purchasing this newest updated to MGT:DotP ask yourself this.
Did you buy this game without reading a review and were looking for two headed giant mode?
Do you expect that the starter deck that you choose should win every match easily?
Do you feel that are the best MGT player in the world so that this game should pose no challenge and you will win every duel?
If you answered no to the first three questions stop right here and pat yourself on the back.  If you answered yes, you may find more satisfaction playing 2014.  2015 returns many features of the first MTG computer game back to the player that have been missing for a long time.  You will be asked to pick your favorite color of deck and given a few options based on that decision.  This starter deck is just like most starter decks in that it has a ton of commons, a few uncommons and a rare.  Finish the tutorial and you are rewarded with a second rare for your deck.
It will next be up to you to optimize the deck as you proceed through the story which will be challenging to start.  After each win your deck has the potential to grow in strength.  Just like in the real world you are rewarded with booster packs which does not always guarentee you a card that helps your deck.  After each plane you have the option to stay on that plane and play random matches for a plane themed booster or move on to the next plane.
Each plane has its own set of cards you can aquire and it will be up to you if you wish to continue your journey and speed through the game or to take some time and aquire additional cards to increase the power of your deck.  As with most MTG:DotP games there are a couple planes that you will traverse through and several challenges per a plane.
If you enjoy the freedom to customize your deck as you see fit and found the previous versions rather limiting then 2015 is a solid purchase.  Multiplayer to start is limited to 1 player per a deck and hopefully gets an update soon.  For the price of $10 you have the ability to get around 80% of the available cards with an additional set being only available via purchased boosters. If the idea of having to spend some extra money to have all available cards for multiplayer turns you off you may want to pass on 2015 and purchase / stick to 2014.

RIME finally arrived, and it was well worth the wait. The visuals are gorgeous and the soundtrack is beautiful. As an audiovisual experience it is breathtaking. I'm playing on a 3 year old midrange laptop, and even though I can't afford to max all settings, I followed the performance hints provided for each graphics option, and found it easy to strike a balance of quality and performance that runs smooth and looks great.
The puzzles are varied, intuitive, and not particularly complicated. Although there are moments of tension and danger, the  gameplay experience is more relaxing than challenging. There are places to explore with freedom, but it is not an open world game, rather it progresses linearly across a number of areas. Still, there are plenty of secrets to find if you want.
The controls work well. The camera has some surprising turns in a handful of places; it does not really hinder the gameplay but it may disorient or annoy you. Thankfully this is very infrequent and for the most part it works just like you expect.
The comparisons with Journey and Ico are obvious, and even The Witness may have been an inspiration. I felt completely immersed in the world of this game, and eager to find out more about the character and his story. I wish there were more opportunities to interact and bond with the friendly creatures in the game, in this sense the game does not reach the emotionally heights of Ico and Yorda's relationship. But then, which game does?
All in all, Tequila have delivered what will surely prove to be one of the best games of this year.

Cons:
As is often the case the game was average in length. Me having finished it i just under 7 hours. However, the game boasts an admirable amount of collectibles and such to bring some replayability into it which is nice.

All in all, I wish it were longer but I am thoroughly impressed with this game. It didn't give away too much too quickly but was a thoughtful adventure from begining to end and left me sitting in awe as the credits rolled. I would highly recommend it to people seeking a thought-provoking and artistic platformer that will hit you right in the feels.

I'm really not sure if I should recommend or not...

Before I go on to the pros and cons...eeeks! these bizarre dark guys really freaked me out first time I encountered them. They're so fu**ing creepy. I can't remember to see something like these in any other game I ever played. Also I can't remember any enemy that I really hated so much like this birdo. He's annoying, relentless, returning and quiet efficient. I'm so happy I reached the next world now...I don't trust that bird.
The pure PRO side:
+The sound is peaceful, relaxing and in appropriate moments tense.
+The world itself is beautiful to look at and has hidden quiet a few secrets.
+Movement and corresponding controls feel fluent (I played with a controller, no idea about keyboard)
+ ^Controller support - it feels like a must for this kind of game, and dev provided :)
+Intriguing story? Okay, I'm stranded, and almost alone so far clichee... but why was the fox trapped? Who is the stranger? Oooh...are these memories? If so, where does the red cloak come from? Wait, is this a prophecy? Will I get this cloak like pictured? Okay, probably more many of interesting questions I'm left with quiet early than a story but I guess the fox will tell...
+ Besides the performance I encountered almost not a single problem (glitchy pushing and one time I was floating stuck on the edge of a platform - lucky me there was a checkpoint like 10s before)
+ Did I mentio nthe Soundtrack already? :P
Aaand for the NONOs:
- I don't think I have to mention the bad performance again.... whoops.
- A little too many questions at the beginning... whats up with the glowing amphores that I destroy?
- Some parts are waaay to dark
- Yay for giving me the option for inverse vertical...nay for missing horizontal
- Sometimes movement started to freak out when pushing the skull-like stones forward (they simply refuse the direction then and push you backwards...)

Sometimes you really have to look careful around to find the way (but most often for the main story it's quiet straight forward). And pay attention to the small details - even the loading screen spoils the main theme of the level. Oh, and it has a bird. A huge bird. And you'll probably hate it (in a good way).
And it has an amazing soundtrack. Really.
Go, play it!

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

First thing you should do when starting a game in Life is Feudal; is to make sure your starting on the right server. Because theres alot of them, and that means theres alot of bad ones.
There are more roleplaying servers than not, which is fair enough considering this is by far the best game I've ever played for Roleplayers. Which would be awesome if I was into that. But I am not. I prefer the open world sandbox PVP experience.
Life is Feudal provides the most advanced way for me to enjoy that very experience. The best part about it would have to be the fact that - even in Alpha - it pretty much all works. Everything that they have in the game currently, mostly all works without any game breaking bugs or glitchs. There are plenty of those around, sure -  but none that make me want to not come back.
This game is slow though. Progression is slow, but rewarding. However if you don't have some sort of goal to work towards in this game then it won't be enjoyable at all. You really do need to be able to envision what you want to create before you begin creating it. And before you even begin that your going to need to do a hell of a lot of basic work just to be able to make your vision a virtual reality. But it is so damn satisfying when you complete each and every little step of your goals.
People you meet along the way will either help or hinder you. Either way it provides more fun, the survival aspects of the game are alot less visible in a non-PVP server - hence I do advise you play on a server that has no issues with theft from other players or murder. This IS a sandbox game and those mechanics ARE in it and they mostly all work.
Plus this game is ALOT more fun when you make enemies as well as friends. No enemies makes your castle pretty useless anyway. So make sure not to join carebear servers.
I might advise to wait a few more months before deciding to buy this game as they are planning on making it some sort of MMO, but...theres a big learning curve to it...so its probably a good idea to get it now just to learn how to start off when its fully released in September.

This is a beautiful game, but not at all what I expected. The store page, at the time of writing, promised, among other things, the following: "Take in a beautiful world inspired by the wonders of the Mediterranean through a fusion of captivating music and color." It also stated that you could "Discover the mysterious island at your own pace."
All the screenshots and videos that we're shown showed a beautiful island basked in Mediterranean sunlight. The reality, however, is that the bright and sunny island is only the beginning of the game, and you'll spend most of the time in underground areas, with the tone of the game changing to becoming more and more sad and melancholy (the visuals match the tone of the game's story). It's quite a beautiful thing all told, and the final reveal, while not unexpected after the "dream sequences" and the appearance of particular wraith-like creatures, is certainly effective on an emotional level. I won't spoil anything.
That said, this is not a free-form exploration game at all. It's linear through and through, with the exception of some areas where you can chose what things to tackle first. There's also a surprisingly large amount of basic 3D Prince of Persia- and Tomb Raider-like platforming, where you climb from ledge to ledge, jump to platforms, and so forth. You'll push some blocks, roll some balls, and use light and shadow to solve the fairly straightforward puzzles.
It's all good stuff and looks fantastic, but it's also very short: I finished the game in 5 hours. There are still some collectables that I need to find, and I assume that will take me another few hours. That said, I prefer to have an excellent short game than a mediocre long one, and RiME is certainly pretty good, though perhaps a tad overpriced considering how linear and fairly simple it is.

It's normal to have high expectations on a game that's been in development for more than 10 years, but to judge it it's important to know a little of its development history to understand why they took so long to finish it.
It was remade from scratch many times because of the engine or graphics being outdated, they wanted it to be perfect, or at least as groundbreaking as the original Duke Nukem 3D was at its time. Due to this fact, many of the original ideas planned for the game didn't make it to the final product as can be seen in its many trailers.
But then, when all hope was lost (with 3D Realms closing) Gearbox appeared and saved the day buying the Duke Nukem license. And then the game was released. Was it groundbreaking? No. Was it awesome? I wish... Was it bad? No, and that's what it's important.
If you don't know the history of its development, the final product (at least the bulk of it, not counting the makeup and multiplayer Gearbox added later) was finished by 2009, and due to budget and legal problems, the game felt a little old even for that time. So probably most of its ideas were nice and new for 2005 maybe, its not bad! But not as impactating as they wish they were (if they decided to change it, it probably would have never been released).
Plot wise, it isn't something jaw dropping, it is something you would expect from a Duke Nukem game: Duke is loved and desired by the women, men admire him, and kids want to be like him, it's all going well until an alien mothership comes to Earth. The problem is, they're not being hostile... yet. As the story unfolds (doesn't take too long actually) everybody finds out that the aliens plan on abducting the women, and kill everyone else, ESPECIALLY Duke Nukem, so it's up to the King to go rescue the babes and save the world once again.
Graphically, it isn't outstanding by any means, but Gearbox did a really good job poilishing it, the blur and depth of filed effects are really well implemented. You can notice a few low res texture here and there (most noticeable on the console versions) but it shines at times like in the Cycloid Emperor fight at the start of the game or in the Mothership battle a bit alter on. What really is kinda of ugly, it's the animations, the characters move unnaturally and don't have many facial expressions, reminded of Quake 4 NPCs. On the other hand, the enemies are very detailed and in general really well done.
In the Sound department, it lacks a more compelling soundtrack, but the voice acting is really well done, Jon St. John returns as Duke doing a really great job. The other NPCs sound a little ridiculous sometimes, but that's intended. The one-liners return and (fortunately for me and unfortunately for others) the old ones come back too. There aren't many good ones within the introduced in this game, but some really have the spirit of the franchise.
Gameplay was one of the most controversial things about this game, I thought it was too linear run and gun with regenerative health (ego) as most FPS games are nowadays, and that's what disappointed me. Don't get me wrong, it's fun to play, but I expected it to be more open ended like Duke 3D. I was hoping for something that would really differ (in a good way) from all the games we have today. There are puzzles here and there and I enjoyed them, to reduce the pace a little to not get too repetitive. The other games references were funny and not offensive like most people think they were, Duke Nukem 3D featured a "dead space marine.." (Duke's voice) and played just like it, guys at Id found it hilarious and not offensive, it's more of a homage than an offense. The guns for the most part don't feel very powerful (with the exception of the shotgun), and the classic funny ones can't be used as they were in Duke 3D because of the 2 weapon limit (4 as an option with a later released patch), the Shrink Ray is overpowered, since it's almost One Shot One Kill, but the Freeze-Ray is underpowered because it takes a lot of time to actually freeze the enemy and puts you in harm's way since it only works in close range.
The loading times aren't as huge on the PC as they are on the console versions, but it is still a little big when you are dying constantly in a specific part of the game. You can't save whenever you want, instead the game uses checkpoints, which actually makes the game more challenging (too much at times but oh well).
Multiplayer is old school. Features deathmatch, team deathmatch, CTF (CT Babe in this case), and King of The Hill. All old school fast paced, not many people play it, but its fun for a while. Weird that when any player dies, they blow up instead of having ragdolls, probably because the guys at Gearbox didn't have time to implement it.
As a game released these days, I'll give it a 6, which is fair, it shares a lot of similarities to other popular FPS games these days (including the complaints). But knowing that it was supposed to be released a long time ago (talking of the actual build, not the old ones), when the ideas were actually "new" for the time, I would give it a 7.8. I think that after all that the developers been through, they deserve a little understanding.

The game is great. I find it rather funny and entertaining, and my only complaint is the framerate.
I'm gonna be apologetic about some things that others have criticized:
The voice acting:
It's not that bad. Certainly better than the majority of anime dubs out there, and really, it's pretty much on par with the voice acting in Skyrim. Which while no huge feat, is still kind of the industry standard.
The dialogue:
Is it perfect? No. But it is pretty dang funny. The charatcers are full of quips and one-liners with a lot of homages (You're a little short for a City Guard aren't you?) and a LOT of self-mockery, especially directed at the previous game in the series, which are subtle, but you'll catch if you play them back to back.
The fighting:
It's pretty straight forward attack-button mashing mostly. But when you do come up against particularly tough opponents you can usually find some way to beat them. Otherwise: go level up. It's an RPG. So of course the mobs that are hard at the beginning (Varns: which are Mummy III army of Anubis style jackal-men) become paper thin foes by 6 hours in.
The plot:
Save the girl. Defeat the evil Emperor. Bad guys from the first game are now the good guys. Pretty standard. Is that bad? I don't think so. It's still an enjoyable story. If you're looking a novel, complex plotline, GO READ A BOOK! It's all plot and no grind! Want suggestions? Message me, I'll give you lists. So unless you're looking to be blown away by some unexpected seldom-before-seen tale of intrigue, wizardry, and shenanigans, it's a good story.
As for the sidequest stories. They're ridiculously over the top, asinine, or just straight up obvious comedic relief. One mercenary mission request is a parent and daughter locked in a cellar because there are angry ostriches trying to kill the daughter by touching her with their feathers and causing an allergic reaction. They sent the letter by carrier pidgeon. Is this serious? Clearly not. To those saying the game's stories are stupid: lighten up. Laugh at the game. Laugh at the genre. They're really picking on RPGs as a genre in this game.
The mechanics:
Plays like a hack'n'slash brawler. I like hack'n'slash brawlers. It can be a bit clunky at times, with your character sometimes crouch to sneak instead of running for his life, but you can fix that by changing the key-bindings I believe.
Lastly, the Personal Info requirements:
It's your name and address. All public information anyway. All information you've already put into Steam likely more than once. Do you really the Polish game designers care that much about you that they're going to stalk you, or ruin their business by stealing your identity? Or send you snailmail? No. It's for commercial data collection. Statistics. By knowing your address, age, and sex, they can precisely gauge who is buying their stuff and adjust marketing accordingly. That's it.

Being my most played game ever, there is no doubt that I highly reccomend this game. It's not as much of a game as it is a platform which you can do pretty much anything. From creating a large scale conflict to simulating everyday life with civilians, arma 3 allows you to do anything you please. The devs are constantly active, providing free platform updates as they release occasional paid dlc. The community is outstanding, truly showing what this platform is capable of. The original PLAYERUNKOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS was first developed on this platform, as well as the origin of all DAY Z type games. The community constantly provides the steam workshop with endless missions, gear, weapons, and overhauls that keep the game feeling fresh.
Arma 3 comes with 3 main modes. Multiplayer, Campaign, and Editor. The multiplayer provides endless fun with other players, from classic game modes like king of the hill, bringing the arma 3 gameplay to a competitive environment. However, community gamemodes such as Battleroyal (battlegrounds) and breaking point (day z) are also very popular amongst the community. In addition, the multiplayer also has a wealth of cooperative missions, which take the squad-based gameplay and puts it to the test against the intelligent AI.
Campaign is a fun introduction to what Arma 3 can do. Although the story and characters is nothing special, almost sub-par, the gameplay is varied enough to keep the player fully engaged. From commanding vehicles to running Guerilla tactics, Arma 3's 3 part campaign keeps the sandbox feel from the other modes in the campaign. Although the campaign is relatively linear, it gives you enough freedom to make the campaign yet another positive of the Arma 3 package.
The editor is where I have spent most of my hours in the game. It allows you to create anything imaginable in the massive canvas that Arma 3 is. In addition, this is where one can see the full potential of their mods. It's really fun just to open the editor up and mess around with all the dynamic features of Arma, and is where u can see all the tiny details the devs put so much care into.
However, Arma 3 isn't without its flaws, and it's got a lot of them.
The engine, although very nice looking, is extremely CPU taxing. Having more than 10 squads of AI shows a very noticeable FPS drop. This isn't a problem on our side, as the entire Arma 3 platform is not only 32-bit, but runs on entirely one core of the CPU. I run a i7-6700k and SLI 1080 tis, and I can barely get 60 FPS on 1440p when I have 20+ squads. It's not as much of a problem to me, but other people with lower end systems will see a huge problem in running this poorly optimized game. However, the game is one of the only first person shooters that is playable on a rediculously low FPS. I used to play this on my laptop at 12 FPS and still had loads of fun.
Another big problem is the AI. The AI is extremely inconsistent, and even though you can set the skill of the AI, they still randomly gain laser pin point accuracy, or just become completely brain dead. That's not saying the AI doesn't pose a challenge, but if you play the game you will notice the AI can be very odd at times.
The engine itself is pretty damn buggy. Actions that should be smooth look really odd, like "vaulting" (not vaulting at all). Picking up weapons and managing load outs is a very laggy process, and glitchy ragolls, animations, and the weird♥♥♥♥♥bipod system remove some fluidity out of the gameplay.
The biggest problem In the game in my opinion is the extremely overly complicated control scheme. Although the game's complexity is half of it's fun, what could be simple control become a hair pulling frustration the more you play. Commanding a squad is abysmal. A simple task of asking a squad mate to heal himself requires you to press a function key, find the soldier and put him in your line of site, then scroll through the god forsaken action menu until you see "heal self", but if he walks out of your cross hair you need to start all ♥♥♥♥ing over again. Not only that, but the function keys as squad selection causes an uncountable number of problem. Since free look is done using the alt key, if I try and get unit 4 to lay down suppressing fire, i click ♥♥♥♥ing alt f4 and the game ♥♥♥♥ing closes and i lose all my godamn progress.
The context menu NEEDS TO GO. It completely halts the fun in Arma when you need to stop and scroll through a menu while your being shot at to OPEN A ♥♥♥♥ING DOOR. The game makes you pull your hair out when you try and loot a body but instead set off the c4 you planted and you ♥♥♥♥ing get blown to hell. The game seriously needs to simplify it's controls to not only make it more friendly to new players, but to keep the gameplay flowing and the heart pumping intensity there.
Despite all it's flaws, Arma remains one of my favorite games to this day, and the endless variety keeps the game fresh. The fun gameplay and in depth editor keeps me coming back every time, and I highly reccomend this game to anyone, even though they aren't fans of the milsim genre.

TL;DR : Better gameplay (particularly coop) with good dynamics but a few questionable choices, still good graphics, enjoyable designs and slightly weaker story and dialogs than the first.
If you got frustrated by the lack of coop campaign for Doom, don't look further, get this game now.
A first person hack'n'slash, fights are extremely more dynamic gameplay wise than most popular coop games with the melee being well developed and fun enough to allow for (chain)sword-only levels.
The procedurally generated levels are very fun, since you can explore and navigate them at your pace. More randomization would be welcome though.
The multiplayer, weirdly enough, doesn't have a chat. Most game end up like Diablo 3 session where everyone is forced to follow th host. With friends though, it becomes awesome.
The rpg elements are a mixed bag, the gems (aka weapon upgrade system) suffer a weird design, with the rarest stats gems suffering most of the time a negative stat that make them hardly interesting to use. The crafting system present is in DIRE need of clarification.
The story is slightly weaker than in SW 2013 though, with the dialogs being more raw insults and less subtle burn like in the first one. Some characters lack development, and the ending is...
And last, the game mostly run smoothly, but can suffer from a few crash. But those days, it's better than what troubles you can get for an AAA title.
In the end ? The game's overall good, though you won't spend a hundred hours playing it like a Borderlands (partly because it's way faster-paced). The rpg aspect could use a development, but since SW1 got some kickass upgrade involving an additional boss fight after its release, Flying Wild Hog has the chance to make this game better.

Arma at its core is a team based tatical shooter, and for the most part builds for and caters to that side of the community. There are also plenty of groups out there that might fit you, for example there are some that are more say semi-casual/semi-serious (which is what ive learned to personally like), and then there is the more realism/milsim aspects of the community. However there is also whatever players in the community have been able to bend the engine to do through the editor, for example Wasteland and Life Roleplaying Servers. Arma is also a pretty open platform for mods, which many groups may use as a requirement, such as ACE, TFAR and RHS. I will say though, once you've gotten use to how they work you wont really want to revert to the base game. Finally it is worth noting that Arma is a CPU intensive game, meaning a higher clock-speed CPU, will give you better FPS (as well as poteintally higher speed ram+HDD/SSD). For this game, to be perefectly honest, a 1080 or even a 960 is kind of overkill and for the most part will not yeild better performance.
