So the Shadow Warrior remake of 2013 was awesome.  Combat was good.  Story was surprisingly deep.   Voice in your head was entertaining.  Levels, while not too elaborate looked nice and were fun to explore.
Fast forward to Shadow Warrior 2.  Combat is good.  Voice in your head is annoying.  Story is weak.  Levels are more elaborate, and still fun to explore, but really show their limitations after a few hours.
Hoji was an entertaining character to have popping out of your head and giving commentary and such.  The chick who eats screen space by showing up in the corner is just grating.
There are some controller issues that may not be a problem for those who use kb/m, but will♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone else off.  Any diagonal movement with the right stick seems to happen at roughly half the speed of up, down, or side to side movement.
The performance is hit and miss.  Sometimes it stutters, despite my fps counter showing a steady 60fps.  So there's obviously some sort of issue.
The menus are a mess.  And there isn't any kind of a tutorial about how to do any of the modding of weapons, or much of anything else.
Since there is no manual save system, we are at the mercy of auto saves.  The problem being, that they can be painfully far apart sometimes.  Near the beginning of the game, I lost about 20 minutes of progress due to a random ctd.
The generated levels kinda kill it for me.  I thought that I had been going to the same three levels over and over.  Then I paid more attention to the world map and saw that they were actually a dozen or so separate levels.  They really should have gone with the hand crafted levels they did in the 2013 game.  Those felt nicely different.  No just a random assortment of limited assets.
It's times like these I really wish there were a middle ground in Steam reviews. While there is a lot to like in this game, there's also a lot that's thoroughly "meh"
To summarize:
I love the combat.  I love the graphics.  The length is decent, with my first playthough clocking in at around 18 hours.  The loot system could use some work, but it adds a lot to the game.  The combat feels a lot more fluid now and the special moves are much easier to pull off.  Basically the gameplay has been improved in every way.
However I don't like the random bag of level layouts.  It just feels "samey".  I don't like the characters.  They're either bland or completely annoying. I don't like the menus.  They're, for lack of a better word, a cluster♥♥♥♥.  The ending is also extremely abrupt, with absolutely no closure.  It just ends.  The humor has also taken a turn for the worse.
I guess I'll base this review on the number of positive features, length of the game, fun, and price point.  Factoring in these things, I will recommend.  Though I should be clear and say that while I did enjoy myself, I was constantly seeing things that could have been done better,   hampered the experience, or just took me right out of the experience.

It's interesting how great games like this one can be swept under the radar, especially from critically-acclaimed developers like Pixel, the creators of Cave Story.
Just ignore the fact that you're a... frog.. janitor.... thing.. and you're in for a real treat.
I was amazed that the game was able to teach you how to play the ENTIRE game with nothing but thirty seconds on the title screen.
This game is essentially Cave Story mixed with Contra.  It kind of reminds me of Mega Man in the sense that your character has some weight on him allowing you to make presice movements.
Lots of weapons to add to your arsenal with satisying upgrades to make then pack an even bigger punch. Bubbles, spreadshots, wide beams, long-range bullets, and a straight up flamethrower. You can also buy health upgrades, so you get to choose whether firepower or stamina is more important to you.
Dont get me wrong, I think this game is really good; good little story, good mechanics, good style. But that's all it really is... good.

This game was a lot of fun to play. The graphics and sounds have a retro style, while having more smooth and modern gameplay. This game reminds me a lot of the original version of Cave Story, when it came out (which, as a retro gamer, preferred). The charm of games, like this one, lies in its effort to emulate the appearance of an older game to appeal to retro gamers. The characters were also very amusing to watch; and their discourse is very understandable to anyone who has worked an office job.
As platformers go, the movement seems fair and balanced. There were no slow points in the game. The weapon system is very well executed as well. You get four weapons and each can be upgraded in an order based on your playstyle. However, each weapon has a definitive purpose and will make certain enemies/boss fights significantly easier. Be sure you buy every new weapon as it unlocks, as it will make things easier for you.
The thing that will appeal to retro gamers; but may upset some new gamers is the challenge. While the game is not especially hard, extra lives are relatively scarce and well hidden at times. While there are save points inbetween levels and checkpoints within the level, if you die too many times and lose all of your lives, you have to restart the level. The levels are very long sometimes, so this can present a challenge in the later levels, which can become somewhat Ghouls N' Ghosts-esque with the enemies numbers. I highly reccomend fully upgrading the spread gun first, then the bubble gun. Upgrade the laser last, for use on the final boss.
That being said, the death penalty is actually a good thing, as gold is permanent and will carry over after death. There is a shop in every level to upgrade your items; so if you get stuck and keep dying, you can go back to the shop and upgrade, helping you push past the difficult point. There is also a health shop at the start of every level, whenever you die, letting you buy much needed permanent health boosts.
All-in-all, the game was fun and I had a good time. :)

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II is the best game i've ever played. Let me explain why.
While Kotor was a great game, the sequel is just magnificent. The story is a lot more original and darker than the first one, more mature, and more serious. It is free of the Star Wars clichés where you always save the galaxy in the name of the Jedi, where you become the Hero in the end. This game is far from that. It is a more PERSONAL story, it has a lot more character than any other game i've played and it has, by far, the best companion characters in the gaming world. Kreia is just pure genius; and the others are great as well. Everybody has his/her own agenda, everybody is a different personality, and in the end, you might be surprised, that not everyone is what he/she looks like the first time. Your choices actually matter; what you say to your companions can either backfire on you, or help you, and how you deal with other people may have consequences that you will only see later. Even the smallest dialogue choices matter in this game.
The gameplay is improved; a lot more skills, force powers, more weapons to choose from, its immersive. The animations are smoother, the music is ABSOLUTELY BEAUTIFUL; and the replayability of the game is great, because you have lots of choices that are different if you play it on the other side (Dark or Light, whichever you didn't play first). It's not like any other SW game where you make a big choice and for the last few levels you'll be bad or good. No. Expect the unexpected.
Because of the rushed nature of the game, it had its flaws in the story, and it had really murky endings, but with the new TSL Restoration Project Mod, it is finally complete. Download that Mod, Play It, and Experience It. By far, it's the best game of all time.
So go play it. You'll miss something truly special, if you don't.

I've played this game twice and I must say that it all depends on your style of gameplay.
The first time I played it was just for fun and my own entertainment.  Lots of scares and all with a ton of fear and struggles.  After a few months I had forgotten almost everything in the game and decided that making some videos of it for YouTube would be fun.  I decided to give it a try and was very disappointed to see that not as many frightening moments occurred.  For example, if a monster chased me then it seemed not to go after me for as long as the first time.  That was a little upsetting because it really got me into the game.  But, I also have to admit that I didn't run straight into all of the rooms and the such the second time around, possibly being the reason that not as much chaos had occurred that time.
Although the second playthrough was not as crazy as the first, I have to admit that the game did take its toll on me.  Multiple times I could of sworn that I had seen or heard something that, upon further review in my recordings, was proven to be a simple hallucination of some sorts.
For those looking to play this game, I would highly recommend it.  But I would take a more carefree style of play with you as well, or I should say, a more adventurous one.
Hopefully this has given you a fair look at this game.  You should expect the best from this game if you allow yourself to enter it with an open mind and are open to the scares it has in store for you.
If you wish to see my gameplay of it, I have provided a link to the first gameplay I had of it down below.  Feel free to use it as a teaser, for it does not provide too many spoilers.  Possibly one or two little factors here or there, but nothing that could potentially ruin the game for you.  For those of you that would like to watch the game in whole, watch the first episode and feel free to follow along in the playlist to all of the parts.
I hope you all enjoy the game.  If you have any questions then please feel free to add me and ask me.  Good luck!!!

Tomb Raider Underworld is by far the best modern Tomb Raider game.
You play as Lara Croft in another adventure through mythical settings.

2. Fantastic locations.  Some of it looks amazing (the second Level, wow!).  Unfortunately too much dungeon and not enough sunshine.
The bad:
3. You can't take screenshots without a workaround explained in the game forums.
4. You should have been able to change the camera depth.  It is too close for my liking.
5. A very contrived plot.
6. Awful Savegame system straight out of console world.  Every now-and-then when saving, my game crashed.
The ugly:
7. Too many enemies spoil tension.
8. Atrocious camera heebie-jeebies in certain spots; like low corner areas.
9. Apparently you can do headshots?  Damned if I could.

This is an almost 8 year old game. And however, it stands out as one of the best of its genre.
I played first when it came out, and my expectations were low, as I thought this was going to be a cheap God of War clone. It turned out I was wrong: combat was simple but satisfying, landscapes were imaginative and vibrant, and the story, while not deserving an Oscar, was mildly interesting. But what won me over was the puzzles. You see, this is in some way a Metroidvania: you can revisit previous locations with abilities you gain during your playthrough in order to get to new areas. The ways you get to use your new gear are sometimes not straightforward and there are more than a couple of clever puzzles in the game. Yes, many abilities we have seen in other games, like Portal, but when you copy things that work and are well implemented in the gameplay like this game does, then it's totally forgivable. Some people I know claim this is the best Zelda title ever, and I agree. Besides War, the main character is a total badass.
When I revisited the game for my second playthrough a month or so ago, I tried to temper my expectations thinking 7 years have gone by and maybe it wasn´t going to hold up well. How wrong was I. Despite, the comparatively low polygon count of the models and backgrounds, the choice of colors and the exceptional design make them look great (this is the old tech vs art design debate), the combat without being as refined as DmC is responsive and satisfying, and puzzles and exploration are as good as ever.
A sign of the quality of the game is that the company that bought the rights to the title is going to release  a 1080p/60fps version soon. Obviously if you have an average PC you should be able to play it at that resolution with no issues.
Do yourself a favor and play this!

This game is excellent, and I enjoyed it greatly. It reminds me of the Soul Reaver series, which I also loved, but with a higher focus on combat rather than puzzles (although there are puzzles).
The game is kind of linear - the main path is, but you can explore around to get some benefits, and revisit old places with your new abilities to reach extra rewards (such as increasing your max health). You will unlock big new abilities and mechanics at specific points in the game, but many combat abilities and upgrades are bought using the game's currency (souls).
The combat is quite entertaining. You have (and unlock) many combat abilities and tools. Your main ways to avoid damage are blocking (which is more useful than it is in other games, though some big attacks are unblockable) and moving out of the way (usually using a dash). Your main weapon is a huge sword, but there's also two alternate weapons (one focused on a bigger are, and the other on stuns and sending people flying away), and they're all quite satisfying to use. These three weapons gain experience by using them to hit your enemies, and you can assign trinkets to them to add small bonuses. You get several ranged weapons, but they're not the main focus (they don't gain experience and you can't assign trinkets to them, but you can buy some upgrades for them). There's also other combat mechanics which you'll unlock, but I don't want to spoil them.
The story is quite good, and it doesn't end too abruptly, even if you do want to learn more about several things (though I haven't played the sequel yet). The story includes characters from several mythologies, but doesn't exactly follow any of them (many details are different from those mythologies), and other characters are new, creating the game's new mythological cosmology.
The graphics are relatively good, although the game's not that recent. The design of the characters and locations is excellent. The music's alright, but it's not particularly memorable. The voice acting is high quality.
The port is good, thought to unlock steam achievements, you should run the game after starting steam (you can restart steam before playing to be safe). It runs pretty well on oldish computers.

Played the new Tombraider reboot and liked it, so decided to try an older TR game as I've never played a classic Tombraider game to the end. Chose Underworld as it's one of the most recent (from 2008). Although graphics are a bit retro, visually there's some fantastic levels as you gyrate through Norse Niflhiem, Valhalla and Helhiem in an epic quest to find out what happened to mumsy (with some great cut-scenes). I found I had to use the walkthroughs (e.g.
as sometimes as it's tricky to spot whats a ledge and whats not (nothing lights up to help).
I found I had to use the keyboard for some jump sequences and my Xbox wireless PC controller for others, and it was never obvious which one would suite best. Tricky controls & dodgey camera angles can become infuriating when Lara suddenly chucks herself sideways and plunges to her doom for umpteenth time, so you might well end up throwing the Xbox controller against the wall at some point - particularly if like me you've never owned a games console. Things like working out how to cling to pillars i.e. release left/right after you leap, take a while to sink in, and just a slight missalignment of the camera angle results in disaster.  Plus when Lara croaks you go right back to the beginning of the sequence, even if you saved midway. Some great acrobatic puzzles for Lara though.
Still other than the occasional tantrum, I really enjoyed the game and completed it in just over week playing in the evenings at medium difficulty  (STEAM says it took 23 hours, mostly spent looking at Lara's a*s).  Overall I found it frustating fun and worth playing (9/10 as I really liked the storyline as well). Doubt I'll play the game again though, so I'd only suggest buying it if cheap.  Now moving on to Tomb Raider: Anniversary which many say is even better than Underworld.

There are worse games out there, in as much as Duke Nukem Forever has never crashed my computer, it's possible to get from the beginning to the end, and you're unlikely to get stuck, uncertain of what needs to be done to progress. That said, it's an ugly game that cribs from other shooters without any understanding of why certain things work and why they don't... Rather than allowing puzzles to function as a break from action, it interrupts them for more tedious "here's two enemies, now here's two more, rinse, lather and repeat" action. The "execution to restore life" idea never pays off because the player never knows if they'll actually get to perform an execution unless they get the freeze weapon... And though they finally included an option to increase the stupid two-weapon limit to four, the player is still going to end up mostly using the weapons that ammo is actually provided for on a given level. The "interactive" elements, like pinball tables and computers, mostly serve to try to distract from the obvious narrow linearity of the levels (and fail to do so). The humor is flat and off-putting, drawing an irate "you thought I would laugh at THAT?" from the player. The use of ugly green dark-vision through much of the game suggests a lack of confidence in the work of the texture artists. And perhaps worst of all for those who fondly remember Duke Nukem 3D, this iteration of Duke is a wuss... Drunk on one beer, constantly having to run for cover in every encounter, and departing more than one major fight flat on his back and passing out. I understand why some people might feel compelled to bear witness to the train wreck when the game is available at a sale price, but honestly... Spare yourself the time and go watch some of the video reviews of DNF online instead; there's probably a lot more genuine entertainment value to be found there.

The new player experience has always been bad. Population has been going downhill ever since release. The reason is that the experience is far higher than it has ever been before. Why is that a problem? Well, in this game every single sailor has a base which also has a growth, and that growth adds to the their abilities. Simple right? Not exactly. Because what comes with ability is sailor count on that sailor. The sailor count will give a percentage. This percentage can range from 0 to 220%. This means that if you have 0%, you have 0 ability. But to raise the percentage you need experts and vets. You can gain experts naturally through battle but you'll need to roll for vets. Yep, gambling system right there. I don't know of anybody who rolls for veterans outside of a veteran conversion "event", if you believe its been raised.
So with the knowledge of ability in mind, lets turn to Blitzkreig, the game mode you'll be playing. Blitzkrieg is LITTERALLY pay to win. There's no ifs, ands, or buts about it. It is impossible to get any high ability sailor in Blitzkreig without using premium items because you'll level out of it(level 60) before you do. Whoever decided to spend more cash then you will have insane repair, insane reload, insane accuracy, and insane speed compared to you. You will always lose against them assuming equal skill, which is unlikely since you are new. I'm pretty sure they will get some teamkill damage on purpose so that they drastically lower their experience and continue to farm away.
Should you endure continued losses because you are a masochist, you will eventually reach lvl 61 and be forced into Great Battle where lvl 120 players will oneshot you from outside the screen and you will then find out that the ability cap is also limited by level and to get to an even playing field you will need to be at least lvl 105, Your battleship will have shotgun spread and your bridge officer cannot spot the shells for tracking at lvl 61.
I've seen talk here praising customization, it's all all a lie. At level 1 to 12 you are using neutral guns for a frigate that is meaningless because there is no real upgrade. However, one you reach Heavy Cruiser(CA) you will only use Best In Slot guns created specifically for the ship. Anything else you are using an inferior gun intended for use on a lower tier ship because of the way gunspace works, which is gun gunspace + ammo until full. This magical system means a Tier 5 Battleship can fit out Heavy Cruiser guns and technically be in the right even though its impractical

If you are unsure about this game, you can always play Pink Hour and Pink Heaven. They will give you a flavor for what this game is like. The sprite work is cute and overall the art is light-hearted. Great, visually distinct artwork all around. There is a lot of challenge to this game and it comes with a progression system so that eventually your powers and skill will grow as you make your way through the games 7 or so levels. What I think is really an outstanding feature is that Hard Mode isn't just the same game again with enemies that are more damage spongey or anything like that. Sure, you revisit the levels from the normal mode, but they are vastly changed and require more precise timing and ability. The bosses in hard mode are also revamped, too, leading to the necessity of tweaking strategy from what you have already been used to. There is also a different, cute story for hard mode, also! Overall, a really outstanding game to play and more than generous demos have been made available to see if this game is right for you. If you enjoy old NES/SNES shooting platformers, you should definitely check Kero Blaster out.

Where do I start? I've been playing this game on and off for as long as I can remenber, and all of my memories on this game have been truly fantastic and some of the greatest gaming memories that I have! Over the years of owning this masterpeice off steam I have accumulated easily over 2000 hours, i'd even go as far as too say 3000 too! Rome total war is one of those games where you cant help but keep coming back too, maybe it is the mesmerising soundtrack, or perhaps the highly addictive week long campaigns; perhaps its the strategic element that it is drilled into the game, or perhaps. Perhaps its a mixture of everything...
The greatest thing in Rome 1 is by far the campaigns, you are plunged into a land of bloody conflict, a land of political intrigue, a land of inter-house dilemas, a land of ploys and plots, a land of *total war*
What is amaazing about this games campaign is the fact that the world is quite literraly your oyster, you can choose to invade anywhere at any time, kill anyone at any place, and wage war on any country for any personal reason. Many a times I have watched my empires form and my empires fall, there is no better feeling than slaughtering a rival faction that has wronged you in the past, or perhaps the feeling of re-conquering what was once your soverign territory, this game has mixed emotions. You actually feel a pang of sadness as you have created an empire through bloody strife and conflict as you remenber the hundreds of thousands of soldiers who died and laid down their lives for you to establish your empire. Or perhaps you wont feel this, maybe you wont have a huge militaristic empire, perhaps you will have a small but economically powerful kingdom filled with merchants and trades, or maybe you just want one or two small kingdoms and you just want to survive, after all. Total war is not for everyone...
The maps in rome 1 are huge and give the player a great empty canvas of strategy at their disposal. The battles feel unique, and they feel like battles, you know that if you loose a certain battle then it will result in a crippling blow for your empire, perhaps your capital is under seige and if you loose then your faction leader dies thus morale is diminished to a minute fraction. Or perhaps you have sent out an expeditionary force to some far off land and have established a small but secure foothold which is under attack from a near unknown force. Each battle has a meaning, and each battle has its own ending. Perhaps your heroic soldiers will become 'men of the hour' birthing new heroes and generals for your faction. No units are over powered everything can counter something, so this game is balanced...
This game truly is a master-peice of a game and i would recommend it to anyone who likes mass exterminating the populus. But unfortunatly it does not run on some pc's on windows 10, and the graphics are outdated and the frames are unfortunatly capped at what seems to be 30fps. If not for theise glithces/ graphical limitations then his game would be a solid 10/10. But unfortunatly I have to drop the final score down to a 9.5/10!

Before Crystal Dynamics took hold of the franchise, Tomb Raider was in dire straits. The downward spiral had finally reached the bottom, and you'd be forgiven for wondering if we'd ever see Lara Croft return to relevancy again. But just like that, Legend was released and all was forgiven, with a tighter knit, better polished, and more cinematic Tomb Raider than we had seen in years. The follow up, Anniversary, reworked the original TR with a modern engine and a handful of additions and fixes to polish it off into something that, while not quite the hit Legend was, set the stage for the final game in the trilogy, Underworld, which fully showcases all the CD was aiming for by combining the best parts of their past two games into a fitting end to their first run with Lara, and a solid game in its own right.
Underworld is a direct sequel to Legend, which means if you haven't played the latter (and preferably Anniversary as well), you're going to quickly become lost in a sea of supernatural monsters, returning characters, and a plot that bites off quite a bit more than it can chew. All that said, it finally answers most if not all of the questions proposed by the last two games, finally giving Lara some closure for all that's happened up to this point, as well as for the trilogy, allowing CD free control to go wherever they like with a sequel. It's not going to blow your mind or keep you thinking about it after the credits role, but the narratives blockbuster mentality is more than enough to entertain and carry the game through to the end (provided you don't stop to think about why anything is happening alone the way).
While Legends focused more on style and set pieces, and Anniversary on classic tomb raiding and puzzle solving, Underworld finally manages to meld these two halves almost perfectly, creating what I would consider the truest expression of Tomb Raider Crystal Dynamics has made. The mechanics themselves have been expanded significantly from past games, with platforming in particular getting a much needed upgrade thanks to Lara's larger move set, which feels far more natural and free form than what we've seen in the past as well as allows for a greater amount of variety in the level designs. The levels themselves have also gotten a boost, now on an outrageous scale that towers above you as you attempt to work your way through them, populated by more elaborate puzzles and a ridiculous number of hidden collectibles to find. Everything that Tomb Raider is known for has been improved and taken on a new scope, but in a similar vein, all the has been wrong with the series for years has been entirely neglected.
Combat, though moderately improved, is still as mindless and unsatisfying as ever. The camera continues to be your worst nightmare, seemingly out to make navigating through levels a living hell and often sending you jumping off in entirely the wrong direction. Numerous frustrating glitches make themselves known throughout, from harmless bugs to aggravating mishaps that make progression incredibly difficult. Most disappointing though is how the level designs can often get ahead of themselves, leaving you scratching your head at the enormous size of them without the slightest idea where to begin. The hint system certainly helps in this regard, but it's an imperfect solution, and ideally one you shouldn't ever need to rely on.
If you have ever played a Tomb Raider game before though, none of this should surprise you. As I said before, Crystal Dynamics has built up what the series does best, while quietly ignoring its issues perhaps hoping they'll be overshadowed or ignored. Personally I'm more than capable of putting up with these annoyances in exchange for the rest of the experience, but I'm definitely beginning to ask myself why I'm OK doing this, or if I should have to (the answer for which is obvious). If you didn't enjoy Legend or Anniversary you will find nothing more to draw you into Underworld, but for those who have yet to tire of Lara's escapades Underworld provides a fitting final chapter in this particular story of her life, if also a signal that it's probably time to move onto something new.

Amnesia is probably the scariest game you can play, NO JOKE. Outlast is a big one too, and pretty scary, but this chilled me to the bone! It is thoroughly scary, and I strongly suggest this game if you want a good scare and story line.
So, plot, pretty good. You play as Daniel, a man from 1839 who drank an amnesia potion because he wanted to forget the bad things he had done. You find a note to yourself, telling you what to do and why. I'm not even going to use spoiler text, I think you should just find out for yourself what the note says, because that note is ONE HUGE SPOILER! So anyways, as you continue the game, you find notes from your journal that tells you your past. By the way, the first hour of the game is just build-up to the scary parts. So give it a chance. There's creepy stuff that entertains you until you encounter the monster.
Gameplay is pretty good, too. You need to stay out of the dark, as it will cause your "sanity" to drain. As you get more insane, your sight becomes more disoriented. The screen becomes blurry, in other words. So to stay out of the dark, you can light torches, candles, and lanterns in the environment with tinderboxes that you find on shelves or in other places. Or you can find oil to light your personal lantern, which eminates light all around yourself. But in enemy encounters, you must stay out of light, even if that means going insane, making it altering your vision, giving you extreme fear because you can't see and you know there's a monster nearby. That's the kind of fear you get in this game.
This game is a total 10/10. Amazing(ly scary)!

This is the first true horror game I ever really played, and now my idea of what a horror game should be has been raised to a standard that has rarely been met. The atmosphere of Amnesia is so immersive, the story so intriguing, that while I longed to know what was going to happen next, I couldn't bring myself to play for more than 45 minutes straight. It definitely broke away from the normal scenario of horror games where, while still being terrifying, you could still defend yourself against what lurked in the darkness. Amnesia takes that safety net away, leaving you with only your brain and legs as your means of survival. And despite the horror aspect, which is done very well, the story is amazing as well. I would recommend this to any horror game enthusiast, as well as to people who may not be very familiar with the genre.
P.S. Have fun meeting Mr. Face.

I do not recommend this game, because it can actually be very fun. Odd reason to not recommend a game right! See the problem is... Enjoying it means obnoxious lenghts of time doing things. Oh want to make a farm, clear an area, teraform area, plow the ground, plant seeds, and harvest crops! Sounds easy, but each step is its own huge grind. On top of that, crops take (usually, but depending on server settings) a real life 24 hours to be able to harvest them. Worse yet if you arent online when they are harvestable, they wither.
Fighting is fun enough, its laggy and glitchy but fun. It feels like a bad connection mount and blade, but dumbed down extremely. The hit detection is off, but not too bad. Combat is absolutely just spam click, however some things like shield bash knock you over and stun you. You can chain this with multiple people. The combat needs a lot of work, its geared for bad players in droves.
Its also not really a solo game, you must find a group. Now several people will argue this, but understand that these are adults who can commit 10+ hours a day to a video game. Are you able to do that? Exactly, me either because we arent shut ins. The game takes huge huge gaps of time, splitting the time load with other players is the only way to survive. Unless you play on a PvE server I guess, but I cant imagine doing that.

All the while there is inevitably some huge 20 person group of euros who is pretending they are back in their countries hayday, griefing everyone mostly when they are offline. Its so weird and socially awkward.
Short story long... Its just simply not ready yet, its a fun little medieval simulator, but im not willing to grind on an alpha game, maybe you are who knows. Try it, its not the worst game ever, its just currently a hot mess.

Shovel Knight is SOOOO GOOOOD!!! 9 hours to complete the main campaign, and there are still 2 other DLC campaigns left to go! Putting my review out now because I've already gotten more than enough game out of the $15 I put into it. Everything else is just a bonus.
Gameplay: 9/10
Tight and intuitive platforming controls. You have your normal horizontal dig attack and a down-attack similar to Mario's spin jump in Super Mario World. That's it. But they managed to inculcate so much depth to it and make the gameplay superbly fun.
Every world is distinct, not just visually, aurally, but also in the enemies that you encounter. And its a heck of a lot of fun to play through them.
A Dark Souls-esque gold-losing system each time you die encourages you to spend your gold on upgrades and discourage reckless play. Some flaws in it because you often are not able to retrieve your gold and feel bad for doing so.
A system which allows you to optionally remove your own checkpoints for added difficulty in exchange for gold is a great addition. However, the game runs out of upgrades very quickly which eventually turns this system moot.
In general, there are some misses, but a lot of hits. Though some of their innovations are a bit wonky, points are given for them trying out neat new mechanics.
Graphics: 10/10
Amazing 8-bit aesthetic, where they legitimately restricted the game's entire palette to only 256 colours.
Very good diversity of aesthetics for all the different worlds. Animations are super smooth and expressive.
Sound: 10/10
WONDERFUL soundtrack. Chiptunes which rival only the likes of Undertale. Able to set the mood of every level perfectly. Excellent boss battle music as well as pieces which bring the feels. So, so glad that I got the version with the OST.
The main themes are great. Some of the boss battle themes are as good as Undertale's. The feels tracks are honestly on par with Ducktale's Moon Theme or or To The Moon's. It doesn't beat any of these classics, but very closely reaches their levels and credit is given for its excellence in a wide variety of types.
Story and Atmosphere: 10/10
A very lighthearted atmosphere for most of the game, with good humour found not only in text but in the animations, sound design, and character designs. The game is oozing with flavour from the get-go.
But the game also knows when to deliver emotional moments, particularly at the end, and I honestly teared up over these 8-bit characters.
It doesn't tell a very complex story. But it wears the classic Hero's Journey on its sleeve and tells it brilliantly. Love the dream sequences, as well as the interlude after every level with Shovel Knight sleeping by the campfire (good application of catharsis).
Shovel Knight's interaction with the other antagonists are also lovingly charming. There is a battle royale sequence at the end that is awesome, and Shovel Knight's own character is developed through the course of the game. In a genre that generally passes on good writing, Shovel Knight delivers it in spades (hehe) and it is a welcome surprise.
Favourite moment: the Troupple King's Dance. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥its beautiful.
In conclusion, every aspect of Shovel Knight is just perfect at what it sets out to do. They reached for the stars and achieved exactly that. What you get is a game that is fun, charming, nostalgic, challenging, funny, and tells a great story—a whole lot of quality content in one package.
Shovel Knight is the pinnacle of independent game development. It takes from the best and discards the rest. This game has succeeded XCOM as my 4th favourite game of all time, and that's saying something, because I invested over 200 hours into that 😅
If you've never touched a platformer before, DO play Shovel Knight! 10/10 👑

I have played many games this year, some good, some bad, but it wasn't until recently that I decided to forget about the reviews and play Duke Nukem Forever for the PC and after I played it I came to a rather disturbing realization, DNF is by far one of the best FPS games I have ever played! No offense to anyone, but I personally think that games like Halo and Call of Duty can NEVER live up to this degree of awesome!
Unlike most FPS games of today, DNF strives to be original and interesting. There was never a moment where I was bored or uninterested, the game was action packed, hilarious, and all around entertaining from beginning to end. It was even more fun than Duke Nukem 3D, and that's really saying something too!
Unlike these so called "critics" who complain about everything, I can honestly say that I can find ABSOLUTELY NOTHING major wrong with the game! Sure the storyline is simple, the graphics are outdated, and the game is slightly perverted, but everyone seems to have forgotten one crucial fact, THIS IS DUKE NUKEM! and when you play a DN game you're not out to embark on a emotional, heart-wrenching, sad storyline that ends with all of your friends and you dying (MASS EFFECT 3). Nor are you out to learn about the philosophy of the human mind (BIOSHOCK). You play a DN game to KICK @$$! END OF STORY!
Critics, fans, and people in general want games that are full of ridiculous plot twists, branching storylines, compelling characters, and amazing multiplayer. All of that is well and good, but sometimes you have to throw all of that out the window and just relax and have fun (AND NOT PLAY AS SOME BORING FACELESS CHARACTER!).
I really don't know what people wanted from this game, but I personally think that it is the best FPS game I have played all year! Not because of a bunch of next-gen stuff, but because IT IS FUN!
I have only one minor complaint, Duke is as near-sighted as I am without glasses!
Don't listen to the critics and fans with unrealistic expectations, buy a copy and kick some @$$!

It's a great game, really it is. Immensely satisfying gameplay and depth that'll make you keep coming back. I started playing in 2011, about a month before the F2P update.
However, with the changes to matchmaking I feel the game has lost a HUGE part of what it was - the community. The legacy server browser is tucked behind 2 menus that no new player would ever think to look into, and the concept of matchmaking itself brings a whole new vibe to TF2 that I just don't like. It used to be that you would find a server that you liked and kept coming back to it, making friends and forming a community. In the 40 hours of Casual I've played in the past month, all I've seen are frothy tryhards insulting everyone for not being their definition of 'good,' coolkids who spam a bind after every kill/win, aimbots, and mutes who never respond to chat or voice. Since there's no community - no regulars, no admins, etc - I felt like I was just being shuffled from match to match, like riding public transportation. There was no connection, not a single memorable occasion to be had.
People like to say this aspect of TF2 ended back when quickplay was added, but I disagree. At least quickplay let you favorite Valve servers that you visited, so there was at least a
at a community. Now it's just meaningless game after meaningless game. I feel that only Competitive should have been added to the game for those who need that vapid sense of player progress in a video game - and even then, don't make it the first thing a player sees when they open the game. Someone who's interested in Competitive will already know about it beforehand. The whole point of adding it in the first place was to add longevity to the game but TF2 was never about its relationship to the competitive scene. There's no one thing it was about, but I feel esports is the very last aspect of enjoyment when it comes to TF2.
I'll still play this game from time to time, see how it's doing, enjoy it for a while. Eventually that same sense of emptiness will come back. This game is just sad now.

If you're like me, you're going to love this game. It's like Harvest Moon for grownups - you fish, mine, forage, chop down trees, build a home and farm. It's definitely grindy, and of course as early access there's a lot that either isn't implemented or doesn't work or is just a bit weird. I was surprised by how playable it was, though, and by how addicted I came to it: just gotta log on and tend to my flax plantation, check on those hides I have curing, make sure the livestock has food and isn't drowning in poop (this does tend to become an issue if you don't keep on top of it).
If you're like my brother you'll be bored, especially with the current state of the game - it is repetitive, not especially dramatic or exciting, and jumping off the mountain doesn't kill you. You have to learn a chain of skills before you can do a lot of things - such as mining before you can actually smelt ore - and some of it can take quite a while. It also requires a degree of teamwork if you want to progress at anything other than a snail's pace.
All in all I sincerely hope the development continues and the game does get a full, stable release - it's always a risk to buy something like this but I personally don't regret the purchase.

Raven has been asked a lot by Activision on ip's they did not create - Raven being a talented studio that has created excellent ip's in the past its the shame that id titles (Quake IV, Wolfenstein *(2009)*) began Greed-a-Vision's dominance on the company; With those two titles They had been given freedom in both Singleplayer and Multiplayer; since then they have been forced into a Formula with Modernwarfare 3's Multiplayer and forced more-so in Call of Duty: Chokes err Ghosts Multiplayer (Along with all of the motion capture and more than half of the singleplayer; with Raven (Aided by members of Neversoft) making something out of nothing with the Extinction game mode; the only positive that is in Call of Duty Ghosts; -
This stays as a landmark title that was enjoyed by just about all who played it. Wolfenstein 2009 had a semi-open world and Raven designed a super gorey fun to gib nazi's in realism style singleplayer; along with a Gun that made IGN's top 10 weapons of all time in a Video Game list; Although Wolf2009 had a very forgettable Multi-Player that saw the title with much less replayability compared to all titles prior; id's Return To Castle Wolfenstein had and still has one of the most popular multiplayer modes.. RIME is a story-driven puzzle-platforming-adventure game. You play as a boy who shipwrecked on a mysterious island and basically at the beginning of the game you don't know what to do and where to go cuz unlike in other similar games, RIME is not holding your hand at all. There's also big emphasis on exploration and enviromental sotytelling which is one of the finest i've seen in years. And since the game is not lolding you hand, you can play at your own pace, explore the world, solve puzzles, look for hidden collectibles, outfits, story related stuff (which is really well hidden) etc. but eventually you need to complete clever but very easy to understand puzzles to progress further. The level's you'll be exploring in RIME is big, but it's not an open world game, more like the levels in the game is more open for you to explore.
At the beginning of the game you'll see a huge tower which is extremely important but i won't spoil what it is exactly, what it does etc. and it's best not to know anything about it. The story itself is thold through enviromental storytelling and really well done in-game cut-scenes with no dialogues. At first it's hard to undestand what's happening and all that, but closer to the end of the game (and especially after you'll finish the game) you'll understand everything and there's a good enough reason to play the game again because of this, not to mention to find hidden collectibles and story related stuff which you didn't found during your first playthrough. I mean, after i've seen the ending i immediately started second playthrough cuz now i know more about the story and want to see some stuff i missed related to it and look at the story and events happening in the game in a different way, and believe me, not a lot of games make me do this after the end credits.
Even though the levels are big in RIME, you really can't get lost cuz usually there's plenty of light sources around the environment which you can light up and mark areas which you've already explored and light overall is really important in game. Every level in RIME is distinct with it's own uniqe visual theme, atmosphere and really fun to explore. And let me tell you, visually RIME is absolutely stunning and incredible game, but at the same time simple and minimalistic in terms of art and design but in a really good way. I really like the art and overall desing of this game and believe me, when you look at the sky at night (yep, there's day and night cycle in the game) full of blinking stars and the moon slowly passing by... ah, at this very moment you'll understand that you're playing really special and magical game. Furthermore, excellent soundtrack which fits extremely well into the game, relaxing and sometimes even meditative atmosphere is also a huge plus of this game. Sometimes you just want to stop playing and look at jaw-dropping vistas, listen RIME's amazing score and just relax for a little bit.
BUT, as a PC gamer i must say this - even though on my system (4790K, 16 GB RAM, GTX 1070) the game runs pretty well with almost constant 60 FPS most of the time with TXAA, the game simply not optimised well enough even for 1080p, not to mention 1440p which is unfortunately unplayable if i don't switch shadows to low. To get almost constant (but nowhere near perfect) 60 FPS i need to switch shadows quality to medium in 1080p. I really don't know why shadows (or whatever it actually is) is so taxing in this game, not to mention that system such as mine should destroy this game even in 4K, yet, i can barely get 30 FPS in such resoluting even with shadows at low. I can asume that maybe foliage or view distance is to blame for all this, but to be frank, The Witcher 3 is a much and much more complex game in terms of visuals, geometry and amount of foliage on screen, yet it performs A LOT better than RIME in 1440p on my system with 99% of max setting and even with HairWorks on.
.
So here it is, i though that anyone who desides to buy the game must know this, but
. Hopefully, Tequila Works and QLOC curently working to fix this, but even despite performance issue RIME is one of the best games of this year and i can easily recommend to anyone how likes games like this. It's as if ICO and Journey had a child and they've named him RIME which has a sister by the name of ABZU.

, cuz it is extremely important to uncover everything on your own to get the best out of this game. So please, for the love of god, stay away from all this and enjoy the game.

I love Rome: Total War. It was one of the first strategy games I played. I sunk hours into this game, playing it long in to the night. Just one more turn... just one more battle... It's highly addictive and great fun.
So why do I NOT recommend this game? Because the Steam version seems to have a serious problem with modern systems.
I originally had the Gold collectors disc (that includes the base game plus the Barbarian Invasion and Alexander expansions). It ran fine on an older Core 2 Duo laptop with integrated graphics on medium settings. However, I'm currently trying to run the Steam version on an HP Pavillion laptop that has an i5-6200U CPU and NVIDIA GeForce 940M graphics card. Deep, compelling, beautiful. RiME is a masterpiece of a game, from its vibrant and detailed visuals, to the mechanics. The moment the game begins, you instantly know what you are getting into. In this review, I’m going to spoil the first 10-20 minutes of the game, and parts of the Steam trailer, so if you REALLY want to go into this game blind, well, do that. I won’t be revealing game mechanics (other than movement), so those will be left for you to discover.
Also note: I am playing the game using the Steam Controller, and have not tried out the keyboard controlls. Controls on the controller are okay, I think I explain more later.

The game is very good at conveying information through gameplay, and not some help menu or dialog. There are no maps, no magic red arrows, no yellow brick roads to point you in the right direction. The game plays on your subconscious, and trusts you to know where you are supposed to go. In the first minute, when you are dropped into the world, there is no path, but you are subtly hinted at where you are supposed to go, via a small rock jutting out of the beach. It points towards the water, and here is where you learn how to swim. You are also compelled to go to the white structure over yonder, but soon realize you cannot reach it. You instead find a path that leads up the cliffs, and into the first real area. When you reach there, a small animal runs away from you. You chase it, leading, or hinting you, to a statue in the middle of the area. You then look around, to find several small beacons. Naturally, you go to see what it is. This is your first objective. In the first 3 or so minutes, the game as already directed you to a location and taught you mechanics without a single line of text.

Another example of this subconscious hinting to objectives is found a little later into the game, maybe 15-20 minutes later. You are in a large open plaza, with many exits. One exit is painted gold (or is gold) and is in the shape of a key. You are subconsciously hinted that there may be something here, as this golden shining color contracts the area’s palette of white, green and blue. This golden key shaped exit can also be found in the trailer.

The game’s visuals are amazing. Something along the lines of The Legend of Zelda, The Wind Waker HD, but with much more detail. It’s colors are vibrant, objectives are clear, the style is defined and consistent, and shadows are smooth. Even the load screens are beautiful. Nothing else can really be said.

The puzzles in this game at first are unique and fun, and require you to learn mechanics yourself, but at time, can be frustrating and confusing. You might have a solution for a puzzle in your mind, but when executing it, it may not work. This is just a small thing, as the puzzles are varied, and when you do solve a puzzle, or figure out a mechanic, it feels rewarding. No confetti, but you do feel like you accomplished something, and are working towards a goal.

Mystery is a big driving point in this game. A mysterious cloaked man can be seen stalking you, like in the trailer. You want to find out who he is. The island seems like it’s in ruins. What is the purpose of this island? Many small things in this game peak your curiosity, driving you to continue playing, and when you do uncover something, more things are revealed, making you want to find out more.

If you like puzzle exploration games like The Witness, this game is for you. It’s visuals are great, it’s gameplay is compelling, the mysteries keep you wanting more, and the puzzles, are simple, and fun to learn how to solve yourself, all like The Witness. Hopefully, this game plays as well as it did on the PC on the Nintendo Switch, PS4, and Xbox One.

OVERVIEW
===========
Gripping and stunning are two words that I HAVE to use to describe this awesome game, it is so very well done!
This is the most artistically pleasing game I have played in such a long, long time!
Full Game Playthrough can be found here :
I started playing this with my daughter (aged 5).  It was a bit too much for her, too difficult at times, and some really scary bits (for a 5 year old) so I am mostly playing this in my spare time.
PROs
======
From the pleasant opening titles to the elegant cut scenes and everything in between, this game offers up stunningly vibrant visuals and overall supplies a heart-warming experience which will wow you as much as challenge you.
The story of this young boy stranded on a strange and mystical island is created with beauty in-mind and it delivers in abundance.
The main character is likable, even lovable and strong; yet he retains his childlike innocence with almost whimsical body language.
The game comprises a night and day cycle and character animations adjust accordingly.
There is no reading required nor verbal dialogue to understand and whilst there are a few scary moments.
RiME is I believe suitable for the entire family (officially recommended 7+) and even includes helpful guides within the game in the form of a fox and a... well I'll let you discover that for yourself, who will help ensure that you continue along the right path.
The challenges are fairly simplistic in essence, primarily comprising of one of three logical or mechanical solutions to resolve, it might sound easy but it will require some exploration to complete.
Further exploration is also rewarded with stunning cut scenes and hidden surprises along the way.
RiME is beautiful graphically, the audio and the music is perfectly balanced and the adventure entices you to keep going with intriguing snippets of what’s to come next and finally the twisting and unexpected storyline ensures that you are engaged throughout.
You're not going to be bored or disappointed with this title for a while, it is truly captivating.
CONS
======
If you’re an older teen or younger adult then the initial excitement might begin to dwindle an hour or two into this game as the calming audio and ambience mixed with the relatively easy puzzles required to aid progression and exploration are likely to become a little dull and laborious.
However, for younger players, and those of us who are young at heart, the fantastic journey should continue on in a state of perpetual joy and happiness (honestly).

First things first, I can admit that this game brought out the wuss in me. Like, more than ever before. And I loved it. Some of that may vary depending on your own tendencies toward an overactive imagination vs firmly-rooted realism, but the game sure does its best to push you toward the former.
I'm sure this game has reached mythic popularity at this point, but I'll throw in my two cents anyway. The world is nothing if not atmospheric, typically in a horrifying fashion. This is largely achieved through Oscar-worthy sound design. The soundtrack alone is enough to evoke the feelings of safety, desperation, and terror presented at the various stages of the game, and that is only augmented by the little creaks, grinds, and growls that seem to emanate from the castle's own walls. The atmosphere here is truly one of the best I've ever seen, so special attention should be paid to it.
The story follows a somewhat generic "descent into madness" path, though there's plenty of neat character writing and evocation of external locales to keep things interesting. And in typical Lovecraftian horror fashion, you can expect mysterious otherworldly forces and beings with increasingly oppressive influence over your experience in Brennenburg. This all falls perfectly into my favorite style of horror, one that emphasizes the ebb and flow of tension with only a rare few cathartic payoffs.
And of course, gameplay. Much of the fame the game has gained I think comes from the feeling of defenselessness people feel thanks to the lack of weapons and sanity mechanic. However, I don't think 'defenseless' is quite accurate; you have plenty of resources for defense, they just rely on your use of movable objects, hiding places, and other mechanisms that simply require spatial awareness. I think this works very well, as it evokes the feeling of living a waking nightmare. The effect is further amplified by the way the monsters, both corporeal and not, announce their presence and seek you out. The result is a classic pursuit predation situation on several scales, and you are the prey on every one.
Alright, that's enough of this. Why don't you own this yet?

So far, the only bad thing about this game is the hands reaching for your money inside. I've played my way through most of the Innistrad block of the campaign using the Life & Death deck, and I will say this: it's different.
DotP15 is more difficult than its predecessors, but it also allows for more freedom. The cards you unlock do not seem to be predetermined and automatically added to your stable of cards. Instead, each win nets you three cards from the zone you are playing in (Innistrad, Theros, Ravnica, Zendikar) which, if they fit with your deck's colors, you can add to your deck.
The tutorial caters to uber noobs and forces you to make potentially bad decisions in deckbuilding. For instance, trading out a 7 mana Resolute Archangel for the 2 mana Raise the Alarm is a superbly horrible decision. The Life & Death deck has so much other fat to trim it isn't even funny.
But in this game, you are a noob again and it will take time to build up your collection.... unless you want to drop some more cash. Perhaps the reason people don't like this game is that it recreates the experience of being a new magic player a little TOO well?
PRO TIPS!!! -- based on a lot of the negative reviews I have seen so far. You CAN change the mana that is tapped when casting a spell with colorless mana. Hover over the spell and wait a second and the mana that will be tapped by default will be highlighted. Tap the left stick to cycle the possible mana combinations.
Also, those people who complained of the menus going slow, use a controller. DotP was made to be played with a controller, and tapping A will cycle past most of the menu transitions.

Ok, so this game has the odd issue with crashing, for the scenarios delete the pre-loaded saves then they work fine, then the other odd random crash issue is solved by saving often.
Another issue is that there's no vehicle to transport sugar processed from your sugar factories, so as a result you cannot make cakes at your bakery. when Olive's have grown from your orchards you have to send the olives straight to either the city to sell, or an olive press to turn it into oil or pitted olives sadly the barn or a silo won't accept them for some reason. I would personally also like it if the chilled storage allowed you to store milk.
There are not many farming simulators from a business point of view out on the market, so if the above issues were addressed this game would be perfect. It does take a little extra patience to put up with the crashing but sometimes you can tell its going to happen (sometimes you will notice the game "Lag" a little when running x3 speed, that's your cue to save the game as it will crash in a few seconds).
There is plenty of different crops to grow, animals to breed, and you earn achievements which you can spend on the skill tree to boost many different things, driver speed, growth rate of certain crops, breeding rates, have your buildings use up less water/electric. you can build your own wind turbines and solar panels and eventually build a bio-gas plant to turn manure and corn into electric!
There are two game modes, scenarios with pre determined objectives and campaign, campaign is a free play mode where you have to "level up" to unlock crops/animals and buildings, however the achievements earned, and your level are saved so if you start a new campaign map you don't have to climb the ranks again! so its great if you fancy a fresh start but don't wish to lose your level.
I apologise for the rambling, I just wanted to write my own little review on this game as while yes it has bugs, but hey a lot of games do -cough EA cough- it's defiantly worth the price and worth it even better in a sale.

A must play for SW fans. If you did like KOTOR1, then you'll enjoy KOTOR2. I played it as a light sided character and greatly enjoyed it. There are tons of items, multiple planets to visit and plenty of story and RPG elements. The D&D3 system is great allowing to customize your characters to great depths. Do you want a dual lightsaber fighter or a powerful jedi master that uses the force or a gun loving sharp shooter? The choice is yours. I took approximately 120 hours to complete the game, with all missions, all characters, etc. The only shortfalls of this game is that is lacks a bit of polish. The videos are extremely small (320 x 240). Also I got into an infinite loop while on Telos. I ended up having to reload an old savegame and looking online to find a solution. Also, some quests can get bugged and prevent you from completing them but there aren't many of those. So this game feels a bit like a Porshe with a few dents here and there. So the engine works great and is fun to drive but little things that are broken in the car and the dents make it "sub-optimal". This game could have been better. So even with small problems, this is overall a great game.

While I recomend this game, I will say it's a vast difference from the last 2 incarnations. This one is more aimed at the die hard deck builders and casual stratagists than the casual players 2013 and 2014 aimed at. That said, it still feels like some things are missing. With the loss of 2HG there is no longer any reason to sit down and play with a friend, this was a huge tactical error in my oppinion, as that mode was the main reason I recomended last years verion to friends. The other big missing piece for me, is all the cards you see used that are not available in the game. I know it's not cost effective and there will never be an MTG game that contains huge set lists, but if you're going to show me something in a game or have me using it in a tutorial mission, allow me to unlock it. Howerver, like all games it has it's pros and cons.
Pro's:
Battle UI - it just feels better and has a much crisper look and feel than the last two year's version.
Deck builder - Finally, you can make your own deck the way you want it within the restrictions of the card list
Booster unlocks - there's just something about getting to open a booster pack of random cards after a duel that makes you want to keep going...much better, imo than single card unlocks
Longer campaign play - having to unlock lists of cards and trying to get 4 of each ensures you stay in the campaign mode beating down random opponents for much longer than you ever did in 2013 or 2014.
Cons:
Storyline is still lackluster - you will find yourself skipping most dialog just to get on with it.
Weak starting decks - if you showed up with any of these starting decks to a friday night magic, you'd be laughed out of the building. It takes a couple hours of gameplay to get a decent deck going, and your still going to have to get use to restarting a good amount of the duels.
Lacks beef - there are good cards, staples and new, but there just aren't enough concept cards to really go full on with a stratagy, you will end up with filler cards to cover things that you just don't have available. This also brings about the existance of pointless cards.
So, with that said. I recomend this game to the solo players, deck building enthusiests, and those that frequented the multiplayer. If you are an avid 2HG with friends, stick to 2014. And if anyone from the design team happens to check this(doubtful), get on some dlc or a patch to give me that pacifism that appeared in my tutorial deck but isn't available in the game.

The core gameplay is beautifully crafted. The combination of stunning graphics and precise detail to how your sword creates gore or even affects walls and objects makes this game very satisfying to pick up. The nifty moveset accompanied by the protagonists cocky one-liners makes it so that you can't help but feel like a bit of a badness. With a nice selection of weapons and the ability to keep every gun and pick up you get, Shadow Warrior 2 gives you the freedom to be the ninja assassin you always wanted to be.
The genius of the game begins and ends with the gameplay however. The story isn't very long or deep and the characters aren't much either. The protagonist is an obnoxious narcissist named Lo Wang who can't stop making bad jokes (although a couple of them do land). To be honest, I think the developers intentionally did this as some kind of jokes itself. The fact that he is not funny...is funny.
Still it's nice to see a game that prioritizes gameplay over story and not the other way around. If you want to feel like an unstoppable Ninja with a slightly sadistic nature for 20 hours or so, buy this game.

"Retro-inspired pixel platformer" is not really a phrase I get excited about these days. Particularly with Humble Bundles and the like, I've been drowning in platformers, and pixel graphics are so commonly used "just because" with few games actually making something creative and unique.
So, I was quite surprised when I gave Kero Blaster a try and immediately felt the need to play through the whole thing. Aesthetically, it has a sort of mixed NES/SNES feel to it, and definitely seemed to be aimed at the early 90's nostalgia crowd. Usually I find this a little obnoxious, but Kero Blaster is much more evocative than most games of that sort, nearly reaching Shovel Knight levels of quality (though in a much smaller scope).
The gameplay itself is solid and appropriately challenging, but reasonably standard Megaman-ish action platforming. The upgradeable weapons help keep it from stagnating too much, starting with a little pea shooter and growing to rapid-fire lasers and flame throwers. I honestly could have done without the old school continue system, where losing all your lives means going all the way back to the beginning of a level, but it wasn't overly frustrating, just a bit annoying on a couple of occasions. The game is also quite short (though does have two higher difficulty replay modes), so I'm not sure how I would feel about it at full price (I got it as part of a Humble Bundle).
But beyond gameplay, it's Kero Blaster's sense of style that really makes it interesting. Adorable characters and enemies, simple yet charming environments, and an awesome soundtrack made it a short, fun, and memorable way to spend an evening. Definitely recommended to anyone who played things like Megaman growing up.

With the Quakecon sale kicking off on Friday, I was a bit surprised to see that there was a Quake 4!  Sure, I got away from PC gaming for awhile and it had been a REALLY long time since I was heavy into Doom and Quake, but I felt a little funny that I didn't know this existed!  With a cheap price I figured it was a must play for nostalgia's sake at the very least. I didn't expect a whole lot out of it, which is good because it turns it's okay.  Not great, but okay.
I run a couple of movie podcasts, so I watch a lot of flicks.  The state of the modern shooter in comparison to classic style shooters compares pretty well to the world of movies.  Most of the time, you like to watch a movie that's well put together, highly polished, engaging and engrossing.  This translates to your modern shooters in the game world.  Games such as Bioshock Infinite or even Deadspace are a different beast than the shooters we all cut our teeth on.  They're deep, they have branching stories, they're well put together. It's a production...an experience.
Jumping back to your movie world. you have another class of movie which boils down to your dumb action or horror movies, stuff put out by the likes of Syfy Channel or Asylum.  These movies are cheesy with no depth whatsoever.  They're there simply to treat you to explosions and special effects, nothing more than the spectacle.  Quake 4 fits in perfectly with this type of movie; there' s no depth to it whatsoever, it's there simply for you to run around and shoot aliens.  And that's it.
Much like watching the movies though, sometimes we simply don't feel like wrapping our head around something deep. We want to munch popcorn and watch stuff explode.  Video games are the same way, and Quake 4 is a pretty perfect fit for those moods.  It's a solid through back to the good old days where you're only concern was checkpoints and finding your way to the rail gun.  The story is a nice aside but really doesn't do anything to suck you into the game.  You're sticking around for the fun of shooting Stroggs and seeing what the weapons do.
There's some sections in Quake 4 that are annoying.  The vehicle sections are slow and clunky which makes them frustrating when you're trying to dodge.  Some of them feel like you're on a rail shooter without a whole lot to shoot at.  The game is way too long for what you're there for too.
In the end though, things blow up pretty well and it play smoothly while showing it's age.  It's worth $5 and a Sunday afternoon.

Continue?9876543210 is literally the most depressing game I've ever played. I don't mean it's just sad, or disheartening, or bad, or deep. It's one of the only pieces of media I've ever experienced that, without fail, makes me feel worse every time I play it. I can read tragic stuff, I can watch sad movies, whatever- occasionally I might even feel teary-eyed- but only Continue? actually makes me feel actually mentally distressed.
In Continue?, you play as the data ghost of one of several failed video game characters, destined for deletion by some sort of cyberspace garbage compactor. In order to survive, you must flee through these strange recycled realms, where everybody talks in an eerie, vaguely poetic dialect of english, mixing terms of faith and hope with computer and video game terminology. Your currency is "Foo" (or possibly "fod", given the somewhat ambiguous font); your extra lives are "Spare Parts". And, most importantly, you are frequently given the choice between two options- "Lightning" and "Prayer". Every time you choose to take Prayer, you create an extra layer of defence at your next gateway town, meaning Prayer is vital to your success in the game. Every time you choose to take Lightning, you randomly destroy some of the barriers blocking your progress to the next level, making Lightning vital to your success in the game.
The game actually has a really great atmosphere- of inevitable doom and the futility of struggling further. I presume this is the intended effect, because it's actually pretty haunting. Some of the "lore", barely comprehensible as it is, actually sticks with you after playing it, the poems and the "prayers" of the NPCs you speak to genuinely some impressive alternative writing. The sound and level design also puts forward this idea, especially in the zones between certain levels.
The other thing that contributes to the feeling of dread and nihilistic despair, however, is the gameplay. In order to survive, you must collect Lightning and Prayer, and the game is utterly unforgiving. If you die without a Spare Part to revive yourself, then the game gives you a "second chance" by consuming some of the shelters you earned with Prayer. This is, essentially, just a way of making you suffer more. Losing even a few shelters will result in a game over once the storm comes. The rest of the game is a mixture of slightly janky minigames (which punish you harshly for losing, making taking part in the encounters a tense gamble) and a race against the clock to find NPCs to talk to to gain resources from. Several of the NPC interactions are basically just random chance- there are temples, for instance, which reward you for providing the right answer to an abstract and unknowable riddle. If one of the NPCs you met in this run told you the answer, then, so long as you remember it, you can pass the test and gain a large amount of Lightning or Prayer. If, however, you weren't fortunate enough to run into that NPC yet, then you have to either guess or leave, having wasted some of your very limited amount of time in the overworld before it begins randomly collapsing again.
If you're feeling charitable, you could argue that the clunky gameplay is part of the metaphor- the challenges we face are random because our lives are not designed for us to succeed in. The controls are imprecise because really, how much control do we have over our lives? Or something like that. Alternatively, your character just handles really badly because the game's a bit shoddily programmed.
As an artistic endeavour, Continue? is actually pretty impressive. It's also the most insidiously soul-destroying experience available to you on Steam, which is why I can't really recommend it. Continue? never gives you any answer or comfort about the existential dread it wields- your character is doomed, just as you are doomed, to be erased and become nothing. Some people describe something similar about Dark Souls- sorry for bringing it up- but at least in Dark Souls it's possible to at least kind of achieve something. Continue? presents a world where the player is utterly alone and totally abandoned, faced with an unfair challenge to extend their miserable existence by approximately a couple of hours if they succeed.

Existential Crisis: The Game
No really, this game, while legitimately good in how it delivers its message, is one of the most depressing games you'll ever play. It's a game about a game where your character dies, and its programming object is freed from active memory, and that videogame character is desperately trying to buy a few more microseconds of time to make peace with the inevitability of being premanently erased by the system's garbage collector. Yes, this is a game that pointedly informs you that, some day, you will die.
I considered it edifying as an experience to have through games, but consider this both a strong reccomendation and a legitimate warning. It's hauntingly beautiful in its effort to gameify the final journey we all must take some day.

I feel bad that my friend bought me this game.
From a storytelling point of view, this is an okay game with a deep message about sentient data (?).
It's a strange idea though, having a self-operating program that actively avoids garbage collection and takes up CPU time sounds like a virus to me.
Personally, I couldn't immerse myself because all the people at the start talked to me like they already knew me and then names were thrown around, and there's some sort of existing sentient data (?) culture going on, and if I were to sit and trawl through the game lore or sit through the cutscenes, it would feel more like a spectacle than something I can invest myself in.
I like the story though, I guess?
Garbage collection being a force of nature that wipes these thinking, feeling creatures is a morbid thought, and that they worship and understand this frailty is also a deep.
But if kind of killed it for me when I thought the lightning specifically targeted the shelter I was in and mercilessly destroyed me.
Wasn't that area supposed to provide me with cover from the random nature of garbage collection, other shelters being taken down as I run for my existence, sacrificing them?
From a game point of view, this game is
.
Unskippable cutscenes (I don't want to watch Simon lie in a field and repeat the same three lines while the camera does a pan around him, I've seen this five times already)
Xtreme Strobe Lighting™ incorporated into almost every aspect of the game makes it hard to look at (there isn't much to look at anyway but that's ok, fine graphics aren't all that important)
Text that is hard to parse, (yes "parse" - reading it isn't enough)
The game pauses whenever you alt-tab even if it's windowed, which means you can't go do other things while you wait for the stupid cutscenes to be over. (yes the cutscenes build up the story but I've seen this one three times already and I'm sick of it)
The red and black text is hard to read because it's in what, 272pt at the four corners of the screen? The Pause menu text is perfect, I wish the rest of the text was readable like that (good use of padding, font-size, line-height that the red text could REALLY benefit from)
No way of telling how many hits each garbage collector monster thing takes to hit, I've had some that die in 1 and some that die in 3
The combat and puzzles are lazy but that's ok? This game leans heavily on story anyway.
The walking collision is pretty bad but only because you can get stuck on stuff really easily.
The only thing I can rag on the sound side is that the sound for taking damage is also the sound for initiating a fight and other things, so it confuses me sometimes.
Oh and if you excuse these bad game design choices as lore or worldbuilding, then screw you, you damn apologist.
