This game is the most mixed-up 'mixed bag' i've ever played.
The good stuff- the idea is amazing, and the game captures the sense of hopelessness that wandering lost around the recesses of RAM might entail. I really like the dialogue too, which has a kind of meaningful meaningless quality, like haikus written by a gifted chimp. The music is quite good, and the basic organisation of the game (wandering around talking to people, finding clues, collecting game resources and then battling to save yourself) is well organised and a good idea for how to conduct this kind of game. So based on originality and thoughtfulness, it would be a 10/10.
However, the execution of the above gameplay is a solid 0/10, and since the gameplay is most of the game, it hurts the overall experience really badly. Generally, the game well captures the futility of trying to escape deletion because it is nigh impossible not to fail over and over and over again, based on flaws in the game mechanics rather than your skill. The combat is incredibly bad, making safe zones suddenly kill you, murdered enemies spring back to instantly and unavoidably shave off half your health (every enemy can do this), and enemies spawn teleported right on top of you to instantly initiate punishing combat with no chance to evade.
The punishment for failure also increase geometrically- every time you make a mistake, the punishment gets worse by 1. For reference, you need to build shelters towards surviving a storm every few levels, and each shelter takes a couple of conversations or minigames to build, with bigger (more effective) shelters taking more. Then when you fail, you lose a shelter. Fail twice, lose 2. Fail 5 times (throughout the whole playthrough), and you lose 5, then 6, then 7 shelters each time. Given how arbitrarily you fail, and that the game actively selects your biggest and most valuable shelters for deletion (i've played it enough to be sure this isn't random chance), the possiblity of getting past level 3 or 4 is extremely low for any given playthrough. Add in poor collision detection with environments (falling off parts of maps to your death), continue screens which also delete between 1 and 7 shelters every time, and randomised puzzles and level order, and you have a recipe for extremly consistent frustration. So I give the gameplay 0/10, with the developer either being really lazy on this element (doing no playtesting to realise what a piece of junk his game is to actually 'play') or really hostile to people who pay for his work (taking the 'avoiding deletion is really hard' story element as an excuse to ruin the gameplay element of the game).
I still really enjoyed Continue?, finding it artsy and thoughtful without being too pretentious. But being almost impossible to finish due to game design unfortunately takes it down quite a few notches.

Before I start an important disclaimer:
If you are prone to epileptic seizures or in any way sensitive to strobe lights, DO NOT ABSOLUTELY DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. This game spams strobe lights like it's Christmas, from beginning of the game to finish. If you play this game and you're an epileptic, you will be as dead as this game's protagonist, before even the intro ends.
But yeah, this game. It's pretty flawed.
As I said before, this game spams strobe lights. It also has it's hard to pronounce name, as well as this 3d pixel style that to be perfectly honest, looks kinda ugly.
The gameplay is the weakest part of Continue, because you are so reliant on rng to not screw you over it's ridiculous. See, in each stage, with gc stages being the only exceptions, your goal is to escape the stage with lightning, while building shelters for gc stages with your prayers. However, lightning strikes at random, so it's entirely possible to have your run ruined all because lightning struck the same already cleared location three times. This is tolerable on large in length levels, but if you get bad lightning strikes on somewhere like the Riverbanks, your run is pretty much over, because you cannot escape in time.
The plot? This game does seem to have a story, but it's a jumbled unconnected mess. Each stage has its own story, its own history, but its all disconnected from the protagonist, which are shuffled everytime you restart the game anyway. The only thing we know for sure is what's on the cover.
And yet, despite all that, despite all these problems, I still love this game. A lot.
The music and the atmosphere are some of the places where this game shines. I don't remember the last time I felt so peaceful when playing a video game. I would download the whole OST if I could. The filters and the sound effects, give the game a weird broken console dream simulator quality that I can't really explain. That, combined with some really touching scenes and you have yourself a game that made me cry at several times.
There's also the message itself. As someone who had troubles accepting the idea of dying herself, I was completely repelled by this game when I first saw it. It seemed to me like just as a game so dark and so obsessed with its own darkness, that it would be completely unenjoyable. It wasn't. It was a journey, complete with thoughts and feelings people may have when they confront their own mortality. And it ended up being one of the most serene games I have ever played in my entire life. I haven't expected to be so pleasantly surprised at all.
So final verdict? I dunno. I can see why people can be turned off by the message and the gameplay and other things. The dev himself said that he made this game this way SPECIFICALLY to repel CoD brogamer dudes. From the name itself, to pretty generic gameplay, I get it. Still, I'd say give it a chance.
If you love these cerebral, borderline-walking simulator type games that are very emotional and sad, maybe this game will give you something. If you are like me and are struggling with accepting your own demise, maybe this game will help you not worry about your own mortality as much and even accept it like it did for me. If you are looking for some neat gameplay or a story heavy game, pass. This game will not satisfy you. And if you're prone to epileptic seizures, dear god stay away.

Gunners can be further broken down to accuracy gunners, reload gunners, aa gunners, and torpedo gunners. Your Bridge officer changes the length of your gun lines, which you can customize by adding or removing rookie sailers. You can also increase your sailors abilities by upgrading them with boosts, training them to increase their skilled and veteran sailers from rookies. Rookie sailers and the red line at the bottom, they upgrade by playing the game and doing damage to skilled which is the white section of the same bar. I was so excited to pick up the sequel to Shadow Warrior. The game had amazing fast paced classic gunplay where every weapon and shot mattered and a surprisingly intriguing story that kept up till the very end. It was lengthy with varied scenery ranging from forests, to towns, to bunkers, and snowy mountains with carefully crafted arenas and secrets scattered through. The light RPG mechanics provided a nice sense of progression that everyone seems to require in games today. The jokes while plentiful were timely and opportune enforcing Lo Wang’s character and contrasting it well with his growth with his relationship with Hoji. Hand crafted cutscenes were littered through the game beautifully retelling the tale of past and current events. The challenge was fair and the enemy variety and placement in arenas were engaging. Shadow Warrior 2 has none of these things and in fact does everything in its power to make sure it does everything worse than its predecessor.
For a frame of reference I played and beat the game on Insane difficulty and base my review and opinions on this factor. I also beat Shadow Warrior on hard and played through most of insane and beat Doom on the hardest non-permadeath difficulty.
Pros
Cons
I could go on forever with everything that I didn't enjoy about this game. I haven't felt this disappointed with a sequel since Dragon Age 2 or Darksiders 2. Shadow Warrior 2 does in fact have enjoyable gameplay when it works. The problem is the monotony of repeat maps, low enemy variety in terms of tactics, showering unnecessary stat stick loot, lack of ammo (barring reliance on ammo shrine RNG), excessive juvenile humor (100x more so than the original), and an embarrassingly bad follow-up story make Shadow Warrior 2 one of the most disappointing, mediocre sequels. This should never ever have been an RPG shooter and whoever made this decision should be incredibly ashamed of what they did to this entry of the series.

After 400 hours of playtime, I think i can inform others about the game. First of it all: It's still an alpha, but the most developed one I've ever played. Combine Minecraft with War of the Roses, and you got your game. The game is, although some mechanics are highly repetetive, very addicting. It's not a game for a few hours a month and without the necessary endurance you will give up soon. If you like crafting, fighting and role-playing with other human beings, then get it and check it out. Otherwise: Don't.
On the positive side you got very good graphics, a great variety of armor and weapons you can choose from and a crafting system that highly supports team gaming. You got a lot of different building, the map is large enough for 64 players and every 2-3 weeks comes an update. The sound is ok, as long as you don't put tanning tubs aside your house..
The skill system is fair and interesting, because on most servers you can only skill 1-2 skilltrees to the max, and it is possible to deskill every time. It is like in Skyrim: With doing certain things, you get better at doing so and with rising skill level there are some other options you unlock. The fighting system is a bit sloppy, but also very detailed. For example: The damage you get from an opponent is the result of the weapon you use, the skill of your weapon, the armorskill of your enemy, the location of the hitbox where you hit and if your enemy is defending with a shield or not. Conclusion: Good mechanics, very high potential overall.
On the bad side you have no game-goals, quests or whatever. Your experience with the game will highly depend on the server you play on, considering if your serveradmins are fair or not and how other players fashion their role on the server. The first time, of course, you will be motivated by building your town with others and learn how to work, but after your village or castle is built, you have no other option then to fight and roleplay.
Considering this, there are also some broken mechanics that must be fixed soon: Since every digged tunnel on the server delays the login time of the players, it is impossible to run a 64 player server over a long time without getting a slow server. Some players on my server have login times beyond 6 or 7 minutes, and when you come to that point it will be extremly hard to get new players to join your server. Others may quit due to this and.. you get the idea, over a longer time your server will get more and more abandoned. There are some fixes to this, but nothing official is implemented yet, a server wipe is in most cases the only solution to get a fresh and playable server.
Another problem is the erasing of buildings: Once built, you cannot deconstruct anything without admin help. This is also highly annoying, because you have to plan really good before building your own town.
So, my conclusion: Don't start this game alone, pick one or two of your friends, start an own server to test things until you feel ready to play on a bigger server. Try to get to a server with active and friendly admins. You may wait until the tunnel-digging is fixed, but if you like crafting & boxing bears, then give it a try.

I never played this back when it came out, but I remember people having mixed feelings. What everyone wanted of course was a sequel to Quake 3, the game that people put highest on their multiplayer pedistals. Instead they got a game not far descended from Doom 3, a singleplayer experience with a multiplayer mode more like the deathmatch from the Doom series. It is, in fact, a direct sequel to Quake 2, dealing witn the human invasion of Stroggos. The game does use the D3 engine and I think it suffers from it, in that they (Raven) wanted to create a game about a grand war and planetary invasion, but the D3 engine is pretty limited to basically a corridor-set of environments. You do often go into "outdoor" spaces but it's pretty obvious you're in a room with a sky texture instead of a ceiling. They serve to break up the long stretches of indoor space, but it feels slapped together instead of inspiring. The weapon variety is nice and I felt like every weapon has its place, and the enemy variety was challenging and kept spice to the game. The boss challenges I felt were fairly boring, mostly uninspired bullet-sponge affairs where I ended up expending most all my ammo while circle strafing, that kind of thing. Overall the game has a short length but the story is semi-interesting enough to make it worth it, including the point at which you yourself change... biologies. Recommend at a sale price for a younger old-style shooter.

Background: I'm a big Quake fan, lot sof time spent in Q1 and Q2 plus their mission packs.  I first got this game in 2006 when I bought a new PC.  I actually got 2 copies. Years later I got a copy on Steam and as part of a challenge to play my backlog, I finally finished the game this year.
This game has a bit of a slow start, and years ago the game just ran slow.  On newer computers the latter isn't as annoying allowing you to move into the more interesting parts sooner.  This game was built from the Doom3 engine but it feels like the runt of the litter in some ways.
The game doesn't really shine till the 2nd half.  I started off having to force myself to push on, but later I wanted to push on.  I wanted to see where the story was going to go, I wanted to see what the next big guns would be .. what the next massive baddies would be, and even where the story would go!  Lets be honest, this is a Quake game, people don't get into it for the story :P
Later on your various weapons get some useful upgrades as well as upgrades to you making you move faster etc.  As I look back at the screenshots I took in January I see so many colourful scenes, I see a lot of gore and a lot of cool scenery waiting to be admired.
This is a game which went from thinking .. I'll finish it one day to thinking that I am definitely going to replay it, and soon!

Reasons why you should buy this game
If the idea of building and fighting to survive in a cruel unforgiving world populated by people who want murder you and steal your flux to finish their warehouse appeals to you then this is probably the game for you. Your story will most likely go as follows. You start as a confused peasant and spend the first day playing the mud. Slowly you learn about the world and eventually you craft primative stone age tools to aid your struggle. After much patience you learn how to build a shelter to shield you from the cold and even learn the secrets to smelting and while using your neighbor's forge while they aren't looking, the art of crafting. Finally after what seems like an eternity you finally have iron tools after which a naked man appears with a stick and promptly beats the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you, taking that shiny new iron hammer and shovel just in spite of you. Doubling back you will forge new tools - weapons. With your humble pitchfork in hand you go to the forest in search of bandits. Unfortunately, you find them. They laugh at you and watch as their buddy beats your♥♥♥♥♥once more with a stick as you haven't the slightest clue how to fight. The next day in exploration you come across a great stone castle populated by several intimidating warriors. You ask to be let in as a laborer and they accept. After days of working on their stone keep they offer to teach you to fight. With stick in hand they kick your♥♥♥♥♥over and over again until the secrets of combat begin to unfold. Eventually you are able to hold your own though you are clearly still an inexperienced fighter. The next day you and your companions go together into the woods in search of adventure. After hours of exploration you come across a populated camp in a clearing. You recognize their faces of the occupants and rush out of the clearing ready to fight. You knew exactly which weapon you would use - the one that had caused you so much pain in the past. Your friends quickly follow eager not to miss out on the fight and the bandits scatter in all directions once they become aware of the unfavorable odds. You give chase and corner one deep in the woods. He quickly pulls out a familiar pitchfork in to defend himself with. Stick in hand you fight him. Although you were once terrified of him you now realize that his experience at hunting mud farmers hasn't taught him to fight. For every hit he makes on you, your weapon lands five on him. He panics and attempts to flee but your last hit staggered him. The following hit ends him. You stand victorious. The circle is complete and now you are the one beating people's asses with a stick.
Reasons why you shouldn't buy this game
I would not buy this game expecting it to fund the plan of the MMO as while it is an epic idea, I do not think that it is a realistic goal for this dev team at the present. From an outside look anyone can see that development is moving sluggishly for a game that is in early access. I get the feeling that a few of their programmers are a little green as I have seen them do stuff like use reserve words as variable names and set the default render range to a rediculous amount causing the entire map to be rendered reducing frame rates of even good computers below 30 (Thankfully has been fixed with a simple edit of a text file). Also for the longest time you could crash the server on command by inviting someone to your group who wasn't in the game. If this team with their present proficiency tried release this as an early access MMO the servers would be empty in weeks from technical deficiencies alone as this team has not demonstrated an ability to swiftly address critical issues like a certain well known crash-the-server-on-command bug(See below).
As time goes on I hope the team improves from experience (doesn't always happen) and expands to include more experienced members. Then and only then will the idea of a MMO be a realistic one

The ONLY thing new about this is creating your own deck. The single player is not true AI, it's deck manipulation that detects player disadvantage and changes the rest of the game to amplify that fact:
-If you start the game with a deck it doesn't like (especially a custom) you'll rarely get a usable starting hand
-If you are short one mana source early, it will make sure you don't get it until it's too late
-Whatever spell you need to turn a game around will be mysteriously absent from your draws
In the actual card game I've NEVER gotten this many bad hands in a row. A few of the archtypes that I have looked at to play have a smattering of cards, not actually enough to make them effective (mostly missing finishers). In the collection, you can get up to 4 commons, 3 uncommons, or 2 rares which makes decks that are rare heavy seem exessively random.
If you're an experienced player this game will sour your experience, and if you're a novice it'll bat you around until you're fed up and want your money back.
As always: the multiplayer experience changes with deck match-ups.

Continue?9876543210 is an interesting game with some potential for frustration. It's somewhat mysterious and pretty good at creating tension while aiming to bring about its philosophical conclusion. We see deliberately low-poly 3D graphics which nevertheless are easily translated into "the world".
The game expects the player to go for several, slightly changing run-throughs, not all of which let the player get to the end. The player is mostly playing on limited time but can sort of recover in mostly unskippable cut-scenes. Will you find the strength to go on or will you find the strength to rest?
+ Nice low-poly design
+ Good music and good atmosphere
+ Special exits
+ Live stories
+ Restarting areas
0 "On the clock"
0 A tad short
- Bad restart method - "Have you tried turning it off and on again?"
- Camera is sort far-sighted
- Fade-ins waste time and make it harder to react
- Controls somewhat lacking
- Incomplete menu with and ambiguous option
The game features a number of modes. There is investigation mode where you run around an area or level, talk to people and gather knowledge which is needed to find an exit from the area and build up shelters, all within a time limit (except for the first level which has slightly different rules). That mode already shows how the camera is sort of far-sighted when giving a perspective view. Enemies will randomly and with increasing ferocity and frequency spawn around you. While the perspective view shows enemies or people in the background pretty well, it's hard to see things in the foreground. This is coupled with the foreground also often going down. So it is possible that you run the avatar towards the foreground/player, run over an edge, be in the air and without control over the avatar while unknowingly steering into an enemy. You have a sword to fight of enemies but to use it effectively you still need to know where enemies are.
Running into an enemy brings you into an action mode of always the same type where you have to fight of a number of enemies approaching you from the air while you play in a 2D brawler fashion, think minimalistic smash brothers. Those fights are easy but time-consuming at first but grow challenging and fast over the levels/investigation areas.
Hint: When jumping and attacking in the air go into the direction the avatar is not looking to make an overhead swing.
Each investigation areas also features up to three other action modes where you are thrown in one of a number of, let's say, mini-games. There are some where you have to find an exit, there are some where you have kill objectives and there is even one where you simply go right.
Action modes mostly offer treasure and performance-based rewards, but failing them results in harsh consequences.
The third mode is a shelter mode where you need to hide from impending doom. It's paramount to have gathered enough shelters or this is where the avatar gets GC'ed.
While cut-scenes offer time for recovery and breaks - they prompt the player before continuing - they are mostly unskippable and it may take you upwards from 30 seconds to get into an investigative area. This is unnerving in connection with the restart feature. You can restart the current investigative area if you feel like you didn't get enough out of it - the game autosaves at the beginning of an investigative area. While the game tells you restarting is an option it doesn't tell you how to realise that option. Instead of clicking the button "Start Over" in the menu and confirming the reset you have to kill the application and restart it, then you are loaded back into the area.
The reset instead means starting the whole run over and losing all progress, not just that of the last area. Imagine my happiness when I found out.
Apart from the "far-sighted camera" problem there is another one with visuals. While investigating you are required to enter houses. When you subsequently leave them the main area fades in, i.e. the world is turned back on before you can see clearly. While you can remember positions of enemies or people and interact with them blindly you are more likely to run into a problematic situation all while running out of time.
Action modes have a number of control problems. First off, navigation is sometimes hard because you don't always know which things you can pass over and which things present an obstacle.
Then, I often felt like I couldn't turn fast enough with incoming enemies. When trying to stab enemies you sometimes only hit when your sword is at or near full extension. So despite facing the enemy and presenting good points they will hit you anyway, reduce your performance and hinder progress in the meta-game.
Specifically the last and fix action mode where you need to turn and jump had me failing jumps multiple times because "up" is somehow not available  when being pressed while changing directions. And yes, I specifically bought a keyboard where ghosting doesn't happen when only two keys are pressed.
I found the gathering of knowledge surprisingly fun, the random life stories are effective towards the game's philosophical goal and I enjoyed the special exits you can find. Even though I played through the game with "full points" I have yet to see some parts of the game.
If you're not immediately put off by its graphical style, I'd say give this a go. With all the little short-comings listed above, I, maybe not highly but securely, recommend Continue?9876543210. Even with its relative shortness of six captivating hours its price tag compares well against the average movie.

Duke Nukem Forever is a game that was in development hell for nearly 15 years. During that time it managed to become what one could describe to be, the most hyped game of all time.
Now, of course no game can sustain 15 years of hype and still manage to be successful in the eyes of it's community right? Well, when DNF was released in the early summer of 2011 it was probably one of the most hated games i've ever seen released.
The game had some serious issues. It didn't feel like Duke Nukem 3D, it was slower, it had a 2 weapon limit, the graphics were rather poor and reminded me of something you'd have seen prior to DOOM 3, the bosses were lame bulletsponges and contained qte's and so on.
Yet still i happen to like this game.
"Why?" you might ask, the reason is simple. It's Duke.
No matter how poor this game is compared to Duke Nukem 3D, no matter how much better it could have been. It's still a thing, and i think that is the most important part about DNF. The game is just so overly happy to exist that sometimes you might actually forget about it's flaws, and just go on bursting the Alien skulls with your mighty boot.
Besides, when you take a look at the rest of the shooters released in 2011 and compare DNF to them. I'd play this one over any of them ten times over.

A long time ago, LucasArts actually made quality titles like Battlefront and Republic Commando. Leading the troop was the Knights of the Old Republic franchise. Now before you play this game, I strongly recommend purchasing the first KotOR game.
Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II is an amazing game. You don't have to be a fan of Star Wars to enjoy this title. It has everything you would expect from an RPG, and also everything you would expect from a Star Wars game. Unlike other games under the Star Wars name that have you blasting and swinging your lightsaber around an area of helpless battle droids and such, KotOR II is somewhat unique in a sense of accomplishment. There are many times where instead of activating your lightsaber and cutting everyone down, you'll have to find your way out of sticky situations with reason or wit. The key to being a good KotOR player is judging when to engage a firefight or when to think things through. Do you attack that Rancor head-on or do you sneak over and poison it's food?
This doesn't mean you'll never see combat. In Knights of the Old Republic II you start off choosing what JEDI class you want to be, (which includes Sentinel, Consular, or Guardian) rather than picking if you want to be a Soldier, Scout, or Scoundrel. This means that right from the get-go of the game you'll have the ability to start stacking up on Force Powers you're going to need in the future. Depending on what you pick, your play style will change.
Guardians focus on swordfighting and combat rather than force powers and skills.
Sentinels mediate between the two, balancing out between swordplay and sorcery.
Consulars are extremely powerful in the force.
Just like the original KotOR, you will start picking skills and feats that allow you to perform various actions. If you put a lot of skill points into Persuasion, you can talk your way out of scenarios before it breaks out into a battlefield. Spend a lot of points on Computer Use or Repair, you can slice into control consoles or reactivate droids to get leverage on your enemies. Then there are skills like Treat Injury and such that allow you to heal wounds faster and give you more HP.
KotOR 2 brings a new feature to the franchise, and allows you to use components and chemicals to create / breakdown items. You can break down a Vibrosword and turn it into components, and then use the broken down components to build a Frag Grenade or Mine.
In summary, KotOR II is not only a great Star Wars game but one of the best RPG's ever created. The story and cast will keep you interested, and the gorgeous worlds from the jungle moon of Dxun to the Czerka Starport of Telos offer tons of chances to explore.
(Plus, be sure to download the Restored Content mod if you plan on purchasing this game, as it adds in TONS of content that was deleted by Obisidan due to time contraints.)

Kero Blaster is an old-school platformer that had huge shoes to fill. From the developers behind indie classic Cave Story, Kero Blaster is a game about a frog salaryman who is an employee of C&F that is going around fixing teleporters and fighting monsters.
GRAPHICS
It's a basic look that suits the game perfectly. Basic 2d sprites and levels with not a ton of big details but it's a distinctive style in an indie scene teeming with retro graphics.
SOUND
Sound effects are on point and the chip tunes are every bit as fantastic as the Studio Pixel projects that have come before it.
GAMEPLAY
It's a run & gun platformer that functions just like how any retro platformer should but better. The various guns are distinctive and never feel underwhelming while our intrepid hero has a nice amount of weight to his jumps and movement so that he moves with just the right amount of weight.
DIFFICULTY
Being a retro platformer, Kero Blaster is pretty tough. However unlike a lot of games that use a similar style, it never feels cheap. Jumps are never particularily difficult to make and enemies & enemy attacks stand out and you never feel like the game cheated.
TLDR
It's a good addition to your library. It's not super long but there are multiple modes which add some meat to the game & it's honestly really charming.

Kero Blaster
Starting off...
Kero Blaster is a game where you have seperate stages and you must beat them to proceed to the next stage and at the end of every stage there is a boss battle which is different and uniquely created.
You use a gun which can fire different types of ammo which can benefit in different scenarios to kill the enemies which you face within the levels.
To upgrade your health and proficiency of your weapon you must earn coins and you can do this by getting them off killing enemies or destroying the shrubery around the map. After a few upgrades of each thing the price goes pretty high so you must wait a while until you can purchase those upgrades.
Positives:
- Gives you at good range of languages to chose from giving variance in the players that can play the game.
- Straight away when the game opens, it gives you a tutorial with the controls on how to play the game which can be good as some smaller games do not do that. Furthermore, you must complete the tutorial to carry on.
- Gives you three save files which is great as you may have friends or family who want to play the game also without overwriting your content.
- The soundtrack is a retro 8-bit track, which is nostalgic to older games from the 90's.
- Gives you a good amount of features, such as new weapons; ways to shoot your weapon.
- Allows you to visit a shop to purchase upgrades for your weapon or you health which can help in the harder levels.
- Levels have cool features as 'Sticky Mud' where its harder to move and you slowly sink which slows down your movement and can be problematic for specific levels.
- Bosses can be quite difficult (Especially the Fish).
- A good range of levels for you to play through (7 Levels I believe).
Negatives:

I bought this game after playing other simulation, sandbox survival games like Rust and Minecraft. I enjoyed the idea that I could build villages and castles, erect palisades and terraform the world to my fitting. What I didn't expect was the god awful mechanics and overall bad design. First thoguh, I'll highlight the few good points this game has.
Good:
- The hierarchial skill tree. its something different, and it would make sense that I need a high forestry and logging level before I can move onto carpentry.
-The crafting system. You can look up what you need, and gather the necessary materials, building better and better tools as you progress.
-THe community. For an alpha game, this has a very strong and friendly community. Joining a guild or gathering a group of friends increases the fun you can have expontentially, and creates a genuine village setting in-game.
Now for the bad:
-The waiting. This game is built almost entirely around the concept of waiting for other things to happen. Every concievable action or movement triggers a progress bar to appear in the middle of the screen, and you have to sit there and do literally nothing for anywhere from 5 to 20 seconds while it finshes the action. You have to wait while you gather plant fiber. You have to wait while you snap off a tree branch. You have to wait while you EQUIP A SHOVEL for christs sake. I understand that performing resource gathering and farming or building takes time, but making the player just sit there and stare at there screen while a progress bar fills is not the way to do it.
- Improving skills. I suggest you find one good server and stay there, because everytime you join a new server you hve to make a new character. This means reassigning skill points to all the different areas (Resource gathering, basic physical abilities, cobat, etc.) It also means that you will spend the first hour and a half in this new server grinding trying to level up your basic skills just so can actually get around to building or farming or mining. Each server admin controls what speed you learn skills at, so unless they've cranked up the learning curve to 200%, enjoy wasting a good chunk of time just to prepare your character to prepare playing.
-Playing solo vs. Teamwork. This is a major compnent of the game. The game itself is called "Life is Feudal: YOUR OWN". Playing this game with a group of friends makes this game about 100% more fun, but more importantly, it makes it 500% easier. The idea is that each person should a special role (blacksmith, carpenter, farmer, etc.) so that you can work together to build your world without everyone having to worry about prodcing their own food or tools. However, this means that if you try to go your own way, you better be prepared to grind for a good ten hours so that you can barely cover your food, resources and tools needs. I get that the game is meant to be played with others, but it shouldn't sacrifice the enjoyment from playing alone. There isn't even a single player option, unless you start your own server and make it private, which can take anothe 30 minutes.
Overall, this game has huge potential, but is ruined by the insane grind and need for others to help you to actual progress. Hopefully the MMO they are making will address this, but as far as I'm concerned, the money I payed for this game was flushed down the toilet.

I don't know why people haven't tagged it this way, but its obvious that this game is a roguelite behind the messages and themes that it contains. Jason Oda covers the whole story aspect pretty well in the about section of the store page, so I will focus my review on the game beneath the facade.
The game mentions that you take on 6 out of 11 levels each playthrough, but these 11 levels appear to be split into two different types where there arent any major differences other than the graphics/map layout for levels of the same type.  The first type being a tag/hide and seek with npcs and the second, more frequent kind, is an open town where you talk with the npcs and try to gather keys,resources, and information. This repetition would be boring if it wasn't for the short minigames in between.
There are at least 5 different types of minigames ranging from platforming to Galaga to zelda dungeons and these different types can come in varying difficulties. If you succeed at the minigames, there is much to gain, especially if you play them perfectly, but they can also be rather dangerous
First off of the roguelite checklist, randomness. Random characters, random levels, random npcs, random minigames, randumb... The first two don't really make a difference, but the random npcs are what make the game. You'll have to get clues and keys from these npcs, but not all are to be trusted.  The npcs never seem to lie about information, so aside from getting some nonsense one liner that wastes your time talking to the npc, the worst they will do is sell you a trapped room. However, since you can get free, safe rooms from the rounds, the npcs really are the least of your problems. The information from the npcs will make otherwise random choices definite, but if you are really desperate for time or resources you can guess questions, although you don't really need to do that to beat the game.
The worst of all randomness is the lightning. The first kind of lightning is used to pave the way to an exit, but there are several exits and its possible that your lightning will hit an empty space, so it is easy for the lighting to be spread out and still not have an exit. These rolls will make or break your runs, they are the difference between having to focus all of your resources just to make it to the next level and being able to safely farm resources with impunity. Then there is the matter of having to find shelter in the storms. The randomness here has the potential to be more punishing when you have few buildings. Some buildings can take 1 or 2 lightning bolts and still stand for the next storm, but too few buildings and these tankier buildings are likelier to be destroyed. Despite all of the possible ways you can get ♥♥♥♥ed by the dice, you do have a decent bit of leeway to messup. Even if you get a few bad dice rolls, you should be able to make those up with resources from playing the minigames well.
Then there is the matter of death. You can use your various resources to get second chances once you 'die', but when you run out of those, you must start from the beginning.  Additionally, the penalty when using buildings to revive gets increasingly severe, while using money to revive, while a static cost, will prevent you from getting more buildings/lightning.
What do you get for replaying this game? Mostly you just get to see different specs of story/dialogue; however, actually seeking out the in game diaries will be detrimental to progressing to the end, but I suppose that's just part of the message with this kind of game. You'll see the different level art styles and see some different minigames, but thats about it. Some roguelites require you to play the game over and over to get direct benefits or crucial knowledge, but any useful knowledge is rerolled with each new game aside from knowing how to play a specific minigame.
In the end, its not close to being the hardest game of the genre since you dont need a truly perfect run to beat the game, but it isn't too simple either. Players have the option of playing the way the developer would, but you could also speedrun it too if you wanted to. I recommend both playing to win and playing to explore in order to get the most out of this game. Finally, for your own sanity, do not play this game in full screen mode unless you want to make it even harder, perhaps impossible.

This is a game i would have a hard time recommending to anyone really.
For a modern game, it has some very difficult puzzles at times, which is one of the only good things about the game. The other thing being Lara looking more gorgious then ever!
The puzzles are never straight forward, and can often be a real brainwrapper to complete. This is really nice, for an age where you are expected to progress by the push of a button.
Sadly, the game has not much else to offer.  The controlls are unusual, especially during "jumping-puzzles" where they shuffle around, literally. Changing the camera angle will change which way the controlls will have you go. This can get so confusing, and it's hard to get used to. It isn't helping much either, that the camera constantly works against you. Sometimes it is also hard to tell if you can grab a ledge or not, this has had me stuck in a few areas for unpleasently long time.
The combat system is probably one of the most boring features of the game, for me it felt incredibely dull, fighting human AI is the worst, as holding down the trigger is all you need to do to achieve victory, as every shot they take freezes them for a frame or two, allowing you to kill them before they can retaliate. Fighting wild life is a whole other game, and is almost too difficult. The camera will always do it's best to get your view as far off the attackers as possible. And it is often hard to avoid enemy strikes. There is alot of very complicated 'special move' controlls, that i never got to use as the combo was impossible to remember.
It is also littered with bugs and glitches as you'd come to expect. The worst of these, being that the ingame physics are highly(EXTREMELY) affected when Vsync is off. Carriable items will fling Lara around, fly away when put down, or clip you through the level. Often grapplehook objects can't be affected either. Why this was never caught in testing is beyond me, As it renders 90% of the physic based puzzles unsolveable. The game also lacks a Steam community GUI, it does however make up for this with flawless alt-tabing. (Have had no crashes with this yet)
In the end, the game fails to mix much of interest inbetween the endless waves of puzzles, boring fights, and difficult jumping session. Not to mention the very repeative enviroments, and areas. Most of the ruins are very alike, altho this is intentional.
The game's main focus seems to be on what it does best, puzzles! But for me, doing nothing else then completing puzzles can get boring very quick, and i oftenly took serval days of break from playing, due to getting bored. Before finally giving up, as i got stuck towards the end of the game. Yet another game i will
complete.
In conclusion, this seems like a decent console port, sadly the PC features feel untested, the shuffling controlls, annoying camera, boring combat system, repeative enviroments and too many puzzles, are not helping it at all. I feel the only two good things in the game is the most gorgious looking Lara to date, and the puzzles.
Beyond that, as i already said, i think it's hard to recommend. But, for 9€ you should get your moneys worth, if you enjoy puzzles.

Massively addictive game. Cannot get enough of it, something about upgrading weapons, armor & gems just keeps me interested. The combat system, when you get used to it, is very rewarding and fun - while I still face some challenges I do feel like a badass now that I have properly levelled up and use the right gems, armor and weapons. Decided to go full warrior class so packed everything into strength and a little into endurance.
Pros:
1. The quests are WAY more interesting than some of the typical RPG quests with some pretty entertaining and, dare I say, mature storylines.
2. The graphics & sound is absolutely remarkable.
3. Variety of things to do i.e. tomb raiding, fighting, hunting, horse riding, sailing, upgrading items, shopping etc. (keeps me entertained for long periods of time).
4. As stated in my opening remarks, the combat system is fantastic and if attacks are timed with defense the results are some excellent fighting routines. The enemies also have certain defense such as blunt force vs cutting damage so when facing say a Skeleton it is better to use a hammer than a sword. It is important to see / know what your enemies are "immune to" so changing weapons is a must to quickly end fights, especially when surrounded (something which the Witcher series uses i.e. silver vs steel)
5. While I am full on warrior, should I wish to switch to range (rogue) or magick (mage) I can use a soul patcher and simple respec my character.
6. The magick system from what I have seen (not experienced myself yet, is the best in it's class - more like Oblivion than Skyrim - where custom made spells are possible, only your imagination is the limit.
7. The different areas are amazing from totally unique (lush islands with gorgeous flora which reacts to your movements, the savana, the deserts, the dungeons, the old ruins, the swallows etc.) each region feels totally unique with even the music adapting accordingly.
Cons:
1. You can see in some instances that the budget behind this game vs other more well know games is less, not based on sound or graphics but rather things like path finding for enemies which can be pretty dumb at times.
2. AI is somethings lacking (and here is a pro tip for folks in the early game) where the enemies have a limited chase distance where they simply reach the edge of this limit and will sometimes just stand there and take arrow or magick damage until they die. (Which was especially useful when facing the giant scorpions for the first time although I did feel a little dirty using this game glitch)
3. Probably as a result of the first point but some of the caves / dungeons are reused but not nearly as bad as Dragon Age 2
4. Possibly a tad challenging in the early stages so kiting is recommended (hit and run tactics)

If I could give this a sideways thumb, I would. It's meh at best. Read to conclusion/TL;DR if you don't want to read the review. My thumbs-up is only because I like MTG. Overall rating? 6.25/10
If you are a hardcore MTG player, this isn't the game for you at all. I got this game because I wanted to reminisce on my days in middle school when I played this game to the extreme. Given that, I recommend this game for the casual player/those that don't want to collect cards and take up space/newbie players just learning. Having said that, there's some serious kinks in this game. The menu icons, SLOW AS ALL GET OUT. Painfully almost. The graphics look great, but that comes at a price; speed. The instant menu features were way better. Also, just skip the tutorial if you've played before, you don't really need it. The 2-headed giant was a fun mode they got rid of, which major sucks too. Sometimes, I scratch my head at it. This is a cool game if you want to just get into basic deck mechanics, see all the new cards, and just have fun with it. But this game SERIOUSLY lacks from an enthusiast point of view (I used to be an enthusiast). You have to win almost everything to unlock cards...which is okay I guess, but there are some points where you have to redo your colors just to get past certain enemies. Also, you don't get access to any other sets with this. That's my worst complaint about this game. I liked some of the older stuff; 7th edition. I got beat in a tournament because some guy used cards from '93 and had a card called Timewalk, where you could take another turn. Granted, that card back then was wroth like hundreds of dollars, but still...it would be nice to incorporate some of the older serieses into this so we can get a TRUE experience. Also, be ready to restart a LOT. If you don't draw the best hand, you WILL lose. You will need to grind for a long time to build up your library, so be prepared to put some work in if you want to succeed at trouncing people and AI. At least they gave us deck customization (finally?) I've been playing on Archmage difficulty, and it's really stacked against you starting out, but it gets better as you go on. You will probably also need (at some point) to buy the card collections, which is a business tactic to help Wizards out since you aren't buying actual booster packs. HAVING SAID ALL THAT, it seems like the cons outweigh the pros. But if you're just casually looking for some once-in-awhile fun chillin' with a Magic deck, this saves a LOT of heartache with regards to buying cards, deck protectors, travelling to tournaments, dealing with the weird♥♥♥♥♥zealots who take it too seriously. Nothing wrong with that per se, I'm just not that kind of player.
Conclusion/TL;DR: Buy this if you're a casual gamer, don't mind spending $5 every once in a rare while (people need to chill on "pay to win", it's more like "pay to make your chances only slightly better", which sucks but they're a company and that's what they do), and you don't want to deal with the hassle of the real game...BUT wait until it's on sale. I didn't mind spending $10 on this game, but I'd advise until it hits 50% off, then you can buy the game and a few card collections for the same price and have a much better experience starting out AND grinding out.

Some people refer to Darksiders as "Zelda meets God of War." I don't think they mean it in a bad way at all because the game is far different enough from those two to make it's mark as a distinguished title.
The comparison to Zelda and God of War are in reference to the fact that this is an action-adventure game with combat similar to God of War and puzzles similar to Zelda. As I said earlier though, this game is different enough from those two that it makes for a fairly unique game experience. Few action games have the kind of puzzles present in this game and almost no puzzle based games feature the combat that Darksiders has.
Even though it's different in it's own way than God of War, if you have played GoW you'll feel right at home with the controls and the combat. You have your basic attacks, magic, and a huge number of combos to pull off. Countering enemies is always satisfying and gives you a huge advantage in that moment. Bosses are also great with each providing a slightly different mechanic to use to defeat them.
One area where I feel the game could improve is the ratio of combat to puzzles. There were some puzzle sections that seemed to go on just a hair too long as I was itching to kill more stuff. Combat is so fun that you end up missing it when doing the puzzle sections (which are adequate, but not quite up there with Zelda). This slightly breaks up the flow of the game and as I said earlier some puzzle stages definitely overstay their welcome. It doesn't help that the puzzles are usually somewhat mediocre (move x to y, push button, etc.). They aren't bad, but it's not like the combat which in itself is pretty exceptional.
On a visual level this is a relatively old game but it still looks pretty good thanks to Todd McFarlane's excellent character designs. Character design is great and you truly get the sense of being in a fantasy/post-apocalyptic setting. Some visual effects are absent as this game was made awhile ago and unfortunately cut scenes are not in 1080p.
Puzzles and visuals aside this is one great game. It's fun and challenging without being frustrating and combat is a blast (when you're not solving puzzles). As far as achievements go there are a number of collectibles in the form of upgrades so they are worth collecting even if you need a guide. A forewarning about achievements in this game though: Some will NOT unlock when they should so keep your eye on the corner of your screen when you expect to get an achievement. I found I had to go back several times to pick up an achievement for beating a boss or collecting an item so make a LOT of saves if you can. This doesn't break the experience though and it only happened a few times so I would still give it a shot at getting 100% if you're up for that sort of thing.
With great combat and a unique art style (even with dated graphics) Darksiders is a great experience. There really isn't too much else out there like it and it will keep you busy for awhile (15-20 hours).

Duels of the Planeswalker - this is my inital response and after having played a game of it online against another player:
It is worth getting if you have problems being able to play Magic elsewhere, or if you are new to the series but even then I would say its sketchy because as fun as it is to build your own deck and face it off your opponents, you can get stuck even at the tutorial depending on your deck you picked - the difficulty may cause a bit of a headache as well but considering I found the AI to be questionable when facing lethal damage... it may or may not affect much.
Because most of the game comes - initially at least - from the deck you chooses that you can't switch or do anything with basically (you can modify it but with no cards until you've won the first campaign to unlock the boosters, it may not actually matter).
The way you make your own deck is fine and unlocking boosters seem to be both easy and grind-able enough for people like myself who want very specific decks going into the multiplayer (altho', now even I will have to deal with the lack of perfect cards and I say that with a smile) so you're most likely going to be able to get the cards you want.
Other than that, its still a Duels of the Planeswalker game with the same things you expect over and over again except two massive flaws in this installment:
The menu is extremely clunky to maneuver and takes a long time to get anywhere if it isn't one of the first three icons... and then you'll still have to scroll thru' after that menu another one, and possibly a third one as well. Its clunky, unneccesary and annoying.
And secondly, something which disturbs a great deal of people - no Two-headed Giant's mode (which is the same as a 2v2 mode in MTG with special rules)...
Overall, the game seems fine but I still wouldn't recommend it unless you have no other way to play Magic.

By far the most amazing underrated game i have ever played, KOTOR 2 was a shining beacon in my childhood. Right from the start the game throws you into a suspenseful story, and it never lets up. Unlike KOTOR 1, where you can clearly define right and wrong (lightside/darkside options), KOTOR 2 muddies the lines that define good and evil and has you make tough decisions, with the early acquired and amazingly well written and voiced companion character "Kreia", further blurring those already hard-to-see lines. You want to help that poor homeless man on Nar Shadda by giving him credits? Think again, because that same act of kindess can make him a target to his fellow refugees.
But what really pulls everything in in this admittedly rushed-yet-amazing game is the not just the complicated moral choices and quanderies, but the feeling of urgency. Wether you decide to stay on the tride and true path of the jedi, or break out as a rogue dark jedi/sith, you can never forget you are being hunted by what must be THE scariest sith lords ever designed. Obsidian definitly took an already amazing game and, in my opinion, made it better than the original.
Don't get me wrong, there are plenty of bugs and holes in some parts of the story, but what IS there is a fascinating take on that Galaxy Far, Far Away.
My rating 9.5/10
Edit: Finally, Steam and Lord Gaben (of the Sith) has finally decided to fully support KOTOR II in all it's glory! with the TSLRCM, I can safely say now, without a shadow of a doubt, that this game is a MUST BUY! Gone are the slightly annoying bugs, and in with the refined content.
My edited rating with full steam support and TSLRCM: 10/10 would kill the galaxy and all the jedi again

i really would like to thumb up this game but i just can't because of so many small details and bugs wich is very unforgivable considering for how long this game is available in store.
the game is unstable, i experienced crash and a few never-ending loading screen. The framerate is ok during battle but incredibly low during the phase where you pick your units.
Let's talk about unit. The balance is bad, not only because of pure strengh but actually considering each unit price when you deploy. For exemple an heavy bolter squad cost 3x the price of the standard bolter with almost no benefice. Or cost the price of a tank 10x more powerfull.
There's a Xp system during battle wich is fine since you keep your units from a battle to the next but there are some huge problems.
When an unit get a new level, you get to pick an upgrade. A talent tree would have been great in this situation but no. Worse, during the campaign xp was reset after each battle. You would keep any finished level but let's say if you were at 99% of the level, most of time (not everytime, its why i call that a bug), your unit was back to 0%.
As a consequence, you would try to kill everything with only a few units to be sure to finish a level, and in same time pray for some rng on the upgrade.
I see a few DLC available so i guess the game isn't abandonned so i really don't understand why these small details aren't fixed yet.

I'm a big fan of Cave Story and this feels like a huge stepback. The controls and platforming feels so unintuitive. I feel as though I've died more to failing jumps (and hitting a monster as a result) than I have to actual enemies. There were some really hard platforming sections in Cave Story too but the controls and booster felt fluid, while in Kero Blaster they feel clunky. Jumping and boosting feels so inconsistent in this, I want to say that the trick to making jumps is by taking your finger off of the directional key then hitting it again while hitting space bar again but I'm not 100% sure.
The gun mechanics in this game also feel strange. You're locked in shooting in a single direction until you let go of the shooting button. Additionally, you can't shoot below while jumping. I don't understand Pixel made this decision as it makes the gameplay feel even more jarring.

Pros
+Very good graphics, weapon models, and animations.
+Amazing soundtrack.
+Hillarious dialogue.
+Interesting story (up until the ending, anyways).
+Large variety of weapons to choose from to meet your enemy slaughtering needs.
+Pretty good RPG aspects to improve certain parts of your character as you progress.
+Weapons feel impactful as you slice, dice, and explode your way through groups of enemies.
+Loot upgrades allow you to make your weapons even stronger, allowing you to kill even more enemies faster.
+Large maps to explore to find chests, secrets, or side bossess.
+Maps are diverse enough to not cause visual burnout.
+Good enemy variety throughout the levels.
+Decently challenging, however becomes a little too easy once you get certain weapons and skills.
+Variety of skill upgrades allow you to choose the way that you play, with the option to reset at any point in the hub world.
Cons
-Multiplayer feels tacked on. Inviting friends is a chore, lack of in game communication method, co-op specific bugs, story progress made while playing co-op will not transfer over to your solo game, some enemies (such as the bunny lord) do not drop loot for clients, some quest rewards are given to the host only (such as the "Like the Wind" skill), requires insanely good connection from both the clients and the host in order to not experience lag, unable to change game from public to invite only (or even from single player to multi player) once you have launched the game, some achievements do not track properly during co op (such as the 50 vanish kills), chests are opened locally and not globally so every player has to open their own chests, and only the host can progress the quests forward.
-Framerate drops in later areas of the game when 5+ superior or elite enemies are on screen. I don't have the perfect computer, but sometimes my FPS would drop to below 40 when fighting groups of superiors. I would also occassionally encounter freezing for brief seconds when speeding through an area and hitting a checkpoint.
-Some of the weapons are way too underpowered (such as the infinite ammo SMG) and other weapons are far too strong (such as the Arm of Orochi). I would have preferred having a more balanced variety of weapons so I don't have to ask myself towards the end of the game "Why am I even using this weapon?"
-Too many upgrades are thrown at you. There are so many utter garbage upgrades that you pick up along the way that just clog up your inventory (even if it is limitless).
-Crafting unlocks way too late in the game and only gives you upgrades based on what part of the story you are at, not based on what level your character is. You also lose access to crafting on new game+ until you reach the point in the story again that it unlocks (although due to crafting scaling to story progress it isn't worth crafting until you are at the very end of the game.)
-No effective mini-map. The mini-map in this game is not very good. I wish there was a bigger version you could use to see the area as a whole that you are in and not just a slightly bigger version when you push m.
Even though I went more in depth on the negatives than the positives, I would  still recommend this game to people who want a fun single player experience with lots of fast paced combat and mayhem. It can also be really fun when played with friends, but be warned of the co-op specific bugs that exist. To avoid some of the bugs, I would recommend making it known via voice chat when the host is moving since some of the bugs occur when the clients are messing around with their inventory during a teleport.

Occasionally I wonder, how many times have I died in this life?  How many Marios have I plunged down bottomless pits?  How many chosen nobodies of Tamriel have I gotten run through?  Alas, the video game lives that have served me, I have not served well in return.  Sometimes in the throes of drink or the in darkness of despair I wonder what has become of those unfortunate sprites, those amalgamated polygons with their illusions of agency.
Continue?987654321 tells the story of one such departed and the game begins with her dying moments.  The machinations of digital afterlife play out before us as we witness the software of souls.  Shortly thereafter, we're given control of our fallen warrior in a run-down corner of the afterlife.  "Where are we," our spirit character asks another. "Well..." he replies tilting his rectantangle head up to ours, "I suppose on a line of code, on a sliver of light, floating aimlessly through the random access memory."  Unwilling to fade peacefully into the digital night, our heroine strikes out to escape the inescapable.
The game unfolds as we move from town to town, one step ahead of oblivion.  Each vignette is a small area to explore and escape.  The player has several minutes of game time in blocky planescapes to find the folks that can grant them lighting or prayers.  Some are vendors, some are quest givers and some are simple well wishers.  There are few ne'er do wells in this well of souls;  everyone is facing the same dissolution.  Their bestowed lightning can destroy barriers to level exits, their prayers raise buildings in the one place where our heroine can shelter against the wrath of the Garbage Collector.
At set intervals the player is thrown into minigames.  Some involve zelda-like dungeons, some are hacks and slashes and some involve a bit of platforming.  All in all, they're quick diversions enabling the player to get more precious foo and ram.  Foo buys you lightning, prayers, extra time and second chances.  Ram is your resistance to the Garbage Collector's pursuing minions.  Run out of ram too soon or fail to escape a level and watch your shelters blasted into smithereens and know that next time you run for shelter, there may be none left.
If the game seems disjointed, it is.  But it works mostly because the minigames are challenging, diverse and fun. And through each disjoint, the unifying metaphor is ever present.  Death is not something that many of us choose to think about.  Perhaps it is a Western mindset, or perhaps it is even gamings' own emphasis on not dying that encourages the avoidance of the inevitable.  Continue?987654321 takes a more Eastern approach.
It is zen-like and Buddha-ful experience, though a bit heavy handed at times. In the squalor of the /apps/Ghangees level, we encounter a npc and her dead grandmother whose foot has been stolen by a stray dog.  But while often grim, it is touching at times and refreshingly self aware:  during a dream the player may approach and ask questions of the great Garbage Collector like 'What is the metaphor?' For which it has no answer.  Between one level and another we're asked to do a short meditation remembering our dearest departed pet.
When games go all philosophy they usually go all pretentious too.  Not so with Continue.  Many of the levels are ponderous locales, but in their pixel precise portrayal of squalor and the evocative conversation of their denizens, there is a comfort in despair. Perhaps the comfort is in acceptance, but either way at the end of the game, based on how long she lasted, the player is told how their avatar met her inevitable death.  Did she escape long enough to come to grips with its mortality?  Or was she ripped from digitalia with wailing and gnashing of teeth?
Continue brings to mind a book I'm fond of named "The Beginning Place" by Ursula LeGuin.  At its most basic level, it is the story of two people who run from their lives and find each other in a broken fantasy world.  When read at that level, the story is a bit uneven and the conclusion unsatisfying.  But when read as the allegory it is intended to be, it's a journey that offers the reader new insight every time through.  Continue?987654321 is not unlike that novel.  If one sits at their keyboard expecting metroid or its latest manifestation, one might walk away slightly underwhelmed.  But when experienced as the metaphor it is meant to be, Continue is far greater than the sum of its mini games, its foo and its ram.  It is a sober reminder of the priceless now, a virtual wise man on the mountain offering wisdom where so many other games merely offer escape, a life lesson to be learned over and over.
Go and wander to lovely, awesome and mysterious places.
Think and feel
Sit quietly and contemplate the precious silence.
Take in the wonder of existence
And then want nothing else from it
Only then will you be ready
- Celia, Continue?987654321

I heard a lot of terrible things about the PC ports of Darksiders. So when I saw them on sale, I was sceptical.
But, I decided to pick them up for a few dollars each, to see if it was worth it.
IT WAS.
Darksiders is basically God Of War meets Devil May Cry meets Legend Of Zelda Ocarina Of Time.
Set in a world where Hell and Hell are two dormant sides waiting to tear out each others throats above
the Kingdom Of Mankind, you play as War, a giant-sword-wielding, demon-obliterating badass.
Pros:
-Incredibly satisfying, good paced combat system that's easy to grasp but challenging to master.
-Looks pretty decent despite itss age.
-The whole game is set in this sort of sub-linear, sub-open world. If you're not directly in a dungeon, you're
free to wander as you please from space to space.
-Puzzles start off easy, and become interesting and challenging towards the end of the game.
-Genuinly decent storyline. Not amazing, but interesting enough.
-Great pacing. Just whenever the game begins to feel dull, a new mechanic is introduced, be it a grappling
hook, explosives, riding on horseback, a new weapon, or so on.
Cons:
-Supposedly has some issues running on some computers, not that I experienced them.
-Lacks graphical settings other than V-Sync and Resolution.
-Basically requires a controller to play. PC controls are blegh.
-A few small bugs in places.
Overall, I was pleasently surprised to find that Darksiders was an absolutely amazing game that I couldn't put down.
It played smoothly, it was fun, the pacing was great, and I loved every second of it. If you have any sort of enjoyment
in brawler style games, like you played God of War or Devil May Cry or anything like them, I definetely reccomend you
try out Darksiders.

Doom 3 is essentially a remake of the original Doom, though series fans will find reimagined versions of almost every monster from both Doom and Doom II in the new sequel. You play as a nameless, voiceless 22nd-century space marine called by the Union Aerospace Corporation to its Mars research facility beset with mysterious problems--the forces of hell, to be exact. You'll end up single-handedly fighting back legions of hellspawn using weapons like shotguns, machine guns, and rocket launchers. As in the classic Doom games, your foes here are liable to strike at any time--often just as you round a corner, grab a much-needed power-up, or set foot into a new area. So, while your enemies will materialize without notice, and may occasionally startle you as they leap out of the darkness, Doom 3 cannot easily be described as scary or suspenseful, but is still an amazing experience at first hand.

TL;DR - Recommended, yes, but with caution. This is an interesting concept that is not always well executed in terms of mechanics, and it's easy to get frustrated.
I really, really, really wanted to like this game. Continue? is a beautiful idea, and has very strange but wonderful writing. I love this style of graphics, so that's another tally in the "Pro" column. The music is nice, and some of the stage designs were really wonderful. A special shout-out goes to the Pink Castle level, where a number of princesses wander about. One of them tells you a story about being kidnapped and taken to a castle, where she awaited rescue. And when no one came, she took up a sword and beheaded anyone who got in her way, forging a new path for herself to carve out a life where she could have peace. It was a beautifully written story that I wish I had screen shots of, but unfortunately the levels randomly generate and I can't quite work up the motivation to play again until I get to that level. Which brings me to my next point…
There are some flaws. Big ones. The idea of semi-random encounter battles that drop you into a sort of mini-game based on some other style of game, mostly arcade-style games from what I saw, is a really great concept that fits the theme of this game and it's story. The downside is that the encounters are frustratingly difficult, to the point of nearly gamebreaking, and ultimately I gave up on this title. It has some other flaws, some in the mechanics (I hit some glitches that required me to start the game over--which is ironic as hell, considering the plot of a game character battling through random access memory trying to buy time to avoid being deleted) and some with the repetitive nature of the conversations and cut scenes that can't be avoided or skipped. I will, hopefully, pick this up again one day. I recommend Continue? because it's an interesting idea with some cool graphics and great music. But take the recommendation with a grain of salt, because in a lot of ways it's very difficult to play through and not the rewarding experience I had hoped for.

*Red alert! *Red alert! Torpedo torpedo torpedo!! Commence evasive maneuvers! First of all, don't let my hours on record fool you. I've played this game from 2007ish to 2012 and stopped for awhile due to work. Since then, I've been playing this game from time to time again and it NEVER fails to amuse me. I'm really glad this game is already in steam! It means more players will discover the uniqueness and awesome gameplay and will also keep this game alive until the end of days! This is the overall package of naval warfare! If you like Frigates, destroyers, battlecruisers, torpedo launchers, submarines, aircraft carriers, fighters dogfighting, bombers bombing and BOOMsticks(Battleships), then this is the game for you! This game is based on the world war 2 naval warfare history and not a fantasy. Each nation you choose have their own unique ships, aircraft carriers, etc. And also have their own strengths and weaknesses. Now to the gameplay. the normal battles are massive! 64 vs 64 players, 128 players in total, can play in 1 battle! Can you imagine all the chaos and mayhem and fun you're going to have!? It will take a little bit of time to familiarize yourself in the mechanics of the game but once you're there, you'll surely get addicted to it. Don't forget to ask other players ingame or in the forums for more info. This is not just another run and gun mindless game because it takes skills and strategy to play effectively. You will need to mind your gun angles when aiming and shooting your enemies. You also need to predict where the enemy is by the time your shells will land because your shells will take time to arrive there. And if that's not enough, you and your target is moving! It's a ship, silly! Ofcourse it will move! Jokes aside. To make it even more difficult, you're controlling everything while you're on battle. Literally everything! From the turret rotations, the gun angles/elevation, aiming, gun firing, ship movements, firing the anti-aircraft guns, sending scouts by airplane, dogfighting, dive bombing and torpedo bombing. Yes, you heard me right. You're not only firing at ships but also firing at scout planes, fighters and bombers trying to send you and your allies to the bottom of the ocean. That is how complicated and deep the game is. But don't worry, you will get the hang of it. ;) It's also a management game because before you start sending enemies for fish food, you get to manage your ship and your crew members in the harbor. You will get the chance to improve your ship's equipment like guns, shells, engines, radar and armor, etc. You will also get the chance to hire skilled seamen and train them to improve your overall ship's performance in battle. You can buy/sell/trade ships, crew members, ingame currency and experience points with its player trading system. The cherry to this game is the harbor assault or the game's war system. Once a week, your clan will get the chance to participate in the very strategic harbor assault and capture each nations' harbors by attacking each tile of their territories until you get to the harbor and destroy their final defense. Once destroyed, you can send land troops to capture their infrastructure. But before that, the territories and harbors are being defended by other clans who captured it on last week's harbour assault. Huge rewards and bonuses, such as ingame currency, etc. awaits you at war's end. You will also get your clan name and logo displayed on the harbor you captured for bragging rights. The game is really deep and massive! I can go on and on about it but still not enough to describe its awesomeness! You must experience and live it. Just play this game and I guarantee you that it's not a waste of you and your friends' time. Infact, your whole life is a lie until you play this game. Thank you for reading and enjoy! - IGN: deadguy69

This is a skill based game, Not pay to win. You can still get good seamen stats ingame. And the stats is way more than enough that you don't need to buy elite seamen or sailors. Wow..... just wow. If you are interested in a game that will have you hooked forever, then look no further than ArmA 3. Now this game is no easy take to run for your PC, this game is more dependant on your CPU than your GPU, therefore you need a pretty beefy CPU if you want decent frames on most situations. On the downside the engine that this game run on is no friend to FPS, this meaning it is rare to get anything over 50 frames per second in multiplayer situations, in my case it depends on how many people are in a server at opne time. For example if you are in a 110/120 persons king of the hill server (unless you have a great CPU) don't be surprised to be at an average of 30-40 FPS. All in all this game is great if you are looking for the most realistic First Person Shooter then this is your ticket. Hope you find this review useful.

I was looking through the reviews and I don't think people are giving this game enough credit. For starters, I saw a lot of reviews stating that the game is "absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; and I would have to disagree. Some people are upset because there is an option for microtransactions. While this might seem like a money grab, it necessarily isn't. Keep this in mind, the microtransactions are there for people who do not have time to play the game as frequently as others. It has been stated in a few forums that a player can unlock every single card in the game just by playing the game, thus making the microtranasctions an option and not a "pay to win" mechanic.
Let's take a look at Hearthstone, Blizzard's card game. They have have a similar formula to this game in that you can unlock every card in the game by playing, or by spending money through microtransactions. There are professional players who haven't spent a dime on the game, and they are just as good as the players who have spent money on the game. It just proves that in order to be a good player you need skill, and the same goes for this game. While expendable income would help one acquire the cards faster, it is in no means necessary.
Moving on, another topic I saw in the negative reviews, is that the starting decks are awful. While it might be a bit unfair to not be told what cards are in your deck before you pick it, the decks are not aweful. As an example, I chose the rakdos starting deck and beat all of Innistrad, Theros, and some of Ravnica on the hardest difficulty with little to no modifications to the deck. Sure there were a few games I lost because I had a bad hand, or the AI had a much better hand, but that doesn't mean the decks are garbage. Now I suppose I have only seen the Rakdos deck so as far as I know the other decks might actually be aweful.
Overall, I would say this game is a nice change in the Duels of the Planeswalkers series and I look forward to playing it more. However, if you are not willing to make your own decks and spend a few hours playing games with AI to unlock cards then I can not reccomend this game to you. I hope this review has been helpful, and thank you for your time.
TL;DR   The game is good and some reviewers are angry.
