Having read the Dev's reply about waiting til you get further into the campaign for the game to shine, I have to agree with them.
Whereas at first there was no visible unit progression, now it's coming in spades. That's lots. And it's good.
So, this is a review of the single player campaign as I have not played the game in multiplayer yet, just viewed some youtube battles.
It's taken a while but the game has grabbed me by the doodads. In a nice way.
You start with a map with a linear progression of battle after battle. There are some scripted well thought out battles interspersed with battles using the skirmish feature of the game. All taking you toward the final battle.
Take your units through to the next battle and wait in anticipation to try out their new abilities they gained from the previous battle after levelling up.
Its fun.
It is not a AAA title. It doesn't have a AAA price tag. Its not how Slitherine does things. But it is cool as a single player comp stomp campaign. Not worth the price if that is solely what you want it for, at the moment.
Maybe with new races IF they each have a campaign released with them too.
There is a tutorial and the first few battles consist of quite basic army lists and units.But as the campaign prgresses you will swing Thunderhammers and fire off Whirlwinds.
It does lack a bit of spit and polish though:
There are no cut scenes, no voice-overs and no cinematic intros.
There is limited unit customization, no re-naming you Terminators 'Nigel Farage' or 'Trump Hammer' if you are so inclined. Makes me sad...
There's very little in the way of engaging backstory for each unit. No tech specs for guns or gun porn. Not even a tiny waaaagh! from the Gremlin units on their unit cards. So yeah, the atmosphere is kind of lacking.
There definately needs to be more mention of experience gain and levelling up in game in the tutorial or at the start of the campaign even.
There are no skill trees to drool over. Bang a great big GONG when your unit levels up in game. Make the +exp numbers fizz and sparkle! <ahem> I mean have a deep masculine disembodied voice announce how the Emperor is pleased with your efforts! Missed a trick here.
The map editor is pretty good, if a little opaque at the moment. No doubt there will be guides coming out from people on steam, and there is reference to some help on the Slitherine webby. But its a pretty decent bit of kit. Can't find out how to make hills yet though.
Anyway I would give this 7.5 out of 10.

Reviews I saw prior to playing this had me expecting a challenging and fun gorefest that is not only comparitable but a competitor to the most recent DOOM installment. Unfortunatley this mindset left me dissapointed.
Pros:
- Gore is really cool, some of the best you will see with any games out there but not the best ever.
- Skippable cutscenes: I would not want to have to live through the jokes and acting that is almost cringeworthy at times.
- Movement: Very fast and allows you to pull off some fun combos with your weapons while soaring through the air.
- Soundtrack: Decent.
- Monsters: Don't feel spongey when playing at an appropriate difficulty level which really helps the gameplay. The monsters are also fairly well designed and can be interesting to play against.
- Threats: Most if not all attacks from enemys are avoidable or dodgeable which is always good in a game like this.
- Graphics: Decent most of the time and some things look great. Sometimes it can be hard to spot things compared to the background but at the end of the day the graphics do the job.
Cons:
- Difficulty: I played on the hardest difficulty and got quickly bored, enemys felt spongey and the guns felt like peashooters, not only that but it wasn't all that challenging to me. I turned down the difficulty so I could mow through enemys but after that the challenge no longer existed and playing felt fruitless.
- Variety: I am starting to get sick of games that don't filter their content. I just want to play the game and get knees deep in it without worrying about equipting tiny meaningless boosts on my bundle of half useless weapons. Some people do enjoy this in games such as borderlands but in SW2 the upgrades and weapon changes just feels too little to take any interest in, therefore managing them feels like a chore.
- Humor:♥♥♥♥♥♥nfart joke humor which is resonates usually with younger audiences. cringeworthy some of the time but you could find a couple of laughs in there.
At the end of the day, if you pick up this game you will probably have some fun and the price is not crazy high. I am writting this to try and give you a different perspective than some of the positive reviews give. This game is no DOOM, but it is a good laugh and entertaining experience. The only reason I cannot reccomend it is I personally did not enjoy it and for people who dislike borderlands for the crazy loot, they will probably not enjoy it so much either. But for what it is I will still give it a 7/10 while not reccomending it to a selection of people.

I went into this game expecting something similar to Borderlands....and that is absolutely correct. The humor and loot n shoot esque style, use of a simplistic skill and leveling system, fast travel, and 4 player CO-OP, is totally Borderlands, and I love it. The gameplay overall sort of reminds me of DOOM 2016 with it's fast paced action and the ability to move around very quickly. The use of gems/artifacts or whatever is also reminiscent of Diablo III, as well as the use of fast travel and loot, and skills. I like the way the controls are too, how you can conveniently switch back to previous melee weapons or ranged weapons, plus the ability to jump, double jump, dash, sprint, etc etc. This all makes me feel like I have full control of the character and allows for fluent and fun gameplay. While this game does seem to draw influences from a lot of other games, it still manages to stand on it's own and feel original, and new. The only reason this game is receiving negative reviews is due to the drastic gameplay change from the first game, while I understand where people are coming from, I think it's great the Dev's are experimenting, It's good to switch things up or else it will get boring. Either way, I feel that this game is an underrated masterpiece, and regardless of were the series goes next, I have already become a life long fan. I wish there was a "must play" option for reviews cause no title fits this game any better.

I had played this game before picking it up on Steam and in the end I decided to do it through here as well, as I kinda miss it, I only had the base game, and it was stupidly cheap. As I usually do, I'm gonna start sharing what the game does wrong, then going up from there.
First and foremost, one of the worst parts of the game has to be the auto-battle option. You see, you'll be doing tons of big battles here, and if you feel like you don't need to oversee this one, you can just let the AI do it for you. However it seems the auto-battle AI is as brain-dead as Trump. I've lost quite a lot of battles because I had a ton of crap to fight and didn't wanna spend an hour doing them all properly. The last one being over 2k of my troops against 200 rebel peasants. F#CKING PEASANTS. AND MY TROOPS WERE HIGH TIER, WITH SIEGE UNITS AND EVERYTHING. HOW THE F#CK DID THAT HAPPEN!? It will make your playthroughs stupidly long, but I seriously advice you to not use that feature at all.
Second is something I'm still not a big fan of. At the start you only have three factions to choose, the three big families of rome (not counting the Senate). However there's a f#ckload of factions, to unlock them you must be the one taking their last area on the map. Why? Why not, for example, certain factions unlocking others at the end of a long game? This way you might unlock a few of them in one game, most likely the ones you don't really want, and will have to restart anew with a faction that's closest to the one you do like, putting yourself through with a faction you don't want.
Lastly, I feel like archers are a bit too powerful at times. Sure, heavy troops can tank those arrows and horse units can just sprint to them and whoop their asses, but then we got archers on horses and the whole balance f#cks itself. Elephants are also somewhat powerful since the auto-balance system doesn't seem to understand what the f#ck they do and usually win insane battles.
That being said, this is a really cool strategy game that still stands strong after all these years that will give you hours and hours of fun for a really low price.
The thing I like the most, strangely enough, is the realism and history stuff on it. It's actually kinda fun to sometimes stop and read all of the stuff the game has to tell you about troops, buildings and such. If you actually don't know much about the roman times, you'll learn a lot in here.
The strategy itself is also really cool. It's not one of those "send all of your troops against them blindly" kind of games. The game is surprisingly deep and there's tons of cool tactics you can use to win even the most harsh fights.
The amount of factions is also impressive for the time the game came off. There's like f#cking 40 or so, from all of those there HAS to be at least ONE you like.
Also, as dumb as it might sound, the dialogue from the captains before the fights are so well written, I can't help but to stop and listen to them constantly. Seriously, they had a blast with those.
Honestly, if you want Shogun 2 but you can't affort it, this is a really good alternative. On a sale it costs like 1 or 2€ and it's completely worth it. Though if you do have the money, I'd say give Shogun 2 a try instead.
TL;DR Edition: A classic that still stands strong by now. While Shogun 2 feels better, this one is way cheaper. If you enjoy hollywood-speeches, then it's already worth the purchase.

A game that explores the concept of death and its inevitability in the face of an indifferent universe. The game could have used more useful dialogue, actually exploring what the player felt, instead of simply exploring the overall tone. The actual game mechanics were unneccessary and felt disjointed from the overall tone the game presented. The game never really allowed the players to fully explore what the characters in the game actually felt. A game that was so emotionally charged could have used some of that to actually get a few messages across. Now then, back to what the game was about, the theme.
To fully feel what this game is, understand that the author had a near-death experince, which helped bring the game about. As such, the game is more of an interactive thought experiment, allowing the player to discover their own nature and feelings toward death, if they let it.
Imagine someone tells you that you don't have long to live, most likely due to a terminal illness. No matter what you do, you are unable to stop it death from coming, but you can postpone it. What do you do?
- Do you spend all your time trying to beat death, trying the newest in the medical fields in a search for a cure?
- Do you exercise day and night to strengthen your body and immune system, to have a chance at survival?
- Do you spend time with your friends, family, and possibly lover(s), to leave them with a shining, memorable piece of you before you go?
- Do you seek closure with those that you have known, trying to bring peace to those you've known?
- Do you seek closure for yourself, spitting on those who've wronged you, and giving the middle finger to the world that allowed you to die before you were willing?
- Do you make an effort to be remembered, pouring your last days into something worth noting in history?
- Do you write a book, pursue your hobbies, and try to die happy and fulfilled, doing the last few things you've always wanted to do?
- Or do you simply give up, knowing what is to come, and die on your own terms?
Death comes for all things. Some run, some hide, most try to postpone it and even reel against the knowledge, unwilling to go into and with that cold, unstoppable unknown. Others are completely unaware, and some are affected by it. Ultimately, all things leave this world, and the question of the game arises.
What would you do in the face of nonexistence?

So we're letting scammers (Chris Ferguson & Co), whose domain was at one point seized by the FBI, advertise their shady product on Steam? I'm talking about an organization that the U.S. Justice Department filed a civil complaint against for allegedly running a Ponzi scheme, and this is getting the stamp of approval from Valve - one of the most respected video-game businesses out there? This is perhaps the biggest example of why Steam Greenlight is flawed like a bottomless bucket. Get it out of here!
More information:

Before we continue we must ask ourselves: what is an experience? Not what is a game, because that is almost too broad to bother trying to put into words. But what is an experience? What is something you enjoy experiencing?
I cannot define this for all of you. An experience changes for each person- it is a variable that makes each person who they are.
Continue?9876543210 (wow that was fun to type out on the keyboard, I slid my finger down the number keys like some sort of badass) is definitely an experience. Whether it is a good one or a bad one is up to you. I personally felt like it made me think a lot about my life and what I take out of it, but I personally do not feel that much of the game other than the thought it provokes lives up to the price I paid for it, even at this discounted price of 8 dollars I paid for it. I personally think thinking should be free. What should be paid for is how the developer makes you think- either through visuals or audio or even story and gameplay.
The gameplay in this game is very basic. You run around and talk to people who usually just jabber on about strange things, but sometimes they open doors for you, and sometimes they sell you things. You are able to choose "lightning" or "prayer" when you enter these doors, and what these mean are up to the player to interpet, but what they do is either randomly spawn lightning to clear the path ahead or spawn a house in a town that is crucial to survive the later stages of the game. After 45 seconds to a minute though, garbage collection or something similar runs and takes you down to play a combat based minigame. After too many of these though, your game ends- but progressing to the next area resets this. So you are in a battle against time to progress to each area.
This gameplay sounds fine, but it is very repetitive. I was about to quit and take a break after the third one of these, but then I realized that there is no save feature in the game- the point is to play the game in one sitting it seems. And so I druged on (and how fitting to relate to the plot of the game), hoping the game wouldn't be TOO much of this. While the gameplay is unique and quirky, after the 3rd or 4th time through, it just gets old.
The music and the graphics are fitting to the theme of the game, but leave much to be desired. I found the graphics and music just plain boring to look at and listen to, and while there are some flashy scenes and very well done graphical choices during cutscenes, the levels look somewhat all the same in exception to a few that look amazing (the level where you're chasing down your reflections in the sea comes to mind) and in the end I just grew tired of it all very quickly.
It's very ironic that a game where you have to find peace with yourself grows harder and harder to get through. I found myself getting very bored with this game very quickly. But it's not about the game right? It's about the experience!
Well that my friends, I do not think is worth my 8 dollars. While it made me begin to think, I feel the game ITSELF did not make me think but rather the themes of it did. I apologize if that may be a mouthful, but it is hard to describe a game like this into words. In simpler terms, I feel like I could have just poked around the website of
and gotten the same feelings I did instead of playing the game. And for that, I do not give it my personal reccomendation.
But experiences change for everyone. Who knows? Maybe you will enjoy it more than I did.

Despite the big thumbs up, I wouldn't recommend the game at its full price. It's good but you can get a lot more with $10 on Steam.
As for the content itself, its atmosphere sort of reminds me of a 3D Sword & Sworcery. However, I found Sword & Sworcery to be little more than a collection of pixel art and mysterious but ultimately meaningless dialogue whereas I found Continue to have genuine meaning that you can connect to your own life. The gameplay is not the focus in either game, but it is at least entertaining in Continue. Where it really excels is in its metaphorical meaning,
It is more art than game, designed to make you think as you race against time to build up what resistance you can to a fate you ultimately cannot escape. There is little replayability; you will discover most of what the game has to offer in a few short playthroughs. But I wouldn't call that a fault considering the goal of the game is to explore a theme, not to provide hours of entertainment. If that doesn't appeal to you, then avoid the game; otherwise, it's something to look into.

A rich experience focused on the inevitable. You follow your main character's journey on the acceptance of his deletion by traveling and consulting with the inhabitants of other locales moments before their Garbage Collection. You have two primary options when speaking with the villagers, lightning or prayers. Lightning will help you escape the current level, or access secret areas that will aid you achieve your closure. Prayers will create a shelter based in your own town, which will protect the player from the deletion storm - literally lightning that deletes objects. Your ultimate goal is to survive long enough so the main character accepts his fate. The attitude at the time of their deletion depends on which villages you have been to, how many, and any "secret" areas you have been to which includes objects from your past and present.
The combat is fairly varied, but not overly complex. It does require skill, and this is certainly not a game you can skate by on without thinking what you are doing. To receive lightning or prayers from certain people, you might need to remember a fact about the town said by another villager. The combat can vary from side-scrolling challenges, to zelda-esque dungeon crawling, to arena "kill-house" style challenges. Depending how well you do can give you bonus lightning or keys which open doors in the villages, which allow you to speak to more villagers. I would advise against those who think the combat itself is the only reason to get the game- you will be dissapointed.
In addition to the combat and memorization, the skill of time-management is needed as well. Each village only has a certain amount of time before it's expiration. You have to prioritize what you need done. This is indicated by a countdown timer in the upper-right, once it hits zero there is a "stage" of degradation (Which varies how many there are by village). You will then enter a random combat scenario. Upon completion, you will return to the village which will have become slightly more hostile. Deletion monsters will roam the village which will delay you in your quest for shelter and closure.
It's an emotional ride that is open to your own interpretation. It does a grim subject matter well and was emotionally captivating enough to tug me along. And for that I am thankful.
Edit: Just would like to clarify on something some reviewers seem to have missed (Even though it's in the instructions). This game does have an auto-save feature each time you load a new area.

Shattered God - Quest For The Divine Relic has a couple neat ideas, but fails in most aspects.
This game is a mix between old school dungeon crawlers and RPGMaker style games. You walk around an overhead map until you enter combat, which is in a first person battle instance.
The exploration is very simple on the overhead map, you wander around, trying to avoid enemies sometimes and open chests for items, equipment and usable bits. Your character moves very slowly when walking, while sprinting looks janky and shakes the screen in an unpleasant way. Enemies have a detection field of view that you can avoid, if not it's onto combat.
The combat in the game is set in an instance that can be against one or multiple enemies, sometimes one at a time. It takes place in first person with you being required to swipe with your mouse across the screen for basic attacks and right clicking during certain moments in order to parry attacks coming your way. The combat is very basic and became boring after even the first three or four fights.
The controls in the game are awful, extremely bad. You are forced to use nonsensical keys, including most of your F1 - F5 keys to do basic functions. It doesn't help that hitting F4 will just close the game entirely without saving, so you could accidentally lose your progress.
There is no options menu in the game so you cannot rebind any of the controls. The game also only runs in one 4:3 resolution that you cannot change. It's 2017, why does this game run in 4:3?
I ran into an instance right at the start of the game where I was testing the combat on a training dummy, but since the dummy is invincible (like most games) I could never complete the battle and as far as I could tell there is no way to exit a battle after it starts. I had to use that F4 key to close the game and start all over with character creation.
The developer has made their own fantasy setting that weirdly straddles the line between serious and seemingly trying to offer some commentary I guess on women's/men's rights. I'm not entirely sure if that's accurate, but it seemed to be the case in the extremely long title crawl that talked about female gods, men not liking her or something and the word Meta as a name was thrown around a few times.
The game looks and plays like a flash game you would find on
five years ago. The artstyle is pretty ugly to look at and lacks imagination, like what someone would draw in high school. The art is inconsistant in quality, as is the dialogue in the game, which has frequent spelling and grammar mistakes.
Overall, Shattered God - Quest For The Divine Relic should probably have a home on itch.io or a flash game website instead of being available on Steam. I was bored of it within the first few minutes and it just lacks enough polish or good game design to be entertaining for long.

For what I expected it is terrible.
What it offers-
*Construction of your own decks. At the start of the game it has you choose a combination of two colors to create a deck.
*An insight to the story of the MTG universe for those that don't read the books.
*A tutorial to learning MTG and construction of MTG.
*A campaign expanding five planes with about five matches each. This totals to around 25-30 duels.
*Online competitive play with up to four people.
Pros-
*(Can be) cheap alternative to playing the actual card game.
*Construction of your own deck(s).
*Quick way to get some games in if you don't have people to play with or don't want to drive to a nearby MTG store.
Cons-
*No premade decks to play as. Only to play against. This forces you to grind up for your cards in order to play online efficiently.
*The deck building is pay to win. Premium boosters can be bought that include cards you cannot get normally. This is slightly adjusted as you can only have a certain number of copies for any one card (4 copies of any common, 3 for uncommon, 2 for rare, 1 for mythic).
*
This is the 2v2 mode that has been offered in every DOTP game until now and was a huge reason for me to buy it.
*The menus of the game are awful. I don't have too much of a problem with this because I use a keyboard but when I do I am easily frustrated.
*The decks you are given are just terrible. Consisting of only commons (from my experience) which requires you to get all of your good cards from boosters.
*Some of the opening draws you have will force you to restart the duel.
Overall, if your looking for a solo experience of playing against other players with a custom deck you may want to give this a try.
But if your like me (and many other MTG players) you will want to play this game 2v2 with your friend against others in two headed giant mode which this game DOES NOT OFFER. I could deal with every other flaw in this game if it had two headed giant but it does not.

It's Duke Nukem, nuff said. But seriousy, speaking as someone who had the game at launch, I loved the game. I expected to find my love mirrored when I went online, but it was not.
The Good: Duke himself. The witty one liners. The immature humor we're used to from Duke. I don't know why people bashed the game for that so much. That's how Duke has always been, why would he change now. If you don't like the humor because you're older and more mature now, fine, but don't knock the game for what the series has always been. That's like going to a bar and complaining that there's alcohol sold there. Was some of it predictable, yes, was it still awesome, yes! The graphics were pretty good to me (at least for the fact that it was in development hell for forever). The gameplay was pretty good with some issues pulling it down at times (see below).
The Bad: Some of the pacing for the game could have been adjusted. I could have stood for some more variety in baddies. I'm not sure about their choice of only being able to have 2 guns at a time. Part of me likes the idea, but part of me wants the old Duke that could carry an arsenal back. The levels could have been a little better, but were by no means horrible.
Summary: I loved the game. It had it's flaws, but if you can put asside the hype it is a good game. It is by no means perfect, but it's not as horrible as the mainstream reviewers would have you believe.

To some of the other reviews, which I feel have been unfair in some respects:
The game can be grindy, yes... But it does not take 30 real-life hours to build a shack.
All you need is skill in terraforming and construction (which are in the same line and unlocked almost instantly) and some primitive tools. If you know what you're doing (and it takes no time at all to know, if you youtube it), you can get a 3x4 plot of land flattened and build a shack in an hour, if even that.
Unless you're building on an extreme incline like a mountain side - which will of course be tons of work.
The game is kind of lame for a solo person unless you love to basically do nothing but build and survive - but that's not the true aim of the game, from what Iv'e seen and experienced.
You can be a lone wolf, yes, but on a server with a decent population it is often much easier to go it in a group.
The point of the game is to build a town/kingdom that is populated by real people that are ready to defend it, and real people that are ready to raid and conquer it. Teamwork is the key here, especially on servers that set the skill cap lower than maximum.
If you want a solo experience, you should go for a "themepark" MMO or a casual single-player voxel game such as Minecraft.
This game - a full-loot, free pvp crafting game with hunger mechanics, complex stats and a no-target combat system, is *not* a casual single-player experience. Don't fool yourself.
Would I enjoy more agressive NPC's that would give a real need to build defenses? Absolutely. But this is just not that kind of game, and there is honestly little need for it outside of a private, single-person server.
Between honorless theives, merciless raiders that want nothing more than to make you bleed and take your land and crafted items, and the ever-present possibility of betrayal from your own neighbors... This game utilizes the same hostile threat that so many others capitalize on - the most powerful, cunning, monstrous and challenging enemies of them all; other people.
And that is more than enough reason to build tall walls and secure storage buildings.
If you absolutely cannot wait for the MMO, buy the "Your Own" version now and get in a good server with decent admins. But be prepared for spurts of lag on higher populated and more developed servers, until they fix tree growth rates and tunnel lag. This current version is more of an isolated testing version in a smaller continent with smaller public and private servers, in which many people and guilds are using for training purposes to prepare for the release of the much larger MMO version.
But all in all, I reccomend this game for its unique and satisfying experience. Think "Wurm Online" with much more fun and heart-pounding combat, and way better graphics.

Kills me to say it, but I really cannot recommend this game.  I played the crap out of the first one, to the point of almost beating it on the absurd highest difficulty (I just refused to spend three hours fighting a single boss in one very tedious and badly-designed fight), but this is NOT the sequel to that game.
The humor from Wang is still there.  He still has a mouth and an attitude, and has tons of great comments as you go through the game.  That's where the similarities stop.
Here's a basic rundown of the major issues:
-the story here is only very loosely related to that of the first game, and all of the neat-looking storyboard-type cutscenes are completely missing
-the story itself is pretty minimal and uninteresting
-truckloads upon truckloads of crappy loot, so you spend way too much time sifting through garbage to find a stack of upgrades for your various weapons
-elemental enemy types and weapon types, which meshes terribly with the combat because big enemies can have resistances you don't know about until you stop and read their description IN THE MIDDLE OF COMBAT
-a lot more melee weapons, but the movesets are extremely limited
-WAY TOO MANY LOOT ITEMS.  Seriously.
-the visuals are TREMENDOUSLY busy; it is incredibly easy to completely lose targets in the middle of masses of particle effects, blood splashes, explosions, and garishly bright scenery
-very sloppy and unsatisfying combat
-bad level design; you're supposed to be maneuvering all over the place, but will CONSTANTLY be getting snagged on scenery
In all honesty, if the devs had replaced Wang with a different character, this have a tough time even being recognizable as something that's supposed to be a followup to the prior game.  Yeah, it's got a coop mode, but that's not much of a feature when nearly everything from the previous title was thrown out and replaced with some unpolished and terrible ideas.

Rome: Total War is an incredible game. I remember buying it discounted at EB Games and thinking 'I can play this for a couple of hours'. Oh, how wrong I was. I played over 150 hours in less than a year (not really an acheivement, granted) and enjoyed every moment of it. The game really put things into perspective for me. It showed me how the centuries-old Greek phalanx was finally swept aside by the Roman legions. Mind you, I was overpowered by them when I first tackled them as the Romans. My only proper disappointment is that Rome is overpowered (to be fair, it was at the time but not as much), Hellenistic pikes are underpowered and Egypt is anachronistic and overpowered.
All aside, I've spent much time playing this and have loved it. Nothing is more fun than tearing chariots to shreds with Spartan spears.

Shadow Warrior 2 makes me very conflicted.
Its got better swordplay, gunplay, amazing graphics, coop, and even more wang.
However, I can't help but feel the game lost some of its flair and style with the inclusion of these hub worlds. Shadow Warrior 2 was a great game, but the more I played the more I felt that the world was more bland not nearly as atmospheric as the areas in the first.
The new mind sidekick doesn't feel as interesting and her dialogue with Wang isn't nearly as dynamic and funny as Hoji's was in the first game. Maybe I haven't played enough but that's my opinion as of now.
I do not think this game needed to become a loot-and-shoot game. There's just something about it that just makes everything feel less rewarding and the menu even more cluttered. Shadow Warrior 2 should have stuck to the strengths of the first when it comes to the way progression is handled. In Shadow Warrior 2013 every time I started to feel bored, a brand new weapon that was completely different from everything else would show up, and usually a new enemy as well. In Shadow Warrior 2 however, you get so many drops and weapons feel like they drop at random, as a result you never get that feeling of excitement or satisfaction of feeling like you've progressed in the game, If that makes any sense.
Despite my overall negative opinions in this review, Shadow Warrior 2 is a great game with amazing graphics and tight gameplay. It's just not the game for me, and if you don't like the formula of shoot, loot, shoot, loot similar to Borderlands, then I don't think you will enjoy this game too much.

For the most part, this can be a fun game to sit down and shoot some AIs for half an hour or so.  It is nice to play a shooter with drop/wind balistics.  The X-ray vision mechanic that lets you watch your bullets smash the organs and bones of your targets is neato.
So what's the problem?  Those are the only things this game has to really recommend it.  The x-ray vision mechanic is the sort of thing that should be a real neat add-on but wound up being the only reason I kept playing the game past the one hour mark.  Everything else was a mess.
-The AI wavers between won't-notice-you-shooting-your-rifle-repeatedly-from-15-yards-away stupid to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t spots-you-and-headshots-you from-150-yards-in-0.01-seconds-as-you-sprint-past-a-3-inch-crack-in-a-wall.
-The rails on this game are extreme.  There is only 1 path to your waypoints.  Sneaking is not an option because of the afore-mentioned AI.
-For a game called Sniper Elite the ranges you almost always shoot from are not very impressive.  Often I had trouble finding a target that was more than 100 yards away.
-The story/campaign was short and very repetitive.  Its very possible to play through it in 4 hours, especially on lower difficulties.
-I would have preferred a game that had me being less of a kill everything supersoldier and more of covert sniper.

Kero Blaster is a side-scrolling action game, which constantly tries to fool you that it's shorter than it really is. At first it wants you to believe that there is only 4 levels in the game, then bam, it's actually 7, and then you find out that there is actually 7 more levels waiting for you in Overtime (or Zangyou) mode. If that's not enough, after beating Overtime mode you will also unlock New Game+, called Bonus (or Omake) mode.
The story of the game is pretty simple - you're a field technician who maintains teleporation devices throughout the world. Unfortunately, these teleportation devices are subject to some interdimensional parasites, which disrupt their work. So you have to reach a disrupted teleporter on foot, going from the nearest working teleporter, always through a very hazardous environment. It all starts simple, but things start to go downhill after your boss decides that having an interdimensional parasite as a pet is a good idea. Yeah, what could possibly go wrong? That's the plot for the first part of the game, the second part has its own plot, which is focused less on saving the day and more on the characters themselves, but I don't want to spoil it here for you.
So there are 14 levels in total, along with a New Game+. It needs to be said that levels share names and visual themes (except for the last one) between Normal Mode and Overtime Mode, but the level design itself differs more and more with each next level. Normal mode and Overtime mode also have different plots and different cutscenes between levels.
Level design is a really strong feature of this game. The levels are difficult, and require good platforming and shooting skills, along with quick decision-making, but you'll really appreciate cool moments of the level that you've experienced - the developer sure knows how to put your skills to the test. The good part is that, however unfair situation may seem, there is usally a key to resolve it easilly. As far as the difficulty curve goes - it's not that spiky, with Normal mode being a preparation for the real challenge in Overtime mode.
The gameplay goes as follows: you go through the level, divided by several stages. Each level has two bosses - a mid-stage boss and a real boss. Somewhere in the level you'll find a shop where you can upgrade your weapons, replenish / upgrade your lifebar, purchase extra HP tanks or buy a ridiculously priced 1-up (which is there mainly for players aiming to beat the game with no gameovers). To buy all of the above, you need money, so how do you get money? There are two ways. First way is a regular one - kill enemies, and they will drop coins (with rare variation of dropping health replenishment or even a one-up). Second way - explore the level and find secret spots and hidden passages, which will lead you to treasure chests / money safes with a substantial amount of cash.
Starting the level, you usually have three lives. Lose them all, and you'll have to start the level all over again, there are no save points to load from, like in Cave Story or even a checkpoint after mid-boss, you always start from square 1, which can get really annoying. The sour relief is that you won't have to beat the mid-boss again if you've beaten it already and you keep all your upgrades with you. The game also allows you to accumulate lives between levels, so you can save some up for hadrer parts if you're playing well on easier parts.
As far as visuals go, Kero blaster goes for a simpler style of early NES titles, like Metroid or Layla. This simplified style with vibrant colors and amount of visuals impossible for original era is actually very appealing to the eye. Additionally, it helps you to identify enemies and projectiles really fast, which is quite important. Also, as the game involves lots of coin-collecting, its developer made sure that coins look really nice and shiny, making you want to grab them, which is a nice touch.
Music gets you in the mood for the game, which exactly what is should do, but isn't something you would listen outside of the game.
For a platforming action game this solid, Kero Blaster has sold really poor, with SteamSpy estimating it around 13k at the time of reivew. If you want to play a hard, but elaborate and well-designed platformer, definetly give Kero Blaster a try.

This is a really fun and well-made little game that I would recommend to anyone who enjoys run-and-gun titles or action platformers. The game was developed by Studio Pixel, the practically one-man team behind indie classic Cave Story (one of my favorite games ever). Kero Blaster, as others have pointed out, is *not* Cave Story 2, so don't go in with that expectation. It's much more straight-forward and linear. But that's not a flaw! The game's goals are simple and sharp: fast-paced action, cool weapons, clever bosses, and a tough but fair sense of challenge. The graphics are cute but a little surreal and attractively weird, and the music is very catchy. The whole package is very much in the spirit of old school NES and Master System games like Mega Man, Contra, Wonder Boy, Adventure Island, etc. It’s not *quite* as hard as those games, but there are definitely some prickly stretches that you’ll need to retry over and over. The final level and concluding boss battles will definitely require all of your skills and some precise timing (I finally beat the last boss with just one heart left after a few dozen tries).
Now, while I definitely recommend the game, I do think that it's a little pricey for what it is. It’s a fairly short game; I beat it in about 6 hours, but maybe a fourth of that time was spent replaying the same levels as I grinded for money or just tried to get past a difficult platforming section or tough boss. If you’re a super-master at platformers like this, you’ll probably be done in no time. This doesn’t mean that the game isn’t fun or worth your while – it’s just that it’s short. There’s definitely some replay value here; the game has a few cool secrets and you unlock a special hard mode after you beat the game for the first time. If you found the basic game too easy and you like a challenge, you should enjoy that mode. There are also a few bonus stages, some other secret stuff, and a boss rush mode. This might be enough content to sell you on the game, but I can understand anyone who might feel that there just isn't enough here. If you're interested in the game, my advice would be to get it on sale.

Summary:
I can only recommend this game to you if you're a real Duels Of The Planeswalkers fanatic and can't live without the next installment. Other than that I feel like you'd probably be disappointed.
The Rest:
As an avid player of the previous 3 games in the series, I was hugely looking forward to this being released. I enjoyed the sealed deckbuilding in Magic 2014, and looked forward to having even more freedom with my decks in 2015. But having now played it, I feel that Magic 2015 is trying too hard to be Hearthstone, and without all the diverse prebuilt decks (not to mention the Two-Headed Giant and Challenge gamemodes) it gets pretty boring after only 5 hours of play, and probably less than that for some others. For me personally that's roughly 1/20 of my recorded playtime on any one of the previous three games, and I could probably still go back and play those some more.
With the complete lack of anything more to do now that I've finished the main Campaign mode, I have to say that it feels more like a demo or an early-access game than a full release title. It wasn't worth the money I spent preordering it, and it certainly isn't worth spending any extra money on Premium Booster Packs.
I hope that Wizards Of The Coast listen to my review, and others I've seen here on Steam, and bring out some sort of update for the game to bring back the long-term fun of the previous games. When they inevitably bring out an Expansion Pack and/or Deck Packs (or card-pool equivilents to Deck Packs) I will think twice about bothering with them this time around unless they make some big changes.
Maybe I'd see it as a better game on it's own, without having to live up to the previous games in the series. But unfortunately Wizards Of The Coast didn't have that luxury, and they've left this Magic: The Gathering fan feeling pretty much done with the Duels Of The Planeswalkers series.

I don't really find myself to be a fan of the horror genre.  That being said, I have somehow ended up with many different horror games, including Dead Space, Outlast, the FEAR series, and, of course, this game.  Of the games I listed, Amnesia: The Dark Descent has to be my favorite.  The atmoshpere is perfect throughout the game, especially in areas such as the Prison and the Choir.  There are a few jump scares throughout the game, which I don't like as much, but are fine in horror when limited, I just don't like the games that are completely based on them.  Amnesia is not one of these games, I find the atmosphere and the setting to be the main part of the horror, along with the stealth aspect of the game, where the main character has to hide in order to survive.  There is no charging through this game, the player must take their time in order to progress, but they cannot be too slow, otherwise the sanity bar drains, and the game gets creepier, hallucinations occur more, and sometimes the game actually changes.
The steam version includes the Justine Expansion, an hour long expansion with the luxury of choice in it, do you wanna be a jerk and let the people die, or save them?  It also includes a little thing called *Remember*, which I have not tried yet.  Both can be accessed through the settings configuration tool that is accessed during launchup.
Positives:
- Horror aspect not based on jump scares, like Slender was.
- It's actually creepy, and the environment is just unsettling.
- There is the perfect amount of the survival aspect- Monsters are an actual danger, and not just for appearence.  The monsters cannot be killed, with the exception of the water monster- the water monster can be killed by bashing it over and over with a box or barrel, until the yellowish blood can be seen and the activity stops.
- Custom Stories
- It gave me 8 hours of gameplay, which is pretty good for a linear horror game.
Negatives:
- I find there to be a lack of replayability in the game.  I've beaten it once, and I don't really need to play it again.  That being said, I'm attempting a speed run soon.  I basically just contradicted myself there, but I'm not gonna play it again without some sort of challenge for myself

This review will primarily be a comparison between this title and the older iterations.
Pros: New cards and mechanics.  New campaign story.  Fully customizable decks as opposed to premade decks with a certain degree of customization.  Booster-pack-style unlocks allow faster progression toward having all the cards available through progression.
Cons: Bright white interface and transitions are not easy on the eyes.  Game gives you one deck's worth of cards and forces you to either run through the campaign with it or shell out more money to unlock additional cards.  Booster-pack-style unlocking makes acquiring specific deck improvements a matter of money or time and luck.  Sound and damage effect animations appear entirely unchanged from Magic 2014.  Ads are still displayed at launch but also sometimes appear before a match.  Certain animations and controls during matches are sluggish, such as transitioning to and from combat and trying to un-zoom from the graveyard browser.  Lastly, it has been recited ad nauseum, but: lack of Two-Headed Giant game mode, or anything besides campaign, practice, and free-for-all multiplayer.
TL;DR: Consider getting/sticking with 2013 or 2014, much more entertainment and less headache for the money.

Magic 2015 is everything to be expected from the yearly releases of DotP, and better. Going through the tutorial (skipping it, been playing MTG for 10 years now) and picking a deck to play with for the non-scripted match and Innastrad was fun because I didn't know what the deck was going to be like because all it did was let you choose the colors that it was going to be. After you beat Innastrad, you get access to the rest of the pre-made decks (which many reviews have been complaining about) and able to make your own deck, or edit the pre-made ones the game came with.
Many people in their reviews also complained about how the decks now work. Instead of getting a card for the deck you just won with, you get a booster with 3 cards for any of your decks that you play with. Or you can buy boosters for a few bucks, which many have been complaining about making it, 'pay-to-win' or you  are grinding for hours to get cards to upgrade your deck. In reality, this is the exact same system that was in the previous games. Either you are stuck grinding a deck to get cards for it, or you can pay a little extra money to unlock the full deck instantly.
The starting decks aren't bad either, while many people may complain that they are, and are also getting smashed '9/10 times on the easiest setting because the AI cheats' The AI doesn't cheat, you suck at Magic. I have only lost once in 2015 so far, on planeswalker difficulty, which was my first time against Avacyn, and the second time I faced her, I smashed, loosing little life. During these games, I have also mulled down to 5 twice and still won, making it so that you don't need 'a great starting hand to win.'(Those were also with the starting deck) In the previous games, all cleared on planeswalker difficulty, I rarely lost as well. Anything that can happen in a real game, playing with real people, can happen in this game.
I feel like this is going to be the best game in the series. I can play how I want to play with the deck I want. It has answered so many fans by allowing deck building and figured out a way to reward players fairly with the boosters. While some boosters may give you a card you need/want, and others won't. This adds more strategy to a highly stratigic computerized card game, where in the previous ones I was playing more on "luck" with the strongest pre-made deck there was in the game.
This is an awesome game for the series. For people that have been playing MTG for a while, they will like being able to build a deck with and have more strategy when playing again either an AI or another player. While this game may feel like Magic Online, just remember they are putting more money into that than you are into this, and Magic Online has a way bigger card library than this game.
Also, if you are having trouble with the clunky menus, try a better computer, I'm running this game with no issues with gameplay or the menus.

ULTRA VIOLENCE and strategic depth to the max!
WARHAMMER 40,000 SANCTUS REACH is everything i could hope for in a Warhammer 40,000 game. It has awesome audio and voice work with inspiring epic war cries and agony filled death filled moans.
Music is top notch excellence alive with ground thumping troop stomping tribalism encased in the armor of classical music as if coming from the very earth with eerie whispers and chant like rhythms.
Graphics are euphoric to experience with incredible detail to units as if playing with tabletop minitures and blissful levels of visual carnage including bodily dismemberment capturing the extreme gore in all its grim ghastly heroic godliness like no other Warhammer game has since Chaos Gate. The user interfaces and different menu screens are all professionally done with stunning art work giving off the perfect mood of the game world's reality.
Optimisation is on the money with everything working flawlessly. The stats and modifiers richness making for game balance which feels miraculous in its execution as i command huge numbers of troops who use morale, cover and terrain with different height levels keeping me smiling and wide eyed like the happiest kid in the world as i have a unit of Space Wolves take a flamethrower to green orky flesh.
When am setting up a attack its very easy to see what the possible outcomes are with all the on screen information giving a very natural elegance and sense of what is going on. Game mechanics are in the style of BATTLE ACADEMY with plenty of morale checks reminding me of STEEL PANTHERS with all the mayhem and chaos going on in the battlefield. Using squares instead of hexes for movement does not feel odd actually feeling quite natural with a game mechanic where you can turn your units facing to focus its attention in a certain direction.
When all my movement and action points are used the game lets me know with a bullet icon above the unit which is great for avoiding second guessing. There is also a button on the ui which takes you to the next available unit awaiting orders. For an ocean's worth of information there is a tactical mode which will reveal all sorts of info about what is going on in the field. Scale feels more personable so am assuming its squad based or in the same style of BATTLE ACADEMY.
Gameplay is more tactical with morale, type of weapons and their range, different terrain types with many variables for cover all effecting situational awareness and combat outcomes. Terrain and certain types of cover can also be destroyed by weapons fire.
Troops gain experience and eventually level up where they become more efficient and deadlier combatants. Between battles such as during deployment you can see how much more experience is needed to level up and if one is acquired the game will let you know so there is no searching huge numbers of your men to see who has leveled up. All armies including the enemy can suffer from friendly fire which can lead to some funny moments when a sure kill ends up taking out one of your own units as well.
Unit characteristics are on the mark with everything feeling as powerfully epic as it should with Terminators kicking humongous tail and Gretchins getting some love being a threat and sinister distraction as cannonfodder.
Sanctus Reach also reminds me alot of Final Liberation from the 1990s with its variety of troops and how many are on the battlefield at the same time including the massive ground cracking monolithic Dreadnoughts.
Another cool thing about SANCTUS REACH is seeing individual men and orks die as the unit is worn down by long range and melee fire giving a sense of accomplishment with each shot or melee attack that hits.
WARHAMMER 40,000 SANCTUS REACH feels like the spiritual successor to the 1990s classic FINAL LIBERATION while still being its own complete different animal a proud wolf bringing home the joy of tabletop gaming nirvana like no other Warhammer game before. I cant believe something this perfect is selling for such a low price.
WARHAMMER 40,000 SANCTUS REACH, BUY IT! PLAY IT! Feel the adrenaline happiness the uncontrollable gaming smile of satisfaction absolute upon your face FOR THE RUSS! FOR SLITHERINE!!! AWOOOOOO!

In my opinion, this is the definitive tournament shooter out there. The sequel, Unreal Tournament 3, was decent but the developers seemingly focused on extracting the best visuals from the Unreal engine and sacrificed on features and gameplay. Then of course there was Quake 3 which was awesome in its own right but just didn't seem to have as much to do.
My only complaint about this game is the lack of modern resolution support. You will need to manually edit a configuration file in order to play with widescreen resolutions. This isn't a problem and is a one time fix per installation but still...if there was ever a game in need of a 'remastered' version, this is it.
The legendary Unreal AI makes another appearance and doesn't fail to impress. You have a good dozen or so difficulty choices so the single player mode can provide a proper challenge for just about anyone out there.
As I mentioned above, the gameplay and features are second to none in the 'tournament shooter' genre. You have your classic deathmatch and team deathmatch modes. You have capture the flag and vehicle combat. You have node capturing styles of play like that made famous by the Battlefield series. There are some other gameplay modes that may be more unique to Unreal but my overall favorite is the "football" style mode in which you can either jump/fall through the goal with the ball for 6 points or fire the ball through the goal from afar for 3 points. Truly unique.

Shadow Warrior 2 makes me very conflicted.
Its got better swordplay, gunplay, amazing graphics, coop, and even more wang.
However, I can't help but feel the game lost some of its flair and style with the inclusion of these hub worlds. Shadow Warrior 2 was a great game, but the more I played the more I felt that the world was more bland not nearly as atmospheric as the areas in the first.
The new mind sidekick doesn't feel as interesting and her dialogue with Wang isn't nearly as dynamic and funny as Hoji's was in the first game. Maybe I haven't played enough but that's my opinion as of now.

Shadow Warrior 2 should have stuck to the strengths of the first when it comes to the way progression is handled. In Shadow Warrior 2013 every time I started to feel bored, a brand new weapon that was completely different from everything else would show up, and usually a new enemy as well. In Shadow Warrior 2 however, you get so many drops and weapons feel like they drop at random, as a result you never get that feeling of excitement or satisfaction of feeling like you've progressed in the game, If that makes any sense.
Despite my overall negative opinions in this review, Shadow Warrior 2 is a great game with amazing graphics and tight gameplay. It's just not the game for me, and if you don't like the formula of shoot, loot, shoot, loot similar to Borderlands, then I don't think you will enjoy this game too much.

I'm a TT gamer and played the 40k TT for several years, i always craved a game that could give me the same sensation. I tried Dawn of war, not my cup of tea. I don't want to build a base everytime i play just to use all my units, and if i take my time the enemies get annoying fast. I still played it but it never quite scratched the itch i had, so i kept looking over the years.
Over time i made a mental list of things that appealed to me and tried to find games to scratch them off, but it was rare. For refrence my list is pretty much.
- Buying units from a list, i want to be able to customise my army and have to think about my choices. I don't want a game that lets me throw units away just to churn out new ones like an endless factory.
- Turn based so you can think things through with no stress, i much prefer this type of games.
- Tactical combat system, Xcom has it down great. Cover, AoE attacks, armor, piercing values and Morale
- Isometric view or 3rd person view that shows animations in combat, don't really find games like armageddon brings that thrilling combat.
- The feel, this is a hard one. It's about the feeling of having heroic battles between armies and that grimdark thing that is warhammer.
I stumbled on this game mostly thanks to my own army on the TT being Space wolves. I always check games with my army of choice in it, i wasn't expecting much. Initial looks made my interest grow, the units looked pretty much like my own real models. I looked deeper by checking youtube and videos.
- There is a points buy system. This is so very rare
- It's turn based. Also rather rare
- It has board like maps, terrain from the TT, tons of units from two armies
- Tactical options, Cover that will influence shots, AoE weapons that can break Morale and make enemies useless, Heroes and huge sized units that are powerful.
Really this game ticks of almost all my boxes, it's a blast to play for me.
There is issues of course but the developers are really responsive and friendly, they are updating rather quickly for such a small team. So all Credits to them for such a undertaking.
Now I do have some downs with the game too, there is no dice rolling it's percentage based maths instead. No customisation on units, can't change weapons or anything. No real flying units apart from orcs that seem to have a chopper, no rune priest for Space wolves (Psyker)
Almost all missions in the game are "Take all victory points, whoever holds most at end of game wins" Wich you basically just ignore and table the enemy.
There is so many possible missions they could add here, like every victory point held could instead give you points at the end of your turn. Victoy achived when certain point limit reached or whoever has most at the end of the game.
More ideas like mission to recover a specific relic or unit that the armies will fight over, whoever has it for X amount of turns wins or gains x amount of victory points. Killing units should award victory points, and give bonus for killing big units.
Maybe even take more pages from TT with mission objectives that generate at the start of each turn giving you small goals to accomplish for victory points? This is the major downside for me in the game but it's quite easily fixed with future addons or patches so my hope here is strong.
I can also add that they also made much smaller units. No 10 man marine squads here, it's 3 guys in regular squad that also fire 3 times each. So it's very different in that aspect, but it still retains the overal feel of a unit.
There is another big thing i wish they had done different, unit Customisation. I love the aspect of the TT to be able to change weapons on my squad, giving a leader a power fist or a flag that improves his unit. This is missing alltogether in the game, the devs state they want units to be a clear role and not make it possible to dilute. I think this is a mistake on their part, customisation is a great reason for people to play again and again just to try different things. I also feel this extends to Heroes who sometimes feel much too weak for their titles, the best heroes are definetly up there as good units but the cheaper ones are borderline useless. Maybe if they had allowed heroes to join regular units it could have been different.
Anyway to summarise, you want a game that feels like the TT? This game is in my opinion the closest you can get. You want a Turn based Warhammer game with point buy system? This is the game. The game suffers some AI Issues and there is still several key units missing that i hope will get added later, but this is a fantastic game for it's price and is an amazing base to further expand upon in the future.
Despite the couple flaws it has i still very much reccomend it to any turn based gamer and warhammer lover.

Shadow warrior 2 released and it was one of my most anticipated games of this year, and I can honestly say that I'm not dissapointed. So I decided to do my very first review on this game.
Shadow warrior 2 is a very good game but it does have its flaws.

*Pros:*
- Really fast and satisfying gameplay
- Well put together enviroments
- Good enemy variety
- Great graphics, though some of the npc's you talk to look pretty bad
- Nice amount of weapons (72 weapons I believe), and good variety between these weapons too
- Really funny and entertaining protagonist
- Decent story for a fps game
- Well optimized
- Good replay value, eventhough most of the replay value is because of the combat
- Cheaper than most bigger releases
*Cons:*
- Boss fights are pretty forgettable, except for the last one because that one has an amazing soundtrack
- The UI is overall decent but the gem UI is a mess (mostly because of the overabundance of gems)
*Other mentions:*
- The CO-OP is a very nice edition to this game, but as it is right now it does need fixing as it is pretty unstable
- The game does have replay value, but something like mod tools or just a horde mode would definitely improve the replay value even more.
- The game is pretty easy, even on the higher difficulties. But this may differ for other people so that is why it is not a con nor a pro
- The loot system is a nice addition I personally think (I love diablo and borderlands, so that is expected), but it does hurt the pasing of the game a bit. It might have been better if the weapons you loot had fixed stats and that you could've upgraded them souls style (like Lil Wang +1, +2, etc.)
Overall this is an excellent game and I wholeheartedly recommend to buy this game, it does have its flaws as stated but it is still a nice package especially for the price.
Any constructive criticism and or feedback for my review are welcome.

DBB is your basic 2-6 player (there is NO single player at all. Please don't forget this) fight to the death brawl game with a ton of game modes, fun retro graphics and a great little soundtrack.
There's a little tutorial stage that teaches you about movement, attacking and everything else you'll need to know (if your friends will stop killing you long enough for you to read) then you're ready to play. If you're not one for reading all the game modes there's a handy little 'game mode collection' which puts you into different modes every round so you don't have to constantly cycle through the main menu.
There are SO MANY weapons, both ranged and melee so you can try and dodge and fire from a distance or rush in and facesmash depending on how you feel like playing. Each weapon has a different attack style (some have knockback, some require charging up and others require you to be stationary) and different special attacks which you build by dealing damage to other players and you can unleash them once your special bar is full dealing devastating damage to those who were foolish enough to remain in your way.
There are a lot of stages and these change between rounds so it doesn't ever feel repetitive. Some are as simple as just being multiple levels, whilst others have lava pouring down, or spikes periodically coming out of the grounds and/or walls. This adds a tiny bit more of a challenge to the game as you don't just have to watch out for your opponents, but also your environment.
My only issue with the game was I had a little trouble getting my controllers to work. Xbox One controllers don't seem to work at all rendering two of my remotes completely useless but the Steam controller and Xbox 360 both worked fine so I was able to play without issue once I plugged those in. The developer was quick to reply when I asked for help though which was a huge plus!

Definitely a departure from the original series and even the reboot before it. All of the one-liners, gunplay, and wacky stereotypes are still there for hardcore fans, but there's been a few changes this time around that change up the formula.
The game doesn't operate on a campaign structure, it's a long campaign with a hub area and missions you accept from within it. I see a lot of people comparing the gameplay to Borderlands but it's really a sparse resemblance. The levels in the game use tilesets with big chunks that get randomly put together, meaning you'll see a lot of familiar areas, but the layout of each area changes mission-to-mission.
The loot works the same way. Chests and stuff contain random loot a-la Diablo, and weapon upgrades are all random little tidbits.
Because of how reliant on upgrades weapons are, it DOES suck sometimes to get weapons that look badass, only for them not to be useful for a while until you upgrade them well.
If the above doesn't deter you and you're wanting a fast-paced FPS with cheesy humor and a load of awesome looking weapons, give it a try.

Kero Blaster is a game that was suggested to me based on my ongoing search for run and gun shooters.  It was created by Pixel (Daisuke Amaya), the same man that brought Cave Story to the world.  Anyone looking for something like Cave Story should turn away immediately.  This isn't to suggest Kero Blaster is a bad game, but rather that it's not an action platformer in the same vein as Metroid.  It's a linear platformer somewhat closer to Mega Man and Contra, but not notably similar to either of those series.
The player takes the role of a frog employed in the custodial sciences department of Cat & Frog Inc.  He is tasked to clean transporter rooms in several different areas. As he makes his way through each stage he obtains new weapons and collects money that can be used to purchase additional health and upgrades.  Kero Blaster's story is bizarre and the game contains many references to the work culture of Japan.  It's fairly humorous, but you might want to read up on the concept of a salaryman in order to better understand everything.  This is even more true if you're playing Zangyou mode, which is definitely something you should do.
Kero Blaster is a relatively short game, doubly so if you only play through on the normal difficulty.  Zangyou mode (zangyou is Japanese for overtime) unlocks after completing normal and is the game's version of a hard difficulty setting.  It acts as a continuation of the normal mode story line and features different bosses and more challenging stages.  If you skip it you're missing half the game.  After Zangyou mode there is also an Omake mode which features a boss rush.  The whole thing can probably be completed in approximately eight hours.  I ended up with a much longer play time because I did all of the achievements except Jacket Rush.  It was a lot of fun and I highly recommend doing it if you're looking for a little more of a challenge than what the game offers by default.  It's probably worth  mentioning that the achievement descriptions for “Save the Gas” and “Cost Effective” are misleading.  The challenge for those two is to beat the game without upgrading beyond two heart containers. “Perfect Attendance” and “Instant Salary” require beating the game without getting “wiped out” which actually means that you can't get a game over if you want them.
Other than questionable achievement text, the game doesn't have many other flaws.  The graphics are simplistic, fitting of the style, and at times sport a surprising amount of detail.  The controls were a little tricky to get used to at first.  The floaty nature of jumping and the way the direction the frog is facing can be locked while firing was a little strange.  Once I got used to it I thought it was fine though.  I'm sure it must be possible to play with a keyboard and mouse but I recommend using a gamepad.  Lastly, the soundtrack is well done and has a few catchy tunes.
Overall, Pixel did a great job with Kero Blaster.  It's a somewhat short but unique and memorable experience that provides a reasonable amount of entertainment for the price.  There is a solid challenge here, particularly for those that wish to do the jacket achievements.  I'd recommend Kero Blaster to anyone looking for some retro style platforming action, people grinding away their days in soulless corporate desk jobs, and those that believe frogs should wear jackets.

For many fans, Rome: Total War will always be the greatest achievement in the series. It is the game that laid out the foundations of every TW game that would come after, and the basic structure that was built in 2004 hasn't ever changed.
For me, the game still holds up. It looks great! And the Total War 2 engine, which both Rome and Medieval II use, actually has far more realistic combat mechanics and atmosphere than the TW 3 engine that subsequent games have used.
A feature I love, which disappeared from every subsequent game, is the ability to look at your cities on the battle map and see them change as you develop them. Even little citizens walk the streets. Why did this disappear?
The UI is dated for sure, but the bones are solid. The game play of the series hasn't really evolved much, not that it needs to, making Rome still very accessible to the modern TW fan. The music is some of the best in the series too.

I'd consider AMNESIA: THE DARK DESCENT a masterpiece. It's not perfect by any means but it over achieves that what it initially wanted to achieve: Being scary/creepy. Amnesia is a game that is not just scary while you are playing the game. It's even scary when the game is turned off. It has that horror that lingers around long after you stopped playing. Amnesia is a game that makes you feel uncomfortable and addicted at the same time. You don't want to keep playing because it's not really fun (in a traditional sense), but at the same time you want to keep playing because you want to explore more of castle Brennenburg and you want to know more about Daniels backstory. And those are the 2 things that make a horror game a GOOD horror game:
1.) Horror that lingers around, even if you are not playing.
2.) The game is intriguing but not intriguing at the same time.
AMNESIA: THE DARK DESCENT succeeds in those 2 points. The eerie and dark atmosphere, the H.P. Lovecraft like story and the superb sound design make this game stand out from the horror-game crowd. I love it and so should you!

Shovel Knight is a 2d platformer with retro graphics. But it is not simply nostalgia bait, it takes the best parts of 2d platformers and adds its own twists to game mechanics. It also has a lot free added content over the years, showing the devs' love and support for this game.
You play as shovel knight, whose main feature (the shovel), defines the combat and movement in the game. You use the shovel to dig up loot, bounce on enemies and scoop up objects to throw at targets (there are more uses to this shovel, and it is affected by the maps themselves). The combat is very reminiscent to that of castlevania games.
Your quest is to battle bosses with their own quirky abilities in their own quirky maps similar to that of megaman, in order to stop an evil enchantress.
The levels are challenging, but can be tackled using a variety of abilities you gain as you progress through the game. It features a Souls-like system where you lose your gold upon death, but have a chance to be retrieved.
Rather than making the game retro for the sake of being retro, the game features a beautiful art design made through the retro style it went for. In fact the style Yatch Club went for probably took a lot more effort than other digital art alternatives.
The music is done by talented composers, Manami Matsumae and Jake Kaufman. Matsumae made music for the megaman games and Kaufman made music for a lot of games, a few favorites of mine are from Double Dragon Neon and Crypt of the NecroDancer. The soundtracks are great, some of which are very popular uploads on youtube; check out Flowers of Antimony!
The story itself is pretty straightforward, however the stories for The Plague of Shadows and Spectre of Torment dlcs are very enjoyable. If you enjoyed the main game I highly recommend these two dlcs, and they're free too!
For a platformer game, this deserves a 9/10

Between the description of the game and DLC, I was lead to believe it would unlock additional cards not included in the base campaign. As it turns out, it only unlocks all the cards already in the campaign for free for you, after defeating the first chapter.
I would not recommend the DLC or Special Edition.
As for the base game, it does include an open deck editor. The problem is you don't really get much more customization then previous iterations of the series, So long as you are focused on one or two colors your options for synergistic cards aren't really much better than the old closed deck system (Re: Actually feels like less choices). In addition, you appear to be locked into a single deck after selecting a color at the beginning. This lead to a little frustration as the last fight in the first chapter included a hard counter to my choice and lead to several restarts before a victory was possible with the cards available.  Normally such a challenge would prompt me to switch to a different color deck, change my playstyle, and unlock more cards for a different deck. (In previous DotP games) however here I was forced to face roll and restart-mulligan my way to a cheap victory. And now if I want to switch to a different color, It appears I would have to do up to 60 random encounters to unlock all the cards I would want for the deck first, (At least I assume thats how it would work, I never got to unlock singles from exploring because of the DLC deception)
In addition to this, its is impossible to complete the entire card library without dropping even more money on now RANDOM card packs as some cards are exclusive to Premium Packs available for $1.99 each. (12% of cards can only be bought) Buying new decks was acceptable in my books, but random cards? I would rather play physical magic or MTGO.
The UI while stylish is a pain to navigate, you are unable to see all the options without scrolling through them one by one. Automatic land tapping is a joke, you have to turn it off and tap manually or it will lock out colors needlessly which wasn't an issue in previous games. The tutorial was much more in-depth this time around, but it felt very long even when skipping through all the dialouge and several times it missed easy damage or had sub-optimal plays that might lead less experienced players into bad habits.
If you don't already own Duels of the Planeswalkers, I would probably buy a previous years version over this one.

While I do have a few minor discrepancies with this title, it's both largely enjoyable and immersive. The capability behind building your own deck from a complete list of cards was long awaited and well received. The card list that we've received is also quite expansive, as far as I can see, which means we've been presented with a myriad of options: they're thinking about the individual.
You do begin the game with a rather poor choice of pre-built decks, but I think that's part of its 'magic'; from the get go, you're tested to use what you've got at your disposal. You start off as, assumingly in the game's context, an inexperienced or at least unknown planeswalker, who then begins to gain the admiration of others, and through a series of challenges, eventually becomes much, much more powerful.
While I've only just begun playing, and I will continue to do so, I am definitely pleased with the new layout; the fresh and very slick colour scheme is striking and strongly representative of the outlying story. The menus do still retain some clunky-ness from its predecessors however, but that doesn't remain a constant issue.
It's also a great title for someone who would only just be immersing themselves into online Magic. The introductory tutorial is very thorough, which aptly pairs with a title focused on the Core Set release; you could argue it's somewhat designed to condition these potential new players.
I've yet to go through some of the features of the game, but I can assure you that it is an improvement. While I'll admit I did enjoy playing around with the preconstructed decks of the various Planeswalkers in M14 DotP, what you receive here in sheer versatile is indomitable.
For those who did not order the Complete Edition, you'll be unlocking the cards throughout the campaign. Think of this as your reward system. I loved seeing what new cards could be added after going through things and trying a little hard. I do think there was a strong drawback in making 88% of the card pool available to players who have the Complete Edition after defeating the Innistrad boss, but that's more likely my personal preference.
I will agree that unfortunately, like the last instalment, there's a large emphasis on simply purchasing the cards like there was with the sealed slots in M14 DotP. However, there's no real reason to purchase them, as they can be very simply unlocked by going through and duelling. We need to keep in mind that WotC are a profitable company, and that of course they're going to want people to buy things. As consumers, you have the choice whether or not you pay the extra for your quick fix.
Whether you're a long-running fan of the game, or just looking to start up, this is a wise decision. However, if you aren't willing to overlook a few flaws, then no, you won't be able to appreciate or enjoy it. Just remember that no game is perfect, some get pretty close, and this one is definitely not subpar.
