After starting a second playthrough I have a few edits to make...
Before reading this reveiw please know that i have not played with multiplayer so i cannot tell how well it works.
If you have already played shadow warriors one and want to play the next game in the series it is important to know that this game is vastly different than the first.  This game has a large focus on loot and trying out new combinations of weapons and upgrades.  If you are looking for a straight up run and gun then you may want to look elswhere, because managing loot is vital for victory especially on harder difficulties.  I personally liked the loot and constant change of weapons and upgrades, but it will not be for everyone.
The mission structure is also very different from the first game.  You start out in a hub town where you can buy or sell various items as well as upgrading your gems later in the game.  You will accept all of your main and side missions in this hub area and then teleport to the mission of your choice.  The side missions are ok, some being more memorable than others.  The story is good and even if you have not played the first game lo wang will explain most of the major plot points that you missed.  The humor is hit or miss, but if you liked the humor in the first game it didn't change much here.
Now the map layout is actually quite good for a randomized system.  Even in missions that have cutscenes foes can start at completely different place than the last time you visited the area and it can easily change how you will handle bosses.  The enviornments are all very well done and do a great job of giving the feeling that this game has it's own world.  Some story and side mission maps add specific features that change the normal layout of the map.  That being said, you will see the same maps ALOT.  While the random layout each time you play is nice and defenitely adds more replayability to the game it would be nice to see a few more enviornments.
The gameplay is soild with tight controls and swords that are actually usefull.  The wierdest thing about the gunplay is that none of the weapons have any recoil; this may be a familar felling to those that have played other twitch shooters but may feel offputting to a COD player.  The combant requires quick movements and an infinite dash lets you quickly move around the feild like an annime ninja.  The story and side missions let you test your skills on several interesting bosses and mini bosses.  Several enimies will be superior or elite enimies that have extra powers and resistances that their lesser counterparts do not have.  Lastly and perhaps most importantly... I really, REALLY would like to see some endgame content besides endgame plus.  Some sort of endless dungeon mode and perhaps some extra challenging raid levels would be an awesome additon.
Now for a pros, cons, and netural list:
Pros:
Good random maps
Loot and upgrades
Quick and tight gunplay
Decent story
Beautiful enviornments
Good boss battles
Side quests are worth doing
Cons:
NEEDS ENDGAME CONTENT BESIDES NEW GAME PLUS
Weird faicial annimations during cutscenes
More maps would be appreciated.
Neuteral:
Lo Wang humor
Overall a good game that is vastly different from the first.  If this game could fully embrace the true feeling of a dungeon crawler and twitch shooter hybrid I think it would be even more of a hit.   I personally would recomend this game, especially if DLC adds more maps and endgame content.

Now if this combat system of Shadow Warrior 2 with its weapons are added to the first game, with bigger levels and Every single enemy of both Sahdow Warrior one and two.. you will have a game of the year title even the Nay sayers wont hesitate putting down the full price to.

I feel like this is a game that plays precisely as it was designed. To elaborate, many reviews point out issues that do exist in the game, but were placed there as being historical details. Cavalry are poor in direct combat, warfare can seem like a ponderous meat-grinder, artillery is viciously deadly, and the mechanics are genuinely difficult for someone more used to RTS games set in more modern eras.
Ultimate General: Gettysburg is NOT an easy game to get into, but it's a fun game if you're interested in the era, and if you're willing to sustain terrible, grievous casualties while you're getting the hang of it. It was crafted with a great attention to detail that someone far more knowledgeable than me will probably appreciate, and it can give you a great appreciation for the bravery of the men who fought the war in reality.
It's a difficult sell, but if it's on sale I strongly recommend it. I feel like I would've gotten my money's worth at $15.

The game runs well under steamos, however the game mechanics are just weird. For example it takes some getting used to the time taken to reload the weapons. The terrain is a shambols, they seem to make little or no difference whatsoever to the game other than if you're behind a hill you can't see your enemy and they cannot see you. The artillary are ineffective at any range and they do too little damage, and are wildly inaccurate. Artillary should be more area effect. Even with a direct hit they don't do much.
There doesn't seem to be any control over what you attack, units just do their own thing. Another issue is that you can't kill an enemy division. At all. Like you can get an enemy down to 10% then they just run for it and regroup. You can't charge them because they run faster than you. As a result of any enemy get behind your lines, there's literally nothing you can do other than just let them get on with wiping out your entire artillary deployments because you just cannot kill them. Even if you threw every regiment in your army at that division it will not die. I just don't understand the logic of this, is this deliberate? Is it a bug? I don't know!
I also prefer a rectangular unit select. I really don't like drawing squiggles around the units I want to select. It's just a faff. The other thing is the time it takes for units to respond. Charge doesn't seem to do anything at all, other than run and then when you get there stand there like lemons, ignore the enemy and die. If I am in charge of an army, i expect them to do what i say, now, and fight to the death to hold positions etc. There doesn't seem to be any tactical bonuses for flanking the enemy or attacking from behind either. Or any bonuses for massively outnumbering an enemy.
The game does have strategic elements that I like, but they are too weakly emphasized. Like in the game "Dark Reign" for example, when you tell a unit to stop, it stops, and it does not fire. If you tell it to stop and fire, it will do so without moving. If you tell it only fire when fired upon, it'll only return fire.  With this game, there's just no control. You're forced to micromanage a load of units that run away at the first sign of trouble and have no common sense. Even worse, there's no way to control them and prevent them doing stupid things. Like how do you target specific enemies for example?

Tears of a dragon is a classic rpg game set in the style of the first final fantasies. it has an overdrive system similar to ff8 and the story is based around a mercenary known as savage dragoon (the creator) throughout the game you progress through his journey of self conflict where he is at war with his inner demon. personally find it quite a strong message and really love the fact the developer has included myself among others who have supported him through the game. I have had the pleasure of testing the game through its start and to see all the progress that has been in the game was truly inspiring and couldnt be more greatful.
I would highly recommend this game to all rpg fans as there are multiple ways of playing the game (trying not to spoil it for those who haven't) the game touches on different forms of gameplay. Good stuff about the game below. Will update this as more updates come.
Right now I'm guessing it's maybe 1% finished. The only content in the game are maps and cars (of which 99% is made by community). But the core is there. Also there are a couple of missions and races to try after the last big update.
There are some amazing vehicle mods out there. And there are a lot of fun maps, too. Most people MIGHT get bored from the current state of the game though because there is almost nothing to do: You just load a map, choose a car, and crash it as you please. Or don't. You can drive around if you want. That's it. Oh you can add a stupid AI to follow you or run from you but that's about it. You can also add multiple AIs. They are also working on AI improvements as well.
Now on to the good stuff:
+ I cannot emphasize enough how good the crashing mechanic is (flagship feature). It's ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. The game's name derives from the fact that they are using the Beam technology on car design (I think it's their own engine). The cars are created out of beams. That's why crashes are so realistic and fun. Every beam gets deformed on its own, according to the applied force, the angle of the force, the momentum and♥♥♥♥♥♥
+ Beautiful graphics. To my taste, this is cutting edge
+ You can even mod your own engine sound
+ Mod maps and cars, or download the ready ones
+ Day/night concept is there (editable)
+ Destruct your car in a variety of ways
+ Multiple cameras (duh)
+ Slow motion at your disposal
+ You're in for a lot of laughs
+ Or join the modding forums on the website and be surprised to find out that someone designed your dream car into the game. Now download and crush it.
+ Career is coming at full release
+ ♥♥♥♥in' A
**The only con I can think of is the required system to play the game at it's full capacity. I'm sure they will optimize it further but right now as it is, the game needs a powerful computer to run. Especially when you spawn multiple cars to crash or enter a foresty area. When crashing multiple cars together, it might lag a lot on average computers.**
It has a vast potential, and the devs are aiming for a free-roam, career thingy, in which you will be able to buy junk cars and reform them into racing machines or pretty eye candies, you will be able to complete jobs, missions, races, deliveries, derbies, free-roam, all of that.
But that would be a long way off from now. They say the game will be in this phase for about a year from now. So buy at your own risk (not that it's a risk actually, there is just not any content right now).
When this game gets finished, it might be the very first 'driving' game that I have given 10/10 my whole life. Because currently there isn't any open world 'driving' game with realistic driving concept which also includes careers and mods. There just isn't any. Any potential rival games that come close to this, either ruin it by sucking at graphics or by making it online, or by making it a linear racing game (don't even get me started on NFS series).
So I recommend it for people who like to smash cars with the best possible physics available, and who like community made cars and maps, and a realistic driving.
There is also wheel support with manual gears.

Okay, after owning and playing this game for the past two years, it's probably time to write a detailed evaluation.
I use an Acer Aspire V5 with a crappy A10 CPU and 8650G integrated graphics. I play this game fine sometimes on low graphics, though I am not able to play at full time at all, just due to the specs. You'll get used to the latency and lag. Remember SSAO kills performance, and adjust other settings until desired performance is reached
The driving feels solid to me. I have had no previous real life driving experience, but this game in my opinion responds better to input than Forza 5, similar to Forza Horizon 3, if you drive properly in this game. Remember to play in a fixed camera view, basically anything but orbit. This is because when the tires start slipping, you can detect and correct the slipping earlier rather than in orbit mode, where the camera is relatively lazy. Remember also specific reactions to drivetypes, like accelerating when an fwd car is in an oversteering state.
Remember to use DELICATE TRIGGER CONTROL. The steering is 1:1 with your trigger AT ALL TIMES. It's extremely easy to understeer by turning too quickly, and to overcorrect after initiating oversteer. Also, the skidding sounds seem inconsistient with what's happening, and it's loud basically all the time, which causes you to overreact. Try to trust the visuals more than the sound in this game at it's current state.
Once you get used to the controls, it's very satisfying. Just remember to be patient, as the controls require caution and delicate control for maximum enjoyment.

The gameplay is decent, the visuals are striking and the dialogue has it's moments.
I'd recommend the game, if the multiplayer worked properly. I've only played a few hours with a friend of mine, and already we've encountered tons of problems that really shouldn't have made it to a live release game.
1) Random crashing part way through missions, especially when cinematics or dialogue is triggered.
2) Only the host player can interact with quest objects (even collectables) meaning the secondary player(s) can't do much except stay near the host and kill things.
3) Only the host can use the crafting system, so secondary players are restricted to what they can buy/loot (no dropping or trading items either.)
4) Dialogue is not always played for the secondary players, meaning the host often has to read off dialogue so their friends can keep up with what's going on.
5) Quest progression is only unlocked for the primary player, so even if the secondary wanted to leave the game to craft/read dialogue etc they'd have to start from scratch.
6) Some mobs (specifically the bunny lords that spawn when you attack rabbits) only drop loot for host players.
7) After the game crashes, or even if the host leaves/closes the game, your keybinds and settings are reset (as a secondary player.)
Keep in mind these are all issues we've encountered within the first few hours. Needs more polish to be a decent multi-player title.

Played the Unreal series since 99. No moddern FPS can even compare to this: the Michelangelo of games. At the time, I'd also played Quake, Doom, and CS. But Unreal....oh my, Unreal. My first true love. She snuffed out all others like candles in the rain.
Every gamer has that one game that just consumes them. Their pulse quickens and their eyes plaster to the screen, your very soul trapped in an enigma of endless time. Years pass as you watch you life fly by at 60 HZ. Your wrists build strong lasting muscle and hardened tendons from hammering on the WASD keys for hours on end. Your index and middle fingers become your future wifes dream toys as you hone your dexterity with years of mousebutton rappid firing. Your heart races as you shotgun dance with your enemies states and countries apart.
This game....
This game needs no introduction. It's name is simple and rightfully fitting: Unreal.
In it's prime, there were thousands of servers on Game Spy. Close your eyes and point, you'd find one packed with dozens of players from all over the globe. My personal favorite was Instagib (one shot kills). CTF, or TDM. I played in a clan that utilized a player built map system called "giant maps". They were maps that looked like your living room, kitchen, dining room, dorm room, bathroom, etc... but you were the size of a penny. 20 guys buzzing around looking like red or blue dots againt a refridgerator or television. "BigPapa290" is strafing on the floor by the door stop, dodging lasers from an onslaught of enemies flying over the cookie jar. Your clan noob "SparklesTheElephant" is straight walking along the bathroom tiles, still figuring out the controls and somehow lands some lucky shot on your enemies veteran "X-L4X69" who's stalking him from the toilet paper dispenser. "DarkCarnage49" is camped up on the shelf by the fabric softener sniping guys off by the furnace pilot light, but "DeepDishPizza" teleports up from the floor in some crazy zig-zag pattern and an epic battle ensues as they jump and double jump and spin back and fourth until one lands a shot. Then, somehow you've found your way into the clothes dryer drum where there is no wall and everywhere is a mirror. There's no telling which way is out. "HabaneroFarts" has also stumbled upon this trap! Son of a B****! In a fury, you start firing at ghosts. Did I hit him? No, that was his reflection. Why isn't he dead?! How the F*** do I get out of this hell!
So you just stand still, hopefully he can just end your misery and you can just die and spawn in the kitty litter box like you were hoping for to begin with.
GREAT SCOTT! the memories :)

For those too lazy to read my full review, this about sums it up:
This game is increasingly difficult to review when you take into account certain factors that have affected it. Firstly, something I must of course say, the game is early-access alpha. It is still in development and so I appreaciate this and will not comment on the large amount of bugs and other "early-access" esque issues that the game has.
I think that the paramount issue with Life is Feudal: YO is the simple fact that the advertisement for the game is misleading. Not on purpose mind, I simply feel as though the developers struggled to catagorize the game they have begun to produce and so consumers who stumble across it are not entirely sure what they are purchasing. I myself am very much into the Mount & Blade franchise and when I stumbled across this game I (and friends from my gaming community) expected it to be like a much larger open world RPG version of the mod for Mount & Blade: Warband, Persisitent World. The game showed pictures of an adventurer moving throughout a completely player made land. This gave me and my friends the misconception that the game was a Skyrim meets Mount & Blade meets Runescape/LOTR Online - what sounded like a perfect compliation.
In actual fact the game is rust meets minecraft. It focuses on the survival aspect far more than the roleplaying rpg medieval aspect. This should be advertised FAR more clearly as survival game fans would appreciate it much more than Medieval role-play fans. Let me try to explain in a DayZ way, the server owners and their friends run around in full armour (like bandits/heroes) whilst everyone else hops from server to server with a few rags, they try to do something but every time they leave the server are forced to try again thanks to a lack of server favouriting implementation. This is fine, particularly in Alpha, but not what I thought when I was buying it.
Good game for what it is in its current stage, but misleading in its advertisement and so that is forcing me to give it a negative review.
Buy the game if you want a Rust esque survival, not a medieval RP RPG MMO sandbox game.

I'm sorry, but I was disappointed in Shadow Warrior 2.
I loved the first one. Since I'm a 80's kid I grew up playing the 90's Build Engine Shadow Warrior and the reboot by Flying Wild Hog was a great return to the 90's style shooter with humor, cool weapons and challenging fights set in awesome designed levels. It had a story that had a layer of cool lore you woulden't expect with a surprisingly good and touching ending to what started as a tong in cheek wang-a-thon with over the top violence and silly jokes. It's one of those games I just wanted to keep playing, the combat was satisfying, the level design was great and there was some impressive scenery with great atmosphere in that game.
The first night I started playing Shadow Warrior 2 with a friend I already felt some boredom sinking in. I tried it for a few more hours the next day, but it didn't really change. The levels have no real direction to them, they are just a simple maze with randomly placed mobs and a objective. Some levels like the City ones just feel utterly empty, with no real purpose other than being a backdrop for enemies to spawn in. And the loot system is just boring, real boring. Checking your drops after a fight or mission is like doing dishes, get the dirt out and place the clean ones in their rightfull place. At least in Borderlands you get lot's of random looking weapons and it's always obvious to see what might be a better choice. Shadow Warrior 2 is like checking a big sack of marbles for scratches and clarity, they all look kind of the same with minor differences. The good stuff is just too sparse. I just issued a refund myself afte seeying Total Biscuit's video, he actually confirmed some things I was afraid of getting to after more hours. There was no cool battles in my session, just mindless bullet sprays at enemies that don't want to die, even if they are the size of a dog.
I can't tell if the story will get any better later on since I stopped playing, but the start of Shadow Warrior 1 was imho way more engaging from the first cutscenes and setup of the story after that opening mission. I was hoping there would be a cooler hook to the story instead of having  to do fetch quests for other characters. It kinda feels like a sequel with a different director, it doesn't feel like right.
Also... the fortune cookies in Shadow Warrior 1 were way funnier imho.

I picked this up on sale awhile ago-- I'm a huge Civil War buff and I played the hell out of "Sid Meier's Gettysburg!" back in the day. This game is basically what "Gettysburg!" was, but updated with better graphics, some neat routing items, larger battles.... and less depth. But I still give it a recommendation because for the price, this is a great pickup.
If you're coming into this game from other RTS games, know that the strategy here is based on morale and forming good lines of soldiers. You need to think like a Civil War commander would-- avoid being flank, try and change the tide of battle with smart placement, and work well to win. I made the mistake in my first couple of games of just walking right at the enemy everytime and I was slaughtered for it-- you have to use smart tactics here.
The level of control is way, way, way too large, however. As in, instead of allowing you to control units at the regimental level like Sid Meier's Gettysburg! did, you're restricted to brigade level units that look like regimental sized ones. Smaller maps are better maps in these kinds of cases, and I think that it's a disappointment that they couldn't make more detailed units (although it's better for accessiblity sake here). I appreciate, however, that you have to maintain control of VP locations in order to win, and that soldier deaths count for so many points in determing victory or defeat. One game-breaking thing that I would do in "Gettysburg!" was move one regiment to a location and capture locations. I was able to do it once here, but it took a looooong time of the enemy ignoring the unit to get the points.
So: like RTS games? The sale price of $2.99 is a no-brainer. Go buy this. Just if you're familiar with its 'source material', it'll be a tad disappointing.

Rainbow Six Siege is exactly the type of game where it can be immensely frustrating at the start but perseverance pays off with extremely rewarding and satisfying moments.
Tactical team-based online games are hard to get right. The overwhelming majority of the time they’re designed in such a way that it’s impossible to lone-wolf it causing frustration with teammates unless you’re in a premade party or a way where you’ll have to rely on them so little you’ll never even notice them. Siege bridges this gap perfectly by having a punishing game that rewards communication by allowing you to get the drop on enemies but at the same time a skilled enough solo player can turn it all around. I personally would still recommend playing with friends simply because due to the nature of the game it can get very toxic resulting in text chat going crazy before people start team killing.
The core gameplay is built in such a way that it stops it from being just a twitch reaction game. You’ll usually die very quickly but it’s not uncommon to make it out of ambushes alive. The health system works well with the guns which have enough recoil to completely disincentivize running around instead of taking a slower more methodical approach. Of course this can cause frustration at times when you get caught out but as you spend more time with the game you’ll find yourself more comfortable and making incredible plays yourself.
Siege is a very replayable game with matches rarely playing out the same. A key to this replayability is how destructible parts of the environment are such as walls and ceilings. This means every time you play the game you’ll always need to be thinking about the map around you as it changes with attackers breaching through walls and ceilings or defenders setting up new routes for viewpoints and navigation. The game offers different characters for you to play as each with their own abilities ranging from shields that can blind opponents at close quarters to poison smoke grenades that do damage to enemies over time. Ontop of abilities they all have their own guns and equipment so as you gain the ingame currency known as renown to unlock them you’ll gradually find ones that can suit the playstyle you’re after. Currently none of these operators or their abilities are tilted too heavily to cause an unbalance however as Ubisoft continue to add more maps and operators to the game for free it is a possibility. Thankfully the developers seem to have worked extremely hard on keeping the game updated and listening to community feedback making it the success that it is today.
As for content outside the multiplayer there’s a few things but nothing brilliant. There’s a single player mode called Situations that’ll get you familiar with the base operators and give you plenty of renown to put towards new operators or unlockable skins. Terrorist Hunt is similar to a training mode where you’ll go against basic AI on a small selection of difficulties to help you with your aim. It’s not great and even though you can play it with friends it’s unlikely you’ll go back to it unless the daily or weekly challenges Ubisoft set for extra renown require it.
Overall Siege is a great online game that has captured my attention away from other online titles. It’s a game that I found extremely frustrating at first but by sticking with it I’ve had some spectacular moments that have made me feel like a pro-league God with a heart that won’t stop racing. Whether or not you’re buying it with friends it’s certainly worth picking up if you’re gunning for an online first person shooter that you can sink your teeth into.

Kero Blaster is overall a great game. It has much charm and kept me hooked enough to unlock and beat all of the main content it could offer. Some may find the story lacking but I prefer this approach as opposed to too much dialogue or too many cutscenes. My only complaints have to do with a few very questionable design decisions that I feel keep it from being one of my top favorites.
There is an impressive controls menu that shows you a whole keyboard to map as you please. I did not play the game with a gamepad so I can't speak for that. I did not notice any input delay or lag while actually playing at any point which is so important in a game like this. You cannot use the mouse to navigate any of the menus though which seems like a pointless limitation. There is a scaling option but it does not work in fullscreen. Such a thing is easy to program, I have done so myself, and I'm disappointed to not see it there as I have poor eyesight and particularly benefit from this feature.
The weapons are designed very well. They all feel unique and serve their own purpose. You may find a favorite weapon but at least every now and then you'll need to take out another one to get an enemy around a corner or beat enemies in a much more efficient way.
The enemies themselves are very fair once you learn how they work and often require you to learn a new strategy to kill them without taking damage. Some enemies don't hurt you unless you attack them and you can walk through them or bounce on them freely which came as a nice surprise as they were annoying otherwise.
You can upgrade weapons and boost your maximum health at certain points in the game. These are usually around halfway through a level, and you're left guessing as to where that is exactly. I felt very relieved whenever I saw one for the first time for each level because I knew it likely meant I got to refill my precious health or get a very welcomed upgrade to help me tackle enemies, sometimes in new ways. The prices are very high however, and I assume this is as a result of one of those questionable decisions I briefly mentioned.
You've got a finite amount of lives. When you die, you lose one and start back and the most recent save, otherwise there is no penalty for death. You do not lose any money by simply dying whatsoever. Saves happen very very often. When you lose all of your lives you get a 'Game Over' which starts you at the beginning of the level with everything you had before and 3 lives. If you happen to be low on health, beyond the rare store or beating the level your only opportunity to gain health is to kill an enemy and hope he drops some. It doesn't happen very often. Sometimes you'll carefully clear out an entire room and only get money. Sometimes you'll kill an enemy to restore three health even if you didn't need it. Sometimes they'll drop an extra life which is a big deal because a life is a free pass to restore all your health essentially.
Every time a level transitions all normal enemies respawn,
. If you're having trouble with a level or boss but only have one life left, then your best option is either to farm rooms and cross your fingers really hard or kill yourself and get three lives. Why not, you'll be back where you started but with a huge advantage in comparison. No real punishment other than consuming your time. I don't think beating a level restores your lives either. While on paper this system may look good, I believe it encouraged the developer to allow elements of trial and error to be introduced and balance things in such a way that accounts for players being more powerful than they would otherwise. It's okay if something is cheap because there's, again, no real punishment. I would much rather have lost all of my progress including the upgrades I bought that level if it meant that the game was more exciting and fair.
The platforming physics are frustrating. They're not buggy and work the way they are supposed to, it's just that they're so intentionally clunky. Movement on the ground is fine but your air control is so painfully lacking that I lost count of how many times I saw my fate at least a second away but could do nothing meaningful
. This happened to me a couple times with things that I had no way of knowing were coming too. Some would call that "artificial difficulty", I just think it's bad design in a game of this sort.
If you hold the shoot button in a certain direction, you're stuck aiming in that direction as you are moving. It's very helpful but you can't toggle in the menu or hold a key to activate/disactivate on hold whenever is appropriate. The way you aim horizontally is also determined by your momentum if not standing still, which makes this mechanic feel very sticky. If you stop shooting in a direction to shoot something that just came up behind you, you can't quickly flip in that direction and you have to unintuitively wait until the character can turn around.
You have
weapons to choose from eventually and have to switch between them one at a time which does not feel good. This is a computer game with rebindable keys, not a console game. I assume it supports a controller but there's no good reason why I can't have a key on my keyboard to select each of those weapons in particular once I get them at least.
I would like to add context to these complaints by adding that I have beaten the true final boss of the freeware version Cave Story (can't write this review without mentioning it at least once) with just under the max health and without any health potions (unintentional gimp). I never felt like Kero Blaster was too hard, it's simply that it can be frustrating for the wrong reasons.
There is a boss rush mode but by the point you get there the game becomes too easy for it to be satisfying in my opinion. There's a timer though and you can easily play it again to improve that time. You can also of course intentionally put handicaps on yourself by not buying upgrades or starting a new file if you lose all your lives.
Again, I did enjoy this game a lot and would recommend it to anyone who likes cute platformers. If you're not a fan of moderately challenging ones and are only going to get the first ending it may not be worth the price however.
It's kind of like Cave Story but more clunky and with less obtrusive of a story. And it encourages grinding. But it's still a lot of fun.

Kero Blaster is a bit of an odd duck. It's the second major release from lone auteur game designer Pixel, who about a decade ago created the absolutely legendary Cave Story. Pixel has made a few small games here and there since then, but this is his second major retail release.
Let me say first that if you liked Cave Story, you'll like Kero Blaster, and that's really because it's just more of the same. A few of the mechanics are changed up here and there and there's a much heavier emphasis on arcadey action than plot and characters, but when you get down to the shooty pew pew bits it plays exactly like Cave Story did.
Something that fans of Cave Story may not like, however, is that Kero Blaster is short, and comparitively easy. Veterans of Pixel's works will have no trouble breasing through the campaign. If, however, you are new to Pixel's games, then Kero Blaster would be an excellent start.
From a personal view, I enjoyed the game a lot, but I did find it lacking in some regards. The "prologue" game Pink Hour gave the impression that Kero Blaster would, like Cave Story, be a story driven exploration game rather than a linear arcade shooter, and I get the distinct impression that was the original intention. Environments are detailed and interesting, and buyable upgrades are priced in such a way as to suggest a longer game. I feel like Kero Blaster is a game that the devoloper got bored of and just wanted to get out the door so he could move on to something new. This is supported by most of the music, sound effects, and even some of the assets and sprites being recycled from Cave Story, which is odd when Pixel is well known for his MIDI music and pixel art, AND because there were new sprites and music in PInk Hour.
Here's the break down:
Pros
- Fun, high action shooter with extremely tight controls.
- Four interesting weapons to choose from, each one feeling unique and special.
- What new sprites there are are cute and endearing.
Cons
- Short, perhaps three hours if you have a lot of trouble, and two if you don't.
- There's very little story. What's there is cute and funny, but it feels rushed.
- The entire game has an aire of partialness, like this is only part of a game. A really good part to be sure, but incomplete.
In closing, I recommend Kero Blaster because it's a fun little diversion, but since it's so short and lacking in plot, it'd be best if you picked it up on sale. The base price is a little much for what you get, but it's still a great game.

Seriously overlooked compared to the first entry in the series, despite this not being a completely finished game (thanks to Lucasarts rushing it for the holiday season, meaning we lost a lot of the game's content). Yes, it is definitely glitchy too. However, I cannot deny the many gameplay refinements and additions it made, including the excellent Influence system. In my opinion the combat had a lot of great improvements too; there's lots of new abilites and fun things to try out, and it still works very well, and the animations are still fun to watch. The story is EASILY just as good, and lengthy, as the original. It is one of the most philosophical and in-depth stories in a Star Wars adventure, ever. It will really make you question some things like the "Jedi way" and what the Force truly is.
The party members this time around are equally memorable, especially Kreia; and yes, HK-47 is still here, as well as a few others (I won't spoil). Some people might be turned off by the lack of Revan and a new protagonist this time around, but I found it refreshing. The voice acting is superb once again, and the light side/dark side thing is in full force again too - no pun intended. There's a lot more decision-making overall, if you enjoy that thing. The story is actually a little different depending on what gender you choose, too. There is plenty of traveling to do; the worlds are large and can be pretty at times. Many of the character models also look much better.
Overall, definitely play this if you enjoyed the first game, you will certainly not regret it, nor will you ever forget it. And yeah, I know I'm reviewing this pretty late. Better late than never, I guess.

After playing this game I had to get the truth out: KotOR 2 is not a bad game, but it is not a shining example of gaming greatness either. However, the game is a diamond in the rough - if you have the patience to read through the incoming wall of text, then I'll explain why. Skip to the end for pros and cons if you want.
The gamemakers were pressured into releasing the game before the planned release date and therefore the game is truncated in a most horrible fashion. The ending is very anticlimactic due to its overreliance on a few dialogue options, which serve to give some conclusion to the story. The AI is dumber than a sack of rocks - enemies do not buff themselves or utilise certain mechanics that forces the player to be smart/flexible. Melee enemies will charge you in an uncoordinated manner and ranged enemies will just have a slugging match with you until they die. And the story tries to have several concurrent plotlines at a point, where you switch from companion to companion, which harms the climactic sequences and that feeling of dramatic tension.
I played as a Light SIde Jedi Consular with the awesome power to KILL EVERY NORMAL ENEMY IN A ROOM WITH 2 ACTIONS on the normal difficulty. All I did was throw Dark Side Lightning everywhere, which was fun for a while in the beginning, although it got boring fast. Then I just decided to do another cool and overpowered thing, which I did in KotOR 1 with my scout+sentinel: I got so many attacks in each round that I could end anyone in a round even without stasis'ing my way to victory. In KotOR 2, I used an aggressive lightsaber form (Juyo) with Master Force Speed, which results in a double-1h jedi throwing 5-7 attacks in one turn with Master Flurry. Vulnerabilities were chased away with the Stasis Field power, since they can't hit you when they are all frozen.
Okay, fine. Combat has improved from KotOR 1 with the addition of lightsaber/force forms and more feats/powers - the game just suffers from a BAD AI and heavy truncation.
I was spared the worst of the truncation, since I installed a mod, which restores a great deal of content. That does not excuse the huge negatives of the game, but it did allow me to experience an introspective quest of self-defense, which was very evident throughout the dialogue with your teacher (Kreia) and your interactions with the force-sensitive companions you gather. The many companions have varying degrees of depth, but Kreia takes the cake with her motives and perspective.
Kreia has (HEAVY SPOILERS INCOMING)
The dialogue with her also reveals some problems between the Force (fate) and free will, with Kreia as a proponent for free will, which explains her actions. (I am also reminded of Nietszche, when it comes to her grayness in the whole LS vs DS debacle.)
Pros: PC mods help (some are easy to install) - combat CAN be fun - dialogue is influential (as it was in the first KotOR) - engaging characters - you get to be as reasonable/psychotic/goody-two-shoes as you want to be - Kreia - if you can immerse yourself then you get a great experience
Cons: truncated game - combat is USUALLY not engaging, especially in the long run - game is a bit drawn out - ending is anticlimactic - game is easy on normal - game is a guilty pleasure - immersion can be hard to gain and maintain - certain powers and tactics are almost gamebreaking in the environment offered by the game
tl;dr game is just alright if you can live with its failures - if not, then it is not for you

Bought this game last week and spent a good 20 hours or so on it this weekend, which is a good sign as is, but lets be fair any decent strat game can pull that out of me.  So, here's what I can say about it.
I have spent the last decade or so pulling my hair out wondering why people don't just make the simple and almost always succesful tactical strategy games I remember from when I was younger.    Nothing too complex, just cover mechanics, AP, decent balance, etc.   So when one comes along I usually get pretty into it.
Sanctus Reach IS a solid tactical strategy game in this sense.   Cover mechanics work well, units are well balanced and have a distinct feel and purpose.  The AP system is well implemented and enjoyable.  There are lots of choices to be made in terms of optimizing your loadout, rarely is one unit universally good.   For that reason I consider this game worth the purchase and I would recommend it.
That said, Sanctus Reach is mostly a very good framework for a great game, as opposed to being a great game itself.  There is no overarching grand strategy of any importance.  Sure your guys level up as you go on, but unit death has limited effects and map progression is highly linear.   Further, while units are well balanced and logical, there really aren't a lot of them at the moment.  There are currently only 2 army types.
Also, the missions are almost all the same.   But I need to emphasize that isn't as bad as it sounds.  While most missions are "Capture the most victory points" it's worth recognizing that you can still get a TON of variety in gameplay from that based on the map layout and your troop loadout.   This is why VP games are still the mainstay of 40k games after so many years.  There are a few more varied missions scattered about, but not that many.
My hope is that DLC will be the thing that takes this from the Good category to the truly Great category.    Time will tell.

This is not a flashy game with expensive CGI cutscenes, but it is a darn good turn based strategy game that perfectly captures the Warhammer 40k universe and is about as close as you'll get to playing the table-top version without spending hundreds of dollars and scores of hours painting your own minatures.
There's not much story, but part of the fun is making it up in your head as you fight a valiant but futile rear-guard action against a numerically superior force, or find half your army cut off and surrounded on a hilltop doomed to fight a heroic last stand.
The detail, in particular with different loadouts and troop abilities, make multiple tactics and strategies viable; there's always more than one way to win, or lose, and the AI while not spectacular is relentless and challenging without being overwhelming or seeming like it's cheating half the time.
In short: 10/10 Would lay down my life in service to the God-Emperor of mankind again...

So, I picked this up on nostalgia factor. What can I say, guys? I feel like the vast majority of games are this way; I install and get just a few minutes in and the experience is just "meh." But, feel obliged to get the most out of my new investment. So, mostly try to trudge my way through the game to finish. It is exceedingly rare that I find a title that is fun from the get go, and doesn't let up. Most feel pretty boring, and somewhat phoned in. I wouldn't say a cash grab or anything, but the elements certainly fail to come together in a very meaningful way. Just an okay experience, overall.

I have always wanted a game where you can get to kill angels and demons alike, a simple hack ‘n’ slash game with brutal themes and gore… well, Darksiders came to my attention on a daily sale, for some reason this title went under the radar at the time, but I got it for 5 bucks, and I totally ignored the whole concept and risked it. To this day, Darksiders still looks fresh and fun to play, with an interesting lore, concept and characters, so I can’t say I wasted 5 bucks.
We are War, one of the four horsemen of the apocalypse, we answer the call for the final confrontation, the ultimate battle among the three kingdoms, Hell, Heaven and Earth. But there is something wrong here, humanity was not prepare for the final judgment, and when you realize that it is already too late, demons ravage the earth and angels fall from the sky to fight and die, you, amidst all the destruction, are blamed for the chaos, The Seventh Seal was not broken! War is imprisoned waiting for trial, 100 years pass and earth is lost, The Charred Council, an entity in charge of taking care of the balance gives you a chance to clear your name, stripped of your powers you seek the truth to clear your name.
Darksiders is usually compared to Zelda because of the puzzles and God of War because the actual hack ‘n’ slash gameplay, but I must say the game deserves some credit and more than simple comparisons. It may look like those games but darksiders delivers a complete different lore and interesting characters that make it really unique and something I always wanted to play for a game. Gameplay is simple, we must regain our lost powers, and abilities so we can defeat more powerful foes, different characters throughout the game help us by striking deals with us and give us directions.
During our progression we can develop certain skills, find new items that increase our health and wrath, artifacts that we can trade for souls and new moves that we can buy so we can kill enemies much more easily. The game’s formula is simple and not complicated, we advanced by hacking and slashing multiple demonic and angelic enemies with diverse abilities and powers, from weak minions to flying demons with extreme capacities, angels, demons, all of them attack you equally. From time to time we will fill a rage gauge, which will help us transform into War’s ultimate form, an unstoppable monster full of anger that kills anything on his way, really useful when surrounded by multiple enemies or more powerful ones when fighting normally.
With multiple RPG elements, puzzles are really fun to complete, they are not extremely difficult nor complicated, but they require to get different tools that will help you reach areas that are a long way off, coming and going from one place to another is really necessary as you advanced on the storyline. Sometimes you will need a tool that is not available at a certain point in the game, so backtracking and remembering where to look is key if you don’t want to miss a secret or a chest.
Darksiders provides a world that has taken over the earth, the world we knew is barely there, collapsed cities and building are part of the demonic scenery, to be honest the design of the realm is awesome, everything looks gloomy, hellish and dead, humanity is no more and demons now dwell in the creation. Depending on the mission, we visit many places with different ecosystems of their own. Textures are decent, there are muddy textures here and there, nothing serious nor ugly considering the world presented here is massive, nothing much to add, the graphics are decent and keep you entertain seeing the various environments created after the fall of earth.
Explosion, power and sword effects are great, you feel every time you hack and slash enemies with Chaoseater and your multiple moves, enemies are tough so they make you feel they can take a lot of damage. The blood and mutilation effects also show a lot of comic-like details, considering the whole concept is based on models that make you see comic in movement, awesome!
Considering that Vigil was not a big company, they really pulled out a great soundtrack, it lives up to the apocalyptic mood of the game, every theme depending on the situation will start playing adding more suspense to the action, absolutely beautiful music for an amazing campaign full of compelling characters that feel alive due to the incredible and believable voice acting, everyone did an outstanding job, all important characters have unique voices, especially War, the voice acting for War is incredibly well developed, you feel his anger, pain and frustration, but also his wrath and thirst for vengeance.
Sound effects are also considerably well done, the flashing of swords, gutting enemies and especially, angels, is rewarding and satisfactory for your ears as well as the many demons and monsters that crowd the areas, the growls and demonic voices are awesome, make you feel nothing is human and everything is out of this world, the apocalypse is alive!
While I consider Darksiders a hidden gem, it doesn’t lack bad things, unfortunately some aspects of the game are considerably awkward, especially some controls, they feel extremely console-like, more so when using some abilities or some other tool necessary to fight certain enemies, you can always bind some new keys to a more comfortable one, some people even like to use an Xbox controller, it all depends on your taste.
Regarding glitches or bugs, I did not find any on my several play throughs, but I did have some annoying game crashes from time to time, nothing that bad, but distracting.
Finally, a bug that is not game breaking but annoying for some gamers is related to the achievements, some of them won’t be completed after you’ve already done them, it’s been broken since the beginning and was never fixed.
As I said, Darksiders has been always overshadowed by other most popular similar games, don’t be mistaken, they may look alike, but this franchise has shown it has potential for more interesting lore to develop and two more horsemen to play as. Also, the whole theme about the apocalypse, angels, demons and the balance between them is something rarely seen in modern video games  as well as being a common enemy for both factions and as one of the game quotes says, “Heaven hunts you, Hell hates you” totally recommended!

Adds to what made the first Unreal Tournament a masterpiece.
Based mostly on the
(DRM-free) version and Unreal Anthology (DVD ROM).
When making a sequel to the much venerated Unreal Tournament (1999) you better damn well get it right. Fortunately for both Epic and UT fans, Unreal Tournament 2004 does precisely that. Taking the misteps out of Unreal Tournament 2003 and adding some cool new features paid off in spades for Epic and UT fans.
This time around, UT looks dazzling - even in 2017. Deathmath, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, Dominiation, and Assault all make comebacks. Domination has a noticable difference in that teams must control TWO check points simultaneously for a few seconds as opposed to multiple check points at any given time. Added to the modes is Onslaught, which involves controling nodes until the opposing team's core is exposed. Both Assault and Onslaught now utilize huge environments and...VEHICLES. Removed is the option to have four teams at once (R/B/G/Y) in TDM and DOM. From the obvious graphical enhancement, which has aged quite well, to the varied gameplay, UT2004 delivers.
While Unreal Tournament 99/GOTY is my all-time fave FPS, UT2004 slides in right behind it for some damn good reasons.
For those wondering where UT2003 went: it's all in UT2004, minus some parts that put fans off. In fact, there's a Mutator that allows for using the UT2003 HUD. So UT2003 is in UT2004.

The melee combat and movement is amazing and really fun.

Shadow Warrior is one of the best shooters of 2016, simply put.
For starters, the game is one of the most well optimized titles this year, I tested this with my 4690K and both my GTX 770 and 1070, and I can achieve more than 60 FPS with both setups and a decent image quality overall; the game scales well down to the minimum spec hardware, that's for sure, and then runs amazingly well on more powerful PCs.
Graphically it has all the options and settings that a proper PC game should have and are within the engine's specs, it even has true HDR support (not that's something that matters today on the PC) and a new NVIDIA peripheral resolution rendering technique called Multi-res Shading, which makes the peripheral section of the screen to render at a lower resolution, thus giving us extra performance at no noticeable difference because it's on the peripheral region and our brains won't notice it as much as the things we're looking at directly. Clever, and it works really well, indeed.
When it comes to sound assets, I can't find any issues either, the game sounds great, most weapons have a different sound from each other, they sound like they're the real deal and they're meant to destroy our enemies into a million pieces, that's what we want, and the music is amazing too with some nice tracks now and then, especially for important moments like the boss fights.
Gameplay is where the game is at though, it's amazing, this is a very, very fast paced shooter where you'll be using the DASH key a lot, both in and out of combat, but it really shines in combat, it's like a dance of death and carnage if you manage to master the use of the dash key and its different movement combinations and aerial tricks you can perform. Also, just like it happens with DOOM, you need to keep switching weapons in a fight, to be able to deal with different types of enemies and their different elemental resistances. I've read some people complain about bullet-sponge enemies but I've finished the game on HARD and there's always a way to quickly deal with these so called "sponges" and that's by carrying a proper weapon with the correct element imbued to it, it's simple.
Furthermore, some people seem to not even use their CHI for anything but healing, that's wrong too, Chi powers can help you bring down some enemies, and even deal with groups in a more efficient way; the game is all about mastering all the ninja arts Lo Wang is capable of, and not just running around with a shotgun: it can be done but it's not what the whole game has to offer, so keep that in mind, it gets deeper than that, believe me.
Now, the controversial part of this game is clearly the LOOT system and its departure from the previous games, especially from the 2013 reboot of the series. This game has loot, like a Borderlands game but not to that extreme extent though, as in you won't be looting a gazillion weapons every level, like it happens in Borderlands, but you surely get a lot of upgrade items to insert in your weapons, armor, etc. Many of these are worthless at first and you should sell most of them, until you reach a point in the game where the forge is open to you and then you can fuse these items into higher quality ones.
But some people don't like this departure from the traditional, linear, design, that's alright but we have to keep in mind the previous title is also a master piece on its own, a proper remake of a crazy first person shooter from the 90's. What Shadow Warrior 2 offers is more of that craziness but under a new less linear format, with free roam options and of course cooperative multiplayer, which are great additions to the original formula.
The gore and violence are increased a lot in this sequel too, and the special effects look amazing, this game has so much going on the screen at any given time, in combat, that it's amazing how well it runs. Also...some of the smoke and fog effects are one of the best I've ever seen for this type of game.
My final verdict for this game is: if you like fast paced, old school style shooters with cheesy humor, over the top violence and cool looking enemies and absurdly over powered weapons...get this game, the price on release is just right for what this game offers (took me 30 hours to finish the game on Hard difficulty in single player, and then it has coop and New Game Plus too), and it can only get lower in future sales and discounts. It's worth the money for the amount of fun I've had and I'll keep having with it in the future, but it's not exactly the same as the previous title from 2013 as I mentioned.
Still, as a First Person Shooter fan, this game is one of my favorites for 2016, along with DOOM.

Shadow Warrior 2 is a great alternative to a lot of the hardcore AAA game titles on the market right now.  The storyline is cohesive and the dialogue is entertaining.
Pros: Visually stunning.  Lots of low-brow humor (You mess with the bull, you get the Wang).  Colorful characters.  Good story.
Cons:
The Fog (and vomit-inducing disorientation) of War
While combat can be fairly fluid, it can also be insanely disorienting.   You are almost never up against just one enemy but  4 - 10.  A good number of them are fairly large on the screen, so fighting that many with a sword tends to just fill your viewable area with giant fields of colors that aren't really discernible from one another. That plus a few of the special skills have you spinning dizzily around often leaves you disoriented for a few seconds.
The Curse of the Neverending Upgrades
SW2 is trying to do what Borderlands did with it's seemingly unending variety of weapons . . . only without the large variety of weapons.  Instead of grinding and picking up a ton of new, colorful, and unique weapons you get a veritable dump truck of weapon upgrades.  So many, in fact, that you will eventually be given the means to turn any 3 upgrades into a slightly better upgrade.  While some upgrades are marginally useful, most contain meaningless stats that don't really effect gameplay all that much.   So in the end, you are left with a massive inventory of pointlessness and a few weapons that you won't even bother upgrading.
Best 10 Hours I Ever Spent
Unless you decide to go co-op grinding (see previous con above about the pointlessness of that) you can beat the game in fairly quick time.  10 hours for my first playthrough, and that includes doing every side mission available.  I might go and give it another look, but for now 10 hours is where I'm at.  At the $39 price tag, I essentially paid $4 per hour for this game.  I dont regret purchasing it, but some might balk at that return on investment.
Overall: The game is a fun distraction.  If you're in the market for something that isn't so far up it's own♥♥♥♥♥to be content with what it is, then give this game a shot.

A+.  This is one of the best battlefield strategy games I've ever played.   Starting with the VERY well researched and beautifully displayed battlefield of Gettysburg.  Top notch.  The forces, of course, are historically accurate as well.  Control of those forces are very intuitive and seamless which is necessary considering this is a real-time game and not a turn-based one.  Understanding the relationship of the different troop types is essential to success and the game does a great job of giving you the tools you need.  As in the historical battle, the game is win-able by either side so it really does come down to the decisions of the player.  I have achieved major victories using either side but it took a few tries (especially as the Confederates--I'll give you a hint NO REST for the wicked).  The artillery and cavalry superiority of the North make winning with them a bit easier, I think.  If you enjoy war games, especially well researched historical games, this is for you!  Again, A+

I've tried to get back into this game several times, but the UI is so poorly designed that it really hampers the playability of the game.  I don't know if the AI is stacked against you or not, but good luck trying to send a brigade of 1000+ troops against any AI artillery emplacement, especially if the charge button is disabled (although the UI won't tell you why).  If you do charge, your brigade will approach the artillery emplacements (which the AI loves to just sit on hills unsupported by infantry), and still utterly wreck infantry brigades over and over again with cannister shot while your units, instead of charging, decide to duke it out with artillery by firing at them (inflicting next to no losses on the artillery).
The morale system is beyond frustrating, again it may be more due to the complete lack of a polished UI, but your units will constantly lose morale.  There were two instances where I had surrounded enemy brigades on three sides, but they refused to break, even after a charge from the rear.  Instead, I found my units, who were in woods, with a commander nearby being shattered.  Their morale would just plummet, and the UI provided no reason as to why, or how to fix the issue.
I really wanted to like this game, but the UI is beyond frustrating.  The movement of units is unique, but poorly implemented.  Your units are completely dependent on your input, and will not self rotate to face an enemy, leaving their flanks dangling in the breeze, instead choosing to return fire at an angle.
Counter battery fire is pointless, as enemy artillery morale is apparently unphased by massive return fire, and the rate at which AI artillery takes casualties is ridiculously low.
Your artillery fire on enemy units doesn't seem to do much, either in the way of casualties or inflicting morale damage.

Magic 2015 has taken steps backwards in all the wrong directions. People have complained for years about many features, or lack thereof in this series. The developers finally listened to people cries for full deck building. While the deckbuilding is robust and the card collection is larger than ever, there is almost no content to back it up.
DotP has been a great online trading card game because it had little competition in the past. Now that there is competition in the form of great games like Might & Magic Duel of Champions and Hearthstone, Magic 2015 is easily overshadowed. You would think that a game series would only add content to the franchise in yearly installments, but Magic 2015 has actually stripped multiplayer of it's best game modes. Two headed giant IS NOT in Magic 2015, and the developers fail to acknowledge that it was one of the best selling points of past games, and the only mode distinguising DoTP from the competition (Hearthstone players are dying for a 2HG game mode, but will likely not get it). The removal of the 2HG was a fatal mistake for Magic 2015, and can be credited to Nik Davidson
.
In the past, cards were unlocked either through grinding (which wasn't all that bad!) or simply manipulating game files to unlock all cards. The developers have done nothing to moderate or squelch people from cheating in past iterations of DotP, and I can easily forsee people exploiting Magic 2015 to the fullest. I would say that Magic 2015 is pay to win since actually unlocking the games full content will cost more than the base price of the game in the form of microtransactions, but I won't because I don't think it will be long before people hack cards into their games and start using cookie cutter decks. Regardless, I do not see myself investing the time to craft decks in Magic 2015 because my only multiplayer options are to 1v1 duel, or free-for-all up to four players - opposed to the past 2HG, and the hilarious Planeschase mode from 2013.
Aside from the removal of the best game mode in DoTP, Magic 2015 has compounded the worst features of past iterations. The menu system has never been strong, and 2015's is the worst of the worst. Navigating the menu is cumbersome, and clicking buttons is extremely unresponsive. Thankfully, the in-game responsiveness is better, but the game is still brought down by slow animations and a boring playing field.
I have been a fan of Duels of the Planeswalkers for years, and a cardboard Magic player for 20 years. Magic 2015 is a huge dissapointment and one of my first regret purchases on Steam. This can honestly be salvaged if the developers patch in 2-Headed Giant, but if past games are any indication, they will do nothing to support the game except release nickle-and-dime microtransactions rather than fix bugs. With over 500 hours played in the DotP series, I am sad to say that I likely will not be playing this game and instead move onto the now better online TCGs.

When you first start up this game, it feels like just another Twin Stick shooter with unique art style. But actually it's got more depth than most Twin Sticks I've played. You play as Prince Rupert, who's flying a Montgolfière, that has the fastest shooting cannon in the world. You're on your quest to prove yourself to be worthy groom for some princess and everybody else who wants to marry her is after you. And your balloon is capable of flying into space and dive 20 000 leagues under the sea. That in itself is the most awesome concept for a game I've seen in a while.
There is a story that gradually unweils as you explore the world and collect various objects and slay enemies. A creative way if you ask me. There is a high chance you'll unlock it's parts out of order, but due to the way the story is written, it doesn't really matter.
For the actual gameplay, it's broken up to two parts- fighing and exploration (even though the world is small). As far as fighting goes, it's your typical shooter. You fly around and shoot at everything. But your balloon is quite fragile and with bullets flying everywhere (this game turns into bullet hell quickly), it's safe to say, you're going to die quite a few times. But if you start taking damage, you can regain health when you stop shooting. One thing that needs to be mentioned- there is no pause button, that's a pretty big oversight if you ask me. You can go back to the menu, but that cancels your current run, you'll have to start over again.
. As far as exploration goes, you have sky and ocean to explore. There are no enemies underwater, but you have limited oxygen. The main reason to dive down is to recover collectables that unlock story and add passengers to your balloon (purely cosmetic).
I have mentioned unique art style. But it's not original- the visuals were taken straight from movies directed by Karel Zeman, namely Vynález Zkázy, or The Fabulous World of Jules Verne as it's known to the rest of the world. Then there is a little bit of influence by Fabulous Baron Munchausen from the same director- few visual references and the overall story feels like something that would happen in the movie. Overall it's a decent effort to recreate the art style, but it doesn't hold up to the source material. So graphics are okay. Not amazing (for amazing visuals you have to watch the movies).
Overall the game looks unique, there's fairly lot to do in it (for a twin stick) and the price is really low. If you like twin sticks, you can't go wrong here. It'll keep you busy for few hours.

Duke Nukem Forever. 15 years in the making and yet here I am, considering if it couldn't have used a couple of more years in development. The truth is though, 5-10-15-20 years it wouldn't have mattered. The problem here isn't lack of development, it's the direction of the development.
All the fluff is there though. Playing this game you will never doubt that this is a Duke game. Scantily clad women are everywhere and you will rarely walk more than ten feet between the various pop culture references, jokes and other nonsense. If anything Gearbox deserves some credit for getting that part of the franchise right. The humor is there, the silliness, the crazy. What they got wrong, is the mechanics.
Playing Duke Nukem Forever is like playing every FPS made in the last 10 years. Gearbox certainly did. They added every cheesy feature the genre has ever experimented with. You got your vehicle sections, your turret sections, your button mashing quick-time events and so on and so forth. Any sense of the fast paced, old school style of FPS that made Duke Nukem 3D the icon it is today is long gone. Instead we have a Duke that's become old and arthritic. This Duke isn't the badass Duke of old. This Duke leans on stamina bars, regenerating health, limited weapon slots, scripted events and linear maps.
Instead of the sprawling maps of Duke 3D, that had you running, jumping, flying and swimming all over the place, looking for secrets and keycards you play through entirely linear and fully scripted sequences and fights you do not allow you to progress until you've killed what the game wants you to kill and listened to whatever irrelevant dialog the game wants you to listen to. The entire experience is slow and dull and there is little to look forward to besides the naked ladies and the occasional proper joke.
Duke Nukem 3D was a masterpiece of adolescent insanity, of old school fast paced shooting, of innovative map design. Duke Nukem Forever has captured the adolescent part but lost everything else in the shuffle. What's left is a mediocre shooter with a bunch of nudes thrown around.
Duke Nukem Forever is not a very good game. It's a game that doesn't stay true to it's old school roots doesn't even compare to the original. Even by modern standards it brings nothing new to the table, just a bunch of rehashed concepts and ideas. Nothing is new, nothing is better than what's been already done.
All in all. For those that have been waiting, hoping for a good old school style shooter, this ain't it. And for those that just want a decent modern shooter to pass the time, this ain't it either. They might get the crude humor right but everything else, just ain't Duke.

I want to like this game I really do. The graphics are not bad for what you're paying for.  My issues with this game is the game play and mechanics. Armageddon is a tile based strategy game which was fun it was turn based and you know exactly what you're getting into. This game is trying to be an Xcom-ish 40k with the best of both tile based and squad based tactical combat but fails. I understand RNG in games like Xcom or Wasteland but this game's RNG wants you to punch your monitor.  For example anyone familiar with warhammer 40k knows what a Melta gun can do, Now imagine a melta hitting lets say a gretchin. This is the equivelent of using a flamthrower on an ant, however in this game at medium range the melta damage is listed as low against and gretchin unit in the open (Not in cover) and does little damage.
Another issue I have with this game is the damage tables are all over the map. A stormbolter shouldn't be able to do more damage against a vehicle than a terminator with a powerfist. On the Melee topic the space marine units such as blood claws, Wolfguards (With frost weapons,Terminator armor or even a powerfist) when engaged in melee is like watching friday night sissy fights (I get it I've read over 100 warhammer books and played table top Orks are good in close combat however so are "Hero" units such as Wolfguard and Terminators) The Orks get reaction hits 100% of the time whereas your Wolfguard maybe gets a hit and for reaction hits you're better off putting a bolt pistol in your mouth and suck starting it. With how many ork units are on every map the damage output of every space marine unit needs to be upped by at least 50% ( A bolter fires an explosive armor piercing round from a semi-automatic or automatic open bolt rifle. Think a Mk-19 on steroids that is in a rifle form) A Melta is a anti everything weapon meant to be a mid ranged anti armor support weapon ( it melts armor and through the melted hole another jet of superheated gases melts everything on the inside hence Melta) Now lets talk about the dreadnaught. The wolf claw should be able to wreck anything it touches however in this game you may as well concede defeat if your dreadnaught gets into close combat (It's a walking mech with insane firepower and armor the only things that can take it out are anti armor weapons, Power weapons or another vehicle deff dread,tank ect.)
Deployment is the last issue I have. there is no logic behind it, no wolf lord with intel would deploy a strong contingent of bloodclaws when the enemy army is fielding numerous fast attack or armor units. No he would have long fangs maybe a predator and some dreadnaughts to support the convoy of rhinos. ( I get that you are suppose to bumrush the exit with a rhino and hope he doesn't get swarmed)
To the developers I don't know if you're either A Ork bias players or you just fail to grasp what warhammer 40k is about but I recommend you pick up a warhammer 40k rulebook and codex's for races you plan on using and try to implement the strengths and weakness of said races. For Example Orks are dumb but have a ton of numbers, They can jerry rig virtually anything and are super tough i.e they have messed up nerve endings and can't feel pain.  Space Marines are a sledgehammer to crack a walnut. The average space marine can take on up to 100 normal men in hand to hand combat add on the fact his primary weapon fires armor piercing exploding rounds that can literally pulp a person in 1 round or in a large orks case 3-4. Now you take the Space wolves (Think Vikings in space) Very diverse military tactics but also very scary in close combat (Anyone who has played against them or with them on tabletop knows what I'm talking about) The basic infantry is the bloodclaw (Throw away melee unit used in large packs to close with and destroy the enemy) and those that survive are tempered and are elevated to the core infantry the grey hunters (Tactical squads pretty much) Then you have specialized units such as Skyclaws ect I don't want to write the whole codex down.
Please in future patches if what you're trying to do is make a tactical  turn based strategy than you need to balance this fast. In the current state I can't recommend this game to anyone who likes Warhammer 40k or turn based strategy games such as Xcom or Wasteland.

This game horrifies me, utterly and terribly. I'm on the last of a fifteen checkpoint trial. I slide around a corner doing twenty-five. My eyes widen in terror when I see a tree clip my back wheel, bending it all to hell and making the race impossible to finish. *presses "R" to restart for the tenth time*
Let me just say, this game is hard. Your car will feel slow and clunky and will squash like a bug at seemingly stupid slow speeds. It is just about as realistic in that regard as it gets. Like any racing game, there are fast and slow cars. Except they all break equally as easy, so don't think going faster is always better.
And as for so many people saying the cars feel like they're on ice, ignore them. If you've ever driven on solid ice, you would know that you can't get going more than a few miles an hour in a decent turn before you're going sideways. A car is held in place by four little patches of rubber each about the size of your hand. Once you break sliding friction, you're boned.
Also, for anyone turned off by the fact that this is a "crashing simulator," I would also disagree. The fun is in the trials. The launching your car off a four story cube in the test world gets boring after a while. There are something like 15 ish trials right now that range from small circuits to long rallies to silly stuff like seeing if you can jump four ramps in a row or make your way down a six-hundred foot cliff. There will be a campaign mode integrated eventually.
The game encourages smart driving (knowing the limits of your car, how fast you need to enter turns, when to accelerate and when to brake). You don't need a steering wheel or pedals, but I'm sure they'd be fun.
The only issue I have with the game is its checkpoint system. First of all, they're huge and kinda ugly. Secondly, if you try to switch out your vehicle with another mid-race, it screws everything up.
