Basically, this game is a huge imporvement on the previous DotP games, as it allows you to create custom decks and fully utilize cards from M15 and older sets, instead of having premade decks that allow barely any customisation and a stale meta, you can pretty much swap and switch on the go as you unlock new cards and get new deck ideas / find something new to netdeck.
But all of this comes at the typical price of having to grind for booster packs ( unless you want to pay for a quick unlock ). It's impossible to tell how much of an impact the exclusive cards will have on competitive games at this point, as this game has been out for about 3 hours at the time of this review.
The tutorial allows newer players to get into the game rather quick, by explaining most details and card effects that magic has. This tutorial won't cover everything though, so you will have to gather some experience in order to get good.
Now, let us talk about the issues that other reviewers have with this game:
1. You can't really see what starter deck you're picking.
Well, that is true. But you have the option to change decks as you play against the Polis Crusher encounter and find a deck you like. You can't change the deck AFTER you have finished the tutorial, so try out some decks and pick your favourite deck.
2. Clunky menus.
I have to agree, the new menu is kind of clunky and you have barely any oversight on what the panels are. One can only hope that they can fix it in the future.
3. The game is too hard.
You can turn down the difficulty, I've had no problems beating Innistrad and a couple of explore missions on the highest difficulty. Maybe you should get good if the lowers difficulty gives you trouble.
4. You have to grind to get cards.
Yes, you STILL have to grind for cards and beat encounters a couple of times. If you don't like grinding or investing money, stay away from the game. I know a lot of people will say that they paid for the game and that they have the right to own all cards. Some people, like myself, enjoy playing more and unlocking cards to improve their decks bit by bit. If you don't like it, as I said, don't buy it.
I would recommend this game, as it is basically just a sequel to DotP with a huge improvement in the deckbuilding ( which is a huge part of card games ) at the cost of some clunky menus.

Screw the haters. Understand what kind of game this is, and you'll enjoy it.
Allow me to elaborate: This game is not the pinnacle of game design, or full of fresh ideas, or show-stopping in any way. What it is is a fun shooter with plenty of throwbacks and references to the 90's/early 2000's. It's not without its flaws, but it is plenty of fun and worthy of a collection, especially for a tenner.
Graphics- No, they aren't great. No, they don't push the limits of anything beyond a low-midrange computer. But they get the job done and do look good while doing so. Pigcops, certain cars, certain weapons, octabrains, and bosses are modeled very well, and you can definitely tell what they are and what they were modeled after (meaning you'll recognize a battlelord right away if you've played Duke3D). Plus, since this game doesn't push high-end setups, it's accessible to everyone.
Sound- Not much to speak of here. The sound is done well. Guns have enough punch. Music is done well. Stereo separation and directional audio does what it needs to.
Gameplay- Honestly, this is where it matters most. You do buy a game for gameplay, not to just look at graphics. Again, don't expect this to rule the gaming world with fresh, innovative play. But, if you're looking for a shooter that's fast, precise, and doesn't do much of the cover mechanic, this is it. Plenty of stuff to shoot, plenty of guns to use, plenty of bosses to fight and die against.
Overall, good for several playthroughs and some multiplayer. This is a basic 2011 shooter with 1998 roots, and they show. I happen to like gameplay like this. If you also do, buy and enjoy. If not, go ahead and move on.

Quick Disclaimer; despite what the Store Page says it is Vista supported.
Kero Blaster is simple, straight-forward run and gun style platformer in a similar vein to Pixel most internationally famous work, Cave Story. Unlike Cave Story, the game has almost no "Metroidvania" elements in it's design. Instead weapons and upgrades are unlocked naturally as you progress through the seven levels. There's no back travel function, so when you beat level 1 you can't go back to it short of starting a new game.
As far as difficulty is concerned, it is easier than Cave Story. An auto save function allows you, for the most part, to effectively retry rooms with no major downside except towards the finale when the checkpoints start breaking up by several screens rather than one. As long as you don't die (and the menu button can be brought up at any point so even if you miss a jump and plummet into a pit as long as you're quick enough you can still retry no consquence.) you can keep retrying infinitely if needed. That said, Hard mode, or "Zangyou" mode is a definite challenge with it's own storyline. It revamps existing content IE new stage layouts, enemies and even boss patterns are slightly or completely different. Long time Pixel fans, or even just players who enjoy a good challenge will greatly enjoy this mode, as normal mode is decidedly lacking in serious difficulty until the last sections of the game.
Gameplay is fun and basically a more straight-forward version of Cave story system with some key differences. Instead of weapon exp, money drops, which can be used to upgrade weapons or buy defensive items like more health or revive jar. Weapons no longer downgrade if hurt enough, and stay consistent. Like Cave Story, each weapon has at least 3 stages. Each one progressively better than the last. Some weapons even have a fourth stage. There's a total of 5 weapons in the game, one of which is a secret. They're all very useful and surprisingly well balanced. If you're the type to stick with one weapon, you'll probably have trouble in certain parts, but for the most part every weapon works exceedingly well in all situations the game presents. In order to max all the weapons though, expect to do a bit of grinding. If you ignore defensive upgrades you should have to do relatively little though, something else rewarding good play.
Music and level design are pretty much what I expect from Pixel. Nothing really stands out as much as some of his other soundtracks, but I still absolutely enjoy Kero Blaster OST. Levels too, probably aren't his best work but his stage design is very "fair". Most area gimmicks or traps are explained in safe areas to give you a heads up and nothing really is "trial and error" about Kero Blaster. It's difficulty is extremely honest and if you die it's usually on you, not because of a cheap death. The story is kind of non-existant, very simple story. It's very cute in a way, particularly with it's foreshadowing.
All in all, it's a nice little sidegrade to his other work, Cave Story. It does some things better and some things worse. If you're a mega pixel fan you'll be happy to know it definitely delivers. If you're a casual fan you'll find this probably MORE enjoyable. Even if you've never played a run and gun platformer before, this game is probably one of the best examples of a place to start. Either way, I hope you have as much fun as I did.

A lot more bad points than good points on this one.
BUT, you might wanna have a look at my (edited now that I got more hours behind me) closing words to know if this game is for you or not.
- Finally being able to build a somehow more "customized deck" !
- The new battle UI is neat (is that even a good point anyway)
- If you're really patient, you can get a lot of cards and shape your deck however you want, tho be prepared for some nuts grinding.
- Menus are goddam slow to navigate in. Looks fancy the first few minutes, but afterwards each menu transition will feel like an eternity. You also sometimes have to click several times on a button due to the slow responsiveness of the UI (probably cos it didn't finish its transition)
- You start with only one deck (yes, only one). You cannot swap decks once you have chosen, and you have no idea what the contents of your pick will be (all you know is the colors inside your starter deck).
- The starting deck is WEAK, and I mean it. Compared to the previous Magic DoTP, the deck feels weak, no fun cards in it that makes you grin, no solutions against many types of deck you might encounter. The result is, AI will♥♥♥♥♥♥you in Planeswalker diff unless you get not only a perfect starting hand but also very good draws. In fact, turn down the difficulty to "Mage" and do some games against a random AI deck, you're not even guaranteed to win, even as a veteran player. The problem would not be with your skills, but because of how weak the deck is. It does look like you can change your starting deck at the very start (tho it doesn't seem clearly visible), but afterwards you're stuck with it until you get enough cards to build a new deck, or to alter your starting one to something decent.
- Grindfest party to build a proper deck. We are very close to a Pay2Win iteration with this 2015 edition. The game now has an online shop in which you can buy boosters (1.79€ for 10 cards) for real money, or an entire card collection for (4.99€). We all get where this is going. And given the facts that even Mage level AI will pown you depending on your starter deck (which doesn't make speed games for farm very efficient at start), you will either have to be very patient or break your piggy bank, the latter being obviously what the game wants you to do. For reference, Only two rares in your starting deck (one at first, and the second when you finish or skip tutorial).
- The land system is broken. Example : Let's suppose you have two plains and two swamps in play, and in your hand you got two cards that each cost one swamp and one colorless mana to play. If you wanted to play both, you obviously would want to pay one plain and one swamp for each.
Well guess what? No. Click the first card in your hand, and the system will often tap both swamps for its mana cost. What the [insert kind words and sing a Bieber song here] hell? You can still tap your lands manually with CTRL, but the system used to be smart enough to leave you with the right mana combinations, which ain't the case anymore. Let's hope this gets fixed.
Well, we wanted a better way to customize our deck, so now we have it. While I believe there is a way to build the "deck of your dreams" (will never beat Shandalar anyway), the game obviously wants you to pay extra money to get what you want. I'm saying this because if this wasn't the case, they could've made starter decks more fun and powerful (like the starter decks in the previous series), and still make other good cards unlockable afterwards, which would've been fair trade. Instead, they made your deck as weak as it can be to either push your patience to the limit or make you break your piggybank. This is not a business tactic I am especially fond of, thus I cannot put a thumbs up for this game.
To clear any misuderstanding, I'm not saying the game is bad per-se. The game itself is solid, and if you're willing to make repeated fights to farm your cards, you'll definitely have fun later on (I can tell without being there yet). I mean, how can it not be fun to make the deck the way you want ?
HOWEVER, and unlike the previous Magic DotP games, you WILL NOT have fun right off the bat. You will first have to farm cards for hours before you have something you can really call a "Deck". In the end, if you know you are willing to spend a decent amount of time to get your cards, I believe you won't regret it and you'll definitely have fun. If not, well...
Have a great day,

Duke Nukem used to be a gun mayhem shooter where you feel like a badass using kickass weapons while spitting cheesy one-liners. You got to explore the map to find secrets to keep yourself better equipped and encounter various fun intractable objects. Now, imagine that game with none of that. Mostly.
While some of the guns are fun to shoot, because you're limited to 2 weapons (or 4 if you choose "extended inventory", which was added after the game release), you don't get to carry around all of them which makes it the worst part of the game. Bosses pretty much require you to carry an RPG, so you’re limited to one weapon most of the times. This game would have been a lot more fun if you could carry all of the weapons just like the classic games.
They added first person platforming which is awkward, but at least it didn't make the game unnecessarily harder to beat. There are occasionally puzzles, but uninspired and mostly easy.
Dodging enemy projectiles and attacks while blasting your way out was a fun part of the original Duke Nukem games, but that is also gone here. Enemies shoot fast (unless they carry heavy weapons) and lock on you, you cannot perform any advanced maneuvers, especially when the maps have so many objects you can run into and most of the battle areas are very condensed.
This game fails to deliver that original Duke Nukem experience and made something that no one really wanted. It’s a bad shooter, but it’s really a good one either. To be fair, it wasn't boring at least, but then again why your precious life waste time on such a mediocre game? There are so many other options if you want to play some kickass mindless shooter (e.g. Serious Sam 3), this game is NOT RECOMMENDED, even for a cheap price.

I'm really trying to like this game, but it's coming at a painful slope.
The voxel art style, rather than enjoyable, helps demonstrate why Minecraft and similar-styled games employ a better use of low-res texture while keeping a solid player engagement. The mid-quality textures most blocks display just serve to make them look awkward in the finished product. Maybe I'm not playing with the right skin, or maybe I should set my graphics card lower, but coupled with a resulting low fps (again, maybe my fault, going on a 3GB GPU) it feels poorly-implemented as of its current stage in the development.
The movement feels clunky. There's no way around it. When you place an object, highlighting the box that object was placed in automatically targets that object, which I understand the idea behind, but the results are a lot of clumsily-destroyed objects thinking I had nothing impeding my way to the ore I was facing. The auto-jump feature also feels very thrown-together, as the awkward textures and automatically-ascending controls make it feel very difficult to navigate an area properly.
The UI is overcrowded. Even after disabling alerts on certain machine parts, you've got your item bar, you've got your tutorial goals/missions, you've got a box that will forever tell you about the item you've highlighted in your item bar (why?), your health window, your power/temperature/biohazard window. These have already shrunk the screen, and made things feel VERY cluttered.
The crafting just feels lackluster, and needlessly complex. I could compare this to having been given a few wooden pallets and a decently-sized toolbelt and being given the instructions "Go make a chair out of these". You've got the wood and tools, but it's just. not. happening. Things are explained poorly, and at inopportune times (I didn't even know I could manually mine until I'd automated my copper and tin!). Some things, which should be touched on more thoroughly, are left entirely unapproached. Also, why does my crafting station have to say "Crafting" like a Portal Turret every time I manually craft something? The first time was cute, but it wore out its welcome soon after.
Fianlly, why does FCE get a free pass for releasing DLC while still in Early Access, while ARK was torn to shreds? I'm not excusing ARK, I'm putting the onus on this game to defend itself for demanding more money for additional content toward a game that isn't even finished.
I've thrown a lot of shade, but please let me say this: I love the idea behind this game. Factorio and Minecraft are both gems, and I can see the inspiration FortressCraft draws from them. However, it takes all the pieces that shouldn't mesh together, and tries it anyway. It takes the laissez faire-style introduction that Minecraft employs, while utilizing similar graphical and resource-management system like Factorio. These don't go well together.
I'd love to see a special tutorial world, where the player has the chance to explore the possibilities more naturally, because there are a LOT of them. Give us a world where we can explore mining, gathering, resource-management, and automation in an organic setting, allowing for goals on multiple fronts working in tandem with one another. I realize it's a challenge, asking for an entire scenario, but as it stands, the steep learning curve is REALLY putting me off from wanting to pick this game back up.

I'm not going to pretend this game is great, it even borders on bad at times but if youre a big wrpg fan you might let some of the bad things slide and see it for what it does well.
Controls are clunky and animations are stiff, but the Gameplay is solid and character progression is good, you have 3 options in how you handle combat, ranged, melee and magic, ranged is probably the worst but i didn't really experience much of it, melee is fairly basic but the skills you can get make it a little better with time, i didn't start to enjoy it until i started parrying(hitting just after blocking) and using my skills more.
Magic is insanely good in this game, it works by combining different effect cards with different elements to create your own spells, i'm not sure how many spells there are in the game but a lot of them are pretty unique and creative.
The story is pretty average apart from the ending, i don't want to spoil it but the last boss is really dissapointing since you don't even fight him head on.
Sidequests on the other hand are great and reminded me of oblivion in some ways, although not nearly as good, you have different guilds that have different storylines that vary in length and then there are a bunch of quests in the world that are both interesting and even pretty funny at times.
Graphically it's a mixed bag, aesthetically it's great, the enviroments are varied and pretty unique for a wrpg, you go from an egyptian savannah area to some sort of asian(Korean or Chinese) jungle and finally to a swamp, the assets and environments are good looking but other aspects like animations and character models are pretty bad.
One final thing to note is that you have to register an account at the beggining of the game to use the multiplayer, the registration is incredibly intrusive and personal if i remember correctly and i saw that a lot of people marked the game as not reccomended because of it, which i consider completely justified, if you however decide to try the mp(and that's if it's still online)you're going to get a pretty great psuedo mmo tier experience with loads of content and even a village manager later on.

First impressions:
Two Worlds 2 is an RPG, similar to Gothic, Elder Scrolls and Risen. It stands out for it’s kick♥♥♥♥♥magic spell system. They’ve come up with this do-it-yourself magic spell card engine which let’s you build custom spells. It’s fun and original - first time I gave the wizard-character a try in an RPG.
The game did a lot of things right and overall left a user-friendly and positive impression.
Pros:
+ Ok graphics
+ Cool character, kinda reminds me of Danny Trejo. Also, he has those small comments upon interaction which sound smart and help improve his personality.
+ Super fast loading time.
+ Ability to save custom outfits in case you need to quickly change from wizard to warrior etc. This should be a genre standard.
+ Mobile teleport platforms was a very good idea.
+ User-friendly mission guide that gives you good overview of where you have to go and what you have to do.
+ Huge variety of enemies throughout the game.
Unfortunately there were those tiny mistakes that could and should have been fixed and improved before the game came out. Those were mainly issues that made the game feel a little immature and green, as if the development team consisted of professionals and amateurs and everyone got to contribute.
Cons:
- I never got the idea behind the name ‘two worlds’. Was it supposed to be something metaphorical? I played as a wizard who looked a lot like Gandalf in his younger years and the events were taking place in a savanna/jungle so more than ‘two worlds’ the game felt like Gandalf’s Safari Adventures.
- Major flaw: the game crashed left and right. I could count as much as 5 crashes in 2 minutes. Then again that truly helped me appreciate the quick loading times.
- Character design was way over the top. All those ridiculous, skimpy armors and gosh, those shoulder plates!
- The Voice Acting ...this was such a major one. When you take a person with a normal voice and tell him to imitate a funny sounding person, then it sounds like a normal person is making funny sounds. That happened throughout the game. Voice acting in this game might be the worst I’ve ever experienced.
- The script/ writing. The dialogues were long and dead boring, the story was unnecessarily complicated + there were completely obsolete characters. It all comes down to really bad game script.
- Something that’s easily forgettable once you’re in-game, but how they implemented Digital Rights Management in this game was not acceptable. The kind of information they asked before I could play the game made me feel very reluctant and extremely uncomfortable.
- NPC movement speed compared to animation was out of place.
- The great paradox of Two Worlds 2 is the ability to outrun rhinos and panthers even though your stamina is depleted after 100 meters of sprinting.
- Swift moving around in combat makes the enemy AI go crazy, they will get stuck behind obstacles and go into attack mode some 5-6 meters from you.
- Banal, unrealistic female characters - a demoness, a vixen and a damsel in distress.
- Battles boil down to how fast you can click the mouse button.
Verdict:
The Cons list became quite long but let yourself not be discouraged by that, those were just minor flaws, all except the DRM issue which kills the gaming world and violates human rights. Overall it was a very positive experience and introduced many new original elements that I'd like to see become a genre standard.

If you're anything like me you'll love this game.
I've desperately been searching for a community based town building game. This game has that with pvp aspects added in. It definitely has a long way to go but if you find a good server you can still get a very enjoyable experience even though everything is not fully implemented yet. The future for this game is very bright and even if you don't buy it to support it's development I would keep your eye on this game for when it hits MMO phase.
Pros: The variety of servers available really lets you choose your own play-style. If you want to go alone and keep it easy you can choose a server with high skill multiplier (you level up faster) and a higher skill cap (so you can do more things). While if you're looking for a challenge you can join a server with lower limits and slower leveling (such as Camelot). For me, I enjoy the challenge and I feel rewarded when I finally finish building that project I've been working on, or that I finally reached that level I've been training for. EVEN if this game was to stop being developed today I know that with the modding community the way it is, and the guys over at Camelot server, this game could still be enjoyable indefinitely. Being a part of community and being needed for your skills by that community is an amazing feeling and really promotes the social aspect of this game.
Cons: Unless skills are set to over 1500 max you'll need at least a few other people to play and build a community with. Some servers are poorly managed and it may be hard to find one that really suites your play style that is consistently up. The game is still lacking in may aspects, but it's in alpha and you are supporting development by buying the game like it is. If you're into playing solo or a lot of heavy action packed game-play you may not like this. If you don't like medieval settings or non-targeted combat (like chivalry or mount and blade) you may not like this game.

You got to explore the map to find secrets to keep yourself better equipped and encounter various fun intractable objects. Now, imagine that game with none of that. Mostly.

Bosses pretty much require you to carry an RPG, so you’re limited to one weapon most of the times. This game would have been a lot more fun if you could carry all of the weapons just like the classic games.
They added first person platforming which is awkward, but at least it didn't make the game unnecessarily harder to beat. There are occasionally puzzles, but uninspired and mostly easy.
Dodging enemy projectiles and attacks while blasting your way out was a fun part of the original Duke Nukem games, but that is also gone here. Enemies shoot fast (unless they carry heavy weapons) and lock on you, you cannot perform any advanced maneuvers, especially when the maps have so many objects you can run into and most of the battle areas are very condensed.
This game fails to deliver that original Duke Nukem experience and made something that no one really wanted. It’s a bad shooter, but it’s really a good one either. To be fair, it wasn't boring at least, but then again why your precious life waste time on such a mediocre game? There are so many other options if you want to play some kickass mindless shooter (e.g. Serious Sam 3), this game is NOT RECOMMENDED, even for a cheap price.

Ahhh Duke Nukem. A classic from my younger days. And then nothing but 15 years of promises and maybes hinted by leaked screenshots.  Fast forward to Duke Nukem Forever and the results are wildly mixed. Positives are the gunplay, voice acting, crude humor and boss fights. Negatives include the platforming elements, BEYOND uneven level design and atrocious load times. The level design was so frustrating. For every clever and fun level like Lady Killer or Ghost Town, they'd throw in a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥like The Hive.  Even the levels taking place outside of Vegas were meh. And the platforming elements. Horrible. Special shout out to Duke Burger Part 2 which irritated the hell out of me. Platforming elements are fine but I found the controls to be a little floaty where Duke would take that extra unintended step and you are back to the last checkpoint.  And the load times, my lord the load times. I died quite a bit in this game as in my old age the reflexes don't work like they used to but I can probably recite every tip that came on during the laod screens. The bottom line is that DNF has some good stuff. The non PC humor, excellent larger than life boss fights and a few well desinged levels overshadow the craptacular levels, platforming and load times. Easy recommendation for $5.

SR is a turn based wargame based on the Warhammer 40k Universe.  You take control of an army of either Orks or Space Wolf Space Marines and engage in turn based combat.
The game comes with two campaigns which consist of a few story missions interspaced with random skirmish missions.  Other game modes include skirmish as well as a mission and campaign editor.
Typically before a fight you will be able to choose your starting force.  You have force points and you pick your army, each unit costs X amount of points.  You can build you force until you have no more points to spend.  Your opponent does the same (Campaign missions are a bit different ).
Missions typically involved battling over strategic points on the map and whoever controls the most by the end of the turn timer wins, although you can also win by wiping the opponent off the map.
Gameplay wise units can move, shoot and perform special moves.  Each unit has separate move points, action points and special abilities (if unlocked).  So a unit can move and shoot and use a special action (like throw a grenade) in the same turn.  No action point counting.  This leads to nice fluid gameplay which is important considering the vast amount of units that can be in play.
For Campaigns, units gain XP for kills and level up gaining new abilities, both passive and active which makes keeping these units around interesting.
Graphically I like it, bit of a cartoony / modely feel but it works very well and it is very satisfying to see your bolters let loose and units explode into gore!  This looks closer to what the table top would than “realism” and works well.
All units are also to scale and when you have loads of units from Bolter wielding space marines to hulking Imperial Knights you get a great sense of scale.
Main disappointments is there is a lack of fluff for the campaigns, no real story per se, just a bit of text on the campaign missions (right now it is 1 campaign mission, 3 – 4 skirmishes, 1 campaign mission etc) so feels a bit disconnected (imo) and the maps can feel a bit bland at time (especially the random generated ones).  The fun gameplay makes up for these shortcomings however and I really feel this game can grow even better with the proper support!

So, Amnesia: The Dark Descent has always been regarded as one of the "scariest games ever." PERSONALLY, I didn't find it that truly terrifying. There were a few jumpscares, but for the most part I wasn't on edge for my full 14 hours of gameplay.
HOWEVER, if you like horror and/or survival-horror, get this game. Just do it. It is intense at many points, and the monsters will throw you for a loop when they do show up.
Also, atmosphere. Just pure atmosphere. You lose yourself in this game. It's amazing at that, without a doubt. The sounds, the lighting, the mechanics; it's all very well done, especially for a game that's over 4 years old. And, as I said before, when the monsters show up, it's pretty intense. You feel like you're being chased. Overall, I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes horror or suvival-horror genres. It's a classic, and definitely worth it.

The game play is simple, as you are provided no weapons (further aiding a  feeling of helplessness) and do not expect any innovative mechanics. In general, the game is like a warm bath of dread. Just let the uneasiness sink in and enjoy the calming descent into madness.

My biggest 2 issues with this game:
Campaign: Holding large territories is virtually impossible due to unrest, I guess that is historically accurate (even on easy), but counter-intuitive to your objectives.
Battles: Unit and camera control are both a disaster. Why they decided against a traditional RTS camera (even though there is an RTS camera option in the game) is beyond me. Moving the mouse to the sides rotates the camera instead of scrolling the map...same goes for the arrow keys. Units themselves are hard to control and rarely do what you tell them to. Want your cavalry to attack a certain squad from behind? Well, first you have manually move them to avoid all other enemies in sight and then they may still attack the wrong enemy. Battles frequently look like masses of pixels trying to get to the enemy, but the game engine doesn't allow that.
A good example of how to do it right would be Dawn of War. Here units first engage in ranged combat, but when they are forced into melee they are actively looking for a direct opponent instead of creating 2 big masses of armies that patiently wait until the front line disintegrates. You can micro manage some of that, but honestly, it's really annoying and just lazy in my opinion.
Apart from that the game is actually pretty good if you're looking for Grand Strategy and the historic battles you can replay from the menu are fun and challenging, but also give you interesting info about what happened back then.
Please, take your time.

I'm proud of Ohgiya. I mean, I'm still embarrassed to be caught playing it, but I feel there's progress. Unlike Men of Yoshiwara: Kikuya, the heroine of Ohgiya is entagled with Yoshiwara for a logical purpose. She has a grounded reason for being there, in contrast to the previous game's heroine, and that means that her reserved innocence in the pleasure district is actually sad and darkly relatable, instead of merely illogical. There is even a route that, for these games especially, is subversively enjoyable: one of the potential love interests is a sex worker by choice, is happy to defend that choice when challenged, and his business savvy and skill at his chosen profession actually save the day-- leaving jealousy and possessiveness aside as the conterproductive and unnecessary negative emotions they are, upholding instead the real romantic values of loyalty and trust. Of course, that's one of many routes, and the rest resort to the usual cocktail of patriarchal, possessive, and problematic tropes that uphold the notion of a woman's virtue = virginity; but the fact that there is one route that I'd consider romantic (leaving aside the poorly written, poorly translated naughty sequences) puts it head and shoulders above its predecessor.
That said-- buy it on sale if you're going to. This is no narrative treat even if it is an improvement: it's an enjoyable mess at best.

Shadow Warrior 2 takes the great sword combat and shooting from part one and adds Borderlands style collecting and upgrading, skills and also adds side missions. The upgrade system improves damage and resistance to damage and allows you to add several improvements to each of the many weapons in the game. The weapon loadout is impressive and nicely varied. Besides the many sword variants there's anything from a bow and arrow up to a nail gun. Side missions can be collected from characters in the main hub map and serve to provide skill points for unlocking and improving additional combat and support skills. Skills improve health or chi (used to power abilities) or add new abilities you can use in the game. You also collect money which you can spend in the stores to buy more upgrades (and sell the crap ones). Don't like the collectathon? Then ignore it and slice your way through your enemies the hard way. Just fit in the highest level upgrades every once in a while and you'll be fine. I personally wish I didn't have to rely so much on the minimap for finding chests and items, though. The cluttered maps sometimes make it difficult to recognise things.
The story and the writing are okay. The humor is what it is and can sometimes be funny, sometimes not. If you already played the previous game, you know what you are in for. If not, you didn't really miss out, storywise.
From the technical side you get a very well optimized game that can really look quite pretty. There are loads of settings to tweak to further improve the visuals or the frame rate. All in all Shadow Warrior 2 is a technically very competent PC title.
There's also coop, though I haven't tried that yet.
This is a solid if not perfect game that is definitely worth its asking price.

As you can see I've spent a great deal of time in this game over the past month I've owned it. Initially I wanted to like this game, I own mount and blade, I love minecraft and I played wurm so this game should be right up my ally.
I'm tired however of games releasing too soon, unfinished and unable to deliver the basic essentials that make a game playable and tonight I experianced all the reasons why this game sucks balls.
Let me start by saying tha tthe optimization for the client is terrible, the polish on the server hosting is worse. Never before have I had to go to the extents I had to go to with a game in order to host my own private server. Your not talking about a simple download and run from steam, your talking unique software for running databases combined with some insanely disconjointed piece of crap software that runs the server. Then ontop of that the server are essentially downscaled version of the MMO, You see this game had problems running a larger map, so they decreased the size of the map considerably and put a limit of 64 players instead of 1000 players (like the original development of the mmo started with) because the game degrades over time.
Put it this way, a successful servers live expectancy is around 1 month. A few weeks into a servers life the amount of stumps (cut down tree stumps that people do not remove because there is no reason to do so) combined with the amount of terraforming and building/npc spawning/crops and tree updates (for growth) means that its common for servers to experiance lag in the morning. This consistantly increases in magnitude until such point that the server crashes continously and requires a wipe.
That is best case senario, worst case senario is that the server is hosted/owned by a compleate moron. That's right, this is a game that admins get super powers and in a world that can soak up a few weeks of your life that is nothing but bad news. I've restarted 4 times since purchase, twice because of admin abuse, once because corrupt database and the last because my community wanted to switch from a full server (the reason it was full was because it was a rare server that actually worked and wasnt hosted/admin by a 13 year old).
And that is not even getting onto the problems with the game itself. Combat skills are hidden behind practially every bottleneck skill progression in the game. Most people will be able to build a castle before they can wieild a sword and wear armour, the reason for this is that the combat system is terrible. The idea of a mount and blade-esk combat system in a game like this is awsome, unfortunatly this game does not pull it off. Instead you have a game with bizzar hitboxes and wierd damage calculations, its clunky and sluggish. People that do not want to fight can flee and you can do nothing about it.
Moving on to death, if your new and you find yourself on the reciving end of more settled players, rest asured that they can kill you 100 times without a care in the world. The mechanics in place are suposed to be that once you reach -50 you can never go back and that is suposed to prevent people going full on crazy killing spree mode. In reality however nobody that starts the game will ever be a threat to someone established, as you need to progress through all the diffrent crafting tree's to be able to craft and wear combat equipment the reality is that this game is not new player friendly. Most people will be the king of thier own little hill before they get into combat skills and that quite frankly is nothing like what you would expect from a fuedal era sandbox game.
the TLDR; if you want this game but fully functional and working go play Wurm or Rust. This game will sap literally days of your time and in a split second everything you have taken weeks to develop will be gone, not via some siege mechanics but by server wipes, bad admins and/or griefers. Stay away from this one, maybe in a few years if they manage to get the MMO launched it will be worth a look again but then again... why wait to experiance less than what is already on the market with Wurm?

It was fun the first few hours but falls flat very quickly once all the cracks start to show. I played the heck out of Shadow Warrior 2013 and it's sad to see that it has come to this. It's a SHIFT-mashing simulator, and a kick in the Wang to the Shadow Warrior franchise
_____________
COMBAT
_____________
The combat is different from Shadow Warrior 2013. No longer can you slash people in half and have them slowly peel away like a banana. No longer are you faced with unique enemies such as shield users, flying gargoyles etc - making you adopt a different playstyle. No longer are you scored on your performance after each battle. No
It all boils down to how much DPS you can put on a target and how much you can mash SHIFT to dodge. It adopts more of a Borderlands-style combat system with number crunching, elemental damages, resistances etc. You will spend most of your time shooting at point-blank with a shotgun or minigun embued with high crit chance instead of doing ninja stuff. I didn't spend any skill points into the melee system at all.
Despite this, the combat you do get is still very meaty and satisfying, your opponents often explode into chunks or take flying lessons. The chainsaws are done right. The shotguns are done right. Heavy weapons are done right. Swords aren't. Precision weapons aren't. Launchers aren't (big enemies dodge them). This just isn't what I was expecting from a Shadow Warrior game. Most enemies can blink, or they constantly jump around. (There's no denying this was so they could move around a randomly generated map)
_____________
MAP DESIGN (Or lack there of)
_____________
The randomly generated levels are the worst thing that could have happened to this game. They lack any sort of memorable set pieces or coherence. I spent 90% of my time looking at the minimap to find chests and coins as there was nothing happening on screen to keep my eyes forward. No natural paths to take you to your destination, instead you end up jumping over rooftops with no restrictions making a b-line to the quest location,
To be more descriptive, the maps are basically a handful of medium-sized randomly generated arenas in which certain sections are 'instanced' depending on what quest you are on. You will be re-visiting the same maps and same locations within many many times throughout the game - none of which are all that unique or interesting
The secrets are uninspired. They often just involve an invisible wall somewhere.. there might be a hint such as an audio or lighting cue. If you re-visit the same map again for another quest you can go to back to the secret again and get the reward multiple times.
_____________
MISSIONS
_____________
They are HORRIBLE. Literally just fetch quests and having to kill a cluster of enemies throughout the entire game, with some very easy boss fights thrown in. You can literally complete the main story within about 2 hours if you ignore the side missions. Enemies scale with you so you can do this easily.
_____________
GRAPHICS/PERFORMANCE
_____________
The graphics as a whole are very nice.. every single piece of foliage moves and the shadows look awesome. The lighting through the trees - to the glowing Neo-Tokyo style streets - the weather effects...it looks great! Water is pretty bad though. The performance is silky smooth, running at 80fps/100fps with a GTX770... but sometimes this tanked to about 11 for brief moments later on in the game.
It's not worth the asking price, get it on sale.

To borrow heavily from Scott Tobias, Duke Nukem Forever deserves "the gentleman's F." It is neither a good game, nor a terrible game (ok, from a technical standpoint it IS pretty terrible), nor does it entail any of the fervor associated with either descriptor. It is, to further paraphrase Tobias, a "failure...try[ing] for nothing and flopping, [achieving] no payoff for compromise." There is potential for good in Duke Nukem Forever; the first two levels or so are likeable enough in a juvenile way, and there are some genuinely great set pieces -- the ghost town, the mine cart bits, the underwater section -- and I found the shrinking mechanism to be enjoyable, in the Duke Burger level anyway. Unfortunately, this game is ultimately dull, rote, and uninspired (and in places rather glaringly offensive), and must neither be recommended nor disparaged for its shortcomings. It truly does deserve to be dropped from a great height.

Sanctus Reach! A turn based strategy game with 40K elements and flair.
This game has a nostalgic taste. When you have played games for at least 10-20 years, you can't avoid feeling this. However, this is a new game which brings the good and the bad with this style. Obviously this game was made for people who enjoy turn based strategy, this is what you will get and can expect to enjoy, nothing more and nothing less. You can play the Space Wolves and the Orks, the only two factions in this game at this stage. The campaigns are focused only on Space Wolves, thus the orklover (heresy!) must sate his or her appetite on playing the orks in skirmish games or multiplayer.
I will begin with the Space Wolves, their campaigns has certain elements of story, although it is also severely lacking. As the player I must admit I don't really know much of the story behind this game at all since there is no real introduction when playing either of the two campaigns. A simple and short video with text and music presenting the theme and the background lore for the coming campaign would have been interesting. Yes I did of course read the texts presented at the screen where you pick either campaign but you might agree or disagree that this information really isn't telling you much about the background story for the engagements. 40K has a lot of lore and background usually, thus I feel a little lost here and can't really imagine myself taking part in the lore very well.
What about the Orks? True there is absolutely no insight at all about them in this game, who are they? Answer is no idea from the game information only. Imagine yourself a new player into 40K lore, you will not understand a thing about these green aggressors, who knows maybe they are the true good guys who simply came for revenge from an old feud? My point being, you don't know thy enemy. Is this really how Space Marines fight, not knowing their enemy? Seems weird that the oldest strategy ever implemented isn't showing itself at all in this strategy game,

Leaving lore behind we enter the most important aspects: Gameplay and impressions. A bad impression stops any player from even starting a game, bad gameplay will halt any player from continuing playing his/her newly bought game and begin the process of Refund. Sanctus Reach offer solid mostly bug-free gameplay. You won't face game breaking bugs here, nor units vanishing into the warp randomly no pure frustration which was not part of your own decision making in the actual game. If you don't scout ahead, expect the risk of getting rushed and mauled by a plethora of weapons, both ranged and melee. It may not happen in all games but the time you do get rushed because of moving forward blindly, there is only yourself to blame. The impressions of this game are "solid strategy turn based game" But it is honestly a little bleak too. The variation of maps are very limited and the colours you usually face except for desert regions offer dark colours only. The problem with colours is that if it is too dark too often, your eyes get tired, your mind can feel tired after extensive amount of playing. However, no one should play any game more than 4-5 hours without pause to begin with.

The deployment of units before battle commences is clunky and arguably unpleasant. Due to the fact that you get randomized units and you can't simply select units from a pool and then place them where you want them to be in the first place. Randomized selection is not a problem itself, but how the user interface is. Mainly because it is a slow process, first you have a big list to the left and already placed units on the map. After selecting the units you want, then you may deploy them. This extra step, deployment after unit selection is an unnecessary extra step which could have been included at unit selection. Picking the randomized units from the pool in the left and place them where you want would have been an easier way to do this. Saving time in multiplayer as well as in campaign/vs Ai.

Santus Reach is focused on Space Wolves and Orks. Problem is, there are only these two factions offered in multiplayer as well. The enormous variety of units for the two factions are not to be underestimated for sure, the amount to tactics and strategy offered when you play a skirmish with randomized pool selection is fun 10 times. But after that, and especially after playing the two campaigns, it is natural that the player would be a little fed up with playing the Space Wolves once again, and then there is the only one option left: Orks. If the developers did not aim to have a living multiplayer scene, then it is all right. However, more factions could have liven up the colours and/or added more variation for the mind. When I write mind, I mean psychologically. The more different kinds of toys you have to play with, the more happy the child is. You can have unlimited amount of choices among one set of toys, but it won't feel special when there are only those you get to play with. It's like indians and cowboys, sometimes you want to play the US army instead or Sioux instead of only Cherokee and Settlers.

In conclusion I am a very happy customer, the amount of hours I could pour into this and feel satisfaction from are apleny. 17 hours, after this amount of time I feel I am done with this game. The gameplay does not offer me more interest personally at this time, I am tired of Space Wolves and Orks, the lack of variation on map colours (There is no jungle, no forests) which made me as a player tired after playing this game, I felt exhausted a few times. from a game! It was a mental challenge to keep focus in the really big battles. The challenge offered in the campaigns was a delight to solve. The gameplay is once again solid in my opinion. Lacking colours, animations and lore might have put me off from continuing playing more. But I must also defend why I am happy despite this, 17 hours of gameplay at this stage is a very big amount of time for entertainment compared to a cinema or going to the theatres. You pay very little for many hours of entertainment in my opinion. It's a steal for what you get! However, I will play this game again if the "life" (expansions, more factions, animations, new maps etc) of the game develops further.

You can tell that the guy who created Cave Story is behind it with the art style in question, but it never hits the same level of charm or story that that game did. It's originally an IOS game that feels more at home here, with simple controls but solid gameplay that relies on good level design and basic weaponry to propel it forward. What it doesn't have is anything that hits you in the mouth, aka the knockout punch to really sell the game, as it's solid in most aspects, but not great in any one either. Some elements have problems with boss fights that let down and an overall sense of having played the game before, but for a title to pick up on sale, it will bring back some memories of Cave Story while you play through it, and it is enjoyable. You have no idea how much time I put into Duke Nukem 3D as a child, hundreds and hundreds of hours, on more than one platform. Duke Nukem 3D helped shape the FPS genre. It's totally fair to say Duke Nukem Forever had some serious shoes to fill.
You have no idea how much I ♥♥♥♥ing wanted to love this game.
I badly wanted, nay, badly needed to love this game! and the good news - it is a fun game. In parts.
The game opens with you replaying the classic 1996 Football field Boss Fight. As the one liners start flowing I breathe a sigh of relief. it's clear they haven't missed the mark too much, but this leads to one of Duken Nukem Forevers' core problems.
It hasn't advanced much at all since the 90's.
Maybe this was the point you may say, but I don't think so. Duke pokes fun at moderns shooters then uses features taken directly from them, such as an Unlimited regenerating health pool and only being able to carry two weapons at any given time.
You can't take the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a game then directly use features from it.
At it's core Duken Nukem Forever is an old school run and gun game. The levels have little coherence and could just as easily be a selection of random events that Duke comes into shooting and shouting one liners.
There are good parts, the combat is entertaining and has a 'classic' feel, the weapons are fun to use (even with overly large models) there are lots naked women, Duke ripping aliens heads off, Ball punching, Beer drinking, and crude humor that the child in me did enjoy.
Huge mini boss encounters are also fun but then you are soon back to some filler moment, when all you really want to do is blow up more aliens with a Rocket launcher.
To it's credit this game has no cut scenes. everything happens through the eyes of Duke. This is important, and I'd like to see more of this 'Half Life' approach in other FPS's.
The really bad moments in the game come from a driving level, broken up with a pointless "Oh no I've run out of gas" moment... and horrible and unavoidable control a shooting turret sections, mixed wioth lots of filler moments.
You have no idea how much I ♥♥♥♥ing wanted to love this game.
Duke - it's great to have you back, but this isn't the game we deserved.

This is the best squad level turn-based grid game that I have played in the past few years. It really shines in the skirmish mode with a great amount of replayability.  I love the fact that you get quite a bit of options when setting up your skirmish battle.  To top that off you get to place your units in chosen tactical locations prior to the battle while in the deployment phase.  Random skirmish maps are really random.  I can use the exact same setting when setting up my skirmish, and the maps are still quite diverse.
The terrain is destructible and many of the units have enough move points to move near the front lines and then back away again, to see enemy units that were covered by fog of war or terrain cover. This allows for numerous tactical and strategic plans.
At first I thought this game was pretty hard, I was not used to the different aproach in how to control the units compared to other games of the same type.  After a few hours into the game I started to like it more and more.
I highly recommend this game even for the full price, It's worth it!  I will be buying any DLC's that come out for this game. I like it that much! So have fun playing, I know you will!

I've always loved racing games, putting countless hours over the years into simulation style and arcade style racing games alike. However, one thing that always bugged me was the lack of realistic physics when I crashed my car. A lot of times, they showed up only as scratches or fender benders, or nothing at all in games like Gran Turismo.
What people get in BeamNG drive is the amount of realism I've dreamed for YEARS. This game is still pretty early in development, so the racing features and AI are still pretty rough, but the soft body physics used are more than enough to keep anyone having a blast for hours on end.
My only complaint about this game is the heavy duty requirements, especially when it comes to the processors. If you have a budget build gaming rig like I do, don't expect to be playing on high graphics lag-free. Still, playing without settings maxed out is no reason not to want this game.

Darksiders was a fun adventure through a post-apocalyptic world overrun by demons. You hack and slash your way through demons and angels as the one of the four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, War.
You explore, upgrade, and fight your way through very different environments and every level brings something new to the table to keep the game interesting. And if you care to backtrack, you can find dozens of hidden secrets that you can unlock using the new items you obtained later in the game.
I found the story a tad difficult to follow and often had to ask myself "Why am I doing this?" but from what I did understand, I found it pretty interesting and I especially found the ending cutscene positively thrilling and left me ridiculously excited.
The boss fights, the combat, the environment, and the upgrades are all great and fun to achieve. The game does a good job of teaching you how to do something and gives you just enough to work with to find your goal.
The hack'n'slash does get a bit repetitive but it's bearable, and I found a few of the upgrades to be really unnecessary, redundant, and a waste of souls (or whatever the currency in this game is).
I can't recommend this game enough if you love hitting stuff with a sword, exploration, challenging boss fights, and engaging versatility in a game that throws something new at you every chance it can.

Does this game really need an introduction? Amnesia: The Dark Descent is first person survival horror game with physics puzzles and stealth mechanics, but I'm sure you already knew that. This game is considered by many to be the apex of horror in gaming and is also known for being the main foot hold for many youtubers rise to fame. But that was just an unforeseen effect this game would have, Amnesia on its own merits is just pants wetting terrifying. The game starts off with you waking up in a dark and gothic castle and having no memory of anything but your name and where you're from (you have amnesia if the title didn't already make that clear). You must find a series of journal pages to uncover your own past and to understand what is going on in this castle. Through out the game you will encounter terrifying monsters that you have to avoid looking at due to a sanity meter, you need to maintain your sanity even though its separate from your health, it's just as important. This games atmosphere is well presented as you find yourself running and hiding from noises and even hallucinations. You will go to amazing locations and solve puzzles that will really test your ability to think under pressure.  However there does come a point where you start to predict the monsters spawn, its almost always after a major puzzle is solved or you've been left alone for too long. But despite any flaws this game may have they are minor to the all around solid design and atmosphere.

Yes, you will have to overlook many typos and bad translations. But the general feel of the game, the stories, the characters, the surprise revelations of each storyline were the best written in the genre.
The stills and characters are beautifully drawn, but they do not vary a lot. There are some games aimed at men that seem to have a greater variety of images and scenes which kicks the entire dating sim games for women to the curb. The music is also, personally, too repetitive. I cannot stand hearing the same song on a loop for more than ten minutes, and it will take you hours to read each storyline. But, obviously, there's a way to turn the background music sound off and enjoy the game in silence or with your own personal soundtrack.
FInally, I wouldn't say the game is worth the full price as it stands at ~18$ CAD. It was worth buying at half price when it went on sale. If you have to buy a dating sim by Dogenzaka, do yourself a favour and buy this one first and avoid all the ones with reviews saying how mysogynistic and abuse ridden they are. 'Ultimate General: Gettysburg' allows you to reign as the commanding general of the Union or Confederate forces partaking in one of the most bloodiest battles of the American Civil War.
The game might be mercilessly difficult for some newcomers commencing their first day on the battlefield, but it also allows time for the player to learn through a mid-tier learning curve. The battles in the game are spread over a couple of days, with each battle lasting a set amount of time before troops from each side call to retire from exhaustion and replenishment.
Orders made on the battlefield could have rippling effects on the outcome of the next few days, and the impressively smart enemy AI will constantly push the player to make split second decisions that can alter the course of the battle as a whole. Falling back from an important defensive position on the field might save a whole brigade from utter annihilation, but losing the position might prove very difficult for the player to retake it from the enemy, hence allowing the AI to use it as a staging area for the next days to come.
Art in the game is pleasant to the eyes, and the gradient colours ironically allows a sense of relaxation even in the midst of stressful decision-making.
In hindsight, the duration of the game is very short with a mere three hours of gameplay in my initial playthrough. However, this shortcoming is cushioned with some replayability in the game, as different decisions made in the battles can allow for very different outcomes and areas to fight on.
Pros:
Cons:
All in all, 'Ultimate General: Gettysburg' offers unique and intelligent gameplay, and presents fresh battle mechanics that are properly executed and rarely seen in the tactical strategy games of today. I personally would recommend this game to fans of the genre, and dare say that this gem will leave an indelible impression on you.

Fun run and gun style platformer from the developer of the highly praised Cave Story. Outside of a few very questionable bosses, the game remains consistently fun. The stages are expertly designed in both layout and enemy placement in order to give a lot of diversity of feel to a game without a huge amount of mechanical depth as well as encouraging the player to use all of the different weapons the game has to offer. It is very difficult to get through the game exclusively using one weapon.
The base game is pretty short (around 2-3 hours) however there is a fair bit of bonus content. In particular, ZANGYOU mode is a hard mode which ramps the difficulty up quite a bit and adds some new content and dialogue in as well.
Overall this game is a masterfully crafted experience that is simple to play but has enough diversity to never wear itself out. Fun gameplay, a cute aesthetic, and amazing music make this game highly recommended from me, even at the full price. Further, there are two free pseudo-demos called "Pink Hour" and "Pink Heaven" which contain similar gameplay though shorter and easier. If you are unsure about purchasing this I would recommend giving them a shot first.

If Cave Story was Metroid, Kero Blaster is Contra.
Completely linear, your objective is always to get to the end of the stage to fight a boss, and then do it all over again on the next. Next to no backtracking or branching paths, but there are a few hidden areas that reward you with money or extra lives. Checkpoints happen on almost every single screen transition, so deaths don't set you back too far nor do you need to remember to hit up a save point. However once you run out of lives, you're sent back to the start of the level, but you get to keep all of your money. So some of the harder bosses get eaiser on multiple tries, since you have more money for better upgrades each time you attempt it.
As for an actual review, it's easy to tell the game was first made for a touch device, with the slightly awkard shooting controls. When you hold fire down, you lock your view to that direction, but can still move freely. After a stage or two it starts feeling normal. The first playthrough is fairly easy, with a few annoying boss fights, but the second playthrough "ZANGYOU" (Overtime) is where the real difficulity is at. The second time through all of the stages get tweaks to their layout, while still keeping the overall shape of the area the same. All of the weapons feel like they have some use, which is good since there aren't many even with the upgrades.
While there's not as much character development or plot as Cave Story, there's still plot and dialog between stages, and the 2nd playthrough has its own as well. However if you enjoyed Cave Story for its music, Kero Blaster does not dissapoint. Overall, if you're into run-and-gun platformers, its a fun game to play through, worth the base $10 to me.

A nice throwback to Final Liberation / Chaos Gate.  Random skirmishes are a lot of fun with a fair amount of options to tweak.  Randomly generated maps are good quality with decent tileset variety.
Graphics look nice and performance is generally good.  Animations and sound effects are pretty poor.  Sometimes a voice line is triggered when attacking.  You are forced to wait for it to play in its entirety before the attack animation commences, unnecessarily lengthening the amount of time enemy turns (or your own) can take.  This is only an issue in large battles and the voice lines are random (thankfully).  It doesn't even seem to correspond to critical hits or high damage attacks.  I had a voice line triggered and thought, "Oh, wow this will be good."  Only hit for 20HP.
Campaign is Space Wolves only, but there are two 20+ mission campaigns.  Unit progression through the campaign is nice and ranked up units receive additional abilities that make them more desirable and effective.  At the start of the next mission, however, it is not easy to see which units are the veterans.  The UI won't filter them from what I can tell, so you have to hunt for them.
Gameplay is incredibly basic.  Cover is either light or heavy and depending on the tileset it is not easy to distinguish between the two unless a view mode is toggled.  Terrain that obstructs line of sight is also hard to distinguish depending on the tile set.  Enemy units will sometimes move through terrain that you don't initially think they should be able to move through.  Units can only move and shoot or enter melee.  Once in melee, units cannot disengage.  You cannot set units to overwatch or any defensive mode (that I could tell).  Units receive one free reaction shot per turn if an emey gets too close in the direction that unit is facing.
EDIT:  Developers patched a lot of the issues I griped about.  Totally worth it now.

- A liitle too bright screen causes eye fatigue.
- Card collections could be bigger and you need to pay for premium boosters to extend collections other than in-game unlockable cards, and it's random.
- No more 2HG.
- Sliding combat area gets annoying overtime, for me.
- I haven't experience AI cheating (as some claimed), yet. Instead, AI got mana flood and few stupid attacks like empty handed swung 1/1 on my 2/2 or glitch like casting Cloudshift "twice on a token" expecting it would avoid combat damage and return to the battlefield.
- Animated menu makes it hard to navigate.
But overall, it's good. Some improvement from Magic 2014.

The game runs on a random number generator, but you can rig it by using the "perks" that you buy one at a time with real money. Usually, players never use these perks, but making a mostly luck-based game into potentially pay-to-win was a mistake by the makers in my opinion. But in conclusion, I definitely recommend you to install this game if you have a group of friends to play with who enjoy relaxed, casual games.

TLDR Other than Shovel Knight it is good. Too bad you need to play through that crap to get to the fun characts (or cheat).
Review is split into 4 parts (basically each character and overall).
Shovel Knight (Worst Part of the game IMO)
Pros:
- Attacking is good most of the time. The battletoads armour is terrible and doesn't work well at all mechanically.
- The dream sequences are a nice break between levels.
Cons:
- Movement is terrible until one of the final levels and even then it only fixes horizontal movement.
- Jumps being near pixel perfect for no reason other than to cause a lengthy backtrack.
- Jump attacks can be activated by pure accident resulting in spike deaths easily because the game picked up a 1/100 movement down.
Plague Knight (Best Campaign IMO)
Pros:
- Unique system for attacking what with mixing different explosions, fuses and throwing styles.
- Movement is much better than either of the other campaigns and actually feels fun.
- Most of the powers gained throughout the levels were useful unlike shovel knight.
- The bomb fish is better than the fishing rod and has use outside of collecting from fishing spots.
Cons:
- The story was pointless and felt like it was only there to attempt to reuse the levels without any changes.
- The vat power was hit or miss when being used, sometimes it would spawn inside of plague knight preventing it from saving you.
- Cluster bombs are inherintly too broken and make bosses and any enemies that should present some challenge a joke.
Spectre Knight (The middle ground)
Pros:
- His unique movement is interesting and feels better than default movement (Shovel Knight) but isn't as good as Plague knight.
- Introductory "levels" for the new powers you buy.
- Upgradable powers allowing them to either gain an additional use or become better in general.
- Using collectables to purchase the powers is better than using cash as money is a joke in the game and this promotes you to at least check the extra areas for the skulls.
Cons:
- The tower map is awkward to traverse and the mirror level select is boring compared to the overworld map.
- Jump attacks make most bosses easy as you can juggle yourself to avoid attacks whilst still doing as much damage as you would be on the ground.
- The armor that saves your life is hit or miss and will occasionally put you into a position where you have to die because you cant progress.
- The inexplicable reason that you cant attack down so jumping somehow breaks blocks.
Overall:
Pros:
- Music is fairly good through each campaign.
- Nostalgia (both a pro and a con).
- Graphics are nice enough to be considered a pro.
-
Cons:
- Moneybags on death are impossible to get sometimes regardless of the character being used.
- Plot is pretty damn bad overall in all of the campaigns so far.
- Stun from knockback will kill you even though you should have time to save yourself.
- You will play the same level 4 times (when king knight campaign is out), with only minor differences being added in the spectre knight campaign.

Sadly I cannot offer anything that represents even a small fraction of an objective, highly professional review, thanks to the lack of my competence. What I got is only my subjective little opinion crafted by my experiences with this amazing game, which I see as a significant pillar and a spectacular peak, not only of the Total War series, but of the strategy genre as well.
I started to play with the Total War series with the first Shogun: Total War back in the early 2000's. I still have the physical copy of that great game in my drawer, next to Medieval: Total War with the Viking Invasion Expansion, and Medieval II: Total War + Kingdoms. As a kid who played a lot with turn-based strategy games like the first 2 Civilization, and Heroes of Might and Magic 2-3 (yes, I am an old fart), i was fascinated by the system and the era Shogun could offer. I was captured by the whole notion of empire building and expansion, and while I respected the whole battle-simulation aspect (which I played for hours back then), I realized that I was much more impressed by the campaign map, with its diplomacy, economy system, constructions, army building, etc. After Shogun I played a lot with Medieval Total War, which became my favorite thanks to its theme, and then for some particular reason, i did not try out Rome. I was not really interested in the ancient era, and jumped right to Medieval II. It was overwhelmingly superior to the two games I played before, and for a short period of time, I thought that Medieval II brought these improvements into the series. But I was wrong. It was Rome.
I borrowed a physical copy of Rome: Total War in 2007 and realized how huge leap this game took from its predecessors in almost every aspect of the game. From the map which changed the whole one province = one army slot type to a more dynamic one with much more attention to positions and maneuverability, the engaging senate system with its authentic theme and quests, till the improved and much more detailed dynasty and family-tree building with an original ruler and general traits system, this game assembled a lot of great ideas, that not only gave it more soul and meat than the previous games, but it also made me identify with certain problem-solving and task performance situations much more effectively.
I bought my own physical copy of Rome in the same year, but it did not live long. In 2009, after tons of gameplay hours, it gave up the good fight.
After playing Rome, I went back to Medieval II, I bought Empire, and also Shogun 2, but I stopped trying out the latest entries of the series. I realized, that none of these games were able to eclipse the glory of Rome. Yes, they added new themes, some new mechanics, new graphics, changed some features, but the core mechanics are still those that was established in Rome Total War, and personally I only see them as bigger, brighter, louder echoes of the same old system, which still keeps its head up high. It may look ancient to some, but this well-crafted piece of gaming is not even close to become outdated.

If you're not sure whether to get this one or the original Men of Yoshiwara (Kikyua), you'd probably be happier with Kikuya. There is less content in this version and I agree with those who've said they didn't like it as much as the first. It also still has the poor translation/editing quality that plagued the first. That said, it might be worth picking up on sale.
---
Again, it is originally a mobile otome game, ported to PC. The quality level mobile otome needs to have to be accepted is much lower - and this game is not especially well edited, with typos everywhere. The romances didn't live up to the first game's romances (with the exception of one guy, whose story was the best in the series, imho) - but the heroine is much more awesome than the first. I'll be comparing this game to the first game in the series a lot, so be prepared.
As with Kikuya, the content rating is approximately "R-18". The images hover at around the PG-13 level at the most spicy, but the language can get pretty direct. If you prefer reading "sweet romances" with closed door sex/no sex, you will not be happy with this story as sex (as brief as it is) is certainly "open door". As for other content concerns, I didn't find it as "objectionable" as the first, but will instead give a blanket warning that this is a game written for Japanese sensibilities with an R-18 content level, set in a fictional historical past. In short - if you're not prepared to be at least a little put-off/offended by cultural differences, you'd better just move on because there might be something here that will upset you.
: The translation quality itself is not too bad. There was very little that made me stumble in terms of understanding the story/what people were implying with what they said. Unfortunately...
: The editing was, as before with Kikuya, pretty terrible. It's not as embarrassing as I found Kikuya's text to be, but there were still lots of typos, missing words/parts of sentences, missing punctuation, confused words (in the vein of their/there); etc.
: It's sort of a mixed bag, as before. Unfortunately for this game, it appears they cut even more corners. There are fewer unique poses/costume changes for each character, fewer side characters who get sprites (I think there were none, actually, aside from the servant), recycled backgrounds from the first game (which is fine since it takes place in many of the same places more or less simultaniously with the first game), and really sloppy CGs in places. (I was fascinated in a way with seeing stray lines in areas the composition of the image actually drew attention to. I assume the deadline was very close for it to have been left as-is.) Without double-checking, I think there were fewer CGs for each route too. Those complaints aside, the art was still nice.
: I think I overall preferred the character design from this game to the first. The characters were fairly distinct from each other, and even the characters that were in similar roles/positions to the characters in the first game looked distinct from each other. (That said - they do overlap quite a bit.)
: I draw attention yet again that this is an mobile otome port. The standards between an otome for PC/console and an otome for mobile are vastly different. The writing is "choppier" and shorter, meant to be consumed while waiting in line or riding the train or something - so each chapter is quite short and there's no real luxury of a slow boil. Even in the best storyline the game offers (IMHO, anyway), the story proceeds quickly and character development can take a sudden and surprising leap. You have to keep this in mind when judging the work (as you wouldn't really compare a short story to a novel either).
Each hero's arc in this game explores the concept of the series premise and how it can bring trouble to not only the man in question, but any woman who might fall in love with a courtesan from Yoshiwara. For better or worse, it's extremely easy to get the "best" ending with each hero, so you're probably more likely to have to take the trouble figuring out how to get the mere "good" ending instead.
I personally didn't find any of the heroes of Ohgiya, bar one, to match up to the heroes in Kikuya. I actually would consider myself very indifferent to most of the storylines and it took me awhile to pick up the game to finish it. For me, Asagiri's (the pretty blond guy who wears pink and purple and smells nice) did, however, make the entire game for me. I'm very glad I left him until last. I might find his route to be the most interesting in the series - but perhaps that is
I had played all the other routes in the series before his and understood the heartbreak of Yoshiwara so well. I can't actually pick out any route in this game as "bad", but I didn't enjoy them as much.
: Unlike Kikuya's "good-hearted idiot", this heroine might be shy and obedient, but is overall quite sensible and has backbone. I rather liked her and found her situation of coming to Yoshiwara to conceive an heir for the family business to be more palpable than Kikuya's more awkward situation.
Ohgiya is probably not going to knock your socks off, but if you wanted to experience more in the world of Yoshiwara, I can certainly recommend it for Asagiri's route alone. (Though I'd personally say to play him last.) I would suggest you try to pick it up on sale, however, to avoid disappointment.

What really shined for me in this one was the protagonist. It can be frustrating to play a character that behaves passively. The lead is much more assertive and straight forward than a lot of the ones I'm used to in these kinds of games, which I found refreshing.
Sadly, I had a hard time connecting to most of the characters and their storylines in this game. There were too many parallels to Kikuya's characters. I felt like the routes lacked depth, likely due to them having fewer chapters. I also found that even though I liked a character's personality, their storyline was lacking. My favorites in this game were Gakuto and Takigawa.
I likely won't be going back to this game too often. Though, it was a nice treat to have after finishing Kikuya! I still thought it was very enjoyable and aesthetically pleasing.
