This game is a combination of good & bad w/ a terrible DRM requirement.
NOTE: This isn't really a "positive" review it's just that Steam has no middle ground when it comes to it's user review rating system.  I just think that this game is more recommendable than not so when it comes to what you get for your money.
STORY & GRAPHICS
The game revolves around a guy (who I guess was in the first game) who's sister gets kidnapped & he's thrown in jail.  He's later rescued by orcs & has to go around the world to raise an army or something.  Anyways, after all the beginning tutorial stuff you get into it & realize, "Omg... What did I just buy?"  Character models look disturbing w/ huge balogna arms & women have the wierdest & ugliest faces I've ever seen in a video game, especially the witch lady.
The graphics overall are something that you have to see.  It definitely feels unique & no other game looks like Two Worlds 2.  The oceans look like jello, the overworld is cartoonish & realistic at the same time.  Everything is unique in an artistic & bad but good way.  The only real displeasing thing about the graphics other than the character models is the terrible motion blur which just adds a fuzz effect to half the screen.  You can turn it off with console commands but you'll have to turn it off every time you launch the game & it does get annoying after a while.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is bad but not unplayable.
Melee is the worst since you can't really get hit in this game without getting killed.  Blocking is pretty useless & it's hard to tell if attacks actually connect with what you're trying to hit & you can't really dodge attacks.
Magic isn't all that enjoyable but it isn't terrible. It has a unique card crafting system that allows you to customize your magics & you have to equip these cards in order to cast them.  With it you can create a variety of spells.  The downside to this is it's completely useless in the beginning of the game & finding cards needed to make the more powerful spells is a pain.
I spent the majority of my playtime playing as a ranged character which is completely broken due to how poor the AI is in the game & as ranged abilities are extremely OP & easy to use.  If it's your first time playing this game you should probably play an archer.
The good part is you can respec anytime you want simply by visiting the witch at the orc encampment so if you want to try something new you're free & able to do it.
Also, if you plan on exploring in this game don't do it at low levels.  Don't go into caves, don't go into areas that you're not supposed to.  Just don't do it.  The game's "progression" system just doesn't exist & enemies in caves are most likely much to high in level for you to handle.  It's basically like Morrowind but much worse since the enemy levels are extremely high for being so early on in the game.  You'd be better off using cheats just to get through it.
The game's world is probably the best part about the game.  It's huge, open ended & has a lot of stuff in it like wildlife, various towns, ruins, caves & lots of enemies to run into.  The downside is that everything in it wants to kill you.  There is no faction system where you'll see lions trying to eat a monkey or anything.  If it exists outside of a town its sole purpose is probably to kill you.  There are some neutral enemies who won't attack you unless attacked first, at least.
There's also a lot of quests to do in this game & some of them have a lot of good humor.  A good early example of one is when I ran into a guy building a house & he said a monkey stole his tools.  Well, I went to find this said monkey & it had nothing on it so I went back to the guy to see what is actually going on.  Apparantly, all the "workers" working on his house were actually armed bandits & he was in the middle of being robbed.  He just made up that story about the monkey hoping you'd think it'd be so stupid of a story you'd notice something was amiss.  Well, too bad for him.  Later when I did the quest again you can see that all the people working on the house are armed & dressed oddly like bandits.  It's a pretty clever way of doing a quest that you don't see a lot of in other games.
The game has its charm that's for sure.  There's a lot of humor in the dialog, lots of skills to upgrade & different ways to build your character, there's a good crafting system for equipment & customization. This is a full open world RPG experience & if you're willing to put up with it's flaws there is some fun to be had within the game.
OVERALL
Overall, the game is good with a side of bad & has issues that just make you not want to play it.  There are some nice moments in the game & there is a lot to do in the open world but the game has DRM which gives you a 3 machine install limit. Any hardware changes to your computer count so if you upgrade your PC more than 3 times you can't download & play it anymore.  You can install it on the same machine unlimited times so if you don't plan on upgrading your rig anytime soon you've got nothing to worry about. You also have to give it personal info such as where you live & meaningless things like your gender.
It's a good game with some flaws but the developers obviously don't care about you even if you buy it so you could very easily pass on the game even if it's on a good sale & I don't blame you if you do.
EDIT:  Changing my recomendation because they added MicroTransactions to a 10 year old game.  It's nice to see the game is still being supported, but why would they add MT's?  You can just use cheats with console commands anyways.

Who is this Game For?
==================
People that relate this game to Zelda have no idea what they are talking about. If I was to make a comparison, the closest game Darksiders resembles is Force Unleashed II. There is not one puzzle in this whole game as far as I could tell in my play through. The game always told you exactly what to do, and if there was something that could be a puzzle in a room, the auto-camera makes sure to zoom onto objects and paths that need to be explored, eliminating any thought process that might otherwise be needed. It’s a straight up hack-n-slash. If that's what you are into, get this title.
Is it good?
=================
The boring linear gameplay, and almost no character progression, does not exactly have a recipe for a winner.
Does it have any problems?
========================
This is a very poorly done port. Horrible controls, no graphics options and the game has a lot more issues. You'll need to check out
if you have any problems.
Final Thoughts!
====================
A laughably boring main character, uninteresting plotline, and a steep learning curve for combat doesn’t help sell the game much. The boss fights are entertaining and the voice acting isn't a marvel. If you could enjoy, say, God of War, but without the storyline, characters, or great voice acting, then you could probably enjoy this game.

Duke Nukem Forever (DNF) got bad reviews overall, but do yourself a favour and mostly ignore them. Have in mind most reviews are biased, and this is suppose to be an old school FPS, with a lenghty campaign (it will take you between 10 and 15 hours to complete if you are an experienced player) and a very fun MP with a lot of customizable options. Have in mind this game was intended for release in 1999, a time when FPS's were simplistic and it was all about firepower and testosterone driven characters, and Duke delivers on both ends. As a direct sequel to Duke Nukem 3D, DNF delivers the same amount of insanity, action and adrenaline as it's predecessor. Compared to todays shooters, it is a dinosaur of a game, outdated in structure and gameplay mechanics, but it still is a lot of fun, and a great throwback to the 90's, a decade that revolutionized video games.
This is how old school games are suppose to be, and if you like crude humour, naked chicks and epic one liners, this game is for you. It took 15 years for this game to see the light of day, so when you buy this, you are getting a piece of video game history. The worlds most famous vaporware is ready to be played. It took forever (no pun intended), but it's here.
Always bet on Duke.
The Good
-Old school badassery in spades
-Easter egg galore
-Fun shooting mechanics
-Epic one liners
-Lenghty campaign
-Awesome firepower
The Bad
-Too simplistic when compared to more modern shooters
-Difficulty level can be a problem to some players (Personally I love a good challenge)
-Style of this game appeals mostly to hardcore gamers
6.5/10

Admittedly a new norm in strategy. The IA and post-battle-decision making, based on the outcome of the skirmish / battle the player just fought, gives the game a incredible replayability. The possibility to pick a random IA, and to boost it - meaning it'll play better, not get a mere buff to its troops - make UG:G a lot of fun to play.
But the better part, perhaps, is the difficulty the game poses. It's not really difficult because of its IA - you can pick an easy / defensive one anyway - but because its mechanics, despite looking very simple at first glance, actually hide a lot of depth to the game. At first, I didn't understand why my brigades lost the firefights. How the morale or condition really worked. For instance, in Total War games - of which i'm a veteran, player since medieval first of the name, and admitteldy the franchise has become a reference in terms of wargame / strategy - exhaustion doesn't really matter. Mostly, troops will get tired very quickly, neither player nor IA will keep reserves, or if so, no more than a couple of units. Mostly, everyone gets tired at the same time, at the same rate, and the battle plays pretty much the same regardless. Well, in UG:G, conditon matters BIG TIME. If you got tired brigades, and infantry can get exhausted pretty quickly after walking up some woody hill, you'd better delay your attack.
To put it simply, the game is one of the best, if not the best at the moment, historical strategy simulation game. It's not arcade. Truth be told, I've recently come to understand it all a little better - how to use your artillery properly, how to time your attacks, how to prepare for your assaults, how lines of sight really worked - and I'm still learning. All those negative reviews bring a smile to my face : only one is above two hours of play. I had no goddam clue about how the game really worked after ten hours, let alone after two. Ultimate General : Gettysburg is a game which requires careful planning, reflexion from the player, and won't just reward you with immediate pleasure. Darth never hid that.
On a personnal side, I say having such an innovative game, especially since it is so challenging, and thus so rewarding once beaten, is a blessing. I bought it straight away when the early access began, and my only regret is to have left this to rot in my library for so long before returning to it. Not having taken the time to dig, to understand, to discuss with other players, and figure out what I was doing wrong right from the start.
A mandatory purchase. A new era for strategy dawns here.

Game is exactly what I expected.  The graphics are great, especially when you compare them to most other 'tactical' turnbased warfare pc games.  The UI does take a little getting used to, but I like it.  I don't think most people have discovered the overlay option ( 1 key ) that gives you feedback on each unit and its action ranges.  It's not really explained anywhere, just mentioned briefly in the manual.  It is very useful for determining full cover.
There are some items that need to be addressed, like how the map sometimes can't be scrolled all of the way, or how you can't tell the experience points when selecting your units before each mission (you can see their current level but not how many points they have towards the next level).  Also, you can't sort during the selection, so that all of each type are grouped together.
A good way to learn what is going on is to start a skirmish game outside of a campaign.  You can experiment with different units and how they perform, and setup a small map area to play in.
If you like 'Fire Emblem' style turnbased games, and don't mind a very shallow storyline then you will love this game.

I don't think this game gets enough credit, although it may get more than it needs at some points. In my opinion, it's a complex game of manufacturing. With recent updates, it changed from being able to carry your raw materials, to having to automate. That itself presents a engineering challenge. Otherwise it's a gem, that should not be overlooked if you enjoy harvesting and games that have a linear progression of complexity. End game is a prime example of how intensly you should have your setup as fine tuned as possible. Major issue with the game "system" is early game you may have your infrastructure setup, but it will need retuned just to push forward with the higher demand of resources/power. If that sounds intriguing and you can handle the blocky world, this game may just be that gem in your inventory.

Sniper Elite v2; you'll either hate it, or love it. My personal experience with the game was great! I loved the campaign, the story wasn't the best, but I followed it to the end. I only wish there was more open maps, and that the ai was better. If you do play the campaign, I recommend you play it on the hardest difficulty because the ai is really bad, but also because you really want to experience the more authentic sniping like adjusting for wind and gravity, on lower difficulties is will simply just tell you where the bullet will hit, and that's frankly boring. What I really loved about the campaign was the gradual transition as you made your way through Berlin throughout the campaign. At first the Werchmact occupy much of Berlin, some buildings are crumbled and some are in tact, as the campaign begins to escalate, the russians enter the picture and now you're fighting both sides, towards the end it is all quite, buildings are nothing more than bricks, and there are dead german soldiers and you will soon be fighting just the soviets. I just liked the transition a lot and I think rebellion did it perfectly.
With multiplayer, it's hard to say, personally I like it, but many people will hate it. You're a sniper fighitng other snipers, that can be good and bad depending on how you look at it. Sure, simply just sitting there bord out of your mind with nothing happening, thinking, this sucks. On the other hand, you're waiting with patience and focusing on what's happening in front of you, waiting for someone to peak their heads out, slowly moving around the rubble, making a mad dash for a building, hoping you dont get shot, and looking over the map trying to spot out something out of the ordinary; that's the way I see the multiplayer and I think its really fun, however the maps should also be bigger in multiplayer for more variety and openess but it's understandable if some hate the multiplayer. Here we go again! So in the 3 years since my first review ive popped in once to update a quick thought. Now i think ill give a last review before the MMO destroys the YO casual community.
So in 3 years we have had the same map. Same resouce locations, same world with the addition of regions which determine nothing, as well as animal spawn changes. This has forced the populated realms, which hope to stay populated, to rely heavily on the PVP or RP aspect. High skill rate servers so you can spend an hour or two maxing menial skills for the glory of combat skills, slaughter and mayhem! Or which seem to be slower RP based servers, where a slower pace lets people build a community. There are also so many dead and empty servers, which always baffles me. Who is paying for that? We have a few large steam groups you can join, but except for these small changes, many of which are player side, the game is the same.
The MMO is in the 2nd wave of beta tests atm, which means YO owners are still locked out of the beta process (unless your initial alpha purchase is supplimented with ANOTHER beta buy in) although the clock is ticking rapidly for that to change. Which means purchasing the game NOW isnt a great idea. You can be patient and wait for beta access or just buy in through the main site. As a purchase for the YO experience? nah, save the money for battlefront 2.
Mechanics for the game are cookie cutter sandbox,basic materials etc , although the largest change is the inclusion of claims, this means instead of needing 24hr vigilance on personal property if you dont have walls yet, all items within claim area are secure from theft, taking away the largely fun aspect of sneaking ways into a base to loot. Also giving the player storage and means to not feel deflated from a midnight burglary.
All this aside, the game itself is still fun. Building a base from scratch with a group of friends is a fun experience, when you have enough people on a server and its fresh it can be amazing and cutthroat. everyone knows where the veins are, the best spawns, etc. The early game fighting is mainly on the site of future towns, this aspect is the best part. Until, the walls go up. Once a few established groups have walls up, the only chance of catching them is outside. This is of course the reason to have walls and a point of medievil genre, but numbers mean a bad idea, an average base is 3-6 people tops, and getting them all on is a miracle. There are a few groups that can pull in 20, but these numbers never last, a server population is only 64 max, and numbers mean everything when you cannot siege or destroy walls within a claim area. The end result is usually the same, unless the server is a chaos pvp frenzy, OR a RP enforced GM haven the servers die once the walls go up. all the land is claimed and the server passes the month old mark.
There is nothing to do IN GAME once your town is established. Besides manufacturing materials, wood, cooking, tools, etc. you are done. Unless building is your only enjoyment, you can build forever. Now the point is that you make it what you want, but after 3 years, ive done that! i tried what i have wanted, played every style and skillset, built everywhere i could, played a hermit cackling in a mountain hut to a peasant lugging logs for a RP overlord. Its done.
I would say buy the game before its out of alpha, simply for the free character in the MMO. Purchase and wait and read the news, then just join the beta. The YO servers are fine for learning the game, but as a standalone purchase i couldnt endorse it. You get access to beta wave and a free character though, so i feel its worth it if youre patient and looking for a taste.
One thing i will say to anyone who is new to the game. DO NOT JOIN A BUILT CITY.  a huge aspect of this game is learning to build and the skillsets you need, what to use and how to do it. you lose all of that when you join a group thats advanced. Instead you simply get everything handed to you, with no understanding of what it all does, mean or how to use it. I have seen hundreds of people join the game brand new, join a base that needs bodies to fight, and get stuck lugging logs for 2 hours, or simply getting completely geared out for war, then told to stand around for an hour while everyone else logs in or gets back to base. These guys last the 2 hours either get bored and wander off and log out, or they rush out in full gear and get roasted in the first fight, again, dissapearing, DONT BE THAT GUY! . take the time to wander around, learn the base game, try to build a few things, then decide if you want to join, Some high rate and skillcap servers you can do everthing solo. when the mmo comes though, you cant.

There are some things about LiF that are really neat: the crafting, the graphics. Building your own medieval town is really such a wonderful idea and I was eyeing this game for ages.
But as a single player (and this game is being marketed for single players as well as multiple), this game has been nothing but a disappointment.
- For solo players, the grind is really the only thing there is. There's no danger and no purpose really to play: any wildlife that may attack you is easily avoidable. There are no other mobs. I had read before purchase of intentions to create quests and mobs, but it seems that those ideas have been abandoned in favour of keeping LiF:YO as a game that relies entirely on PvP for non-crafting content.
- The grind is real. It took me over thirty RL hours to flatten the land and collect the mats I needed to build a small shack. This was after tweaking settings so I could have a chance in hell of creating anything on my own. As much as I love crafting, it's going to take absurd amount of time -- hundreds and hundreds of hours -- to build anything. But with no danger present in the world, there's no purpose to build other than aesthetics.
- Some of the cool features in the LiF video are -only available for the MMO-. This is not the MMO. There are no crafting games here. The island you get is small and not likely to get bigger. No quests planned. The only thing in the world is you. And the tedious grind of creation.
- Speaking of the MMO, that's where the devs are focused. Buying LiF: YO isn't giving you a version of the MMO: it's giving you the redheaded stepchild of the family. It's sickly, underdeveloped, and simply not getting any of the attention that they are lavishing on its brother. Reading the official forums makes it clear that this isn't likely to change. (Seriously. Go look at the list about the differences between YO and the MMO. You may find that the feature you're purchasing this for doesn't exist in the YO version.)
Don't get me wrong. I really want to like this game. I'll keep my eyes on it and see if maybe the devs have a change of heart about the PVP-only content. But LiF is too much effort for very little pay off. Even if you are a solo player -- especially, even -- I'd highly suggest you wait for the MMO when it comes out.

Edit 2: Im 185hrs into the game and I'm not really interested in playing it anymore. The devs have done a marvellous job at addressing some bugs and play issues and most of the things in the negative reviews that players have complained about have been fixed, so the game is shaping up nicely. But if you look through the negative reviews of the game, there's a common complaint that has not been addressed, the lack of an Army Builder for choosing your units. And this one issue is what kills the re-playability of this game.
Sanctus Reach randomly generates your force selection each time you play it. There's no way to really choose the units you want. Every game is about the same in terms of the units that are selected for you to choose from and therein lies the rub. It's true Sanctus Reach offers a lot of unit variety. There are a good number of tanks and special units they have put into the game and some campaign missions allow you to sample them. But beyond that, they wont show up in non-campaign Skirmish missions. Land Raiders, for example are so much fun to use. And the Orks need to have access to Warbikers to be competitive in multiplayer, but you'll really never see them listed in your force selection. In fact, in a 6000 point game (current max), you'll be lucky to see more than 2 tanks ever listed. So your force is always comprised of basic foot soldiers, and therefore you'll always be fighting a foot slogger battle which gets boring after a while. You'll never get to play a mechanized assault, or an armored spearhead. Or dabble around with what ifs using different force structure.
I've wanted to setup a mission where I have but only 2000 points of Space Wolves vs. a horde of 6000 points of Orks and use mostly tanks for both sides... but Sanctus Reach wont let you. There are hardly any tanks in your list, and it's really sad that you cant customize the enemy army either. The devs have said to use the editor to make custom mechanized missions, And I've tried, but its not easy. I started to learn how to do it and the editor is very powerful, but getting o the end where you actually have a mission to play isnt something I have figured out yet.  I havent seen any tutorials or downloadable campaigns by anyone in the community either. It's one thing to have a quick skirmish mission that you can set up in seconds and entirely another when editing a mission takes countless hours.
So the verdict for me is a no, I dont recommend this game because in the long run you're going to get bored of being forced to play every battle using the same exact troops and force structure. Its always a foot slogger ground troop battle each and every time and maybe one or two tanks, three if you get lucky. It becomes dull and repetitive and its not fun anymore. They have all these great units that are fun to play with but it blows my mind that the devs won't let you use them. It really ruins the fun.
Edit: I wrote this review after playing it for several hours. You can still read that initial review below. Right now Im 35 hours into the game and its so much fun! Its nearly addictive the more you learn how to get the game to do what you want. This is an Indie title that was just very nicely put together. I'm learning how to make my own scenarios with the game editor with truly EPIC style armies facing off on both sides. This is some of the most fun I've had playing any 40k title in a great while. There's a couple minor issues like the UI and units being a tad clunky to use, but once you spend a few hours playing the game it's a non issue and it all works ok. The Force Organization doesnt spawn a unit list that allows you to field the kind of army you want, you get to be somewhat choosy but its random and flawed. Instead, you'll have to learn how to copy and edit an existing mission if you want the freedom to explore what it's like to have a completely mechanized force with Titans go up against a huge Ork horde. But the nice thing is the game allows you to do pretty much what you want once you start using the editor. Oh, and 35 hours into the game and not ONE single crash. Its coded very well and very stable.
Original review:
If you like the table top game, FINALLY Straylight Entertainment and Slitherine Ltd. have made a 40k game that gives us just that. This is a table top like experience. It's not like other 40k games. There's a good number of fair to poor 40k games on Steam right now, and this isn't one of those lousy titles. For example, I remember playing Space Marine when it came out and my shoulders slumped when I saw the way you got health was by killing an enemy. What? WTF? Somehow the life essence of a dead ork heals your wounds? Stupid! And then when a jump pack marine lands, every enemy around you gets knocked off their feet in commical fashion. WTF! Stupid and over the top! And then Dawn of War, Oh God where do I start at how ridiculous it was. So If I had a Marine squad in the field that was depleted, I'd just click on reinforce and "grow" a new marine next to the other ones. LOL! So Dumb! There isnt any of that silly crap in this game, thank the Emperor!
What you get with this game is something that you can sink your tactical and strategic fangs into. But first you'll need to open the game folder and find the MAPVIEW.TXT file and change the 'Pitchlimit' to 35 from 10. That way you can get a models eye level view of the battlefield in addition to free camera rotation, pitch and zoom. That's nice. It sucked before I found that file and changed it. I also noticed there's a lot of text files that seem to make this game quite moddable. Thats good. I'm guessing as is typical GW fashion, there will be expansions for this for all the various armies GW sells. And I bet customizing some new armies might be able to be done with mods.
Skirmish mode offers a lot of customization. You can even go into an editor and make your own campaigns or missions. I browsed this a bit and all the tools are there to setup whatever kind of battlefield you can imagine, but I didnt see water tiles... I also couldnt figure out how to raise the map height, but CTRL+Clicking lowered it to create depressions and trenches. That will be fun. As it is, you have about 7 or so different maps and you can pick some more variations of those, customize the weather, unit choices and victory conditions and force points. The last part is pretty exciting for me. The first skirmish I played, I was surprised at how the AI managed to hang on to the VC objectives and even flank me and take one where I wasnt paying attention, but I stomped the AI pretty good. So being able to give the AI more force points allows it to have more units. Or you can setup reinforcements to come in at a certain time. It seems very cool. I cant wait to setup a massive Ork horde and fight them all to the death heroic style.
I havent tried the campaign yet, but being able to carry over unit experience will be interesting. What it does I dont know yet, nor how long the campaign is. But seeing that you can create your own campaign leads me to believe that you'll be able to DL other players campaigns and that will be cool if that can be done. There should soon be an enormous replay value. And when other army DLC's come out, oh wow... But for $29.99, I think this game is a STEAL. Its a fun tactical game that plays smart, looks slick, has great terrain and model details, and the units are varied and behave very specifically depending on type. It is much like table top chess with stuff that shoots guns, rockets and flame throwers, with skimmers, jump troops, and mini-Titans! I'm loving it so far. I've read there is also a hotseat mode whereby you can have a friend over and fight an entire battle from one computer. I'll update this review later, but I'm off to play this game, over and over and over... you cant do that on a table top game. Takes too long. In thirty minutes, I can get a 2000 point game over and done with. Awesome!

Updates sometimes involve balance changes. This is great as it adjusts progression to account for new features and mechanics, but may change how old bases work on new versions. Balance changes are intended to be used from start to finish, and when played as such you shouldn't ever notice. Aside from having to adjust old setups like this, older saves are forward compatible in my experience. There are technical workarounds which take around 10 minutes for using old balance with new features if you want to update, but don't like the balance changes.
Most negative reviews are indev problems from people unwilling to use existing workarounds, as the game is still in development. Arma 3 is a military sim, sandbox game made by Bohemia. Although it is an expensive game, it contains many hours of fun, gamemodes and story missions. It can supply from the minimum of 50 hours - 10,000 (as 1 in 3 people have over 7,000). Don’t rely on the bad reviews about the performance. The performance is good, you just need a good computer. Don’t get a game that is out of your specifications even on the lowest settings because obviously, your game will break and crash and it will be all over the place.
WARNING: I did buy this game in the Arma 3 Apex Bundle in the summer sale but I have never experienced the gameplay that Arma 3 DLCs have to offer as I have mainly only played PUBR and KOTH.
The gameplay offers many gamemodes like GTA (Grand Theft Arma), PlayerUnknown’s BattleRoyale (PUBR), KOTH (King of the Hill), Deathmatch, Survival and End Game. The singleplayer gameplay is bad and not recommended to be played unless you can afford all the DLCs. In the case of people that have not purchased the DLCs, just play the fun part of the game, not the single missions. The gameplay can give you a valuable experince for a long period of time such as 50 hours+. Do not give up on the game 2 hours into the game.
Quality and Settings - The game ran at low frames at first (about 4fps). This is because, most likely, the settings are set to the default which can be medium - ultra. It is recommended to spend about 1 hour going through each setting in depth until the game runs well. I eventually, after a hour, changed the settings so that the game ran at 30fps which is successfully playable. The view settings is a good addition as you can choose between first person (like Call of Duty) and third person (PlayerUnknown Battlegrounds (PUBG is originally a Arma3 mod)). It can suit both a third person and first person player and possibly both at once. The game can also look very pretty and realistic. Also including the realism mechanics that links to to the gameplay.
Overall, this game rated with DLCS is: 10/10
Overall, this game rated without DLCS is: 20/10

This has to be the most overrated game I have ever played. Not only is it not scary, it's boring and cliche. It's pretty to look at, and has some cool room designs, but that's about it. The game fails at storytelling hardcore. You find these notes/diary entries that supposedly hint to bits and pieces of what's going on along the way, but the reality is they often are a lot of yapping without providing any actual new, interesting information about the story. Oooh, mysterious artefact, like anyone gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥ The "sanity level" is nothing new. Eternal Darkness did it first, and I feel like the sanity level is a good-sized part of what made this Amnesia's reception above what it deserves.
The monster mechanics are both BS and incredibly stupid. Monsters will generally "spawn" as triggered by discovering something or progressing a puzzle. When the game is feeling especially unfair, the monster will spawn practically right on top of you. I hope you have lightning fast reflexes and have memorized every single corner in this dungeon maze, because if not, have fun running to your doom. That's the BS part. The stupid part is that often the monster's spawn period is finite. Yes, you heard me. They don't stick around. Solve a puzzle, a monster spawns. Find your hiding spot or whatever, and wait for them to pass out of sight or leave the area. Once the coast is clear, congratulations you can wander freely because that monster is forever gone. Spooky atmosphere, my foot.
The two points I give this game are for being pretty, and for having a fairly compelling, and relatively creepy intro where you discover the note about Daniel's memories. But it all goes downhill after that.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is kind of a survival horror, where you actually can't do anything about monsters. Hiding is a good strategy. Darkness is your best friend, but also your biggest threat.
Alright, these were a few out-of-review sentences, now something about the game itself:
Amnesia doesn't have a really epic graphic, but it really makes out for the atmosphere, wchich is by far purely amazing. The well-made audio cover also adds to the horror-style.
Game uses the mechanic of "Sanity meter" - if you lose it all, you'll fall on the ground and will be unable to move for a few seconds. Standing in darkness for too long or looking at monsters will make your sanity drop pretty fast. There's also a health meter. Your main light source will be a lantern and tinderboxes.
Our horror runs perfectly without any problems, but I encountered a few glitches (falling through the floor, missing models), although these aren't really annoying and won't happen too often. The monsters' AI is good, but not perfect. They sometimes bug on doors / walls or ignore all sounds. The storyline can be a little bit confusing, but if you collect all the puzzles and match them, then you'll understand it.
There is also an option to play custom stories (fan-made bonus stories, you can download them on Mod DB, for example), which really extends the fun of playing.
Now everything what I said in short words.
Pros:
-Amazing atmosphere
-Scary monsters
-Good storyline
-Well-made audio cover
-Neverending fun (Including main story and fan-made custom stories)
Cons:
-Bugs 'n' glitches
-Can be too confusing in a few times
-Not everyone may like this concept of game
Personal rating: A great classical horror, which should be in every horror lover's library.
Traditional rating: 9/10, greatly recommended

KotOR 2, despite being chronically unfinished, is probably the best Star Wars RPG out there and here's why:
The story and especially the writing are absolutely phenomenal. The guys at Obsidian have managed to create a game that feels like Star Wars without any of the clichés associated with it. Where the first installment had a whiny Han Solo, a force using Leia and Chewie as carbon copies of their originals, this game puts multiple twists on most stereotypical Star Wars characters, fleshing them out so much more. Hell, even though all a certain Astromech droid "says" is random beeps, you know exactly what he wants to tell you, without anyone going "What's that, Lassie? There's  boy trapped in the well?". It's just that amazing.
On top of it all the game features the best wirtten female character in any video game ever, but it's hard to praise the writing without spoiling the story, so I might as well stop now. Just so much: The game covers a multitude of philosophical questions, especially when reading between the lines, so you should be prepared to think while playing.
The graphics are dated, RTwP combat with DnD rules isn't everyone's thing but the same thing can be said for Planescape:Torment and it still is widely regarded as a (the?) classic RPG.
Things of note if you have played the predecessor:
While the graphics, animations and UI have remained pretty much on the same level when compared to KotOR 1, the characters' build diversity has been greatly increased, making things like a gun wielding Jedi viable options.
The combat itself hasn't changed much, except for a few extra skills and powers or new enemies, of course.
Loot is now randomly distributed and modding items as well as crafting them have been greatly expanded.
The story itself covers quite a few events that happened before KoTOR 1, although the game itself is set later. Due to this, I'd recommend playing the predecessor first (especially since its big twist would otherwise be spoilered). Otherwise, you might get lost, concerning the order in which things happened.
As so many others have already stated, the game's main issue is the fact that it's unfinished and unpolished but this can largely be fixed by downloading and installing the TSLRCM, a brilliant modification which restores a lot of cut content to the game, such as the great droid factory. Also, while the game now has widescreen support, I'd still recommend the Widescreen Fix mod to un-stretch the UI.

So, Life Is Feudal – what a spectacular game concept and with the level of developer commitment that has been displayed thus far, I am excited to see what the finished product will look like.  Let's just get the summary out of the way so you don't have to read a wall of text if you don't wish to do so.  I will detail everything later.
The Summary:
LIF:YO is a stand alone game that is being developed completely separate from another project the devs are working on (MMO).  The price tag is a bit rich for an Early Access game, in my honest opinion, but that $40 was well worth it simply due to the fact that have on record almost as many hours as many of my “fully polished” titles in my library.  There is plenty to do but at the same time, it is very possible to hit a brick wall until other features are added or tweaked.  Overall, if you like a game that simply takes time and effort to create something very cool and organic, this game is for you.
The Deets:
You start off with nothing more than the rags on your back.  It is up to you to find a suitable area to sustain and survive.  Is the game possible to play single player?  Absolutely with some tweaking of settings or multiple characters.  Is the game more fun to play multi-player?  By far!  Either set up your own server or join one to play with more people and make the game really exciting.  Build up your defenses, barter with your “neighbors,” master a skill set that no one else in the area has mastered to make yourself a more valuable asset to the community.  All of these things take time and effort to accomplish, but the reward is that you have built something to truly take pride in.  Fixing a broken down wall isn't as simple as replacing a couple blocks.  It takes mining materials and the skills of multiple trades to raise the wall again.
Resources are diverse enough to offer quite a bit of exploration and travel to various locations.  Are they a bit too sparse?  Maybe.  But for what the game is now, it feels appropriate.  Use the materials you have to refine your skills and make higher quality items for trade or protection.  The possibilities are numerous!
There are quite a few bugs... there's no denying that, but the devs seem to be on top of things as long as they reported accordingly.  There are some balance issues within the game that make it falter.  Again, the devs will surely address these before the game is finalized (hopefully by Q3 of next year as they plan).  The UI and combat can definitely feel clunky and unresolved, but over time, it will get more and more optimized to better suit the needs of the game.
Essentially, what you have to remember is that this is an Early Access game and there are going to be bugs.  But if you can past those bugs, horrible optimization, crashes, etc. and realize that the game offers far more positive ideals and possibilities, you enjoy the crap out of it.

If you liked "Shadow Warrior 2013" because  it successfully brought back all the essential features of oldschool nostalgia, please take a moment to read this before pressing the "buy"-button for its sequel. What you have to know and consider is that "Shadow Warrior 2" may still look like "Shadow Warrior 2013" on screenshots (and it even looks better), but it is a very different kind of game.
It's now more or less like "Borderlands": An FPS action-RPG with tons of "loot", overbearing RPG-like weapons/skills upgrade-system, bullet-spongy enemies, and a "hub" with "missions" set in semi-procedurally generated settings (instead of a string of linear hand-crafted levels like we used to see in times of the original  "Duke Nukem" and "Shadow Warrior" games).
Whereas most people seem to see these changes as clear and welcome improvements over the game's predecessor, I for one can't. What I want and expect from a "Shadow Warrior" game is the simple yet addictive 90ies formula to first person shooters, just with upgraded graphics and handling - something that "Shadow Warrior 2013" did so convincingly.
As "Shadow Warrior 2" actually starts out like a traditional "linear" FPS, it took me a few hours to notice that something's "off", but when I got to the "hub" and suddenly received fetch-quest "side missions" from NPC, all the fun evaporated in a mere matter of minutes.
I own all "Borderland" titles. I tried to like them - like everyone else seemed to -, but eventually had to admit I simply didn't and couldn't. A gazillion of modifiable weapons and endless looting and grinding is just not my idea of fun. In my opinion, less is more here: I would have been very happy with a few carefully placed upgrades and weapons I can look forward to.
Also, the  more I play "Shadow Warrior 2", the more I notice that it was quite obiviously designed with 4-player co-op in mind - at least that would explain why, in single player mode, vast stretches of the maps feel beautiful-but-empty: They had to cut on enemies to balance the campaign for when there's no friends to help you.
Despite the "thumbs down" icon, I am ready and willing to agree that "Shadow Warrior 2" is not a bad game as such, though - in fact the overwhelmingly positive feedback is certainly quite justified IF you appreciate the translation of the "Borderlands" concept into a (refreshingly) different setting.

But if you're like me, and rather want to enjoy some oldschool FPS gaming nostalgia: You have been warned!
PS: For comparison's sake, I'm now playing "Shadow Warrior 2013" again too. This game would have been almost perfect if it only hadn't cut the bossfight with the Kyokagami Sisters everything seemed to lead to at one point. From what I've played so far this game is very good. It's very different from the first game, as this is much more open world than the linear story style of the first game. This game has a loot system, where you find different upgrades for you weapons including more damage, elemental damages, fire rate, and other upgrades. The game also has aparantly 70 guns, some you can either buy from stores in game, or you can get randomly, or scripted, by enemies. The movement mechanics are perfect. Theres no stamina bar, so your able to jump and dash around enemies to jump in, deal damage, and jump out without taking any yourself. Combat is well done as well, it seems that enemies dont scale to levels, and instead only scale to the difficulty, meaning that leveling up is just for obtaining skills.  I have only run into a few visual bugs and one major bug, props glitching into each other or being able to see under the map in some spots, and a major bug being that my friend had gotten stuck inside of a rock, with the only fix being to cancel the quest we were on and going onto a different one, which changed which map we would play on.
I plan to update the review as I get farther in the game, but so far its a fun smooth game.

Shadow Warrior 2 has great Combat, amazing movements and solid weaponry.  That all good but you'd think that Shadow Warrior 2 will be a huge step up from its predecessor?  The focus on 4 player co-op, bigger better levels and more of the Wang would make the experience so much better?  The game is strongly well optimized which is the greatest thing that Flying Wild Hog did so right and the visuals are a sight to behold.
Clearly, alot of the effort went to the game combat system.  It's amazing then that so much has gone wrong...  Not only did Shadow Warrior 2 not revamp most of the fundamental flaws from the 2013 reboot.  It makes them much much worse.  The inconstant Role Playing Elements is some the dumbest mechanics I've ever seen in a shooter.  The laughable difficulty, lame♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, and poor story makes the game not that memorable.  Oh, the level design and questing is very abysmal, all of which I'm being unpleasantly reminded of both: Borderlands & Dragon Age II...  It's downright lazy to make a game this shallow and repetitve so quickly right after you did all of Act 1 missions.  The game never changes its rule, it all stays the same throughout the entire game.
Now, not all of it is so bad.  The game combat is so much better than its 2013 counterpart.  Thanks to much improve controls and shooting.  Doing sword abilities no long requires you to press each key movement twice.  Now it's done by pressing one key and the RMB to do the job.  The movement is very good, I really enjoy my time constantly airdashing my way through most of the terribly generated levels in the whole game and it can also be useful in combat since you no longer have to worry about the annoying stamina from the 2013 reboot anymore.  The weapons are pretty decent.  I find the shotguns and grenade launchers the most effective weapons in the game, the assault rifles, pistols and RPG's are decent at best.  The Melee weapons (including the Chainsaw) are your best friend and you'll be using them way more often in higher difficulties or so.
Oh speaking about higher difficulties...  You'll be dealing with tons of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t bullet sponge enemies with elemental resistance and ammo is scarces as hell.  Even with the right equipment, you can pretty much breeze through most of game without stopping.  Once you noticed that it is impossible to resist the urge to do this when your fighting and so damn boring on the hardest difficulty.  Either way, your going to finish the game in just 2 hours or less if you bull rush through the game story on easy or normal.  On Hard and Very Hard it will take you awhile to go through since it makes the enemies so unbelievably strong but still easy to kill if you decide to careover your previous character build from your 1st playthrough.  If you decide to do everything it may take you about 14 hours to get everything done, if you're achievement hunting that is!  There's little reasons to replay the game, since most of the missions are pretty the same♥♥♥♥♥♥  Go from point A in a large randomly generated map to point B, kill that one target/pick up/talk to generic NPC, teleport back to the hub and tell the quest giver its done and accept the reward.  That's all you do in the game.  There's are 5 main bosses total (mini bosses are terrible btw) in Shadow Warrior 2 and they're not too bad but not the same great boss fight level like from Bloodborne & Hyper Light Drifter.
Looting isn't very interesting.  In fact, the looting makes the game shocking more restrictive than actually having fun to play around with.  Why do you need a gem to do Duel welding?  Why is there explosive round gems?  Why is there denonate gems or someother useless stuff?  Why, what, why?  Just ingore those gems and get those both: weapons and elemental gems.  so you can buff up the damage and get at least good bonus upgrades.  Ignore the gems with negative side effects.  You don't want them.  You can use those things in the melee weapons since it has no effect on it and you pretty much make your melee weapons insanely overpowered!  I'm honestly suprised that you also have co-op, armor and power gems to make yourself at least stronger, but I didn't care much about it since they rarely add much to gameplay.  (I could be wrong on that.)  You also have Karma that returns again in Shadow Warrior 2 and you also pick up perk cards that you find thoughout the game.  It'll give you a new perk to make Lo Wang even better in combat.  So you got to choose carefully on you want your build to be setup.  There's no redo options I think but that wouldn't matter since this game isn't that fun or funny to play!
As much I love the visuals in 2013 Shadow Warrior.  Shadow Warrior 2 does provide a good looking experience but since the game is disappointingly designed to have pointless randomly generated levels.  You'll mostly encounter more the same areas over and over and over again.  Worse they often change color just to think the level is different when its clearly not.  There are some original levels early on but that quickly goes away, I can guarantee you that!  While the character model look solid at best, the NPC aren't that good looking and the cutscenes are pretty basic and dull.  The evironments aren't really any speical compared to the 2013 reboot, I did like how the cyberpunk city look. (Don't know if it was a lame reference to the upcoming Cyberpunk 2077 or Blade Runner?) Most of the game visuals are sadly wasted in Shadow Warrior 2, you do get to see some good effects like trees reacting to high winds storm and the rain effects are good, but that's about it.  Performance wise is great and I'm very happy the game works so very well at launch.  Even so, there some framerate hitches when you apporach to a checkpoint or when battles get way too chaotic but that just a minor flaw.  Sound design is mostly carried over from the 2013 reboot with some new ones for the new weapons and stuff.  All solid, nothing else to say...
Oh right, co-op...  I didn't bother touching on it.  I'm hearing people on steam claiming that its broken right now.  So yeah, I got one last thing to say about this game, is the bland story.  The 2013 reboot had a strong narrative that works very well, even if the humor was not the greatest it could've been but that ending had me in tears...  The sequel story is pretty much a complete throwaway in an attempt to get you to rip and tear through hordes of demons and robots alike.  And once you're through this very short story (10 or 11 main missions total) you're treated to a lame sequel bait ending that just as bad like in DOOM 2016 that also has a horrible ending.  Seriously, Flying Wild Hog?  This is the best you can come up with?  In the end, this game is a huge letdown.  This game had the potential to be a pure run & shooter done right like the original DOOM and Serious Sam.  However, the developers chosen wrong.  Instead of keeping the old school FPS formula intact, they've just decided to throw it out of the window and replace it with a poor mans version of Borderlands & Dragon Age II all in one package.  While the combat can good fun at times and movement is godtier.  The sad reminder is that this feels like a generic RPG Shooter then it does being a proper Old School Run & Gun First Person Shooter!
Overall: I'm not going recommend Shadow Warrior 2!  Stick to the classic Shadow Warrior, the 2013 reboot & Original DOOM!

I would say that Swarmriders is the most enjoyable concept thus far from Walter and, with a bit of work, could be turned into a high quality game. For now, it's a bit short and plays far more like a proof of concept than an actual game, lasting a total of ~5 minutes for 100% completion if you get the hang of it fairly quickly.
One major improvement compared to the Ubermosh series is that it plays far more "fairly." Whereas Ubermosh likes to spawn enemies above and below you in a way that's hard to react to, this game warns you far in advance of the challenges you're about to face. The controls are also responsive, but it's easy to get lost in all the explosions and forget exactly where you're firing in some cases, just like in Ubermosh. It may only be a difference of a centimeter, but it's enough to make the difference between clearing the screen and being swarmed.
One of my biggest complaints is one I have with all of Walter's games here on Steam, and it's that most of the games don't really go anywhere. They don't develop. They're short, somewhat one dimensional arcade experiences that are more or less predictable. If more time was spent creating a deeper game, perhaps with levels or something at least, the quality would improve dramatically as the structure is already mostly solid.

With every update I hope things will get better. And still, several months after playing, every update just makes me want to play this game less and less. And that bothers me, because I got several friends of mine to play this game and now none of us touch it anymore.
I'm just going to list a few things this game introduced that just took away from the experience of playing it.
-Okay I don't even think I need to explain the new landscape. I know it supposed to be an alien world, but the cold survival in the forest feeling was much nicer than the now framerate eating color splash it is now, especially when the colors don't mix on the ground correctly. Also you can still get tree trunks, despite there not being trees.
-This was awhile ago but this game actually had music, good music! It was in the original fortresscraft and while it had bad syncing issues with the time of day, it was really good, it added atmosphere. Now we have "ambience", which was actually introduced as the new "music" and when I first heard it before reading the patch notes I genuinely thought it was a sound glitch. To anyone wanting to play this game, you can turn it off with CTRL+M. I recommend doing that.
-The amount of instruction pop ups in this game now is absurd, completely and utterly absurd. within less than 60 seconds of beating the tutorial I am hammered with a step by step instruction guide that you can't turn off, that constantly plays a notification noise whenever you do anything. Remember when you could explore a survival environment at your own pace? Well the game now thinks you're going too slow and will continue to pester you until you do something.
-Add on to the above. Arther, will, not, shut up. And he will sometimes say things that the instruction pops up are repeating to you as well, over and over, until you do it. There is apparently also now a noise for when ARTHER gives you some of his power, which is nice, if it didn't repeat every 3-4 seconds because you lost 1 power from being cold.
-Using the scanner still sometimes results in the scanner echo noise taking much longer than it should to stop, meaning this, combined with the "ambience", creates an unpleasent ringing sound in your ear for several minutes.
-There still isn't any notification if you take damage from something, such as your burning ship, or if you get shot by a slime thats too far away to make the noise. So you may just randomly die if you don't notice your health bar going down.
-The game once again enforces very strongly on a two hopper, 1 smelter design despite the fact I have used, and proven the use of, a more efficient use with 1 hopper and a filter. This wasn't an issue until ARTHER had a notification pop up for when you have an add/remove storage hopper attached to a smelter. I am not sure if my method even still works however as I wasn't able to tolerate my most recent playthrough to the point where I could get a filter. I have brought this up in the forums in the past and was promptly disregarded.
This game is just not player-friendly. I understand that new players will need help with some things, I do, but you need to understand that some people like to figure things out on their own, or play their own way. And this game no longer allows you to do that. You have to play it a specific way or the game will annoy you constantly until you do. The visual aspect of the game is now dead. The music is gone, and unless your preferred playstyle is exactly what the game wants, it punishes you for playing it.
And I feel bad for posting this, since I know the developer puts a lot of work into the changes they do, and they are very active in the forums. When I first saw the dapper support DLC I was almost willing to buy it just because of how much I respected the developer. But I was hesitant to get the Frozen Factory DLC because of how I saw the game going (I never bought either), and now I'm regretting buying the base game. It just isn't fun anymore.
This game has never been as fun and enjoyable as it was in Early-Access. Regardless of all the content they put in. And its reached the point of being unplayable for me.

First my System:
Intel I5-3750K with 3.40GHz
16GB RAM
AMD R9 380 with 4GB
I played the game on Ultra Settings, i had 65-70 FPS, even when there was rain, lightning or grass and trees that swung with the wind. But when i entered a level, the FPS dropped down to 30 FPS, but after a few seconds, normal FPS of 70, when i encountered enemies in masses the FPS was at constant 50 FPS, no problem. But sometimes the FPS dropped down to 20 FPS, in the middle of the fight, out of the blue! Even when there was only one small enemy left. Might be a Hardware Issue, but the Problem was even on lower settings.
Then,there is the gameplay. The gameplay was supposed to be a mix of a First Person Shooter and a First Person Hack'n Slay, but the Guns were so underpowered, one will find himself playing most of the times with the many swords you get. Even for smaller enemies you need entire clips to put one down.
But, there are of course positive aspects, like for instance, the music. It is nicely made and always fits the occasion. When you are in walking around, nothing happening the music plays in the background and is calm, when enemies attack, it changes to a louder agressiver tone to show that you're in a fight. When you're fighting especially large hordes of enemies including a Mini-boss the music swells up, gets more menacing till you defeat them and the music reached it's climax and then ebbs away until it's reaching the normal sound again.
The grafic is nice, it is of course no B*ttlef*eld or and C*ll of D*ty, but it is still very beautiful to watch and play. The wind chimes in the grass, the rain which pours down from time to time or the bright neon lights of the big technocratic City,it all makes the game come to life.
Also the're is the Story of the game. You meet characters, who are not just there to push the story on. You will find throughout the game books and scrolls that tells their background story, or other storys, how the Nobitsura Kage (the sword from the first game) was made for example. Of course, the fortune cookies are back, but this time only for entertainment(?) because they apparently don't give you any health back, unlike in the previous game.
The Weapons. You get a decent amount of Swords, Chainsaws, Pistols, Submachine guns, Assault Rifles, Miniguns, Rocket Lauchers and others. Even when the guns are quite underpowered, it still is fun every now and the to dash guns blazing against an large group of enemies.
The upgrading system for your powers and your weapons are an nice feature, too. You can attach up to three upgrades to your weapons, which makes them deal out elemental damage, or you can upgrade Smgs and pistols to Dual-wield, what makes them in exchange slightly less accurate and also the reloading time increases. You can upgrade your Health and your Chi to an higher amount and even self-regenerating. You can decrease the freezetime for your supernatural abilitys as well as increasing the amount of time you can use them.
Overall, i can recommend this game to everyone who liked the first one, is into the old 90's Shooters or anyone who is into Sword and Chainsaw fighting action, it really feels like one of those 90's First Person Shooter packed in all new grafics.

Normally I do not make a review for a game which I have played so little of. But from what I have seen so far, I cannot possibly recommend Ultimate General: Gettysburg.

-Concept itself
-Acceptable graphics
-Fitting soundtrack
-Flexible customization in settings
-Adaptable scenarios
-Terrible troop placement. Moving your troops in UG:G is a massive hastle. In order to do so, you must click and drag to where you want the selected unit to move. Sometimes I have experienced clicking on a unit and it not registering. I'd have to mouse back to the unit and click again, which wastes a huge amount of time relative to what I have available. Often times, that unit overlaps with the one next to it because it's pretty difficult to estimate the size of them when I'm trying to deal with 1800 men fleeing from 600 men and a single unit of arty (we'll get to that latter). When ordered to move a tiny bit ahead, the entire unit breaks from their organized battle line into a mob and becomes easy pickings for artillery and troops firing at them.
-Horrendous system of 'morale'. Morale is impacted largely by the General and artillery. Yes, artillery, a normal part of 19th century warfare that these troops are accustomed to, will cause morale to drop in half after firing a few times. As mentioned before, I've had a unit of 1,800 troops retreat after a single unit of 23 arty fired one volley at them. This makes having engagements of any kind difficult, considering your troops will just break and lose 300 men.
-Union forces definitely overpowered. Confederate infantry is absolutely abymsal and will get crushed by the Union every day of the week.
One volley of union forces=200 fatalities in one of my units
One volley from my unit=10 kills. Yep,
. I counted. The opposing forces were only one level topographically higher than mine and yet they dominated my troops. It's absurd, historically inaccurate, and quite simply enraging. I can't play a campaign where even the most cautious and gradual tactics by me results in a pyrrhic victory at the most, and a 'major defeat' at the least.
Some of this may be wrong, but it's what I personally saw and experienced. So, again, I cannot recommend this game on account of its poor mechanics and unbalanced nature.
P.S: I have been playing strategy and grand strategy games for 6-7 years now. I am not someone who just started with the genre. I have 1,000s of hours in various titles and games from Total War to Crusader Kings.

Honest to its roots, Sanctus Reach is the most Table Top like experience you will find on the PC. It is not the full rules version of Warhammer 40,000, but rather a sensibly streamlined version that allows you to get playing fast. It's an excellent fit for digital Table Top gaming because it strikes the right balance between enough choices to provide depth but not so many as to baffle a newcomer.
The graphics deserve particular praise as the miniatures are exquisitely detailed. The developers used Games Workshop's own maestro of miniature painting, Duncan Rhodes as a point of reference. If you've watched any of his figure painting videos on youtube or buy your Nuln Oil in 5 litre pots, you'll know what I mean. ;)
On gameplay, it uses squares rather than hexes for movement which I personally feel is better. If you've experienced XCOM game play and like that style you'll find this a good fit. Combat is turn based of course, as it should be, and typically the only things that the enemy can do during your turn is reaction shots. The whole thing is deceptively simple, right up until you walk into an ambush.
This is definitely one of those easy to learn games that has enough depth, challenge and replayability to keep you happy for a long time. You can play the campaigns, skirmish mode which is randomly generated, create your own maps and also use the play by the email system against other players.
All in all this is a lovely game. Whether you want a quick blast or long strategic play through.
In Summary
If you like Warhammer 40k and wanted to try the Table Top games, this is for you. Veterans of Table Top will also enjoy this too, because you can play it without hours of setup. If you've no special interest in 40K but like Turn Based Strategy, you will find this on a par with XCOM & XCOM 2. If you find a friend to play against, so much the better.
Highly recommended. And I will say it again, those in game miniatures are fantastic. They look just like the real thing.
Oh, one more thing. Rumours are that there may be more expansions with other factions. Please PLEASE let it be so. I vote Chaos and Eldar.

Warhammer 40,000: Sanctus Reach Is a turn based tactics game that has a deep and rich gameplay with layers of tactical complexity, housed in a weak UI.
Video:
Text:
This is a EXTENSIVE game, and a few paragraphs of text cant do it justice, please watch the video for the best impression of the title.
So lets starts with the weakest part of the game - the UI. Its a very complete UI, with a ton of information and functionality that is available everywhere. But even so it always feels very clunky, and actions other games take time and effort to polish so the user has the smoothest experience are left very cut and dry in the title with many extra mouse clicks needed to performs actions that don't really need it.
The same applies to things like the Editor, which is GREAT, but also very hard to use with names and UI elements being cobbled together with less care than almost any I've seen.
But, having said that the extensive Campaigns, campaign maps, editor and levels are very cool. Diverse gameplay scenarios are played out and the game offers a very cool take on digitizing the warhammer tabletop experience. With smart and methodical play being rewarded and studying your opponent and your unit compositions being paramount for success.
Animation and Art quality wise the game is a mixed bag, with the various models looking fantastic and pretty detailed, but the various movement, attack and death animations being hilariously stilted. the units look like they belong... until they start to move and feel like cheap imitations of mighty armies.
The turn based A-Sync multiplayer is a amazing addition as always and allows for methodical play and the AI is quite well put together.
In about 30 hours of play I've spend every match learning something new, from Armour VS weapons, movement compositions, flanking and harrying and so on - the gameplay is rich and rewarding, because in the immortal words of the A-TEAM... "I Love it when a plan comes together".
To bad the UI makes you want to torch the building the plan is being made in.
Great if you enjoy slow paced tactical turn based strategy, but offers little else beyond that.

First time I write a review here, so I might as well write it proper.
As I see it, Sniper Elite falls between a number of chairs. It tries to have it's cake and eat it too, and suffers greatly due to it. It's part stealth, part action and long range focused. Problem is, there is no good way of planning attacks, the gameplay is linear and the sheer number of enemies makes this game in a much poorer condition than it could have been in.
The offset is pretty good. There aren't alot of games that focuses on the role of the sniper/marksman out there, and so far nobody has really suceded in recreating that aspect of combat. The game tries to come off as realistic, having it's balistic model as one of it's most adverticed selling points. And to some extent, the bullet physics are great, exept bullets can't penetrate anything, even a wooden fence can stop these bullets. Only thing it actually does penetrate are foilage and bodyparts... the latter it doess rather well.
The levels of the game does not invite the player to plan their attacks, as I stated earlier. In addition, there is far to much focus on close quarters combat for this to really take the art of sniping seriously. Snipers and marksmen are mainly covert operators, and they are usually only used for high value target and recon, not as the one man army portrayed in this game. The gameplay is repetative, unintuitive and plain booring in the long run, and it's far from as interesting as it could have been.
It does, however, provide some entertainment if you have nothing else to do for 30 minutes, but as a game to sit down and enjoy for an evening, it doesn't serve at all.
Hope that you'll find this review helpful, comments are welcome.

Let's cut to the chase: This game is great.
The Breakdown:
7/10 Story- The story follows Karl Fairburne in the last days of WWII. His initial mission is to assasinate five German scientists, as they have connections with the Nazi V2 rocket project. Unfortunately, things do not go as planned, intel is gathered, rockets are blown up, convoys are stopped, facilities are infiltrated, all in all, a solid storyline that accentuates the urgency of each mission.
9/10 Gameplay- The player must remeber several core game mechanics (remeber to shoot the red fuel caps, not just the fuel tank), but other than that, simplistic, point and shoot, bullet drop, things like that. A veteran to TPS or FPS games will have no problem at all. Unfortunately, I am not a veteran, so it took almost twenty hours more than it should've.
7/10 Graphics/sound- This game was released in 2012, but the graphics hold up (medium graphics settings was good enough for even my picky eye). Very immersive, you can almost feel the gun pumping in your hands and feel the bullets plugging into the enemy's body. This is due to an amazing sound engine, along with some amazing sound people at the helm.
8/10 Realism- Obviously no army would have bright red fuel caps that explode upon impact with a bullet, but you can see muzzle flashes and the bullets whizzing past you. The bullet cam is extemely cool, when you snipe somebody you see a camera following the bullet as it kills the person. Grusome, but very cool. Healing is non-realistic, you are good as new is seconds. There are the little things, too, like NPCs carrying on conversations about the war, what they'll do after, how they never wanted to be a soldier in the first place. I occasionally think about sparing them, as if after the game credits roll, they'll go back to a little cottage in Russia, sitting down with their family. But I kill them anyway because they try to kill me and oftentimes do. They can smoke, try to heal their incapacitated comrades (Russia joke), even drink vodka or coffee.
That's about it. Buy this game, play the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it, then come back and weigh in on the discussion.

This game surpasses its reputation of being horrific. It is also interesting, mysterious, and awe-inspiring. It provides a cold trip to the past, leaving you to piece together the events surrounding the setting and characters. I very much enjoyed the voice acting and dialogue along with the puzzles and plot.
Surprisingly, the game did not end quickly. I found it satisfyingly long, but I should mention I took my time to go through it. There is quite a bit of content to take in and think about while not being overly complex. There were a few minor parts that I could not figure out, as I felt that I had "already checked everything", though this could be due to my lack of patience; merely walking in this game can be scary and stressful... backtracking is not something I was always willing to do unless I was certain I had missed something. The path is not completely linear, in that it frequently lets you choose where to go first and decide the order in which to do things, though the "correct" order is often made clear. This provided me with a sense of freedom as every new area allowed me to decide where to go first.
I found that certain aspects became less scary or thrilling over time, however the developers did a great job there as I frequently had something sufficiently new to deal with, keeping the game fresh and forcing me out of my comfort zone. I want to add that I experienced the most intense "jump scare" of my life in this game, and that was after I felt I had been desensitized to most of what this game had to offer.
I want to praise all of the specific details that I obsessed over while playing, but I will leave that to the reader of this review to experience for themselves. How I wish I could share the sense of wonder I had while trudging on through this cryptic journey... I don't know what else to add here except to keep an open mind while playing, and to really try and immerse yourself in everything this game has to offer. If you're like me, a beginner in the field of Lovecraftian and weird fiction in general, I feel there is no way you won't get swept away by this magnificent creation from Frictional Games.

I'm just gonna put It out there. It's monopoly, nothing too simpler about It. From the creators of miniclip came Business Tour online. Not going to complain, nor any hard complaints from me.
Up to four players at a time, can perfectly work with two or three, free for alls or 2v2's, however you like. This game is heavily based on luck, rng, and hoping you have enough properties to avoid bankrupcy.
I played one game with one other person, and I can say this from experience, It can snow-ball pretty hard if one of two players has more than half the properties on the map.
How to win you're thinking? Simple. By three ways you can,  buy all four resort areas (Which are actually on all sides on the board respectively) Two, you buy 'on four sides' three lined properties, In this case three combined respectively, makes sense. Or option three, force your opponent to go bankrupt.
This is what I was saying about the snowball effect, you have one person owning a three squared area and you land on that you pay the one who owns it money, (And hope you don't run out of it) Making a full ring around nets you 300k, there on the corner tiles are
"Lost island" In this case, you lose between 1-3 turns."
World championchip, more or less upgrades a tile to give it more value i.e: I have a property thats 150k, I land on world championchip and select it, goes up to 300k in a sense.
World tour: You can go on any unclaimed propety tile on the map, also can do a loop around for 300k. Found it nice to land on this space often, though you have to pay 50k to use it.
Tax tile: Near the end theres something called a tax tile, aka you land on it, you have to pay money, simple.
The issues in my opinion.. Gold, chips. "Why?" You may ask. Simple.
Gold: The premium currency, more or less you use this to buy ingame items, change chance cards, roll different dice, hell even buy chips.
You can already see the problem, if someone dumps 100 dollars buying gold they automaticly have an advantage, be it rolling evens, odds, or rolling 'again' to get away from paying property.  Oh yeah, those 'chance cards' can be very useful, to VERY self deabilitating,  Hell the one game I played I hit a chance tile, 'protect a single property from being bought' Okay, that looked nice. Rolled another. 'Pay twice the amount of rent the next time you land on it' W-wait.. what? So rolling onto a 512k property turns it into a 1 mill rental? You see what I mean? It's entirely based on luck.
Also theres a limit on how many you can use, like two to three dice-edits per game. Etc.
Chips: As much as I like having chips and a limiter, yes. Chips are a limiter. You can bid as low as 100, up to 1000. You start with 5000 chips.  If you're reckless you can lose those chips within five games. I'm sure you can get more over time with dailies, or just logging in, but of course you have the option of paying for chips, 20 gold for around 5000?
I get why people are getting angry over the game 'it sucks, It put me on lost island continually' I don't exactly blame you for being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off either.  But in the end, what can you blame, yourselves? No. It's just rng and luck.
Also noted a weird graphics glitch from time to time, not too crippling, but annoying.
Not a bad game Miniclip, though honestly you should tweak it.   6/10. Would recommend with friends.  4/10, something good to pass the time by yourself, can't recomend it by myself though. Good game.

Darksiders is an action adventure game that while competent, doesn't really bring anything new to the table. It's a mix between a God of War styled combat and Zelda exploration and puzzle solving.
Pros
-Nice combat that gradually introduces new weapons and items to use
-A big world that allows for a bit of exploration
-Good amount of upgrades for both your weapons, moveset and other modes
-Not that many items but they all have their purpose that makes them unique
Cons
-Not enough enemies. In a game where the combat is one of the major elements, it doesn't help when you usually only fight 5 or so enemies at a time. There is also little enemy variety.
-The world is huge but doesn't feel natural. With no towns or relevant NPCs or sidequests, it feels like a giant corridor. There is little reason for backtracking other than getting to chests you couldn't reach before, which you either have to do  every single time you get a new item or wait until the end of the game when you already have every item
-Enemies placed outside of dungeons are repetitive and sometimes a few zones won't even have any enemies at all
-Too easy, both the combat and the puzzles, safe for a few examples near the end.
-Nothing new about any element in the game. All items and puzzles have a certain "been there, done that" feel to them.
Conclusion: I realise that I listed more Cons than pros, but I still enjoyed the game. It just seemed to be dragged down by a lack of originality and a few amateurish flaws like the overworld's design and the simplicity of both the items, their function and the puzzles themselves.
I recomend it to anyone who enjoys this type of game, unless you're craving for something new and original, which darksiders doesn't provide at all. It competently follows the mold of all the elements in most action/adventure games, nothing more, nothing less.
