So, that was Ostwind, or as called in the weird english translation "Windstorm".
I gotta say, if you are looking for action, you can already stop reading and move on to another game.
The most important thing before you start:
Positive and Negative about the game:
+ Fantastic voiceacting, i played the game in german and in english and i can assure you that the voices, also the subtitles are well done.
+ Soundeffects are realistic (When you ride over asphalt, dirt, gras etc.)
+ The game is based on the original Ostwind books and movies, includes some of the original characters.
+ There is the possibility to ride in an Open World
+ Different but simple tasks to do, like catching other horses in small races, jumping, collecting lost items, taking care of Ostwind and making sure that he's clean and happy.
+ The Developer(s) are very active in the forum and tend to answer on questions and problems within a short time.
~ The game overall is rather short. You are done with the main "quests" after about 3-4 Hours if you are quick.
And to mention it, there is no replay value for the mainquests at all.
Afterwards you can do some extra sidequests in the Open World mode of the game, collecting items and discovering hidden places. Or try to beat your own best time in the jumping / running races. That will take you about 2-4 more hours.
~ There are sometimes visual bugs, like missing animations while playing with Ostwind in the Paddock. Then hes hovering around instead of using his legs. It's also possible to ride outside the map and to get stuck in certain objects.
~ The Price for the delivered content is too high in my opinion. for the 6-8 hous of playtime you get, 9,99€ would surely be a fairer pricetag.
~ The open World Map could be larger, as far as i remember it´s only about 5x5km large. Sounds bigger than it actually is, because a lot of this is not accessible due to invisible walls in front of trees / water.
~ More (different) wildlife would also help the game, since it feels rather dull at most areas. Maybe some ducks in the water, Pigs on the fields or more birds would change that.
- The music. It's not completely bad, but after about  30 minutes riding freely, the loop gets really monotonous and annoying.
- Many people say the graphics are great. Sorry, but i can't sign that.
They are not ugly, but also not great.
The game is made with the Unreal Engine, but never really using the full potential.
You see lazy made 2D plants and flowers here and there, and alongside the good looking normal 3D trees, are also 2D tree "walls".
Whoever had the idea that this combination looks good... just NO.
You can't use the Unreal Engine and then celebrate like its 1996.
- The controls. As mentioned already, do yourself a favor and switch from mouse to keyboard controls.
I didn't realize that i can change it at first, and got pretty annoyed by the standard (mouse) control settings.
PS: if you have a question that wasn't answered above, feel free to leave a comment, in english or german, on my profile.

I am blown away by the effort put into making this unique RPG. The real selling point of the game is its complex magic system. I've never seen a game before that lets you construct your spells piece by piece in order to create completely unique effects. Even better, it integrates force mechanics which allows you to throw objects of the scenery at enemies or toss your enemies into the air, or at each other. I greatly enjoyed tossing the corpses of my enemies at other enemies.  I also enjoyed spawning a small army of hellions and granting them all flame armor, causing percent damage back to my foes whenever they attacked my army. My only disclaimer is (spoiler alert) the game does a poor job of tying up loose ends. Once you beat the final boss the game abruptly finishes and there's nothing else to do. You main love interest is never seen or heard from again and all you can do is finish up side quests you hadn't touched yet. There's no closure on a number of story arcs. Basically, enjoy the game for what it is in the present. If the developers of Two Worlds II happen to see this review, please include an endgame or some type of cinematic at the end to tie up the loose ends.

This was my first experience with Frictional Games, a studio that has quickly become one of my personal favorite game studio's still in operation. This game is, and probably will be for some time, the quintessential Frictional game, as well as one of the quintessential games of the Horror Genre. Its astounding to see how much influence this game has on its Genre, with games such as Alien Isolation, Outlast, etc, all of which have the distinct mark of a horror game that arrived after Amnesia's groundbreaking success.
The story is simple, Your name is Daniel, you are trapped in a strange, seemingly haunted castle with no memories. Disoriented and confused, you discover a note from your "former self" which tells you the following:
1. That you must travel to the inner sanctum of the castle and kills its owner, Alexander of Brennenburg.
2. That there is Something hunting you, this entity, known as the "Shadow" is described as a living nightmare, and will chase you relentlessly.
With that, the Dark Descent (pun totally intended) begins. From the getgo Frictional does a stellar job building atmosphere, and establishing the haunting presence of the "Gatherers" (the games main enemies" without granting a single dangerous encounter (at first). These creatures moan, wale, and shamble about in the beginning just out of reach and sight, simultaneously everywhere and no where. Sometimes you hear their moaning and discover one directly behind you, posed to strike, only to realize that it is a hallucination, as it evaporates into dust. Other times upon entering a room, the monster shambles menacingly into another, its motion and being seen just through the Corner of your eye, only to find nothing should you investigate. The Gatherers are strong players from the beginning, even without the actual danger.
The Atmosphere of this game is also amazing. Every bit of the castle is rendered and created in magnificant creepyness, from its creaking doors, rotted wood and destroyed stone. Doors fly open on their own, lights swing in non-existant wind. Voices ranging from Whispers to screams echo along the empty halls. Even more disturbing is the Shadow's effect on the enviornment, creating an unnatural flesh that grows and creeps along the walls and floor, hurting Daniel should he touch it. Even without any real danger, this game is horrifying.
Once the danger exists though, it becomes as omnipresent as the fear it creates. The storage was the first room I encountered with an encounter that was meant to be dangeroud (not counting the Gatherer early on which you have to run up to in order to be attacked by). While the guest room may also be an early encounter (and a stellar one at that), the storage proved to be one of the most intense, nerve wracking moments of the game. The inky blackness causing distortions on the screen while the Gatherer's shambled about, searching for their prey.
The sanity aspect of this game, flawed as it is, also adds quite a bit to the overall feel. You experience Daniels fear and insanity as it sets in first hand, which creates this wonderfully horrifying sense of reality amongs the fantasy, almost german expressionistic enviornment.
All in all, Amnesia is a masterpiece, a testament to just how scary a game can be, and a milestone in its genre. Many years from now, while other games have faded and become stale and dated, Amnesia will continue to fright and delight its audience with its atmosphere, gameplay and story.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg provides the best way to experience 18th Century warfare at its finest. There is a extreme ease when it comes to manuevering, whether its the Army of Northern Virginia or the Army of the Potomac. Simply click on a unit and drag the intended path of travel, you can also hold down control and right click, then rotate until the unit is facing the desired direction. The only time troop movement can get wonky is when they move up very steep hills for example Culp's hill gives my troops fits and Ill find them not even moving or facing the wrong way somtimes it works out and they do actually get to the desired position. In terms of sights and sounds, the audio (when wearing headphones) is actually awesome, especially in the more heated sections. Sights can be lacking at times being the Units are sprites however I must say the map looks great and actually when you have large amounts of units lining up and engaging one another, the large clouds of smoke along with reloading and firing animations also look cool in large numbers. Content this game is well worth the price even though it is one battle, every single battle feels distinct and different each play through. You may sweep the field as the Union on the first day and push the Confederates back off of Herr's Ridge. Or as the Confederates you may push the Union off of Cemetery Hill....etc. The battle can also last up to 4 days aswell. There are 9 different difficulties along with the "boost ai" option always being there for whatever difficulty is chosen. Each difficulty varying in aggressiveness of ai, and the overall difficulty of the battle.
The Army of Northern Virginia and The Army of the Potomac are very different armies. The Confederates consisting of Highly spirited troops who lack the efficent weaponry of the Union, can take volley after volley. They Confederates are really lacking at long range volley exchanges. It is more wise to close the gap when using the Confederates as close range combat is something they tend to excell at. Their artillery is also extremely lacking, specfically in terms of range the Union arty can hit you with canister shot and be alot further from your men then the Confederate arty (where it seems the Union troops have to be right on top of the cannons in order for them to be in range for a canister shot). This is very cool to be able to play two very different armies however it seems as of late (The latest patches) the Union have an advantage and this wasnt always the case. As back when the game first released in 2014 the Confederates where able to just walk through walls of lead seemingly and not waiver.  The Multiplayer is almost non-existant it takes days to get into a game with an opponent. All in all this game is one of the best games featuring 18th century warfare, I've heard rumors that the developers plan to expand to other battles of the Civil war which will be really cool. I feel the sky is the limit with this soon to be series (hopefully) , that they can capture the Napeleonic wars along with the 7 years war and many more. I highly recommend this to any strategy player.

I held off buying this "sim". After throwing away money on previous TML bus games I swore I'd never get another product from them. But a few youtube videos made it look like this one is different - and I decided to buy it. Should have trusted my initial instinct.
This is NOT a simulator. It's a console-like pass time at best. Seriously? No force feedback? No halfway decent drivetrain simulation? No ammount of pretty map building can make up for the lack of basic simulation features. Physics? Pffft, who needs those, they're for nerds. Wooden linear steering, no force feedback to speak of (a jolt when you crash into something doesn't count!), no acceleration unless you bury the pedal all the way, incorrect gearbox behavior, completely wrong suspension behavior... I'm not asking for project cars level of physics, but at least something? At least ETS or OMSI levels? Nope, no soup for you.
The fact that this has been out for over a year, had numerous updates, and still doesn't have force feedback support, shows you exactly where TML's priorities are. They added a radio DLC, but not force feedback... They're just gonna go on adding more map eye candy and bus DLCs which are all going to feel and behave exactly the same; and meanwhile the core of the game, the driving experience, remains on the level of a phone app. And it really is a shame, because the map is gorgeous and has so much potential. But all that potential is wasted. OMSI: Horrid graphics engine, good sim. Fernbus: great graphics engine, horrid sim.
Big thumbs down. And still... I'm hoping that some of those things might be addressed. If they are, I'd change this to a thumbs up, honest. But being familiar with TML's past, I'm not holding my breath. Hoping Lotus will get completed soon...

The game was brilliant, I played the game for hours - with many more to come - almost everything in the game was perfect, the variety of weapons, the dlcs, even the hours you spend cramped up in a corner with your squad dead is fun; which leads you to ask - "Why did you rate it a thumbs down?" - unfortuantly, the AI in this game are... well - crap.
In the game their are different game difficulties, recruit being the easiest, and elite the hardest, but it only effects one thing; the reaction time of the enemy. The enemy in the game are *incredibley* overpowered, its like fight a level 100 Warrior in WoW with a level 50 Rogue - It is near impossible. Dont get me wrong, on some missions the AI is well balanced, but on some (Signal lost - This drove me insane, if your going to buy the game have fun <3) it was noticable on Signal lost and onwards, the enemy is described as 'Better trained, with better gear' you are supposed to kill these enemies with a pistol with 1 mag :/ .
I'll be honest - that wasnt the hard part, if you find some AI with their pants down, you often kill them, get their rifle and vest, but its when you have to go through a large town which is the near impossible part. The AI have aimbots (No literally - they actually have aimbots which usually lock onto you - then their is no escaping) they have X-Ray vision (You can be laying down on the top floor of a house making no noise, suddenly you hear "I'VE SPOTTED AN ENEMY!" then you are gunned down) They have eyes in the back of their heads (This is partially with the aimbot, but if your sneaking around behind them, doesnt matter how far really, if you are behind them within about 200 metres, they usually just *know* your there, then they turn around and let a spray of auto cut you into little pieces)
Those few things let the game down significantly, stealth is almost non-existent in the game, so your only hope on 'Signal lost' is to run, gun and pray you dont get bombarded by helicopters, a spray of 50. from boats, some guy with an automatic weapon 200m on a roof top south of you, or that you've actually killed the enemy (Yes, ammo in this mission is a major thing, it takes about 5 shots from the pistol to kill an enemy (So at the start, assuming you dont miss - you will miss a lot- will take out the two guys at the start. And once you get the rifle it takes 4 - bare in mind that they are semi's - the enemy *will* have automatic, aimbotting, spider sense weapons which will destroy you even if you are 500 metres away.
There is also no melee - so if you out of ammo - your ♥♥♥♥ed- have fun reloading as save and doing all that again!
Personal note to devs: I doubt you read these but for the love of god PLEASE revisit AI targeting, stealth and radars (I forgot to mention that once you fire a single bullet, every AI starts rushing towards you, I remember running up against 8 AI on one of my goes at this mission)

This is probably the nicest horse themed game on Steam right now, even if it is a movie series tie-in. I'd never heard of Ostwind before seeing this pop up in the store, now wishing the movies were more readily available on this side of the Atlantic.
The open world is 25 square kilometers of meadow, lowland and pine forest, mixed with farms and a few logging operations. The forests and open areas are filled with AI animals like deer, wolves, and birds, plus cows and horses in a couple spots. Solid ambient audio plus the relaxing soundtrack means you'll probably spend more time free-riding through this than questing.
The quests themselves switch between timed races, item delivery, tracking down escaped animals, and finding things like Mr Kaan's lost horse carvings that are scattered throughout the map. There's also locations from the movies to find, and a couple secrets too.
The horse is defaulted to steering with the mouse, and triggering jumps and speed bursts through the mouse buttons, although this can be changed and the game does support controllers.
Overall, Ostwind's definitely worth its asking price, but you'll want a decently beefy computer if you're planning to run it on its highest settings.

Sim UK Junior RATING (70/100)
===============================
Longevity: 8
Fun: 7
Educational: 5
Positivity + Equality: 7

UPDATED REVIEW
=================
Ostwind Windstorm is a German movie & franchise which has not really been experienced in the UK/USA before now.
Checkout Loads of our gameplay here :
5 Year OLD Gameplay Here :
Having played this game for a few weeks now, with my daughter and on my own, I feel that a more in-depth and updated review is justified.  I still recommend this product but now I can offer more detail about the game itself;
The game appears to follow a pre-existing storyline, of which I am not knowledgeable but the general premise appears to be;
Windstorm only allows the heroine to ride him and together they don't like tournements....her Grandmother (who I think owns the stables) always tries to encourage more enthusiasm and in the long run I think tournements are where we are heading.
The game increases with difficulty, but not complexity as you progress through each quest.  As you complete more quests you can apply upgrades to Windstorm;
- Stamina,
- Speed,
- Resiliance
- agility.
This make future quests easier.  Quests include;
- Mazes,
- Pursuits,
- Training,
- Discover / Hunting,
- Showjumping
Horse care consists of four mini games;
- Cleaning shoes,
- Brushing,
- Cleaning stables,
- Play
PROS
======
- For my 5 year old daughter this is great!  Especially the free roam feature.  She can happily (and on her own) explore without getting stuck anywhere and see lots of great views and animal wildlife (deer, fox, cows, Hot Air Balloons, Low flying Aeroplanes, and more...).
- Seems to be a lot of content, not run out yet!
- Increases with difficulty, not too much but does increase skill requirements and concentration.
- Good introduction to children about animal care.
- Just looks and plays nicely
You CAN play with a controller, you just need to turn on keyboard controls (makes no sense) :
CONS
======
- My biggest annoyance is with the Horse dynamics, they are limited.  You will bounce off of many things, rocks, trees, grass, vehicles and whilst this is good for younger players it looks a little unrealistic.  I would also like to see Windstorms head move and not his entire body when turning, like a real horse would lead, but this is fine for youngsters with imagination.
- Whilst Windstorms energy is persistent horse care is not, if you clean the stable and then click on it again, you will repeat the challenge.
- A little cheesey at times :-)
FIRST LOOK REVIEW
===================
Gameplay :
Ostwind/Windstorm the game is theoretically the first attempt at introducing the franchise to Britain and the Americas etc..  This is immediately previlent as the game's introduction is all in German without translation or subtitles.  Thankfully the game itself does offer both English subtitles and English actors and has been done to a high standard.
The game looks very nice graphically, we are not talking next gen but certainly captures the horse enthusiasts imagination effectively.  My daughter is 5 and has been hounding me to get this game since release and I finally decided to give the game a chance and I am semi-satisfied with the game as a whole.
Pro's
=====
- Very pretty to look at
- Has some nice mini-game + educational in terms of horse care
- Nice audio and environment/characters are pretty decent
- Has captured my daughters imagination straight away
- Relaxed semi-linear approach to gameplay
Cons
=====
- Controls are less than brilliant (feel detached from the horse)
- Although controls can be changed versatilitity is limited
- No controller support
- Horse animation and riding physics are dated and less than realistic (But OK for kids)
- Lack of depth...example: Cleaning the horses hooves has a double ended tool but only one part can be used.
- The storyline and characters are a little shallow (again fine for Kids)
- Repetetive (at this time) time trial...quickly take something somewhere....time trial....Quickly find something...time trial...
Overview
========
This is a modern(ish) and pretty looking title with a focus on horses and the characters from the films, from this aspect it is a perfectly fine and happy game that younger children and horse (or Ostwind/Windrow) enthusiasts will no doubt enjoy.
We are only a little way into the game but concerns about how much content is included are beginning to appear, hopefully as the game progresses more content will emerge and new challenges will become available.

This game is super realistic...Focuses Largely on teamwork, Takes a few dozen hours just to create a basic mud hut by yourself. Giveing you an idea how hard it was to live back in the feudal era, and the importance of living with a organized group.
For being in early access, It has so much content, you cannot possibly get through it all. Its too slow paced for me, so I will wait for some added features that will make the game more appealing for solo players who just like to survive.
Pros: 1.This is the closest thing you will get to a mutiplayer/realism medieval simulator. (Aside from Kingdom Come:Diliverance that is more single player and much much better looking)
2. buildings are beautiful, for such a large world with lots of content and with a big enough group of friends anything is possible starting as a bunch of mud hut savages who kill people on sight to building a wall to keep up other savages, and then thriving as a huge kingdom who still kill people on sight but with more deadly weapons and fully tanked out armor.
3. Loads of content...for being in a alpha stage...it feels more like a beta, best part is they are adding more.
even though I am taking a long break from the game.
Cons: 1.You need a group to surivive or have any fun with it, your best chance is to wander around like a naked pleb and find a group. To know if they are friendly, make sure you have the mic setup...or people will kill you on sight for not communicating since banditry/stealing/murder is very common and penalties for doing so are spirit breaking.
2. Its a very time consuming game. This is a double edged sword *no pun inteded* I find myself in the middle with this, If the game could make it exciting from the start to the end game as well, I would be putting much more time into the game. But leveling and many of the RPG elements are useless if you find yourself constantly starving searching for food (this is why you need lots, and lots, and lots, of peasants to farm for you- thus teamwork is the cornerstone of survival)
3. Make sure you are on a server with good ping, this is obvious...Don't be that BR guy that joins a Canada server/US server with 300+ ping...you will get rekt unlike most shooters where its the otherway around. Also communcation is delayed on high ping servers for you, so having crisp ping pong conversations makes the game much more enjoyable...as well not watching people rubber band.
.I recommend this game because the concept is very good, Its worth keeping an eye on and see this becoming a very successful game even if its for a nitchy group of people -like myself-

After the huge innovation of Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, KOTOR2 had high expectations. It introduced advanced upgrading; a more fleshed out and expanded story; more force abilities; early game choices/customisations; and allies that you could get to know, gain influence with, and overal interact with, with much more depth.
From the get go, you're flung into a mystery as you find your character recovering from being held within an abandoned mining facility. I won't spoil the story for you, but I will say that it it never gives in - also raising new questions, and spawning many branches which act not only as side missions, but also to add more detail to the main story.
In KOTOR2, you start the game as a jedi, as opposed to becoming one later in the game. There are more force options, and more feats that make each of the 3 classes really distinct. This, combined with the game's element of choice, and a light/darkside meter, you will find it is a unique experience for each player.
So, for those who enjoyed the original KOTOR, this game will serve as both an extension to the story, and the means to get back into this amazing experience.
For new players, however, this game will still be blast to play. It features an easy to understand character creator, and a solid tutorial in the beginning. I would recommend playing the original KOTOR first though, to really understand both the gameplay; and more importantly, the story.
Kotor 2 is a fantastic game, and one played through many times. Each experience is unique, and the characters and story are really engaging. And I've currently just started my third playthrough at the time of writing this :)

Overall, this is a mediocre game. It runs around 40 hours with completing every quest. The game world is interesting if cliche, at times. Basically, it's just good enough to hold your interest and suck you in but you will never once be wowed by it. Part of this is because quests are all loose and disconnected with barely any relation to the main storyline. The only time I felt compelled at all to learn more about the game lore was during my stay in the swamp village. This particular part of the game was well done, and if the whole game played like this it would have been better off. Guild quests also feel loosely connected and offer no benefits to completing them outside a title that only you will see in your character screen (as opposed to something like Elder Scrolls, which it clearly borrowed these ideas from).
Combat system is passable. Magic system is creative, but makes your mage specialization and approach subject to the cards you find on your quest. For me as a mage, the game revolved around tedious hit and run tactics until I got my first summon card halfway through the game which insantly made my mage insanely overpowered. That said, I give them props on doing something unique here.
My biggest gripe is with the end. An already mediocre plot throws in an unneccesary and flat out stupid twist. But worse than that is the final boss battle which is reduced to a "line up the crosshairs and shoot" ordeal. It was not exciting at all, just tedious. It took me 3 tries. And only because it was so unenjoyable and disappointing to me that I refused to die even one more time just to waste any more time on it. As for the ending, what a worthless wait that was. The ending is flat out awful.
In summation, this is a good investment during a steam sale. You can't really beat 15 cents per hour of entertainment.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a survival horror video game by Frictional Games, released for Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X, and Linux platforms. The game features a protagonist named Daniel exploring a dark and foreboding castle, while avoiding monsters and other obstructions as well as solving puzzles. The game has earned two awards from the Independent Games Festival and numerous positive reviews from fellow gamers.
Amnesia is an adventure game played from a first person perspective. The game retains the physical object interaction used in the Penumbra series, allowing for physics-based puzzles and interactions such as opening doors and fixing machinery.
In addition to a health indicator, Daniel's sanity must be managed. Being in darkness too long, witnessing unsettling events, or staring at monsters will reduce Daniel's sanity, causing visual and auditory hallucinations and drawing the attention of monsters. Light sources help restore sanity, and if none are available Daniel may use tinderboxes to ignite candles in wall sconces and candelabra, or deploy an oil-burning lantern found near the beginning of the game. However, the number of tinderboxes and the amount of oil available are both limited, and standing in a light source also makes the player more noticeable to monsters. The player must balance the amount of time Daniel spends in light and shadow. Sanity is fully restored once Daniel completes an objective or progresses the game's story. It may also be restored by staying in the shadows until Daniel passes out, but this leaves him extremely vulnerable to any nearby monsters.
If a monster spots Daniel, it will chase him until he's out of sight. If spotted, Daniel must flee, as Amnesia does not give the player access to weapons. Daniel must find hiding places or barricade doors with rocks, chairs and other obstacles; however, monsters are capable of tearing down doors in their path and kicking obstacles out of the way, and move extremely fast once they have spotted their prey. Players can also choose to hide Daniel in the shadows, at cost to sanity. Monsters who lose sight of Daniel will search for him for a time, but will eventually leave and vanish.
Overall I would recommend this game. 8/10

Shadow Warrior 2 is a fast paced, action-packed FPS that has tons of loot, and a whole lot of wang jokes.
You are Lo Wang, a lone mercenary on a mission where something goes terribly wrong. You are thrust into a major conflict between hordes of demons, and the enemy forces belonging to your nemesis. The story is interesting. It’s not profound or anything, but it’s very amusing at times.
Most of the gameplay revolves around combat. You have a wide variety of weapons, both for ranged, and melee. Personally, I am a huge fan of the melee combat, where you get to jump and dash all over the place, and stay constantly moving. I absolutely loved the gore; dismembering, and slicing down enemies was an immensely satisfying experience. The guns are fun to use too, and there are definitely times where you will want to keep some distance, but melee combat feels so much more intense for me.
I played the game solo on normal mode. It took me 9.5-10 hours, and I had expected it to be a bit more challenging. In hindsight, I should have played it on the next difficulty setting, but I still had a blast playing it. If you’re looking for some fast-paced action to play by yourself or with friends. Shadow Warrior 2 is a lot of fun, and it reminded me of DOOM combined with Borderlands co-op and loot system. Overall, it is a really fun game, and definitely worth playing.

Aside from the unnecessary complication of having to complete the tutorial stage before being allowed to co-op, what kills this game for me is that:
-The combat is too floaty. It feels like it was made with a poor multiplayer netcode in mind. Enemies just start waving their swords around and you take damage despite being 2-3 feet away from them. It's almost as if like there was lag, except I'm in single player, so obviously the hitboxes are very exaggerated - again, it's as if the combat was designed to compensate for laggy players or perhaps a poor netcode. It doesn't feel like a proper shooter because of this.
-The clunky, unergonomic UI. If you're going to make a drop-in, drop-out co-op game, you NEED to keep a sense of speed and accessibility in mind for your character/inventory menus. The UI for your character's skills and weapons and whatnot is... not necessarily complex, but it's very unintelligible, if you just want to get something done quick. It's a huge buzzkill. When me and my friend played, our first reaction almost at the same time was "who the hell wants to sit in this menu for 10 minutes to figure it out, I'll just use whatever weapons the game auto-equips for me, I don't care...".
Aside from that, my personal opinion is that this game's graphics are overblown. There's so much visual fidelity that the actual enemies just blend in to the explosion of colors and particle effects everywhere you look. Shadow Warrior 1 looked amazing, without taking your enemies out of the visual focus. The Unreal Engine 4 circlejerking in this game is just too much for me, and I find it hard to focus on my enemies. When you put too much detail in a game, everything just melts together and it's hard to get a read on what's happening any more.

It's rare that I give up on a game so soon into playing it but this would be one of the few times that it happens. I couldn't tell you much about how the game itself plays except that it really does lack anything which could be considered entertainment. The notion of a tower defence Minecraft-esque game sounds appealing but the way it has been done is just needlessly tedious. There are many mods for Minecraft which offer what FortressCraft is doing here but does it far better.
Whats more is that the game is just plain unpleasent to look at. The UI itself is messy and vague. The environment itself is dark and neon in a way which isn't interesting or visually appealing at all and can be done much better as shown by games such as Subnautica. The draw distance, even when maxed, is actually far less than what Minecraft it capable of with shaders applied so you have this distinct horizon not very far away and the surface clutter can be seen hovering over an invisible landscape that has not yet loaded. The items held in the players hand block a good 1/4 of the screen which is distracting when you're looking around. Due to how dark the game is and how crucial machines are all blocks I found myself having to carefully peer at the screen to tell if I was looking at a hopper or a smelter for example. This unwieldly design also extends to the controls which cannot be rebound to new keys from within the game it would seem.
The game is just an unwieldy mess of ideas that have been mashed together and don't really work when taken as a whole. I've refunded this already and I would suggest that nobody touch this game.

Though in its current state the price point for Shovel Knight is higher than most retraux indie titles, I cannot emphasize enough that it's worth every dollar. If you absolutely can't spare 25 dollars, Shovel Knight: Specter of Torment is available as a separate game for only 10.
This is a game that nails the concept of a game-defining central mechanic that has been polished to a mirror shine. The core gameplay of each character is a unique platforming mechanic that is intuitively integrated into each level, and while Shovel Knight is pretty challenging by default, I found that it was rarely, if ever, because I didn't understand what to do. Each campaign uses the same assets but remakes the levels almost ground-up around the abilities of the character, never leaving you feeling like you're playing a level designed for someone else.
Casual audience fear not: collecting everything you can and spending your hard-earned gold will give you more tools to use, allowing you to change up your gameplay or make the overall experience easier with multiple kinds of skips, emergency measures, and safety nets, but all of them are in your control as the player and you can wean yourself off of these tools at your own pace. For those who've beaten the game already and want more, harder content, there are a myriad of ways to challenge yourself, from playing again trying to collect every single hidden knickknack for that perfect save file, to a New Game+ with a formidable difficulty spike, to the ability to break checkpoints for money, to a series of challenge levels that you can play from the main menu.
A lot of the other odds and ends, particularly body swap, are mostly just extra bits that I think are nice. They don't add much value to the game, but I think being able to mess with the gender presentation and pronouns (independently, even) of pretty much every major character is amusing and while it doesn't mean a whole lot to me personally, it probably means a lot to someone.
On the subject of the characters: pretty well all of them, including many minor NPCs, are oozing with charm. The retraux graphical presentation may not be high resolution, but it's exceptionally smooth and colorful, and there are many characters, setpieces, and animations that just straight up look cool.
I got Shovel Knight early on - not by kickstarting it, but definitely before the addition of Plague of Shadows - so I may have paid less than its current asking price (unfortunately I just don't remember what it cost back then). The base game that I owned was easily worth 20 dollars if not more. Treasure Trove has solidly pushed it over the threshhold from being worthwhile to an uncommonly good value for a video game. Just get the thing already.

I know, this game was developed for over 10 years. The critics say horrible things about it. But I don't care! The single player story was really fun and varied. It's designed as a continuous adventure, like Half-Life 2 and other modern games (so it's not split into levels). It puts you in the heat of the action with many big guns. It has some puzzle-ish elements too (again comparing to HL2), so it's more than just shooting. Not boring, nicely varied. Examples include driving a monster truck or jumping from a burger to burger in a kitchen while being shrunk. People seem to complain the most about being able to carry only 2 weapons. First of all... they've already added an option to carry 4 weapons, you can find it in the menu. But the game is completly playable and fun keeping the limit set to just 2. You find a lot of guns as you play. Rather than carry it all, find a new one, replace your low ammo weapon. You'll get enough opportunities to fire them all.

The graphics are horrible. I never saw a game with worse graphics ever. It is like playing a game from 20 years ago. The lighting is ridiculous weird. In the most case, it is so dark that you cannot see anything. Once you initialized a scan or stand before a light/torch, it get so bright that you cannot see anything still. >.>
The optimization for rendering is bad too. I have to set all the detail to lowest with 1/2 resolution (Yes, I have to play the game in a window which sucks) to make it run at around 30 fps. At the same time, I can play Minecraft very smoothly so I assume it is this game's problem.
However, I really love factories-designing games. Although similar to factorio, this game is really creative in its own ways.   I really love how energy is transferred through lasers. I also love the concept of hoppers (which are similar to inserters in factorio though).
Also, I really love that you can go (almost) infinitely deep in this game. It really gives me a sense of being in a 3D world. factorio is 2D obviously. Although Minecraft is 3D, the height limit thing is just annoying. When you are playing Minecraft you can get to the bottom very quickly. It feels like being in a paper world.
Last but not least, I also love the "op-ness" of the main character. You basically get the ability to fly (even though really hard to control), infinite long reach, and very fast health regen from beginning. You also almost lose nothing when died. All these settings really let players get into the actual designing instead of worrying about getting to some where.
Anyways, although the graphics is extremely bad, I will really recommend this game.

I just can't go back to laying down one conveyer belt per click after playing Factorio.
*edit*
Turns out I was wrong!  And so were the YouTube videos I watched!  Steam Reviews works again!
Still have more time before the next Factorio patch, so will try again this week.  Would have been nice if the interface or in-game help had explained this after I had laid down the ore miner or looked up conveyer belts in the in-game help, but I understand many games are too busy being awesome to explain themselves.
*edit edit*
Well, previously this was a negative review.  This isn't wholely a positive review either, wish there was some more shades in the middle for Steam.  As I mentioned previously there are some teaching issues.  Mass-building/build-to-me really should be in more help files or hand-hold explained (not the rest, but something as core as that should be clearly laid out from the start, especially on any kind of not-hard-mode).  At the very least it should show up in the help files of commonly mass-built things like conveyer belts.  Additionally the quest/tutorial system that is trying to tell me generally what to try building next started useful but then got very seperated from my current progress, recommending things that I had already done/experimented with a long time ago at sometimes and then recommending things that are way past my tech level (or usefulness) at others.
Also, you don't normally expect a Nvidia 1080 with a i5-6500 CPU to hit framerate issues in games, but the center of my base where most of my conveyer belts meet causes noticible chug.  Some gameplay mechanics to encourage spreading out or optimizations would be useful.
I also prefer the inserter model from Factorio instead of the way hoppers and belts interact here (that may be due to me paying Factorio first, but I am fine with the different ways they do power).
But... building conveyer belts in 3d... digging and building elevator shafts... carting energy to deep mines and barely making it back to the surface before hypothermia sets in....  Very enjoyable in a similar but different way than Factorio.  (although similar to factorio, killing bugs is a bit meh, and the starting wasps have a longer range than the starting turrets, which is frustrating)
*edit edit edit*
Framerate issues fixed.  When the game starts up, the launcher was pre-set to "fantastic".  Downgrade that to "good" and the graphics quality does not noticibly go down, but the framerate improves around your core considerably.  Turns out the developers consider "good" the effective top-tier for their game.  That's fine, but was not expected and I didn't feel it was communicated that well compared to expectations for that kind of launcher.

The game was brilliant, I played the game for hours - with many more to come - almost everything in the game was perfect, the variety of weapons, the dlcs, even the hours you spend cramped up in a corner with your squad dead is fun; which leads you to ask - "Why did you rate it a thumbs down?" - unfortuantly, the AI in this game are... well - crap.
In the game their are different game difficulties, recruit being the easiest, and elite the hardest, but it only effects one thing; the reaction time of the enemy. The enemy in the game are *incredibley* overpowered, its like fight a level 100 Warrior in WoW with a level 50 Rogue - It is near impossible. Dont get me wrong, on some missions the AI is well balanced, but on some (Signal lost - This drove me insane, if your going to buy the game have fun <3) it was noticable on Signal lost and onwards, the enemy is described as 'Better trained, with better gear' you are supposed to kill these enemies with a pistol with 1 mag :/ .
I'll be honest - that wasnt the hard part, if you find some AI with their pants down, you often kill them, get their rifle and vest, but its when you have to go through a large town which is the near impossible part. The AI have aimbots (No literally - they actually have aimbots which usually lock onto you - then their is no escaping) they have X-Ray vision (You can be laying down on the top floor of a house making no noise, suddenly you hear "I'VE SPOTTED AN ENEMY!" then you are gunned down) They have eyes in the back of their heads (This is partially with the aimbot, but if your sneaking around behind them, doesnt matter how far really, if you are behind them within about 200 metres, they usually just *know* your there, then they turn around and let a spray of auto cut you into little pieces)
Those few things let the game down significantly, stealth is almost non-existent in the game, so your only hope on 'Signal lost' is to run, gun and pray you dont get bombarded by helicopters, a spray of 50. from boats, some guy with an automatic weapon 200m on a roof top south of you, or that you've actually killed the enemy (Yes, ammo in this mission is a major thing, it takes about 5 shots from the pistol to kill an enemy (So at the start, assuming you dont miss - you will miss a lot- will take out the two guys at the start. And once you get the rifle it takes 4 - bare in mind that they are semi's - the enemy *will* have automatic, aimbotting, spider sense weapons which will destroy you even if you are 500 metres away.
There is also no melee - so if you out of ammo - your ♥♥♥♥ed- have fun reloading as save and doing all that again!
Personal note to devs: I doubt you read these but for the love of god PLEASE revisit AI targeting, stealth and radars (I forgot to mention that once you fire a single bullet, every AI starts rushing towards you, I remember running up against 8 AI on one of my goes at this mission)

This brings back so many memories... The first actual pc games i played were Unreal Tournament 2003 and Unreal Tournament 2004. These two games got me into pc gaming, not just because of the gratuidous violence or the simple way the game is laid out to you, it was the fact that they have almost endless replay value. Yea, the graphics dont look as good as they did back then but they were never developed for the extreme high definition displays we use today, But they still look amazing, especially since even if you have a lower end gaming rig, you can still play it with graphics maxed out.
The fact that Steam only has UT2004 and not UT2003 is a big letdown especially since they are missing a few other Unreal games, but with the supply of mods (if you know where to look and find them) adds even more fun, i didnt know about modding when i first played, so with the user created content floating out around the web...it basicly creates a whole new experiance .
The Pro's
Low end rigs should have little trouble if most of the hardware is from the last few years (i even tested it on my old compaq laptop that hated running games and got 30-50 fps on medium to high settings)
Nearly unlimited replay value
Multiplayer is still up//LAN//Dedicated server/hosted(pay-to-host)/listen servers(you host as you play)
Tons of mod content ranging from skins, voice packs, maps, mutators, gamemodes and more.
Includes unreal editor in game files so you can create content
Custom Mappable Controls
Setting to toggle gore for people with weak stomachs or children
Plenty of weapons and vehicles for all the violent fun
Singleplayer
Voice Chat for those who know how to set it up
Power-ups granting damage bonuses, invisibility, and more
Play alone in instant action with bots and manipulate the ai difficulty ranging from a basic dummy ai that can get kills on you occasionally up to the God-Like ai that paints whatever is behind you with your blood (useful for practice)
So much more that cant even be described
The Con's
Often first time startup can be problematic with some higher resolution displays(simple fix by changing certain values in the games config, search google for fix)
Mod content can sometimes be hard to find due to some file servers permanently archiving files or hard to understand install instructions
Steam wont allow multiple instances of the game running (For example you open the game and set up a dedicated server, you cant open another instance of the game to play on your dedicated server unless you are smart enough to outsmart steam...hehe im not sharing my secrets..)
Some resolutions dont always scale just right when using an HDTV as a monitor (lots of trial and error finding a resolution you are comfortable with)
Overall Unreal Tournament 2004 gets a 9 out of 10

Negative:
-Had to rebind almost EVERY single key, because for some reason E = jump and SPACE = activate, as well as other horrible binds. Some important things aren't even bound to a key at all with default settings.
-Combat is not always very responsive. I will press the key to block.. he won't block. release the key, do it again, still wont block. Annnd now i'm dead because he wouldn't block.
-Drinking potions is not always very responsive. "drink a health potion... i'm telling you to drink a health potion.. i've spammed the key about 12 times now..." annnd now i'm dead because he woulnd't drink a potion.

Overall, I think this game is a rather significant downgrade from the first, which I enjoyed a great deal, but still a fun game.
First, the pros
+Fantastic lighting and particles, as well as enemy dismemberment.
+Weapons all feel pretty good to use, especially chainsaw (the camera can be a little wonky though)
+Mp seems like it could be a lot of fun, haven't tried it out yet.
+Some weapon upgrades are pretty cool, like the weapon modes and ammo types.
+Environments look great.
Cons:
-Some character models on npcs are absolutely horrible (especially the yakuza boss. That close up you get in her first encounter is quite frankly terrifying.) Enemies look good however.
-Voice acting for secondary characters sounds like it was done in the office by a dev. Akward pauses, flustered, rushed dialogue. Wang is still perfectly cheesy ofc.
-RPG system is more annoying than anything. Swarms of +x% items swamp your inventory, adding a significant amount of tedium to the game.
-Sidequests are more often than not incredibly boring. Go to x, get key, kill boss, done, with the same enemies as in the main level. The "boss" is usually just a bigger version of regular enemies.
-Some levels are literally copy pasted. The third scroll quest is literally just a smaller segment from kamika's aparment quest.
-This may seem small to some, but I think it is really important; the characters are so much less endearing. The jokes, instead of being (usually) cleverly asinine like in the first, have forsaken any cleverness whatsoever. Kamika is a poor replacement for Hoji imo.
-The game feels much less polished, and has a lot of filler. Big, empty levels, instead of the tightly designed ones from SW2013. A lot of enemies, while visually different, are functionally identical.
-none of the beatiful handrawn cutcesnes from SW13.
-Melee combat feels a lot spammier. No heavy attacks, shurikens, blocking is useless
-A lot of weapons, but a lot are functionally identical. Some fun exceptions.
-No point system, which encouraged flashy, stylized combat.
-Level design is weak. Hunting for secrets is tedious on such large levels, encouraging you to run through them as quickly as possible.
-Enemies are too tanky and deal too little damage. Instead of fast combat, this just results in a grind fest of dodging and spamming until everything dies.
-Chi system is pretty awful, at least when it comes to healing. Instead of healing you to 65% health, it can heal you to full, making health management a vanity.
-Large level designs make kiting, instead of arena combat, the best option on harder difficulties.
-Enemies dont feel like a challenge, just a health grind. Bad AI, massive health pools/resistances on tougher enemies.
Overall, I was very disappointed with this game. It threw away the formula that made SW13 so great for me; Almost uninterrupted, satisfying combat with a focus on the theatrical.
Instead of this, the game was padded it out with generic rpg mechanics, vast amounts of downtime, and generally watered down from the original reboot.
For some unfathomable reason, the devs decided to copy all the weak parts of borderlands: grindy side quests, an overwhelming amount of tedious percentages, oversized and boring levels, and bullet spongey combat.
For once, Mr. Wang, bigger does not mean better.
tldr; Go play the first game, it's a lot better than this one.
PS: I haven't actually mustered the will to grind through the rest of the game, will update this review when I do. Doubt much will changer here.

Having played the Total War series since the original Shogun, including the newer installments, Rome: Total War still stands as the one I believe is best.
The graphics are certainly a bit dated, but even then they aren't horrible. The gameplay however is where this game really stood apart. The factions felt much more significant than a lot of the other games, while also not feeling TOO different, so it feels like you're fighting on equal terms more or less. Got a choice of quite a lot of factions, but the map itself isn't overloaded with different forces, and you're able to play all of them yourself once unlocking them, something they stopped allowing in later installments.
Then one thing that I really like in this game, which I believe only showed up in Rome and Medieval 2 is the idea that your Captains (the leader of armies without Generals) can actually be adopted into your family and made a full on General for their accomplishments. Such a nice feature, as if you have an army going around and doing really well, that Captain deserves recognition. In general I liked the family tree system as well. Medieval 2 had a lot of this, but I felt got too bogged down by the religion system, whereas Rome has no such drawbacks to me.
Overall I'd rate this game very highly, especially if you enjoy the Total War series.

I'd put this game at 4 out of 5 stars, and I consider myself a fairly harsh reviewer.  The thing you're paying for in this game is a deadly opponent that will match you in actual strategy.
The main selling point of this game from the standpoint of a war strategy veteran is the competency of the opponent AI.  The computer opponent has 9 different behaviors to choose from that act as difficulties.  This is in stark contrast to the strategy game norm where your "difficulty" options are based on enemy statsitic buffs to give it an edge over the player.  Your UGG opponent gets smarter, it doesn't become a sharp shooting bullet sponge.
The AI regularly does a tactical retreat into kill zones, provides screening fire for its units as it tries to out-flank you, and uses your line-of-sight restrictions to move troops about behind hills to hit you from weakpoints on the final two AI behaviors.  It is a master of defense and a ruthless attacker.
The battlefield is nicely detailed and you'll gain a familiarity with the Gettysburg area that you didn't previously have.  Places like Cemetery Hill and the Round Tops will take on a new life as you progress through the stages of the battle and find yourself forumlating strategies to take some of the most famous defensive holdouts of the Civil War.
The single battlefield complaint is entirely valid, and I believe that's the one thing that stops this game from being a 5 star piece of art.  I can see how the limited area is good for the AI's ability and how it could become increasingly difficult to add in more battlefields and get the AI behaving well on all of them.  While you're always fighting on the same battlefield I would also argue that you aren't always fighting the same battle.
I find that I got my money's worth a long time ago, but I still keep coming back to this game.  It's really light on micromanagement and focuses on grand strategy.  The controls are super easy and your units are fairly intelligent at doing things on their own- it is really easy to take long breaks from it and come back.  Recent updates to the game have made Confederate victory in this game very difficult to achieve on the last three difficulties (still haven't done it after 96 hours) and I find that I like having it around as an "ultimate challenge".  This is probably not a game you'll sink 1000 hours into, but I feel like the price point is more than fair.

This game is in the Ultimate General series of historical and strategical games. You play the civil war in the US as either the Union or the Confederate. It's very well executed, the maps are very large and there's tons of them, they all look unique and have multiple strategies. Some maps are based on woodlands (giving off cover), some are basically next to a town (giving off tons of cover but makes battles a lot slower, also slows movement speeds), some are a mix of two etc. In my time of playing, I did find that the Union was superior to the Confederate units as they can eliminate even Pettigrew squads (2K Confederate units) when outnumbered as they (seem) to reload faster, have way better and more accurate weaponry and artillery and don't flee as often because of this, so you can actually hold your ground longer than the "hardened war veterans". It's just really unfair and doesn't help make the game fun at all. It's just such a chore to watch everyone die off to the Union playing as the Confederate. Another thing that needs improving is the reloading mechanic. Sometimes artillery just refuses to reload, in which case they are just there, not doing anything but being targeted by enemies. So basically: combat needs work.
Despite the flaws, it's still actually pretty fun. Strategies do have a big effect on the outcome of a battle, such as flanking. Other things as a full frontal assault is, well, it doesn't have the largest effect for a strategy. The exchange of unit speed for cover is also very interesting, it doesn't have that much effect on how much slower units will die, so again, I just think it's a number that is there, but nothing is being executed. In the overview I said that the maps are very large, which they are, but the units just take forever to navigate even just a small distance, which gets even worse during forest map matches.  You will be surprised how much an effect this has. Heck, even while setting the units to run, they do take quite some time to reach the end goal. This makes me not want to use even a flank as it's just going to take up so long of the battle time to set up. Artillery needs an improvement in terms of movement as well, they will often refuse to lock onto an enemy squad for no apparent reason. They're in range and they're already spotted. Until, of course, it's too late and the brigade is now just debris. The movement planner is helpful to find where every unit will try to move, however. Especially when trying to encircle the enemy. You will not need to check every unit seperately as the movement arrows are always on screen.
As solid as a 2cm sheet of plastic. It's alright enough to be used for many things. But it can certainly be improved. I may have a stack of 1K Union units attacking a single 1K stack only kill, lets say, 200 enemies every reload turn. This makes very little sense as 80% of my units have the aim of a potato. I'd understand 450 units every reload turn, as then it's more realistic I suppose, but this is the main reason why battles can even take up to an hour and some minutes. The main feature of the game should be more solid than what it currently is.
Pros:
Pretty fun
Large scale battles
Large maps
Very detailed
Pretty graphics
The UI doesn't get in the way
Cons:
Combat and Movement need work

If you like Factorio or Minecraft with tech mods, you must buy this.
If you don't know what I'm talking about, but you like Automation, Logistics, Production, Multi-tasking or games that can actually feel alien, hard or challeging, then you should try it out.
Although the 'FortressCraft' name may make it seem like another one of the infinite Minecraft clones and knock-offs, the only thing it shares with Minecraft is the voxel-based world. A bunch of other things can resemble modded Minecraft, however, it's still unique and easily stands on its own.
FCE is all about exploring and finding resources, and getting machines to exploit those resources for you. Instead of spending most of your time manually digging and mining, you'll spend your time actually thinking, planning and implementing solutions of all kinds, expanding your base and coming up with cool machine designs and setups to do boring work for you while you run around using your time where it really matters.
I've first played FCE years ago, and now that I came back to it, it's much different. There's a lot of improvements, from visual, to technical and gameplay improvements, which really makes it all an even more solid experience.
If there's one thing I would complain about FCE (and how it changed), is that some things take insane amount of resources to craft. Indoubtly those were (re-)balancing attempts, but I'd prefer more sensible requirements.
I'm still barely on the mid-game, though, so I can't give a proper, full review on its balancing and wether such high requirements make sense.
To be really concise, FCE is not for everyone. So I do recommend you check videos out if you can.
It can be time consuming and it will make you think about solutions and designs when you're away from the game. It might make you draw setups in notebooks. It might make you want to stick solar panels wherever you can.
The developer, after all those years, still works on the game. Which is why I'll be buying the DLCs soon - it's really admirable to see someone working on something for so long after it's release, without it being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t features or updates.
There's something satisfying about striking the earth, exploiting an alien planet's resources, and using said resouces to murder the innocent creatures that lived there before you.
Become an Evolved FortressCrafter today.
PS: I should mention: This game has the most cool, fun and satisfying "grappling hook" I've ever seen in a videogame yet.

An excellent homage to classic platforming games of previous generations. Well designed levels and mostly frustration-free experience that has plenty of challenge for fans of the genre. With great pixel art and one of the best 8-bit soundtracks, this game is packed with quality and charm. Every character/boss in the game is unique and memorable as well as a lot of fun to fight against.
The game isn't perfect though, as I find the instant death spikes and pitfalls a bit annoying at times, especially due to the large kickback you receive when touching enemies. Luckily there are infinite lives in this game so you don't have to worry about replaying a whole level over and over again. When you die you drop some gold, which is a nice idea but unfortunately wasn't well executed. Most of the deaths in this game are going to be from spikes or pitfalls, and many times the gold you drop is stuck in a wall or far below a reachable place above a pitfall, so you cannot always retrieve your fallen gold. This isn't too big a deal though considering the game gives out gold like crazy and I always found myself buying everything about 60% into a playthrough.
Overall one of the best platformers ever made. Takes all of the best aspects of classic platforms, removes some of the hassles (although not all) and dishes out some great levels and tunes in the process.

, because you only have one CPH. The good

- the magic system
The bad
- the game setup / activation
- getting online with friends

In depth
graphics : actually pleasantly surprised, probably the main reason i carried on playing for as long as i did.
optimisation : with graphics as nice as this i was expecting to have to put in ultra crappy quality to play on my macbook 13’ 2012 but it actually runs fairly well.
the magic system : definitely the strong point of the game for me with a really interesting use of cards to create new spells. you basically have 2 main cards, one which will give the basic action on the spell (if it’s zoned, blast, aura…) and an element card (fire, water…). you then have 8 modifier cards than will modify the main effect of the spell. the most interesting being on the aura or zoned spells. you can make anvils fall out of nowhere and then create a tornado around you picking up the anvils and giving you this badass shield of anvils that spins around you. for each spell you can then add a whole new secondary or third effect where you can do everything i just said all over again. so for example a homing fireball than the creates an electrical zone around the enemy.
the game setup : as everyone on here has said, the game setup is ridiculous asking you for a ton of personal info before you can even start playing the game.
getting online with friends : after convincing a couple friends to buy as it was on sale, i was eager to try out the online mode which seemed to be more fun than the solo campaign. you start off by choosing a class such as two armed combat, fire mage, ranger…etc which will already have a few skill points in a selected skill tree, which makes in more fun when playing a mage but when playing a close combat close it means you basically have every skill you need from the start of the game, i fail to see how your character can evolve much throughout the game.
the dialogue : omg, seriously? and if this isn’t bad the french voiceovers are even worse.
the quests : thingy want’s you to get something from thingy 2, but before thingy 2 will give you what you want, he want’s you to help him by getting something he needs from thingy 3… etc etc. i can’t even remember what the main quest is any more, plus the fact the each npc talks with these terrible voiceovers for 5 minutes each time you go see him i’ll bet you’ll be skipping what they have to say after the first 10 minutes of playing. i ended up skipping everything then just looking at where i had to go on the map.
combat : fights in the main story are tedious to say the least. you’ll find yourself repeating the same actions over and over because you haven’t got enough money to buy a new spell book, at lvl 10 i still haven’t even got half the money i need to buy a new action. another thing is some enemies will have auras around them that does damage when you get too close. if you have chosen to fight with close combat weapons you will die every time forcing you to use a bow or magic, seeing as you haven’t put any points into these in your skill tree it will take you forever just to kill one of these damn creatures.
Conclusion
I wanted to like this game i really did, being on mac and not being able to play skyrim this looked like a good alternative but hell i was wrong. if i could’ve got multiplayer working with friends then i think a would of at least of got some fun out of it even without it being anything very special but as it is i wouldn’t recommend getting this even on sale. i now have to find a way to refund two friends after i convinced them to buy this crappy game.

When I first booted up this game (as someone who enjoyed Darthmod for Empire Total War, a mod whose lead designer now works for Game-Labs), I was confused and mildly annoyed: units seemed unwieldy and inflexible; playing as the Union I was unable to conduct the fighting retreat the first scenario demanded; the UI and controls didn't quite allow me the flexibility and fine control I wanted; Confederate troops seemed too numerous and nigh-invincible on the charge.
As I stuck it out, though, some of the nuance crept in, and now I find myself heartily recommending this game. It is, as you might expect, similar to the Total War series, but it's different in several ways: for one, units will not, as in Total War, act as clockwork automatons until their moral breaks and then flee the field completely. Instead, infantry brigades advance, waver in the face of overwhelming fire, break, and then reform out of the line of enemy fire. Permanently defeating an enemy unit is unlikely, but doable if you have massive local superiority. Control of formation and frontage isn't as fine-grained as in Total War, but it's also less relevant, and skew-whiff lines are usually the result of sprites moving into or staying in terrain that provides cover, which is usually a good thing. Cavalry is almost nonexistent, but that is, as I understand, a function of the ACW setting, rather than a design oversight.
There are a number of scenarios available, many of which can be played in order through the main battle - the game's version of a campaign, which requires you to general one of the two sides throughout the three (or four, if things change from history) days of the Battle of Gettysburg. This requires you to keep an eye on the future and preserve your units, even at the cost of ground - sure, you can sustain 50% casualties to your elite brigade on the first day fighting for Oak Hill, but by day 3 you're going to feel the lack of quality troops. The custom battle functionality lets you select individual scenarios and play those out without worrying about future engagements, and there's a number of interesting and challenging ones available. I can't speak to the quality of the multiplayer as I haven't tried it.
There are some issues, though: for one, the tutorials and online guide, while okay, aren't quite as detailed or useful as I'd like, leaving the player to work certain things out through frustrating trial and error - like what those stars by unit commander's portraits mean, or what general units are really for. The default map-view, while pretty, isn't very readable and really should have the optional contour lines enabled by default. It's often difficult to read which ground overlooks which, and whether what looks like a small rise is actually dead ground overlooked by nearby terrain, even with the contours enabled. Similarly, the line-of-sight system works well (when a unit is selected, areas where it cannot see are darkened), but isn't adequately explained and is a little too subtle at the default settings. These sound like minor issues, but in a game where good placement of artillery is crucial, they can be serious problems.
The rest of the UI is decent, albeit a little bland - again, a little more explanation of what each gauge represents and what effect that will have on your units would be nice. Similarly, there are some confusing UI choices regarding General units - selecting a general will highlight all the units recieving a buff from the general's presence, which is fine. What's not fine is that this highlight looks exactly the same as the selection indicator, leading to early circumstances where I wasn't sure if moving my general would move all those units out of position.
Further, the controls, while an interesting setup, have some issues in the PC version. There's no selection box, and while the draw-around-the-units-you-want system is cool (and must work well on tablets), it feels a little counterintuitive, although it does allow some nice fine selection of units. It's not particularly easy to quickly deselect units in the heat of the moment, leading to me ordering my brigades to march in a circle while attempting to select more units. The drag-the-unit-across-the-map method of unit movement is very, very cool and I like it a lot, but I'd also like a more normal right-click to be implemented alongside it. This would also make the use of the game's rare cavalry units a lot more intuitive, since using them to attack isolated artillery units requires a lot of move orders that cross the artillery's position, rather than a less micro-intensive charge order, which doesn't quite seem to work with cavalry.
The only real gameplay complaint I have is the balanced AI's tendency to make a bunch of aggressive moves just as the battle timer runs out, thus seizing more time for itself to put your ragged forces under pressure. That might just be a failure of my generalship for showing it weakness, though.
If it sounds like I'm harshing on the UI, that's because it's really the only thing in this game I have a problem with. Other than those issues, Ultimate General: Gettysburg is a near-perfect strategy experience. Not huge in scope, but perfectly executed, with a nice visual style and deep, complex gameplay that's tunable to the level of difficulty you want. I'm planning to check out Game-Labs' Naval Action at some point, but mostly I'm waiting eagerly for the next game in this series (and hoping for a French Revolutionary/Napoleonic setting).

When the most annoying element of a game manifests itself within the first few minutes, it colours your perception. So when I found I was issued with only 30 rounds of ammo for my Thompson SMG, I readily picked up an MP40 from a fallen soldier—with 7 rounds in it. That same machine gun had been emptying magazines into me for a few minutes like his fellow guns.
I was concerned. Would they make this an ammo restricted game to force me into a particular playstyle? As opposed to clever (or poor) level design? Indeed so!
All enemy soldiers seemed to carry only 2-13 rounds of ammunition for their primary (only) weapon, except when firing at you; where mother nature appears to provide them with ample rounds. Sure, your sniper rifle and innacurate silenced pistol have rounds aplenty, but close in fighting chews through ammo like blazes (because SMGs are also wildly innacurate in this game).
Also, in sniper v sniper situations. They seem to know where you are at any point in in cover. No point in sneaking around to a different point (they do on occasion) they will immediately snap shoot you—with only your amazing health to allow you to absorb the first round and get off a quick shot.
Sniper Elite V2 is not as 'intelligent' as say ARMA2 and is essentially a tunnel shooter. Have fun but don't expect any actual realism in a firefight: except with the sniper rifle balistics (although they might overplay the effects of wind—they don't give any external cues for direction), and the interspersing of the very clever internal anatomy scenes of bullet penetration. Pick up when cheap.

I really wish I could recommend this game, I really really do but I can not agree with the direction the developer is going.   I have had this game since the early days of early access, I've had fun playing it but it's never been "finished" and time after  time I have to set it aside before picking it back up due to ground breaking bugs. Scroll to the bottom for the TLDR;
I've had worlds corrupted on me, ones that have had hours worth of work put into them
I've had major work lost due to sudden crashes
Several updates have causes existing worlds to no longer be loadable
Granted all of these are while it was in Early Access, frustrating but can be expected from a game in development (hence putting it aside and trying it again later)
Well it's been out of Early Access for a while now so I thought I would give it another go around, unfortunately there are still issues that while not "game breaking" are 'game breaking'.
I have a HTC vive and the game starts up in VR mode every time, unfortunately VR mode isn't useable as the game won't load pass the world creation "into", even while loading the resolution is lowered to the point that it's not even playable.  That's fine, I can play it 2D except:
There is no way to force it not to start Steam VR
When it starts Steam VR it doesn't start it properly causing Steam VR to error out until restarted
I have to catch the right time in the loading screen to hit space to switch over to 2D mode
Then there the other issues with the game:
Still crashes occasionally
When you exit the game it doesn't quit, steam thinks it's still running and won't let you restart until you quit steam and reopen steam (not just the game)
There are still issues with block placement and Orientation and getting everything to align correctly
I understand that the developer needs income to continue development, and I'm good with the fact that additional content is coming in the form of DLC but am rather on the fence with the patreon content.... There is something to be said for the privilege of getting early access to something, but some of those items are in my opinion "Core" items, that should be part of the base game (Mutators, since mods break achievements) as well as the fact that the "base" game isn't finished and is still buggy.  It comes across that new content is being developed to bring in income, bugs are being fixed while new content is being made but of course new content takes times and effort (which in turn slows down bug fixing), it leaves a bad impression on me that new content is being made to bring in income before the base game is even  finished.   The fact that the content is good and useful is conflicting, I want to support the game and the developer but at the same time I won't be buying DLC for a game that still doesn't function properly.
TLDR version;
I really want to like and recommend this game but I can't, it's still isn't complete and New content is being released before bugs are fixed in the base game.

My orginal review:
This game has potential, yes, potential. It's an evil word that is thrown about and often the ones who spring forty dollars on a game are quick to adopt it.
It's fun to play, for sure, especially when there are more people working in sync to alleviate the artificial wait times. The wait times are a mix of a blessing and a curse, they give the feeling of accomplishment when you are finally able to see your hard work pay off, but this is all a ruse when you realize that there isn't really an end to a means since the endgame comes down to pvp which is still a work in progress and from my experience a long ways from being substantial. (I.E. Horses and almost all the weapon skills are not implemented.)
The real reason I am NOT recommending this game is the lack of updates. YES I KNOW THIS IS EARLY ACCESS. They have been working on this game for over THREE YEARS before it got greenlit, Do yourself a favor and research it yourself, their PR will gladly say that they are working diligently on the game, but the fact is there hasn't been any substatial updates for years. That is not a good track record, especially concerning the core mechanics of the game which are not even implemented.
PROS
-Combat is not like Mount and Blade
-Crafting system is detailed and involving
-Fun to work with others towards a common goal
-Open charachter development
-Open world development
CONS
-Combat is not like Mount and Blade (Yes, it's a pro and a con)
-Artificial wait times
-The graphics are pretty horrible (Think Asheron's Call with some realistic photo textures for SOME things, ick)
-Many have problems getting it to load and be stable
-A lot of strange lag and bugs
-It's over 3 years old and still early access
-Lack of end game content
-Not much freedom when constructing things (Prefab building, etc)
I suggest you read over their official website, especially concerning their progress before you purchase, I also recommend researching other games that are close in genre and half as expensive.

It has issues running on Windows 10 at the moment.
To fix the problem do the following (as originally commented by Steam user "tacobob", but I can confirm, this DOES fix the issue)
Go to
C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Unreal Tournament 2004\System
and look for and open UT2004.ini
Find the section with the below entries:
[Engine.Engine]
RenderDevice=D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice
;RenderDevice=D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice
;RenderDevice=Engine.NullRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=PixoDrv.PixoRenderDevice
Replace the "D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice" on the first line with "OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice" (without quotes)
It'll look like this:
[Engine.Engine]
RenderDevice=OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice
;RenderDevice=Engine.NullRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=PixoDrv.PixoRenderDevice
