310 Hours played, a dozen or so servers.  PVP, PVE, Raiding, etc.
- $40 is very expensive for a early access game.
- Definitely got $40 worth of fun out of LiF
- Right now the amount of fun you will have is heavily dependent on the server you are on.
- There are servers with  house-rules and servers without rules.
- The skill progression of the game is completely different for each server as well as several very important factors, all tweaked by that specific server's admin to test those settings.
- You need to find a server that will play at the speed you want to play, with the amount of people you want to play with, with the rules want to abide by.
- The PVP is not broken although you will find swinging with a wooden shovel is not very effective when compared to a claymore and the hitboxes are a little iffy.
- There are currently some serious bottlenecks with how much you can do to a server before it starts to get bogged down.  Cutting down trees and leaving stumps, excessive mining and building are no nos
- Remember this game is an Alpha, and as much as you want daily updates with groundbreaking new material you are basically signing up for a testing job
- All this being said, actually creating stone walls, metal tools, suits of armor, etc from nothing but what you find and build is incredibly satisfying.  To go from a naked guy with a handfull of cookies to the proud owner of "The Vault", a walled in farm, and the highest quality producing iron mine on the server (all while being constantly harassed by raiders) provides a sense of achievment i've not found in many other games.
- Soloing this game is tough but i find just one or two other people is all you need on any server with a skill cap of 1000 or above.  Large groups are very fun to play with but some people are picky about which job they want to do.
- I wont be like the rest of the reviewers and pretend to know whats going on behind the scenes with the devs but as far as my experience goes they have been great, Bobik personall replied to a question i had.  LiF sees an update every week or two.
I heavily reccomend this game, but at the price its at its tough to say go and buy it.  If you are into games with steep learning curves, coop gameplay, building/mining games, sword slashing, or just plain living Feudal, go for it!

Firstly - take the recommended/not recommended ratio with a pinch of salt. Lots of people are complaining because the game asks you for personal information. That's not really a reason not to recommend a game, and personally I just put in a load of made up gobbledegook and it didn't even care.
So, why don't I recommend this game?
Well, I love open world games and RPGs but, frankly, this game is meh. Not
as such, just meh.
The combat is meh.
The characters are meh.
The story is meh.
The adventuring is meh.
The online stuff is meh.
Even the alchemy and crafting stuff is meh.
Despite being a huge leap from the original Two Worlds (*shudder*), Two Worlds II still has it's sloppy moments - one example is that hit boxes are poorly framed. You can stand directly behind a bear and it'll somehow be able to hit you with a paw swipe while facing the wrong way. If you've got a shield and try to block the bear's magical paw attack, your character will still use the sword blocking animation, as though he's forgotten about the massive bit of wood strapped to his arm. Simply put, there's some lazy 'that'll do' style programming in aspects of this game.
Which takes me onto the combat 'meh'. Yeah, you've got good variety and generally it
, but for the most part it's a clunky affair and a lot of enemies can be overcome by running around them in a tight circle and randomly slashing. Ranged combat doesn't really work at all unless you let the computer auto-target for you which is a bit *yawn*.
And that's if you can even find much worth fighting between all the trapsing around you do. Two Worlds II does look nice, but nice enough that I want to run down a path for five minutes just to fight
pack of wolves. Add to this that making money is ridiculously easy and, well, why would you even bother?
Again, it's not that this is a
game. It really, really isn't. It's just, well, what's the point in buying it? It doesn't surpass any recent title in the Elder Scrolls or Fallout series. Kingdoms of Amalur is superior to Two Worlds every way, Witcher 2 has more solid combat, characters and story telling... hell, even if (like me) you're not a massive fan of MMOs, you'll still get a similar, but better, gaming experience from WoW, Neverwinter, Elder Scrolls Online or Diablo 3, just to name a few.
If those other games didn't exist, then sure, I'd be drooling all over Two Worlds II. As is, in the open world RPG genre these days, you need to go big or go home. Unfortunately, Two Worlds II just isn't up to scratch compared to these other titles, so while it isn't a bad game, I also wouldn't recommend it when you could just as easily get a far better one that does the same sorta thing.

Fortresscraft Evolved is similar to the major tech mods for FeedTheBeast, with an emphasis on defending your factory from waves of enemies.  The graphics in FCE are good, but you can still play with an older PC - I'm using a GTX 650 and it's fine on medium settings.  There are many features that make it easy to build large structures - cosmetic and functional.  The Frozen Factory DLC is highly recommended - it adds a significant amount of content to the game.
The difficulty settings focus mostly on "how much time do you want to grind away", so if you are a busy person, you can still enjoy the full content of the game without "grinding."  The game is more about building, planning, and some exploration - it's not as action-oriented as FTB.  In fact, the monsters mostly ignore you in FCE - the monsters are all trying to attack the center of your factory.
Summary:   If you enjoy tech mods for minecraft, check out Fortresscraft Evolved.

The graphics are ok but that's about it.  Little attention paid to realities of actual civil war combat so the battle simulation is terrible.  They decided to use brigades instead of regiments as the basic tactical formation with no options to alter the basic formation.  The AI units inflict disporportionate casualties on a player and it takes over 75% casualties to cause an AI unit to break.  Fought one scenario where the Texas brigade started with 1700 and was down to 300 before it broke.  Player units break after 10% casualties.  AI artillery is too good and the player artillery is useless, choosing its own targets despite orders.  The ranges on the various munitions make no sense, shells which are only fired from rifle cannon have a much longer range than the game suggests and canister is not outranged by infantry fire.  The AI units frequently fire from out of range positions and the cannon are able to fire indirectly over obstructions from masked positions the player can't see.  This game will not help anybody understand the battle of Gettysburg, test battle alternatives, or grasp the reality of Civil War combat.  I don't recommend this game.

I don't usually write reviews, but after buying this game and looking at all the negative reviews, I thought I'd better step in and tell my point of view, to let the developers know, that there are still people out there who believes in this game.
When I first thought about buying Fernbus, I thought about it for a long time, mainly because of all the negative reviews, but I still went ahead and bought it anyway because it looked fine to me in YouTube videos and so on. And now with a few hours of gameplay I must say I don't see ANY obvious bad things. Yes, there is the AI that can be a pain sometimes but it is mainly in the cities, yes there is a bit of freezing but it's VERY RARE for me, and only when it's loading a new part of the map, and also the freezing lasts no longer than 1-2 seconds and you're off again. How can that be a problem for someone?
The things I like about Fernbus is that it has a huge map to explore, and the traffic makes it even bigger, as you constantly have to keep your eyes open because they've tried to simulate the real world traffic by having traffic perform lane changes in the middle of everything, overtake on the right on the highway, police pulling someone over etc.
I also like the fact that they've focused so much on that YOU are the bus driver and YOU have to do things, you have the responsibility of transporting a group of passengers from one place to another, and you therefore have to count them, check their tickets, make sure they're comfortable with the temperature and wifi connection, open the doors for them etc.  and I think many people may have forgotten that.. they've forgotten that they're the bus driver this time, and not the demanding passenger in the back or the backseat driver.
I've made a list below of things that still needs some attention but i'm sure the developers are working on. Check it out and see if you would be able to live with it or not, which I am sure you would.
- Timeplan still needs some work. Sometimes it puts the ETA too long.
- AI spawns in close to you, but far enough away so you don't have to brake or crash into them.
- Other FlixBus busses drive too fast into construction areas on the highway causing them to crash.
- The bus kind of jumps a bit forward when you press the throttle after a stop.
- AI waits a little too long before driving after the AI in front has started moving.
As you can see, those are MINOR THINGS.... and it doesn't make the game crash or anything, I haven't even experienced a game crash as of yet.
If you like Euro Truck Simulator or American Truck Simulator as well as OMSI Bus Simulator, you will also like this game, and the good thing is, it is still getting developed and I believe a game like this has unlimited amount of things that can be added to it.
Thank you for reading my review and have fun playing.

I have been a long time fan of the Duke Nukem series and I enjoyed this game like any other first person experience. I will say I have a few complaints myself but I enjoyed the game overall. I am glad to see that the game did not receive a large number of DLC to seem like it was a money pit. I thought that the Doctor Who Cloned Me to be rather fitting for the game and it was worth the price I got it for. Okay, back to the base game. The UI and AI are fully functional and it provides a challenge but definitely possible. The level design is fairly linear but sometimes allows other approach options and the environment in each level is finely made into a very believable scenario. The control and overall functionality of the game is solid as well as sticking to realistic arsenal choice. Allowing you to carry only two weapons or four if you allow it in the options, you are deciding what weapon is best for each encounter or just to fit your preference. Also, the EGO system makes it similar to Halo's shield system or anything like it. I like that they decided to do something different but I think the old formula of medkits and armor is sufficient. Also, the arsenal is not to far from your arsenal in Duke Nukem 3D but that is not bad. The weapons that are new are the Expander and the Impregnator Gun. Also, the Freeze Ray can't shoot projectiles but only a continuous beam that recharges. Then the Shrink Ray is not a weapon but a story component that changes the combat somewhat since you will be very small. Well, to conclude, I thought this game was a success and I found it very enjoyable and well thought out. Even though it took practically forever to release, the game was good, I would recommend this game to any that wish to play another entry in the series or first person shooter fans.

TL;DR for each game under their review and a sum of TL;DR at the bottom. Be aware that my ratings attempt to be as accurate and fair as possible and have some worth to them, thus, why none of the games are 11/10, even though in the usual rating they deserve to be.
This game is incredible. The amount of joy and entertainment I had playing this(and rage) cannot be fit into words. Shovel Knight is a masterfully made game made by intelligent people. Although I have an extreme hatred for the Plague Knight stage, every other stage is articularly made and have sly inspirations to past Retro games. This  is a love letter not just to Retro games or people who grew up in the Atari/NES/SNES age, but to gamers in general. It's a work of art and an incredible one at that. This doesn't focus on trying to cheat you by cramming as much content as possible, it does the opposite.
The first Shovel Knight game is an incredible ornament of inspiration and originality. The game doesn't just pull assets from old 8-bit games, but every asset is original, even including the sound. The first level made the absolutely best impression and set forth a whole realm of possibilities simply from its breathtakingly perfect design. Never have I felt a game so fresh like this in a long while simply from the first area. Even if I absolutely hated the Explodatorium and the
in every way, every other area of every other stage made up for it. Each area is brimming with both inspiration and originality, showing true skill and artistic love put into each area. It may not be the best game for those who don't enjoy platforming, but it more than makes up for it. The story may be a little generic, but it still touches you and does it best. The characters are likeable, if not absolutely loveable, including the villains. The game itself is incredibly difficult in later stages, but in no way does it make you want to quit. It makes you challenge yourself to rise above the challenge and to defeat the obstacles in your way to victory, the music, the atmosphere and even the characters cheering you on! The Soundtrack is beyond anything I could have expected and I honestly listen to it constantly out of Steam. It's that good. There's even a twist in the second-to-last area that I will not spoil...
A sure buy all on its own. Everyone needs to buy this gam-- no, this
A beautiful, breathtaking game that is as close to as perfect as a retro game can get. Elements of platformers, metroidavania and the like make it not just an instant classic, but a legend.
8.8/10, an incredible, breath taking experience with very few kinks. Everyone should have this experience, even if they're not a gamer.
This wonderful game has received many mixed reviews. Many people hated the ways the character Plague Knight moves, many people enjoyed it. I for one greatly enjoyed it. Plague Knight may have identical stages as Shovel Knight, but with secrets that lead to heavily modified parts of the stages. The game in itself is tweaked where Plague Knight's abilities are much better put to use. Everything good in Shovel Knight with a few cons, but it is definitely still a buy. It's very hard to put this game into words, however. On one hand, it is the same stages and bosses as Shovel Knight(save for a couple,) but it feels like an entirely new experience. Plague Knight plays so differently to Shovel Knight and the tweaks feel so different from the original game that it feels like a completely new game. The abilities of Plague Knight vary in more ways than one from Shovel Knight. Multiple combinations of bombs and abilities to fit every situation. Not to say that the game isn't difficult, it's still very difficult like its predecessor, but not to the point of the player wanting to rage quit. The Story is also very enjoyable. Plague Knight's personality with his companion Mona is extrordinarily likeable as he's on the quest for the ultimate potion!
It's breathtaking, to say the least. I may even love it as much as the original game!
A different character with the same stages, but what feels like a completely different adventure. The story is fun, quirky and at times relateable. So many things to discover and even a little edgy for those in to that sort of thing!
8.7/10 A ridiculously fun game with the same stages but completely different feel of its predecessor.
I will say that the first stage gave off a horrible impression. It was lackluster and even annoying and felt very uninspired, like a run-of-the-mill Steam greenlight Metroidvania game. However, after getting past the first stage, the capabilities finally shun through the craggy, even unlikable surface. Specter of Torment is an edgier, darker prequel to the first two legendary games. Its mechanics are not for the newcomer and is meant for those who have already played the first two games. Specter of Torment requires precision, fast thinking and for you to control your reflexes. It definitely has a lot of great moments, but the beginning can be rather... boring, at the least. Once you get into the later parts of the game, it becomes a wonderful adventure with unique new abilities and fresh stages that show that the developers are still working hard to bring quality content! As stated, the middle and ending parts are the strongest parts of the game, with new stages based off of the original game, with the same bosses that have some rather... new tricks up their sleeves. The game is defeinitely worth the buy if it's by itself, but it's a sin to miss this game with the rest. The story is a little generic, albeit heart wrenching once the story of Specter Knight comes to light. The "Order of No Quarter" origin story is definitely pretty cool and how each of them came to become united. The Ending is where everything comes together, however. The Ending alone is what makes the experience well worth the beginning and everything you may or may not enjoy.
A bland beginning, a wonderful middle and end. Worthy of the name Shovel Knight but still has its kinks to work out. Heart wrenching story with the usual charm of the Shovel Knight series.

There is a demand for hardcore sandbox action in this environment and as an MMO it can be profitable for decades, just look at the EVE:Online model that has thrived even with internet spaceships which turns alot of hardcore RPG'rs off. This old game has been around, it has survived all the newer Total war games and in my opinion it is one of the finest games that was ever created by the Creative Assembly studio, it is one of those games that has survived the "Test of time" and there are not many of those types of games you can find that are like that.
Currently there is a steam award thing going on and i chose to vote this for the test of time, because you can't beat what is a perfect product that keeps beating the new ones, even it's successor Rome II TW isn't as good as the original Rome TW. It is one of those games you come back to play again and again and the replayability of the product is pretty good. No one campaign is ever the same and the music is just right, not too exciting that it gets boring too quickly and not too dull that you start ignoring it all the time. the beat is right for each thing you do. From a standing army waiting for orders hearing the tension in the music to ordering your attacks as your enemy is starting to rout and you hear the song change to it's best bit.
You can create whole armies from several towns and easily have enough to wipe out any enemy along the way, potentially bringing 8 full armies to any one fight and if your enemy attacks you it could be even more with the potential of having over 10,000 units on the map at any one time. it is that kind of epicness that you can't find anywhere else.
The graphics are dated these days, however that is the best bit about the game because the graphics are so simple is what makes it easy to play the game, with medieval 2 TW you have disappearing flags or flags behind other flags, you get into a fight and you don't know where everything is at that very moment. in Rome TW, you know where everything is and it is a simple layout that works, in my opinion it is the only UI system in any TW game i can rely on in a fight.  Also when you have more graphics it makes it harder to pick out everything you want in any given fight. a simple bright color on the soldiers and horse units makes it much easier to find them.
One thing i will always like the most out of any TW game is the charge mechanic, when men charge into their enemy, they all try to get into the fight unlike with medieval 2 TW where only a few fight and the rest spread out behind waiting for their turn. but most importantly is the horse charge mechanic, when you got a few groups of horse units, you got mobility on the battlefield, charging into tightly bunched enemy groups can kill a few dozen in the first charge. you just can't find that kind of strength in attacking your enemy with a later game.
To me, Rome TW will always be the game i like the most out of any building game and one i am likely to be playing for years to come. One i can easily recommend.

This game is
Gut-wrenchingly, keyboard-smashingly, 'Jesus♥♥♥♥thatguyshotme♥♥♥♥inghow' hard. It has a steep learning curve and even at 300 hours I find it difficult, despite almost encyclopedic knowledge of operator strengths and weaknesses, maps, and breach points. My potato aim might have something to do with this I must say, but the point still applies. It is difficult. Map knowledge is needed, especially because of the game's main draw.
This is the absolutely awesome destruction system.
Whilst at times, the all-or-nothing destruction feels annoying (for example, a 50 calibre LMG cannot punch through a milimetre thick bit of sheet metal, or a stair railing, but can destroy walls, hatches, wooden barricades, people, car batteries, complicated electronic devices, floors, garage doors and more,) almost always it feels incredible.
Smashing through walls like the Scottish Kool-Aid man, or shotgunning open new lines of sight feels satisfying. Walls crunch and crack with force and noise behind them. Guns rattle and ping loudly and recoil is hefty for the most part. Bullets hit with a satisfying meaty 'thwack,' and due to the punishingly quick time to kill, (one hit headshots, most guns
end you in a second,) you always feel like each engagement has been a proper fight.
To explain why this game is liked, I'll take you through an average round. The map is randomly selected from a pool, and 'Operators' are picked. These operators are all elite special forces members, ranging from the well-known (SAS, FBI SWAT,) to the more obscure (BOPE,) and they all bring along specialist gadgets with them.
These gadgets have wonderful interplay with one another. An attacking operator, Thermite, can blow through reinfoced walls, but he can be blocked by the defending operator Mute, who has EMP signal disruptors that prevent all electronics from working. Thatcher however, another attacking operator, has specialist grenades that can take out Mute's jammers, letting Thermite open a 'big ♥♥♥♥ing hole,' to use his own words.
That's just three of them, incidentally.
Returning to the round. Whilst the defenders blow open hatches, lay out barbed wire, reinforce walls to prevent breaching charges and bullets from leaving them defensless, and generally prepare for the storm,  the attackers have a different job.  All of them have thrown out little remote-controlled drones, which scoot around the map, searching for opponents and the objective. When the timer ticks to zero, it's off their drones and away they go, using their newfound intel to plan a path to the objective, which might be a biohazard device that needs securing (in a sort of TF2 capture point kind of way,) one of two bombs that need defusing, or a hostage that must be rescued.
Now the attackers have to be careful. Defenders might be peeking out of windows, or have clever little traps set up in order to punish hasty rushes. Once the round is done, it's time to switch sides and repeat, the once-attackers now shoring up their defenses in order to repulse the once-defenders.
The map variety in which you do this in is truly excellent. From a presidential plane to a biker clubhouse, from Brazillian favela to Russian kafe, no two locations are quite alike, all of them requring different ways to be seiged.
That's the good. Now onto the bad.
The hit registration, tickrates, matchmaking,  bugs and glitches, and balance is
Rubberbanding was a major problem with 30 ping only a few months ago, and the so-called 'Operation Health' didn't do much to correct a lot of the ongoing issues the community had. Combined with liason Epi over on Reddit leaving, and people are quickly becoming disenfranchised.
It needs some proper loving before it can truly join the ranks of giants among FPS's, but Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege promises a tactical, team-oriented shooter, and delivers a tactical, team-oriented shooter.

You find yourself alone on a beach, wearing nothing but your trousers and carrying a handful of cookies for survival. As you run towards the nearby forest you see four men in leather rush up a nearby road with crossbows in hand. You decide against your better judgment to follow them up a mountain. You watch from behind a tree as they stealthily get into position below a larger force of heavily armed people. The scene before you begins to unravel; There is a vast mountain fortress with high walls and an impenetrable gate. The defenders are raining arrows and bolts down on top of the besiegers who have chopped down the trees and used them to erect palisade walls for cover. The group you followed is allied with the defenders, and just as they are about to open fire the attackers spot them. Swords are drawn and chaos ensues. Two attackers and three defenders are ultimately slaughtered, one taking a crossbow bolt to the back of the head, and the rest falling to melee combat. As the leather archers retreat to their own stronghold, the battle ends as the injured and exhausted attackers make their way back to their Viking kingdom to count their spoils and nurse their wounds. A protracted, two hour long siege on a mountain fortress, all taking place within your first in-game day. You run to some corpses and find gear, running off into the woods to begin your own adventure, and avoid the bloodthirsty feuds of warring nations.
This is Life, and it is Feudal. The above is an example of something which happened on the server I play on, and I am sure on many others as well. The game itself is something many people have been waiting for - a true role playing game where you take on the task of a builder, farmer, carpenter, blacksmith, miner, forester, healer, alchemist, and so on. Players must work together to survive, establishing settlements and hunting wildlife, mining deep tunnels and clear cutting entire forests. Everything you build, or grow, or cook, must be made from things gathered elsewhere, bringing a sense of true accomplishment to completed tasks, doing away with the instant gratification many games provide for us these days.
Will you be a bandit? A Thane of a Viking keep? A humble farmer serving under a just and noble lord, or a wandering merchant selling his possibly ill-gotten goods to the highest bidder? The choice is yours in Life is Feudal, and for an early access Alpha game, it is arguably one of the best games to date in my opinion. Aside from the random crashing, and a few mechanics in game that one would expect to be completely possible but are not implemented yet, I would strongly recommend this game to anyone and everyone who loves medieval times and role playing games.

A unique and addictive mix of puzzle, physics and racing; which RedLynx has been mastering for what must be a decade now. I've been playing the RedLynx trials games since waaay back when they were just 2D Flash games; so they've come a looong way.
However - I ride a motorcycle daily, still do trials biking on my bicycle, and have ridden actual Trials motorcycles, and I actually prefer the handling of it's predecessor:
.
The prettiest graphics of any Trials game to date; with fantastic gameplay to match.
There's a wide range of beautiful environments and props for you to not only race in, but also create your own tracks in (with a bewildering amount of customisation). Your rides and riders can be personalised too, with (most) items being unlocked with progress and paid for with the in-game currency you earn. The rider can now do tricks in midair (once you unlock them) for that extra XP and show(off)manship. Tracks are varied, clever and engaging. And for those hardcore completionists, there's three side achievements for every track which range from simple to-dos to entire minigames. Lots of extra fun and value. Oh, and in case you didn't know, there are also Online and Local multiplayer modes too.
Handling that can be hard to understand and predict.
I will say, the bikes move at a more realistic pace than ever before, feeling like they have real weight an inertia. But hit a bump or land from a drop, and sometimes those physics go out the window with a bike that surges and bounces like a space hopper, or jams/judders in a way that seems to stall the bike. Evolution had a bit of this too, but it made sense as the bikes felt light and twitchy. But when a hefty bike does it, it's hard to react, and harder to counter (the heavier bikes mean less airborne control). Performance also struggles too - The game isn't overly complicated, but it seems quite demanding on CPU and GPU power for what you get.
A great time wasting and skill honing game for people of all ages and gaming levels. Definitely worth buying if you see it on sale, but you may as well skip Steam and get in from uPlay directly (as you have to use uPlay anyway). However, if you're rig isn't very powerful, you'd be better served getting Trials Evolution - it's just as much fun, and probably better value.

Unique, beautiful graphics style, sounds of battle and authentic map of Gettysburg encourages to get more information about  bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil between Army of Northern Virginia (CSA) and Army of Potomac (USA) and lot of joy and satisfaction from playing.
We can play  Campaign, where we choose to fight as Confederate or Union general, fight some single, Custom Battles with many, different AI difficulty levels or face people thanks to Multiplayer in 1v1 fight on several maps.
Multiplayer is very emotional - although there are not as many maps as in singleplayer, there is enough number of battles we can fight with another player. By winning we rank up from 2nd lieutenant to Lieutenant general.
Also, there are differences between CSA and USA soldiers - Rebels are more courageous veterans; Yankees are less brave and experienced, but have better equipment and deploy more efficient artillery.
Personally, I would recommend this game not only to people who are interested in American Civil War and love strategies, but to everyone who likes military history. UGG, created by a small group of passionates can compete even with biggest well-known strategy games.

Plenty of territory to explore over all different sorts of maps, from tropical islands and seaports and much more.  Paved roads, dirt roads, offroad!  Who cares?  Find the nearest hill, plant the pedal into the carpet, and see how flat of a car pancake you can make.  Physics are exceptional, I spend as much time writing off cars as I do panning the camera around them and admiring the phenominal amount of detail and time that was put into the crash physics.  Absolutely love this game, few minor bugs with certain vehicle body panels, but nothing that hinders gaming from my experience, constantly updating so look forward to new content: vehicles, maps, physics and mechanics updates. This game is just plain awesomeness. As I said in other platformers reviews, one thing that I notice about some 'retro' games on steam is that some are just considered retro because the pixel art and such. This is not a bad thing at all, I'm a sucker for any kind of pixel/8-16 bit games, but it's hard to find some who actually plays like an retro game.
Shovel knight plays like an old school platformer and brilliantly added some modern elements like the relics, fuses and curios - respectively the itens avaiable for shovel knight, plague knight and specter knight which makes the character have some special moves, different attacks and defense gadgets. Each one of these makes you play differently according to your strategy when you grind through a level. That means you can finish a level or kill a boss in different ways. And although the controls are simple and very fluid, it's tricky to master specially with all those options.
The graphics are amazing, great pixel art style, very detailed. As for the sound effects they're awesome and the soundtrack is glorious. For me, Shovel Knight's ost is one of the best of all time. Overall, not much to say about the technicall aspects of the game presentation.
About the gameplay, as I said before it's very fluid and every time you die, you feel like it's totally your fault. Easy to learn, hard to master is what I have to say about the game mechanics. The trickiest one to play is plague knight, but when you get used to this character, you'll find this campaign awesome. The enemies are placed in challenging spots, you'll probably die a lot if you rush into the levels. This game is that kind which you have to understand the enemies patterns and then attack. Same for the boss battles, which are epic and fantastic. If you got the patience to learn the boss battles you can easily defeat them without taking any damage. Even though this is a hard thing to do it feels very rewarding.
I've played all 3 campaigns and the specter knight one is my favorite. Your reflexes have to be spot on, there's almost no margin for error and the controls are 101% precise. That made probably the most challenging character to play, but also the funniest.
Overall this is one of my all time favorites on steam. Everyone should get this game.

This old game has been around, it has survived all the newer Total war games and in my opinion it is one of the finest games that was ever created by the Creative Assembly studio, it is one of those games that has survived the "Test of time" and there are not many of those types of games you can find that are like that.
Currently there is a steam award thing going on and i chose to vote this for the test of time, because you can't beat what is a perfect product that keeps beating the new ones, even it's successor Rome II TW isn't as good as the original Rome TW. It is one of those games you come back to play again and again and the replayability of the product is pretty good. No one campaign is ever the same and the music is just right, not too exciting that it gets boring too quickly and not too dull that you start ignoring it all the time. the beat is right for each thing you do. From a standing army waiting for orders hearing the tension in the music to ordering your attacks as your enemy is starting to rout and you hear the song change to it's best bit.
You can create whole armies from several towns and easily have enough to wipe out any enemy along the way, potentially bringing 8 full armies to any one fight and if your enemy attacks you it could be even more with the potential of having over 10,000 units on the map at any one time. it is that kind of epicness that you can't find anywhere else.
The graphics are dated these days, however that is the best bit about the game because the graphics are so simple is what makes it easy to play the game, with medieval 2 TW you have disappearing flags or flags behind other flags, you get into a fight and you don't know where everything is at that very moment. in Rome TW, you know where everything is and it is a simple layout that works, in my opinion it is the only UI system in any TW game i can rely on in a fight.  Also when you have more graphics it makes it harder to pick out everything you want in any given fight. a simple bright color on the soldiers and horse units makes it much easier to find them.
One thing i will always like the most out of any TW game is the charge mechanic, when men charge into their enemy, they all try to get into the fight unlike with medieval 2 TW where only a few fight and the rest spread out behind waiting for their turn. but most importantly is the horse charge mechanic, when you got a few groups of horse units, you got mobility on the battlefield, charging into tightly bunched enemy groups can kill a few dozen in the first charge. you just can't find that kind of strength in attacking your enemy with a later game.
To me, Rome TW will always be the game i like the most out of any building game and one i am likely to be playing for years to come. One i can easily recommend.

LiF is one of the games I've been playing since starting my break from a different game earlier this year so I'd like to share my views on LiF as well.

As others have said, it will not be for everyone, and the MMO version (LiF) vs the private server version (LiF:YO) are two rather different beasts.  Having been in the alpha for LiF, the biggest difference between the MMO and personal server versions is simply the size of the map, the lack of the "claims" mechanic (think of this system as a combination deed and guild/nation mechanics in Wurm Online), and the server owner's ability to mod the server.  This includes going so far as to restructure the skill trees, the exp rates, recipe requirements, and even the animations/models, they just need to provide the modified client files for you to use.

Looking at map sizes, for the LiF:YO map, if you are familiar with Wurm Online, it is roughly the size of Cele and shaped like a mini-Indy (big mountain in the middle, various terrain types between the mountain and the waterline).  On the MMO map, the LiF:YO equates to about 1 map "grid" in size (map was something like 12-15 by the same if I remember correctly).

I've actually been playing mostly on a modded server for the last few days, the admin/modder has been keeping in-step with the developer and releasing updates the same day as the official client files.  Currently there are only 3 truly modded servers (actually requiring modded client files) accessible to the public.  Custom server configurations for exp gains, number of animals, etc... do not require modded client files
*Updated*

Honestly, I'm enjoying LiF about as much as I when I started playing Wurm full time a couple of years ago.  Like Wurm Online a few years ago, there are a lot of things that are still in the early development process, and more than a few things that are just fun when taken as part of the overall system.  To me, it really does feel like Wurm Online back when Golden Valley (GV) was the starter town and the mainland was premium only.

The two biggest things that I think players coming from games like Wurm Online specifically need to keep in mind is that in LiF:YO there is a built in need to interact with people unless the server has the skill cap set high enough (3000+ skill points), and there is a progression dependency to all skill progression.  If you want to build castles, you need to learn to terraform->refine construction materials->construction->masonry->architecture, you cannot simply jump into one skill to hit the next skill unlock and then forget about the base skill.

As with any other game, you'll either like it or you won't, but either way, it's a personal opinion/preference that only you can decide on.

Roguelight: Really nice rogue-like game, which has a very interesting play with light, nice gameboy-like graphics and many upgrades. I've reached level 3, and I plan to try it a bit more to see if I can finish it. You can get this game for free or pay what you want here:
Detective Chirpums: The game is mostly filled up with dialogs, with only 3 puzzles and some dialog choices that don't seem to matter much (you just get a different dialog response). It's not a great game, but it's OK.
Hets: cool graphics, randomized levels, you get upgrades when you finish a level. Not too bad, but after playing it 44 times, I got bored and decided to never play it again.
Laz Knitez: joust game with shooting mechanics and some weird power-ups. Played it for a couple of minutes (by myself) and quit. Could be nice with friends, but it is boring alone.

I recently had the pleasure of replaying Knights of the Old Republic II with the Restored Content mod.  Taken as-is, KotOR II is a fantastic, if unfinished, successor to the first KotOR.  The fanmade Restored Content mod works to add in and finished content that didn't quite make it into the retail release while also stomping out the many bugs that plague the game.  It is an absolute must-have for the game.
The game's main draw is its rather ambitious story, weaving a tale of shades of grey in the otherwise bipolar Star Wars universe.  Thematically, the game might even have less in common with Star Wars and be more of a cousin to the classic Planescape: Torment (a personal favorite), which is probably why I enjoy KotOR II even more than its outstanding predecessor.
If you enjoyed the gameplay of Knights of the Old Republic and/or Obsidian's singular style of storytelling, give it a shot.

Trials Fusion has quietly become something of a minor masterpiece. With the normal content plus season pass and MAX DLC there are a pile of things to do in the game, and it should keep any player busy for at least a solid 40 hours. We haven't even touched the 20k plus community tracks. From the active online through to campaign and whatever else you need, there really isn't any way you could go wrong with the MAX edition, which includes all the DLC plus the new MAX stuff for 40 bucks. This will obviously drop in price on certain sales. I honestly have very few complaints at this point in time. So let's discuss a few things:
A lot of the cranky reviews cite either Uplay or the newest DLC, released long after a the yearly season pass, as problems that make them feel angry and mad. Neither of these issues is even the slightest bit of a problem anymore. If Uplay is not running correctly for you in 2015 it's your own fault. I have absolutely zero problems with it and haven't had any major problems with it for well over a year. It's a solid service, if unneeded, and really it doesn't belong in reviews for this game anymore.
The season pass has expired. It was never meant to be a free DLC for life kind of thing. Only an idiot would keep thinking that a season pass somehow connotates free DLC for life. The new content is suitably priced anyway. Taken as a whole there are literally no problems with this game. At its release I could definitely agree it was a little lighter on content and the price was too expensive for not having a functional multiplayer; as well it was buggy and unfinished. But that simply is not the case anymore. Everything you would ever need is now included in the game, but polished to a high degree.
The unlocks are decent and the various bike upgrades and ability to change colors and wheels among other things is a nice feature to keep you busy. There are a decent amount of extras for those interested that kind of stuff. You can use acorns, the new currency, to buy special additions like new body styles, outfits, and faces. You also unlock a decent amount of stuff just from normal playtime with the original currency. Acorns currency can now be purchased for cash if choose to do so. Leveling up in game seems to grant a decent amount of acorns as well.
The meat of the game I am very happy to say is very solid. Graphics have been given a large boost and it shows throughout the incredibly varied environments. With the season pass you have access to a multitude of different locales and each has its own vibe that is fairly unique. As far as comparing this to Evolution Gold well this one is a lot different. Fusion is more extreme, with the themes of the environments and tracks taking on a totally appreciated craziness that really never lets you down. Both games are worth owning.
Evolution is more grounded, where as this one just goes for glory and throws in some very imaginitive and well-constructed tracks that take you from the fiery pits of hell to the most futuristic skyscrapers of an advanced civilization. And everything in between. There is no game that does racing quite like the Trials series, and the devs have seriously stepped up their game.
There are the usual medals to earn, but there is also three achievements on each stage that can find you hunting down squirrels or activating secret switches for special achievements. These will keep a lot of people busy that have gotten their golds the first couple times through.
Besides getting gold medals, the idea is that you may want to try and compete on the leaderboards. Cracking a top 5K time will definitely give you the challenge you need and should entertain the skill levels of all players. Add in some wonderful multplayer action and dozens of hours will pass before you get tired of this one.
I run this in 4K with a single 970 on the highest settings and it mostly holds a stable 60FPS. A few drops here and there on certain courses. It's a beauty of a game for sure. It might have some nitpicks here and there, but for the most part no Trials game has ever looked even close to this lovely.
All in all this is now a great game. Support for Fusion continues and multiplayer is still very active. So get on it. It's worth every penny.

the game has a very steep learning curve that requires a lot of micro management and getting used to the game's controls which were very hard for me to get the hang of initially being used to Total War Napoleon's method so anyone jumping into this from that game be prepared to face some catastrophic losses as your "maneuvers" turn into massed blobs that are shredded by prepared guns.
The game also makes no compromises in wanting you to conform to its mechanics istead of customising the experience to your wants. this has led me to a great deal of frustration, as i can't choose the composition of my army, reinforcements arrive at set times, battles end adruptly at times (when i was winning them!) with no option to continue, cannons won't fire when ordered to, units fail to follow orders sometimes, and the reasons for these circumstances are vague or completely opaque. Thankfully the community is there with detailed guides and explainations and is a must if a player wants to get a grasp on this games various quirks (although some of the guides out there have a slightly patronising tone).
i'm very tempted to rate it no as frustration has so far outweighed the fun that i've had, but those moments of fun when i was able to play the game exactly the way it should be played have so far kept me interested.
bottom line is i can't see this or any other game with similar mechanics being more than a niche title for strategy die hards, however if you buy it on sale (like i did) and can invest the time the rewards are certainly worth it.

Grab your rapid-fire plasma gun, hop on the back of your futuristic motorcycle and prepare to hang on for dear life as you gun down the massive swarms headed your way.
Walter Machado has once again delivered a game (Free to play, no less!) that offers short, high-octane bursts of cyberpunk gun-toting action. With a soundtrack that has a similar heart-pounding vibe to UBERMOSH and UBERMOSH:BLACK, you'll definitely feel the adrenaline rush as you try and outlive the swarm as long as possible.
So far a very solid game that has its basic gameplay nailed right down and the graphics are a nice retro nod. My only criticisms is that there is some occasional slowdown when there's a lot going on and sometimes the clouds that form after you gun down enemies can obscure your vision, but that does very little to detract from the fun that this is.
I look forward to future content. Though as for some suggestions: Variety in the swarm would be nice, maybe some gun upgrades here and there and if there are gun upgrades, then maybe work in a version of the class mod system?
All in all, this is definitely a game worth playing. And if you like it, then I highly recommend buying UBERMOSH and UBERMOSH:BLACK and supporting Walter Machado with future projects.

Fernbus Simulator is far from finished and far from perfect. However, for true simulation fans, its bugs and flaws can be overlooked, for a short while, due to the immersive gameplay and attention to detail offered by TML. Anyone who has played OMSI before will find this to be a breath of fresh air in comparison!
The game has a comical interface and on launch I was slightly worried about whether this cheap, arcade-style UI would be reflective of the gameplay. Fear not, however, it is not. And I believe in a simulation, the gameplay is FAR more important than the UI so I was happy to overlook this.
I started off my adventure on career mode by creating a route which passed between another city (2 stops in total). I launched in the virtual world and I was instantly struck by how decent the graphics were for a driving simulator. I'd liken it to a GTA style feel, albeit with far less detail. I liked how you could walk around the world and the coach and check in the passengers before driving away. You do this with a cool little phone handset, and you even have to open the luggage compartment for certain passengers. I think realism could be improved further by allowing luggage to be picked up and actually placed in the compartment, but I'm glad the feature exists nonetheless.
Once everyone was seated, we set off. The driving physics still need work but certainly aren't bad. Just, if you are used to OMSI/ETS2 you may feel it is slightly more acadeish, but definitely not as much as the other cheap bus simulators you see. It is still playable and realistic enough. The buses have various functions like AC, door locks and refueling which makes the game more interesting. As well as being able to stop to refuel, you can also stop for rest breaks where you have to check the passengers on their return to make sure everyone is back - another nice touch.
In terms of actual gameplay, you just follow your GPS between stops. I feel the timings provided on your route planner are FAR too generous. They need to be tightened significantly, as much as half an hour in some cases. Not the end of the world, however.
The optimisation is better than OMSI but still far too inconsistent. Jumps and stutters need to be removed. I am hoping this is a priority for the developers.
All in all, if you like ETS2 (and not just to mess around on multiplayer) you will probably enjoy fernbus. If you like ETS2 and OMSI, I am certain you will get enjoyment out of fernbus.

Start game, first thing to look for: Settings menu...  Ok; there is none.
Guess I'll go create a world (no other available options).  Start typing in the world seed, go to click "ok", mouse cursor has vanished... Ok, so it's gonna be like that, eh?  Hit "enter", mouse is back... Strange way to start things off.  All menu's to this point are waaayy too big (playing on a 43" 4k monitor), but yeah, whatever, I'll probably find the settings in-game.
Start the game, watch the initial cutscene which I guess trying to explain what's going on?  Get into the tutorial, but have absolutely no clue what to do, anywhere.  There's zero consistency in the presentation of information, no idea what the keys are (as I didn't find a settings menu before starting to check!), and the tutorial is pretty vague.  Information is arbitrarily displayed when your cursor is over random items, but there's nothing to really direct you.  I patch together some basic directions (pretty sure I missed half of course), one screen tells me to craft something, which I do from a menu (without the slightest clue as to its material requirements, purpose, or process), and bam, the tutorial ends... wait... what?
Absolutely nothing learned in the first 15 minutes of the game.  I figure out how to "dig", make a hole (figure why not?), can't get out, tutorial didn't cover that (or anything else really).
Whatever.  Enough for now, Exit game. Screen whines something about trying to compress something or other... Let it run for 30 seconds... Says you can exit, but nothing is clickable (even if it was, none of the buttons display when being pressed, etc.).  No progress, alt+tab / force-close.
This game needs a serious tutorial/UI overhaul before it's worth wasting any time.  FWIW, I can manage to build asparagus staged rockets in KSP, I've finished Factorio (*with* bobs mods), etc.   The basics of a tutorial/etc. should be well within my capability to grasp, yet somehow, the first 20 minutes of this game were about as clear as mud.
[update - 01-Mar-2017]:
Well, I took the plunge and gave it another go.  I reset the world, played the tutorial up to the point it dropped the shield.  Honestly  -- it looks exactly the same as it did before.
The UI is absolutely terrible in every regard.  Maybe it's my 43" monitor/4k resolution -- but the text is enormous, the dialogue boxes are all at minimum opacity with crap going on directly behind them, the fact that all of the icons are fuzzy and look like excessively-inflated 16 bit art that doesn't match the rest of the landscape rendered in "fantastic" mode.
The tutorial gives you a set of directives that you follow because you're told to, not because they provide any compelling narrative, or stitch together actual game mechanics, etc.
And then at the end of this little mini tutorial, there's a robot floating off to your left, with the text "press h [blah blah blah]", but when you turn to look at him, he perpetually shifts away to sit in your peripheral (and the text rotates away, so if you missed it, you can't read it now).
Bottom line, DjArcas: have an actual UI dev take a poke at your game, if you can't draw somebody in during the first 15 minutes of gameplay, then they're never going to discover what's beneath the hood, and that's your lost/flipped sales at the end of the day.

While Sniper Elite v.2 is a unique and interesting game with well-built mechanics and physics, it unsurprisingly has no story.
To elaborate, single player is highly enjoyable - by no means is it terrible. It works properly, is immersive, and is captivating. But I did not purchase something I could acquire for free, I had purchased something that would hopefully fulfill my lust for PvP sniping. This did not occur.
Rebellion, quite clearly does not care about their community that have put up with their abhorrent DLC useage (You do not HAVE to buy them, but if you want more than a handful of maps, a Walther Gewehr 43, a Springfield M1903A1, a E.W. Maschinenpistole 40, a Thompson M1A1, and a few explosives you are going to HAVE to buy the DLCs.), and various connection issues. A game like this could have easily flourished if proper support was given to the community and if things were different. However, this is not the case - Rebellion's support team after repeated reports of server connection issues demanded it was a local issue, and therefore not their software's fault when in reality, people on the Xbox 360, PC, and PS3 were reporting these issues which are still unaddressed officially and have no proper fix and do not have one in sight with the advent of Sniper Elite V.3 which, I am sure will have the same DLC useage and connection issues but I shall not jump to any preemptive conclusions but Rebellion has made it quite clear with their lack of support for Sniper Elite V2 (Instead of fixing the issues, we had gotten two more cliched, poorly-written games that were so short they may as well have just been DLCs, but I digress.) With any hope, I was wrong about my assumptions of Sniper Elite V.3 but I severely doubt it. The only way Rebellion could possibly find more players to populate their game servers is to correct the lack of a progression system. (While I do not disapprove of DLCs being used to acquire weapons, there SHOULD be a goddamn progression system that allows you to unlock normal, run-of-the-mill firearms with DLCs offering unique and special firearms.)
In short, Sniper Elite V.2 has a strong and enjoyable yet poorly-written single player with an absolutely terrible multiplayer set with connection issues, poor netcoding, and no progression system allowing you to unlock firearms without buying them.

I have always loved being a sniper in video games and when I found out that there was a game where you play solely as a sniper I knew that I had to get it.
This game is nothing like COD so if you are looking for something like that then just move along. That being said this is a fun game that combines stealth and sniping and although it is fairly short (10 hours) I find I have no problem going back and replaying the missions over again.
As far as game play goes, SE:V2 has ties to Ubisoft  and so some of the mechanics and animations of the game are similar to those of the Splinter Cell series (I sometimes like to imagine that protagonist is Sam Fisher's great grandfather). The selling point and most talked about aspect of this game is the slow motion kill cam, which allows you to watch your bullet fly through the air and into the target, in visceral and often brutal imagery.
The game does have it's flaws but I feel that they are fairly minor and are easily overlook-able.
TL;DR: Fun, Not COD, Bullet Kill Cam, Buy it.

Well, I fixed the little issue, amd drivers are so bad, anyway, I have come back with a different review, one of a more positive one. firstly I love the unreal tournament collection, it's always been my favourite FPS and I've never stopped enjoying the game, even if my record track says differently, secondly I recommend this game for a few great reasons:
1) Unreal Tournament brings hours of enjoyfull FPS combat, using amazing and fun weapons, like the flak cannon, a great shotgun-like weapon that fires flak at things or the redeemer, in my opinion the best weapon in the game, a mini nuke launcher that fires slowly but blows the hell out of a small area with one shot, great fun when you play it with an all redeemer setting!
2) You know those basic team-based FPS games that just bring in simple gamemodes like CTF or TDM or just basic DM? Well, how about a game that brings in more gamemodes than just that, like vehicle CTF, where you attack the enemy and take their flag using awesome cars that range from air to an artillery car to a tank to a little buggy that holds a blade that cuts through enemies! Then there's Onslaught, a fun game mode where two teams compete to capture key points to assault the enemy core directly it also involves vehicles, then there's assault, a fun attack and defend story-like driven game mode where one team defends their objectives while another must attack, the attackers win by completing the objectives, defenders win by holding back the attackers!
3) The vehicles! Who doesnt want to like those vehicles? Firstly we have our basic melee and ranged vehicle, the scorpion, this is the one packing those blades, as well as a special type of gun that has a beam similar to the link gun, but charges and then, when it hits can kill a basic troop instantly (as long as it's fully charged) and a manta. Next we have a kind of reconaisance vehicle, the manta, this is special, for it is the only ground vehicle that is allowed to jump, it also holds a plasma-based weapon system that fires two plasma shots at a time, holding down shift allows for vehicular manslaughter kills. Here's my favourite: The Leviathan, a 5 person manned vehicle that's main weapon is a rocket launcher (and the point defense weapons the other 4 people can man) and it's secondary, only capable of firing when the leviathan is deployed, is an ion cannon, capable of 1-hitting most things, it's great fun to have! Here's another of my favourites: limited only to the editors choice edition, the cicada. An air vehicle that's primary is missiles fired wildly at a single location, secondary is a lock on that, when held down, can fire multiple missiles at that target. The vehicle holds 2 seats, the second is a downward turret that's primary is an acurate high-firing turret, kills unprotected people and light vehicles easily, second fire is a harmless 'decoy' if you wish to call it that, which confuses locked on AVRIL and Raptor missiles, causing them to target the decoy instead.
4) The maps, ah the maps, though I may not know them off by heart I can tell you that there are tonnes of maps and they're all great fun to play on, ranging from ons-arcticstronghold to DM-junkyard to AS-convoy! ONS/DM/AS are all abreviations for their full game mode name, like how ONS is onslaught and AS is assault.
5) The campaign, I think one thing that made this game series great was the campaign, the campaign for the UT series was always great fun, in UT 2004 you'd be tasked with making to the top of the tournament leaderboard through hours of great fun and sometimes tricky missions, first you would have to do the qualification ladder, getting you into the tournament, then it'd be the team qualifications, where you fight other teams with you just hand made team in TDM trying to get fully qualified into the game, then it'd go on into different tournamnet ladders, firstly being the CTF ladder, then domination and it'd keep going until you'd completed all the ladders and become the champion of the tournament, from time to time you'd get challenged by an enemy team in little challenges known as blood rites or head to head where you'd fight against that opponent for their member in replacement of one of yours, though that's just the blood rites, head to head is a 1-on-1 DM challenge where the first person to get the set amount of frags (kills) wins, and takes with them a certain amount of cash from the fight!
Also, I recommend using Nvidia drivers, as when my friend (and I) tried using an amd driver it messed up the system, deleting a folder and also screwing up the graphics, other than that it's great fun!

So, for all of you holdouts out there, I'd like to talk a bit about my favorite game of all time. The gameplay may not be for everybody (although I and many RPG fans do enjoy it), the original release was a shell of a game, and yet, KOTOR 2 has cemented it's spot as my favorite game of all time for years. 6 years, in fact: once TSLRCM 1.5 (The Restored Content Mod) was released in late 2009 and articles started to circulate, I replayed for the first time in years and fell in love.
Gameplay: With the Restored Content Mod, it's essentially the same as the first KOTOR (necessary to really enjoy and understand the second one IMO). There are some new powers and feats, there's some rebalancing, but it feels pretty much identical. Same engine and all. If you've played KOTOR, Skip this.
The gameplay involves a fusion of turn based and real time RPG mechanics. You encounter enemies, and can pause to click on enemies and select actions for you and up to two party members, similar to Dragon Age and Mass Effect. Characters level up and learn new feats (vanilla character enhancements and new moves) and Force powers (if the character is Force-Senstive).
Out of combat, you walk around in real time and click to interact with things. In conversations, you have many choices for dialogue (over 5 isn't rare) and each one is fully written out (no misunderstandings from a conversation wheel!). Think Fallout: New Vegas (Fun Fact: Obsidian developed KOTOR 2 *and* F:NV).
Graphics: The game came out in 2005 and looked kinda dated for back then. The game can clean up nicely with mods, but it will not be looking anything near as good as even the original Mass Effect. Still, the graphics do their job, and the environments and skyboxes are both well done. Characters have a subtle range of facial emotion. Atmosphere is good.
Sound: With TSLRCM (I can't recommend it enough!), the sound becomes a strong part of the game. Weapon sounds are more pronounced and consistent, music is timed well and highly atmospheric, and you forget about the early 2000s graphics. Voice acting is excellent, with a few exceptions amongst minor characters you may see in side quests. The main character is not voiced, however.
Story: Much of the story and atmosphere of the game is best to be discovered as you play, but a general summary is fine. You play as a Jedi Exile (Canonically Female, named Meetra Surik), who was banished from the order for helping lead a war call to protect planets from the Mandalorians against the orders of the Jedi Council. The Council's reasons for staying out of the war are vague and are meant to be. The war ended with great sacrifices, and your connection to the Force was lost. This unique backdrop sets the tone for a complete deconstruction of everything Star Wars. There are somewhat legitimate Gray Jedi builds (unaigned and with bonuses from certain armor or weapons), Nihilistic overtones, and Sith like you've never seen before.
KOTOR 2 is without a doubt my favorite game story of all time, even beating out Deus Ex and Half-Life. It works so well as a deconstruction of everything Star Wars. This is not your ordinary Star Wars game, and if you have at least watched the movies and played the first KOTOR, you are in for what I would dare call a storytelling masterpiece.

Shadow Warrior 2 is a semi open world first-person shooter and a direct sequel to the 2013 Shadow Warrior, the reboot of the original from 1997.
You play as Lo Wang - A katana wielding, one-liner cracking, demon decimator. That's right. I am that cheap.*
The game takes place 5 years after  the events of Shadow Warrior. Demons now roam our realm and it's up to Lo Wang to slice 'em, burn 'em, freeze them, electrocute them, blow them up and of course insult them in hilarious yet badass ways.
The story isn't anything special but can be quite enjoyable for a 80's action flick fan like myself. The ending was kind of dissapointing. While the final boss fight itself was totaly rad the final cutscene felt...Unfinished. It gave me the same feeling Deus Ex: Mankind Divided gave me. The feeling that the ending was cut short.
The gameplay itself is outstanding!
, ladies and gents! Such a vast variety of weapons!
Borderlands tells us that they have billions of different weapons which is of course a lie. Borderlands has about 15-20 different weapon models. The only difference between assault rifle X and assault rifle Y is the stats. They look exactly the same. In Shadow Warrior 2 you actually get 70 different weapons. All the weapons look different, have different stats and feel different. That's something none of the Borderlands games actually achieved. Sure the snipers felt different than shotguns but there were not many different weapon models.
You can carry up to 8 weapons with you at all times. We have six shooters, pistols, submachine guns, automatic rifles, bows, sniper rifles, shotguns, minigun, LMGs, demonic weapons, claws, shurikens, katanas, bats and more. Pistols, automats and submachine guns can be dual wielded and ALL weapons can be upgraded. In fact you can even craft upgrades. Weapons can also do elemental damage such as fire, ice, electric or toxic damage. Melee weapons have special skills like charge attacks and 360 no scope spins. You can even chainsaw monsters and/or people.
The gameplay is really something special. The game is separated into different sandbox areas. You can dash, vanish (be invisible for a certain amount of time), sprint, heal yourself and double jump. You can even go into somekinda demonic killing frenzy. Now you can also have 8 different weapons with you at all times and there's a lot of different barrels and pods laying around. This all means you are guaranteed to get some epic large scaled battles. I once managed to aggro pretty much the entire sandbox and the battle was glorious!
Shadow Warrior 2, unlike it's prequel, can be played in 4 player co-op. Each player will play as Lo Wang himself but others will see you as a random ninja.
I understand there is no such a thing as a bug free video game but I honestly didn't experience any bugs or glitches in the game so far. The game runs fine and seems to be well optimised.
You can go from ultra to the very very low so if you have a beast PC you can enjoy the full beauty of the game while those with dated PCs can enjoy the game worry free as well. Just without seeing how detailed and awesome every single weapon looks.
Lo Wang is badass and hilarious, graphics are OK, voice acting is quite good, the music is just awesome and the price is just right. I have only three complaints: The game felt a bit too short. Took me around 13h to finish the game. It's also way too easy and the game ended in a weird way.
All in all it's still a good value for your money. You can always start a new game+ or hack through demons with your buddies.

Factorio meets Minecraft. For those of you that aren't familiar, this game is about planning and constructing logistics systems to gather and process material (Factorio) set in a voxel based world with essentially no limits on the ways you can build with those voxels. (Minecraft)
If you like Factorio, go ahead and get FortressCraft Evolved. I think you'll like it. If you like Minecraft however, you may want to watch some game-play videos, as there are many aspects of Minecraft that don't exist in FortressCraft Evolved.
This one really gets your brain going. Resources are abundant on default settings, but difficult and time consuming to extract. As such, intelligent and cleverly constructed logistics systems will provide an immediate advantage to players with the smarts to create them. Maximizing the available resources is a constant goal, and to that end the player can continually upgrade or change their systems in attempt to better utilize what's available. On top of that, building is a key mechanic to the game and players can spend as much, or as little time constructing decorative building as they desire. Oh, and there's a wave defense mechanic slapped over the whole game. Not really sure how I feel about that, but it doesn't get in the way.

This is an updated review. Recommendation remains the same.
I hate tower defense games, and I despise them with a passion. There are a few exceptions, if they are cleverly hidden or done in such a way that a player does not feel punished for playing an overly specific strategy. FortressCraft Evolved, accomplishes this feat, so I give it a glowing recommendation.
Let's start this off by saying it is less about "building" a base in the sense one would in other survival games. You are essentially building yourself a self-sustaining factory that will get increasingly more complex, and better defended in a nearly endless cycle. Oh, and you're going to have to do this with a constant threat of aliens that will scale their attacks to how well you are doing.
This does not mean the game is punishing you for doing well, but rather rewarding you with better loot, and always having some sense of urgency. There is a tipping point where you can outright utterly crush the alien threat if you so choose. With the Frozen Factory Expansion, ending one threat allows you to focus on a new threat, or fight both at the same time if you are feeling adventurous. With many survival games, it gets boring once you hit a certain point, but in FortressCraft Evolved, the game will try harder to wreck your progress.
Naturally, the player is not going to want to lose all that progress after investing many hours into their elaborate base. This is not a problem, because once the aliens kill the CPH, they all leave. They don't blow everything up to get to it either, so they rush that part of the base and only that part (with exceptions). Your goal is to have enough firepower to prevent that. Which, with a giant mechanized spider warmachine, turrets, missile launchers, and your crappy laser rifle, give the player lots to work with. Of course, keeping missiles stocked, turrets powered, and the spiderbot fueled is the player's responsibility.
This may irritate some players, as they'll either feel "too rushed" or "not rushed enough" which comes down to player preference, not balance. There are also some people who feel the game is too grindy, yet there are settings to speed things along, so if this is a complaint, they never bothered to actually use them. Many of the negative reviews are people who either A) Didn't follow the integrated tutorial. B) Did not check any settings ever. C) Had issues that Unity caused, not the developer. This isn't some rampant fanboy comment either, as the same issue arose in several other games at the same time!
To add to that, the developer is active, and involved with the community. Visiting streams, streaming while working, and on several occassions personally fixed a bug on the spot. I'm not joking, I had a bug and brought it up on stream, and that bug was fixed within minutes. There are few developers that care that much. Yes, they are blunt too which might seem a tad arrogant, but at least you know where you stand. Sometimes a suggestion is met with a good discussion about "why that won't happen" which means that the developer has a vision, and not prone to "feature creep". Despite a few heated discussions personally (usually on why not x feature from Factorio), I still felt respected as long as respect was given. For a game review, I mention this because developer interaction is important, even long after the game has left Early Access.
If you can swing it, I'd highly recommend the Frozen Factory Expansion as well. It adds more stuff, a new enemy threat, and is a seemless transition from vanilla to the expansion. With another Expansion down the road, there has been a lot of new free content that has been added as well, so the game is still going strong.
Overall, I recommend FortressCraft Evolved. I would like to mention that as a fan of "logistics" style games like Factorio, this game feels right at home so I enjoy both for different reasons. Co-op is stable, and quite fun. I play with the same group for a lot of different games, and every playthrough we're always trying/finding something new. For the hours I've put in, the money I've spent (even on the dev's Patreon) has been well worth it.
It's an okay shooter, but it honestly isn't anything special. get it if you like, but if it doesn't grab your interest immediately then don't even bother.

Life is indeed Feudal, but unfortunately this game is futile.
At the time of purchase, this game was advertised as Life is Feudal, then they made a hard right turn and shut down their original servers used for testing the MMO of this game and repurposed it for "Your Own", a small 3kmx3km island that resembles RUST only that it is set to a medieval time scale. The game promised group oriented combat and large group vs large group sieges to claim land and castles of such grand scale that it truly did blow everything else out of the water, including the Persistent World mod for Mount and Blade.
After the game's EA release here on steam it was clear that they were completely derailing from their original intent of the MMO, and sought to make some extra cash. That's wonderful and all, but the simple fact that they openly said, " We're looking to fund LiF:MMO with all the money we earn from LiF:YO..." makes this game dangle ever so slightly over the toilet that snaps at it with hungry jaws.
The marketing idea is flawed, fine, maybe the game is good enough to overcompensate.
Let's look at some of the keystones for the game:
Built with Torque 3D ( HEAVILY modified)- While this engine looks decent enough, it's not even capable of handing a 16 player server with minimal terraforming, the rigging is so clunky that most of the hit boxes actually twist with the character's movement, which translates into mangled hitboxes that are impossible to land hits on when you can clearly see the head of your hammer or the blade of your sword going through the body of the other player.
Bi Weekly Updates- While the updates seem frequent enough, the content that is updated is more of a "hotfix" nature and not an actual Update to the game or its content.
Developer presence- The presence of the Devs is definetly felt, they seem to be making a good bit of appearances on the forums both in Steam and in their own bug tracker. This could be both bad and good, as the more time they spent scrolling through the forums.. the less time they spent fixing the heavily modified game engine that requires a lot of love due to the fact that the engine is not designed for such a game, even with modding... it's limitations are clearly visible.
Terraforming- The trailer made it look sweet right? Well... unless you dig a tunnel in a straight line then you need to expect gapping holes in the world that will cause you to fall beneath the playerworld and into a vast underground sea. The other side of terraforming, which doesn't involve mining, is almost a death sentence to the server. Get a group of friends to terraform your lands so you can properly build your kingdom and you'll increase the time it takes to load into a server by 10-30 minutes. The more you change, the longer it takes for the server to give you the files as it seems to be replacing ALL the local files with modded files from the server.
Building- You can't do it alone unless you crank up the skill cap and become the God of All Skills. The only way to enjoy the game is to do so with atleast 3+ friends on a server that has skillcap/harvesting/growthtime all cranked up, and even then it will take days to complete small projects.
Online play- I can only consider this an option if I'm part of a private server, as the game does little to nothing to stop griefing. Between folks digging unrepairable tunnels throughout your village, to people deconstructing your homes and putting unremoveable campfires in their wake. This game's Troll factor reaches that of RUST, minus the hacking... they did a good job of preventing that by keeping ALL files server sided.
Servers- So, this is the fun part. Even a high end server can barely run this game without hourly spikes of lag that have been dubbed, " Morning lag" due to the obsurb amount of trees and plant growth that all require 2-4 calls to the database before updating. Each time you change a value, the client requests information from the database and the database requests information from the client... multiple times for the same change.
Inventory- If you have OCD, step away. The inventory bags are nothing more than visual vomit. You COULD take an hour to organize the herbalist bag of yours... but your friend will still see visual vomit when he opens it, due to all inventory placement being clientsided.
There are countless other issues that arise when you talk about the keystone features of the game, and I understand it's an embryotic alpha, damn near a tech demo, BUT.... the icing on this wonderful cake is the fact that the game doesn't properly used your video drivers as NONE of the video display adapter profiles are implemented into the game yet... want some more sweetness? a 16gb rig still gets  "Out of Memory" errors from playing the game for less than 5 minutes.
Last but not least, the bug tracker for this game is a mile and a half long, and seems to be at a stand still.
Overall, 2/10 but 7/10 when played with friends.
Would not recommend.
