Sniper Elite is fun. The Singleplayer (which not many complete, because most people get into the Multiplay right away) is really cool. It felt kinda too easy though. The Campaign features several different authentic locations from WW2. The AI is kinda good. I've seen lots of games that where equally nice but sucked at AI. Here the NPCs take cover and remain there depending on the location they saw an enemy / bullet. You have a lot of nice (but static) voice-overs in cutscenes as well as right in the mission. The graphics is really great although you dont need a killer-machine to run it. Even with a mediocre PC you get really good frame rates and still have a really nice visual experience.
The Multiplayer is really straight forward and can be exiting at certain moments. But it looses its touch quickly because it doesn't have much new to it. It is like battelfield but with a focus just on - well - sniper rifles. Also on the hardest and seemingly most realistic game mode you can't do much to your rifle. Next to a hold breath-focus-option and different zoom-sizes you have no zeroing, no different sights, no different ammunition, no rifle jams (I mean come on - its 1944), no features that give the weapons mechanics some real realism. It is just plain pew pew without any interference.
After completing the kinda short Singleplayer Campaign (it took maybe like 10 to 15 hours - without collecting all of the collectables (gold-ingots and shooting-all-winebottles), I played the Multiplayer for some weeks but I have stopped now playing the game at all, still hoping for some Updates or even some cool DLCs - especially a new compaign, some new Mulitplayer features, a realism overhaul ... some things like that would make me jump right back into WW2. The game itself is really cool and immersive, but it misses content and realism/options. I definitely would buy anopther DLC campaign and probably new multiplayer features.

Short review: I did try to like this game but just the fancy graphics didn't really do it.
The UI is not tht great; the graphic as mentioned is pretty good; although animations for the passengers is a joke; with people going through the floor, look all the same and jitter in place when the bus approach the stop.
Cities look all the same; there is not enough variety for the buildings and roads; which look nothing like the original cities. Some textures are really low detail.
Sound is decent; nothing much that you can expect, beside engine noise and other effects.
The bus drive decently, it is not a full sim; and matter not that the game support spring physics. There is some parallel wth how a big rig should drive, but you can tell that it is not a full simulation. Pushable controls are nice, although you need to get in a specific view to interact with them; so can't drive and push controls, unless you have them mapped to keyboard.
The gameplay could be interesting if the AI of the cars would be decent; instead you get stuck in neverending jams because AI is so atrocious that does not find a way to avoid other cars or back up. This was OK 10 years ago, not today. Also you can run over red lights with no penalty. There is no damage to the bus to repair, so you can go offroad or on sidewalks, withouth any penalty.
The progression in career mode is not affected by mistakes; you get few penalties on the xp, but it is usually 1-3 points per infraction, against hundreds of points you gain for reaching the stops. If you are late, no big deal, same if you run red light, speed cameras, hit other cars, drive like a maniac.
The idea of getting out of the bus is nice, but all you do is to check ONE BY ONE the passengers, and either they have the right ticket, wrong ticket or no ticket at all; they interaction is close to 0, and simply disappear; like Train simulator,  instead than hopping on the bus. Beside fueling and check tickets, there is no other gameplay for the first person part; nice to add it but if there is nothing to do with it...
And in one year that this game has been released, some serious bugs are still there since launch; the devs seems interested in DLC and new games, instead than fixing this, so it is disappointing to see such behavior, when some serious issues still persist.
I can't suggest this game, until bugs are fixed and AI improved radically, The only nice thing is the bus, with clickable elements, but if the rest of the game is sub par, there is no incentive in playing it.

You will find out very, very quickly from the first mission that this is not your typical fps or third person shooter. You cannot just run-and-gun into enemy territory, like in Cod, Battlefield, or any other fps that you have become accustomed to playing over the years. This is no doubt one of the most, if not, the most realistic, tactical, strategy-based fps, and third person shooter available on the market. Right off the bat from the first mission of the campaign you will be in prone mode, sniping, and crawling all the way to your objective, which is always around 900m away. If you make even the slightest noise via the rustling of grass near an enemy, they will look for you, they will alert the many reinforcements nearby, and they will kill you, FAST. I knew that I would not just be able to run in and move on to the next objective in about 5 minutes, just as I would in Cod, or Battlefield. I died a ♥♥♥♥ load of times, but not just from sucking, but from having to adapt to such a realistic system and tough mechanics. This is the closest you will get to a real life military experience, if you do not wish to join in real life, that is. Though the maps are absolutely massive and the graphics are breathtaking, don't expect to explore much, because there are enemies hidden in bushes EVERYWHERE, and they will shoot you, and you will be dead in a matter of 2-3 precise shots, if you are standing still. Playing with friends, using the radio, using commands, tactics, and everything you would do in a real war situation is the most immersive, and heart-pounding gaming experience I have ever had. To all you 20th history lovers, such as myself, I highly recommend you subscribe to as many Ww2 mods through the workshop as you can. The Dday and Japanese invasion mods are the best ones. If you are also a Star Wars fan, such as myself, it is an absolute must to subscribe to the SW Opposition mod, maps, and the many other incredible star wars mods available for Arma 3. You will need the apex edition so be warned when purchasing, if you want to have the best Star Wars experience, and the Battlefront game that fans have always wanted, you must purchase the apex edition, in order for the SW Opposition mods and other maps to work. This, along with its outstanding independant game developer support and having the Eden Editor there for anyone to create their own maps at will, is amazing. I have spent most of my hours just creating new animations, models, and scenarios for myself, with the Star Wars mod mainly. For the most immersive, hilarious at times, and realistic military gaming experience, Arma 3 is a must have. Arma 4 is rumoured to have entire planets explorable, so fingers crossed. Really awesome, fun, and surprisingly deep, Shadow Warrior 2 trumps its successor on a few levels.
-Way more customizability, adding light-RPG mechanics to a really fun shooter, with all sorts of trinkets to constantly evolve and improve your loadout.
-Gorgeous graphics and satisfying combat, melee weapons in particular feel especially more satisfying after the first game. Enemies split and break apart, and tons of gore abound, Killing enemies in SW2 is its own reward.
-Co-op, I mean, its fun to play with other people, right?
-Lots of locales, lots of enemies, and even sidequests give this game longevity that most other modern shooters offer.
-My only misgiving about the game is that I really don't care about what's happening in the story. The nature of the multiplayer and RPG aspects make the story feel very incohesive and it's kind of all over the place. I usually skip about half the cutscenes, but don't really feel like I'm missing much.
Regardless, it's a very fun shooter which looks great, plays great, and has to potential to keep players playing long after its release.

Anyway this game should be getting 90%+ I think on recommendations, its being brought down by the DRM unfortunatley, but IMHO it's well worth jumping through the hoops to play this amazing game.

So I'm going to cut right to the chase.
The Good: An extremely accurate physics engine that does its best to simulate real life as closely as possible.  "Official" cars included with the game destroy and deform for the most part as you'd expect they would (you get minor bugs here and there but this doesn't often happen unless you completely mutilate a vehicle).  The official selection of cars is small, but steadily growing.  You get a selection of cars, trucks and SUVs with varying trim levels and options that you can customize. They're all very highly detailed and behave as you'd expect them to behave.  In addition to vehicles, there is a wide variety of other machines and devices you can use to destroy vehicles (including a roller crusher, a rollover sled, a giant hamster wheel and a car cannon).  The environments provided are again few, but nicely varied and include sections of countryside, small towns, racetracks, industrial areas and more.  The really big pro here?  The game is totally open to the modding community.  There are lots of cars, props and maps available to drive, and they run the gamut from plain family cars to rally specials and science-fiction wonders. The modded terrains range from rally stages to highways to elaborate obstacle courses to who knows what else.  The official terrains are very well designed and pretty, if a bit lifeless.  They're also quite large and have a lot of little secrets hidden all throughout them--secrets that can often only be accessed by a particular type of vehicle.
The Bad: Despite being in production for well over two years, the game is still a long way from being done.  There are lots of features still missing (there is no multiplayer, AI is primitive at best).  And then there's the other problem--this game is a MASSIVE resource hog.  All the physics calculations are done in real time.  There are ZERO canned crash animations, unlike a game like GTAV.  GTA uses canned animations to save on CPU overhead and preserve framerate.  Beamng.drive does not.  Because of that you are going to need a very good PC to run this game on high graphics settings and keep a reasonable framerate.  Also, because of the early state of this game there...really isn't all that much to DO.  There are a few "scenarios", basically all time-trial races, but other than these there's no real point besides driving around and figuring out new and inventive ways to destroy a late 90s pedo-van.  Also, this is a car-based driving game with car-based controls.  There are working boats and aircraft in the modding community but the control scheme is not designed to accomodate them.  Because of that they can be very hard to handle.  Another point against--the game works decently well with a gamepad (The X360 controller is supported natively), but to take full advantage of it you are going to need a decent steering wheel and pedal setup.  DO NOT attempt to play this game with just a keyboard and mouse.
So should you buy this game now?  Well that depends.  Are you the kind of gamer that enjoys driving games?  Can you make your own fun?  Do you like to break stuff?  I'd say if you answered yes to at least two of those three questions, you should give this game a good hard look.  If however you're the kind of gamer that needs direction, needs to be given something to do, this game probably isn't for you.

FortressCraft Evolved is a great game that gets nowhere near as much recognition as it should. Though often compared to other things like Minecraft, FC:E is far removed from the style Minecraft presents and should never be considered in the same vein.
You're on an alien planet, for a start, crashlanded after a great big asteroid smashed into the station you were about to dock in. So, where to begin? Well, you start with a Central Power Hub, some simple machines, a fantastically powerful Build Gun (which is upgradeable) with which you can mow down mountains or build massive plateaus with little effort, and you have to find yourself some resources.
With the handy Scanner, you must scan the world around you to be able to research new machines, ping for ores, and plunge the dark depths of the grandest caverns you have ever seen to discover new resources further down, beneath the surface.
Then comes the automation part of the game, which is arguably the largest part and a great logistical challenge. You'll have to start with simple automation: getting Copper and Tin to your smelter. A few conveyors, a storage hopper or four, and before long you have bars with which to build new items, blocks and machines. Next comes Iron, which is deeper down in the ground. Then Lithium, though this ore is deep enough to attract the voracious Mynocks to your conveyors, which fuel a dark threat hidden in the caverns if they eat stuff off your conveyors. So, after having placed some turrets and provided enough power, you have Lithium safely automated.
So, now with plenty of bars to spend on base expansion, what does an accomplished crash survivor like yourself have left to conquer? Worry not, for there are still several hurdles to overcome. Enemies will come to find your base, attracted by the increased energy your base produces as you expand. Vast deadly caverns lying below those precious Lithium veins provide new challenges and environmental dangers. Hiveminds stalk your base, lying in wait for that one block of conveyor not covered in turret fire to plant a Mynock on it.
As your base grows, so do the dangers, so there is never a dull moment.
That's all I will say, since you really should experience the game for yourself. I have more than 900 hours in this game, and I have enjoyed every one of them. There's nothing quite like putting all your hard work to use in calling a bombardment from orbit to exterminate your enemies. For the price, this game is absolutely worth it!

Shovel Knight is a metroidvania platformer that invokes retro feelings from classic games like Castlevania or Megaman. Shovel Knight doesn't just look like a retro game but perfectly captures the essence of those games as well through extraordinary level and boss design, as well as providing a satisfying challenge and refusing to hold your hand. Shovel Knight felt to me as if it took inspiration from multiple other games, both old and new, and weaved them all together to create a truly unique experience in an over-saturated genre. From boss battles that almost seemed to draw inspiration from the souls series, to level design that seemed straight out of Castlevania, Shovel Knight isn't just a game with a retro skin, it's a flawless callback to classic retro games of old.
So, Shovel Knight is a platformer, yes, but to me I felt more like I was playing an RPG first and a platformer second. This may sound like a bad thing but I honestly think that Shovel Knight mixes the two extremely well, you can buy items and complete side quests just like in an RPG, but when it comes to dungeons and bosses expect lots of jumping puzzles and verticality. Speaking of dungeons and boss fights, both of these are designed exquisitely; every area you go to has some kind of obvious theme and there's secrets everywhere for you to find. Each boss fits into their zone perfectly and has abilities that match as well, the bosses also have a surprising amount of difficulty to them, which gave me some Dark Souls vibes. You can't just mash keys to get through the bosses, you have to pay attention, use your items responsibly, and actually think the fight out rather than going in there and shovel smacking your way to a shallow grave. I think the bosses work so well because of each individual bosses design, but also because Shovel Knight controls excellently. You're going to be doing lots of jumping in dangerous places, places where one wrong step could spell your doom, and not once did I ever feel that my death was due to faulty controls. The tight, but simple, controls also make navigating the levels more fun since you aren't going to be tearing out your hair after failing a jump or dying in a way that was unfair. Shovel Knight's controls work well with its simple combat system, pretty much just a few basic attacks. You can buy a handful of special attacks at a shop later in the game, but honestly I never found that they were much use and instead were really just too bothersome to even worry about. Shovel Knight manages to take this simple combat system and make it harder by forcing you into mixing combat and platforming in order to progress through the levels. Mixing the combat with the platforming is actually really fun and you get scenarios where you chain attacks together, bouncing between enemies in pure joy, that really make you cherish your experience with Shovel Knight.
Now speaking of enemies, there is plenty of variety here too, usually the enemies you fight are in some way themed to the zone, which adds something to the boss experience as well since you feel like you're building your way up to the main fight itself. Sometimes the enemies can be a little frustrating and there's definitely a place or two where I feel the developers may have overdone it on the difficulty, but overall the enemies are placed well and aren't too hard to deal with. Shovel Knight isn't all about the combat though, there is a pretty classic story here too. Your old fighting companion, Shield Knight, with whom you've faced countless horrors, has been kidnapped by the evil enchantress and you're setting out to save her. This is pretty barebones, but I honestly think that Shovel Knight should be focused on minimal story, with maximum gameplay. The classic story works well because Shovel Knight is supposed to be a cliched classic of a game, with our great hero setting out to slay horrible monsters and rescue his friend, you really don't need much more story than that here. Shovel Knight manages to get you to actually care about this Knight and his companion quite a bit, even though you never see either one's face or hear a voice, because Shovel Knight conveys emotion through audio.
Now I've gone over how Shovel Knight has a simple but effective combat system, extraordinary level design, and notable influences from other amazing games, but there's one thing that truly sets Shovel Knight apart: the artwork. I'm not just talking about the gorgeous 8-bit inspired graphics, but also a soundtrack that deserves to be up there with the greats like Hotline Miami and DOOM. Shovel Knight's music is used to almost be the characters voice throughout the game; the soundtrack perfectly captures the feeling of each zone, be it creepy music for fighting the undead, or upbeat chiptune tracks to keep you on your toes during a boss fight. The sad moments of Shovel Knight are made even sadder through the music, making you actually feel a bit for this cliched action hero and his noble quest. Shovel Knight doesn't just rebuild the image and feeling of a classic NES-era fantasy world, it also flawlessly recreates the sound.

Yacht Club does a very, very good job of bringing back the nostalgia with Shovel Knight. This 2D side-scrolling platform game is indeed reminiscent of the era of 8-bit consoles, from the simple pixel art to the retro-inspired soundtrack. Shovel Knight doesn't lack in testing one's skill or mastery in platforming, as every stage is a challenge. In fact, I consider clearing a particular stage to already be an achievement in itself, since there have been far too many times when I have frustratingly restarted some stages  again and again. Finishing a stage means having carefully studied the area -- with all its secrets and surprises -- and being able to execute your plan perfectly and without error. I'll be honest that there were times when the game just seemed unfair, and perhaps it was by a stroke of luck that I passed some particular areas. Nevertheless, I would definitely recommend Shovel Knight for those who miss the familiarity of platform games, and for those who are up for a frustratingly good challenge.

I really want it to be good. It's a huge game. You spend a lot of time in the begining on two main islands. Both feel pretty large. The melee combat is just gross to experience, range is either way too easy or way too hard and doesn't feel natural either way, magic is fun to mess around with but is also hard to use in combat especially if you have allies with you. That fire bomb spell doesn't know what the word friendly means. Doors are hard to open, jumping is grotesque, running looks and feels stupid especially if you prefer to carry a staff or polearm. I can't express enough how clunky this game feels. For a game with so much content, i'm straight up mad the fighting actually makes it unenjoyable to play.
It's not even like this game is that old. There are no excuses. Especially since the first in the series had the same problem and they failed to fix it. And the fact the game freezes while it loads the next area sometimes is really annoying.
On a positive note, this instalment improved upon the first Two Worlds in a lot of ways. The world is bigger, there are more kinds of enemies, cooler weapons, better story, necromancy is legal yay! However, it's just as clunky as the first game and really quite hard to play because of it. If the mobility in Two Worlds didn't bother you then you will definitely like this game. I really, really, really want to like this game, and for a while as I was starting out, I did. The elevator pitch is more or less "Factorio as recreated in Minecraft", and the first person element really does add that much more to the exploration aspect.
Unfortunately, once you've got an assembly line set up for your most basic resources, the entire game's progression of tech trees turns out to be deliberately balanced a step or two behind parity with your current progress, such that you are
sticking your neck out, collecting stuff manually, and being forced to stretch your current equipment to its absolute limits to gather the new resource for the next tier of equipment, at which point the process repeats itself. It's less a game about automation as it is a never-ending masocore scavenger hunt. Which is a damn shame, because if just a bit more common sense were applied to the tech trees it'd be another masterpiece of the "explore, collect, build" genre. You still might be able to get something out of it, but I would advise caution. It's more nefarious than it looks.

This game, though, was developed by the indie company Game-Labs.  If you want to know upfront if I'd recommend this game, the answer is yes, with just one caveat - although the tutorial is adequate, its still pretty basic, and the online guide is missing some things, as well.  So, if you really don't like having to work some things out on your own, or consult Steam guides, you might give it a pass.
Now, for some more detailed Pros and Cons:
PROS
- Strong presentation.  There's not much music, but the opening/title screen theme is nice, and the sound effects in gameplay are realistic.  The portraits for the different generals, colonels, majors, etc. are all well-done, and aren't just lifts of old black-and-white photos.  The map is very nice, quite accurate and detailed.
- The AI is very good, and comes with a lot of customization - there are nine, different AI settings, based on aggressiveness and difficulty, and you can mix and match to create your desired strength of opposition.  There is also a Boost AI setting that can be enabled, though I have yet to be brave enough for that.
- You can tell that the designer is knowledgeable about both Civil War and Gettysburg history.  I just recently finished Gettysburg by Allen C. Guelzo, and UG:G gets almost everything correct.
- Branching scnarios - let's say you're playing as the Union, and you manage to hold onto the northern ridges in town through the first day, instead of losing them to the Confederates as per history.  This will prompt the game to give you options for your next strategy - launch an attack on a Confederate position, or withdraw to the southern ridges.  If you choose to extend your right flank with an attack on the Confederates and succeed, this will then also lead to additional, non-historical scenarios.  This is also true for the other side, but I have only played as the Union forces so far.
- Replay value - you would think that a single-battle game might not have much, but I've been through it several times now; partially to see if I can score a more decisive victory than was recorded in history, and partly because I haven't done as well as I would like to, and want to achieve better results.  The different, branching paths, plus the possibility of a Pyrrhic victory (winning the battle but losing too many troops) are strong motivators to play some more.
CONS
- Although the branching scenarios are great, sometimes they can be a bit perplexing.  For example, as the Union, I secured part of the map that historically had been lost on the first day of fighting.  While this did lead to the branching paths described above, the text briefings indicated that I'd had to reteat to Seminary ridge anyway.  While losing the ground outright does not result in an option to launch an attack to take it back, such that your strong performance still results in a change of sorts, it would be nice if all of the scenarios branched directly off the actual results.  Most do, but some don't.  I suspect this disconnect comes from trying to create alt-history divergences that still fit into the original scope of the battle.  It's not a huge problem, but it's somewhat disarming.
- Some aspects of gameplay, while fully revealed during the course of play, are not explicitly mentioned in the tutorial.  Artillery fire, for example.  When you select an artillery unit, you'll get an FOV cone and can click on enemies within the unit's FOV to attack.  If the FOV cone is darkened, rather than bright, that means the unit has no line of sight.  Likewise, if you click on an enemy unit to attack, and it simply flashes briefly but does not remain highlighted in red, that unit is not within your artillery unit's line of sight.  No line of sight = no firing.  When you click on a unit that is within your line of sight, the enemy soldiers are highlighted in red, not just for a moment.  If you click over somewhere else and come back to your artillery unit, it's targeted enemy will still show up in red highlights.  These are the visual cues that tell you whether your artillery is placed correctly so that it will attack the enemy, but you have to figure them out through gameplay rather than being told explictly.  Honestly, I expect to spend a lot of time with a strategy game, learning, so it's not a big gripe on my end.
Overall, I think this is a very good game, with good presentation, good historical accuracy, nice design, branching scenarios and most importantly, it's a lot of fun.  There are a couple of issues that may render it unsuitable for some, depending on their preferences, but I think that most Civil War enthusiasts will enjoy it.

TL;DR version: highly recommended for Civil War or military history enthusiasts. Good AI, very good replayability from a dynamic campaign and many individual scenarios, and mechanics that force you to take into account the morale, fatigue, and cohesion of a unit instead of just its size.
Full Version:
Overall, I think this is a very good game. It reminds me of the 1977 Avalon Hill game Gettysburg's advanced game, which was a great simulation--just incredibly taxing as a board game. Making it a computer game instead hides a lot of the bookkeeping and tables that are involved in a board game, and the whole thing flows better. In fact, the mechanics are similar enough that I wonder if the people who designed this didn't look at the Avalon Hill game for inspiration, at least in part.
The game is very unforgiving of mistakes, and forces you to keep track of your forces--not just their number of men, but their overall state as well. Troops have a "Morale" rating, which is their will to keep fighting, and a "Condition" rating, which is a measure of thier cohesiveness and fatigue. If Morale is depleted, the unit will break and run, and if Condition is depleted, it will be less effective at maneuvering and firing--accurately depicting the fact that Civil War combat relied a lot more on morale and unit cohesiveness than actual casualties to put a unit out of action. That brigade that just broke and fell back behind your lines can be sent right back into the fray, but you'll lose a lot of troops for very little gain.
The campaign is something I haven't seen in any strategy game of this type--it's split into bite-sized engagements, in which you control a part of your army rather than the entire thing. Based on your performance in one engagement (and sometimes on general strategy decisions you make between battles) the game will decide the reaction of the AI general and generate the next scenario, in which you units' casualties, morale, and condition will carry over--so don't burn out your army on the first day.
Speaking of the AI, it's actually very good. There are three different difficulty levels, and three different aggressiveness levels. They do make a difference in the AI's behaviour. I played the beginning of a campaign as the Confederacy with the AI on balanced mode--moderate difficulty and aggressiveness--and by the evening of the first day I controlled all of Cemetery Ridge except for the Round Tops. I started a new one on the same difficulty but with a defensive AI... and all of a sudden it didn't make counterattacks I could beat off and exploit, and I found myself running up against well-positioned troops that shattered my advancing units. It radically changed how the game played, and I always have to work to outmaneuver it, I can't rely on taking advantage of the "idiot AI."
There's an array of individual scenarios, both historical and hypothetical, which let you try out a particular possibility without having to play an entire campaign to get there. Quicker, easier to get into (although the later scenarios put you in charge of more units, so you've got more to keep track of), and a good learning tool to use in the more drawn-out campaign battles.
There are some bugs, like artillery seeming to forget the target it's been ordered to fire on, and the artillery in general is difficult to master (you almost have to be proficient in actual Civil War era gunnery). But the learning curve is worth it, and it puts you in the same shoes as the actual commanders. You feel the tension as you watch an attack go in or a lone brigade desperately holding until its support comes up; you feel the gut-wrenching pain as you watch the number of troops in a unit melt away, desperately hoping the attack is worth it. As a Civil War buff and reenactor, and as a military history enthusiast, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who falls into any of those categories.

Rome: Total War is a superb game, and remains very fun to play even 12 years after release. It was the first of two Total War games to use this engine (called simply TW Engine 2 by Wikipedia), and while its successor had more complex strategic layers, more unit variety, and better tactical battlefields, it somehow lacked the charm of this one, in my opinion. Each faction plays very differently, having access to different unit types and requiring dramatically different strategies, which results in every playthrough feeling like its own epic story. Sure, the game has its inaccuracies, quirks and problems (save often; don't rely on alliances which you aren't paying for; and study your units in battle, as many of them require a little extra micromanagement than they should), but you'll forget about all that the first time one of your onagers takes out an enemy seige tower that was nearly ready to spew a hundred angry Macedonians onto your walls; or the first time an elephant runs amok through a pitched battle, tossing dozens of men aside or trampling them underfoot; or the first time your General's bodyguard makes a desperate final charge into the enemy's rear and actually turns the tide of battle.
To make this game even better, it has a large and dedicated fanbase, which has been producing mods of incredible scope and scale. Projects such as
and
can give you what feels like a whole new game at no cost. It should be noted, however, that most mods require game version 1.5, which is available only through the expansion game
.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game. I dare say that it's one of the most memorable strategy games ever made.

So, I read the reviews. I must admit I was weary about buying this game. Alot of negatives for reasons that are too important for me in a simulator.
However, I commited, and I was pleasantly surprised. It's not as bad as people make it out to be. Sure, the optimisation is pretty poor, dropping from around 60 on highways to mid 20's in certain parts of the cities, and stuttering is freqent. I have played alot of OMSI 2, and I don't ever get above 30 on that, so for me, in a simulator isn't too bad. Does need to be worked on though. The graphics are fairly good. Has the typical really detailed player vehicles and then quite bad AI vehicles, and textures aren't amazing for the rest of the environment. However, in a sim, again, it can get away with it. The colour scheme on this game is unique, but I like it. It has quite a realistic tone, but the bloom is sometimes a bit much.
The AI are pretty rediculous. Stopping for no reason, merging/changing lanes at stupid times without looking, being unable to navigate the roadblocks and heavier traffic efficiently. Ended up having to use the pavement and hard shoulder a few times as they simply weren't moving. I'm sure this is a high priority for the Devs though.
I really like the addition of checking passengers tickets/passes and selling tickets. That's realistic and also gives the player something to do when stopped. Plus being able to play the briefing and enable/disable certain things such as WiFi, toilets, kitchen and other things is fun and adds more detail.
This leads me onto the timings. Arrival estimates are way too late. Driving at the speed limit, carefully, I still made it to my final destination half an hour early. Passengers didn't seem happy the first time but the second time they were happy they were early, so I don't know if it's good or bad.
Playing with a G27 was passable, but needs work. Steering, braking and accelerating performed as they should, but with a lack of any useful force feedback it was pretty lifeless and steering at speed was difficult. There only seemed to be force feedback for the rear axel, and then that only activated over speed bumps. So that needs a lot of work to feel realistic and engaging.
Going to try this game with the Delan Clip when it comes, I'm sure that will be okay.
There are alot of interactive options in the Coach, however once turned on most don't need to be touched again until you start a new game completely. This is farely true to life though, so it's acceptable.
Overall, it's good. It's still got a hell of a long way to come, but it's good and I enjoyed my first time playing. (3hrs straight/2 routes).
I can't really imagine it going on sale, so you know where to get this game cheaper (over $10 cheaper too), which I think is a more acceptable price. I won't be picking up the added bus though, as I think that's likely to decrease in price when the game gets closer to full release.
The thing with simulators is that not everything needs to be perfect. In GTA, we expect a polished game through and through, as the activities you can partake in are so vast. AI cars need to be real models as the player can drive them. Buildings need to be well textured and details need to be maticulous because the player can go anywhere at any time. In this sim, you drive a coach. If the coach is nicely textured and built, handles realistically, and is interactive enough to be interesting, it's okay if the rest of the world and vehicles lack a bit.
Overall, if you have played OMSI and like it, played ETS 2 and liked it, played Train Sim and liked it, you'll probably like this too.

It's got the classic style of strafe and shoot but the modern style of carrying two guns at a time, and with so many awesome weapons to choose from, this was a poor design choice. Who was this game for? Duke Nukem fans. But even they are deterred by the poor choices that designers made. Some of this stuff is even too immature for Duke Nukem. A lot makes sense, like the beginning, sort of. But then you get things like punching aliens in sensitive bits Duke assumes they have, or picking up a turd and throwing it around. Yes, we were able to urinate in Duke Nukem 3D, but that doesn't mean there needs to be more bathroom jokes, or nut-punching. I like the fourth wall breaking, I liked kicking a cyclops eye through a field goal post, I liked the finishers of kicking enemies in the head, or increasing my ego with minigames or looking at myself in the mirror, because Duke will be Duke.
This game has your standard Duke story; Duke gets mad at aliens for stealing his favorite girls, Duke sets out on revenge mission, President hates Duke, Duke flips off aliens AND President, Duke swears and does immature things, fun shooting, fun shooting, fun shooting, minigames, minigames, minigames, and so on and so forth.
But this game makes me think that Duke's time has come to and end. In the late 90s, it was like Duke ruled, but his reign quickly ended with an array of crappy games and this one is no different. Duke has one good game, and unless some serious changes are made, that's all there will be.
I do have one idea for the future of Duke: A game about him getting older and him going in search of a son he didn't know he had, his son is the antagonist, mad at Duke for killing who he thought was his father, but Duke is his father. This gives you all those opportunities for movie references, bad jokes, but having a new experience with new enemies, a new antagonist, and a plot-twist. This would even make it so Duke's son becomes the protagonist in a sequel that could possibly be funded if the game really does change Duke. Possibly even a 2-player co-op sequel where one player is Duke, and the other is...  you guessed it... LUKE. That's right, you'd hear "Duke. You killed my father." "No. I am your father." "That's not true! That's impossible!"
Anyways, onto PROS and CONS:
+ References to previous games
+ Reference to the long wait for this game
+ Ego instead of health
+ Ego boosts
+ Items you can use to change the tide of combat
+ Classic strafe and shoot combat
+ 80s movie references
+ Duke is back
- Duke is back
- Disappointing after the long wait
- 80s movie references may be too dated, now
- Unreal Engine is not used to its potential
- 2-weapon carry limit
- Humor that's just immature and not smart or funny
- Same aliens, less interesting experience
- Physics glitches
- Standard Duke story
- Some really frustrating mini-games
- What's with the low decal count? Least violent Duke Nukem since the original side-scrollers
- All that stupid, f***ing sexism

SWARMRIDERS is a flying dropkick to the face with its frenetic gameplay and eclectic metal tracks.
In a time when distracting us with hollow trailers that blast sh*tty dubstep noise at us is all the rage, game developer Walter Machado shows a rare display of confidence by telling us exactly what we're getting in the box. Through an Update Post and video accessible on the game's Store page, we get an honest look at what's offered. This is a stripped down game, distilled to its essential parts like a scrapyard goliath. (Well, maybe more like a cool Erector Set, it's a small free game after all.)
Desaturated, almost B&W pixel graphics give the game a raw vibe. Shocks of color accent important bits, like player health, bullets, and the enemies' glowing...optical...sensors? It could be their bungholes for all we know, all the more reason not to let them touch you.
Gritty Guy pilots a rocket-bike over a black desert while Tough Chick blasts at an endless horde of creeps with a purple laser shotgun. The longer you last, the more patches/achievements you collect. That's it, now you know the game. No power-ups and no do-overs in this twin-stick shooter. I imagine SWARMRIDERS would gobble all the quarters at an arcade, it's addicting, like licking peanut butter off a knife.
A mass of enemies tears♥♥♥♥♥towards your riders from the left side of the screen, enemies that flank to the top and bottom tend to coral you to the middle right side. It's possible to comfortably stay in that sweet spot early on, but eventually you'll be forced to put your reflexes to the test as you frantically weave around the increasing enemies, sometimes even charging directly into the oncoming horde, gasping for precious seconds of breathing room.
Lasting 150 seconds earns you all 4 patches and achievements, and while not impossible, it can definitely feel like it. Aiming with the mouse feels like the aiming reticle is cutting through a layer of molasses, you may need to externally twerk your mouse sensitivity because the game doesn't have any built-in options (other than "kill" or "die horribly" of course). However, it plays great with a gamepad, the controls are snappy.
Like Machado's previous UBERMOSH games, the music alone is worth giving these games a go. There's post-apoc surfer-metal, groovy cumbia-metal, and even a thrashing of booty-thumping cyber-metal, like something out of a Batman Beyond episode.
The "title track" is my favorite, it plays over the sketchy painting of our two protagonists blasting the gunk out those alien starfish creatures with the maybe buttfaces. It's a melanchololy tune that hints at a dark past and blazing future, which we know almost nothing about because there's very little lore shared by the developer. This game's intro screen gives us one sentence, explaining these events take place hundreds of years before the UBERMOSH games. The lore in those games is more enlightening, but even combined they only give us a few sentences.
I think this is to everyone's benefit though. This way the dev doesn't have to sweat an elaborate backstory, but through pixels and gameplay gives us enough dirt on this series to plant the seeds of our own crazy headcannon (like the slanty-lettered blurb at the top of this review). Walter Machado birthed one of the most fascinating universes in video game history, and he did it with only a handful of sentences! Your imagination will run wild fleshing out this 'verse and its characters, their schemes and motivations, their uncertain future.
Thank you, Walter, for this gift.

I honestly had problems writing this review. With my numerous attempts at writing a decent introduction I found myself thinking about this game much more than I should, considering it is just a dumb, unambitious hack 'n' slash title...
I remembered how this game started a series which never reached completion, as THQ's bankruptcy halted all plans for future entries after the second one. Should we be sad about it? I mulled over all those opinions about War's journey being a calque of successful story of Kratos from God of War. How funny is that? There are so many H'n'S games, GoW did not start them nor was it the best game (/series) of this type. I thought how many people will even read this review, considering that everyone who wanted to own Darksiders already has it, either cursing or celebrating it (or maybe doing simply nothing...?).
Oh? I accidentally wrote something akin to an introduction. Sweet!
At the beginning, I stated that this game is dumb and unambitious. While this is technically true, as the game never overstepped its bounds with its design, there is no reason to label it as "bad". Quite the contrary, you can have a lot of fun tearing apart various opponents, searching for hidden treasures and solving environmental puzzles. Just do not expect any narrative depth or involvement with characters. The story is quite straightforward and the big twist is not quite as shocking as it should be, but nothing can be described as cringeworthy, so that's a plus.
The combat is enjoyable, especially further in the game when your power grows with every upgrade bought from demon merchant, every weapon added to War's arsenal and every ability found. There is also a decent number of enemy types and bosses to unleash your power on and make 50-or-so combos. Add in some finishers and you should have a satisfying combat system, right? Unfortunately... in practice it falls short sometimes, as it is bit less varied than it could be. You might be a bit disappointed once you realize you can get only 3 melee weapons, 2 ranged and, uh, one horn, for crowd control. The number of possible combinations is really small as well and some of them can be unlocked only after the weapon levels up (yeah, you have to use a weapon to level it up and THEN you buy a new combo or upgrade those you possess). Furthermore, the game does nothing to encourage or award combat variety. You can just stand in one place and spam one technique over and over, you get no points for trying to be stylish. Dodging is also a bit strange, as it seems to be a bit too slow but I suppose it makes sense with War. Just look at some artwork of him!
In Darksiders if you are not in combat or exploring (which is really nice, by the way - many nooks and crannies to look into and an ok level design) you are probably solving some puzzles. All of them are quite easy, although you might want to pause for a bit and look around before going for the solution, as in many cases you can find treasure chests or precious artifacts in the puzzle areas, saving you a lot of time you would otherwise have to spend to find that one chest with the awesome armour piece you missed. Quite curiously, many elements of Darksiders - especially puzzles - remind me of the Legend of Zelda series. You go to the dungeon, find a new item, proceed through the dungeon with the help of said item and finally fight a boss... which at some point requires your newly acuired item. Simple and sweet.
What I am trying to say through this review is that Darksiders is a simple, decent game. While it might not invest you terribly in War's story, it can help you relax and have some good time. Who knows, maybe you'll want more? The sequel is supposed to be even better and it is always good to start at the beginning.

The best arena FPS of all time, perhaps tied with its predecessor, Unreal Tournament '99. My 200+ hours are all without having played a single match online and I could easily spend 500+ hours on each game mode. So far I've barely played CTF and played a few matches of each game mode and spent the rest doing nothing but Deathmatch and some Team Deathmatch. This also excludes my huge amount of playtime on the disk version. This games balancing is fantastic, the gunplay is almost arena perfection and the amount of content shoved into this game is insane. I'd happily pay $70+ for this game today (don't get any ideas though, game developers).
++The original Unreal arsenal is back once again making for some more classic Unreal gameplay
++The amount of maps, character models and game modes will no doubt keep you entertained for hundreds of hours
++Movement is entirely unique to the genre, even within the Unreal series itself, and adds up for some frantic competitive arena action
++SinglePlayer tournament ladder is a huge step up from both of the previous Tournament games in the series
+Some really good remixes of UT99 music
+The gore is a large improvement from UT99 (and UT3) and it's awesome to see limbs flying every which direction
+AI is really ♥♥♥♥ing  good
+Huge variety of character models and many choices between them
+Enemy clarification is easy and the game gives you visual and auditory feedback from the games' systems very well
+A vast array of mutators
+Total control of gameplay options in every concievable way and settings to allow you to choose your look and style any which way you like
+Almost every song that was also in Unreal Championship rules
+-The music isn't as good as Michael Van der Bros' and Alexander Brandon's (and other composers) work on UT99 or Unreal but it's certainly not bad, just dissapointing in comparison
-+Maps are not as good as UT99 but they're not bad and therefore not a case of quality over quantity as there's still plenty of both
+-Game doesn't look that good with some unimpressive lighting and an unnattractive art-style. Not ugly, and visual clarification is easy, just not as good as it probably should look for a game from 2004.
-The new game modes are largely filler and gimmicky. Not without their merits, but they're still pretty poor.
-Some maps either seem to limit the movement options too much purposely or weren't made for them in mind, meaning you can't traverse the level as easy
-Performance is okay but high resolutions aren't supported without file editing and to get perfect mouse control you have to do some file tweaking due to the game crashing on Windows 10 if you pick Raw Mouse Input. Game also crashes on majority of Windows 10 computers if you don't get a fix. More of a hassle than anything.
-Maps such in comparison to other instalments in the series
-Accident dodge is infuriating and common. A key to dodge would be far more helpful
-I like the audio, but the actual quality is low and badly mixed
--Playing this as a single-player game is impossible unless you do nothing but deathmatch. You could be the greatest of the great, but when your teammate AI commonly stands around doing nothing and you face the entire enemy team alone in a game of CTF when you have the flag, skill is irrelevant. The AI has so many issues that make any game mode other than deathmatch a pure chore. Here's a list of AI issues: AI are deaf. I have seen a case where a guy was defending the flag but he was useless because he was looking the other way and despite being 2cm away from the eenmy taking the flag he couldn't see them so he didn't know they were there. It's very common to see team mates standing around doing nothing which makes me want to destroy my monitor every time. It's common to see team mates totally ignore the fact that you have the flag or ball and don't defend you and instead run off to grab a link gun. AI love to pick up equipment, even if they have the whole enemy team behind them when they have the flag. AI don't miss with the flak cannon at close range. AI don't miss with the link gun secondary. AI dodge incoming attacks from rockets and etc. even if they're not looking at you and should have no sense of them being fired at them, which is ridiculous. AI have no dodge downtime and can dodge all they like, whereas you have to have a short break before dodging again. The list goes on and on. If you play this for deathmatch solo it is amazing. Any other game mode, including team, don't bother. These issues happen at easy difficulties as well. At Godlike? Team games are up to luck basically.
--Weapon balancing has severe issues. The 2 main hitscan weapons, the Shock Rifle and the Sniper/Lightning Gun are far better than anything else in all situations except maybe the Flak Cannon. Arena FPS is meant to be about dedicated weapons to specific scenarios. There should be no weapon to rule them all, and yet there's two (technically 3).
--Level design is far, far inferior to UT99. The main issue I have with it though is that every map seems to have every weapon on it. That means those 2 all-scenario weapons are on every map meaning everyone's rushing to get those weapons and every game plays the same. In UT99, maps sometimes had a focus on a weapon or a group of weapons. This game has the vast majority of maps having every weapon included, but who cares about the rest when you have 2 hitscan weapons to get.

Despite all the hate it got due to feeling unfinished and buggy, I believe this to be the best thing ever produced in the Star Wars franchise. Because if you look past the bugs, you'll find a deep and (unlike with the original KOTOR) meaningful story. KOTOR 1 was basically the original triology set thousands of years before - it felt like a decent Hollywood movie with some choices available (that still neded up in two generic endings). KOTOR 2, on the other hands, is a deep psychological trip into the darkest corners of Star Wars universe, with phyilosophical questions popping out on every turn, making you question what right or wrong actually are.
In short, if you want a more action-oriented, classic story - roll with KOTOR 1. But if you want a deep and meaningful story with characters that have flaws just like any other real human being - play KOTOR 2. It is an awesome game.

Edit: After a developer reply on how to fix the crashes this runs smootly now (it never crashed since 2 hours at least). So i edited this to reflect more about my experience.
However i still leave this review as negative, mostly since there is no "neutral" button, and since positive would not reflect what I exerienced / felt, while playing it.
I must admit, that I havent progressed further than starting some basic automation.
The UI get's in my way too often, and the tutorial is minimal, not explaining you lot's of things.
Geting into automation is way too tedious at start.
There is some weird sound problems for me too, like if i scan down there in a hallway the shrieking echoes forewer, having me to turn down the sound to an allmost absolute minimum.
While the idea might be nice, the 3 dimensions just make it horrible for me personally, since the grappling hook probably needs hours of training to make you go up and down a mining shaft without dying every second time (after another two hours i found that shooting it repeatedly towards the wall while "falling" down a shaft you can actually land...). Digging deep and then bringing those materials back (automated, not running down there every 5 minutes) is a pain at the start too.
The idea of needing unidentified blocks to scan for research is in my eyes not really good game design. An increased amount of ore or other resources per research would be much more apropriate (or did i not progress far enough still?).
One of the things that hinder me most is the limited energy at start. Just because of this, and for no other reason i run forth and back 10 or more times to just set up a mine and build the conveyors and energy supply for it. While it could be fun to dig it, find a way for the belts and the energy transmition it gets dull, because 50% of the time is "running forth and back for energy".
Some things are really nice in there too. Like distance not mattering for interacting with things, or the "build to me" feature. Unfortunatly nothing of this is explained in the tutorial, and i had to check some youtube videos and guides to even get the basic understanding of the game (and i'm one of those that dont like to have to watch let's plays to understand a game, i want immersion and learning in game).
There is potential in it for sure. And i'll check on it again some time later.
TL;DR:
If you want a stable good factory builder then I recomend Factorio instead.
If you want pure tower defence then there is 100 such games around.
If you want a blend of both and you love 3d then this one is it.

If you like complex games that make you think and experiment and don't mind a little rough around the edges gameplay/difficulty curve typical of a one-man development studio, you'll most likely get your money's worth out of this title.
An interesting and fun take on a survival, factory building, and tower defense game. After crashing on a frozen planet, you're forced to bend that planet to your will in an attempt to destroy the native life threatening your very existence. You'll dig deep and unearth the resources to build ever more complex machines and the defenses to protect them. Don't let the voxels used in the game fool you, this is not a Minecraft clone even though there is a creative mode available. The real draw is survival. If it's too difficult, you could always bring a friend as FC:E is also multiplayer with both local and dedicated servers available!
This is a true indie gem written solely by DJArcas who streams most of his development and is accessable via Steam forums. This title has come a long way since it has come out of Early Access and now has a full expansion titled the Frozen Factory, which further utilizes the chilly methane gas filled caverns found hundreds of meters beneath the surface of the planet. There is another planned expansion that will focus on even deeper layers near the planet's "core".
DJArcas is also toying around with bringing VR to FortressCraft: Evolved. You can't do much except for touring your factory in VR, but it's still pretty neat. You do need a pretty hefty PC to run the game without VR, and enabling VR makes this requirement even more paramount.
Most of the negative reviews are from veteran players that are upset about "recent" changes to the game that force you to
build machines and production lines (a.k.a. play the game). These changes include not being able to carry unlimited amounts of ore in your inventory and being unable to smelt ores underground. This is done to force the player to utilize the plethora of machines and automation at their disposal to accomplish these tasks and craft their factory. I'd like to reiterate that these negatives will have no impact to new players of the game as they haven't been spoiled by these shortcuts. This is akin to the players complaining that there is now fall damage in-game and now have to work around it (yes, this also happened). If you absolutely have to cheat, FortressCraft: Evolved is also Steam Workshop compatible and has mods available that basically enable cheating.

A short, free game given as thanks to the UBERMOSH community, SWARMRIDERS is an endless runner type game mixed with a twin stick shooter and backed by a vaguely industrial soundtrack. Use WASD or the left control stick to move a bike around the screen, and right stick or mouse to aim your shots at swarms of flying robo squid thingies chasing after you.
I've yet to play any of the UBERMOSH games, so I've no idea how this ties into them at all since there's no explanation for anything, but then again, everything about the game is intentionally minimalist. There's only one enemy type, no form of upgrades or real progression, a pretty basic art style, and a handful of music tracks. It comes across not too dissimilar to a bonus stage between main levels of a bigger game, or at the very least like a neat little browser title, but I get the sense it really isn't trying to be anything more than that and is content to be a neat little distraction with some slight challenge, hence why it's being offered free.
It's entirely one-note in almost every way, and while that's not necessarily bad for what it sets out to be, it did end up leaving me wanting more, though not exactly in a good way. If anything, it mostly made me wish for additional features more so than actual content. As best I can tell, unless it was being completely masked by the music, there's no other sound effects in the game. That lack of audio feedback really hurts it and makes it feel devoid of a certain amount of pep and life that I think it would greatly benefit from, especially as I wasn't particularly into the music that it relies upon so heavily and I ended up muting the game after 10 or 15 minutes (sorry to all those that love it). Nor are there any kind of settings or options, so I couldn't do anything to address those issues either. It would have been nice to be able to turn off the cursor whilst playing with a control pad, but maybe that's just me and everyone else would be thankful to have it.
There are no additional modes to try or leaderboards to work through, or even a score to rack up, nothing to do other than last as long as you can and unlock a few achievements. Depending on their skill levels, some might do that their first try and get no more than a few minute's worth out of this, others might spend an hour or two on it and never get bored in the slightest during that time. I do really wish this was something greater with some substance that I could really sink my teeth into and play for hours, but as it is I mostly found it an adequate time-waster that has its charms but that you feel could go a whole lot further if it had just a little bit more.

I love this game. Its bullet physics, and the visceral impact the game displays to you is all awesome, and probably worth the purchase alone at the right price.  However, instead of presenting you with a lot interesting sharpshooter scenarios, the game tends to put you more into a meat grinder, by throwing wave after wave of enemies at you.  There were a few times during the game where I had to make a complex shot on my target.  Those instances were fun.  But, they only lasted maybe 2 minutes a piece.  The rest of the game revolves around shooting Nazi A, Nazi B, or Nazi C, (or Russian A, Russian B, or Russian C).
It stops being a sniper game, and becomes a standard shooter.  The times where I had to time my shots to coincide with artillery shells exploding were awesome.  There needs to be more intersting things like that.  Or, if they are going to force me into a building to retrieve a document, I would like to have some sort of melee or takedown option because I always favor stealth over guns blazing.  Overall, now that I have thought about it enough while writing this review, the game is kind of cheap.  Which can make the awesome bullet cam seem like a gimmick.
I can see how someone would think the entire game was basically that, and the rest is just cheap window dressing (i.e. great bullet cam... lame story, cheap enemies, meat grinder missions, poor voice overs, repetive music).  I'm a little torn on this game, but I can't recommend it.

My friends always try to get me into Team Fortress 2, but there's a slight problem: they're all mad good and I'm hella stupid at first-person shooters. So when Lead and Gold: Gangs of the Wild West came out, I was excited to switch over to that and be on a more level playing field. It's a fun game (that I don't suck at), but I don't think I'll be able to convince my friends to switch over for more than a couple days.
Lead and Gold is a third-person shooter set in the gold rush era (that's the mid 1800s, kids). You play as one of four different gun-wielding badasses out to get rich and mow down anyone else in their way. The characters are pretty standard in terms of gameplay. There's the pistol-packing cowboy, the sniper rifle hunter chick, the shotgun-miner, and the all around rifle wielding lawman.
I love the Old West aesthetic of Lead and Gold. The characters ooze style. The Deputy wears garters and a bowler hat, so I'm pretty much in love with him. And the Trapper is Davy Crockett, reincarnated as a sexy chick. Of course, style doesn't mean the game looks great, because it doesn't. It looks OK, especially for a downloadable title, but it's not pretty.
The game looks and feels a lot like Team Fortress 2, with a bit of Counterstrike mixed in. Each character has his or her own special moves as well as these inherent abilities called Synergies. The characters radiate a positive effect to nearby teammates, rewarding teams for sticking together and acting like a team. As players rank up (by earning EXP through killing enemies and whatnot), the Synergies get stronger.
The six different game modes mostly focus around getting or defending large sacks of gold. There are Capture the Flag type events, mad dash "grab it all" events, and even more classic deathmatch style modes. All of this takes place in small old west towns, mine shafts, rural farmer homes, etc
I like the team dynamic of the game. Teammates can revive you if you get shot down, provided your opponent doesn't come up and blow your face off while you're down (of course you can keep shooting at him too). And the ammo is unlimited, so you never have to stop playing to run around and look for that elusive shotgun ammo spot.
As far as which version to get, it's really a tossup. There are more people playing on the PC servers, but that's probably because the game has been out for a while on Steam. I saw no major differences between the PC and console versions.
Well, I don&#Array;t think Lead and Gold is going to replace Team Fortress 2 for any of the fans out there. There&#Array;s just not a lot in the game, but what is there is fun, stylish, and cool. If you&#Array;re more of a casual multiplayer gamer like I am, then Lead and Gold is neat game. Just don&#Array;t expect to be playing it for months on end.

I primarily play the single player campaign. What makes it great is the way you can vary the difficulty. The enemy AI, the ballistics and the tactical assistance can all be changed. With ballistics set to most difficult, you have ridiculously lot of bullet drop and wind sensitivity. It's still appropriate for the distances at which you encounter enemies in the game,  0 - 300 meters.
At the mosts unrealistic setting, the tactical assistance will give you a little red dot shows you exactly where the bullet will land, which may be way off your aim sometimes. I personally enjoy the game most when all that is switched off, though. Then I get to fire the rifle, see where the bullet lands, adjust, and get my headshot! Of course, it's even more satisfying when I can land the bullet where I want it on first try. In my opinion, all games should have bulletdrop and wind sensitivity like this. If you don't like it, you can reduce it or even turn it off which will make bullets go in a completely straight line.
The AI is as unrealistic as it is in most games. If you fire at someone, you don't expect them to run between cover objects exposing themselves. You expect them to hide and flank you. Flank they do, but they don't hide.
The graphics is excellent. It's really beautiful and hardware friendly when you turn off the nicer stuff. Using playclaw, I've seen that my Geforce 560 Ti is maxing out giving me 1920x1080 @ about 100 fps, while the 4.5 year old i7 cpu is only running at 25%. Depending on how multithreaded this game is, that might mean that I could put more GPU in there and get even better performance (increase the image quality and still run framerates above 90 - my screen can do 144 Hz). There are games that are poorly programmed and will require you to have a ridiculously fast CPU to get 40 fps, while the GPU still only runs at say 30%. That's not the case here. The game engine is excellent, and it shows as the designers have been able to make a really beautiful game using it.
The sound is spectacular. I don't mean that in a completely good sense. The sound quality is great and the sound processing as well. But the sound of my boots echoing off anything in almost every situation is quite unrealistic.
There is a lot of blood from exploding heads in this game. You know you want it.
The game is full of obvious trigger lines, which I think is stupid and takes the edge off the experience. I know that I can sit here for an hour and nothing happens. But if I take one more step, enemies will swarm out. Also, the enemies seem to be deaf, as they may (appear to) be standing around the corner but not still not react to the sound of a sniper rifle.
From a single player perspective, I rate this game a 4/5. What I would have wanted is:
* higher bullet damage (If I aim right, one shot will do but that's not always the case)
* at least twice the campaign length
* some more open settings with longer sniping distances (perhaps 400-500 meters) where it actually gets difficult to hit the target
* a more fluid game experience (less triggery-like) where the enemy will actually eventually find me if I hide, never letting me completely clear out an area and feel safe.
Still, I highly recommend it, as it's fun, gorgeous and can be played in so many different difficulty settings.

It really, really, really pains me to tell you not to buy this game. I want to enjoy it--I do enjoy it, in fact--but I cannot recommend it because it constantly crashes to desktop.
I originally tried to play this game with a Keyboard and Mouse, but I gave up early on when the controls became much too cumbersome. I got a 360 controller a week ago as an early Xmas present, and decided to reinstall it because it would be perfect with my new controller!
When the game is good, it's a fun romp toward a bizarre Post-Apocalyptic wasteland populated by angels and demons, and you play a Kratos-lite a**hole bent on revenge for some or other betrayal that I can't remember. Long story short, it's got a little bit of Zelda mixed in with dicing an endless supply of demon fodder with your assortment of oversized steel weapons.
Unfortunately, not long after reinstalling it, I discovered that it would crash to desktop every time I played, anytime between 5 minutes--and sometimes less than that, even!--to an hour. The game is about as bad as a Bethesda title on Launch Day, but it has little to motivate players from investing the patience to complete it (I'm only playing it because I have nothing else to play at the moment and am trying to clean up my Steam backlog a little bit. I figure I've made it this far, I might as well finish it).
That it has little to motivate players doesn't mean that the game is bad--I'd give it a decent 7.5-8/10 if it didn't constantly crash. And the severity of the issue is compounded by a terrible save system that is governed by your entry into an area, and it will not usually save what you did in an area unless you reach a scripted monster fight/checkpoint, or move to a new area. Picking up items (with the exception of Armageddon blade pieces) will not trigger the save system, either. So if you grab that obscure Abyssal Armor piece and the game crashes--even if you saved manually upon acquiring it, you will have to do all that again when you restart the game.
I have scoured forums online searching for a fix or workaround, but I haven't found one that applies to my machine (I was able to play The Witcher 3 on medium, and this game runs perfectly--except for the crashing--on high settings).
As it stands, do not buy this game.
Buy it. Buy it now.

Plenty of role-playing afficionados will likely claim that the first game is superior, but you can take it from a lifetime Star Wars fan: everything about this game really just captures me.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg, is a great indie strategy game, in which you command either the Union or Confederacy during the Battle of Gettysburg, June 1st-3rd/4th of 1863. The game has a top down command style, with good sound and graphic qualities. The premise is rather self explainitory, yet this game allows for a very immersive view of how the Union and Confederacy fought at Gettysburg, as well as how geography played a major role in the battle.
Honestly, this game is a little light in gameplay features, but the impressive and easy-to-use functionality and mechanics completely make up for it.
I wish that this game was expanded into an entire Civil War game... It would be so good. The mechanics of the game really do have much more potential than just this game. That said, this is a great start, and a great game.

Two Worlds 2 is a good game, but it is not a great game. I really liked the first Two Worlds and TW2 is almost as good, but there are a few things that really bothered me.
The controls seem like they were made for a console game and at times it is rather difficult to have good control with mouse and keyboard even with customization. E.g. run, block and sneak are all on the same key, often causing confusion in the heat of battle (it is less than ideal when you are trying to get some space between you and an attacker and you end up trying to block instead).
The game also clearly seems to give meelee fighters an advantage over casters and archers. My favorite play style is that of a stealthy archer. You can not do that in this game. Sneak attacks can only be done with daggers. Archery in general is rather difficult as the auto aim can not be turned off and it does not know how to aim ahead of a moving target, causing even a high level archer to constantly miss even low level and even slow moving targets from relatively close distance. It is a bit better with sniper mode from a great distance (where auto aim does not lock), but it is really annoying nevertheless. Also there is no first person mode, so your characters elbow tends to get into the way, blocking your view of enemies.
Finally there were also quite a few bugs (dialogue skipping, and wrong shaders getting loaded occasionally, among others) that cost this game points.
On the positive side, I really enjoyed the story (which unfortunately felt a little rushed in the end) and the many side quests all of which are well written and entertaining.  The crafting system is simple and fun.
I loved the lack of classes and the freedom to customize your character skills. There is a lot to explore and discover, which is always nice. The graphics are quite good, though not outstanding for todays standards. All in all a good game for RPG players looking for something to spend some time on. I got it for a real bargain around Christmas and I would definitely recommend it for that price. I would not buy it for the full 19,90 it is costing right now, though. Better wait for another special again.

The game SHOULD be everything I'd like, hardcore theme, attack/defense, fortifications adding a new skill to learn, a bunch of unique operators with awesome gadgets.  However this game has WAY too many issues.
Firstly, spawnpeaking is super easy to do.  The only thing stopping enemies from rushing you is a two second timer before you're detected.  However I've seen a guy sneak out, get detected and get three kills before the game says "Hey, here he is!"  I feel it should be more of a sniper attack deal where you take half your hp after five seconds on top of the detection at two seconds.  Just to keep spawn peaking down.
Secondly, hit registration is horrible.  I've had moments where I sniped a guy in the face, but the game says I missed the shot.  You can say "Oh, every game has latency" however this is coming from a Widow main on Overwatch, who is a sniper, and I end up with an 75+% hit ratio.  This game, I feel I'm downright lucky to hit something.  Which is a MAJOR issue.  You have to learn how to get a hit easier, by not aiming at the person.  Which is horrible to do since that breaks any sense of "Realism" the game is going for.  Let alone a number of hostage/bomb sites that are horrible, such as the fish in a barrel.  A spot where an enemy can easily kill anyone in the room from a small window that they just have to climb up. Ect.  Frankly I say steer clear of this game.  It's clear Ubi and EA aren't able to fix the issues as Operation Health (A time where the game fixes issues) Only served to decrease the time it takes to find a match, yet still made sure all the problems are still there.  I've nicknamed it operation flop more than anything.
Like I said, it's an awesome concept, I should love the game totally, however the execution is abysmal and should be avoided for that reason.

BeamNG is a unique little soft body physics simulation gone car simulator which means it solves a lot of problems with driving looking wrong in other driving games. Things like cars having incredible shock absorbers when landing jumps is not present here. There's no magical forces like in other simulations and cars respond properly to impacts and hard landings. Miles beyond Nextcargame. This is at the cost of CPU performance. You NEED a good CPU for this game. your graphics card doesn't matter so much yet
There are a few things to be aware of; it is an alpha with few features and many bugs present. Currently there's no game as such. Just a way to play with the physics engine. Tire models aren't up to scratch yet so while driving is realistic(ish) all vehicles handle very lazily with a kind of unavoidable floatiness. There isn't a massive quantity of content either. What there is, however, is fun to play with.
If you want a physics sandbox then buy it now. If you want a driving simulator then wait for it to become one. If you want a realistic bridge building simulator... wait for it to become that.
