This is definitely one of the best racing games I've ever played.  Its fun, realistic, and creative, thanks to the dedicated mod community and wonderful devs who keep us updated on their website
with a weekly summary of their work.  I've put at least 20 hours into the game before it came on Steam, and I have no intention of stopping.  This game already has no ceiling to how amazing it can be, and there isn't even any sort of structure to the gameplay.  Its a simple load map, load vehicle, drive to your heart's content affair that is both incredibly relaxing and engagig.  I love making rally courses to run through without wrecking and just running through them over and over.  There is no time limit, no opponents, and no objectives.  Only you, the car, and the road.  The great bit is that each game is a new adventure because there aren't any rules as to where you can and can't go, leaving it up to you to decide how to explore and play with the environment you're given.  And then there is the main selling point of this game: the crash physics.  How the devs did it, I have no idea.  Watching your car get bent in half around a tree after a botched high-speed turn is a sight like no other.  For those of us hell-bent on obliderating our cars, there is a map called "Insane Testing" by Insanegaz on the mod forums featuring spikes, loops, giant stairs, huge drops, high speed cliff races, and all kinds of terrains to smash your vehicle on.
As well as being a great game to play, it is also a great game to mod.  The world editor can be accessed by pressing F12 in game, and it uses a simple and intuitive UI that makes it easy to create your own content.  On the coding side, everything is done in LUA, which is incredibly simple to learn.  Installing mods is as easy as downloading one from the forums, unzipping the package and dropping the folder into the appopriate directory within the game file ("Levels" for new maps, "Vehicles" for new cars, etc.).
Of course, there are a few problems with the game, but that is to be expected of a private Alpha build.  The engine sound is the same for all cars, and the tire screech is not pleasant either.  There is currently no multiplayer, although I expect that to come eventually.   At the time of writing, the dev team is in the process of crafting a massive update nicknamed the "Race Update" because it is to add a structured race system complete with laps, checkpoints, and working AI (non-player vehicles are currently a feature, and they do have AI, but only "Flee from player" and "Chase player", both of which are tons of fun already).  Some of the controls are a little obtuse (I'm sure they're just placeholders that will be changed by Beta), and there isn't any GUI for customizing your controls.  In fact, you have to find your inputmaps.dae file and manually edit things, which is a little annoying, but not a game-killer.  While the crash physics are amazing, the rest of the graphics fall a little short.  As a whole, the textures are somewhat lifeless and the lighting isn't advanced enough yet to add a solid tonal feel to the game.  BUT, the game isn't anywhere close to being done and I am quite impressed at the quality and sheer amount of fun present in this piece of software.

Not really fun for me, but you can see the reviews and notice I'm the odd one out.
The mechanics are very simple: jump and shovel.
This is both a blessing and a curse, as the player doesn't have to overthink the controls, which is great, but also leaves a lot to be desired when you get annoyed with the gameplay.
And I'm surprised not many other people are.
From what I've played it is painfully slow, and since the controls are simple, overcompensates with annoying, difficult levels. There's no dash, so you WILL watch yourself die, over and over, and then get that nice nostalgic 5 second long death screen where you watch all the money you've earned taken from you, followed by another 3 seconds to re-pick the same level on the map. Maybe that emulates the "good old days" but I personally find that frustrating when I'm already annoyed enough and just want a straightforward, no delay way to give it another go. It just feels like a waste of time. Let me press A and re-spawn.
The enemies are just dull nuisances that aren't really dynamic enough for me to give a damn. I feel like I'm grinding my way past them, and when I kill one, I have to wait around to pick up all their gems. Again, it's too slow.
If you find yourself excessively frustrated, and maybe just want to give the story a fair shot, there is no way to turn down the difficulty either, which is really the worst part, because you can't even give it a chance if you wanted to.
I don't recommend this game, but that's just me.

The sequel to the classic Knights of the Old Republic, this crude, notoriously rushed title fails to measure up to its predecessor. The development of this game was passed on from Bioware to Obsidian, king of inferior sequels, and it shows in the finished product. Obsidian added virtually nothing in terms of gameplay, instead opting to focus purely on a new story. The result is a trite experience that necessitates suffering through the same rather dull combat system found in the original. While the excellent plot of that game justified dealing with its combat mechanics, you might find it shockingly tedious to play through another game under exactly the same circumstances. More, the quality of KOTOR II's plot pales in comparison to that of the original.
Buy this game if you're starved for Star Wars RPG gameplay; but don't expect it to live up to the standard set by its predecessor.

The Sith Lords is a sequel; however, it is also a Star Wars sequel, and Star Wars sequels are one of the few that have generally managed to avoid the curse associated with that label.
That being said, this game has always had a bit of a stigma attached to it; it was a followup to a massively popular RPG on the original Xbox and the studio creating it was under alot of pressure to both A) release it quickly and B) deliver another hit. They were given only a year by the publisher to get it together and push it out; the result was a game that was slightly buggy and rushed. While it was fully playable, epic, and far deeper than the game it was a successor to, there were always elements to it that left fans wanting more.
Enter the hardcore PC RPG-gamers and their love for modding. There is a mod for this game - which thankfully, miraculously, works with the Steam version - that essentially restores KoTOR II to its original, intended glory. When Obsidian was making this game, there was a large amount of content that had to be cut from the original version in order for them to make the December 2004 release date; that has all now been restored by a dedicated team of awesome volunteers. All of the idle characters, ineffectual prompts, and sealed doorways that led nowhere in the console version of the game can now be accessed thanks to some clever RPG fanatics and their digging around in the source code of the PC version.
I won't lie; there are still a few glitches and bugs that make keeping multiple save files for a single playthrough an absolute necessity - but all of the cut content - interactions with party members, additional dialogue, ways to make your NPCs more powerful, even an entire extra planet to play through - can be accessed via the 'Restored Content Mod'. This makes an already excellent (albeit incomplete) d20-system-based epic Star Wars RPG even better. Both games are available on Steam, and collectively serve as a prequel to Star Wars: The Old Republic.

TF2, the first-person, team and class based shooter released by ValvE studios on Oct the 10th, 2007, is one of the greatest game's of all time. The gameplay, while there are still issues (hitreg being the largest one) is perhaps some of the most dynamic and interesting of all time. It features 9 distinct classes, each playing completely differently from each other, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. While some classes are definitely better than others, most are applicable in at least SOME situations (the only possible exception being Spy.) Movement is one of the most important mechanics in the game, with only a very small number of weapons impeding others' movements. There are some classes (notably Pyro and Heavy) which are fairly easy to pick up for new players. There are some (like Spy and Sniper) which have incredibly high skill ceilings. And there are some (like Scout and Engineer) which combine both. The game also has over 100 functionally unique weapons, insuring that there is almost always something to do, some new combination to try, or some new application of said weapons. Visibility, usually is very well preserved in maps, with a lot of lighting and very few dark shadows to hide in, the game is very well lit, allowing you to see other gamers in your vicinity. Readability is also incredibly well excecuted in the game. Very few cosmetics (we'll get to those later) both affect readability and are not seasonally locked. As for customization, this game has a lot, with nearly 1000+ cosmetic items, and nearly 750 available to obtain right now, very few cosmetics sets will be the same. Weapon skins also often have randomized patterns.

But in this case I think the technical issues are bad enough to be a non-starter. To clarify, the underlying game is a blast, from what I played, but to get 25 minutes of gameplay I had to put in about 3 hours of troubleshooting across two different (and very normal) computers, a PC and a laptop. There's a solid mix of server problems (uPlay AND another Ubisoft connection, both of which can, and for me did, fail often) which immediately reset your saved progress (it's always-online), graphics problems, and start up problems; all persistent across both computers. More irritating, the demo worked fine after a bit of work, and the full game did not: the demo uses uPlay but seems to save itself a lot of trouble by not attaching your progress to your account.

+ There’s an abundance of different (though basic) gameplay mechanics; from upgrading weapons via blacksmithing, to alchemy, lock picking (surprisingly one of the most fun lock picking minigames I’ve played), and even some stealth mechanics thrown in to offer some variety. And, while the combat is relatively simple, there’s a good variation of skills to use (including ones for melee and ranged weapons, as well as spells) that prevent the combat from being too repetitive or bland, and allows you to tweak your character to fit your preferred playstyle.
- Easily the biggest negative for me is the lack of difficulty scaling. What this basically means is: if you want to play the game just for the main story, you will have an exceedingly difficult time doing so (even on Medium difficulty). The game will force you to resort to cheap tactics in order to beat boss battles/hard encounters and run past most of the enemies throughout the dungeons, unless you complete side-quests (which there are plenty of, but I don’t think it’s fair to force the player to complete them in order to have a fair chance of defeating the main obstacles the game throws at you). This ends up making the game artificially difficult, as no matter how well you utilise or level your skills, you will have a needlessly problematic trek towards the end credits if you don’t complete optional content (unfortunately the final boss itself is rather awful as well, so I wouldn’t blame you if you felt like quitting before reaching the end)
- While there are plenty of side-quests to complete, the world itself--which may be big in scale--doesn’t really encourage exploration. There are simply vast masses of land that don’t contain any meaningful sights nor secrets worth discovering, which is a shame because the world itself is quite pretty
- Again, like the first game, the wooden voice acting and weak sound design in general don’t make much of an attempt to immerse you into the world of Antaloor; though I will admit, the music itself is very charming and partially redeems the sound overall
- Lastly, the story itself is predictable and forgettable; no interesting main characters and nothing that hasn’t been done before.
• Though people claim the game has severe DRM, all it really is is putting in a serial number, and using online activation to verify your purchase (which only needs to be done once). It literally takes only 30 seconds to do so... unless you forget to uncheck the checkbox which tells you to register (which makes you enter personal details, but this isn’t required to play the game at all). But, if you hate ‘DRM’ in any form (excluding Steam DRM), then by all means don’t bother purchasing the game.
“
starts off as a rather clunky experience. But, once you start getting into the swing of things, you will find yourself enjoying the game more and more as you delve deeper into it. While the game is just a basic open-world RPG, with both poor and good qualities mixed together, overall this and the first game have an undeniable charm that makes them memorable (and admittedly better than they deserve to be). With some more polish here and there, this game could be even better than I’m giving it credit for.”

I like this game, yet I should also give a heads up to anyone expecting an accurate civil war simulation, in which this game isn't.
Starting off with the bad, the UI is very basic and gives you no access to formations, or any way of helping my unit to defend itself, where in this time period there were formations a unit could use to defend themselves.  For exa; building fortifications, digging in, nothing like that is in this game whatsoever.  Fortifying was made an option in the mobile version, yet was left completely out for the original.
Many can say "UGG has great AI" or "UGG has fair AI" however both of these are wrong to an extent.  The AI will always get a boost in casualty rate, no matter your choice for playing as the Confederates or the Union.  Selecting a more difficult AI type only results in more casualties for you, despite this AI using the same strategy/tactics as the AI below it.  The AI as a whole is capable of effectively attacking or defending, making it smart, yet higher leveled AI only seems to rely on higher casualty rates, nothing else.
Bugs are terrible in UGG, from artillery disobeying your orders and switching to a different target despite it being in range of the target you wanted it to hit, or infantry not firing, etc.  These are common and should be fixed, they probably won't unfortunately.
The game does a great job in accurately depicting brigades, generals, positions, how the units look, etc.
Overall this an above average game, and I would recommend it if you can get past some of its faults and know anything about the history of the Civil War, or Gettysburg, but for the average person, I do not recommend this game.

Duke Nukem Forever is a shallow, crude imitation of better games released before it. In other words, it's bad. Read on at your own risk.
It's even more puerile than
, and with even less relevance. When 3D came out in early '96, at least that game's aesthetic was an earnest step in a new direction: video gaming entering its adolescence. It may not have been particularly tasteful or mature, but at least it was a better direction than the cynical, even-more-outrageous toxic masculinity and objectification of women on display here.
The developers at one point said their world-building was genius because everyone in-universe takes it completely seriously. It more often comes across as tired, aggressively moronic, disgusting, or a combination thereof. On the rare occasion the writing manages to rise above that, it's still usually not great. In 3D, this sort of stuff, while still a bit cringeworthy, ultimately played second fiddle to the great gameplay. Here, the
seems like it plays second fiddle in both quality and importance.
The only plus I can give the writing is that it's an unwitting dystopia. Duke is our hero for saving humanity multiple times as
is more vulnerable than ever. We see massive monuments erected in his honor, awards bestowed, his own fast food chain, and even a dedicated Vegas casino complex. Thanks to his hero status, normal people are emulating his forceful personality enough that American society has become more aggressive and sexist. This still doesn't make up for all the hamfisted, often outdated references.
DNF makes its alien invasion story feel tiring quicker than it has a right to. There's a couple characters here and there, primarily Duke's friend General Graves and his boss, the less-than-perceptive US President. You'll see the plot 'twist' concerning him a mile away. Captain Dylan the infantry commander is notable for how vulgar he is. The rest are unremarkable or cannon-fodder, with two in particular I'll get to soon.
There are a couple inspired touches, but they're needles in a haystack. For example, whenever Duke is knocked down or kicks open a door, the animation and camerawork is pretty nicely synced - and it's satisfying to kick open doors here. The dynamic, breakable lighting is also a nice touch, as is keyboard navigation in the menus ala 3D.
Then you see another low-quality texture that
have flown in 2004 and you remember what game you're playing. I mean the graphics aren't the worst thing about this game by far, but they stand out pretty early as a sign of things to come. It makes DNF seem like a prolonged boxing match between the power of human talent and the ravages of time.
The writing reaches its nadir in the alien hive, about midway through the game. Here we have - trigger warning, folks - rather graphic depictions of sexual violence against women by the alien invaders. Yeah, I know this was hinted at in 3D, but it wasn't nearly as graphic or tasteless. Here in DNF, it's not hinted at, and we hear Duke snarking at all of it like nothing is out of the ordinary.
Soon you come across two characters that were never more than one-dimensional parodies and servile sex objects for Duke, and this is the important part, right up to their final painful moments.
we come across alien boobs embedded in a wall which Duke can play with and snark about while women scream in pain and horror all around him. The most he can do is mercy-kill them while unconvincingly stating it's 'better this way'. The whole thing is, and I'm saying this with
charity, not the best fit for a parodic series about a manly dude blowing stuff up and obsessing over babes.
Now, the gameplay.
It is largely derivative of Half-Life and Halo, but not as good. Most of the game was dated when it came out, really. Maybe if you're a 'retro gamer' you can appreciate that, but you'll still feel this game should have came out at least 6 years before it did.
DNF's gunplay is serviceable enough not to be totally awful, although it really is more Halo than Duke. The option to carry four weapons (because 'Duke isn't Halo!') makes the game easier at the cost of destroying what little verisimilitude it had and making it hilarious when Duke literally wishes out loud that he had three guns late in the game.
My favorite weapon was actually the pistol, a relatively modest weapon that rewarded accuracy. Most of the other guns felt sloppy and unsatisfying, although the shotgun deserved credit for stopping power. The aiming and movement are just a little 'off', too. Occasionally the movement gels well with what's going on but oftentimes it's just weird.
I was initially surprised by how quickly I was progressing through the campaign, but there's a decent amount there - enough frustration and filler, at least. It took me around 10 hours the first time on Hard difficulty. Some of the puzzles and player directioning hint at competence on the design team, but not enough of it got through. There's enough world interactivity to match DN3D, but without the benefit of being new or unique.
The game's structure is a far cry from 3D's open levels, which would be forgivable if it was good. DNF's story may be in the background, but it's ultimately more of a driving force than 3D's. Said predecessor is masterful in comparison, building off Doom with its labryinthine levels and even less intrusive plot. DNF really wants to be more like
, with linear progression supplemented by spoonfuls of "plot" and even vehicle sections.
Those sections aren't the
driving, like how a leftover $1.50 pizza bagel isn't the
snack. It certainly can't make up for long loading times & small level sizes comparable to Invisible War in their ridiculousness.
I didn't entirely care for the way you increase your regenerating health (or "ego"). Even when it becomes a blessing on harder difficulties, you still have to run away from combat to regenerate. That's hardly "badass". It feels like Duke is more vulnerable and washed up than he thinks he is, whether he knows it or not; further evidence of this is that he only needs to drink ONE beer pickup at a time to get really drunk. It also gave the devs an excuse to mash Call of Duty's influence into their potpourri of a campaign, but I digress.
Overused QTE events, mediocre turret sections, routine boss fights, annoying enemies and encounters that border on unplayably difficult round out DNF's list of features. The Grand Canyon-esque difficulty spikes in those battles indicate a lack of playtesting. For a game that took 15 years to make.
In fairness, the final level & boss battle was surprisingly decent. The giant Enforcer-versus-mini Duke battle was also inspired, even if you had to juke it to win. It's not worth playing the rest of the game to get to either point. Ladders meanwhile are probably the most interesting thing in the entire game: you press a key to get on and you actually
the things. It sacrifices juking potential for actual ease of use.
Multiplayer is old school 'run for the biggest guns' with a handful of diehards. The starting pistol at least proved powerful enough that I didn't die
the time to the weird hit detection, because the weird hit detection also worked in my favor. The My Digs feature might have been interesting if it wasn't partly sexist and if the game was good enough to play and unlock stuff.
DNF is a big disappointment if your expectations are anywhere above the level of 'budget shooter'. Duke was a product of a specific time, a vehicle that didn't need to be revived so acrimoniously to create what is essentially a parody of action blockbusters by way of Adam Sandler. Don't even buy this if you're a masochist. It's not worth it.

In my opinion, this is still the best Total War game to date.
Rome's got good combat, decent unit roosters for different cultures, good siege mechanics & decent city "building/development". You can also build forts & watch towers on the strategic map.
Rome was made before the switch to the new engine, which means that each individual unit actually fight on an individual level, trying to hit enemies & block incoming attacks, instead of the crazy 1v1 kill-animation system. This have a major effect on how battles turn out & how they're conducted. If you got more units of similar skill & situation, they tend to do a fair bit better, instead of it just being a battle of attrition. Projectiles are fairly strong, but as far as I can tell, don't home-in on targets & ready, large shields greatly negate their effectiveness.
I should mention that the music is the best in this title by a land-slide, it's always fitting & it's always get's you in the right mood for the situation.
The one thing you may miss in this if you're used to the later titles is the naval combat, it's automated in Rome. Also, the graphics are very dated. Camera controls are janky & visual feedback is poor compared to later titles.
Compared to the other Total War titles, there's only 3 other games that even come close to being as good as this one: Shogun 2, Medieval 2 & Empire(after milions of patches). I haven't played enough Warhammer to tell how it hold's up yet, but it looks promising.

The game is ok. It looks more like an early access then a full game but this is the problem with all german simulators. They never seem to be full releases.
The game has two modes of play: Arcade and Realistic. In arcade you pretty much think only about driving while in realistic, you need to face a lot of other details like changing gears and passanger requests.
The AI is quite dumb but this makes it more realistic becasue there are a lot of unexperienced drivers out there in real life too. Somehow, the driving feels more realistic then in ETS2 or ATS. Maybe it is because of the map scale which is bigger and the roads are longer. Also, it feels more alive because of the passengers comments on your driving when you are speeding or having accidents which makes it up for the lack of music during driving.
*EDIT November 2017 : They have added a DLC which makes radio in the bus finctional. It is a paid DLC with about 70 songs, mostly in english.
You get to make your own routes and choose what bus stops to add similar to Bus Simulator 16, Probably this is the begining of implementing a sort of company management into the game. Hopefully the devs wont stop adding features to the game and atually make it feel like a full release and not as an early access.
Like all other german games, this too suffers from optimization issues. If you can overlook the 20 FPS then you should buy the game it is neither worse or better then omsi, bus simulator, notruf 112 or cityconomy or train simulator regarding the graphic performance.
Personally, I am dont mind the  low FPS, and I actually get  like 25-30 FPS on low-medium graphics on a lower spec PC then the recomended.
*EDIT November 2017: It seems thay have worked a little on optimization but it is still heavy on the computer but it works very smoothly now with everything on low inluding shadows
A little tip for the people feeling nausea when driving in this game, remember you need to spend some time testing the game settings and graphic options. Remove the vehicle tilt, bloom, motion blur and post processing. Also set anti-alizing to low or medium. It shouldn't make you feel dizzy in this way.
What I like about the game is that it offers the possiblility to select the year date in a calendar and drive the route in winter, spring, summer and autumn. You can also set the time of the day. The nice touch to this options is that you can set your own PC time and date automatically and so it is giving you the time of driving right when you are playing in real life.
You are not earning any money in this game so you can do as many accidents and speeding tickets as you like. They are not affecting you negatively in any important way. The only thing you earn is experience and you unlock some things by gaining levels. i guess it is only 4 levels and you unlock things like Night driving and speed passenger check-ins.
The Skylaner DLC is very good. At least it is the only way to get a new coach in the game. It looks nice and has different sound then the main game MAN's

Thay have faster acceleration but some poor sond. All in all it is worth the price just for collecting more buses. you cna later costomize with various paints.

'If you snipe in a video game, you're a social degenerate.' - ELPRESADOR
As much as I agree with that philosophy, this is the only game where I make an exception. The reason why I like Social Degenerate Elite V2 is because it's a shooter game with a WWII setting. As someone who has enjoyed playing many WWII shooters (mostly Medal of Honor) I just had to try this game, since WWII shooters aren't being developed as often as they used to be. And like those games, this game was very fun to play, particularly because of its single-player campaign.
The campaign doesn’t really have that great of a story. You’re just some guy going around assassinating German scientists that want to defect to the Soviet Union, but Rebellion somehow messed that up and made that somewhat uninteresting. Maybe it’s because the story isn’t that deep or intricate. But again, for me it makes up for it for the fact that it takes place in Nazi Germany. And seeing landmarks in the game, such as the Brandenburg Gate, was pretty cool.
An interesting game mechanic implemented into the game is bullet ballistics, which is wind and gravity affecting how the bullet travels through space. It is easy to learn how it works playing on Marksman difficulty (normal), because using Empty Lung shows where the bullet will travel. (Just without wind though)
I do not recommend that you play the game’s multiplayer because everyone goes full-degenerate and camps like a wimp. Eh, well what do you expect from a sniping game? This is especially awful when playing Capture the Flag because you’ll get killed by someone (most likely with a sniper rifle) who is camping near the flag.
Playing co-op is fun, but it’s strange because many of the co-op missions are not canon to the single-player campaign. The co-op campaign is also strange reason being that the second player isn’t in any the cutscenes. I mean heck, in House of the Dead the second player is shown in the cutscences and that was a game that was released in 1997. However, this does not mean that co-op is terrible. It is quite enjoyable so find someone to play it with.
In conclusion, I’d just like to say that despite some problems this game is probably one of the best WWII shooters I’ve ever played. I might even go so far as to say that it is THE BEST I’ve ever played. Ever. If you want to play an awesome WWII game then you should probably get this game because it is a gem that is truly outrageous. (Hurr durr Jem and the Holograms reference)

This is rather a military simulator than a game.
You'll find that you have to actually learn to play, not in the sense of getting good, but actually getting to know the key binding and various mechanics. For example, you have a separate button for setting up the bipod of your rifle, and can adjust the height of your crouch with ctrl + W/S. You have to know how to display the compass, hold your breath, change stances, use the radio, switch aiming modes and walking speed... Half the keyboard is bound to something, and sooner or later you will need all of it.
The realism also dictates the pacing - you don't run 36km/h, you run 18km/h while sprinting, and you cannot sprint for too long or uphill. Your weapon sways and wobbles if you dont rest it on a bipod or a rock or a tree trunk. You don't charge in and kill everyone - one or two bullets and youre gone. Most of the time youll be walking and running around, trying not to be spoted but spot the enemy. This may be boring for some, but if you want to get a bit closer to actual warfare than Call of Duty, this is a game for you.
Multi is very much about teamwork. Without your teammates, you are nothing. This isn't a game you'd want to play as a "random" - you need a team.

Ok.  Not working on Windows 10?  No problem!  At least until the next Win update breaks it.
Go to C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Unreal Tournament 2004\System
and look for and open UT2004.ini
Find the section with the below entries:
[Engine.Engine]
RenderDevice=D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice
;RenderDevice=D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice
;RenderDevice=Engine.NullRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=PixoDrv.PixoRenderDevice
Replace the "D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice" on the first line with "OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice" (without quotes).
It'll look like this:
[Engine.Engine]
RenderDevice=OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=D3D9Drv.D3D9RenderDevice
;RenderDevice=Engine.NullRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=OpenGLDrv.OpenGLRenderDevice
;RenderDevice=PixoDrv.PixoRenderDevice
I've tried the NullRenderDevice and Pixo and the only one that worked every time on my new machine is the OpenGL though pixo works sometimes.  Once it runs you can play around with the settings as you see fit.
You're welcome!

I really enjoyed learning and testing Life is Feudal: Your Own. Even though it's current content is limited, this game has absolutely AMAZING potential. The concept is truly awesome. However, there are some pretty serious issues with the game.
Aside from exploiters and trolls, the engine the game runs on is utterly terrible. The engine cannot currently support 64 people (or even 20 very active players) without a substantial amount of serverside lag. This isn't something that can be fixed. It has to do with a memory limitation of the 32 bit process that the engine uses. Until they remake the game on another engine, an MMO with 10,000 people per world will be entirely unplayable (no matter how much they break up the world into individual areas with their own server).
Secondly, the combat system, while very interesting in concept, is horrible. I understand what the developers were going for, but what they designed is too clunky to be enjoyed.
Lastly, the developers are doing an excellent job smashing bugs and fixing other errors. Even if they can fix the exploits and remaining game-breaking bugs, it is still difficult to recommend LiF:YO for $40. The server and engine issues cannot be fixed without using a different engine. The only exception would be if someone has ten to twenty friends to play with and are willing to wait a few months for more content.

Lead and Gold, is a third person multiplayer shooter taking place in the mid 1800s, in which two teams (red and blue) battle out each other across various gamemodes, or you can play co-op with another buddy and fight off waves of enemies. Note: I haven`t played all the objectives at the time being, due to the lack of players, I may edit this if I ever get a chance to play more objectives.
So lets get to it:
What I like:
- Graphics arent too bad for a 2010 game.
- It is fun, especially for a casual gamer.
- 4 types of "classes" or characters that have they`re own advantages (we have the blaster, who basically has a shotgun, we have the gunslinger who is also for close range but has a high rate of fire with his pistol, we have the Trapper who is basically a sniper and also has a pistol, and lastly the deputy who has a rifle which can shoot medium-long range.)
- Teamplay is promoted, health regen is faster when you are with your teammates, as well as the revive mechanic
- Sound isnt that bad, although would prefer if characters said something to give them more presonality.
- Movement is crsip and good and responsive.
What I dont like:
- First and formost, the lack of players is really noteable in this game, which is shocking, given the fact that the developer gave away over 300,000 keys for this game. (there are literally 2-4 servers at a time, thats it)
- Gamemodes arent really original (Shootout which is basically team deathmatch, conquest, gold fever which is basically co-op for 2 players, greed where the objective is to get as much as gold sacks to the team`s drop zone, robbery where the attacking team has to destory the bank vault and get 3 gold sacks back to their dropzone, powderkeg where one team defends and the other destroys the objectives with powderkeg).
- Lots of lag due to the lack of players.
- Also, there is zero motive to keep playing this game, what I mean is that there is no real progression (or leveling up) system in the game nor there is any character customization, and there arent any real stats of you, unless if you go to dig your stats in the leaderboard.
- 5v5, I want there to be more players, 5v5 is alittle less, but then again given the small playerbase, it doesnt even matter.
- It would also be better if there were more maps and maybe more gamemodes as well.
- Boring menu screen.
- UPDATE: After playing the other gamemodes, I have to say they all just feel more or less the same.
LASTING APPEAL: THIS GAME HAS GOOD VISUALS AND GOOD MOVEMENT AND IS REALLY FUN TO PLAY AS A CASUAL THIRD PERSON SHOOTER WITH THE 4 CLASSES, BUT THIS GAME IS KILLED TO THE FACT THAT THERE IS A LACK OF PLAYERS, LACK OF ANY PROGRESSION SYSTEM AND LACK OF CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION AND IN THE END NOT GIVING THE PLAYER A REAL REASON TO KEEP PLAYING THE GAME. I WILL RECOMMEND THIS GAME, AS I HAVE RECIEVED IT FOR FREE, BUT AT THIS STATE I CANNOT RECOMMEND FOR PURCHASE.
8/10 - FREE
5/10 - FULL PRICE

Quite the fun multiplayer shooter, but has some problems with cheaters and there aren't many players. Somewhat recommended.
The game features 4 classes with distinctly different capabilities, but it's also well balanced enough that all 4 perform well and get picked fairly evenly. So even though the game's no longer in development, it's still fun to play because nothing is overpowered. Unfortunately, there's the occasional cheater. And even 1 is enough to ruin a game. Usually it's someone who's playing the one class that has an indirect weapon, and throwing that weapon very accurately at people they don't have in their line of sight. Or ambushing them with suspicious frequency. I'd wager there's a working wallhack for the game out there in the cheatosphere.
Still, when there are a few players and nobody's cheating, it's one of the most fun shooters I've played.
Especially noteworthy are the classes. They're all fun to play. Two of them are a short-range shotgunner and a long-range sniper, whuch have to, respectively, rush in or stay at a distance to be effective. The other two are the short-mid range revolver guy and the mid-long range rifle guy. The reason they all work is that pretty much all the maps are varied enough to allow it. There are usually some open areas that allow sniping, plenty of buildings for short range skirmishes and plenty of cover all around. And the characters move fast and rarely die from a single shot. So firefights are exciting and full of movement and usually last a few seconds.
One of the unique things about the game is that when you run out of health, you get knocked to the ground instead of dying immediately. You stay knocked down until an enemy finishes you off, you choose to respawn, or a teammate revives you. And a couple of seconds after being knocked down, you become able to shoot slowly and inaccurately with your sidearm. Still, most of the time you'll just end up getting finished off almost as soon as you're knocked down.
When you do die, you can respawn either in the base or on the spawn flag, which any player can pick up from the base and carry around until they get killed. When the flag is dropped, players can still spawn on it, and teammates can pick it up. If an enemy picks it up, it's teleported back to base. This is a cool way to let players jump right into the action.
And it also tends to keep most of the team close together, which is great because of 2 other features - synergies and healing. Synergies are bonuses that every class gives to every teammate in range, but they don't stack. So to get full bonuses, you need 1 each of the 4 different classes reasonably close together. And you also get a slow passive healing effect if near teammates.
This passive encouragement of team play is great for the game's CTF-style modes. Except it's actually Capture The Gold, and when you're carrying the sack of gold you're super slow, unable to jump, unable to shoot, and can be seen by enemies across the map. So you need your teammates to cover you. The same goes for modes that require carrying a barrel of gunpowder, with the added danger of the barrel exploding after a couple seconds if it gets hit by a bullet.
Other game modes are the typical team deathmatch and capture-the-point.
Maps are generally good, and some feature oldtimey machineguns in fixed positions, which are fun to use. Although one of the maps has a machinegun in a rather overpowered position near the center.
The maps generally prevent enemies from getting into the spawn area, but a lot of the time the fighting will be around one of the spawns, with the attackers throwing dynamite into the spawn. Usually though, the defenders can hold their own, unless there's one of the aforementioned cheaters among the attackers.
Gameplay aside, the game has a nice atmosphere. The visuals, character designs, maps, sound effects and music are all consistent with the semi-comical Western feel the game is going for.
Finally, at the time of writing, the game is somewhat short on players. It's rarely possible to play outside of evenings in European timezones, and even then there's rarely more than one game going and often none at all, with some players joining if I host. Since this is a multiplayer-only game, a further dwindling of players will make it worthless. But, fears of a multiplayer game running out of players are often a self-fulfilling prophecy, so don't let this stop you. It's a good game, worth your time.

Sniper Elite is an interesting write-up here, cause it has equal amounts of ups and downs. I didn't play the co-op or multiplayer, just the campaign. It takes place entirely in Berlin in 1945 at the end of WW2 and draws a number of gameplay elements from Half-Life, Thief, and puts them into a WW2 shooter. Although it's not a shooter in the general sense of the word; it utilizes a narrative progression like Thief and semi-linear levels like Half-Life, and that's where the ups and downs come in. The levels are very linear compared to what a sniper might really be in, and there isn't a whole lot of calculating and planning of your moves. The AI is a mix of both smart and dumb, will detect you from absurd distances and sometimes spawn RIGHT where you just were/checked.
It's a gorgeous game with interesting mechanics and fair bit of polish, but i definitely ran into a few bugs of stuck AI, shooting through objects, and other minor glitches. The pros are very satisfying slo-mo cams, explosions and general shooting handling, but it'll likely be either a moderately entertaining playthrough, like it was for me, or it'll be too simple and linear for some. Still worth playing, and looking into, especially if it's on sale.

I feel like i have enough experience to fully know this game inside and out. I bought it in 2008 for the xbox orignally, after playing the first one. Actually I didn't know a sequel existed until a year after I finished 1. I needed it so bad I would not leave my parents alone.
Playing it then it was a ♥♥♥♥ing experience that I loved, but I didn't think matched the first one. Now I see it's because I was younger and I wasn't fully capable of understanding the subplots and characters here. Then, the happy sci-fi star wars adventure Kotor 1 offered was unbeatable to me.
The first thing that will stand out to Kotor 1 veterans is the game is just darker. The UI goes from a blue to a more drab green/olive. The environment is darker as well, with planets set at night, during a dark tropical storm, in space (dark), in space stations where everyone is murdered except you (it's also pretty dark and in space). The one planet that reminded me of Kotor 1 was Onderon. The cityscape nature and cantina brought me back to Taris. The storyline of 1 was you're just a small time Republic soldier who survived a Sith attack on his ship, turned out to be force-sensitive
, trained, and saved the galaxy following a quest to two of your favourite Star Wars universe planets and some beautiful new ones.
The storyline of two follows a new Sith that emerged after the pyrrhic victory of the Republic in 1, or their defeat as you can choose how 1 ended. As opposed to Malak's sith in 1 that sought to build his pseudo fascist empire, the new sith only want the complete genocide of the jedi. They are not a militant force, relying on cloaked assassins to stalk and jump you. You must track the remaining jedi council survivors to stop this threat, as well as find out what truly happened to you and your exile. The characters in 1 were great and I remember them all fondly, but 2 offers characters that you don't just like, you understand. The usual example is Kreia, who will explain to you her take on an indivualist type philosophy she follows, trying to mentor you. Whether or not you follow her teaching and prove to be her greatest student is up to you.
The next thing that I believe stands out is the soundtrack. Jeremy Soule isn't composing this time, now it's Mark Griskey, whose OST is very subtly but noticeable different. With the theme of the game, the new soundtrack is more ominous and brooding. Soule's music is great, Oblivion has my favourite OST of all time, but in 1 his battle music was weak imo, Griskey's battle music is really inspired and goes perfectly with each setting. His "peaceful" music is fantastic as well.
The combat is more of the same, no new feats or anything. New animations tho really makes you feel like you're beating someone's♥♥♥♥♥now instead of ripping their heart out like in 1. wtf was that grabbing animation for melee combat. it looks way better to fight now.
However, the game was super rushed, Obsidian really has bad luck with that. Highly recommend downloading the restored content mod- now avaliable on Steam Workshop®! It adds new cinematics, dialogue, characters, and quests. Basically it completes the game.

I consider this a must play for anyone who likes Star Wars, sci-fi, a great story, or an immersive universe.

All honesty though, this game has come quite the way from it's original conception. Back in the day Unreal was an amazing shooter and still to this day still holds highly to it's acclaim. The mods have helped significantly to keep the game interesting.
Unreal Tournament is most likely known for it's obscene commentary, extreme gore, and weapons that aliens look like they developed. Before you start playing multiplayer, there is a campaign available that will get you ready for multiplayer. In UT, you may customize your character from a large select group of races in which each have their own attributes. The guns in this game are absolutely fantastic. They range from basic shotgun and rockets to energy weapons that will vaporize an opponent. I should say the guns are one of the main reasons why this game got so big; the fact they also introduced alternative firing with both the same amount of strength really plays to the shooters advantage. The game play itself compared to other shoots is a little fast as players move throughout the map with speed.
is quite basic but includes sprinting, crouching, jumping, lateral movements and double tapping a movement button will make the player roll forward. Like Halo, you won't find many players standing still to take a shot as you are absolutely vulnerable when not in motion. What blew my mind was one map I played online where I was not only able to enjoy the basics the game came with, but some crazy yahoo out there took his time to make vehicles (that resemble warthogs), ghost sort of looking vehicles that can jump vertically up and down, tanks and of course a ship that flies through the air. The mods get pretty crazy and some maps feature fixed guns. Game modes that are available in this game are standard deathMatch, team deathMatch, capture the flag and double domination (which is sort of like King of the Hill). Upon killing a lot of opponents or collecting adrenaline, players can use it for regeneration (Down, Down, Down, Down), invisibility (Right, Right, Left, Left), faster rate of fire (Up, Up, Down, Down) and faster movement speed (Up, Up, Up, Up) - (pint size and berserk are also available but I do not know the proper combos... yet). This adds an extra depth to already an enjoyable game. Picking up more health, armor or even ammo is quite easy and shouldn't be too much of an issue to get the gun you want. It's how much can you dodge while you're getting there. I should also add the maps I've come across so far have been superb.
The
are as good as they can be for their age and an update to them could make or break the game. It's vintage-ness is what's really appreciated.

If you're a fan of Shadow Warrior (The Reboot and the original) you will love this. It's slightly different, less linear due to the (Alleged) partially procedually generated levels. But overall, the♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, the combat. Arcadey and ♥♥♥♥ing incredible.
We got wang, we wanted more wang, we got more wang. That's the way(/ng) it goes).
I completed the Story Mode and All Side Quests (And a majority of the achievements) on No Pain No Gain (Insane) Difficulty in roughly 40 hours. As someone who is a completionist, I was surprised that I didn't even need to get all Achievements just to get my money's worth.
As someone who wholeheartedly values the logic of £1 Should Equal 1 Hour of Game Content, [Cheers Spoole], this has thouroughly impressed due to the length alone.
On to the basics;
Overall I loved the look of this game, especially with the HDR option enabled for my 4K panel. Looks beautiful at max settings without, but colours obviously look more vibrant with HDR enabled.
This game is very well optimized. I have a 6600k OC'd@4.2Ghz, GTX 980 at stock speeds and 16GB DDR4 Quad Channel at 2400Mhz. I have played through this entire game twice now at 1440p, Max Settings. 60FPS without dropping a frame 99% of the time (Motion Blur, Chromatic Abberation, Film Grain, etc, were disabled, they make games look worse IMO) the only time I dropped frames was when I encounted some very weird but incredibly rare physics glitches that causes dead enemies to connect with the level environment, causing framerate loss. But I doubt most people will even encounter this.
Combat is smooth. And I mean smooth. Responsive, sharp controls. Dodging and slashing, connecting hits on enemies you can't even see makes you feel incredible as a player. It makes you feel cool, it makes your wang very, very hard....Not to enjoy as you cut enemies to bits with the procedual cutting system that really just adds to the experience in a practically minor, but aesthetically major way.
Pros+
+Optimized for all sorts of set ups and GPU's. Widescreen, 4K, 144Hz, SLI. You name it, this games got it. That's just how it ♥♥♥♥ing should be.
+Gameplay is silky smooth, responsive, fun, engaging. Combat can be as slow or as fast paced as you want it, Enemies always keep up (Or Vice versa)
+Game length is notable. Longer than the first game at least. I completed the original Shadow Warrior Reboot in just 11 hours. But this lasted, as previously mentioned, 40 hours on my first playtrhough (Although I did die a fair amount of times in the early stages of the game when I had crap weapons (and no weapon mods)
+Soundtrack is excellent. Really blends with the combat well, helps keep you focused. Which is what game music should be used for.
Cons-
-Certain characters...All characters, fail to be memorable. Character relationships come and go in minutes and when you do finally take interest in a character, or part of the narrative it's already done and dusted before you can truly become invested.
(Sub-Con based on first Con) -Kamiko is nothing like Hoji. No witty banter, just a couple of jokes and insults thrown about. But she isn't an endearing character. She's not interesting because the story doesn't try to make her such.
-Story is too short on it's own. Between missions you feel like there is some diaglogue or content missing.
-Weapons can be achieved at certain later points of the game, but are useless due to one easily finding or being awarded better weapons from earlier quests, ultimately making the weapon count partially inflated..
Overall, in conclusion. There is enough wang to go around!
No regrets.

It's a fun game that has a lot of annoyances that add up fast.
-Line of sight, while good in theory, is completely broken. At times I would have regiments have to walk to within 20-30 feet of enemy regiments on the same level in order for them to start firing (and of course the entire time that they're walking up, the enemy regiment is shooting them to bits).
-Morale is broken for the campaign. I don't know why they wouldn't have your troops get a morale boost inbetween engagements. The amount of times I started a battle with troops already about to rout was ridiculous. And then of course your reinforcements come in and are all ready to rout as well. No reason morale shouldn't be at 50% minimum at the start of a new engagement as opposed to 10-15%, particularly if you've had nonstop victories before.
-Speaking of routing troops, this game suffers a major Total War flaw in that when one of your regiments breaks, they don't always retreat back towards you. I've seen countless regiments of mine break and proceed to run straight into the enemy army and just get annihilated. I just had an engagement where one regiment broke at 850 men and then proceeded to run around in circles in an open field why enemy artillery just destroyed them until they were down to 250 men and stopped retreating for some reason.
-Charging seems to be broken. I tried it twice and both times my regiment charging engaged the first enemy regiment and then just kept walking through the first regiment to try and fight the ones behind it all at the same time. Maybe it was just some weird glitch for me but I quit trying after I basically lost two separate 1,000 man regiments from them doing that.
-For some reason, having my troops on an elevated position and firing downhill at an enemy regiment results in my men taking more casualties regularly (I recall at least four separate occasions where I had 1,000+ man regiments with high morale and only facing one enemy regiment had this happen to them). I'm not sure I understand that logic.
-The amount of time in engagements is pretty short. You can't ever wait to setup your forces before attacking because you'll have no time to actually capture your objectives.
-The fact that I did a campaign as the CSA and had three different maps where I captured both Round Top and Little Round Top is just stupid, no more explanation needed.
-What constitutes a victory/defeat is pretty inexplicable. I'll have a map where I inflict more than 8,000 casualties on the enemy than my own casualties and capture all but one of the control points and have it say a draw.
-It also seems that the casualties don't actually matter much from past engagements. The AI always has several thousand more troops than you every engagement, regardless of how many you killed the previous one.
This game is fun for about an hour or two before you want to just break your computer after all of these things add up. It has a lot of good ideas that just weren't executed well. The fact that troops don't get a morale boost inbetween engagements is inexplicible, particularly when you go to the next day. Line of sight is broken for the most part. I know this seems completely negative and that's mainly because most of the top reviews already outline all the positives from the game so I don't feel like doing the same. Like I said, it's fun for an hour or two and I do enjoy it. There are just a lot of small things that seem like they could be easily fixed but aren't.

What i like about sequels is that you get to compare previous game to a new one and you can see what developers wanted to change, how they improved the game what elements they removed and so on. Shadow Warrior 2 is truly a big step from the previous game that was released in 2013, going with new engine and getting rid of linear boxy levels and adding open maps where you can roam around and choose your route to objectives, loot chests and fight demons & Yakuza.
In multiple ways Shadow Warrior 2 did everything that it should've - they kept cool sword abilities and guns and added some more customization to them via new gem system (Similar to Diablo, where you socket stuff into weapons) they removed stamina altogether and added Chi system that lets you use certain abilities like heal, stealth and Chi wave among other things. Instead of going via level by level in linear manner, now SH2 has a Hub system where you can enter shops and pick up side quests.
While the game still does crash alot in Co-op i think its rather great addition to the series and gameplay is rather fun. If your reading this review from weeks after release i bet its already fixed. I really did enjoy this game overall, however I would not spend $13.99 on it at this moment. This game is well made graphically and most interactions happen without a hitch! The graphics are nice and the overall feel of the game is good.
However, a few points that I was not a fan of is the music in the game, there are only like 3/4 tracks that play on a loop and they feel more of music in the game, as opposed to background music. What I mean is that you're more aware of the music being there and always being there and being on a loop, that it gets annoying at times.
Okay, "music not that big of a deal, I play it on mute and have my own music playing in the background" exactly, it's not a huge deal at all, just a slight annoyance at times.
This game is also very
hand-holdy at all. Which is both good and bad.
It's good because it lets you get right into the game without annoying tutorials taking up your entire first week/month of the game, so that's really nice.
On the other hand, because of that the game is very much just "Okay....GO!" and you just start wandering around until things happen.
Which, I do get part of this game
exploration, and the exploration, map size, things to see are really nice, vast, large, etc. I loved the exploration in this game and how large the maps were and the things to do and see in each of them! It really made the world a lot more interesting than that of like Stardew Valley.
Overall, I would recommend this game, but not yet. There is so much that can be done with this game that I am excited to see where it goes from here, as it is still in Early Access. I will certainly be following this game and wanting to see what happens in it, because it was good, but not quite there yet(I feel anyway)
Maybe one day I will feel it's worth that price tag, but at this moment I would feel more comfortable spending $7.99-9.99 on this game. But that's just my opinion and I certainly wouldn't tell anyone to
get this game and support the dev team, as they did a great job and I'm excited to see what they do with it!

This is the first game I have purchased while still in the Early Access stage. Normally, I steer clear of these as I have heard so many horror stories about games never being finished and the developers basically running away with the money paid to them. However, the previous reviews had mentioned constant updates from the developer, and... WOW! They were not kidding! This simple farming sim game in the vein of Harvest Moon and others like it appears to be as much of a passion project for Hudell Tales as Stardew Valley was for Concerned Ape.
Please do not let my low play time for this game (half an hour, at the time of writing this) deter you from taking my words to heart when deciding whether or not Orange Season is a game you would like to spend your money on. I have played every Harvest Moon title since Friends of Mineral town, even so far as to continuing with both the Harvest Moon series and Story of Seasons games following the split between Marvelous and Nastume. Stardew Valley is my most-played game on Steam, and I even have it for the PS4 because I adore it so much. So, believe me when I tell you I have plenty of experience with these sort of games and can tell when I see a good one - even if it is still being developed.
I'm not going to lie. There are a few issues I ran into with the game, but these were mostly just small bugs and they've already been ironed out as far as I can tell. Bugs such as these are going to be present in a game which is still in Early Access, and it bugs me (pun not intended) that people always seem to focus on them when reviewing a game which has not been "officially" released. Any such issues I have had have been MINOR, and have not affected the gameplay as a whole to the point where I had to scrap my save and start over.
One of the biggest problems I have with the game - which is more of a nitpick than an actual problem - is the lack of choice in the character creator. While I appreciate that the developer has recently added in the ability to play your character as transgender (yay inclusion!), you still must play as the generic male or female model type with only the ability to change hair and skin color. Yes, I know the Harvest Moon/Story of Seasons games are pretty much the same, but Stardew Valley gave us a wide variety of things like hairstyles and clothing items to choose from in order to make every character unique to their player. I am hoping more options will be added into a later update. Yes, I know mods are a thing for the game... but I have not installed any of them and probably won't until after the game's final release in order to preserve things as the developer intended them during the ongoing development cycle.
It's saying a lot when the only true complaint you have is a lack of variety in your own character model, I think. That's why I can confidently say that anyone who is a lover of farming sims and/or a fan of Stardew Valley and looking for a little more of that sort of game to scratch their itch should seriously consider picking up Orange Season. Even with the game still being in Early Access, you will not be disapppointed! On the contrary, with the constant updates and additions from Hudell Tales, you will only have more to look forward to as time passes with this game in your library.

Amazing platformer. It looks like one of those typical Indie games with 8 bit graphics and soundtrack but where Shovel Knight truly excels is its gameplay. Since the difficulty's steadily increasing with each new level, the game proves to be quite challenging and even frustrating, especially for beginners (with DS esque gameover mechanics where you drop some of your gold/souls after dying but only have one chance to pick it up). But just like DS, once you get the hang of it, the game's actually really fun to play!
Right now there are only three campaigns available (Shovel of Hope, Spectre of Torment and Plague of Shadows) but they aren't too long so you get bored after a while but at the same time not too short that it might leave the impression of an "incomplete" game. It's just the appropriate amount of time for an indie game.
The soundtrack by Jake Kaufman's very impressive and manages to make the game's world even more vivid. Even if you die a million times at the same spot, you just want to stay for that awesome level music, or wouldn't you?
So as you see I really enjoyed playing Shovel Knight and... you know what? Just buy the game. You'll see soon enough what I mean.

I just looked at how many hours I've played this game and I was surprised to see the number 75 before me. 75 hours. Then why do I still feel like I haven't gotten enough of this game? No seriously, I can't get enough of this game! I LOVE THIS GAME!!
I love the control, the graphics, the lighting, the cheery tunes, the day/night cycle, the dynamic weather system, the amazing repaints from dedicated fans of the game that can be found in Steam Workshop, the exquisite attention to detail on buildings and surrounding objects, the horrible traffic that can drive any man completely insane, the police inspections, the terrible roads I have to drive thru when road construction is underway, the immersion level of dealing with highway traffic, the frustrating realism when I have to re-plan my route due to roadblocks, the ability to exit the vehicle and have the option to take a peaceful stroll and enjoy each city's unique sights (as long as I can remember to respect my work schedule that is).
Now don't get me wrong, this game wasn't all flowers and rainbows when I first got it. I had quite a few issues, plenty of game crashes and those dreaded moments of despair when I thought that the only thing I could do was just give up but thankfully, to some good old tweaking, lots of googling, opening up topics on the game's Steam discussion page or in TML-Studios community forums I managed to get great support from other gamers with similar issues and from the down to earth developers who always offered their great advice and eventually resolve my issues. What I really like is the excellent level of communication between the devs and the players which eventually leads to a constant flow of patch updates that only makes the game better and better.
I am looking forward to what the future has in store for this game. I would like some changes made and hopefully some new features that will add to the immersion and realism in the game like for example: more expansion maps, the ability to adjust our driver's seat position and also adjust our vertical viewing position, getting an auto re-route of our destination on our NAV system when facing a roadblock, multiplayer feature, more new bus designs as dlc and finally to maybe someday have the ability to actually be able to mod the game to our hearts content!!
To sum up, I most definitely recommend this game to each and every one of you, whether your're a sim fan or not, this is an experience you'll always remember.

From the convoluted interface to the zombies on the bus stops to the lackluster physics, this IS still a decent attempt at a game. An attempt, no more. Another ten years of education for the development team and we just might have had a game. This product is certainly not a game.
As King Arthur said in one famous movie, "You make me sad". This is precisely the feeling I got from playing this. I always have high hopes for German releases (my father is German, I know well the punctuality and commitment to precision and quality that they usually display) but this time I really feel let down. Remember OMSI? Now, that IS how you do things the German way - a bit bland, but polished to the very extreme. This thing... it does not show a single hint of a promise there.
A gtreat premice, and a very amateurish execution. If the team does nail it down some couple of years along the way, I will be happy and re-buy it. For now... let them prove themselves and the we will see. In the meantime, I would advise agaist buying this.

This is rather a military simulator than a game.
You'll find that you have to actually learn to play, not in the sense of getting good, but actually getting to know the key binding and various mechanics. For example, you have a separate button for setting up the bipod of your rifle, and can adjust the height of your crouch with ctrl + W/S. You have to know how to display the compass, hold your breath, change stances, use the radio, switch aiming modes and walking speed... Half the keyboard is bound to something, and sooner or later you will need all of it.
The realism also dictates the pacing - you don't run 36km/h, you run 18km/h while sprinting, and you cannot sprint for too long or uphill. Your weapon sways and wobbles if you dont rest it on a bipod or a rock or a tree trunk. You don't charge in and kill everyone - one or two bullets and youre gone. Most of the time youll be walking and running around, trying not to be spoted but spot the enemy. This may be boring for some, but if you want to get a bit closer to actual warfare than Call of Duty, this is a game for you.
Multi is very much about teamwork. Without your teammates, you are nothing. This isn't a game you'd want to play as a "random" - you need a team.

My first impression of this game was graphically it looked very appealing. Upon further playing it, I found odd simplistic qualities that somehow was able to grasp my attention and keep it. I easily spent an hour in this game my first time before realizing how much time went by. This can be a good strategy game for some while others may find it extremely boring. This game will either appeal to you or it simply won't.
Ultimate General : Gettysbourg throws the gamer in a room staring at soldiers on a battlefield that sits comfortably on some table. The story follows the American civil war between the Union and the Confederates. The difference here is that history can potentially re-write itself and that battles can carry on for days. The
itself is actually quite simplistic and very easy to use. The challenge is how to approach each situation (like any game right)? In this particular game, one does not simply produce units out of a factory or thin air. Rather, units every so often may come as reinforcements. Depending on the battle, reinforcements may not come at all or very late in the game. I'm not a huge American civil war buff so I cannot comment on the accuracy of everything historical in-game. I can mention, however that there are a lot of facts and a timer that will try to accurately end the battle. The battle can obviously go longer than expected but going too far over the original clock will stop the game. Everything seems as accurate as can be to me.
There are different units that have different abilities in game. Union units are more technologically advance while Confederate units excel at close quarter combat. Skirmishers are basic units that do not have too much range but are obviously meant for close combat. Archers have a longer range but aren't as efficient in close quarters. Artillery is a cool unit type that the player can use to decisively manipulate the outcome of the game. Artillery is able to choose between shell, canister and solid shot. Shell is mid-range and will hit units in the target impact area. Solid shot is used from afar but cannot take out as many units as shell does. Canister is sort of a rapid fire feature that can take out many soldiers in one go. Issue here is that the artillery has to be in pretty close range to reach the units. Grabbing any random unit and watching them follow the arrow you've so nicely drawn out on the map is satisfying. Selecting individual units can be done by simply clicking them. To select more than one group of units, click and hold the left mouse button and freely draw a circle, encircling the units that you want to pick. I find this to be a neat feature that others games should perhaps follow. Choosing exactly who you want is a lot more powerful that picking specific units with a square.
The AI is definitely no push over. They will react in real time to whatever movements you make on the battle field. They can also get extremely annoying (in a good way) with their artillery that'll blast you from afar. Troops owned by the player also have a mind of their own. If they are getting bombarded and completely destroyed they will retreat on their own will. It can be annoying watching troops run away from a fight but they can come back and support when they calm down. Orders that could be given to units is move, run, fallback, hold and charge. Charge will have your units engage in hand to hand combat with the opponent. The Confederates have the advantage here as they are given a more aggressive stance.
The
are appealing and are done decently well. You cannot zoom in all the way to see the blast effects but smoke/gun effects are all there. The HUD contains some useful (and colorful) information for the player. These four categories are quite important : morale (green), condition (blue), cover (yellow) and reload (red). The higher morale means the better your troops will perform. Conditions allows for you to choose the "run" option to move quicker on the battlefield but depletes the longer the displacement. Cover is an especially important one as it will definitely give you a leg up on the opponent. If you're not in some woods or on a ridge be extremely careful as your troops are extremely vulnerable. Reload obviously indicates when the troops are ready to fire. Points are awarded for certain points being captured which is made extremely evident without disturbing the eyes.
are decent and are suitable to the game. It would be nice to hear some in-game dialogue or more explosive effects.
Overall, not a bad game but I would certainly say this is not recommended for everyone. It is somewhat of a simplistic RTS that sometimes will not demand too much micro-management. This isn't necessarily true at all times but some people that have tried the game seem to think so. I think a little bit more could have been done to immerse the player by giving them more of a immersive role in the game rather than simply planning everything. If this was the goal to simply be a planner, then the game succeeded in it's role.
RATING : 6.95/10

Since I've finished the tech tree I feel I can write a fair review.
The game is basically Peasant Simulator, and it's a really good concept with a lot of promise. There's a few things it does really well and others it doesn't but luckily the bad ones are easy enough to fix.
Let's get the bad out of the way:
* This is currently a grind because of how many loading bars you have to suffer through to do pretty much everything. This however is a placeholder until they get minigames added for each task. It's singlehandedly the most unappealing thing this game has. Even if you get iron and steel tools they don't speed the process up, they're just lighter so you can carry more, which is a disappointment and I feel should change and add a multiplier to. Skills don't speed up the loading bars either, just unlocks things.
* There is no property protection system at time of writing. If someone finds your stuff buried under a pile of dirt, well then tough luck. There are a lot of ways to get around this though, like creating multiple mule characters or being clever with how you hide items.
* It's an grind until you are able to make metal things. But after that things get really exciting because your options explode.
* No guilds or land claim systems at time of writing either.
* The whole skill system and UI is uninuitive, and the wiki is pretty much required reading for your first time doing anything. There is no tutorial beyond an F1 menu that tells you what your hotkeys are.
* Performance is pretty unoptimised but that's to be expected of a game in alpha.
Now for the good:
* Mount and Blade style combat. Need I say more? It's also got a Total War sort of formation system as well, provided you have enough people.
* It has a focus on team-based gaming since the skill cap means that no one person can solo everything. There's a huge focus on trading and co-operation. If you play this alone it is going to take you forever to do things. More people means everything goes faster and has a set role to specialise in. I really enjoy that sort of aspect. Fun scales with how many people you're with.
* Even in this early state the range of things you can build is absolutely fantastic. Towns actually have a meaning and a function and grow naturally with what you're doing. I've had my small shack with my friend grow into a respectable-looking trading outpost and that's just with two people.
* The community is generally friendly. Just keep a respectful distance from their settlements when you talk to them or otherwise they may interperet you as smashing and grabbing, which is a fair assumption.
* The building and placement of items is really incredibly freeform. Options to finely raise, translate and rotate pretty much everything. It really allow for a fluid and natural looking set of buildings.
* It's got a really solid terrain deformation system. If you throw a bunch of dirt or rocks on a hill they will slide down the hill and raise it as it would in real life. It's quite impressive - never a seen a game deal with soil and gravel as fluid-like before. It also remembers properties of substrate. Fertility of soil, what kind of ground material you're dumping etc.
As it stands, LiF has a ton of potential, and if you're playing with a medium-large group (4-5+) you're gonna have fun.  I don't regret paying 30$ for it when it was on sale elsewhere. Really looking forward to how they grow the features and fix the issues.

Now if you guys want to know what the actual game is about, continue reading.
So what's this game about? Well, you create a character and assign it starting stats. You pick a faction out of 3 (I'm pretty sure this will determine building types later) and Name you Character. When you start, you spawn randomly in a world. (Currently one static map) and you are thrust into the role of someone who is new to the world. You'll need to find food and Shelter.

There's various skills that you can level up, by doing different things. And each skill branches off from base skills. For example, if you progress down Forestry eventually you'll get to Logging, and leveling logging will eventually get you into Carpentry. The system in which the game is laid out on, is extremely deep. The game gravitates everyone to work together, much like in actual old medieval times!
The game naturally pushes you to work and play together, and not artificially either. Interactions with other players are intense and require you to decide if you want to use diplomacy, or perhaps just all out go agressive. Life is Feudal offers so much deepness that you'll quickly realize, that you're actually role playing the trade of your character. No other game has immersed me so much that I would play out the role of my character.

Gothic IV Arcadia, Demonicon, and Witcher.
You and your sister have been kidknapped by the evil wizard Gandahar who rules the lands with an iron fist. You escape from prison with the help of the last remnant of the Orcs who fought Gandahar in a war years ago. You must work with the Orc's and the mysterious woman who leads them in order to rescue your sister and defeat Gandahar.
The magic system is probably the most insanely cool thing in any RPG ever made. Want to make it rain anvils and then cast a tornado armor spell right afterwards to create a tornado of anvils that destroy your enemies.... I know I do. The crafting system allows you to destroy crappy equipment to upgrade good equipment. You can also augment equpiment with gems to increase stats and damage. The game has a delightful sense of humor and never takes itself to seriously.
The game doesn't have the greatest graphics, but the main issue is that the blurs can really mess with your eyes. The controls aren't bad but they take some getting used too because they are a bit loose. The inventory system gets to be a huge mess after a while. The magic system is very difficult to understand at first and some spells along with stealth in the game are totally useless eventually. That being said I created an healing/phoenix spell invisible mage that wore plate armor and dealt massive AOE damage so it is possible to be an uber mage when you know what your doing. The voice acting and story aren't mind blowing by any means, but then again neither was Skyrim in that category.
Two Worlds 2 is a generic RPG with an amazing magic and crafting system. The game has some major faults, but if you can look past that and enjoy the humor and charm it can be amazing.
I value Two Worlds 2 at $15 and $20 for the Velvet.
