I speak of the first of the Shovel Knight stories specifically, as I have yet to get into the others.
I have a love/hate relationship with this game.  Why?  It reminds me of the "good ol' NES days."  If you actually recall those days accurately, and not just through a haze of nostalgia, you'll remember that some of those games were TOUGH!  And FRUSTRATING!  And I don't mean tough or frustrating as in how modern games are.  I mean tough as in you'll have to die just to figure out how to use certain items, get past certain areas, etc.
I die and die and die.  Sometimes I find interesting artifacts that may make certain parts of the stages easier.  Over the course of many deaths, I slog forward an inch at a time, only to die and go back to the checkpoint again.  But at least I get really good at getting past that one inch of screen.  Too bad the next inch of screen is more of the same BS but different enough, so I'll have to die there too, in order to learn how to get past it.
As you get further into the game, the platforming becomes ever more intense.  At least the controls are tight, and the game is made for a controller.  Don't even bother trying this game with a keyboard/mouse combo, I'd say.  The precision necessary is too great at some parts, unless you're a keyboard god.
If you find yourself getting frustrated easily at challenging games, I would say take a pass.  If, however, you have a sadistic streak for tight platformers, go ahead and buy this game.  After all, you're getting 4 games in one.  Maybe I'll like the other stories better, but Sir Shovel can straight shove it, as far as I'm concerned.  I get much too angry playing this game to enjoy it any.  If you've ever watched Mike Mattei of "Angry Video Game Nerd" fame, you'll understand the rage of which I speak.

FortressCraft Evolved is a game that takes place in the distant future. You start out in
a terrible, freezing planet. At first progression is slow. You will likely need to cling to your Central Power Hub (CPH) to power your suit, or suffer a hypothermic death. Before long, you will likely set up automated means of collecting ores and smelting them into bars. There is a ladder to progression in the sense that you must set up automated mines for new tiers of ores, set up logistics to get the ore back to the base, create machines to assemble devices, and eventually upgrade you suit to go deeper and discover newer ores. However, spread out across the planet, are creatures called hiveminds. They are encased in a thick, resinous shell that can only be destroyed with high-tier explosives/machinary. After a while, the hiveminds will become a problem, as they will spawn 'mynoks' (cis) on top of your conveyer belts, which will eat passing materials. This causes the hivemind's shell to grow, until it reaches/destroys your CPH. As well as that, there are swarms of wasps that will attack your base on the surface, and will attempt to shoot acid at your CPH to destroy it. //// EDIT:
10/10
A year later (since my first review, I've had this game since release date, August 2013), and I still love this game. For those worried about indie games being abandoned, don't. There's been a heap of progress since I first reviewed it, and it's all good. It runs better, it looks better, there's more maps and more cars and more features. Handling has come a long way and now with 0.4.2.0 we have possibly the final iteration of the tire model, achieving extremely accurate slip angles.
The maps are just spledid, Jungle Rock Island is only 4 sq km and it's got all sorts of things to explore - lighthouses, tunnels, industrial complexes, landing strip, and more. East Coast USA has a whole town with each house highly detailed and realistic. There's also a hidden aesthetic that no one discusses, sort of like Portal 2's bleak and ruined facilities, BeamNG.drive's maps are all largely abandoned, desolate and decrepit, which makes them a perfect place to drive/hoon/abuse/drift/crash a broad selection of cars.
I must make a point of saying that there aren't a lot of cars, only 12 now but three more coming in the next update. This is NOT an issue, it's an opportunity to get to know the various styles of vehicles, each one representing a different era and body style, and each one being highly customizable. You'll soon realize that unlike GTA V, the best car is not the fastest car, it's the one suited for the application. There are track cars, which are fast but unruly on bad roads and are intense to drive - there are old cars, which lack the helping hand of ESC and TC but make up for it in brute strenghth and simplicity - there are cheapo cars, which don't really do anything well but are a lot of fun to throw around and do what a car is supposed to do. Each car is not background visual for a shooting game but instead a work of art that the game is centered around. If you played GTA V like me and spend 99% of the time going back and fourth to los santos customs, and enjoyed the cars aside from the super cars (Futo, Rebel, Sultan, Blista, etc) because you just liked "regular" cars, then consider this game.
as a closing statement...just...just look at my gameplay hours. Yep. Those don't lie.

BeamNG.drive is the best game I've ever bought. If you like cars, but can't stand NFS physics, this is the game for you. I stumbled onto Fantasy Farming: Orange Seaon while looking for a game that would interest my 13 year old daughter. She loves the Harvest Moon series but honestly most of the recent titles are virtually the same, using a tired forumla and backstory with little innovation or change based on player feedback. Orange Season attempts to bring a fresh look at the farming/relationship/exploring gameplay without reinventing the wheel. At this, being early access, it has hit the nail on the head. My daughter, who is as finicky as they come, loves it. Now my son loves it and so do I. Updates are frequent and meaningful, making me feel good about my investment. Thus far, the developer seems very in tune with his growing fanbase and by all accounts, I believe this game will grow into something special and fun. I can't state it enough; Please remember that you are purchasing an early access game and thus will not experience all the planned features right away. As it stands right now, I believe the cost is worth it but if you prefer a completed game or feel you will be disatisfied by discovering content in game that is not yet in use then you may consider waiting a little longer until key elements are introduced. Overall, I love it and had to scratch my head for a few minutes to pull a few cons out. Even then, they are basically centered around the fact that it is early access.
Pros
- Great retro graphics.
- Satisfying gameplay.
- Helpful new ideas and features that you always wished for in Harvest Moon.
- Tasks are varied and interesting with a touch of humor that my kids appreciate.
- Nice variety of activities to engage in, not just watering 50 stalks of corn every day.
- Great for relaxing, no pressure, gameplay to either kill a few minutes or a couple hours.
- Looking for a use for your underpowered laptop? This will run on it.
Cons
- Early access. Understand you are not buying a complete game.
- Key features of this genre such as relationships, marriage, family not been fully implimented.
- Limited use of mouse. Controls center around keyboard/controller use and can be mildly inconvenient for avid pc gamers.
I will update again when more major updates are completed.

By now, Amnesia’s reputation precedes itself. Youtube is full of players screaming into their mics at petrifying monsters while running deeper into Brennenburg Castle or hiding in its darkness, praying the monsters don’t find them. Amnesia: The Dark Descent has become one of the scariest games of all time and it fully deserves to stand with the best that have gone before.
What makes The Dark Descent so petrifying? Different players may answer differently. Those brave (or stupid, depending on your point of view) souls who venture through Brennenburg Castle in total darkness may say the always foreboding, almost always oppressive atmosphere of the fortress and the unpredictable nature of the monsters (and jumpscares) that roam its narrow halls the greatest sources of fear. Others who tentatively explore with headphones glued to their ears may claim the unexplainable, disembodied screams and sobbing wafting down the damp corridors or through the clammy walls the greatest sources of discomfort. Others still who play late into night may believe the disturbing story of a descent into terrifying madness the source of their nightmares. For me, it was all of these.
The atmosphere of Brennenburg Castle is fantastically crafted. The player starts in the upper levels of the castle, many of which are bathed in light from windows, and steadily progresses lower into the fortress. These passages are often filled with water, and the walls covered in harmful organic overgrowth with fewer sources of light, making the player ration both oil and tinder boxes. I was at first eager to explore the upper portions castle and it took a relatively long time for anything to actually scare me. For some, this is a big turn off. For me, it made me even more terrified when the scares started and much more apprehensive to wander away from light, especially if my supplies were low. I have to admit, however, it always seemed just as I was running out of oil for my lamp, I would find more. Miracles, perhaps, or great testing/level design. Perhaps a little of both.
One of the most terrifying aspects of The Dark Descent (and what sets it aside from the rest of the pack of horror games) is that the player has no means to fight the monsters that shamble through the corridors. If you feel afraid to be alone in the castle, your fear is gravely misplaced; you should be afraid because you are not alone. The monsters are rather intelligent and hiding while in their sight will not fool them. I spent many long minutes flat against a wall next to a door and in a dark corner surrounded by dead pigs hoping a creature wouldn’t be bright enough to peek around the corner. There are only a few kinds of monsters, but the most terrifying for me was the most unique: the invisible Kraken, which lurks only in the flooded passageways. It could only sense me while I was in the water, but this made the scramble for dry ground even more desperate as I could hear the realistic splashing of heavy footfalls close behind my own.
The Dark Descent could have been scary enough with all of this, but then there’s the story. Daniel (the character you play as) has woken up with amnesia and must descend into the depths of Brennenburg Castle to regain his memory. Sounds cheesy enough, right? Wrong. The premise is cliche, but the way it has been crafted is not only a disturbing, but also shockingly believable look at human nature, and how far some will go for protection and power. The loading screens give some unrelated pieces of the story at different times, and the player can learn more by picking up pages from Daniel’s journal which has (of course) been scattered around the castle. Daniel also gets a sort of “audio memory” when he enters certain rooms. These helps set the stage for puzzles or rooms to be encountered, but it’s largely up to the player to piece these all together. I was amazed that many of my questions were actually answered by the end, considering I did not always go out of my way to find journal entries if monsters were near or I was low on oil/tinderboxes.
Up to this point I have given almost all positive criticism of The Dark Descent, but there are a few--albeit very minor--things that did raise my eyebrow and I cannot let them slip my memory now.
Especially in the early sections of the game, the player is given light tutorials (in game) about how to navigate, read the health and insanity “meters” in the inventory, and hide from monsters. Since the tutorials take place early in the game, they take place in the upper levels in the castle, and when taught how to hide from monsters the player is instructed to hide in closets. This would be all well and good if there were monsters where there are closets (in the upper levels, not including the “tutorial.”). When the monsters did actually start appearing, there were no closets to hide in (I did not see a single closet in the lower levels). While I found figuring out how to hide added to the intensity and scariness of the encounters with the creatures, I feel the tutorial is slightly wasted since I never hid in a closet again.
I also wish there was more variety in the puzzles regarding the machinery in the castle. There are some genuinely good puzzles in here (some deceptively simple) but about half of them required me to either find gears, pull levers, arrange pipes and other similar actions. Nothing unbearable, but by the end of the game I was beginning to feel more like an exasperated mechanic than a petrified amnesiac. Every time I went into a new area of the castle, my thought was “What needs fixing now?” instead of “What is lurking in this room?”
The Dark Descents’ legacy is only destined grow, considering the number of horror games that already imitate its style and mechanics, as well as the ability for players to create and play custom stories within the program. Whether or not you decide to venture into the darkness of Brennenburg Castle, you will certainly encounter Amnesia’s non-combative design influencing the mechanics of other games you may play. Just knowing it all started here may be enough for the faint of heart to handle.

Ok, I love this game, it has great gameplay and a steady preogression all of the way to the end.  I am on the fence about recommending it because of how buggy it is, which I will explain later.
The Good:
Gameplay consists of a voxel based mining simulator with base defense elements. There is a heavy emphasis on automation with mining rigs doing nearly all of the mining.  If you are smart, it shows in the machines and networks you build. You can build incredibly complex machines to do things like assembling rockets and feeding them into your rocket launcher, or you can build the rockets and hand feed each turret's hopper.  FC inspires you to be creative out of necessity.  I bought the expansion pack three hours into the base game, 117 hours and I'm just at the front door to the expansion pack.
The Bad:
If you aren't smart, this is going to be a really hard game.  Some things aren't intutive and are missing, like more of things sometimes/always going north from a hopper or energy source but no big compass. Which means that some configurations only work when the machine faces a certain direction. I would also expect at least one entire base and save file to be lost due to god know what because
didn't respond at all to my email. You will lose so much progress.  Don't make any huge works of art.  I found a way to get items from my broken base's save file so I could finish my review.  Also, you can only kill 3 types of enemies with your gun. Using your gun is a hassle. The grappling hook is so cumbersome and frustrating to use, because of how you get caught on things and dropped (down a mine shaft).  Also the BFL is completely broken or has unlisted usage requirements. And the Laser Borer kills you even when it is turned off.
The verdict: Get it, there are bugs. Lots of bugs. The base I lost was a one refinery, two turbine dump.  The base I have by end game has 7 refineries and two towers of turbines. (It also has hedge mazes and a cabin.  Because it takes 30-40 minutes for the end of game weapon to charge and you have to fire it 4 times minimum to beat the base game.) In the end, the gameplay is solid. 90% of it is trying ot figure out why something isn't working. Is it the supply line? is the ore exhausted?

Despite the obvious youtube bait, this game is actually a lot of fun. It's an interesting take on the point and click genre, and it may not have the typical tropes of a P&C, but the fact that it is a large map puzzle game that will often have you back tracking and thinking outside of the box to enter a new room definitely fufills the criteria. It's also an interesting perspective on the survival horror genre. In most survival horrors (Silent hill, Resident Evil, Fatal Frame...etc), the player is vastly unprepared (similar to Amnesia), and the controls are intentionally hindered to give a feeling of helplessness and struggle within the game's universe. However, with Amensia, the game controls just fine, but you have nothing to defend yourself, and that arguably creates a bigger sense of helplessness, and a real feeling of frustration, because you know what you want to do, but you cannot actually complete the thing you want to do because of the monster in your way that is pretty much unbeatable other than running away and finding a new way around.

Take the tradional Star Wars forumula. Black and white characters, the combination of blasters, light sabers, the force, and various other technological wonders.
And then scrap the black and white component. Or hell, combine them and make grey.
Meet KOTOR 2. Arguably one of the best RPGs I have played to this date, and with a fantastic universe backing it. The original KOTOR was an exceptional game (and they're very much alike) but it fell into the traditional Star Wars cliche which I mentioned in the first sentence. What Obsidian has done with this game is nothing short of a marvel, and they've managed to create a fantastic game absolutely loaded with character development, information to read and learn about, and a fantastic journey.
Characters are anything but one dimensional, often having hidden motives that cannot be deciphered until it is too late. The counter to this is how characters are developed, and the player is presented with many opportunities in which to learn more about his or her companions, even right down to their innermost secrets. Interactions aren't purely about the player themself, but also from character to character. Different combinations have their own interacting dialogue whether it be between each other, or to various people you meet along the way. Certain characters can be convinced to take up a different view point if you are successful in persuading them, and change drastically in their behaviour as a result. If you play through this game without getting to know your party, you're missing one of the largest aspects about it. Characters are believable, and aside from the rather static way dialogue is done - almost real.
Your choices throughout the story have a huge impacts later on, sometimes even completely changing how a certain section plays out. This leaves room not only for replayability, but for a sense of intrigue. Consider your actions carefully, because they might just come back to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥- unless that's what you'd like. Enjoy the game as you cover large portions of the Star Wars universe, exploring many strange and foreign worlds in your galactic quests to discover what exactly happened after the original story in KOTOR.
Do yourself a favour and pick this up (along with the content restoration mod, google it - get it). You won't regret it. It is solid as a standalone game, but enhanced if you decide to pick up the first game in the series and play through it. A lot of subtleties will be otherwise missed, and you won't be as involved without doing so.

I had zero expectations - and was still disappointed.
The reason is that despite much time spent troubleshooting, I couldn't get the game to start. Normally that would make me completely discard the value of a Steam review, since that is probably the user's fault (or a problem on that specific installation or hardware). But I'll explain a bit about why I'm even bothering to write this review.
In my case the game alternated randomly at startup between two problems:
- The launcher (eventually) displays the "dreaded" NBE-1013 error message, which indicates a network connectivity problem. Despite the launcher showing that it has network access, is logged in and all servers are alive. The developer page which you are led to, explains that it is a temporary issue because of gameserver maintenance (hint: it isn't - VPN'ing to other regions gave same error). That explanation currently has a rating of "150 out of 900 found this helpful". Yeah, me neither.
- The launcher manages to start the H1Z1 executable as fullscreen for a split second before crashing. The log file only says "ProcessSyncEvent GameIsReady destroyed." No other hint whatsoever what it choked on. Then what is the point of having logging enabled on a "work-in-progress" software?
Now I'm a very tech-savvy, and even going through the game's own logs and every relevant troubleshooting suggestion I came upon didn't let me solve the problem, or at the very least, give me an indication of what the cause was. Connectivity? Blocking VPNs? Driver issues? Security issues? Just plain bad programming?
One of the most common troubleshooting-suggestions I came upon, was to enable "Run as Administrator" for the relevant executables (H1Z1 uses a "Launcher" system). Hello, this is 2017? Yes, the game may have Early Access-status, but it's been 1½ year since launch. Something so basic should have been solved long ago, seeing as it appears to be a common problem.
Overall the Early Access moniker must be taken literally, as this does not seem to be a solid product yet. "And it's not just me, I swear".

Quite possibly the most important work of Star Wars fiction of the 21st century, no joke.
Sure, the engine is decrepit. The world is a sterile mix of ferrocrete, dead plants and brackish water. Its design is  dated by  overwhelming inventory, filler sidequests and needless tabletop RPG-isms. What makes Sith Lords such a classic is its attempt to take the moral conventions of Star Wars apart and challenge them repeatedly before turning them upside down.
It undermines every act of compassion and altruism, while dismissing capricious acts of evil. It deconstructs the carefree scoundrel and puts him back together again, and it balks at a faraway galaxy of long ago engaged in zero sum conflicts. Simply put, it advances the themes of Star Wars by challenging every piece of fiction that has come before it.
If the game get's better mechanics, buy it, if not, don't buy it.

Type of Game:
First person or Third Person Multiplayer Medieval Survival Sandbox Open World Simulation
Version Played:
Early Access PC version through Steam
Similar Games:
DayZ, Rust, and to a lesser degree the Mount & Blade series
The Good:
An epic game world filled to the brim with content, whether it be things to craft or items to use, the game world has no limits on what you can do.
Everything you see is reachable and harvestable.
A very strong medieval aesthetic, which makes the game stand out more so than the competition (i.e. DayZ, Rust, etc…).
Multiplayer is this game’s strong suit with a great enjoyment to be had by exploring the medieval landscape with a buddy or two.
The crafting, building, and surviving aspects of the game are much more exciting when experienced with a friend
There is a level progression system, which you typically won’t find in games of this nature.
I only say this because a progression system is much more fun in a survival type game and brings with it a sense of urgency that you would find in a PDL genre-type.
The map is always present, which usually isn’t the case for these games. This makes coordinating a rendezvous with your friends much easier and drastically improves the multiplayer experience.
As you’ll find with other game’s of this type, the relationships with other players is a fascinating experience. For the most part other players typically pursue a Lord of the Flies mentality and will often exert their power over those that have a weak footing in the game’s hierarchy. However, when you encounter other players that are helpful it makes the game much easier to digest and enjoy.
The Bad:
Life is Feudal is very clunky and not polished at the moment. Menu and interface options aren’t intuitive and present themselves as overly complex.
Complete lack of a tutorial, which is understandable for an “Early Access” title, but you should be aware none-the-less.
Single-player is difficult to swallow as most other players will just grief you over and over again. Playing with your friends is the only way to currently guarantee a good time.
Outside of the medieval aspects, this game is more of the same if you’ve played Rust or DayZ. I would argue that the features are much deeper than what Rust has to offer and Rust is Life is Feudal’s closest likeness.
Can you play it while the children are awake?
Due to the nature of multiplayer shenanigans, I often had to play without my sound on. Other players are often rude and mean, which can lead to profane language and crude lingo. There is also combat and violence, but I felt as though the graphics weren’t grand enough to matter in that regard.
Did I make time to complete it?
As a multiplayer game there is no completion per say. I did build a number of structures and survived for a number of hours.
Redlight or Greenlight?
This game is currently at a redlight.
The content that is currently offered is just not worth the asking price of $39.99. If you were a gamer that REALLY enjoyed Rust, then you will be getting your money’s worth in this title as the content is better. Outside of that demographic, I just don’t see the appeal of paying a large amount of money to experience a lesson in human nature (i.e. griefing) and confusing gameplay (lack of tutorial). This may change as the game updates, so please check back here for any changes in my preview.

Life is Feudal: Your Own is definitely a product of our ongoing craze and love for the survival, sandboxy, constructive and destructive genre, while taking another step towards its logical extremes. The game is a beautiful one, the graphics and the lighting do not fail to impress, which helps bring life to a vast world filled with trees, mountains, swamps, beaches and the ocean itself. Although at the time of writing the game is clearly an Early Access one with plenty of missing features, what's there is evidently plenty to hook people in.
The game gives you plenty of options on how you'd like to play it. You can set how fast or how slow your skills level up, from a glacial crawl to rocketing into masteries. You can set skill caps, either letting the player master every profession, or give them just enough to master one and dabble in one or two others. The latter adds an incredible amount of flavour, where you see farmers who are actual farmers, carpenters who are actual carpenters. They've specialized, they've mastered their trade, and although they may have the ability to help out here and there, they'll never become the town's second blacksmith. To some this may sound bad, but look at it this way: this is Life is Feudal. You're building a town, and in this town everyone, every player, has a purpose. They become gears in a grander machine, where everyone relies on everyone else.
In that kind of game, on that kind of server, you won't find that one guy that's a master blacksmith, carpenter, architect, herbalist, and so on. You won't find a massive castle built by a single person, vast and full of every imaginable thing, but equally lonely. During my play I was invited to join a town. A small one, admittedly, but immediately the community became evident and clear. You had farmers with their plots outside the walls. You had the blacksmith with his shop, a herbalist with another. I was lucky enough to be apprenticed as a carpenter, witnessing wood cutters at work, hauling timber to their newest farmhouse.
That doesn't mean it has to be though. If you're the kind of person that prefers the Minecraft approach, worry not! As I mentioned before, the skill rates are completely up to you. If you want to master the art of logging from peeling the bark off a tree, you can set those settings up and just jump in. You'll be able to master every skill and build your own little kingdom. This goes in multiplayer as well, meaning you can have a small group on a high skill rate server that'll be able to rival a low skill rate server's larger community.
Nothing is perfect however, and this goes doubly for early access. I don't fault the game for any of its bugs or glitches, but it helps that I honestly didn't run into many. The only thing that actually showed up was that sometimes items wouldn't load in and I had to restart the game. No crashes, no memory leaks, no massive frame drops out of nowhere. The frame rate, admittedly, was pretty awful even on the lowest settings, but that's par for the course during early development. It can only get better. Yet this doesn't leave me with a lot of complaints! The UI is a little clunky, but that tends to be cleaned up during development. Wolves are a bit deadly when you're starting off as well, making running into one early on a deadly affair -- and honestly, that's about it.
There's already a good selection of servers out there with a modest but dedicated population, too. For anyone who's been seeking a game like this, I find it easy to recommend. Just be warned; this may be a little too hardcore for a jump directly from Minecraft, at least for some players. For the rest, that's most definitely a good thing!

The Power Rangers look like Academy Award contenders by comparison.
After being led around by the nose for a while, you'll be told to search a large room for a switch to open a secret door. This might not be so terrible, but you're forced to walk at about the speed algae grows. After enduring this, the only possible relief is to write a bitterly acrid review, as I'm doing now. Here are some fun phrases you may find useful in yours:
- What's what the arm-waving? Are they making fun of epileptics? Not cool, guys.
- Why must this be the way I discover that I've died and gone to hell?
- I wish this game had a corpse so I could desecrate it.

This is a great strategy game, very realistic. And unlike what I initially thought, you don't solely play the Historic battles. The first battle when you start a new game is the same, but depending on what happens the next battle(s) will be different.
Each battle is called a Phase, and there are 3 Phases in a Day, and 4 Days in a Campaign/Game. When you complete a Phase, depending on what happened, you are given 3 choices that vary from abandoning a position, taking it back, etc. and that will be the overarching objective for the next phase. However things can still change drastically which will then alter future battles and decisions. And by the way, Unit condition and moral for specific divisions carries over to the next phase, so fighting smart and keeping your troops in as good condition as you can pays off.
From what the manual said, there are 80 different scenarios it picks from depending on what happens in a battle and how far along in a campaign you are.
You can play either as Confederates or the Union.
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys strategy.

Right now I would term the game as shows promise but you need to understand what it is and where it stands.
Obviously enough this is a farming life sim game in the vein of Harvest Moon. You farm crops, explore caves, forage, fish, socialize with the villagers etc, etc. Those who are generally into the genre know what to expect and for those unfamiliar the above mentioned is the core gist. Which brings us to the question of how well that game does at achieving this premise.
To put it simply it is really rough at the moment. Many of the core mechanics are in place though the socializing aspect is currently extremely shallow with most of the villagers seeming to have no real routines, villager dialogue being limited, interior designs are fairly rudimentary, and character creation is bare bones being my main criticisms at the moment. However the game as it currently stands is by no means bad. Rough yes, it definitely needs a lot of work but at the same time you need to remember that this is in early access and from what I've seen the dev has been communicating on the forums and has been taking criticism into account.
So what it comes down to is this. I'm recommending this game on the basis that for a early level foundation it is a good start and I have faith that the dev is going to work hard at implementing features and improving based on feedback. If that is good enough for you and you want to support the game and the dev then by all means buy it. However if you are looking for a complete product right this second then I say hold off. If you are lookign for some guarantee that the game will eventually be amazing I can't give that to you. As of right now I recommend the game only if you want to support the games continued development and are okay with throwing money at a currently incomplete title in the hope that it may eventually expand into something great.

Ahh, another farming simulator hits Steam. As a huge fan of the Harvest Moon series, I definitely put aside some money to purchase this game. Please bear in mind that I only got up to Spring 27, Year 1 and basing my review on everything I've seen so far.
Unlike other farming simulation games, the main character was not left to tend to a farm of a deceased relative, but in fact had aspirations to become a farmer since they were young. The first day you are introduced to the mayor who helps get you settled into your new home along with another farmer who helps teach you the basics of farming. After a quick tutorial, you can take your character outside the farm and begin exploring.
Pros
+Controller support
+Nice looking graphics
+Several different crops to grow in each season.
+Characters are unique and have different personalities.
+Tasks available to complete.
+Several different animals you can raise.
+Being able to edit the contents of the shipping bin before it's shipped. Very helpful if you accidently put something in you needed.
+You recieve a dog on Spring 2, Year 1.
+One of the coolest features, which reminds me of Animal Crossing, is being able to write letters to other characters, including your mom!
+Lots of areas to explore and forage to collect.
Cons
-Not much to do in the first couple days. I found myself running around town several times just to kill time.
-No map to help keep track of exploration.
-Some of the building/store times of operation are weird. Why is the library only open for 7 hours in the middle of the day?
-Female playable character not implemented yet as of 4/22/17.
-Only two skin choices.
-Some NPCs have no unique text and/or stand in one spot all day, every day.
-No storage unit to put extra things you don't need/want to collect.
Suggestions
= Add a statistics panel to track various stats such as conversations had, products/produce shipped.
= Add a relationships page to track relationships with characters.
= Add collectible shells at the beach.
= Add an in-game calendar.
= Add text to the television.
= Add a map.
= Add images to the character's text box.
= Add voice over to the opening cutscreen.
= Add being able to get a cat.
If any of these things are already in-game and I just haven't unlocked them yet, please let me know. Otherwise this game shows great promise and I look forward to any and all updates! Brian Hudell is working very hard to provide the best customer service experience he can and has already provided several updates using suggestions from players.

This game is
Gut-wrenchingly, keyboard-smashingly, 'Jesus♥♥♥♥thatguyshotme♥♥♥♥inghow' hard. It has a steep learning curve and even at 300 hours I find it difficult, despite almost encyclopedic knowledge of operator strengths and weaknesses, maps, and breach points. My potato aim might have something to do with this I must say, but the point still applies. It is difficult. Map knowledge is needed, especially because of the game's main draw.
This is the absolutely awesome destruction system.
Whilst at times, the all-or-nothing destruction feels annoying (for example, a 50 calibre LMG cannot punch through a milimetre thick bit of sheet metal, or a stair railing, but can destroy walls, hatches, wooden barricades, people, car batteries, complicated electronic devices, floors, garage doors and more,) almost always it feels incredible.
Smashing through walls like the Scottish Kool-Aid man, or shotgunning open new lines of sight feels satisfying. Walls crunch and crack with force and noise behind them. Guns rattle and ping loudly and recoil is hefty for the most part. Bullets hit with a satisfying meaty 'thwack,' and due to the punishingly quick time to kill, (one hit headshots, most guns
end you in a second,) you always feel like each engagement has been a proper fight.
To explain why this game is liked, I'll take you through an average round. The map is randomly selected from a pool, and 'Operators' are picked. These operators are all elite special forces members, ranging from the well-known (SAS, FBI SWAT,) to the more obscure (BOPE,) and they all bring along specialist gadgets with them.
These gadgets have wonderful interplay with one another. An attacking operator, Thermite, can blow through reinfoced walls, but he can be blocked by the defending operator Mute, who has EMP signal disruptors that prevent all electronics from working. Thatcher however, another attacking operator, has specialist grenades that can take out Mute's jammers, letting Thermite open a 'big ♥♥♥♥ing hole,' to use his own words.
That's just three of them, incidentally.
Returning to the round. Whilst the defenders blow open hatches, lay out barbed wire, reinforce walls to prevent breaching charges and bullets from leaving them defensless, and generally prepare for the storm,  the attackers have a different job.  All of them have thrown out little remote-controlled drones, which scoot around the map, searching for opponents and the objective. When the timer ticks to zero, it's off their drones and away they go, using their newfound intel to plan a path to the objective, which might be a biohazard device that needs securing (in a sort of TF2 capture point kind of way,) one of two bombs that need defusing, or a hostage that must be rescued.
Now the attackers have to be careful. Defenders might be peeking out of windows, or have clever little traps set up in order to punish hasty rushes. Once the round is done, it's time to switch sides and repeat, the once-attackers now shoring up their defenses in order to repulse the once-defenders.
The map variety in which you do this in is truly excellent. From a presidential plane to a biker clubhouse, from Brazillian favela to Russian kafe, no two locations are quite alike, all of them requring different ways to be seiged.
That's the good. Now onto the bad.
The hit registration, tickrates, matchmaking,  bugs and glitches, and balance is
Rubberbanding was a major problem with 30 ping only a few months ago, and the so-called 'Operation Health' didn't do much to correct a lot of the ongoing issues the community had. Combined with liason Epi over on Reddit leaving, and people are quickly becoming disenfranchised.
It needs some proper loving before it can truly join the ranks of giants among FPS's, but Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege promises a tactical, team-oriented shooter, and delivers a tactical, team-oriented shooter.
If you love modding and destroying cars in 100x slow motion this game is for you. Full stop.

Its a very nice 3D version of Factorio (+minecraft). I know it isn't exactly like it, but it has just VERY strong Factorio vibes to it.  Not as complex in the long term maybe or maybe it is... And not as polished yet, with all the fancy smart UI solutions, Factorio has) , but thats balanced out by the 1st person perspective and the 3rd dimension.
Also the UI looks a bit clunky in places.
EDIT: Sadly i have to edit something in here: The game, despite some flaws, is great and would be well worth the  money. The Frozen Factory DLC only becomes relevant later on so try&buy first tha base game and get the DLC later if you like it.
BUT: things like patreon donators exclusive (preview)features and skins sold in what's effectively  microtransactions(Mini DLC) leave a bit of a bad taste.Even though they are "just cosmetic" and you don't even see it (1st person). It's a very thin line to walk between extra support/money, for whats a very big and time consuming one-Dev project, AND possibly scaring potential new "normal" players off and getting negative reactions from existing ones, by paywalling features.
Paywalling ON TOP of the normal game expanding DLC which are already not cheap.
It starts to feel a bit much....
edit end.
That 3rd dimension. makes things much more interesting, immersive but also nicely confusing.  Walking THROUGH a messy (first) factory is a greater experience than watching it from far above.  And of course there is the 3rd dimension thing.  It goes DEEP. Setting up a little (or big) base in a huge cave 500+m underground feels good but is challenging due to the balancing issues.
There isn't really a goal and target though. Maybe thats why it's going for somwhat more micromanagement. It becomes effectively a tower defense game, with monsters/aliens attacking your base increasingly.
It  adds a strong Minecraft part to the thing, which makes it different to factorio.  But thats the world, the blocks, the digging (though MUCH faster) and the mining. The crafting on the other hand thankfully feels much more intuitive, much more Factorio then Minecraft(+Tekkit&co)
Some balance decisions are a bit questionable. Like the first real ore smelter being so far down the research tree. You're stuck with the 1 free one for a long time and can't even move it for a long time. Also wrong choices in research can get you seriously stuck (Suit heater&Toxic filter!). And there are some gaps in research/access to resources.
Especiall since you see no tech tree. Or get advise qhat you need first or in order to get a much needed technology (Heater, Toxic filter) Only google tells you, what you need for what later on
.
While i don't always like the balance and think, it gets way too grindy later on, It's flexible enough.
The game is open for modding. I use a personal mod that makes stuff much cheaper and moves certain things down(or up?) the tech tree. Equally there are game options and mods to make it more challenging. So you can adjust it to your needs. The steam workshop has a decent amount of mods.
Also due to all storage systems being (imho) undersized, it remains despite automation, more manual and demands more micromanagement in the longer run, then factorio. Then again, imagining some of the gigantic Factorio factories in 3d graphics ... it would be hard to do it with any performance left-
It doesnt need a longe step by step tutorial to the perfect facility for me. Although i would have appreciated the information that conveyers simply transport stuff vertically as well. Its mentioned nowhere. There is ingame help and a context sensitive handbook. It's not perfect though. So you'll not get entirely around looking stuff up externally.
The world/game creating options have several parameters suiting new players. Like  the amount of ore or day/night settings. Like keeping inventory on death. I can't possibly imagine doing the deep game without "dying back home".
Maybe with much more experience.
But if you liked factorio and look for something  kinda similar but in 3D AND can forgive a few rough edges, its really worth it (maybe at reduced prize).
PS: It runs stable for me, native 21:9 support, although it looks VERY stretched at the sides.Graphics not amazing but nice enough. Lighting at times can be annoying. But overbright pipes have been fixed in recent update. Full Steam workshop support. All is ok on the technical side. Performance is also ok but can get wonky later with very large and complex factories.
Can't really tell about multiplayer. Improving it technically seems a major focus in dev though.
PPS: There is no Steam or game option, to change language. So its only available in english. Apparently translations are work in progress and will come.
PPPS: Warning: This game is as time-eating as Factorio. Everytime you look at the clock its two hours later then you wanted to stop playing.

Great hack & slash puzzle game with an interesting story. You have a badass sword, a badass gun, a badass ride and a badass dude to control. The game feels fluent and fun, plays through almost on a single breath (not literally).
The fighting feels good and rewarding, bosses require you to make out their pattern, there are many puzzles you need to complete and they all are well-balanced. The RPG element consists of buying abilities and upgrades, and leveling up your weapon.
The storyline is developed nicely through cutscenes and dialogues, with you being in the middle of all the action. The visual side of the game is great, animation feels fluent, you get slow-motion on special finishing moves, there aren't many misleading elements (background parts that look like they should be interactive). The music is okay, but one of the oftenly played tracks reminded me a lot of one of the DOTA 2 soundtracks.
There are some bugs in the game, however, it sometimes crashes for no reason, steam achievements work only for the first game launch after every steam launch, so if your game crashes - restart steam as well. The controls can be a bit odd sometimes, like shooting over the wrong shoulder, but I haven't played with a controller, maybe it's better there. Also, occasionally the game just leaves you in the middle of nowhere with a task, wondering where the hell is the place you need to be in.
I'd recommend getting this game if you like the hack & slash genre or puzzles, or both, it's definitely a great choice. Even if you're not much into it, Darksiders will probably find a way into your heart.

It's difficult to explain why this game is a fail, because it does so well a lot of the time.  The problems are difficult to describe as well, because they are not consistent.  Everything seems to be fine, and then it all stops making sense.
For somebody considering making a purchase, I would make these general warnings:
1.  Units are not placed properly.  In the vast majority of the battles where the campaign manager places the units, you will commonly find brigades belonging to the same division and even corps. spread far apart.  This has implications for effectively using your units to work together.  If you do take the time to identify the various units and give them movement orders to get together, they will spend that time under fire and be all shot to hell by the time they finally get in proper formation.  If you just accept the placement and adjust the lines, they will suffer badly from morale penalties.
2.  Artillery simply does not follow orders.  Don't even try.
3.  The strength of units is wildly inconsistent.  Brigades are commanded by generals with a start system where more stars means a generally tougher unit.  The problem is the wide disparity between the reliability of the one-star brigades, which most of the Union brigades are.  (Most of the CSA brigades are much much stronger.)  I've seen two one-star brigades do just fine defending in cover with their corps. commander nearby.  I have also seen the entire Union III corps. run from cover when taking fire from two (2!) CSA brigades.  They fire one volley and run.  In cover, tightly linked, with corps commander nearby.  There isn't much more you can do to "encourage" them.  When 4500 guys run from 1500, I really do have to call fail.
IN general, it's just realy mystifying on how to properly command Union troops effectively.  (I haven't tried CSA.)  Just when you think you have it figured out, they find some mysterious reason to break, run or just plain start walking around.
What makes this even more frustrating is that it isn't like this all the time.  Most of the time, things are fine, but when they stop working, they really stop working.  And you don't know why.  Whatever mystery is embedded in the AI that makes your troops fickle isn't documented, either.
The game was designed by a well-known TW modder.  I think we can safely say there is a big difference between modding a working game and designing a working game.
I tried.  But this game just doesn't make any damn sense.

Darksiders draws inevitable comparisons to Zelda and god of War. Its a shame that it is never as smart as the first or as satisfying as the second.
The combat in bland, simplistic, overused and repetitive. You cant properly mix weapons in combos, in fact, most combos are 1 button sequences like: X, XX or XXX. If you wana be a pro try holding X for a sec. Yeah...
Off course sometimes you also have to dodge, but considering how much the enemies telegraph you their attacks I can say you almost have time to check your email. And don't let me start on the "finishing" animations, so frequent and repetitive that got me tired of them after 1 hour of game.
Overall the flow of the game is very contrived. A lot of it feels like filler, especially the underdeveloped platform segments. To make worst, most puzzles feel uninspired and tedious, riped off directly from zelda games, but without the same level of polish in its execution.
There is constantly something gating your progress that don't feel like it was needed and the ways you solve problems always sound like they took triple the time they should have taken.
Its not terrible, for sure, and has semblances of being a fun game on a few moments, but on the long run is boring, which for a game is almost a worst sin.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #40 - Darksiders
My first reaction to Darksiders as I played it was that it was very reminiscent of God of War.  I don't consider that a bad thing, but it's hard not to make the comparison as you are hacking and slashing through demons.  But I think it would be a disservice to simply call this a God of War clone, as there are some differences that make Darksiders stand on its own, particularly with it's emphasis on puzzles.
The art style has a comic book influence to it, and I thought it worked well.  The only negative is a relative lack of graphic options.  You can change resolutions and set v-sync, but otherwise there are no real customization options.  This isn't a dealbreaker to me at all, and I would still recommend this game.  I'm definitely looking forward to spending more time in it.

Pros:
-Awesome story, except the ending of the main story. Otherwise, the quest is meaningful and realistic, your character can speak and his response is meaningful throughout the story and side quest. This make the game become more interactive (in other game like Skyrim or Neverwinter night, you can only response with dialogue, no voice, no speak back and forward between you and NPC)
-Charming music
-Graphics is beautiful for a game from 2011. Vast desert, corrupted lands, dark dungeons, fresh forest. The world is smaller compare to skyrim but more quality and less repetitive.
-Day and night circles. NPC go to work at day and return home to sleep at night.
-NPC response to your action, they run and scream when you hit them, then guards will try to beat you and they are while powerful. If you pull out your weapon when guards are nearby, they will surround you and ask you to sheath your weapon. When you break into people's home. If the owner see you they will ask you to leave and if you don't leave, they will call the guard.
-Combat system is realistic and fun:
Melee is included block, counter attack, combo, passive and active skill, dodge, step back and strike, while blocking you can strike at choose direction by pressing move button + left click. Due wielding, two handed, one handed with shield or touch or nothing, all these options have skill to support them, for example you can strike enemy with the torch and deal %100 of your physical damage as fire. Different weapon have different skill to support them: axe strip enemy shield, mace stun them, etc. Some skills can be use with any weapon.
Range is very powerful, you can snipe, you can shoot power fire arrow/bolt deal area damage, shoot arrow/bolt that create a decoy, when decoy expires or dies, deal % of your physical damage as spectral damage. Poison and frost arrow/bolt that slow enemy. Frost option deal a small area damage while poison is single target but deal damage over time. With the pirate dlc, you get access to the crossbow, which provide a different using mechanism and fighting strategies.
This game has the best magic system, you can create a lot of spells by combine magic cards together. You can make stone rains from the sky and then create a tornado that make these stones flying around you and hit enemy. These are hundreds, even thousands combinations. Air, life, lightning, fire, power, force, water, ice, psyche, corpse, poison, decay, trap, summoning, area, etc.
-Crafting and alchemy system
-Teleport system: besides the fixed teleport gate, you can create your own teleport gate as many as you want and spread them across the world.
-Nice lockpicking system
-Fun mini games
-mod-able
Cons:
-Lack variety landscape: no winter, fall landscape.
-Lack variety of races, the variety of monster is okay but I still want more.
-Only one dragon.
Conclusion:
Two worlds 2 is a must play game. I played Skyrim and Oblivion, the worlds is vast with a lot of side quests, but everything is repetitive and dust story. When it comes to quality, I choose Two Worlds II and its DLC pirate, meaningful quest chat-chit and dialogue, different quests outcome, rewards and different ending in DLC. This the first open world game which I truly want to replay.

After finally charging the OET, I feel like I can write a bit about FCE. I nearly gave it a thumbs down, but I think, overall, it deserves a recommendation. Most say it's a combination of Factorio and Minecraft, but it largely reminds me of Power Towers, a TD custom map that involved defending your base with towers that needed to be routed power from power generators. I enjoyed the grand majority of my [thus-far] 150 hours in FCE, despite ignoring the missions most of the time and playing my own [undoubtedly slower] style. Even not on sale, it's easy to get your money's worth out of FCE, with plenty to see and do. If you don't like busywork, there's plenty of tools for automation to build a base limited only by your imagination [and PC specs]. My biggest complaint is lack of polish, including user customization; for example, the music is ofttimes just whistling tones, just begging to be turned down or off [there's no setting in the options to adjust only the music volume, nor a setting to disable music all of the time - it must be switched off every time you play] - just little things like this that drive home that this is an indie game that needs some more love around the edges. Dev seems to listen to the community and continues to add content [even as DLC - which costs more than the base game?!? - it's an excellent value]. In-Game handbook and wiki seem to be incomplete/out of date, but I think there's some focus on improving this coming up [why the official wiki doesn't have info built directly from in-game data beats me]. I only ever played single player, so no comments on MP.
+Gameplay
+Style
+Fun factor
+Value
-Lack of polish and easy-to-find answers
-Occasional community hostility
Overall: 8.5/10
tl;dr: If you like base management, defense, mining, and don't mind indie quirkiness, there's no reason to not check out FCE. You could watch for a sale price, but it's well worth the everyday price.

I'll start by saying that I am having an amazing time with this game.
That said, it's definitely a niche offering. I used to play a heavily modded Minecraft (let's start by not pretending the game isn't influenced by Minecraft), but there was always the issue of mods not working well together. Different machines needing different sources of power, for example. Then everything would break when there was an upgrade. It was a hassle. FCE provides the experience I was looking for w/o that hassle. It's more akin to a 3d Factorio than Minecraft.
There are negatives, of course. FCE has the nickname toilcraft for a reason. There's a lot of manual labor involved in ramping up automation. Resources are generated slowly, and you'll spend the first several hours waiting for ore to smelt into bars, even AFTER you know what you're doing. You start with one ore smelter, and there is a lot to do before you can even build a second. I find the slower pace relaxing, but I'm old. YMMV. I like the fact that I can carry on a conversation with my wife & watch TV w/ her while playing.
There IS a rapid resources mode now that makes this somewhat less of an issue, but you'll still be doing a lot of running around manually smelting stuff for hours to get things going.
The world is also really bleak and depressing. That's by design, but after a while it gets to you. A bit of biome diversity would have been nice. I haven't tested it, but it also doesn't seem to have Minecraft's nigh-endless size. It's big enough, though.

At first I found the controls quirky and things not explained as well as I would have liked through tutorials or other aspects of gameplay. However getting past that initial "breaking-in learning phase", the game turned into what I would describe as an OCD addiction that spanned for weeks of fully enjoyable gameplay.
If you are familiar with Factorio and liked that game, then the pull of this game will be familiar in the way that you research and progress. This game however is a 3D sandbox world where you can dig/place blocks in - in addition to setting up your factory / logistics operations. Want to run conveyor belts up the side of an elevator shaft that you just mined down to and discovered a new type of ore ? You can do it.
There is a campaign overtone and events that trigger as you become more advanced in your base and this extends into the expansion as well. Even after fully achieving the goals the campaign set in place I still felt like going back to improve aspects of my base to get better throughput.
If you enjoy automating systems and solving logistics problems or sandbox games I would highly suggest a playthrough or 2 of FortressCraft.

This game is like the next Minecraft, but in 3D.  It's starting out just as funky and buggy and lacking, in my opinion, however I can see that it's turning into something darn great.  The only real issue I have so far is all the darn progress bars.  I don't really like them, I'd much rather have a minecraft-esque style of harvesting things.
By that I mean more live-action; if you held down left mouse button to harvest bark or search for things instead of just click and let a progress bar fill I feel it would be more engaging.  It could be something along the lines of every tick there's a %chance based on your skill and other variables that you get whatever item you're trying to get, be it flint, bark, etc.  And making it so there's little mini games for fishing and the like would be pretty great too, I feel.  Yet, honestly, that's really my only complaint.
There are a few issues with terrain generation, yet I'm sure they'll get that smoothed out.  I mean I saw seams in the terrain where there was nothing but void beneath them.  It was kinda amusing, actually.  Similarly I'm sure they'll get more tooltips into the game that explain more stuff.  While it's great to have it like Minecraft where very little is actually explained in the game, the fact that the simplicity of Minecraft isn't there makes it so that things like descriptive tooltips and the like are absolutely needed so I'm sure they'll work on that as they already have some good tooltips in the game.
I've never liked the idea of having to go to an external site or having to watch video tutorials to get even the basics of a game, I've always found that to be clunky, especially when a simple pop-up tutorial on the basics would serve the player far better.  I'm not saying that everything needs to be explained, yet the basics should at least be pointed out so the player doesn't have to stumble through the first couple of days wondering where or how on earth to get flint or rock.
Overall it's an excellent start to a truly extraordinary game, it's beautiful, it's entertaining, it's engaging, and for being in alpha it's already impressively well done.  If you're not interested in the bugs and troubleshooting but you still want to play a sandbox-builder game with surprisingly beautiful graphics and good gameplay then this is, without a doubt, a game you absolutely want to follow and keep your eyes on, there's great things coming from this, I'm sure.  If, however, you actually don't mind, or even like, being part of the testing process, random crashes, strange bugs, and all that jazz AND want to play a game like I just mentioned then this, right now, is completely for you.  You can be a part of gaming history and usher in a truly unique and amazing game!

Firstly Sniper Elite V2 is a fantastic sniping game and I recomend you play it ether on the hardest difficulty or a custom difficulty where everything effects your shot.
The game is great at what it does, sniping, you feel sneaky as you crawl in to position, you line up your shot, modifying your aim to counter wind, gravity and distance and it's oh-so satisfying seeing you landing a headshot every time due to your built knowlege of handling the game's mechanics, the rifles feel powerful and accurate as well as sounding nice too, you can set traps such as trip mines and place dynamite where you can shoot later so there is a certain strategic element to the game, there's a few enemy types I've encountered so far: soldiers armed with SMG's, some armed with more accurate and powerful rifles and other snipers where you have to find them first and generally are harder to take out (due to their distance and high elevation) but now the bad.
Quite simply, Sniper Elite suffers when you're doing anything BUT sniping, you do have 2 secondary weapons, a SMG when things get hairy in close quaters and a silenced pistol for sneaking and taking enemy's out stealthily.
Oddly you are not at all accurate with these weapons, the reticle for the pistol is relatively decent but it's not tight enough to land certain, percise headshots from a distance making it's usefulness limited, the SMG's ammunition is limited, forcing you to scavange, the crosshair suffers the same problem, the crosshair could be tighter, which is understandable as it is a fully automatic weapon so it causes less of a problem but the shooting feels "serviceable", mediocore even, nothing really thrilling about it but better aiming would make it less of a headache.
There are un-official stealth sections (no failure state if you are discovered), generally I give them a couple of tries to get through them un-detected but the game's engine is terrible for such a thing, the enemy's vision is sharp, expose a leg or so and they will see you, accidently take a single step while running, they will hear it (even in a middle of a warzone with bombs dropping), there's no radar, no tracking, no helpful way to seekout enemy's or move from cover to cover, no meter's or hide in the shadows,  just your slow crouch-walk, moving bodies and choice of using your okay-ish pistol and a stiff stealth kill from behind, that's it, it feels like a absaloute chore to slog through and everytime I just give up and blast my way through with the help of explosives.
Despite this glaring downside, Sniper Elite V2 is a fantastic sniping game, great for anyone that prefered the role the sniper class.

Otherwise, this game is definitely a classic of the TW series. The pros greatly outweigh the cons.

I've been wanting a replacement for my old Windows "Sid Meier's Gettysburg (SMG)". This review is a comparison for others who want to do that. It is not quite the same as SMG, but it's close enough to enjoy, with similar dragging control mechanisms for brigades and troops, and some nice enhanced artillary, charge and grouping functions. "Ultimate General: Gettysburg" has smooth graphics on my 4 year old system running on Linux Mint 17 [64 bit]. The pace is better than SMG, and getting a basic game going before reading the manual was easy. That said, I completed my first battle and found that I need to read the manual to get a level of control I would be comfortable with. The basic drag and move works well in transitioning from SMG, but my inability to execute formations and concentrate attacks as I am used to from SMG did cost me. Looking at an engaged unit does not immediately give a view of the unit's health, but there are advanced indicators at the top if you have a split second to flick your eyes away from the action. It works without any crashes, black sceens, bugs or system tweak requirements on newer computers. If you want to replace your old SMG game, go ahead - it is not quite a clone, and I felt  it lacked some of SMG's polish most felt not so much in-game, but between scenes and on the intro, Considering the age difference between the games I found those rough edges disappointing, but the game is familiar in enough ways to recommend to another SMG player.

Overview: Darksiders is a decent hack-and-slash adventure with an angels-and-demons theme. You gather equipment, solve puzzles, explore dungeons, and fight bosses, killing hundreds of enemies along the way. Collectibles and some character progression make the game a little more interesting.
Dungeons are typical networks of rooms containing puzzles and treasure. To get through them, you solve puzzles, get items, and fight a boss at the end. The puzzles aren't usually too easy, but some can be tedious to get through due to slow movement speed and back-tracking.
The game's story is decent, if somewhat sparse. It's revealed in disordered fragments throughout the game and doesn't answer all the questions it produces, but it's not a bad story overall. The last cutscene is amazing.
Environments are varied and detailed, and a few are downright amazing. The world is semi-open; it's made of several corridors branching off from a couple of hub areas, which you can explore freely after you've opened their paths. You won't be surprised by the dynamics of the game's world, unfortunately: Everything is scripted and highly invariable between saves, so there isn't a lot of replay value to be found in the world design.
Environments and objects alternate between being logical and completely nonsensical. I often try to figure out why game worlds look the way they do, and this one was an entirely mixed bag. It's best not to think too hard about this one. Still, the game has some great eye-catching areas, but they're unfortunately rare.
On to character progression. There's a decent amount of it, mostly achieved via incremental equipment upgrades and items.
One thing I liked was how the game continued to introduce new mechanics and items almost to the very end. New and useful equipment is semi-regularly obtained until you need to face the final boss.
While most of the game's progression is incremental and item-based, there is one small element of "organic" progression: Your primary weapons have an XP bar that gradually fills as those specific weapons are used against enemies. XP can be very slow to gather: Weapons only have four levels, yet they usually won't be maxed out by the end of the game unless you deliberately grind for XP.
Now for movement controls, which have a few minor annoyances. Darksiders has a dodging mechanic, which is required for surviving encounters with many large enemies. However, depending on camera angle, your dodges will sometimes go in the wrong direction. Most of the larger enemies deal huge amounts of damage and require you to dodge in exactly the right direction at exactly the right time, so this control discrepancy can be an incredibly annoying death sentence.
War is completely unresponsive during/after certain actions, which can be easily to accidentally trigger due to overlapping controls. Some of these combat moves will lock your controls until they've completed, which can often lead to unavoidable damage. The worst of these takes about five seconds to complete, which is an eternity in combat.
You can't grab onto most ledges, since the only ones that let you are scripted to do so. Sometimes you will unintentionally fall into chasms or lava, since many ledges only look like they can be grabbed.
The game's world can be a slight bore to get around, because War's main movement speed is a light run. You can fast-travel and eventually get a mount, but much of the time you'll be on foot. The game also has a lot of uneventful back-tracking and filler areas, so boredom is inevitable when you just want to get from point A to point B.
Despite its serious tone, Darksiders heavily utilizes a "fantasy cartoon" aesthetic, with a tendency for the ridiculous and impractical. Many objects and environments have nonsensical designs and features, but at least they look interesting.
As an enthusiast for pre-industrial combat tools, the weapons and armor are particularly bad. Most of them are obscenely bulky and unbalanced for no apparent reason. To be fair, almost everyone in the game is a superhuman immortal; their equipment would have to be much bulkier to withstand the immense forces exerted during combat. Even with that in mind, the game's characters could still benefit from more practical gear.
True to bad fantasy design tropes, the only female warrior in the game has unusually light and form-fitting armor, and wears high heels. That's right, this game's only female soldier wears high heels in battle. Good job, developers. /s
Stability-wise, Darksiders is... adequate. The game crashes and freezes on occasion, and some permanent issues can rarely tarnish your saves.
In particular, the game hates being minimized or tabbed out. At best, it will lag when you tab back in. At worst, it will eventually crash.
Unfortunately, Darksiders has a bad case of consolitis. There are no video options besides brightness and fullscreen resolution, and the controls can't be re-bound. The game heavily prioritizes controllers over the mouse and keyboard, regardless of which is actually being used.
That said, M+K controls can be awkward much of the time; third-person hack-and-slash games are pretty well-suited to a controller, and this is no exception (especially with this game's consolitis). Fortunately, most of the game doesn't require much finesse with aiming and camera movement, so playing with a controller works best most of the time.
However, there are a few aiming/shooting sequences where mouse+keyboard controls are vastly superior, but if you have a controller connected, the game will force you to use awkward and sluggish thumbstick aiming. It's tolerable, but unpleasant.
In summary, I like Darksiders. It doesn't have as much freedom as I'd like, the designs can be a little ridiculous, it's kind of unstable, and organic progression is almost nonexistent. Even so, it's still an enjoyable experience that inspires feelings of both familiarity and novelty.
Strengths: Gameplay, world design, story, mild challenge, exploration
Weaknesses: Mild instability, consolitis, limited replay value (almost everything is linear, scripted, and invariable), occasional issues with movement mechanics

Shovel Knight is a fantastic retro throwback that recaptures not how games played or looked on the NES, but how we remember them. Tight controls, a catchy soundtrack, clever level design, visually appealing spritework, and multiple campaigns come together to make something even greater than the sum of its parts. I highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys platformers, retro games, or enjoys having fun to any capacity.

This game has given me quite the interesting experience. For the slightly high price of 25 dollars, you basically get a 3-in-1 pack, and you will be able to choose which one you play based on your character type.
Pros:
Starting with the basics, I obviously just chose the OG Shovel Knight. Throughout this journey, I found myself enthralled by the adventure. I have to admit, the gameplay mechanics were somewhat simple, but that isn't always a negative point. The storyline in itself may seem generic, however the game has incorporated scenes throughout the game that makes it touching and emotional. A very clear example of this is given after the first level (SPOILERS) where you are asked to save Shield Knight, your partner, falling from the sky within the dream. This campfire scene becomes very symbolistic throughout the game.
However, if you are looking for a more dynamic gameplay mechanic, definitely go for playing Specter Knight (from Shovel Knight: Specter of Torment which is included in this game). There is wall climbing, slashing in mid-air to travel and an entirely different upgrading/shop system. So if you are less into story, you can get just Specter of Torment on Steam for around $10 (base price).
Plague of Shadows (the third playable character that comes in this pack) also takes a whole different perspective into the game and plot. Taking the perspective of Plague Knight, you use your special alchemy powers to constantly throw bombs and jump around at great heights. This character introduced a great "mix and match" system with what types of traits you wanted your bombs to have that you unlock and purchase with your collected coins throughout the levels. Great way to keep every playthrough fresh.
There are still many general concepts throughout all of these that make Shovel Knight so unique. Every level is cleverly designed to keep your brain solving small puzzles and organizing your next move along with certain places where you need to physically act quick. Death has a fair penalty of taking 1/3 (I believe it is around that much) of your current gold and letting you take it back when you respawn. This motivates you just enough to let you keep playing, without being so harsh where you just want to quit.
With only a quick glance, it's hard to tell that this game has much substance besides "defeating levels, bosses and repeat", but that is actually incorrect. There are plenty of hidden secrets in every level or world to discover. Even upon finishing the original campaign for Shovel Knight, the difficulty has changed as the save file turns into something called "Game+", allowing me to experience it again but with a more challenging situation to keep the fun of the game alive.
This game is...well...just really fun. The soundtrack fits the game almost all the time, and nothing is too complicating or impossible, but definitely not just any plain game. I think my money was well spent. 10/10
Cons:
-(When on Mac) can't leave the game without quiting it.

First things first, Duke Nukem Forever isn't as terrible a game as everyone makes it out to be. It may be an antiquated, haphazard, unpolished game. But honestly I've played many other FPS games that had far lower investments into themshelves. And too its credit DNF does have things that are sorely missing from modern shooters, or all games for that matter.
Duke Nukem Forever is, for a lack of better term; a varitable cross section of FPS delevelopment. Like the real rings of a tree, you can see all the growth of the genre. And for better or for worse, its a neat little history lesson or sorts. But in some sections this trip down yesteryear way does wears thin.
Ultimately, if you ask me, DNF is a victim of circumstance. Not because it took thirteen years to come out, but because during that time the FPS genre had become standardized. Today a shooter isn't a shooter worth playing if it is without a robust multiplayer, a sense of realism, over the top melodrama, HATS, and if it isn't military shooter. Forget about it. Than comes a game from an era that didn't have rules. And because of that, we simply scroffed at our roots.
