First off, I am unsure why so many people had trouble with the drm? It may possibly come down to connection issues but i only entered my keycode for the game and dlc and continued on. As what you may consider a "veteran" gamer, the whole "register" thing is quite an old system. However the game clearly allows you to skip it and play without registering.
Tl;Dr Magic in this game is awesome, if you enjoy games with interesting and fun or even over powerd magic systems (Morrowind i'm looking at you) then you will adore this gem.
Anyway onto the review, I mainly will be looking at the Magic system of the game, there are a number of other reviews that can properly describe and highlight the games other excellent aspects.
To be honest perfectly honest, prior to reading a few of the positive reviews for the game, I believed it to be a bit of a joke. The graphics from the screenshots looked poor, the combat seemed clunky and generally the whole thing looked a little bit of a mess. However despite these lingering doubts in my mind I persevered. Getting past the tutorial I had already decided to be a mage. (My usual choice due to magic usually being a bit of hax) Magic in Two Worlds 2 is probably one of the things that makes it so great.
Generally in TW2 skills are aquired through the acquisition of skill books, don't worry the books are quite plentiful, I havent yet completed the Second chapter and already have unlocked every mage skill and there is always the option of purchasing them from respective guilds/merchants for reasonable sums of money. After you have unlocked the skill you spend points into them to level up, nice and easy.
Magic however, differs in that rather than just having spells and combat abilities solely unlocked through skills, it requires you to craft spells using "Spell Cards" these spell cards are received as loot, in chests or as quest rewards. Depending on what skills you have unlocked you can then put the cards together in "Spell Amulets".
Spell cards consist of the
Effect cards: Fire, Water, Psyche etc
Carrier cards: Missile, AOE, Enchant etc
Modifier cards: Damage, Homing, Protection
Depending on the level of your skills you can stack cards to increase the power of their effects, as well as the sheer number of combinations. At first you probably will only be able to create a very simple "magic missile" type spell but as you begin to collect a greater number of cards the possibilities start to expand.
As an example I will describe a recent scenario that played out during my game. I had a quest to clear out some cultists from a number of houses. My spell reportoire consisted of a Fire spell with two stages, the first spat out three homing fireballs, when the fireballs hit the AOE stage activated, because i had added a "time" modifier onto the spell the AOE fire explosion stopped being straight damage and became a meteor shower lasting about 10 seconds. So each of the three missiles would start a meteor shower ontop of the damage they inflict.
The results are quite devestating. However after numerous attempts at destroying the cultists within the house proved fruitless, they seemed to be easily shrugging off the damage. So I switched the spell to use Ice and Lightning damage instead, still the the cultists proved immune to most elemental damage. The beauty of this system is how easy it is to experiment, it merely requires you to swap a card or two in the amulet in order to completely change the spells effect. I eventually defeated the cultists by changing the missile card to an earth card, dealing physical damage and the AOE aspect to a Psyche card, which cause the enemies to turn against each other. It was awesome :)

Overview: Darksiders is a decent hack-and-slash adventure with an angels-and-demons theme. You gather equipment, solve puzzles, explore dungeons, and fight bosses, killing hundreds of enemies along the way. Collectibles and some character progression make the game a little more interesting.
Dungeons are typical networks of rooms containing puzzles and treasure. To get through them, you solve puzzles, get items, and fight a boss at the end. The puzzles aren't usually too easy, but some can be tedious to get through due to slow movement speed and back-tracking.
The game's story is decent, if somewhat sparse. It's revealed in disordered fragments throughout the game and doesn't answer all the questions it produces, but it's not a bad story overall. The last cutscene is amazing.
Environments are varied and detailed, and a few are downright amazing. The world is semi-open; it's made of several corridors branching off from a couple of hub areas, which you can explore freely after you've opened their paths. You won't be surprised by the dynamics of the game's world, unfortunately: Everything is scripted and highly invariable between saves, so there isn't a lot of replay value to be found in the world design.
Environments and objects alternate between being logical and completely nonsensical. I often try to figure out why game worlds look the way they do, and this one was an entirely mixed bag. It's best not to think too hard about this one. Still, the game has some great eye-catching areas, but they're unfortunately rare.
On to character progression. There's a decent amount of it, mostly achieved via incremental equipment upgrades and items.
One thing I liked was how the game continued to introduce new mechanics and items almost to the very end. New and useful equipment is semi-regularly obtained until you need to face the final boss.
While most of the game's progression is incremental and item-based, there is one small element of "organic" progression: Your primary weapons have an XP bar that gradually fills as those specific weapons are used against enemies. XP can be very slow to gather: Weapons only have four levels, yet they usually won't be maxed out by the end of the game unless you deliberately grind for XP.
Now for movement controls, which have a few minor annoyances. Darksiders has a dodging mechanic, which is required for surviving encounters with many large enemies. However, depending on camera angle, your dodges will sometimes go in the wrong direction. Most of the larger enemies deal huge amounts of damage and require you to dodge in exactly the right direction at exactly the right time, so this control discrepancy can be an incredibly annoying death sentence.
War is completely unresponsive during/after certain actions, which can be easily to accidentally trigger due to overlapping controls. Some of these combat moves will lock your controls until they've completed, which can often lead to unavoidable damage. The worst of these takes about five seconds to complete, which is an eternity in combat.
You can't grab onto most ledges, since the only ones that let you are scripted to do so. Sometimes you will unintentionally fall into chasms or lava, since many ledges only look like they can be grabbed.
The game's world can be a slight bore to get around, because War's main movement speed is a light run. You can fast-travel and eventually get a mount, but much of the time you'll be on foot. The game also has a lot of uneventful back-tracking and filler areas, so boredom is inevitable when you just want to get from point A to point B.
Despite its serious tone, Darksiders heavily utilizes a "fantasy cartoon" aesthetic, with a tendency for the ridiculous and impractical. Many objects and environments have nonsensical designs and features, but at least they look interesting.
As an enthusiast for pre-industrial combat tools, the weapons and armor are particularly bad. Most of them are obscenely bulky and unbalanced for no apparent reason. To be fair, almost everyone in the game is a superhuman immortal; their equipment would have to be much bulkier to withstand the immense forces exerted during combat. Even with that in mind, the game's characters could still benefit from more practical gear.
True to bad fantasy design tropes, the only female warrior in the game has unusually light and form-fitting armor, and wears high heels. That's right, this game's only female soldier wears high heels in battle. Good job, developers. /s
Stability-wise, Darksiders is... adequate. The game crashes and freezes on occasion, and some permanent issues can rarely tarnish your saves.
In particular, the game hates being minimized or tabbed out. At best, it will lag when you tab back in. At worst, it will eventually crash.
Unfortunately, Darksiders has a bad case of consolitis. There are no video options besides brightness and fullscreen resolution, and the controls can't be re-bound. The game heavily prioritizes controllers over the mouse and keyboard, regardless of which is actually being used.
That said, M+K controls can be awkward much of the time; third-person hack-and-slash games are pretty well-suited to a controller, and this is no exception (especially with this game's consolitis). Fortunately, most of the game doesn't require much finesse with aiming and camera movement, so playing with a controller works best most of the time.
However, there are a few aiming/shooting sequences where mouse+keyboard controls are vastly superior, but if you have a controller connected, the game will force you to use awkward and sluggish thumbstick aiming. It's tolerable, but unpleasant.
In summary, I like Darksiders. It doesn't have as much freedom as I'd like, the designs can be a little ridiculous, it's kind of unstable, and organic progression is almost nonexistent. Even so, it's still an enjoyable experience that inspires feelings of both familiarity and novelty.
Strengths: Gameplay, world design, story, mild challenge, exploration
Weaknesses: Mild instability, consolitis, limited replay value (almost everything is linear, scripted, and invariable), occasional issues with movement mechanics

Preface: I used the Restored Content Mod while playing this game.
KotOR 2, this time brought to us by Obsidian Entertainment, at first glance appears to be its predecessor's hotter, younger cousin.  There are many fixes to complaints I had for the first game: better menu system (inventory management still needs work), cleaner, faster, better looking, containers show if they're empty, datapads are read automatically, even walking in spacesuits is faster (although it looks funny, seems they just upped the animation speed).  There are more force powers to use, cool special character abilities, and there's better rollplaying since there are a lot more options to what you can do.  For example if your level in Treat Injury is high then more dialogue options open up for you allowing you to truly play the game how you want!  Or...it actually doesn't.  This game was *extremely* aggravating at times.  Once again the designers felt like it was a good idea to throw you into 1v1 duels, so the belief that you could actually roleplay was a mere fantasy that is ripped from your fingers less than a quarter through the game.  To make it worse, there are sections where there are *unskippable cutscenes* right before duels.  This is the biggest pain ever, especially if you're already getting annoyed at the required 1v1 battles you go through.  I would highly recommend ignoring anything but force and battle prowess (melee too, blasters blow), not only for your main character, but for *all* of your characters.  That's right!  It wasn't bad enough making your main character duel, now a large portion of your companions have to do battles (or even entire segments of the game - ie long dungeons) by themselves.  The worst offender of this has to be the HK factory, where you're expected to use HK-47 against an army of droids.  It was terrible, I literally *could not* play through that section the way I built my HK-47.  It made me feel as if I was playing "wrong".  No game should have that effect, *especially* an RPG.  Luckily this game has a console that you can enable because that was the only way to struggle through that section of the game.  As if this complaint wasn't bad enough, the *most important* part of an RPG, the storytelling, wasn't very good.  I enjoyed the journey of the original much more than I did in KotOR 2.  Even *with* the rcm I felt like some of the character's backstories were done halfway through the game and the plot and storytelling was convoluted to put it lightly.  Your companions *attack* each other, seemingly without consequence at times.  It was confusing and distracting.  And the ending straight up sucked.  It was literally dialogue choices, and this is coming from a guy who didn't mind Deus Ex: HR's ending.
This game didn't just need a restored content mod, it needed a drastic overhaul, fix, and rewrite - that's the only reason I can recommend this game - the modding community.  It's really big, even to this day.  The RCM is the tip of the iceberg, and if you didn't like the way the game did something you can probably fix it.

I've had this game for a good 1-2 years before they added it on steam and i love it. If you are the kind of person that LOVES crashing cars, then GET THIS GAME. The physics are unreal. They are incredible.
Pros:
- Incredibly realistic phsyics
- Great graphics for a physics based game
- Greats mods (maps, vehicles, engines, etc)
- make your own custom maps
- vehicles are great
- TONS of options for your cars (not quite total customization, but you can change the colors, engines, type of car [i.e. make a care the "off-road" version of that car and much more], etc.)
- shadows are great
- modding this game without the steam workshop is very easy
- it is in alpha state, and yet i have not had much trouble with any bugs. Maybe a few here and there but it's in good state right now
- there are 5 motion options: Realtime, 2x slower than realtime, 4x slower than realtime, 8x slower than realtime, and 100x slower than realtime
- car crashes are unbelievably realistic and awesome
Cons:
- You will need at least a decent computer to be able to play this game
- shadows (at highest setting) take A LOT of memory and can cause, depending on your kind of computer, a 5-50 fps drop (since my machine isnt the greatest, i lose a great amount of FPS if i put shadows on high. I lose about 30-40 FPS)
- i personally did not enjoy the default maps that came with the game. BUT there are AMAZING custom maps on the forums that you can download (mods)
Final verdict:
If you like crashing cars, get this game. If you love realistic physics in videogames, get this game. If you are looking for a racing game, this game might not be for you. YES this game IS getting a racing update, but i doubt it will be as good as other games that are made specifically for racing (forza, burnout, need for speed, etc.). But i hope the team at BeamNG proves me wrong on that statement :D

The horror genre is pretty much crap nowadays. A monkey with a keyboard could produce what some like to call a "scary" game. Why? It's all just jumpscares! Jumpscares, for those who don't know, are when a sudden unexpected event in a form of entertainment is meant to startle the player/viewer. These are often put into a game to make them seem "scary". This game does have a couple of those, but it's truly terrifying due to the one rare peice of gold in a game: atmosphere. Atmosphere alone in a horror game can drive it home all by itself! "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" is the most prime example of "atmosphere over jumpscares" that you could possibly find. It tears at your true fears and never holds back on the terror. The game could be worth a full $60 and still be worth it, but $20 is a platinum deal. Bump off another $15 and you have the sale of the century! I can gurantee that if you hate jumpscares, but enjoy a good, creepy, pee-your-pants type of horror game, you will not be dissapointed in the slightest.

The only real threat are the enemy snipers, these are incredibly hard to spot before they start shooting at you. Meaning that they will almost always get the first shot off. This makes fighting these enemies not a spy vs spy challenge but more a fishing game with yourself as bait.
The story isn't much to speak of, prevent the Russians from obtaining V2 tech. Shoot some scientists, kill bad guys. Most missions will be completed by killing every guy on the map, sometimes you have to be sneaky until you kill a special guy. Crawl around, shoot, rinse repeat. All in all, an enjoyable but somewhat mediocre game. But I hear good things about the zombie expansion.

Hail to the King, Baby. Duke Nukem Forever is the sequel to 3D Realms' classic Build engine first-person shooter Duke Nukem 3D. After a VERY long (and troubled) time in development, DNF was finally released in 2011. For the most part, the mainstream gaming media panned and generally sh*t on it. Many oldschool fans of DN3D who had waited a very long time for this game's release also cried foul. I am one of those longtime DN3D fans and i have to say, after playing through DNF the first time at launch and more recently a 2nd time, i still truly don't get all the hate for this game. IMO it's great fun, a fitting continuation of the franchise, and a decent return to gamedom for Duke. Usually intense, often amusing, occasionally frustrating, but immediately enjoyable and entertaining throughout. While not perfect, it's certainly not a bad game and i feel it definitely deserved better scores than what it received. Don't let the negative press decide for you, try it for yourself.

I played the old Side Meir's Gettysburg when it came out and loved it. I've been playing Ultimate General for a while and feel that it is superior is someways, but the old Gettysburg had some advantages. I think Ultimate General blows the old one away in graphics and fluid game play. I like the way you can group units and move them as one. I'm very impressed with the live action, but think the old game was better in the following ways;
1. You could march units in column form and then deploy at a designated spot in a number of ways (wedge, refuse line...)
2. You could manipulate individual units. Say deploy 3 reg and have one as skirmmers watching you flank.
3. You could deploy a whole brigade as skirmishers
4. The calvary was more versitle. Able to move as calvary and then deploy in line.
5. The old units had experiance points which could be added to by where they were in line, location of Division commanders, cover....etc.
6. If a unit was in line they would automaticlly start to fortifiy,
All in all its still a great game. I would highly recommend this to anyone into real time combat games. Def worth the price. If the good people at UG would take the above into consideration it would be a perfect game.

THE FOLLOWING IS A PRE-PLAYED REVIEW OF DARKSIDERS II: DEATHINITIVE EDITION. I HAVE NOT SUNK A SINGLE MINUTE OF PLAYTIME INTO THIS VERSION OF THE GAME
So I've been reading the reviews for Darksiders II: Deathinitive Edition. I still hate the term Deathinitive. Let me go on the record saying that right now.
Anyways, reviews are mixed for DSII:DE, and this may turn people away from actually considering getting it, because Mixed Reviews means that the game is at about 60/40 or 50/50 on good/bad reviews. But there is a very valid reason as to why this is.
It is because the PC Gaming community which I happen to be part of is a bunch of self entitled little ♥♥♥♥♥. We have people whining that, because they bought DSII, but not all the DLC, they should get DSII:DE (which features a graphical upgrade AND every single DLC released for it), they should be getting the game for free, , because they are just getting a "graphical polish that should have been there in the first place" (in their eyes), as opposed to getting it at 80% off (about 6 bucks American). Let me be clear. These guys are whining because they have to pay SIX BUCKS. PS4 and Xbox One users have to pay full price for the game. These guys get 80% off of a game on release day. RELEASE DAY! How often do you hear about a game being 80% off for ANYONE on release day?
Besides. Don't blame Nordic Games for this. Blame Steam for making it impossible for Nordic to reward their fans the way they wanted to anyway. They intended to give a free copy of the Deathinitive Edition to anyone who had bought Darksiders II plus the DLCs, but Steam forced their hand to have it be those who had bought the Darksiders Franchise Pack (Darksiders, Darksiders II, the soundtrack for both, a Darksiders Prequel Comic, and all the DLC for Darksiders 2 wrapped up into a single-purchase package). My previous post already went over the various Loyalty Tiers available, even having a tier for "New members of the Darksiders Franchise", read, people who haven't paid a single red cent for their games.
So yes. A full two-thirds of the negative reviews are just entitled brats whining about having to pay 6 dollars for a game that costs 30. ♥♥♥♥ them.
The rest of the reviews complaining about 1.) how buggy the game is, or 2.) being unable to purchase Darksiders II now. As in, the regular version, NOT the Deathinitive Edition. The second category of negative reviews can be safely discarded.
Bugs in a game, especially on launch day, should be expected. Some of the bugs listed are in fact quite valid. Example: Some of the reviewers bought/unlocked/played the game on the first day. They all had the same issue. The game would get to the main menu, they would start a new game, and they would Crash to Desktop. And they wrote an angry review saying "don't buy his broken game, ♥♥♥♥ nordic games for ♥♥♥♥ing with the game"
And that is a very valid review for a very valid problem. If you can't play the game, any price above free is too high to pay. Thankfully, after the bombed port that was Batman: Arkham Knight, Steam has a refund option, an option these people took. But that wasn't the end.
See, those that stuck around beyond the First Day Crash bug found out something. Nordic was listening. and Nordic started fixing the various bugs players pointed out. Starting with the Crash Bug, which was fixed on day 2, which is why it is referred to as the First Day Crash Bug, because it was only experienced by people who bought the game and played it on the first day. Since then, over the past 15 days, Nordic has been responding to any bug reports they get, and dealing with them accordingly. Did you have a Season Pass to Darksiders II? Email them proof, and you will get a Steam Key to the Deathinitive Edition. Just activate it and boom, done. The game is yours now. Many of the issues the negative reviewers are complaining about (excepting the ones whining about paying 6 bucks for a thirty dollar game) HAVE BEEN DEALT WITH.
REPEAT FOR THE PEOPLE IN THE BACK. NORDIC GAMES IS ACTIVELY WORKING ON FIXING ANY AND ALL ISSUES THAT GAMERS FIND WITH THEIR DEATHINITIVE EDITION OF DARKSIDERS II.THEY ARE NOT BEING WB GAMES AND LEAVING IT A MESS LIKE WB DID WITH ARKHAM KNIGHT. THEY ARE CLEANING IT UP AND MAKING SURE IT WORKS, TO MAKE SURE EVERYONE CAN ENJOY THEIR GAME. AND I CAN SAFELY SAY IT IS THEIR GAME, BECAUSE NORDIC GAMES HAS IN FACT RECRUITED THE OLD DARKSIDERS CREW FROM VIGIL GAMES (Hopefully to work on Darksiders III)
One final thing to note. Apparently, according to one reviewer, a lot of people were complaining about how DSII:DE wasn't running at full 60 fps on max settings even though they had super souped up rigs. This perplexed this user because he had a modern rig, and was experiencing the same things. He found a fix for this. And it apparently is that you just need to rollback your hardware to an earlier version, and it will run like a dream (Applicable to NVidia users, cannot speak for AMD). Don't ask me how that works, I don't have a ♥♥♥♥ing clue. Also the System Requirements section on DSII:DE is now slightly archaic and innacurate.
So the vast majority of the negative reviews on DSII:DE can be broken into three types of people
~~People whining for paying 6 dollars for a AAA game (even though this AAA game is at about a third of the cost of a Standard AAA Game. CoD sells for about, what, sixty bucks on release? and its ♥♥♥♥ing CoD!!!)
~~People griping about bugs, but didn't stick around for them to be fixed
~~People who found the game running less than absolutely perfectly on frames per second, and blamed the game company, instead of their hardware
SO. WHEN YOU ARE LOOKING THROUGH THE REVIEWS OF DARKSIDERS 2, DISREGARD THOSE TYPES OF NEGATIVE REVIEWS ENTIRELY, BECAUSE THEY ARE ♥♥♥♥♥ING AND WHINING, NOT BECAUSE THE GAME IS BAD, BUT BECAUSE THEY ARE ENTITLED LITTLE ♥♥♥♥♥.
Instead, do what I do when looking at buying a game. Read the reviews, yes. It's how you find out if a F2P multiplayer game is F2P/P2W (Free to play, pay to Win). Those types of games need to be weeded out and destroyed. But as for everything else, read reviews, but watch some gameplay footage on Youtube. You'll get some spoilers, sure. But you will also get a look at the style of the game. The controls, unfortunately, you won't know unless you play it. Some people like the control scheme for Brutal Legend, some people don't. That's a case by case basis that the reviews can't particularly grasp.
As far as my review for Darksiders II goes, here it is.
Zelda-esque puzzles, God of War's hack and slash combat, Brutal Legend's fantastical art design, and some of inFAMOUS's platforming style all get together and have a big, massive orgy pile in Diablo II's dropped loot mechanic, and Darksiders II was the baby. If you liked a majority of these things, then you will enjoy Darksiders II, I can almost assure you.
So final verdict: "Is it good?" I hear you ask, to which I say "Yes!"
"Is it for Everyone out there?" I hear you continue, to which I respond cheekily "Is ♥♥♥♥ing anything?"
If you liked Darksiders and have been considering getting Darksiders II, go ahead. At this point, if you are looking at this page you doubtlessly know about KotOR 2's reputation for being buggy and incomplete. Just to make sure you know: this wasn't the studio's fault - LucasArts gave them less than half the time they actually needed to finish the game. Still, a review isn't about what something could have been but rather, what something is.
If you liked KotOR 1, KotOR 2 is more of that but refined, enhanced, and... admittedly, yes, buggier. However, the bugs (in general) are rarely crippling and the more serious ones tend to be both not universally experienced, and tend to only occur in side missions (like swoop racing). As for gameplay, combat is streamlined while still providing plenty of options for variety what with blasters, lightsabers, Force powers, and special attacks. Feats, equipment and their myriad upgrades, and to a lesser degree skills allow for crazy amounts of customization while remaining simple enough to easily understand.
The story is really where KotOR 2 shines through, though. As mentioned before, the game was a rushed job and much had to get cut at the last moment, however aside from the final stretch most missing plot threads are in the minor side quests and are only missing the very end that some may not even notice. Dialogue is natural and is one of the few examples where dialogue trees actually work well. Very little exposition (if any at all) is given straight through endless monologues, but is woven in from bits and pieces grasped from various characters (including the main - no amnesiacs here) including some who outright lie (and well, might I add)! Every playable character is well characterized with great personalities and motivations that are believeable enough not to make us question why they hate everyone else on the ship stick to the main character regardless (except maybe Visas...)
This game is also much darker than it's predecessor. It's enough that whether you liked or were simply lukewarm towards the original Star Wars trilogy of movies while the new trilogy left you cold, you are practically guaranteed to appreciate this game. On the other hand, if you really liked all of the Star Wars movies you may find the departure from the standard too much for your tastes. Honestly, despite the lightsabers and Jedi, there are points when KotOR 2 almost doesn't even feel like Star Wars (which I actually liked, to be honest).
One last thing that is worth mentioning - while a significant portion of the game was unfinished at the time of its release, a group of fans have been digging up the not-quite-removed game files, finishing them up, and reconnecting them to the game. It is very well done (particularly for a group of fans digging through broken scraps), adds much to the game, and helps fill in most of the holes in the story. Just search for The Sith Lords Restored Content Mod.

Okay. Now that's out of my system: onto the actual game review.
First, the bad. The story is just okay. It's not bad, but it's not exactly rivetting, and it's downright boring the second time through. The inventory system is still held-over from Baldur's Gate and KOTOR 1. It's completely unmanageable without a notepad. If you're following the chronology of Bioware games, this won't be fixed until Mass Effect 2, and it gets worse before it gets better. The fact that you can make any character a Jedi is cool, but it makes any levels taken before that absolutely worthless. Once you can use a lightsaber, even owning anything else is just stupid.
Now the good. The story is pretty okay. It doesn't have great re-watchability, but I did find myself caring about it the first time through. For the second playthrough, it's a serious chore to skip through all the extensive dialog. The fact that you can make any character a Jedi is really cool. Gameplay-wise, it's a little hokey, but story-wise it's really neat. And let's face it, lightsabers kick♥♥♥♥♥
This is a pretty good execution of the Dungeons & Dragons/Star Wars d20 system. It's far more playable than Baldur's Gate 2 (in my opinion), and much more fun than Neverwinter Nights (again, that's just imho).
The AI. Hmm. What can I say? Like much of this game, it's okay. You can absolutely just keep track of one character and let the rest do what they want, and you'll be okay. But if you pause every round and issue specific orders to each character, you'll be done with battles a lot faster and probably live longer.
Overall, I like KOTOR 2 better than the first. I prefer the characters, I like that the interactions with your party members affects the game, and I like that any character can be apprenticed as a Jedi. It's also great that you choose an actual Jedi class right off the bat, rather than choosing a non-Jedi class initially, then having to essentially start a new character once you become a Jedi. But the story is very simplistic, the inventory system is still a mess and the graphics were mediocre even when the game was released.
So I give KOTOR 2 a B-. Objectively, I suppose it should be a little lower, but this is one of the Star Wars games from the golden age of Lucasarts, so I'm a bit biased.

It's hard to put Shovel Knight into words even if you grew up with 8-bit nintendo games.  When the resurgence of nostalgia games came about in the mid 2010s, a good chunk of them kept the stupid difficulty for the sake of nostalgia, and most people used it as a selling point. And in a sea of intentional mediocrity, comes this diamond in the rough. It not only uses nostalgia as a selling point, it takes every advantage of today's technology and what we know of what can make a quality product that newcomes and veterans alike can enjoy.
I hate to crib from another source, but I think Redlettermedia's Previously Recorded game review of Shovel Knight really drove home the difference between a cash in of nostalgia and an inspirational homage of what people grew up playing. Shovel Knight delivers the latter in absolute spades, and no, I'm not making a god damn shovel pun out of that.
Since i'm bringing up inspiration, let me give you an idea of what this game is in terms of what I played when i was a kid. Mechanically speaking, this has the movement and platforming of a GOOD Mega Man game, with combat resembling duck tales, the map system of Super Mario Bros 3, and the forgiviness, polish and charm of Kirby's Adventure.
Remember when I said taking advantage of today's technology and knowledge of what can make a good product? There's subtle things in play that just make this game so good. It's an 8-bit game, and there is no intentionally digitized voice acting, so every character you meet including yourself has a bit of an "accent", and you can tell who is talking just by listening. From the sneaky Plague Knight to the towering Polar Knight, you can tell they added personality just from all the little things, and that's not even mentioning the animation.
I said it before. This game is a real diamond in the rough. You need to enter it knowing that out of the sea of lazy chiptuned, intentionally difficult 8-butt videogames out there, this one right here is the standard bearer to which all games should aspire to be. Just ♥♥♥♥ing fun and enjoyable.

While this game has tremendous potential, it is nowhere ready to play.  This is not pre-alpha software, this is in the developer unit testing stage.   In a few months of hard development I think this game could be something pretty awesome but at this stage I wouldn't recommend spending your money to assist the deveopers testing their code.
The user interface is clunky at best, the game is completely unforgiving but also gives no assistance to the player, the crafting lines, although intricate, make no sense and EVERYTHING takes way too long.   I continually get a deadlock error that crashes the game and then when I trie to restart it tells me to wait for the game to close.  It takes 5 minutes for the game to close so I can go back in and find I lost my last few actions.
Myself, I can't sit and play a game that tries to mask frustration as entertainment.  For example, wolves that are nearly unkillable to a brand new player, but spawn in your chosen settlement area, When you die you loose everything plus stats and skills.  To top that off you spawn in one of several points around the island and you have to start all over again, trying to make it back to your grave.  When you arrive there you are killed again by the same wolf.
I don't necessarily disagree with the concept of requiring multiple player/crafters to progress.  But to be able to make a steel sickle to harvest (yes i know you can use a flint one) you must have a prospector/miner/smelter/forger of appropriate level.  But you also need to have flux to make steel and to make flux you have to have an alchemist.  But for the alchemist to have a better chance of finding herbs they have to have ... you guessed it ... a steel sickle.
Frustrations like this make the game feel like the developers making it are figuring things out as they go.   I don't believe it is unreasonable to expect a developer to have figured out how to fill in a tunnel while they were figuring out how to dig one.
I don't recommend this game at this point, however, in 6 to 9 months it might be playable.

For me this is one of the games that I can play for a very long time.
But be warned that this game is not for everyone as it is complex and takes time.
Time for gathering resources depends on world difficulty and can range from fast to taking forever.
Base building time is not so much affected by difficulty (once you have the resources) but takes some thought to have a good layout. You can even screw up without knowing until it is too late. For example when you do not protect your conveyor belts and have uncontrolled hive mind growth.
So before starting I recommend to read some guides and/or the wiki. If you are not willing to read then you may have a hard time. The tutorial is very basic and the ingame help is not enough to understand everything in the game. There are no scenarios or extended tutorials that show you how to master the game.
Once you know how things work out it is really enjoyable to build up your base and to automate the tedious processes.
The frozen factory expansion is not required immediately for this because it extends the late game. Have played over 100 hours and just about to begin with the additional content. For that amount of playtime it is well worth it in my opinion.
The user interface is the part of the game that needs the most improvements. It makes some tasks more complicated than they should be. If you are deterred by this fact then better wait for improvements. It already improved over time but still needs more time.
My recommendation:
If you are looking for a complex game that requires time or already played minecraft with technical mods like industrialcraft (especially if you like Gregtech) then this is likely a game for you.
If you are looking for a game with less complexity and quicker progress you should look into Factorio first and come back once you need more ;)

Star Wars - Knights of the Republic II: The Sith Lords is the sequel to one of the greatest videogames of all-time, Star Wars: Knights of the Republic. As you can imagine, the game has a lot to live up to. How does it fare? Pretty damn well. In terms of gameplay and technical (graphics, animations) prowess, KOTOR II is superior to its predesccesor. The narrative isn't quite as strong, due to KOTOR II's inconsistent second and third act that waste the narrative potential that was set up by the game's first act. The ending, in particular, is very, very underwhelming. Also, the villains of the game (Darth Traya, Darth Sion, and Darth Nihilus) don't reach the heights of the original KOTOR's Darth Malak. They are decent, servicable villains but don't get enough screen time and character development for them to be as memorable and compelling as they could have been. So, is KOTOR II better than KOTOR? Yes, and no. There are many moments in this game that are above many RPGs, including KOTOR itself, but many times it deliver in a way that's great but still not as impactful as you know it could have. I know LucasArts didn't give Obsidian that much time to develop this game, so that's why see such a great feeling of inconclusive incompleteness. Still, despite that, KOTOR II is a masterpiece. A very flawed one at that, but still a masterpiece nonetheless.
*P.S.- There's a "restoration mod" for KOTOR II that fixes many of the narrative probolems the original build suffered from. This version of KOTOR II is the ultimate cut, and it delivers on most of the potential that the game has. It almost trumps KOTOR, but the original is still king. Get the mod if you can. It's great--and it will change the game drastically. :)

DNF tries to better itself compared to Duke games of old, be more than simply a ‘pickup n play for ♥♥♥♥♥ n giggles’ game. The problem is, the entire premise of Duke Nukem is ‘pickup n play for ♥♥♥♥♥ n giggles’. Duke isn’t meant to be Gordon Freeman, Sam Fisher, Agent 47 etc. Duke is meant to be Duke.
The bottom line is, if you want a decent game, that’s got some good moments, and can put up with annoyances of the modern FPS additions, give it a try.  But classic Duke this is not.

UPDATE: It's been quite a while since I made my original review, and while the vast majoriy of what I said then still applies, there are a few things that have changed, all for the better! The game still has wonderful softbody physics, scratches still do not appear on the pain and the game still eats up a lot of my time. However, I can gladly say that BeamNG.drive now provides a much better driving experience. All the cars handle very realistically (not necessarily nicely however) as a lot has been overhauled. You now have control over tire pressure, tires will heat up, the engine will heat up, suspension has been completely overhauled and generally, the game handles a lot better. On top of that, there are several new official maps and vehicles, and lots of quality mods available. BeamNG.driver still isn't the best looking game on the market, and still has places to grow, but it's still certainly worth picking up and it keeps getting better and better!
ORIGINAL REVIEW: As someone who's been doing small track racing in beat-up 4-cylinders since I was 11, I know a few things about damage modeling. I'm very picky with car games, especially ones centered around carnage. Beam.NG, is in my opinion one of (if not the best) soft-body car physics sandbox games out there. The damage portrayed is pretty darn close to the real thing. While it's not perfect it's as close as 2014 technology can really let us experience. Since it's still in Alpha, scratches and rubs don't appear on the side of the cars, but I certainly hope they will when the game is finished. However, while the damage modeling is wonderful, as far as a driving experience, BeamNG.drive doesn't deliver. If you want tight, accurate and realistic car control, look elsewhere. As of (Aug. 14 '14) BeamNG.drive isn't great to drive. The controls are sort of laggy, rear-wheel drive vehicles are near impossible to drive and the standard transmision is rather awkward. That being said, this game is still in developement, and I certainly recomend picking it up. As is, demolition derbies are sort of possible, but just messing around is tons of fun. I certainly enjoy it, and I want this game to become fully polished, so buy it and help it become the perfect driving simulator sandbox thing.

Overall BeamNG.drive is one of the best soft body car shenanigans simulator out there, and it's completely worth its price. I bought the alpha early on, about a year ago, and I'm still having fun with it now. If you like the physicsy simulationy type of sandbox game you'll definitely be impressed with BeamNG.drive and end up messing around with it for a long time (and that's not including the wide variety of mods available)!
There's a racing mode and other new features coming out soon, and I hope they turn out as well as everything else.
Regarding Next Car Game, NCG is more of a desruction derby focusing on wide areas and chunks of destruction with a ton of broken pieces flying around; it's more of an action-orientated
. BeamNG.drive is a realistic physics simulator sandbox. NCG and BeamNG.drive are both good at doing what they are designed to do, but in my view they're pretty different.
The physics are extremely realistic and efficient with minimal glitching; every crash inflicts different and varying amounts of damage upon each vehicle.
The cars are detailed in terms of aesthetics (the detail of the exterior and interior of the vehicles) and mechanics (wheel torque, suspension, chassis integrity) with results extremely similar to their real-world counterparts.
The graphics are decent with no visual effect bugging as of now. The sound works for what it is but isn't made all that well; a sound overhaul is planned.
The mods are plenty and great, very high quality. You can pilot airplanes and do the coolest trix.
There are many controls and it is sometimes hard to press all the buttons needed to control vehicles. Vehicles can sometimes feel sticky or slippery.
For those who are willing to take upon themselves the challenge of reading a huge block of text:
BeamNG.drive is one of the most realistic car physics/damage simulators up to date. Utilizing a real-time soft-body physics engine powered by Torque3D, it successfully emulates breakable and malleable surfaces applied to cars. The physics demonstration that BeamNG.drive is capable of is nearly identical to real-world movement; footage of in-game crashes have been compared to real-world test crashes with minimal differences.
It's amazing how the physics are simulated, with every surface on every car bending and breaking differently in every situation (surfaces are warped in accordance to the surfaces they come in contact with resulting in unique damage, rather than calling up a stored "damage model" when a car hits something a la GTA car physics or the such). This is where the "Beam" of BeamNG.drive comes in. I'm not that knowledgeable about the details of the physics simulating but it can be thought of like a detailed, intricate grid on a surface with each point moving when it hits something. I have not encountered many bugs in the physics so far, but if pushed far beyond real-world limits the physics do cause model glitches. Sometimes meshes and textures will crumple and stretch weirdly after paricularly intensive crashes. For what it is, however, it works wonderfully and efficiently, even able to be run on a medium-powered laptop with some lag spikes only during intensive car mangling.
Each car is crafted with a keen eye to their details; the mechanics of a vehicle and the aesthetics are both represented. Each car has its unique statistics, with varying engine types, suspension, handling, and et cetera. The handling can even be changed, with options for a sportscar-like experience, offroad handling, and other presets. (The actual in-game control handling can be changed as well, ranging from an arcade control scheme seen in most car games to a full, realistic "driver's seat" experience. However, as of now the control is sort of lackluster with a keyboard since the left and right keys make the steering wheel turn all the way to either side; the cars sometimes feel sticky or slippery.) The detailed aesthetics can also be changed, as the cars are modular and can have parts added and removed. This also ties in with the modding capabilities of the game, which I will get into in a bit. Because of all of the attention paid to making everything as realistic as possible, the seven vanilla cars each have their own unique feel and excel at different tasks (again much like their real-world counterparts).
In my opinion, there's not much to say about this aspect currently since the focus of BeamNG.drive is realistic physics simulation. The graphics are decent and look great when maxed out, but they're nothing special currently (as you can probably see in the trailer and screenshots). There are some post effects which help to smooth everything out a bit, and there are a spattering of particles here and there. The particles do add a lot of effect when used correctly in screenshots and cinematics. The camera following sometimes goes through the ground if a car is tumbling or spinning but overall works as it should, providing smooth views of third-person and first-person views (although there's no model actually driving the cars). That covers the basic graphics system, I think. The sound isn't as good as everything else, but it is clear and works its part. The engine sounds, tire screeches, and et cetera are the same in every situation on every car but the actual sound clips are clear and concise. In slow motion the sounds run in realtime and are very loud, but other than that I can't think of anything too jarring. There is some ambience as well, and it is decent. The developers are planning a sound overhaul, however, so I am looking forwards to that.
The modding capabilities really expand the possibilities of BeamNG.drive, with more detailed vehicles, intricate maps, other fun and interesting mods. There are many high quality mods that have qualities comparable to the actual game. One of the most well-known modders on the BeamNG forums, DrowsySam, has even helped the devs with some things. Of course, as mods, they aren't completely perfect but as I said, most of them are top notch. There are even mods for planes, and althought the physics for those aren't as realistic and smooth as the car physics, they're still pretty awesome (the devs haven't had air travel possibilities in their mids yet so hopefully you can see how cool that is), I'm also not going to say too much about this, since you really just have to install some mods to get a sense of what they can do.
The controls are a bit weird, with the arrow keys controlling vehicles, the numpad and a right-click-and-hold controlling the camera, and various other key combinations for respawning, changing gears (in manual control mode), switching vehicles, and activating slow motion to list a few of the commonly used commands. It works, but sometimes it is hard to access multiple commands, for example, when trying to record something (movement, camera angle, and slow motion for example).

I finished the campaign after several play sessions and 7 total hours in game. At first I was blown away by the sniper mechanic and especially the kill cam. This is a beautiful game and I had fun even though I usually do not enjoy stealth games. I did find the game to become alittle repetitive after a few missions and could only stand to play one mission at a time and then needed a break. The game does give some freedom in how to handle situations/missions/enemies. You can watch patrol routes or individual enemies and line up the perfect shot, set booby traps, or silently eliminate a target. Several missions also provide enviromental conditions to mask your actions. So if you enjoy stealth/sneak games then the sky is the limit here. I personally don't enjoy that dynamic too much and found myself running and gunning through missions. The game does allow a fast paced and loud approach with the only drawback being that it sometimes punishes this behavior by overloading you with enemies. Sniper Elite is obviously centered around the sniping mechanic and I think it does a good job of making that function fun and interesting. I wish there were more long distance shots but it is satisfying to fire that perfect shot at any distance and watch the impact with the kill cam. As long as you don't tire of this central mechanic then the game will be fun. It can grind on you alittle if you play missions back to back. It also reloads at checkpoints when you die or when you continue from a previous session so that can get alittle annoying to play the same area over and over especially if you continue to die further into an objective. I did not play CO-OP so I can't comment on that. I briefly played multiplayer and the match I was in was fast paced but I bet if you had a server full of patient snipers then it would be a blast in a methodical cat and mouse game kind of way.
I think this game is worth it especially if you can snag it on sale or in a bundle or something. Its not going to change your life but its different then alot of games out there and that coupled with the 7-8 hours you'll spend on the campaign means its worth a shot. (Ha Ha!)

Yes, this game is scary. Your first 30 minutes will be the most scary, and you'll want to stop playing forever. Your next 2 hours will be strenuous and make you want to uninstall the game and never hear that horrible music ever again. And dear God, the monster spawn noises will be playing in your head every second you're asleep for at least a month.
However, when (if) you finish the main story, you'll end up wanting more. So you try the Justine story. You haven't seen fear until you've seen the Justine monster. So once again, you stop playing for a couple days... But then you come back.
After you finish the Justine story, and there's nothing more to do, guess what? You can download custom stories online.
These custom stories make the main game child's play. These are created by demented, crazy, unforgiving people in the community that want nothing more than to make you crap your pants. They trap you in horrifying situations where you have to face your worst fears, and you don't have a choice. But you love it and you know you do.
So bottom line, buy this game. It's $5 during sales, and it may be the most important $5 you spend. Eventually, you reach the point where it isn't scary, it's just fun and you become addicted to breaking dishes and running past monsters you threw boxes at.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg, is a brilliant game. Graphically it doesn't compete with any games of it's type really, but the strategy and thought that goes into it is just what Total War lacks. Ultimate General is a very diverse tactical game, where your mission is to pick either Confederate or Union, and win the battle of Gettysburg, which ultimatly saw the fall of the Confederate States. I am a Confederate supporter, so I always play Confederate. I am good at strategy games, but I am yet to win a Battle as the CSA. I came so very close, but their troops just aren't as devastasing as that of the Union. This game is very realistic, and it takes unit positioning into account well. A silly mistake could cost you a flank, and the AI has the intelligence to seek this opportunity. Confederate Units don't generally take as much of a beating, I have noticed. I have used 2 v 1 on good Union units such as the Iron Brigade, and only just won. Moral is a problem for the CSA, and I notice they are happier to run generally, than take a beating.
I haven't yet found a tactic that works, it is a very challenging game. Where you place your units, height, cover etc, really matters, and judging it wrong will cost you, most likely.
I really like this game, and it get's very intense towards the end just because of the sheer amount of units on the field. The battle is broken up into parts, and sometimes you have to take the decision to push on a certain position of he union army, seperatly from the full scale battle. Afterwards, you may be taken back onto the full battlefield with all of your armies, and all of the enemy against you, and you have to crush them ultimatly. I do find the time limits a problem, as I am not a very agressive player, and last time I was winning as CSA slowly, but the game ended as I ran out of time.
It really takes a lot of practice, it is NOT an easy game to play, but it is fun. I reccomend it 100%, especially to those that like the game type, or the era. 10/10, the CSA will win some day...I am trying.

The first hour or so of this game was frustrating. The developers did not include much in the way of a game guide or tutorial, however Dartis actually has an awesome tactical guide on steam. You can find it
.
If anyone is having trouble with this game, or finds it to be flawed I highly recommend reading this guide. It goes into detail about things like condition and morale, which play a huge role in charges, retreating, etc. Once you know these concepts god damn does this game become fun! The past 10 hours (as of now) since the first hour I played has been only enjoyable.
It is tactical, brutal, tense..the ground in front of you changes hands six times, canister shot after canister shot being poured into the lines. makes me excited just thinking about it.
This is a game of patience and maneuvering. It is a fair amount of stand and fire, fallback and replace the line with reserves, and so on, just like the actual civil war. However a cunning, opportune massed charge or flank attack can break through and roll up the enemies line. The important thing is being able to utlize this advantage, which in the actual civil war was sometimes not taken advantage of (as in, a charge that broke through had no real plan for afterward and would be repulsed).
So it is purely a strategy game. What will you do after breaking through? Do you have reserves to follow up? Are you going to/have you created a salient? This game reminds me of chess in some ways, in that each move must have a larger plan, must have something it is following up, and you must be ready to counter any move the opposition may make.
No game is perfect but in terms of pure, straight-forward strategy with a fantastic historical flair,
comes pretty dang close.

Ok this is my first ever game review, I've followed this game from the start, seen Youtubers play it, wanted to do it on my own channel, saw the mixed reviews and having played it, thought i would put forward my latest opinion (15th March 2017).
Fundamentally, the game does a lot right. The actual driving of the coach/bus is well done, visually it's very nice, the coaches and their controls are well detailed. There have also been plenty additions from the last time i saw the game to now. (such as the GPS having different scales).
Are there issues? absolutely.
The biggest undoubtedly is the AI. Generally it's ok bar 2 pretty major details. 1, Juctions/intersections, they can get a bit confused and end up blocking them a bit too regularly. Not ideal but not a game breaker. The second one however... kinda is a game breaker. The AI on the autobahn/Motorway has a horrendous habit of stopping. and i don't mean "hit the breaks and avoid a crash" kinda stopping, i mean "they've hit hit an invisible wall, done 100km/h to 0km/h in 0.01 seconds and we're about to rear end them with our 20tonne coach at 100km/h" kinda stopping. (And you do). Given so much of the game is on the Autobahn that's a fatal, fatal flaw rendering the game a struggle at best.
But no, i'm not going to sit and rip the game to shreds, it's generally very, very good. It lacks a lot of polish in certain areas but aside from the AI stopping issue, nothing you can't work around or live with. Ok i have had one random crash to desktop already so perhaps stability is a slight concern, and yes, out the "box" i don't like the settings (road markings didn't appear on roads for me until they were a few ft from the frony of my coach etc until i turned all the graphical settings up to epic mode, for example).
I do recommend it on the basis that other bus sims are just as, if not a lot more generally unstable and less user friendly (Hiya OMSI), or are just plain nasty. Fernbus, even with the current issues is still a very pretty, enjoyable bus sim. Just go in expecting issues for now, realise you'll probably get a few crashes, have to spend time configurating the game for your machiine and the controls so they are sensitive and sensible enough to work with and you'll probably be surprised that once you're past issues, the game does a lot more right than wrong.

After spending a while with no hack'n'slash games in my library, I browsed some of the higher rated games and found Darksiders on sale, and I must say it was a steal. The quality is a lot higher than I was expecting; considering I'd never really heard about Darksiders. It's often compared in a negative way to other games like it, like God of War, but this is a very unique game, with unique themes, characters and lore that are quite interesting if you're into angel and demon stuff. Even after playing Devil May Cry (the first four games) this game stacks up pretty evenly overall. It's combat system isn't as deep, but it's world is much larger and is more varied with puzzles that require you to use your brain; something that not many games like this do. There's also a good amount of platforming that blends well too.
Pros:
-The story is very interesting once you've finished
-The combat is fun and satisfying, with challenging enough enemies and bosses to keep you on your toes
-Progression is great, as nearly everything you can find adds to your options and arsenal
-Collectibles were fun to find (yes, were - I have no intention of hunting down everything after getting the achievement)
-Voice acting was good, though I found some of the attempted expressions from demons rather cheesy
-War has Liam O'Brien's voice and a BFS.
Cons:
-The story isn't clear until the end. A lot of the game, I didn't really understand the goal.
-The secondary weapons feel a little redundant, considering you have to use a weapon to increase its power.
-Collectibles require backtracking to find all of them. I really don't like this, but that's preference.
-Pc port has achievement problems. It took quite a lof of effort to get all of them, but it was worth the effort considering how fun the game is. The problem relates to achievements just not unlocking when they should - it may happen if you alt tab out of the game or some similar action.
Overall, if you like adventure, hack'n'slash, or angels/demon settings, you'll want this game. 8.5/10.

Hello everyone, my nickname is Atlantis and in most cases I keep that name aswell,
I had my own concerns when I heard the first time of this game. "Another Survival Game?" I thought, but the medieval theme catched me, so I bought it a few days later trying to figure out if I could trust the developer.
As a new player I was a little bit confused what to do, there is currently no tutorial or any help at all from the game itself. The current UI is working but aswell as confusing as some informations show up when you hit the right key on your keyboard, for example your skills (L), your character page (P) or simply your inventory (I). But luckily, the developer have added some helpfull entries on gamepedia.
After my first steps and configurations I decided to jump straight into the multiplayer. Why? Because this game clearly is about teamplay! If you have read it by now or not, some server aswell as the planned MMO will have certain settings that will cause you to play with others to gain better weapons, a house or simply better tools. I will not go further into this as I am not writing a tutorial here ;)
Currently the server performance is quiet good, although some of my mates I play with reporteed multiple crashes since the latest patch, don't forget this is an ALPHA (some like to forget such things). I enjoy the moments of gathering materials to build a building, a wall or just weapons or armor. And you will have to gather a lot! This game is extremly slow if you compare it to something like Minecraft and you don't have the chance to build your houses on your own, rather then setting up predefined houses (check the wiki for more).
Combat is quiet fun but not balanced right now, slashing weapons can do decent damage, but the bleed that can be applied to you is a death sentence, aswell as some heavy crossbow that kill you nearly in a single shot. This is something that hasn't been worked on since I joined the alpha, but I believe this will be looked at.
Graphic and game performance are moderate, if you have a decent pc and you have some lags, it's because of some bad server maintenance or overload of objects on a map.
The sound ingame is as right now clearly nothing special. Sometimes a sound is bugging and playing in a loop until you finally decide to restart your game.
Yes restart, because reconnecting/disconnecting is not implemented yet!
All in all I recommend this game for anyone who is a fan of survival, teamplay, medieval and is ready to invest some time into a game and not expecting to have a big giant castle on day two.
Here my personal opinion in a shorter version:
+A lot of skills
+A lot of crafting recipes
+Teamplay needed
+Patches every second week
-Soundquality
-Missing guild/friend system
-Missing longer roadmap (I like to see a plan cause it shows some "organization")
-Combat unbalanced
-Some Crafting recipes needs to reworked
-No horses :(

got my alpha code in email because i had played it a while ago. last time i had played it, it was very similar, but a lot more buggy and had less content. that was probably 1-3 years ago, i cant remember. but i had only played it for an hour and got fed up with it before uninstalling it because it was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
NOW, it installs over steam, has longish loading times (who cares though), the controls are kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for m+k but work if you're patient and learn to tap and feather the keys you can deal with it, and the graphics (artstyle) are fairly nice, but a little lacking contrast in the colors.
The game runs fairly well, considering how much♥♥♥♥♥♥is actually being drawn on screen and how the devs implemented it (see: placing a bunch of objects on screen by hand). Which means: its really nice to explore and see the sights, but you need a powerful computer to do it. I'm running a 768mb 460gtx and a first gen i7. With all graphics up to high (except the garrys mod-esqe post processing) I get about 15fps while completely stationary in a forrest. with most things on lowest or low (lowest threshold until the game looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥due to flat meshes and NO shading) I can get up to about 55fps.
there's a lot of pop-in for random tree areas and buildings, which isnt really a big deal but worth noting.
the car handling itself is fairly difficult, because at low speeds the cars handle alright but once you speed up, the fps chugs randomly, the cars feel like they're on ice and makes crashes/flips inevitable. It almost feels like they're trying to make you crash. This is neat for showing off your crash mechanics (which i admit are incredible, i ripped out a part of my steering on one side because i high centered over a large rock and couldnt control that wheel much) you can ctrl+r to reload your vehicle and drop five feet away, but the location drifts a little to one direction each time and you can easily be stuck in a load-loop into a wall or trees or some other obsticle with no way out except to keep hitting reload unti you come out the other side. Pretty annoying, yet..... somehow satisfying when you're free.
If I get a wheel or controller, a more powerful computer, and they keep adding content and fixing bugs, I'd say this game could be the driving sandbox (gta style raging/romping) equivalent of a walking-sim type game. There are jumps, trails, roads all around the island in grand touring style, big meadows, swamps, ponds, beaches, abandoned buildings a la ken block, and lots of things to smash your car on and have to reset. It would make a VERY nice exploration/relaxing/personal satisfaction driving sim with a high potential of adventure.
My biggest desires for adds/fixes for this game are:
1) customizable suspension and drivetrain settings to tweak
2) them to keep adding more content because I like the style they're doing it in (the offroad 4x4 stuff is REALLY nice)
3) optimizations ZOMG<---
4) better color palette (its not bad, just leaves something to be desired and feels washed out when out in the open)
6) more cars!!!
7) the handling to not be so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (maybe this is just because im trying to control a sim driving game with a keyboard)

Right now, the game isnt worth much if you dont like driving around irl or in gta games. I dont know much about the pacing of the dev, but Im going to go ahead and say they're slow as ♥♥♥♥.
In a few years, maybe this game will be really cool. But, until then, its very much in alpha and has been for a long time. If this is your thing, cool, if you can't entertain yourself by driving around and exploring in a very buggy game, steer clear of this one for now.
sound: 6/10 (nice directionality, but all cars sound the same and stuff isnt very dynamic. great ambience. not too buggy.)
graphics: 7.5/10 (if you could get it all to run at a decent fps with no pop-in or stuttering, it would be VERY nice.)
menus: 5/10 (lots of options, yet somehow still lacking options. average to bad organization. very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ loading times.)
art: 7/10 (cool, sterile, matrix like maps. really cool idea of loading up a world feel. surprisingly immersive. "cozy".)
playability: 4/10 (sub average. frustrating experience driving around on the roads, but very pleasurable 4x4 experiences.)

First let's do the obious: Would I recommend this game? Yes, but with big disclaimer. At it's current state there is not much "game" in this game. It's just incredibly accurate physics simulator sandbox with cars in it. But as an engineer I've lost my heart to this thing. I've banked incredible hours into this game before steam release just crashing stuff and sometimes generally trying to stay on the roads.
Let me open that "generally trying to stay on the roads" don't even think about that trying to do anything else than crash cars into various objects next to the object you aimed for with just keyboard controls. The cars are incredibly twichy to drive without precision control like in any driving game aiming for high- to ultra realism in their drivingmodel (and no driving aids). Xbox360-controller, yes good start, but I would recommend somekind of steering wheel for any tries to stay on roads. Altought at this moment you should be prepared to do some input mapping manually with notepad etc, if you have older or more exotic wheel and even then force feedback is no-go (Xbox360-controller works great straight out of the box).
Then few words about cars and tracks included at this moment. They are good start, but one sportcar one 90's saloon, frontwheel driven hatchback, van, musclecar and pickup are quite limited choices (I won't mention the threewheeler as it is right now completely undriveable). Also out of the six maps there is just three actual ones to drive around and they have very little variance between them. The rest three are just empty map, big hill to make your car look like raisin and a crash testing field. But as with this game's spiritual predesessor ROR there are community made maps and cars, and oh boy there are those. Ranging from poor mods made by sticking something like Audi R8-model on the games sportscar Jbeam map without modifications to it (so that the car stars to crumble before it actually hits anything) to completely custom made models where you actually can nearly put your crash results next to euroncap footage and not see no big obious differences. Altought most of the older ones you can find most likely won't work correctly as they made some changes lately that can break models made before that update. From the map side I've not yet come accross a incredible map, but some ok-ones I've tested. This tought I'm sure will selfcorrect as this game comes available here in steam as this game includes as far as I can understand pretty comprehensive level designing and customising tools. NOT USERFRIENDLY, but comprehensive!
As I wrote would I recommend this game at the start, let me end by writing what I've like to see in this game. Firstly ofcourse is to see some actual "game"-like systems implimented. Some of these like basic checkpoints for racing etc. I've understand are just few updates away, but that career mode promised in that trailer sounds like a dream come true if they manage to get it out sometime. Second thing I'd like to see is Steam workshop support for easier installation of the community made models and maps. Third I'd like to see more cars and maps in the vanilla version, mayby even if they would manage to get some real cars licenced for this game it would be great. But as car makers are what they are I understand that this might be just a pipedream and we'll have to settle just in the community made mods in that front...

Yumsters 2: Around the World is the unofficial spiritual successor to Bad Rats.
Featuring a similar production quality and budget as Bad Rats, Yumsters 2 pulls no punches in providing the best that indie games have to offer.
The gameplay revolves around pulling brightly-coloured dinosaur worm things (Yumsters) across chains of fruits (at a blistering 60 FPS). They eat the fruits, and you get money for it. Later on, you use the Yum-money (the yummey) to purchase a generic albeit not racist musical instrument from whatever region of the world you're in (Egypt, Mexico, Japan etc) which you then use to play a rhythm minigame that rivals the depth and complexity of titles such as DmC: Devil May Cry and Michael Jackson: The Game. The intricate plot of Yumsters 2 is very well-paced, engrossing the player in a profound tale about brotherhood and personal growth as they advance from level to level.
Yumsters 2 offers a plethora of graphical options to make it perform well on all systems, such as "Fullscreen: on or off". The soundtrack of Yumsters 2 is also very prodigious, featuring a whopping three minutes of looping audio. Sometimes if you score a good enough Yumster combo (a yumbo), "Rules of Nature" will start playing, congratulating the player on their Yumsters skill. Yumsters 2's voice acting is top-notch. Captivating quotes such as "Commander ready" and "Tumma" (???) are delivered magnificently, rivalling the emotional and compelling narratives of titles like Metal Gear Solid.
"Do you think fruits can bloom even on a battlefield?"
"In the Middle East we don't hunt foxes, we hunt Yumsters."
If you liked Bad Rats, play this. Yumsters 2 may very well be the "Citizen Kane of video game".

, which, instead of playing out over the course of the entire Civil War, focuses on its most famous confrontation. The game is a lot of fun, blending historic names and locations with alternate courses of events that keep games fresh and exciting. While it might not be concerned enough with its historic accuracy to please those most interested in a history lesson, it’s a game that should be on the radar of anyone with a passing interest in the RTS genre.
handles the flow of its campaign extremely well. Obviously Gettysburg, being a real battle in a real war, had a distinct outcome- the Union defeated the Confederacy on the third day. It’d be pretty boring if players were tied to the ebb and flow of the real battle, but the game instead plays like a choose your own adventure novel. The first battle always starts out the same (except for your choice of playing as the North or South), then after that, depending on how the battle goes, you’re given a few choices on what you want to do next based on how much damage and land each side took in the previous confrontation. You can decide to make your next objective taking over a location to earn Victory Points (basically just number for how strategically valuable different locales are to the overall battle), to protect a certain front, etc. Additionally, unit losses carry over from one campaign battle to the next, meaning that even if you’re dominating there’s still reason to be careful. Thinning out your larger brigade at the end just to finish a little quicker may seem like a good idea, but it’s going to come back to bite you in the next round when the opponents get lots of reinforcements and you’re suddenly overpowered. These combined to make each of the three campaign playthroughs I tried vastly different, which was great.
Unlike some strategy games, most forms of resource management aren’t something you’ll have to worry about in
. You won’t have to try to be a careful spender, keep track of research trees or raise combatants’ stat points, etc. You don’t even have to worry about what units to produce. In fact, the entire management side is really quite simple. There are only two things you need to keep track of among your soldier groups: morale and condition. Morale is what you’d expect- the willingness to fight.
does a great job of being simple enough for anyone to learn in a short sitting, but deep enough to keep you learning and perfecting your tactics deep into subsequent playthroughs.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg has just one thing that speaks for it self, that makes up everything, gameplay feeling and emersion! Game-labs, the creator of this game is the creator of Darthmod for Total War series, and the experience gained modding Total War clearly shows in this game!
The graphics are obivously not Total War graphics, but it`s not even the purpose. It`s there to make you feel like you are in a tent 3 km from the front line looking at a map of the battle, and getting reports about troop movements. As a seasoned gamer my conclussion has been that in these days when even simple graphics can look good and fill a purpose, who need the flashy animations of Total War games? The graphics of Ultimate General: Gettysburg is indeed simple, but beutiful, and gives the player the opportunity of feeling like master general, drawing out lines of attack on a map.
So it`s pretty much established that it`s the feeling and gameplay emersion that trumps good graphics in most cases. At least in my opinion. In terms of gameplay, I do really recognise some things from the Empire & Napoleon games from Creative Assembly, that reflects the creator`s previous work. But I have the feeling of everything having been improved upon and well thought about. How you have to place your troops, when you move them, and how to engage is basically about looking at the surroundings in the map and at units stats moreso  than in previously mentioned games. It`s noticable that Game-Labs have improved on many things from Total War, and created a far more historically accurate battle simulation. There are really stuff here that Creative Assembly would be wise to consider if going back to the Empire franschise of the Total War series.
Since this game obviously is about one battle, the game is not like Total War, were one battle is one major set-piece battle that takes 15- 45 minutes, and that`s it. In Total War this fills a purpose, given that you also play a grand strategy game on a large map filled with several battles. Instead Game-labs focused on one batte and came up with something really clever;  You don`t really fight the battle of Gettysburg all at once. You fight larger skirmishes as a part of the bigger, several days long battle. The campaign is non-linear, and how you fight the campaign depends much on your overall strategy decisions in and between battles, since you carry all your troops with you from different battles. In between battles you have options; Shall I reinforce flanks? Should I hold the line no matter what? Should I do tactical retreat? All these decisions make each playthrough unique. Especially since you can decide how your AI opponent should behave. This has made me come back to the game a couple times and realized that I`m not fighting the same battles, and I can suddenly find myself pushed up against the wall by something unanticipated. This makes the relatively short campaign really interesting and replayable.
Ultimate General: Gettysburg is unique game, that the RTS and history nerds defintely will enjoy!! I`m falling into both of those categories, and I did! :) I recommend it for anyone who enjoys tactical battle games set in historical settings. For the sequel under development, I would only ask a few things of Game-labs, and that is to include more than one battle and perhaps make som of the details stand out as 3D in the otherwise 2D landscape, such as houses, towns treas and ridges. Otherwise it`s a great game as it is!
