This game is to Factorio what Minecraft is to Terraria. (If you didn't get that: Fortresscraft Evolved is a 3D Factorio.)
It is complex and requires some patience/time to get the hang of things but, once you do, it's a blast. You go to sleep thinking about how you're gonna automate the extraction of ores, how to optimize power distribution, etc., and wake up eager to put your ideas in practice. If you are not afraid of some hard work and like figuring out how to make things work efficiently, you're probably gonna love this game.
It also must be mentioned that this game is being done (you could say it's still in Early Access, there's a lot of content yet to come) by a single guy, which is baffling.
----------
I'm going to adress some of the points raised by most of the negative reviews to try and set your mind at ease in case you are considering buying Fortresscraft Evolved--and because I believe this game deserves much more praise than it seems to be getting:
1 - It has some rough edges indeed (a few Help texts missing, some not quite clear, conveyor belts blinking every now and then, the Spiderbot getting stuck, ...) but they are all minor issues. All the machines and everything else that matters works perfectly. Since the game is being developed by one person, I think that's forgivable and his priorities make sense.
2 - The UI is not beautiful, but you get used to it really fast and it fulfills its purpose just fine.
3 - The tutorial kinda sucks indeed (you gotta take a look around your base to spot some signs telling you what to interact with and how) but it gives you the basics and its extremely short (I hate long ones.) A small message will pop up on the top right corner of your screen after the mini-tutorial is done to suggest you what to do next so you don't get lost. If you keep an eye on the help-box on the lower left corner of the screen when you point at something, and check the Help Book when needed, you can figure pretty much everything out. (Land your pointer on any item in your inventory then press H and said item will show up on the top of the Help list... I think it's neat how that works.)
4 - Some claim the Dev is an A-Hole. Well, I never talked to him directly nor anything but I've seem him answering appropriately and politely to every single Steam-forum topic/question I looked up. The guy seems to work a lot and hard, apparently answers every single question about his game personally and who knows what else, and we, players, can also be annoying with our requests/demands/suggestions quite often so... I think the guy is doing the best he can, I didn't actually see anything that made him look like a jerk.
5 - I read about performance issues. I, myself, have an average computer and run Fortresscraft with fixed 60fps and never had any issues other than the eventual crash (rare, about 6 in 70 hours playing so far.)
6 - "The DLC policy." Okay, this does suck at first glance. The game is not really finished and there's already a DLC. When you are playing, your research one tech tree or go down to a certain layer of the underground and realize you can't mine these ores because you don't have the DLC, or can't build some of the stuff you just researched for the same reason. It♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off too--specially because nothing warns you you need the DLC to do this or that, it's just there like everything else and then... you can't do it (and that's the worst flaw in the game for me.) But then I went to take a look at the Devs writings and some other stuff and... well, the game sells well during sales, but not so much in between them. The guy needs money, like everyone else. But the thing is: he deserves it.
I was playing and run into the problems I just mentioned. I quit it to check on the DLC and wonder whether I should get it or not (not on sale, and it costs 30 bucks here in my country while it must be 10 or so for Americans... and our wages are lower as well so I'm paying, essentially, about 6 times more for it.) Well, long story short, after I read everything I did (the Dev's Patreon page, the spread sheet with his schedule for future updates, ...) I just came back and got the DLC, for the reason I said above--I believe the guy deserves it. Fortresscraft is a great game but, sadly, its sales rate doesn't do it justice. So I'm helping him out by buying a buckload of content with the Frozen Factory expansion (only one other game ever inspired me to help out, and that was Tales of Maj'Eyal.)
7 - Most of the other complaints seem to be mistakes. People who couldn't find a certain item, or figure out how to decently farm a drop, or where to find something else. I had no problem of the sort--it's all there. In the worst case scenario, you can Google it and you'll find the solution.
----------
So, summing up: Fortresscraft Evolved is great fun and pretty solid for a one-dev game. If you get it (and I recommend you do) I suggest you get the DLC as well. If you don't, by the time you need it you'll realize it's worth its price and probably end up buying it anyway, like I did.
And don't be intimidated by the game's screenshots. Fortresscraft Evolved is intricate, but it's not that garish fanfare they make it seem to be--unless you want it, of course, but it's totally NOT necessary.
----------
One last detail: you can become a "Patreon" by donating 10 bucks or so monthly to the Dev (so with the steady income he can hire a 2D and 3D artists to help him out.) Patreons get some aesthetical bonus items and beta-access to new stuff.
----------
EDIT: Ok, now that I sank some 200 more hours into the game, I gotta say you spend a lot of time just waiting for resources to pile up--and by "a lot" I mean about 2/3 of the time.
The base game "ends" when you charge the OET (Orbital Energy Transmitter or, as I like to call it, the Over-Exaggerated Timewaster.) Anyone who played 150 hours or more spent about 100 of them just piling up resources to have enough power to charge this thing and defenses to survive the non-stop, overpowered waves of monsters that come when you actually start charging it. If you manage to do everything right (enough power, enough defenses) it's gonna take you about 10 hours to charge the OET once. You gotta do it 4 times. You just sit there, waiting while it charges, because there's nothing left to do until it does.
After that's done, you get into the DLC (if you have it, of course, which I do.) At first it's fine, then it starts to get a bit grindy once again, until you are finally able to build a machine called "The Magmaborer" which is to the game's expansion what the OET is to the base game. But, doing some quickly calculations, it turns out it's about 25 times worse than the OET. I closed the game--and never went back to it--as soon as I realized that (the OET itself has already been the biggest time-waster and the most artificial game-time increaser I've ever seen in my life.)
That stuff needs to be balanced.
Nonetheless, when you're actually PLAYING the game, it's great--so my positive recommendation stands. Even with the OET crap and the Magmaborer even-crappier crap, I'm still glad I bought this game (and the DLC as well.)

In order to progress beyond a certain point in the game you need an item called a Perfect Faceted Eye. It's a drop you get from killing creatures in the game world, or supposedly get from creatures in the game world, me and my friend found none after more than four days of game play. No matter how many slimes, wasps and or other creatures we killed we never got this drop. We tried multiple worlds, increased our threat level, built slime magnets, killed everything in site for hours and hours and hours and still no drop. The problem is you need at least a few of these items to mine crystal and without getting any in drops you can't even get to the point where you can manufacture your own. Crazy huge flaw, feel like I wasted my time and money, should have multiple ways to get this item and or mine crystal and without it you pretty much hit a giant wall that you'll never be able to get around. Tutorial is a little weak too, like for the longest time I was possitive that you could not add items to the hopper. I was amazed when I found out it was the T key. LOL, no drag and drop option like everything else you literally have to select it in your hot bad, face the hopper and press T. A little funky but not enough for it to be a problem. Fix your drops and I'll come back and give you a better rating. Until this I honestly can not find myself recommending this game to anybody.
EDIT: I just wanted to add that if you look online this is clearly a problem that a lot of people are having and is something that isn't taken seriously by the developers or the community for some reason. I can only guess that most people are not having this problem but after 70+ hours, my friend having played 190+ hours, and after receiving every other type of drop except this specific drop shows that there is a problem with this game. Warning: Extremely long, mixed rant and story ahead.
It doesn't show, but I've spent dozens of hours in this thing, I swear.
I bought this... thing because Angry Joe recommended it to people who love really, really open world games. As a fan of Garry's Mod, Skyrim's WORLD (not the combat) and free-wheeling, massive games like Wind Waker or Mass Effect, I thought this might be up my alley. I'm not "terribly" pretentious when it comes to graphics, and I like European games. I thought "Hell, why not." Bought it at full price. With the DLC.
I had no idea what I was in for.
Joe, I love you man, but your tastes and mine are not the same.
But first, the good. The World: You can pick a direction or a distant mountain or tower, and walk there. I love that in any game. But there appears to be three huge continents on the map: THIS IS A LIE. There is ONE continent, ONE small island, and ONE SWAMP. THE THIRD CONTINENT IS A LIE. Also, if you like generic Asian land, Savanah Land, and Swamp Land, then this game is totally for you.
The graphics: The environmental graphics, while often repetitive, can almost be breath-taking at times. At full graphics I'm sure it's quite nice looking, especially the ambient lighting and textures. I particularly like the undead swamp, abandoned Asian town, wasteland, and initial savannah area.
That being said, the character models are quite atrocious. While they weren't exactly repulsive, they were very, very ugly, in a charming sort of way, and suffered from an armor designer with tastes very similar to the horrifically awful taste in the Dragon Age games. Seriously, Bioware, shoot that desginer.
Anyway, another somewhat bright spot in the awfulness is the spell design system. I love anything which allows you to summon creatures, and worked like hell to get where I could summon a massive army of skeletons to do my evil bidding, wiping out whole villages of hyena-men in a massive melee beneath a piercing bright moon on the blood-soaked savana. That totally kicked♥♥♥♥♥ as well as wiping out outposts with hordes of rock golems, or my undead horde murdering fishmen in some idiot's flooded basement.
There were some quite memorable side missions, the most well-done the very early on "Fluffy the Dog" mission. That was a quite excellently executed buildup and execution of a damn creepy horror level. Playing at 3am with headphones to hear that soundtrack in the final room (you'll know it) was truly nightmare fuel. Also that bit where the the guy was being buried alive, and the undead swamp, had really quite nice, stark imagery and fairly well realized concepts. I really quite liked those parts, when it was being marred by...
The bad: And how much bad there is.
First the writing: It is quite, quite awful. The side characters (and there are too many of them) are, for the vast majority, flat, lifeless constructs who dole out missions. I can remember a few of them mostly a corrupt embalmer, the grave digging guy, and the creepy priest. And some of the more major characters, the gay captain, the witch, the demon priest, the one British guy (?), the orc chick (Bioware relationship it most certainly was NOT) and of course the Big Bad himself. I actually was genuinely interested in his backstory, and to see how he and the main character were really very similar: both ruthless sons-a-♥♥♥♥♥es, who just happened to go down different paths. Definitely not a novel concept, or particularly well executed but I liked it anyway.
Further comparing it to Bioware and Skyrim, I appreciate that everything was fully animated and voice acted. Not many games has the cajones to do that.
However, that being said, the extremely annoying protagonist caused me to remember why silent protagonists aren't so bad after all: he never shuts his god-damn mouth. He dispenses a tiny pool of one liners upon dispatching his feeble enemies which RAPIDLY grate on the nerves during extended play sessions.
That, and all the voice acting there is is EXCESSIVELY awful voice acting. Seriously. It is very very bad. But, in a morbidly enjoyable sort of way, I guess. You can always skip it if it really starts to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off (which it may).
The other truly terrible bit of the story is the cutscenes: Every one of them is overly elaborate, horribley mo-capped, butchering-the-art-of-cinema awful. Seriously. These guys need to learn about a little thing called subtlty.
And speaking of subtlty, the ending twist may just be the worst thing ever. Yeah, both of them. They just plain suck.
Now to break down the meat of the game:
There is only one good class. Forget about the complicated spell casting system, because this is how EVERY, and I mean EVERY battle works. Summon deads. Deads distract enemy/form human wall. Throw the same basic spell 500000 times because it is the only thing that recharges fast enough until the deads vanish. Resummon. Repeat until target dead. Repeat ad nauseum with every single fight, and by that I mean the 1000s of enemies you will face in the course of this game. Utter lack of damage resistance means attacks from tough enemies often kill you instantly.
Archery is broken and horrible so rangers are stupid and don't exist.
Horse combat is utterly non-existant. I get that we can't all be Mount and Blade, but horses are worse that useless.
Only fighters have enough damage resistance to be worth playing, but their fighting is possibly even more boring. Spam attacks, wait for idiotic MMO cooldowns, and slavage armor so thick that enemy attacks don't even graze you.
PvE is totally unbalanced. If an enemy succeeds in wounding you, pause time, make 5000 health potions, then drink them.
The stats system utterly lacks subtelty. Put all your points in health and strength. There is absolutely no point to multi-classing. Dark Souls this AIN'T.
Horrible boring enemies that make JRPG's slimes and bats look clever. Ooh, my club and I are SO scared of skeletons.
I truly hate when ostriches, hyenas, boars, and rhinos, all of whom should hate each other, gang up to kill you. It's lazy.
And you may have heard of the final boss battle on a forum. It is one of the most truly pahtetic, disgusting and spectacular fails of a fight I have ever seen in gaming history. I don't mean that lightly.
All in all, it's frustrating, it's idiotic, it's droll, and it's very boring at times. But there are many points where I had fun.
So I'm sorry, Two Worlds 2. I simply can't recommend you to the world. I can only say to those would be buyers out there: if summoning a horde of skeletons to kill a herd of rhinos sounds awesome, or an extremely clumsy approach to sexual assualt (shudder) is your cup of tea, or you LOOOOOVE horrible MMO combat: By all means. Play this... thing. It's your funeral.

UT2k4 is, with little doubt, the pinnacle of the Unreal franchise with the largest variation in game modes, best maps, biggest arsenal, and one of the best AI opponents of its time.
It took almost four years for Epic to create a sequel to Unreal Tournament, and they were aiming high with a proposed yearly series. Sadly, they started with UT2003, which changed and removed so many things that despite the initial success it flopped hard: so much so that they had to release Unreal Tournament 2004 well ahead schedule. Thankfully they listened to the fans, and not only gave back every removed game element, but created an amalgam of the best features of UT2003 and UT ’99.
The action is faster than ever, but not to the point where it is disadvantageous to a new player. Old weapons and map types complement the new ones, offering a variety not just in play style, but in game modes– including a Halo-inspired vehicle-using war scenario.
The campaign also received an overhaul. You still need to complete all but one game type to win, but the small changes made sure that each play through can be different: instead of set maps you are given a small pool for each stage. For death match enthusiast 1v1 and team DMs are offered as optional challenges, boosting the possible team management strategies and game time to even higher levels.
Some of the game modes like Bombing Run (a cross between Blood Bowl and Counter-Strike) and Double Domination (Domination with camping strategies) weren’t received well, but against bots they can be one of the fastest-paced modes you can play. And even if you dislike them, the other modes and the myriad of high-quality player-made map packs can ensure longevity even after all these years.

Now you're probably wondering what kind of game this TI really is, huh? Well let me try to explain it briefly: TI is the way the community always wanted it to be, a better and quicker way of playing where experience points is not required to unlock weapons only in-game credits which is given after every match played and that gives every new player a fighting chance. Below you'll find all sorts of information regarding the game, take a look you might find something helpful.
I like this game a lot. It allows you to get guns permanently, there are achievements that may take you a long time to get, a number of maps and modes to play (after the latest update), driving maps which quite a number of FPSs do not have, and also several skins you can purchase to have a different and a more badass look for your own character. To be honest, I got hooked on this game for months and I still like this game a lot more than other FPSs I have played before. T.I. is also not so much of a 'pay to win' game compared to some of those I have played. Yes it is true you can purchase stronger guns when you are only a level 1 with real cash, but even so, everything can be bought with in game money other than skins. So I personally wouldn't call that pay to win, since you are just buying things to have it faster. It's not like you bought a gun that's only purchaseable with real cash. But well, I respect the opinions of others if they do disagree with me.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic was a good roleplaying game developed by Bioware. KOTOR 2, the sequel, was developed by Obsidian. The core differences here is that Obsidian still legitimately cares about making a good stat based RPG and not a shooter with romance options. I think I'm projecting modern Bioware shortcomings here but KOTOR 2 took everything that was wrong with the original and tried very hard to fix it. The game is by no means perfect, and you WILL need to download one of the Restoration Project mods to fix bugs and add content that was cut but as a role-playing game KOTOR 2 is still absolutely great.
Your choices matter, the whole game is seeing how the consequences of your choices play out. This whole game is about choice. The characters are excellent, the writing is everything you would expect of an Obsidian title. The game almost starts out as a satire of Bioware cliches but quickly becomes its own animal, allowing you to explore a deeper aspect of the morality of the Star Wars universe that a lot of games never do.
While this game certainly is not perfect, I find it better than the original in nearly every way. That said, I do recommend playing the original before you ever get started on this, the original game is still a good title and deserves the respect its earned. There are better RPG's out there, but you won't find a lot of them on Steam yet. For what it is this game is great and I love playing it.
8/10 would play again.

While I am a big fan of the Extended Universe of Star Wars, it was the Knights of the Old Republic series that really set me up to explore the universe outside the movies.
The second installment improves a lot from the first game. It delves deeper into the Old Republic and the struggles of the Sith and the Jedi. Replayability: 4/5 - Each class offers a different way to play, so playign through as each class poses its own challenges, despite the story remaining the same.
Graphics: 3/5 - Even somewhat subpar for its time, the graphics aren't the best, but a great story canmake you forget this.
Story: 5/5 - One of the best stories ever told in a Video Game, ever in my personal opinion, it's is for sure one of the best ever told in the Star Wars universe.
Overall - 5/5 - Despite glitches and some frustration, SW: KOTOR II is a rare gem that has a story that can overcome its problems.

There will be a lot of people saying: "MUH Operation Health, MUH Hitreg, MUH Bugs."
and it won't ever be. There is not a single game that is perfect. every game has its flaws, and its up to the developers to fix them.
The base game is overwhelmingly fun. The game has a lot of customization, as you can choose operators, then their guns, then their gadgets, then the customization on the weapons and so on. You can also change how your operators look.
The game is pretty balanced. None of the operators are overpowered, you just need some time to learn how to counter them, but there are some operators that are underpowered, such as the infamous Lord Chanka. Tachanka's concept makes it harder to balance him, but there are some great ideas in the community that might help buff him well.
Developers pay attention to the game, and they try to fix it. Yes, sometimes one fix creates even more problems, but they fix that as well. Some players were annoyed by the fact that the Year 2 Season 2/3 was delayed, but Operation Health was worth it in my opinion.
Graphics are amazing. The level of detail on the map and guns and operators is surprisingly good. Yes, there's the occasional Valkyrie that looks horrifying, but otherwise its great. And hey, IQ's butt balances it out. You can download the Ultra HD Textures pack, which is completely free, for even better graphics.
Now for the doomed topic, the Hitreg. Yes, it is problematic, and yes, it causes a lot of rage, but it's not THAT bad. I also have problems with it sometimes, and I have raged a lot because of it, but not much lately. Operation Health did its job and fixed the hitreg (mostly). Sometimes the ping causes you to see that you hit someone but in reality you didn't, sometimes its the game, but come on. It's not as bad as the community makes it out to be. The occasional unregistered headshot is once in twenty matches. There is a lot of footage showing the hitreg problem and titled "Operation Health", but as I said, it's not that bad.
The updates are few, urgent hotfixes are pushed out often. The updates do bring in a lot of content though, including huge buffs and nerfs, new gameplay mechanics, interface changes, and the seasonal updates bring the new operators.
So, all in all, the game is extremely good, tacticool (not tactical), great graphics-wise, the developers pay attention to the complaints, the mechanics are great, the game is balanced, so I would definitely give it a shot. I have nearly 600 hours on the game and I'm still not bored a bit.

(TLDR at bottom, if you don't want to read it all.)
As far as I can tell, if you read the most helpful negative reviews, you'll find everything I would have said myself (lack of game presentation polish, business practices, rude developer and rude close followers of said developer). Even the ones that are a little aged at this point still ring true in a lot of ways.
A lot of people compare this game to Factorio for its similar logistics puzzle/mining and refining automation premise, and to Minecraft because they both have a "blocky" world that you can dig around in, I guess. If you liked Factorio, then I feel that these are the main differences you should be aware of before you try Fortresscraft out:
-While Factorio is much looser in how it handles player progression (It's there but you don't really have to follow it very closely), Fortresscraft has a far more linear progression path in general. Sure, you can expand your mines, or your filter systems, or anything else when you want to, but the developer has a very strong vision on what he expects you to be doing at X point in the game, and the game is made to remind you of what you should be doing at any given time. Constantly. You may like it, you may hate it. I grew to dislike it, and you can thankfully turn some of it off, but not all of it.
-Unlike Factorio's two dimensional world, Fortresscraft incorporates a third dimension into gameplay. This is probably where the Minecraft comparison comes into play. You can build into the sky or dig into the ground for what looks like far longer than it would take to hit any sort of world border, but you should know that there's nothing in the sky (that I know of), and that after a certain depth, there isn't really a point in digging deeper (that I know of).
-Fortressscraft is far more complex than Factorio. Sometimes this is interesting and adds some fun to the equation, but there are other times where it feels like needless padding of gametime being moved onto the player. There are a lot of machines that craft one item, and only one item. Some of these machines aren't very used either, just collecting dust until the off time you want it to craft whatever it crafts.
While the differences between the two games are largely subjective tastes that you may love or hate, here are some cons that you'll see in many other reviews:
-The UI, while often displaying a lot of information to the player, is often unintuitive in how it displays this information, and in my opinion can be quite ugly. It also often lacks basic convenience features found in many other games, such as the more common stack management keybinds. Be prepared to click and drag your items a lot.
-Progression is slow for anyone new to the game, or anyone not interested in busywork. There are many systems in the game that function at a snail's pace until you sink in the time and effort to expand your mining or logistics systems considerably, and it often feels like an artificial means of padding the game's gameplay hours for marketing purposes. While some of the information is there, a new player is probably going to have a rough time learning the game's complicated and often nuanced systems. The in-game documentation can help, but seems to often be written from the perspective of someone who already knows the nuances and doesn't really see why they need to be explained, in my opinion. This attitude shows in bright colors if you try to ask for help on the forums, and that's not really just in my opinion. More on that below.
-While there are some very nice and helpful people in the general community, you're going to get very familiar with the same gaggle of people who seem so passionate about the game that they come off as passive aggressive, snarky or downright rude. A quick browse of the comments in the review section will show you about a dozen of them. Unfortunately, this attitude is often demonstrated by the developer himself. If you're coming in expecting baseline respect and consideration for you as a community member, or even as a paying customer, you should prepare to be confused and disappointed, especially if you have any questions or constructive criticism of the game. Replies include "Maybe you just don't have the IQ for this game :)" and "Well, it was obvious to me, so I don't see a problem with how it's presented". There's a small book that could be written on this point, but I won't get that deep into it.
TLDR: I don't really want to rant any longer, so I think I have a nice summary of my feelings about this game. In a word, I feel it's all about patience. The game was fun to me after, and only after I was patient with the game's unpolished presentation, the unituitive in-game help system, the pretty steep learning curve that's partially caused by the lacking tutorial/in-game help and the deplorable help often received on the forum, the clunky control scheme, numerous naggings to do exactly what the developer expected me to do in the game, the abysmal way I and others were treated as community members and customers by the developer and his followers, knowing little to none of the concerns or criticisms of the game would ever be taken seriously by anyone not paying into the developer's Patreon, and finally, the clear financial infleunce the developer's refusal to get a job to support the game has on the game itself. The game is still definitely in early access, and being "released" was to get more sales. It means absolutely nothing for the game's state. There's work done on the base game still, but the game's clearly going to be sold in DLC parts now. Frozen factory is a huge part of the game and it's looking like there's another DLC release coming soon. No game should be unfun until I'm patient with it and the aspects related to it for a number of hours.
Finally, to the four followers and the developer who are undoubtedly going to thumb down and debate this review in the comments like children, I'm just going to tell you now that you shouldn't bother. I have the IQ for the game. I know how to play. I muscled through the crappy tutorial and the crappy UI and watched video after video teaching me what I should've been taught in game. I loved Factorio, so this "genre" is for me. I actually enjoy the idea of a more complicated, more content rich Factorio in three dimensions. What I don't enjoy is how this idea was implimented in Fortresscraft. There's too many valid criticisms that are just being ignored, and often openly ridiculed for being provided.
Fortresscraft could've not only been as good as Factorio, but it could've easily been better. It feels like such a wasted effort to me, and the fact that Factorio has over 10 times as many concurrent players than FC is completely understandable, not to mention an all time peak that crushes FC's. That's not even mentioning that Factorio has a standalone client off of Steam and it's only been on Steam for a relatively short while, so it's even higher than that.
But hey, I'll just take the wise advice I've seen given on these forums. "Haha. That's great. Please by all means take your attitude elsewhere. We have no need of it here."

TL;DR: Kill cam footage is awesome, but the levels are confined and can feel constraining.  Gameplay and controls are fine - think unpolished Rainbow Six Vegas (or Gears of War).  The AI can spot you too quickly to be anywhere near realistic.  The story is... meh.
The story is just okay.  Your mission is to get intel on the Nazi rocket program before the Russians do.  I don't really know how the levels are linked together, or where you are and how what you're doing will impact the big picture.  There's a lack of combat variety in the levels, and the AI is too damn smart.  Most of the levels are streamlined, with a few hidden paths here and there, but for the most part you're going to be moving from point A to B without any other options.  If there's a loud noise that will drown out the sound of your gunshot, and then you snipe someone from a distance, how the hell does their buddy standing 15 feet away (and looking the other direction) know exactly where I am?
Gameplay and controls are fine and feel similar to Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Vegas (though not as polished as TCRSV).  I wish that they had an idicator so you could tell where you were throwing things before you threw them (grenades, rocks), but I'm not too picky.  Hell, it's a grenade... all you have to do is get close enough anyway.
Despite all of that, the kill cam footage makes this game worth it.  Shooting someone's skull off is pretty cool in slow motion, but shooting their grenade (causing it to explode) or shooting their nuts off (and watching them pop as the bullet destroys them) is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing cool.  90% of the reason I bought this game is because of the kill cam, and I am not a bit disappointed.
Don't buy this game at full price.  Wait until it goes on sale, or better yet, purchase it from the humble store.

Rise of Keepers:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

You have been chosen to defend the mighty Solaris Blue Crystal! Rise and defend it at any cost against the onslaught of the enemy’s waves. Now….. do what you have to do to keep it safe. Keeper!

Rise of Keepers is a Tower defence/RPG game type of game where you have to defend your base (the blue Crystal) against waves of enemies. At the start of the game (single player), you will be able to choose what type of difficulty you would like to play. You have 4 in total from Easy to Survival. The difference is the number of enemy waves you have to dispose of. Easy has 8 waves in total with 15 minutes interval between them, where the hard one has 25 waves with 5 minutes interval between them.  For survival, you will play until you die and you have 5 minutes interval between the waves too!
Between the waves, you will have to gather resources to build your defences; chopping trees and picking large rocks will be your main prerogative at the start. You can build warehouses, each of which will give you an additional 2 workers and they will help you drastically with gathering the well- need resources.  Then you will be able to explore this huge map and come across animals you can hunt easily and some who we shall consider dangerous…. A bear for example! Foxes, deer and wild boars will give you experience points and food when you kill them (and they do not fight back, they run away).  As you explore the map you will find treasures which will be very helpful to your keeper.
To upgrade your base not only will you need to have enough resources but your keeper will need to have reached his next level experience to be able to do so. When upgraded, you can upgrade your towers, choose to level up your keeper attribute, but the most important is that your base gets additional points - more points you have the harder it is to destroy.
From the keeper’s point of view, at this stage you will be able to play with only one keeper but based on what I can see, you will have up to 27 keepers on the final version to play with. 9 keepers with strength attribute, 9 keepers with agility and 9 keepers with intelligence.

The designers have put a “Road Map” in the options which tells you when and what upgrade will come through.
On the final version, PvE & PvP multiplayer modes will be available. This game is well presented and enjoyable to play for an early access but it needs more content, in my opinion.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good concept
-	Nice graphics
-	4 levels of difficulty
-	Single and multiplayer modes (final version)
-	Good price point
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Needs more content
-	No achievements / trading cards
Rise of Keepers is an early access at this stage but has got GREAT potential and you can pick it up at a bargain price.
This is one of the games I will keep a very close eye on!

UPDATE 10.12.2015: The new price is much more reasonable, while my points about the state of game remain same, if you are intrigued by the gameplay as I was it is not that of a pick up with the current price.
With the basic workings of the game let me move on to the technical state of the game. To begin with and to remain on a positive way let me mention the visual part of the game. Menu of the Rise of Keepers reminds me of Dota 2 and promises a lot, at this point though, most of the options are "greyed out" and one can only try the single player mode in which one gets to choose from four different difficulties which differ in the number of incoming waves and the time one has between each wave. Discouraging may be the absence of the settings menu (Unity?) which is accessible only upon the start of the game from desktop and lets player change resolution, graphics fidelity (no separate options for different settings), select the monitor he wants to display the game on and to change input keys.
The visual quality of the game itself is pretty decent. The textutres look actually pretty great and from the aesthetic standpoint the Rise of Keepers looks pretty fantastic, that is, until something moves. The animations need a lot of work to match the overal visual quality of the game at its current state.
I do keep repeating "at its current state" a lot, don't I? Well, as I have stressed out at the beginning of this review, this is a very, very, VERY early alpha release and as such suffers from lack of content and technical problems. While the game did not crash once during the time I have played, my FPS were going unjustifiably wild considering the graphical fidelity of the game as well as my hardware. Average of 25 fps with drops below 15 with more units spawned on i5 and 660ti with the way the game looks is not acceptable even with best quality options on fHD. On later stages, with more units spawned, the game also suffers from an input lag (in singleplayer!) at the worst it took from 5-10 seconds for the game to register my mouse clicks making the game basically unplayable. If the developers manage to fix these problems the Rise of Keepers will be a much more pleasureable experience; However that won't be the end of developers work.
What I would like to see possibly in the next update apart from the technical fixes is an improved interface, possibility of seeing the stats of the enemies on click and tooltips in the inventory. If I was the developer of Rise of Keepers I would focus on fixing the technical issues and improving the interface first and foremost before releasing the new content. Multiplayer and more Keepers would be great but at this point what the game needs more is fixing and improving not expanding. I would also suggest to hire some native English speakers to proof read or even write the texts and to do the voice acting, possibly with at least some higher quality microphone if you cannot afford a studio. You might also want to ask the youtube community to do that for you in exchange for a free copy of the game and mention in the credits. You probably won't get any of the big names; However anyone with a decent setup and native speaker level would probably do better than the current voice actors (sorry guys, don't take it personally).
To sum this up, is the game currently worth the asked price? Hell no. Will it ever be? Possibly; However the devs really need to work their butts out since this is just the beginning and they have looooong way to go. I would recommend buying this only if you really want to support the devs and are willing to risk that the game might end up unfinished considering how much work is left to be done here. Playing at this point is really just alpha testing and I would suggest to wait for the later versions.
I will be updating this review in the future to reflect the development of the game.

After reading some reviews on here I was a little unsure of getting Fernbus (as I have OMSI2 for bus simming) so i did a little research on Twitch and Youtube, and came to the conclusion, I'm getting it!
First off it is very different to OMSI in the fact it is an intercity long distance coach simulator, not an inner city route runner like OMSI is. Installation was a bit of a pain but this was due to me needing my C++ updating to cope with Unreal engine, once this was done I was into the game. My PC is what i describe as MID range (see specs for what I run) but despite previous reviews I'm getting very good FR and no crashing as yet (6+hrs).
I'm really enjoying the game, the handling feels like you are really driving a heavy and full coach! passengers wait to be checked in/buy tickets, which really adds to the immersion. The scenery is in a 'development' stage, but looks really good for me, I really like the weather effects too!
As with everything, this sim isn't perfect, but the little quirks are easily forgotten, and nowhere near as frustrating as OMSI2!
All in all I would reccomend Fernbus as it is a fun and great looking simulator that is constantly being worked on to improve.
I would say it isn't as good as something like ETS2, but it is very close, and tbh a silly comparison as they are totally different games, but fernbus is the ETS of the coach sim world!
Buy it, learn it, be patient and I know you will grow to love this.

This game isn't for everyone, that's a fact.
The game is mostly about resource gathering, processing said resources and the infrastructure between. The game is slowpaced, it WILL take time before you have everything set up as you like it and even then you are very likely to rebuild it later as you figure out better ways to do things. It will require quite a bit of thinking ahead and possibly a few world restarts once you reach a point in your current world where rebuilding everything is just too much of a hassle.
Each restart will be much easier than the last though as you learn more tricks. What took you 2 hours before, may now take 30 min and when you have played for quite a while not even that long. The time it takes to do stuff is usually down to player skill, be patient and you will get a lot from it.
If you do decide to stick around for the first 10 hours, you are very likely to play at least a 100, and that is without the DLC Frozen Factory (have a look at the positive reviews, most have well over a hundred hours play and still haven't run out of content). The larger part of each update is also available for free, no paywall here unless you've already spent said 100 hours and want at least 50 more. There are a few bugs, but hey, you just spent a dinner for two and the bugs will disappear at the end of the month.
And lastly as I said this game may turn you off quite quickly, please have a look at lets plays before you consider buying and if you do, you won't regret it.

DISCLAIMER: If anyone notices I left out UT2003 completely, there's a point to that, and that point is likely parallel to why it only took a single year for another UT to come out.
What can I say about this game? The Steam hours say nothing about how much time I've actually put into this game. I first bought it a day after it was released in Canada (That would be about 4 weeks after it was released in the US, based on exchange rates at the time), which would have been when I was 15 or 16 years old. I'm nearly 27 now, and I still hold many fond memories with this game, and will continue to make great memories. It doesn't often see a lot of replay, but the once or twice a year I do jump back into it, I stick to it for at LEAST a week before moving on. That says a lot for an 11 year old game. A lot of other games that age I just can't jump back into because it's just too outdated for me. That, or I've grown up enough to realize that the game actually sucks balls.
UT2004 is an FPS, and like the name says, you're in a Tournament setting. You get points for "frags" (kills), capturing flags, holding positions, or whatever else depending on game type. The game is won when either team, or individual player in Deathmatch, reaches a certain goal parameter set by the campaign, yourself in Instant Action, or the Servermaster in Multiplayer. For example, in a Team Deathmatch game, the goal is always going to be the team with the most points collectively. This can be either a set limit, or it can be a timer countdown in which the team with the most frags at the end of the timer wins. The best part of this game, though, is HOW you get your frags. Even in the vanilla game, there are at least a dozen weapons to choose from. For the most part, these weapons are ranged, but there are one or two melee weapons (Who wants to use those, though?). I don't want to spoil the fun for those who are new to the game, so I'll tell you about my favourite: The flak cannon. This weapon was in the original Unreal Tournament, as well, and in it's return, it's packing a meaner punch. Here's what it does: The primary fire throws a dozen or more slugs of white-hot shrapnel at fast speed, ripping your oponent to shreds. Use this fire up close, and like a shotgun, you're bound to make it messy. The secondary fire is more of a mortar, in which the shrapnel is launched still encased, and then explodes into shrapnel on impact. Imagine taking that out in Call of Duty.
I have to be super honest, I've never actually fully completed the actual TOURNAMENT (The "campaign" of the game), but I was never really looking for that when I bought the game. I had spent the previous five years playing Unreal Tournament, and 99.2% of that time was playing Practice Sessions, or in the case of UT2004, Instant Action. This is, in my opinion, the Brains of the game. Instant Action is where all the experimentation unfolded. Anything that you downloaded or created yourself was first tested in Instant Action, where it was put to the test with or against computer AI bots. The bots in this game are incredibily intelligent, and also very customizable. To find out more, and there's a LOT more about Instant Action, play the game and experiment yourself. It won't ever get old.
When it comes to modability, that's where UT is the most memorable. You get the basic package, which is amazing on it's own and has hundreds of hours of gameplay, but then you also get FULL modability of the game. They even include a full UTEditor where ANYONE can jump in and make maps, good or bad, mods, skins, sounds, graphics, textures, ANYTHING. It's one of the most awesome things I've seen when it comes to a game. And then those who aren't so good with game editing could easily just check community hubs and sites for content. This was what DLC was before it was corporatized and had a price slapped on it for good measure. This is how it still SHOULD be, and I'm glad Steam came up with the workshop. I'm happy there are still a lot of good developers who provide open modability, as well. I just don't see it in this scope anymore. UTEditor was relatively simple (For those who are into it) and basically right there for you to curiously click on and figure out. To put it in perspective, I was creating maps and doing minor mods to UT99 when I was 12.
That's about all I can muster for UT2004 right now. There's WAY too much to really rave about, and I don't want to talk circles around anyone. HIGHLY recommend this game. 9.5/10

The effects and simple yet smooth graphics are enough to pull you in visually. The sound is superb. And the gameplay brings it all together perfectly. Just a great atmosphere altogether. When enjoyed in the dark with a headset with no clue what you're doing this game can certainly get your heart racing.
You're stuck in an abandoned castle with nothing but a lantern with limited oil to burn and a few welcoming tips such as how the sanity system works and that the rare light sources in the game are your friend. The narrative unfolds through startled memories triggered by interactions with certain items, entering certain rooms, and notes found throughout the castle. The voice work is top notch and adds feeling to the story. Progression is made by doing some basic puzzles, exploring for items, and of course running away as fast as you can the second anything makes a noise or moves! There's a good sense of involvement finding the clues and making old machines work to progress to the next area.
Playing fairly cautiously I only died 3 or 4 times that I remember (one was scripted to advance the story) and finished the game quicker than I would have liked. I thought there were some clever puzzles but never anything overly challenging. Then I was quite disappointed in the anti-climatic ending, that while presented some ending options, did not present a challenge of any kind. I think this game could have used one last puzzle challenge to make it feel a little more rewarding.
But regardless of any minor negatives this was a fun little game that I got in a Humble Bundle somewhere along the line so it was absolutely worth it. Though I will say I was surprised to just look up and see a $19.99US regular price. Wait for a discount for sure, but do take it for a whirl.

Amnesia is a rare game that manages to create an immersive, visceral world directly from the start, and continues to keep the scariness running all the way through without fail. Even though I told myself that I would not allow myself to be scared by a videogame, I have to admit that every time I booted up the game, I would spend the rest of my playing time darting glances over my shoulder and turning on nearby lamps.

Opting to forgo the “silent protagonist” route, Amnesia instead chooses to have your hero narrate the adventure through notes that you have placed around the mansion, hoping you would find them later on. Although you begin only with knowing your name, the story begins to take Lovecraft-ian turns quite early on, with several memorable beats sprinkled throughout in regular intervals (the first time you encounter another living creature in the mansion will be memorable for sure). I felt that the story in Amnesia was a bit jumbled, but this was possibly intentional, and as you progress through the game you can come to your own conclusions as to who the true villains are.

One gripe I have with Amnesia is that I felt that there were certain points in the experience in which I was simply unsure as to what I should be accomplishing or where I should go. Your inventory holds a notebook and memo pad which automatically fills with objectives, but I felt as if I possibly should have been playing with a memo pad of my own next to the keyboard to jot down puzzle solutions found in notes scattered about in drawers and boxes. I’m admittedly not very clever when it comes to adventure games, and I know I expanded my playtime by bumbling around the solution to several issues, which I would usually solve by accident.

Another thing that I came to learn about Amnesia was that, in all, the game really wasn’t THAT scary when I started to break down the experience. Your encounters with monsters are actually few and far in-between, and the general dreadful mood that the game creates is actually just “insanity effects” as a result of running around without a lamp. Once I discovered that there was no real threat from having blurred edges on my screen, and that the cockroaches crawling around me were only in my character’s mind, I had no real fear with barreling down black corridors. I actually wound up finishing the game with a giant surplus of lantern oil and tinderboxes, because I felt no need to light any candles and torches as I passed by. Besides, the darkness is your friend more often than not, providing plenty of hiding spaces to peek out of, which is very important as you have no weapons with which to fight. Every encounter must be escaped from in some way, which often brings out the most thrilling experiences.

Still, this is a fantastic experience that I want everyone to try, even if only once. It’s fun, and reminded me of late-night Resident Evil sessions I would have with my buddies many years ago. Recommended for all.

My first game...i spawn on the beach with nothing but the clothes in my inventory and five cookies to sustain me. i start walking along the beach picking up branches by nearby trees, flint from stone piles, and the occasional bit of plant fiber from the grass. crafting a primitive axe i start marchin up the beach. its a beautiful looking world with a few minor graphical glitches (that are soon going to be fixed)
Stumbling upon two ppl on the beach just chillin i walk up slowly saying "Hey"...expecting the classic dayz death of being pummelled to the ground and then tea bagged profuscely they instead just said Hey!"...........i know what your thinking.
This is not a game for everyone. it certainly takes time to build things and get your skills up to a level where you can do other things...so you inspect some trees..get some bark...then u start cuttin them down n eventually sawing them into planks n crafting furniture and so on. After about 20 minutes i made my way inland to a lake with the server admin and 12 other guys. after gettin the teamspeak address and everyone talking to each other we had a plan.... Splittin up into various teams gathering logs, terraforming land, gathering food, we soon had a proper little settlement of rubbish huts and a campfire complete with kitchen and herb garden. Ok so the combat isnt quite sorted yet and the interface isnt perfect but ive still poured 60 hours into the game and more in the future. We made friends and we built together and still do. From a simple village we now have proper walls to protect ourselves, a complete foundry, 2 warehouses stocked to the brim, farms and an orchard, armour and weapons...have we gone to war with anyone?? not yet as we are taking tributes of rope from some of the villages... although im pretty sure our two northernest villages are secretly about to wage war when they finally put they put guild monuments in...its a simple bit of Roleplaying but thats quite nice about this game.
Players in our server are mostly friendly and over time our humble little band alone on our island now has 5 villages some with 3 people in others with 5 and some with more. we have had one time of bad pvping on our island and looting hasnt become an issue....we did have about 10 guys come in once but they all raided one guys hut killed him n took his stuff but i think it was their first game cos after about an hour n all they had was a tannin tub they couldnt use...a coop they couldnt harvest from n a big house construction ready to go but they all left the game and havent come back for weeks. its a complicated little game that has quite alot of charm aslong you dont mind working with other people.

Obsidian, the king of sequels! Known not only for the sequel to KotOR, but also the sequels to Fallout 3, and Neverwinter Nights, and also making the 3rd Dungeon Siege game. One thing we can learn from these guys track record is that while they will sometimes make a decent engine seem a lot more buggy, they have a good ability to craft an even better story than their predecessors (most of the time). And that is no different in KotOR 2.
Taking the ball that Bioware handed off, and running full force with it, Obsidian brings players back to the world of the old Republic, and puts them back in the role of a Jedi, and his or her team as they battle the evil forces of the dark side, or ultimately succumb to it. More so in this game than its predecessor, you actually feel the changes in your choices having an impact on your entire team, and people you meet.  You can be the good jedi, following the righteous path and helping those in need. You can go straight evil, and fell those who get in your way despite being good natured. You can be sneaky and devious, neutral, or whatever you wish. Most dialogue paths have a good number of options to change the outcomes. Ultimately though, it either leads to a gain in light or dark side points, or nothing at all. So play it how you want!
KotOR 2 is a team based RPG adventure game, with 3D visuals, and battles happening in real time, with a mix of turn based elements that use the age old 'dice rules' method for any moves you may choose to dish out to your foes in the heat of battle. You see enemies, you choose your moves. You can also switch between one of the 3 currently chosen party characters at will at any time, during and out of battle to strategize. And over the course of the game, you will find a number of teammates to accompany you on your adventure. Some required for the adventure, and some can tag along based on choices you make. Like in most RPGs, you can gain new skills and abilities by leveling up. Speaking of which, the level cap from KotOR 1 has not been rasied, but rather, removed!
Rather than taking place on 1 world, like in most RPGs, KotOR 2 will have you venturing across many different planets on your journey. Aside from a lengthy first few areas, the game opens up into something grand and open ended after about the 3 or 4 hour mark, with several planets to explore. You will travel from planet to planet on your ship, the Ebon Hawk, which is also where can converse with your entire team. Once on a planets surface, feel free to explore the locals. Shop, talk to people. Do side quests. And more! There are a few mini games even to be found in the game, including a card game, and a sort of pod racing mini game.
While there is a lot to be said positvely about KotOR 2, it is not without its faults. The game is still a bit buggy, but not as much as when it first came out. Animations can be a little off when interacting with objects. Characters can get still get stuck. Sometimes characters will stand in odd places when conversing, and more. Also, there is little adjusting for graphical settings. You will pretty much need to mod the game if you want to play it at your monitors resolution. It can be a hassle, but it is easily done with the right tools, and very much worth it. Modded, KotOR 2 looks a helluva lot better than what I remembered playing many years ago.
Bottom line, if you are a Star Wars, or an RPG fan, you owe it to yourself to pick up one of the games that helped pave the way for games like Mass Effect. Buy this game!

The best way I can describe the Darksider series is an interactive book.  The lore is so creative and so good, the driving force for me to push into the game was to findout what was going to happen. I want to recommend this game, but I can't right now.  It needs improvements.
The graphics are good and the sound is ok...though I do wonder about the "jungle drums" that randomly play in the background.  The AI can pull off good maneuvers, but it can also fail miserably.
The mechanics are overly simple to the point that they can cause problems.
Examples:
Morale...your grizzled veterans (blue or gray) often have morale swings similar to American teenage girls having mood swings while watching Twilight.  Your men can stand in the open with no cover and have so much enthusiasm that it puts cheerleaders to shame.  You can also put them in a very good position and find that they are so depressed that they might need a psychiatrist and a smiley face balloon.
The combat capability of a unit is dependent on whether its commander has a PhD in Motivational Speaking (inspiring) or if he is lactose intolerant and boring.  If he is the latter and isn't worth his milk, your soldiers will forget how to load their weapons and will shoot very slowly, even if they are veterans who have fought in 10+ battles.
Artillery can shoot straight through some of the hills.  Its effects are very random.  The enemy once fired about 8 cannons, in total, at one of my brigades a half mile away (directly to the front of the cannons).  My unit lost 350 out of 800 men.  I don't remember anyone having laser-guided bombs in the 1800s.
I am convinced that my soldiers are actually Canadians because they are so polite; if you move one of your brigades too close to another brigade, one group of chaps will politely step out of the way.  The problem is that when they do so, they can go straight at the enemy and get shot to pieces.
Infantry will only fire volleys.  The developers took the time to allow cannons to fire different types of ammunition, but they were somehow unable to give you the option to tell your infantry to either fire a volley or fire at will.  Firing a volley at the beginning of combat is good, but most of the time you would want your men to load and fire as fast as they can afterwards.
Victory...capturing certain pieces of ground is the primary objective.  Your men could be completely surrounded on a hill and cut off from supplies, but it matters not.  I once had the highest level of victory at the highest difficulty setting because I used my entire army as cannon fodder to take objectives.  The game didn't care that I had almost completely destroyed the ability of my Confederate army to defend a single tree from a handful of rabid squirrels.
Historically speaking, the developers seem to have left out a number of Union units that were in the battle, so they end up being short thousands of men (I am especially looking at your troops, Generals Meredith & Cutler).  If it was a dozen here and there, that's a margin of error and is perfectly fine; when it's thousands, it's Abraham Lincoln's carriage sitting on concrete blocks without wheels in front of the White House.
I used to do volunteer work at the battlefield with park rangers, so I know more about the battle than many.  I do not expect the developers to read a dozen books on the battle, though a couple short emails to the National Park Service at Gettysburg to verify information and proof-read would have been helpful.

With almost 900 hours spent on this game, this game is still one of my favourite fps.
Gameplay: This game has two modes: Terriost Hunt and Multiplayer.
Terriost Hunt: You can play Solo or matchmake with other people, but essentially the game modes are Hostage, bomb, and terriost hunt. All AI are relatively easy to take down and good for a first time player to know the map and setting up your own keybinding for your keyboard.
Multiplayer includes casual and rank games. After the Operation Health patch, matchmaking and connecting to a game has been far better. In first season, you'd wait minimum 3 minutes for a casual and maybe 5 minutes for ranked. A lot less disconnections due to server and personally, the game only ever crashed once in my area.
Overall: Ubisoft has been pretty spot on with patches that fixes occuring problems that us palyers face. A big improvement from season 1 with new operators, new maps, fixing their servers, ( I think also graphic upgrade). Like most fps, besides buying the game, you have the option to go FTP or using earned "gold" or credit card to futher purchase equipment, skins, charms, etc. They have the Alpha packs now that's the same as CS:GO crates, but you don't need a key to open nor pay money. You'd just have a chance after every game to unlock a random equipment.
Negatives: Besides the high pitched kids playing this game, there could be more game modes. Since AI and multiplayer gets repetitive, but that would mean a big patch for a redesign of a system for the game mode. Character unlock takes forever if you don't buy the season pass. Occasional glitches here and there, but it's resolved faily quickly. Hit boxes aren't 100% accurate, but it depends on which side of the coin you're on.
Expecting many more updates and changes for this game

I bought this as part of the Darksiders Franchise pack because I actually thought that Darksiders 2 looked better...
But I figured I'd start on Darksiders 1... Bottom Line: Great game. One of the most interesting, fun and great looking fighting games ever. Great characters. Amazing bosses. Fantastic environments.
This game is really awesome. I like many aspects of this game more than Darksiders 2, even though Darksiders 2 is a really good game, despite some problems. In this review I make many references and comparisons to Darksiders 2.
The combat in Darksiders 1 I feel is more fun and satisfying than Darksiders 2 for a few reasons but the biggest one is my favorite combat move:
Harpoon Tackle.
(NOTE: FOR MAXIMUM COMBAT EFFECTIVENESS DO NOT PURCHASE POWER STRIKE IF YOU INTEND TO USE HARPOON TACKLE)
There is no better way to charge into combat for a direct strike than this move, and coupled with an evade move it provides a quick in and out for tougher enemies. Harpoon Tackle is a hard, sharp, thrust that covers quite a distance. There is only one real issue with this move in the game and that's if you intend to use this, (you'd be a fool not to) and you also purchase Power Strike which uses two of the same buttons as Harpoon Tackle. The problem with this is that Power Strike, which would be a fine addition to the moves list, triggers often when you are trying to use Harpoon Tackle. Power Strike has a really slow wind up which can leave you vulnerable if you use it at the wrong moment. If it triggers when you are trying to use Harpoon Tackle that is definitely the wrong moment.
I made the mistake of purchasing Power Strike after four hours of gameplay. This move left Harpoon Tackle so unreliable that I had no choice but to restart the whole game. Yet, it was hardly a chore to play through this game once again. Still, a major flaw and/or bug in the game system which should definitely be resolved. It totally breaks the gameplay completely for me.
Harpoon Tackle on the controller uses RB + X + a direction on the left stick or forward if you are locked on a target. Power strike is simply RB + X without the stick. The problem is that Power Strike will trigger often even if you are holding a direction or forward, especially if trying to use Power Strike in rapid succession. This is a major problem in the combat system. However, if you avoid purchasing Power Strike this problem goes aways entirely and the game is just freaking awesome.
The overall pacing and area layouts seem to be based off of games like Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. The idea is that you gain certain power-ups, gear or abilities that allow you to get through certain obstacles and/or enter secret paths and ofcourse progress to new areas. The weapon and gear progression are linear as well as the story progression. You really only have one mission. I see a lot of people considering this type of thing negative in platformers or in fact in many fighting games. But I see a game that is extremely well put together. It's like short-stories or short-films in how it's crafted into a very tight artistic form. It has a symmetry, a geometry, an architecture that is something that unfolds as you go along.
I definitely prefer this style of game world to whatever they did in Darksiders 2. Which wasn't bad but it made it sort of pointless. Sure there are a bunch of sidequests you can do or not do and you are free to explore any area, but you might also run into some enemies you have no chance in hell of killing until you reach a higher level and get way better gear... and that's just plain wierd sometimes. Especially, for this game. it sort of makes no sense. I guess that's the very nature of RPG style gameplay. It seems to be a trend that most franchises adopt nowadays. Perhaps it's to increase replay value or give players choices as that seems to be desired by a vast number of them. I personally don't see why everything has to end up the same. Some choices are irrelevant or just don't add much to the sense of adventure when you run into a boss you're suddenly very excited to fight and you can barely drain a few pixels from his health bar before he one hit kills you. Oops, I guess my very open ended choices means I get destroyed when I'm very freely and open-endedly explored some awesome new area.
Not that I don't appreciate open-world or RPG or free choices, but it's now such a rising trend that good, old-school style games are being converted into something they're really not supposed to be. I like Darkisders 2 and some RPG elements and things like that can be kind of fun or whatever, but I think that the feel of the original Darkisders game was lost somehow
Darksiders has a natural, story-driven gameplay that evolves as you progress. In many ways it is much like the Legacy of Kain series. War has a singular purpose. He's not concerned with random entities and talking and getting to know people. There's no confunsion about sidequests. Like, "should I do this now or proceed with my main mission." Also, there's no confusion about gear. You go into every battle fully equipped and you handle it based on your abilities. It makes for better mastery of the combat system.
Darkisders 2 has a move that uses the same buttons as Harpoon Tackle, but it's nowhere near as powerful, quick, or effective. It also doesn't trigger as flawlessly when trying to activate it. Overall the combat in Darkisders 1 is far more fluid and solid. Besides the combat moves, the camera is far more stable. It also has absolutely no issues running at all. Darksiders 2 had terrible lag/stutter until I used Radeon Pro (external graphics tweak program) to fix it. This alone is a terrible, terrible way to sell your game. I don't know if it's issues porting or whatever, the damn thing was released in 2012. 3 years is way more than enough time to release some major performance patches and there's no excuse for this behavior. Luckily, Radeon Pro is totally free (how very generous of Radeon Pro). Indie devs do way more to fix and improve their games than these people did on darksiders 2.
Darksiders 1 has some problem it seems rendering correctly when you are looking through portals. It doesn't just show where the second portal is showing, it shows like an xray... through where you're facing or something like that... Anyhow, it's not right. It doesn't make it impossible to see through, but it's still annoying. That's one graphical problem.
There are some places in the game where the frame rate drops, especially if you have forced vsync, but it's the normal slower framerate symptoms. The game still runs consistently even if the framerate is dropping. Whereas in Darkisders 2, if there is any drop in performance from perfect 60fps, the whole image stutters violently and unsmoothly. I said it before, but seriously, patches should have been released for this at some time during the 3 years since release.
In conclusion, Darksiders 1 exceeded my expectations by far. Compared to Darkisders 2, Darksiders 1 has:
-smoother combat
-smoother camera
-smoother performance
-better pacing
-better story
-better game layout
I felt the need to mention Darkisders 2 here because in some ways I was really disappointed. Although, I did play it and like it and even do recommend it, especially if you can manage to get a fix for the initial major performance issues (because there still are issues even with fix).

This review is based on the alpha version of the game, up to the date August 11th, 2014.
If you like realism, destruction, and cars, this is the game for you.
I'd like to begin by discussing what exactly Drive is. Drive is a state-of-the-art physics simulator that runs Torque 3D as the main physics engine. In this environment, every movement and input is calculted and recalculted over and over again as the game moves. So, as you come around a corner with your tail out, the computer is taking your car's weight, road surface, throttle, brake, gas, size of the contact patch of the tires, and many more variables into account every second. This allows the game to make an accurate representation of what is going on. Continuing with my example, if you nicked a bump in the road, millions more calcultions would take place, throwing the car around and whatnot. Another important feature that is simulated is air, which, for the time being, is being experimented with.
"So, what do you do in this physics game?" Well, most of us from the beginning have been obsessed with cars and destroying them, so, that's what we do. We take vans and drop them onto hatchbacks; we take hatchs, and put jets on them, and then run them into the wall at 300mph. We also create the game. Due to the producing company's small size (under 15 people total at last check), the community up until now has aided in adding content to the game in the form of maps, vehicles, UI apps (compass, speedo's, tachs, etc), and more. Others constantly push the game, such as accidently making a working plane and several helicopters that are flyable (albiet with primitive controls, depending on the model). As a gamer, having all of this content available for free is awesome. And it's usually good quality stuff that the creators have put hours and weeks into. And it's free.
"I'm a creator/artist/coder/computer wizz. How can I get involved?"
I'm not sure how this'll work with the game porting over to Steam, but up until now, you would do whatever you'd normally create aand then put in the game. It's quite simple, and the game itself is built to be modded easily (the devs even have a wiki on how to do it). Modelors can make their models in any 3D program, export to COLLADA, create a "JBeam" file, and you're in. Obviously it takes more than just that, but it's a very straight-forward process that even a beginner could do successfully.
"Should I buy this?"
Yes. There's more in the game that can be covered in this review without getting boring, but it is an extremely well-done game. Even though it's only in alpha, it's a pretty good game. Tech support from the community and devs is great, and gme-wide issues are quickly resolved. The physics are great and getting better, the view is spectacular, and who doesn't like smashing cars into each other? Oh, and did I mention the DLC is free? The DLC is free.

Nothing but problems.
The lighting system as it is currently implemented is completely broken.  Bloom effects are amped-up through the roof while ambient/"natural" light is nonexistent, making this a very dark game - such that it is borderline unplayable.  I cannot begin to describe how difficult it is to see anything while playing.  Reference the attached images and judge for yourself:
Depicted is a subsurface coal vane about 1-2 blocks below the surface that has been exposed.  One screenshot shows the coal in natural light, the other with a flashlight directed at it on maximum power.  Also included are screenshots of various tunnels being illuminated by a flashlight on maximum power.
There are very few user-configurable audio or video settings.
- No brightness/gamma control
- No UI scale control
- No key binding (must exit and change within the Unity launcher)
In addition, the control scheme is extremely awkward.  It is completely alien to that of any other game, including Factorio and Minecraft.
For some reason, this game implements a savefile compression system that activates after you confirm that you want to exit to desktop.  This system will operate for well over a minute before allowing the game to shut down unless you cancel it by clicking "exit now".
The sound design in this game is a bit of a let-down.  It tries way too hard to be a blend of retro-futuristic bleeps, bloops and machine sounds, but ends up sounding more like a bunch of stock files that were tweaked in Audacity.  This is not a deal breaker by any means, but it really helps to make this game feel like a cheap one-off.  (The main menu alone contains audio elements that pop and crackle as they move around, and at least one horribly obvious 60Hz ground loop.)
I cannot in good faith recommend this game to anyone.  I was very hesitant to try it based on the other negative reviews below, but I purchased it for ~$12 w/ DLC nonetheless at the recommendation of a friend.  I will be refunding this title immediately.
Caveat emptor.
To the developer(s?):  The main problems with your game are not related to lack of features or content.  Your game is
in need of usability refinements and technical polish.  When it comes to your UI and lighting systems: Instead of trying to defy convention at every opportunity, take a few hints from other games that have been massively successful.  In addition to everything mentioned above, focus on the little things that make a huge difference - like placing "tutorial" elements into dialog boxes, instead of floating them above peoples' heads or behind machines where they will never be seen.
System specs for reference:
2560x1440 144Hz display
GTX 980ti
i7 5820k
32GB DDR4
(All overclocked)
