If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Shadow Warrior 2 is very different from Shadow Warrior 2013. SW2013 was a linear story game, but this is a lot more like Borderlands. I played this on difficulty 2/4 single player. There's a tl;dr at the bottom.
There is a little hub world, with a few shops and NPCs that give you side quests and main story quests. The game is NOT open world. To play a mission you open your map and teleport to the area. From there, you carry out the mission. When you are done, you can revisit the area and free roam. Levels are randomized (NOT RANDOMLY GENERATED) when you spawn in. However, I noticed the same few prefabs popping up several times in completely different quests not long after each other.
There are different elemental effects: Fire, Electricity, Ice and Toxin. Enemies can be resistant, weak and invulnerable to these. These can be applied and removed to weapons at any time.
Speaking of weapons, so far I've collected quite a lot. And they all look very different. It's not the same few gun models with different colour pallettes, but completely different models.
Throughout the game you collect many (like, a metric ♥♥♥♥ton) of modifiers for your weapons and passive abilities. Stuff like +11.6% damage, elemental effects with different potencies, etc. This can be really cool, but I think you get way too many. By the end of a level I would have found like 30 new modifiers. Most of which do the same thing but with +-0.1% difference. If thats not enough, you can combine 3 mods to craft a random one of greater strength. I say random because I combined 3 mods that involve guns using 2x ammo per shot for +50% damage, and got a mod that shot multiple projectiles at once (kind of like a cluster bomb).
Information in this game is quite overwhelming. With hundreds of modifiers, loads of different enemies with different weaknesses, trying to balance mods and make my weapons useful while being surrounded by drops is insane. I scroll through my list of modifiers and I have no idea what the ♥♥♥♥ I should do with anything.
There is no punishment for dying. When you die, you respawn at the last checkpoint (usually 3-10 seconds away from where you died) immediately, enemies have their health restored and you lose a bit of cash. That's it.
It's pretty repetitive. Mini-Bosses have the same mechanic (when you deal 50% of their health, they go into a stasis effect and summon a few strong enemies. Once these are killed it wakes up and the fight continues) and theyre not very difficult. A few areas look pretty much identical to each other. Many times you run into a locked gate, where you have to backtrack to get a key. One time I had to rescue a dude in a cage, then in a different mission an hour or so later I had to rescue someone completely different from a cage in the same spot an identical area.
Despite all of this, I'm still enjoying my time with the game. It does feel very repetitive at times and it's pretty easy (at least on difficulty 2/4) and despite the fact I feel overloaded with information and choice with modifiers and weapons.
---------------------
tl;dr
+Very different from SW2013, more borderlands-esque
+Well optimised
+Looks very good
+Lots of unique weapons and modifiers for them
+Randomized levels
+Satisfying visceral effects
-Information overload
-Repetitive quests and areas
-Too easy
(-No real punishment for death)
If youre a fan of SW2013 and borderlands, this should be a game worth getting, and I think the devs did quite well with it.

This review is based on the alpha version of the game, up to the date August 11th, 2014.
If you like realism, destruction, and cars, this is the game for you.
I'd like to begin by discussing what exactly Drive is. Drive is a state-of-the-art physics simulator that runs Torque 3D as the main physics engine. In this environment, every movement and input is calculted and recalculted over and over again as the game moves. So, as you come around a corner with your tail out, the computer is taking your car's weight, road surface, throttle, brake, gas, size of the contact patch of the tires, and many more variables into account every second. This allows the game to make an accurate representation of what is going on. Continuing with my example, if you nicked a bump in the road, millions more calcultions would take place, throwing the car around and whatnot. Another important feature that is simulated is air, which, for the time being, is being experimented with.
"So, what do you do in this physics game?" Well, most of us from the beginning have been obsessed with cars and destroying them, so, that's what we do. We take vans and drop them onto hatchbacks; we take hatchs, and put jets on them, and then run them into the wall at 300mph. We also create the game. Due to the producing company's small size (under 15 people total at last check), the community up until now has aided in adding content to the game in the form of maps, vehicles, UI apps (compass, speedo's, tachs, etc), and more. Others constantly push the game, such as accidently making a working plane and several helicopters that are flyable (albiet with primitive controls, depending on the model). As a gamer, having all of this content available for free is awesome. And it's usually good quality stuff that the creators have put hours and weeks into. And it's free.
"I'm a creator/artist/coder/computer wizz. How can I get involved?"
I'm not sure how this'll work with the game porting over to Steam, but up until now, you would do whatever you'd normally create aand then put in the game. It's quite simple, and the game itself is built to be modded easily (the devs even have a wiki on how to do it). Modelors can make their models in any 3D program, export to COLLADA, create a "JBeam" file, and you're in. Obviously it takes more than just that, but it's a very straight-forward process that even a beginner could do successfully.
"Should I buy this?"
Yes. There's more in the game that can be covered in this review without getting boring, but it is an extremely well-done game. Even though it's only in alpha, it's a pretty good game. Tech support from the community and devs is great, and gme-wide issues are quickly resolved. The physics are great and getting better, the view is spectacular, and who doesn't like smashing cars into each other? Oh, and did I mention the DLC is free? The DLC is free.

There's a lot to BeamNG Drive. It's probably best known because of the amazing, unique, real-time physics make the cars deform very realistically.
Most games that have a decent damage system only seem to deform very well somewhere past the more gentle bumps and bashes, but somewhere before the really extreme, high-speed crashes, that would turn a car into mangled pulp, which does take quite a lot of joy out of that insane crash-stunt-thing that you managed to pull off.
BeamNG, though, as the damage is calculated while you are crashing, will have the cars deforming well no matter what end of the scale you push it to- you can watch the very slight deformation that comes from driving a car slightly too hard, and see the little dents and and bashes, all the way up to the car being crushed to such an extreme that the car is left only a couple of inches tall- a phenomenon that is usually caused by setting the gravity to a level that makes the cars float off the ground, before suddenly changing the gravity levels to that of the sun itself.
But, although that is all amazing, and can bring a LOT of fun, and be interesting to observe, it is not the focus of the game, and it is, for me, not the best part of the game.
At the time of this review, there are three environments that I consider particularly noteworthy, and a few smaller environments.
All of the maps are extremely detailed, and contain a lot to explore. They don't even prevent you from leaving the roads!
Sure, there isn't a huge amount to find away from the beaten path, but if you're like me, then you've probably had that moment in a racing game, when you've just stopped and looked at how beautiful the landscape is, and had a strong desire to go drive all over it.
BeamNG won't surprise you with anything super-amazing if you try to do that, but it won't disappoint, either.
That hill will be there, and you'll be able to actually drive all over it, and it will be almost exactly what it looked like it was- although, I will note that it will, in one or two maps, while still turning out to be what it looked like, Also reveal that at the bottom of the other side of the hill, the map suddenly ends in a void.
It isn't a huge thing, but it would be a bit more immersive if they'd thrown a random ocean there, or something.
Then, of course, most importantly, there is how the cars feel when you drive them. This is probably the main point of the game, and the most important aspect of any racing game.
Now, they handle very realistically-there are a few issues to iron out still, but heck, it's an early alpha game and they've already got it THIS realistic? It's pretty insane.
But, I'm going to focus on how it feels to drive them. This is the most important point for most gamers, if they are not hardcore simulator fans.
A lot of people have been complaining that the cars are too hard to control, but I'm just using a Logitech F710 -that is, a gamepad with the layout of a PlayStation controller, that emulates a 360 controller, minus the deadzone- and it isn't TOO hard to control the cars.
They’re a little hard to control if you’re trying to push them to their limits, but they’re not too hard, and you can always just drive them gently, which is plenty easy.
In fact, I don't understand why this game is getting flack for how hard it is to control the cars, when games like Assetto Corsa seem to have few complaints, yet, when I'm playing Assetto I often find that one minute the car feels like it's very stable, and despite the fact that I'm starting to slide it, it feels like I have a LOT of control- then, suddenly, because I applied slightly too much throttle, I find myself backwards and in a cloud of tyre smoke, without any warning, wondering what just happened.
BeamNG, though, feels so...Natural. Nothing feels forced. If I push too hard, I can see very clearly that the car is slipping out of my control, which sometimes gives me enough of a chance to catch it before it spins- or, at the very least, to put the game in slow motion so that I can watch as the dents form in the car.
Y'know, I've always had a thing about watching cars leaning and/or bouncing on their suspension. I can’t really describe it.
This game succeeds in giving me the same kind of feeling I get from watching a car's suspension smoothly dealing with a sudden change in elevation, or dealing with the weight shifting to the front of the car under heavy breaking, in real life; I don't remember ever getting that feeling from another game.
And, of course, I could talk for days about how detailed, and beautifully designed the cars in this game are.
They are very similar to cars that are in reality, yet they are not blatant ripoffs; they have their own look, and their own charm...
Rather like real cars do.
They are FAR more detailed than the models in most games, and if you pay attention, you'll notice that the interior of the car is actually part of the model, and you can see it in all it's glory from 3rd person view, if you manage to get the camera to be looking in the window.
...I'll stop here, before this gets any longer. Even as it is, it'll be a pain in the neck to proofread.
I will note, though, that the game is very resource intensive. back when I got the game (the day after it was first released), I only had an old-ish laptop, and, as I expected, it got an average of about 20 FPS with the least CPU intensive cars, which was not very playable. But, I now have an AMD FX-8320, which is OC'd to 4.4 GHz, and a Sapphire 7870 HD, and it runs the game as smoothly as a Codemaster game's menu animation.
You should make sure that your computer has enough power before you buy the game, or you may be somewhat disappointed. And, don't expect to be able to run a tonload of cars, either.
If you have a good CPU, you'll be able to run about 6 cars at once.
Also, don't expect a complete, polished game, because it isn't. It's an early alpha release, being worked on by a VERY small team, and this game is more advanced than any driving game before. EVER. So don't expect it to be developed at lightning speed. The devs are releasing updates at a good pace, but the bigger changes and features can take a few months to implement, and there are a few [small issues] to deal with at the moment, such as slightly tacky engine sounds.
TL;DR: Amazing physics, good graphics, good maps, good devs, good game. Shut up and take my money. And the money of whoever is reading this review, for that matter.
I expect I'll come back in the future and update this review as the game progresses.

If you like Big Pharma, Inififactory, or Factario you might want to check out this game.
Personally I think if you like Kerbal Space Program, Rim World, or Prison Architect you might also like this game.
First thing, even though this is a voxel based game, it is far from a minecraft clone. That was the biggest thing that made me hesitate buying it, but I am glad I was wrong about that.
The game is far from perfect. There are bugs and annoying things. However, the dev is constantly working on it (and if opt into one of the branches you get nightly updates).
In the course of a year, the game will seem like a completly new game with all of the the additional features and content. Yes there is DLC, but there are still free content updates as well. However, even if there was not, you are more than getting your moneys worth with this game.
I find it rediculous how peopel will hem and haw over buying this when it is on sale to like $5. If you like the game you get 100's of hours of gameplay (Many players get 1000's of hours). If you don't like it, you are only out $5.
The fanbase is supportive enough that many people donate to the dev through Pateron. This is one of those games (like Dwarf Fortress) that will continue to be in development for years.
I won't go into the details of the Pro's and Con's or anything like. Plenty of other reviews do that. I will just say to check it out.
EDIT:
Just a thought I recently had. The 3D FPS nature of the game will mean that setting certain things up will take longer than in games like Factario (even ignoring Factario's blue print system).
Thinking about it, I just wanted to emphasise the similarities to Infinifactory.

Fast version:  This game is slow, the temperature mechanic is interesting but frustrating, the game is complicated in a non fun way, building things is okay and the monsters are annoying in a non fun way. FortressCraft Evolved is like factorio mixed with minecraft.  With all the cons of both.
******************************************************************************************
Complexity
******************************************************************************************
Factorio gets its complexity through simplicity.  FortressCraft gets its complexity through complexity.
Factorio has these eight raw resources: wood, coal, iron, copper, stone, oil, water, alien artifacts.  Very different and used for different ends; of these most everything is done with: iron, copper, oil.  Simple, it becomes complex as your create new resources.
FortressCraft has 14 (? by the wiki) ores alone, each one can be turned into plates, wires, coils, pipes, and PCBs.  It also has 13 (?) other resources which you find, they can be very hard to find based on your starting seed. (Organic Rock I am looking at you).  FortressCraft also has 11-13 (?) items dropped from mobs that you need to collect.
I will start with my frustrations with organic rock.  You need organic rock to make smelters, why? I have no idea.  Organic rock is sometimes found in caves.  Caves are dark and cold.  You only have so much battery to keep yourself warm and the cave lit, so bring 1000 torches made from coal they provide light and warmth.  But don't stand too close or they will begin to overheat your suit, stand precisely something like 1.5 blocks away from it or it is worse than not having one.
The first time you look for organic rock it will be easier as you can scan for unknown objects, not all of them will show up but hopefully a couple will.  As a new player instead of collecting all of them you will likely be like, "wtf is this weird thing, i'll scan it for the research when I get back."  After this there is no organic rock scan to use later.
All this to make a couple smelters.  But smelters also require tin plates and Basic PCB (the copper ones) and all the dependent research.  See the problem.  Fortunately the game starts you off with one smelter you can use, that will deliver you the high throughput of 4 bars per minute at a 4:1 ore to bar ratio.  This leads to maybe being able to make a smelter within the first hour of playing.  Don't worry you will definitely be mining enough ore with the extractors provided. The game will constantly bug you to improve the extractors and also bug you that they are constantly offline as they are backed up. If only I could smelt all this ore.
You will be manually running around fetching ore for several hours as conveyors require a copper bar and a tin bar per square. 2 bars each, 2 conveyors per minute, need hundreds of conveyors to connect mines to smelters.
Then you need to build the machinery to make plates, wires, coils, PCBs.  Keep in mind storage is very hard to come by as hoppers are very expensive early on, so you can't just build a storage bin for each of these materials immediately.
Now you can make the research lab (if you didn't accidently spend all your research points on everything else and screw yourself permanently.)  The lab itself takes a lot of copper, but smelting copper is trivial right?  That isn't the problem with the lab though, the lab can consume 15000 power per second (pps) and the assembler can consume something like 500-1000 pps.  Up until this point power has been trivial, an extractor takes roughly 2 pps, the smelter takes somewhere around 5-10 pps.
Do not connect your lab directly to your central power hub, it will take all the power just to charge its own internal buffer.
To combat this you need to make more power generators and energy lazers and probably make a new coal mine at this point, so while you are waiting on the metal to set this up, you are waiting on the lab to finish its research, also did I mention that about now you are going to get attacked, better build turrets.  Also did I mention that your lithium mine will probably have a bunch of plants eating all the ore on the conveyor you built, better build some more turrets and batteries and lazers to power it all.  But you need those for the lab too, better get more smelters going, but guess what your suit also needs all that power so you can find more organic rock without dying of hypothermia.  Also you can't leave your base because a bunch of wasps are attacking and they don't seem to stop coming and you need that lithium to build those batteries and the purple plants keep spawning and you need to shoot them too.
So you run around killing wasps, trying not to die from hypothermia, out of research points, making sure lithium isn't getting eaten, and collecting metal bars so you can hopefully do something is this silly game.
You have now been playing for ten hours.
******************************************************************************************
How it fails
******************************************************************************************
It is so hard to explain how needlessy complex and slow this game is.
To pull from minecraft and factorio, the furnace is made out of stone blocks.  It makes perfect sense, the limiting factor is how much ore I can find.  Which leads to needing more furnaces, which leads to more ore, etc.  It is an exponential that I want to ride up.
To mine something in FortressCraft it needs an extractor, lets assume we have those.  They need power, each one needs at least a basic laser of power.  Lets assume we have those.  They each need to have line of sight to that laser or have batteries to connect them all and the laser needs to be powered likely by another laser.
So what should happen is I run back and forth making this mine amazing and making my smelting amazing too.  But you are bottlenecked constantly.  Your new basic smelters will take 8 ore per bar, so we need about 4 extractors.  Which is 4 basic lasers, which is either going to be some crazy triangular setup to keep line of sight or you are going to need 16 ish batteries.  For each of the three basic ores, maybe more lasers for lithium as it is found deeper underground and more everything for copper as you will need a lot.
That many lasers just isn't going to happen early on so we will need to upgrade.  Good news there is a better type of laser available early on, the MK1 laser is 10x stronger than the basic laser.  So we can just point one in that direction easy.  Next the conveyor belt can only carry one ore at a time, so perhaps we need to use normal conveyors instead of basic conveyors but replacing the conveyor is being bottlenecked by the very smelting we are trying to upgrade.  So lets just smelt the bars right at the mine its an 8:1 throughput increase.
But each smelter takes a full MK1 beam of power, now you are running multiple MK1 lasers to your mine and you have the same problem you had before.  Plus smelters stop working at lower elevations (for some reason?).
FortressCraft is like 4+ seperate linear functions instead of one happy exponential.  And once you finally decide to stop increasing one of those functions none of the others can increase either.  For myself it was power for the lab, I just stood there feeding plates, PCB, and research packs into the lab for hours.  It was already running 10 power generators out of energy, even at that my 1 million coal mine was already draining faster than I would like.
It is always the same answer: There is a solution to that, that you can't make.  I can't even talk about how research works as I am out of space. Basically you scan unknown blocks, there are only so many unique blocks in this game.
The controls seem to lag a little bit, but its a fun and well detailed game.

The Campaign is tons of fun and has many different game modes. My favorite being Assault, an attack & defend objective game mode. There are powerups and different abilities that you can obtain from getting max adrenaline such as Speed, Regenerate, Invisibility, Berserk, Pint-Size & Camouflage.
There are loads of mods such as the original Alien Swarm & Killing Floor. Theres was also a mod I played but I cant remember the name, You started on a roof with fences on both sides and a spiral stair case going down into a lab, Only weapon you had was a translocator & bullpup machine gun. You could set the number of AI players & glitchy zombies. AI would run down and you'd hear over the radio (we're under attack, man down) etc. 2Spooky4me :S
Definitely try it out if your a fan of Fast paced Shooters.

TL;DR: You will put many hours into this game before you see any significant progress. The game does not instantly reward you. You will spend lots of time on the wiki and in forums getting answers to your questions. If you plan to play alone, you're choosing to make the experience much harder on yourself. To get full enjoyment of the game, join a village.
If you're looking for a relaxing game with a deep crafting system, the ability to create any conceivable design for a village (within the limits of the game mechanics of course), a challenging yet rewarding gaming experience, then this game might be for you. I'd like to first address the reasons I believe people would not enjoy this game.
1. You will not be instantly rewarded for your labors. It takes time to erect a clay hut, to construct a house, to build a wall. If you've played Rust, you're more familiar with the ability to simply gather a certain number of wood and clicking the structure you wish to build. In LiF, it's much more tedious.  The gathering process beforehand along with acquiring the skills necessary to even gather those materials are a discipline in and of itself. Once you do achieve the appropriate levels and gather all materials, you can finally build your structure, that is if it's on level ground. If the ground is not level, you must terraform. If you're not familiar with terraforming, this game is a perfect introduction. All it means is diggins out dirt and leveling out the terrain.
2. Lack of NPCs. This, in my opinion, adds an interesting dynamic to the game. It forces players to cooperate in ways they may not have before or have always refused doing. However, the amount of time and effort it takes to gather certain ingredients makes it almost advisable to establish some form of trade contract with another player to help with your experience.
3. Weak PVP system? Long story short, killing other players can be an immense challenge considering their abilities. For example, you can always run into a village in full armor and a two-handed sword and murder a player who's unarmed, and lacks armor with ease. Of course, this is assuming you have the appropriate levels to even wear armor which you have to craft and you can only craft that armor if you have the appropriate gathering levels to get those ingredients. This is why cooperation is stressed in LiF because you can have different players have various roles (blacksmith, carpenter, herbalist, etc) and you come together to build a flourishing experience. Anyway, I digress.
Assuming both players are in a consenting battle, it won't be shortly won as the targeting system is physics based meaning wherever you swing is where you'll do damage. Since the game is in Alpha it's not always accurate. Of course you can move around and block and there are even crossbows to attack at range. And the game does not reward you for killing others. In fact, in a way it punishes you. You have a prayer skill which is measured by something called Alignment. Everytime you do damage to another player your alignment decreases. This means, if you die with low alignment, you will lose skill points and the lower your alignment the more points you lose. However, you do have the ability to invite a player into a "unit" which makes it so alignment is not lost during combat. You can begin to see how random death matches actually hinder the assailant and simply inconveniences the victim.
4. Bugs. If you purchase the game in this current state, you will notice bugs here and there. They do not significantly impact your experience nor does it take away from the game. All the necessary components are in the game and you will be able to play it just fine.
5. Intense graphics requirements. Many players including myself have to lower the graphics settings to lowest to avoid sluggish gameplay. But I have to say even with graphics set to lowest the game still looks great.
If you can get past these points and are still interested in playing the game, I just barely scratched the surface. I recommend giving this game a chance to lure you into its creative depths and challenge yourself with a very intricate game. You may not be instantly rewarded, but the rewards you do receive are damn good.
No level system, no unlocks, no 12vies, no standing still, no outstanding price. Take it or leave it this is the best game on the market.

Unreal Tournament 2004
9 / 10 (2004)
When released in 2004 this was the third iteration in the seminal Unreal Tournament franchise. Renowed for intense and over the top deathmatch in single player and multiplayer mode, this game delivered unprecedented adrenaline overload and cumulative sleep deprivation following installation to your hard drive.
I installed this game (2015) and played single player mode on a W7Pro 64bit / Radeon 6870 without any hassles and no 3rd party DRM. I reconfigured my keys in game to my traditional FPS set up and was fragging away within minutes, and then came the adrenaline, I loved it. This was my first time playing this particular release; the controls are responsive, the weapons (10) balanced and very tight, and the giblets abound. I played for an hour on maximum graphics quality without a single hiccup. I did not test multiplayer.
Previous versions that I have owned and played extensively include Unreal Tournament, Unreal Championship (Xbox), Unreal Tournament GOTY (2000 PC / XP), and  Unreal Tournament 3 (2007 PC / XP). This version fits perfectly in the expected rank of the series for graphics, map design, and audio quality which of course was top notch for 2004. This Hall of Fame franchise belongs in everybodies collection.
Q: Why did I install this game?
A: They added cards. It's madness ; )
[note: I purchased this in 2010 in a bundle, not just for the cards!]
Buy this game Unreal Tournament 2004 if you want to taste classic deathmatch style with polished maps and gameplay from this era.
Purchase Unreal Tournament 3 (2007) if you want more recent graphics with much larger and better maps, improved graphics and more complex gameplay options.

I've played this game more than any other game, well over 700 hours.  I will play for a few weeks every day and then move onto something else, however FortressCraft keeps pulling me back, at which point I start a new game.  The game is constantly updated with new stuff.
You start at the crash site of your ship, with a few machines and a brief tutorial.  When I first started over a year ago, the game didn't have a guide to the early game.  Now in the corner of the screen the game will suggest what you should focus on.  You can follow that or not, but I think it's helpful to new players.
The game becomes like a tower defense after your base threat level reaches 100 or higher.  Your threat increases the more you build machines and generators.  You can build Threat Reduces to bring that number back down, something I did when I first started playing, to avoid the wasps which shoot acid at your Hub.  I have since found out that it's better to focus on defensive turrets and arming your SpiderBot with blasters.  At threat level 100 to I dunno, a few hundred, only a few waves of some wasps will come at you.  The higher the number, the more waves of higher numbers will come.  Eventually when you get into the 1000s larger bugs will attack and when you get higher still giant creatures will spawn.
The focus of this game is automation.  I used to try to do everything manually, taking 100s of trips up and down into deep caverns to retrieve ore.  Many new techologies have been added to the game such as transporters and lifts to automate the process.  BTW don't use conveyor belts below like 75 or 80m because creatures will spawn on them and consume your resources.
I should note that I play on "scarce" resources and power, meaning it takes more ore to smelt into each bar and less power generation.  I also play on Clumsy death, meaning I drop my inventory items upon death and have to make a corpse run.  "Scarce" difficulty really increases the time needed to progress.  After spending 100s of hours discovering new, better ways of doing things, I think I have a pretty good system going.  I haven't really watched any videos or read any tips on playing this game.  I prefer to figure out things on my own.  There are videos and guides out there to help you get started, offering tips to optimize your efforts/resources/time, etc.  I could've saved TONS of time by watching these but I like to discover better ways of doing things on my own.
The game seems intimidating at first, but it's addicting!  The developer has added beginner tips and technology guides you can see by pressing "H".  Also before researching, highlight a technology and press "H" to see what machines the research will unlock.  This is relatively new and very helpful to make research decisions when starting out.  I recommend suit upgrades, mining upgrades, and power upgrades first.  Also mine as much coal as you can!  You will need tons in the early game before better power generation methods are available.  I recommend starting on the default "plenty" resouces/power.  It will greatly shorten the time needed to really get going.  Research requires research points which are gained by scanning unknown plants and materials.  Scan everything!  You will eventually gain enough research points to research everything, but it's best to choose carefully in the early game so read the help guide to make the right decisions.
I highly recommend this game, it's one of my favorites and it's always fun to discover better ways of doing things.  If you want a game with fast progression and quick rewards, this may not be the game for you.  Researching in the early game takes a lot of time and you can quickly run out of coal to generate power.

This is an amazing game with a lot of charm in it's writing and setting, a great soundtrack, tight gameplay, great level-design, and can be pretty challenging while being fair.  This game is an NES-style game done right and nails everything from the limited color palletes and pixel-art to the constrained music, but with all of the lessons we have learned over 30+ years of gaming on what to do and what not to do in game design.  You will also see very clever game design decisions in this game, for example: there is a checkpoint system in the level so you don't have to retread the entire level if you die, however, if you want to you can break the checkpoints and they will drop more money which creates a nice risk-reward system.  The first level is also pretty easy but drops a decent amount of money, so if you are having trouble, you can replay that level over and over again to get better gear and upgrades if you are willing to grind a little bit.  Those are just some random examples of things I've seen in this game that exclaims that these devs really know their stuff, and it shows through the entire game.
If that isn't enough, there are two other modes you can play in where you play as 2 different antagonists.  The first is the alchemist which, I'll admit, I'm not a fan of.  It felt like a really cheap remake of the original levels with a twist which, imo, felt kind of lazy.  There is still a lot of differences, but they all seem minor.  Same levels just remixed a little bit to work around different mechanics that the character you use has.  The second, however, feels like a completely different game and an independent game unto itself.  The character and his mechanics are a huge departure from the original game with very unique levels (although there are some similarities here and there, especially for the first stage).
So, for both the original and the spectre of torment, the full price is definitely worth it.  I would encourage you to not wait for a sale and support it at full price if you can afford it, otherwise pick it up on a sale the next time you see it!

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is an ambitious indie game that set the bar for a horror game experience, defining a new level of immersion that games of its genre had attempted to achieve but fell short. Environment, lighting, expertly constructed sound effects and music, and powerful psychological effects create an atmosphere that immediately instills awe, reverence, and dread all at once. With the stage set as it is, the game mechanics, storyline, and progression maintain and enhance the experience, thrusting you into the world and filling you with panic, fear, and desperation, but the game keeps you wanting to see and learn more about your surroundings. The power of visual, aural, and mechanical queues is on full display here. And all of this comes at an affordable price. How can I not recommend it?
There's even player-made custom storylines that you can play as well, so the game's livespan is greatly extended. Truly a wonderful purchase that all gamers should experience.

Hands down the first game recommended to any fan of the Survival Horror Genre and arguably the most frightening game ever made.
You awaken in an eerie castle, unaware of how you got there and unaware of your identity.
The story is told through a journal that is collected by you throughout the game, helping you piece together who you are and why you are there...but stay in the light - for your sanity drains in the darkness.
The castle forces you to explore it's dark corridors by making it necessary to gather resources. You must have oil for your lantern, wicks for the candles in the hallways - you can find the items you need by looking in drawers and cabinets. However, do not ever forget...you are not alone.
Danger is around every corner and every door of the castle...and you are completely defenseless. Running from the threat is your only option and you better find a good place to hide.
In the end The Darkness will have what it wants...one way or the other...

After having played H1Z1 for some hours now I must admit that it's not a bad game but at the same time  it's not a good game either. I would put it somewhere in the middle. In fact this game can be very addicting at times.
Pros:
Optimization:
this game is very well optimized. H1Z1 definitely beats Player Unknown in the optimization department! But this game does use up a good amount of system ram. Minimum specs should be at 8GB of ram and recommended specs should be at 16GB of ram. My computer peaked out at around 9-10GB of usage in most of my play sessions. H1Z1 uses very little video memory however. My RX 480 averaged around 1.5gb on my RX 480.
Graphics:
Superb! The graphics in this game looks really nice for a game of this type. This being an older game then Player Unknown H1Z1 is still on par graphically and again runs much smoother!
Windows 8.1
I7 4790K 4.4Ghz
RX 480 8gb
16GB ram
1TB ssd
Cons:
Gameplay:
The green toxic gas advances far too quickly. I died mostly by the advancing gas and not by other players. That's not fun. I think that the speed at which the toxic advances needs to be slowed down a bit. Doing this would give players more of an opportunity to search buildings and to get to the safe zone. Also, this game is in dire need of a first person shooter only mode. As it is now you can only play in third person with the option of putting your character in first person but doing that will put you at big disadvandage.
Sound:
Sounds in this game needs a reworking. Inside buildings for example gunshots can be heard loudly from across the map. So loud in fact that it sounds as if the one doing the shooting is inside the building with you only to found out that they are quite a distance away. Also, footsteps needs to be toned back at bit. Again, they are way too loud even when crouched.
Hacking:
It's questionable, but there is a good chance that there are hackers with aimbots, speed hacks, and inviniciblity hacks. Players that are running around zig zagging, jumping and landing perfect headshots? Players, that appears to be running faster then most. Players that doesn't seem to take hit damage. Hackers ruines the experience for me. Hackers will just tell you that they are having mindless fun and so what's the big deal. But having fun at who's expense?
Variety:
The gun and clothing variety that is found in the Battle Royal mode is way too limited. Which results in everyone pretty much having the same gear and setup. Maybe this was done to keep the game running as smoothly as possible but once I realized just how limited my choices were in this game I started to get very bored very quickly.
That said, given the fact that Steam doesn't allow for anyone to vote neutral and given the fact that this game has more cons then pros in my opinion. Its a thumbs down.
Overall, 6 out of 10

The story and art are interesting and enjoyable with a passable soundtrack (standard cinematic affair, not particularly special).  Unfortunately the gameplay design and programmers have really dropped the ball with what would have been an otherwise great game.  The controls are just terrible and awkward, even on a 360pad.  Most input lacks buffers and are otherwise unforgiving leaving lots of situations where you fall of ledges other games would have been tolerant with jumping or pressing a button repeatedly to charge something because it only accepts key down in the right state and a tad before.  Other clunkiness comes from the terrible camera which you will not only fight, but affects your dodge input.  Anyone who is a fan of the Zelda franchise will feel right at home with the concepts, but frustrated to no end with the awful controls.
Oh, it also crashes frequently and I just found out that for whatever reason it's failing to deliver achievements.  The only way to get the ones it randomly decides to drop is to reload the game before whatever awarded it and try again.  Did I mention it autosaves?  Well, that's actually a good thing considering the port crashes... frequently.
I mentioned the design was a bit off.  There's lots of of show and tell to the point it's distraction.  The game gives you an unskippable cinimatic for finding a puzzle.  Then showing you the puzzle you just solved was solved.  It tells you how to use every minor item/environmental effect in the game, then hides random bits of information like it's trying to be clever.  It doesn't cater to the casual or the hardcore gamer, but tries to find some middle ground leaving the game to feel inconsistent.  There are mandatory events with specific rules (only special kills, throwing kills, protect the minions, ect) that most other games would make optional diversions.  Rather than exploring it's mostly linear routes with backtracking.  I can't even remember the rest, but expect enough design nuisances that you will probably have no sense of immersion in the game (well, assuming the crashing and clunky controls don't ruin it for you first).
-----------
Overall it feels like the budget for testing and bugfixing was cut, which is a real shame given the great amount of effort that went into the art and writing.  If you're a fan of the franchise play this game, but to anyone else I can't recommend it.

Wow! I had picked up Darksiders expecting some kind of God of War clone (which it is to some degree) and a so-so experience, but I was totally blown away. The story is actually good and there are some prominent voice actors that you may recognize (such as Mark Hamill as the voice of the watcher) playing important parts here and there. Gameplay-wise it’s basically like GoW with a lot less QTE plus a generous helping of Metroid Prime.
A good chunk of the game will have you using various new items and techniques to explore the environment, unlock areas, find upgrades, and solve puzzles in order to advance. Fast travel is implemented in a unique fashion where you enter serpent holes e.g. mini-levels where you run over appearing platforms, giving a bit more of a feeling of going somewhere than just instantly appearing at another location.
The controls are pretty solid and I only found myself struggling with them when trying to get war to jump off of climbable walls or when trying to get him on his horse (it doesn’t always respond right away). The AI seems to range from really aggressive to pants-on-head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ depending on the strength of the opponent (small fry will casually stand around as you slaughter their teammates, big guys, not so much). Puzzles in Darksiders are generally more of a matter of finding all the components as some of them have critical parts hidden from plain sight. They’re pretty much just enough of a challenge that it isn’t a cakewalk but still enough to give you the satisfaction from solving them. As far as finding secrets, the game gives you various items that can either highlight their location on specific maps, or one particular enhancement that reveals ALL secrets on the current map (it’s an easy to find enhancement too).
Overall I have to say I was pretty satisfied with this game and can’t think of anything really bad to say about it so I’d definitely recommend it to anyone who likes action games with a bit of exploration involved.

BeamNG.drive is a physics simulation from some of the same people that brought you
and some of its top quality mods. When comparing the two, it is evident that lots of lessons have been learnt and that each developer has improved greatly in their respective field, resulting in state of the art physics that simulate every single part of a vehicle/object with almost true to life accuracy (with accuracy and efficiency being improved as development goes on), near perfectly modelled fictional vehicles that each represent a certain type of vehicle, resulting in a diverse, albeit small selection (
) , and fantastic
that push the graphics engine,
to its limits. Currently, the Small Island map is my personal favourite mainly due to the recent overhaul that added so many little details. I hope Dry Rock is also updated in a similar fashion.
In terms of gameplay, it is currently just a sandbox, but a planned update will bring timed races (no advanced AI YET) and online leaderboards to the table as the first step in the direction of given gameplay, but I still think the sandbox will be where the majority of the entertainment is.
The game is very moddable, all sorts of vehicles can be added, including helicopters and planes, levels can be created in the in-game level editor, and LUA files that make up quite a lot of the code can be freely edited to tailor your experience to your liking or even add features. A feature that I quite like that has been created by the community with LUA scripting has been changing the engine sound depending on the vehicle that is being used. Mods should only be downloaded from the official forum's showroom and downloading from anywhere else will either leave you with some kind of malware or very disappointed.
The current sound system is a placeholder to avoid people moaning about "sound not working" really, with a single engine, skid, and crash sound making up the entirety of the vehicle's vocabulary (can be modded though) and a few ambient background tracks. This will be completely redone eventually.
The vehicle's handling characteristics can be quirky at times with some seemingly random veering at very high speeds and vehicles losing friction too easily, but the physics will be continuously improved and tweaked to ensure maximum authenticity. I can see this rivalling high profile racing simulators in the future.
The game needs a fairly high end CPU (or more specifically, a CPU with fairly powerful cores) in order to run the physics smoothly. My i5 3570k can run 4 detailed vehicles smoothly, but those with certain AMD CPUs may struggle. Even though they have lots of cores, each core is quite weak. To run the game at max graphical settings, a fairly powerful GPU will also be required, but most semi-recent mid range video cards should be able to run it with lower settings fine. The tech demo will be updated soon so I suggest going to
and trying it out before purchasing.
I've probably sunk hundreds of hours into it so it's safe to say that I've probably got my money's worth.
I think that is all I currently have to say, but I'll probably remember something else in 5 minutes.
TL;DR:  Physics, mods, don't complain if your ZX Spectrum doesn't run it at 120 fps etc.

"When will we take a break!?
"I'm going to get thrombosis!"
"When are we going to have a break!"
*gets on the speaker*
"I'll turn this bus right around! Do you want to go back to Leipzig!?"
Okay, full disclosure, I play lots of Omsi 2, so I'm used to flawed but brilliant driving games, and no, Fernbus is not nearly as flawed as Omsi is but if you wan't /flawless/ game play Fernbus does not have it.
It is fun though, and it'll only get better. If Omsi 2 is one end of the spectrum and say ETS 2 is the other end, than Fernbus sits between them.
Graphically its pretty good, they use the Unreal engine. I have noticed some flickering on occasion I can't get rid of with either in game settings or by setting my GPU to a non-overclocked base setup. The Audio is good, the sound of the bus is realistic and it changes if you open a door or a window, very nice. The passanger voices and the ambient sounds are also good.
Problems come with the gameplay. The traffic AI is not horrible but will need work. I've seen cars spawn or despawn on the road, and there have been a few major pile ups on the road. To its credit, the game rapidly despawns vehicles involved in those events, I haven't had any accidents because of that.
The game seems to have a problem with in game events. For example I've been told I'm off road when I'm sitting at a light. Also they need to tweak timing in the game. It seems that if I go the speed limit I'm chronically early. There is no way to reset the clock ala Omsi so you'd have to sit at the pick up point. If your ten, fifteen, or more minutes early thats just ridiculous. Also the passangers will complain about needing a break and there is nowhere to do that anywhere close. So they keep complaining until you drive into the oncoming lane. Well no but it gets annoying.
I have a G27 steering wheel and the game had no problem recognizing it, though to set the steering sensitivity to anything nice you have to use the "assistant" that tells you to turn the wheel all the way left and right. If you want to not have to roll the wheel a lot you need to turn the wheel as far left or right as you want not what its capable of.
I still like it though. I didn't go in with the expectation of perfection and the game is very playable. The cities are very detailed, not cut and paste urban areas either. It seems they've put effort into getting various German cities to have some realism. The traffic can be atrociously busy but you have the option to set how much you want from 0 to 100. I've found 35 is good.
Its not Omsi 2 bittersweet and filled with flaws that make you work for your fun, but its also not at the ETS 2 near perfection level. You get detailed switches and knobs that work, a good driving experience and actual passangers to check in with tickets or smart phones. You can do multi city runs, have to keep up on fuel usage and the weather can be anything you want from sunny all the time to dynamically changing. You also have road events like re-routes and construction that can be set from 0 to 100.
If you love driving games (not racing, you'll never go over 100KPH) this may be for you. Its rough, yes, but it works and Aerosoft seems to be working on it so it can only get better.  This, however brings me to my final complaint, the price. I think its a bit over priced for being not quite ready for prime time. Yes you get a tremendous amount of road to travel with interesting places to go, but ouch.
System: i7 4790K, Gigabyte 980ti G1, 16 gigs Crucial Ballistix ram, Windows 10

Fernbus Simulator is the ultimate coach bus simulator available as of now. I had the opportunity to drive in Germany and I have to tell you that the autobahn in this game is right on the point, the random events and the realistic road works are great additions to the long journeys. With the 1:10 scale the map feels huge and can provide a very nice experience driving around on the complex road network and through the ~40 cities.
The game is very intuitive and gets you started real quick with the Arcade mode, where you don't have to deal with anything and you can get the bus moving instantly. But the simulator also features a Realistic mode, where you can control everything from opening/closing doors and luggage doors, shifting gears, operating the air conditioner, the exterior and interior lights, the retarder and traction control, restroom clearance, reading lights, WiFi on/off and so on... These controls can be operated from the cockpit by clicking buttons or by keybindings, and there is also a quick control (Hotkey Wheel) on the bottom of the screen which can be toggled by Numpad keys! The keybinds are of course customizable and you can set up whatever controller/wheel you want.
And if you miss something, don't worry, the passengers will surely let you know. :)
The options are extensive and I don't really miss anything. You can set up pretty much everything: traffic density, camera steering, mouse wheel mode, event frequency, weather, time & date...
The simulator features a free play mode as well, so you can even walk around in the cities if you feel like exploring.
Truth to be told, the game is not perfect but it is constantly being worked on, the developer team reacts quickly to community feedback which is always a nice thing. The few minor issues are AI and graphic optimization. Don't expect to run this on Ultra mode on a medium tier PC. But expect nice free content patches as said in the DevDiary videos like: modding and steam workshop support, TrackIR support, additional cities like Kassel, performance and AI improvements...
Altogether I'm happy with how this simulator turned out, you can really step into the shoes of a FlixBus coach driver in Deutschland. I recommend this game to everyone who likes coach bus simulators.

Hands down the first game recommended to any fan of the Survival Horror Genre and arguably the most frightening game ever made.
You awaken in an eerie castle, unaware of how you got there and unaware of your identity.
The story is told through a journal that is collected by you throughout the game, helping you piece together who you are and why you are there...but stay in the light - for your sanity drains in the darkness.
The castle forces you to explore it's dark corridors by making it necessary to gather resources. You must have oil for your lantern, wicks for the candles in the hallways - you can find the items you need by looking in drawers and cabinets. However, do not ever forget...you are not alone.
Danger is around every corner and every door of the castle...and you are completely defenseless. Running from the threat is your only option and you better find a good place to hide.
In the end The Darkness will have what it wants...one way or the other...

Gameplay repetetive.
Setting we already know.
Killing germans. Been there done that.
But what is it then that makes this game special?
It's the way it does all these things.
so yhea the gameplay is very repetetive. all you do is move from A to B, set up and shoot a couple of nazi's through their head.
But how. The sniping mechanic in this game is as realistic as i've seen so far in a game.
Do it right and they won't know that you are there. ♥♥♥♥ it up and it's game over. You won't be able to take that much hits so stealth is key.
But expect the frequent fire fights. And that is also something to prepare for. Set up some trip wires, or place a mine under a dead soldier.
The sniping mechanic is the point of the game. And that is it strongest point.
It can be customised to with, But if everything is enabled, it will be as real as it gets.
Take the bullet drip into consideration, and be sure that the wind isn't too strong. Even the gun you are using makes a change in how the bullet drops.
But as soon as you pull the trigger the fun happens. Did you hit the target or did you miss?
Always a fun to see when you actually hit your target. Watch as the bullet slowly enters the enemy's brain and launch small bits of skull and brain through the air.
Level wise, It is nothing really spectacular. Mainly it are the common urban World War 2 settings. (in this case mainly Berlin). With sometimes a country side mission here and there. And the missions are pretty linear.
But is that taking away the fun. Not for me.
Weapons.
Not many weapons are featured in the game. Some pretty common World war 2 sniper rifles. (Even some japanese models, Don't ask me why. Since the japanese aren't even mentioned in the game). A couple of common sub machine guns. And some traps.
But in this case it is in fact Less is more. Because even though there aren't that many guns, They all differ quite a lot from each other. Each sniper rifle has it's own pro's and cons. And that is what makes the difference.
DLC, It's not that spectacular. Some maps, some guns.
But one map in particular which i find oddly enjoying. Of course i am reffering to the Kill Hitler DLC.
Nothing feels better than putting a bullet through the head of Hitler himself. Or at least a video game representation of him.
So sniper Elite V2.
It is a nice game. Not the best game ever. But gameplay wise it's something new. Not something we frequently see in this age's third person shooters.
It's a game that is nothing special, but also a lot of special all in once. that is what makes it great.

OKAY, rewriting review time. This game has matured so much since I've had it. I've played it daily, I've watched it grow, I've poured many hours into this game and interacted with the community. I taught myself many driving techniques with this game (with some mods so stalling a car is actually possible). This game was the exact game i've wanted since I was a little one playing Flatout 2 on my Xbox. Does it have problems? Absolutely. Do these matter? Absolutely not. I can't get enough of this game. The physics are satisfying, and feel real. I've yet to play a game that can make me cringe when I hit something as small as a trash can at low speed like this one can. The cars are unique and beautiful and every one is labored over to give it the exact characteristics of real life equivalents. They're fun, most imporantly, and I can't get enough of whipping the hatchback (Ibishu Covet) around a corner, or abusing the hell out of the Offraod version of the Pickup (Gavril D-Series). Even the level design shows detail, with maps being unique and having a variety of roads and ways to have fun, be it rallying through country in a small Japanese compact, or tearing up the streets in a souped up American Saloon, or ignoring roads and trails in a jacked-up delivery van. Yes, $24.99 may seem risky for an Early Access game, but these devs absolutely show promise. They constantly update the game, they constantly interact with their community, and I've even had conversations with some of the staff... They're great people, and they love this game like it was their child. They prioritize keeping the game updated, fresh with fun and new stuff, and fixing major problems. I can't tell anyone what to do with their money, but I can more than recommend buying this game to anyone who consults me on it. Please do yourself this favor.
Quick notes about this game:
-ABSOLUTELY USE A CONTROLLER OR WHEEL, keyboard is still fun but is nowhere near as great as the former two options
-Fairly demanding, don't expect to have 10-car derbies with a laptop. Even my i7 4790k and GTX 980 only do 9 cars at once on certain levels before it becomes difficult to play
-Bear with the devs, there are problems that pop up... With this in mind, do go to the official BeamNG forums for help, the community and devs always find solutions to these problems

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I haven't followed the Shadow Warrior series very much. I didn't play the last game (the demo didn't impress me too much), and I had not played the original DOS game either, so I was coming into this with no real expectations (other than a certainty that this couldnt be as fast and smooth as the recent DOOM).
Well, suffice to say, Shadow Warrior 2 has proven to be a pleasant surprise indeed.
A lot of people are comparing this game to Borderlands, Diablo and even the aformentioned DOOM reboot. Personally, I think a better comparision would be Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces 2. Like that game, you'll be fighting with three primary toolkits; magic (called Chi here), guns and melee weapons. Also like Dark Forces 2, melee combat uses movement combinations to dictate the type of attack you unless (though it is far more advanced here). Add to this the sprawling and often vertical design to the levels , its hard to think of this as anything short of a spiritual successor to that Lucas Arts classic.
Where this game does differ from Dark Forces is in its speed and violence. This game is FAST, rivaling (and occassionally suprassing) the pace of DOOM 2016. Combat is so hectic that you'll end up resorting to button mashing in a panic for the first few levels. This works for a while, just long enough to make you doubt the depth and quality of the games systems, but after a few missions, you'll gain a deeper understanding of how to control both your movement and sword to unleash more deliberate attacks and manouvers. Just in time too, because button mashing absolutly stops being viable once the training wheels are off, and the enemy numbers start going through the roof (and the levels get bigger).
Once you get the hang of it and have upgraded both your Chi and arsenal, each battle turns into a strangely ordered chaos. Particles fire off every which way as you leap, zip and slash your way into the hordes of monstrosities. The pace and flavor of these fights almost makes you feel like you're starring in your very own action anime', amidst some fantastic environments that range from neo-tokyo style dystopias to warped japanese villages. However, for how beautiful these areas look, they are also where the game starts to stumble.
The game is supposed to have semi-proceduraly generated levels, though I couldn't tell you if it had any real effect. Areas are very clearly recycled multiple times over, leading to each zone eventually feeling inconsequential. The game itself is still so much fun that this becomes little more than a small annoyance, but it is one I do hope the devs will address either with patches or expansions/ DLC's. Less easy to ignore is the use of invisible walls and clunky nature of the mantling system. To put it bluntly; as much fun as dashing and jumping is, it is NOT as smooth and cleanly executed as in DOOM. Several times I'd try to catch onto a rooftop that was well within range, to no avail. Some roofs would keep pushing me off    as if I had hit an invisible border, and at least once I managed to walk on top of a level because I had jumped over some invisible barrier. Granted, this last one only happened once, but the fact that it was possible at all is somewhat odd.
Speaking of bugs; there was also a funny instance where a boss battle had began, but I had accidently back peddled too far back before the lockdown door could close, thus creating an impassible barrier between the enemy and myself, leaving us to awkwardly stare at the door and get nowhere.
Those are about the only real issues I had though. The plot- such as it is- is okay, niether great nor awful. It's chuckle worthy now and again, with a couple of laugh out loud segments, but the meat of the game is in the fights, not its dialogue or plot. Speaking of which; some reviewers online have complained about the humour being overly juvinile and falling flat. I myself am not generally a fan of crass humor, but I didn't find anything so off putting here. Many people have commented that the central joke is &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, but honestly, I felt more like the joke was that Lo Wang isnt as funny as he thinks he is. Certainly, the characters he's surrounded by are only barely tollerating his antics, which more often than not does make for some funny scenes.
Anyhow, all in all; Shadow Warrior 2 was a TON of fun. If you're coming from DOOM, this is an obvious next step. If you were a fan of Jedi Knight: Dark Forces 2, this should be a no-brainer.

10/24/16: The devs released a major patch that introduced a lot of fixes to the game.  I still get random freezes fairly often, but I haven't experienced any FPS drops in multiplayer again (yet).  As such, I'm changing my review to a RECOMMEND.  Although the story is complete garbage, the characters are extremely cliche and utterly forgettable, and the random level design isn't memorable in the slightest, the gameplay makes this an enjoyable experience for the price point.
10/15/16: Review is a NOT RECOMMENDED due to the broken state of multiplayer for myself and others currently.
The game itself is okay.  It's fun, though there are tweaks I'd like to see.  That's not what I'm here to talk about, however.
The multiplayer is a mess (for clarity I am playing "cooperative" with my brother).  Whoever is the host experiences the game and has a blast.  Whoever is the client gets the short end of the stick.  They don't see info on what quest is active.  Chests frequently don't show up on the minimap for them.  If the demon rabbit spawns and is killed, no loot drops for the client.  Desync issues when using chi-blast to move many objects at once.
These are all moderate/minor problems.  The big two:
1. Clients do not receive any progress towards quests in the game.  Once the client disconnects, they will need to redo all story missions to catch up to where the host was.  It is Dark Souls style, where "cooperative" isn't really cooperative, so much as it is temporarily assisting someone in their own universe.  It's not really "coop" as you don't work together towards one goal.  The host works towards completion of the quest.  The client follows the host around being a drone.  Imagine Borderlands where you played with a friend for six hours, gained many levels and gear, but then once you disconnected you needed to redo all the story content on your own as you were back at the tutorial.  It's unacceptable, frankly.
2. FPS drops for clients are severe, especially around elite demons.  The client will experience a persistent FPS drop to unplayable levels (~10 FPS) while the elite enemy is alive and nearby.  This persists until the enemy is dead.  All graphical settings were reduced to minimum and all other tweaks were examined.  The game also hung/crashed a few times while my brother (who was the client) tested all the settings.  Nothing worked, so we have abandoned the game for now.
The devs are still pushing out updates to deal with the slew of other problems I'm reading on the steam discussions and elsewhere (crashes and unable to progress past the first stage are the biggest two I still see occurring).  If an update is pushed out and resolves the stability issues within multiplayer I'll change my recommendation to a yes, though it will still come with a clarification that the game is not true "cooperative," which I am heartily disappointed by.

I really wanted to like this game. The grapple mechanic is really cool, so are the glowsticks, the hiveminds are huge and imposing, and it runs pretty well. But there are multiple design decisions that are very annoying, and I found myself asking "why?!" much more often than any game since the n64 days.
Here are some of the thoughts I had in the first couple hours:
Is it day out? All the fog and excessive shadows are making it really hard to see stuff. Maybe I can change the gamma in the settings. I can't? That's annoying, I'll just turn off the shadows. Okay... nothing changed, that's annoying.
Wow, that's a deep hole. Maybe I can find some or down there. Wait, why did it suddenly get so dark? I could see everything when I was looking down, and I can still see the lit sky above me. That's annoying.
Good god! What the hell is that damned noise? Oh, it means there's a crystal nearby. I don't need those yet, so I'll just turn down that sound. Oh I can't... that's annoying.
Okay, I have some ore extractors set up with automated power delivery. I should automate smelting next. Oh, I can't make  a smelter without some research. It's annoying that I need to do research for something so basic. Fine, i'll move my starting smelter so I don't need to wste time carting resources. I can't? That's annoying.
Well, if I can't bring my smelter to the ore, I'll bring ore to the smelter. Wow, the conveyor belts are pretty expensive in terms of resources AND time because of the lack of smelters. I'm going to need a lot of these too. This is pretty annoying.
Oh cool, lifts are much better for getting in/out of my iron and lithium mine than the grapple. Oh shoot, I can't actually get the lift shaft all the way down because there's an errant coal vein in the way that I can't remove. That's really annoying.
Geez, I finally found enough of this obscure resource that I can't scan for to make smelters for all the starting materials. I finally can begin sutomating something interesting. How long has it been? 4 hours... huh... I don't feel like I've completed very much. That's annoying...
Do you see the pattern here?

You crave a thriller that psyches you out, as opposed to resorting to cheap horror tropes that set out more to disturb or disgust.
I've had 3 Amnesia-related nightmares (no really) and spent the first night after playing it looking at my cupboard, bracing myself to run into it if my bedroom door started getting kicked in.
And yet I still come back for more.
The horror genre is currently saturated with remakes of loud noises and things jumping out at you to rip off your head and eat it in front of you. It's frustrating and is more like developers just trying to repulse and upset you, than actually create a terrifying yet exciting experience. But this is what Amnesia does beautifully: It psyches you out. It doesn't milk the "hey, you've opened a door - Let's have 50 spiders jump at your face" but just drip-feeds uneasiness with a brilliantly cultivated environment to the extent that you're jumping at your own shadow and freezing when you hear creaks of floorboards...
The tension just mounts further as you have no weapons and must make do with limited sources of light (lest your sanity crumble). Nothing exacerbated the sense of dread more than sheltering by a single candle in winding labyrinth of pitch black corridors and rooms - with nothing more than 2 tinderboxes and a drop of oil.
The story is also superb, even if you don't get scared by the game. You wake up with no memory and a hand-written note from yourself... and that's it. As you progress and find more scattrered notes, diary entries and flashbacks - you unearth the dark stories of what's occurring. It's grim in places, but tastefully done and drives the story well.
2 people playing, taking in turns, tends to get the best result. Good scares but a lot of laughs.

Duke Nukem Forever may not be as horrible as disappointed fans make it out to be, but it is certainly far from Game of the Year.
Pros:
- Duke's personality is entertaining, which sometimes adds to the feeling of the fight.
- Fun weapons such as the Freeze Gun and Shrink Ray.
- Inventive puzzle concepts, though some poorly executed.
- Great final boss battle true to 90's shooters.
Cons:
- Absolutely terrible minigames that don't function well.
- Horrible and stupid achievements that require aforementioned mini games.
- Poor difficulty balance. Most of the game is too easy while other parts are frustratingly difficult.
- Campaign is full of filler sequences.
- Extremely distasteful imagery involving killing naked, bound, pregnant women.
- Terrible voice acting.
Duke Nukem Forever plays like a mildly entertaining 2004 sci-fi shooter, but there is no king to be hailed to in this game.

If you enjoyed the late 90's "Sid Meier's Gettysburg!", you'll love this game. It's impossible to say this isn't influenced by it. While Meier's offered a greater level of control over regimental tactics e.g. formations, orders, etc., Ultimate offers a more streamlined approach to orders which lets you enjoy/evaluate the big picture instead of micromanaging your units. The map is beautiful, and terrain plays a big part in making decisions. Scenarios directly influence each other, with unit positions and strength carrying over. If I have any criticisms, it's that cavalry is useless for anything except scouting your flanks. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of RTS, maps, or the history behind the Battle of Gettysburg.
If you enjoy sniping, this is the game for you!
